11100417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11100417.value: 與中樞神經系統不同，外周神經系統通常被認為在受損後具有強烈的軸突再生能力。不過，有關論點並非完全正確。近端外周神經損傷的受損軸突需要再生一段頗長的距離來重新連接其目標肌肉。礙於受損軸突的再生速率非常慢（每天一毫米）， 患者的感官及運動功能復原亦因此變得有限。我們早前的研究已經展示了再生中的軸突必需於35天（在實驗小鼠身上）或10至12個月（在腕管綜合症的患者身上）這段「關鍵時期」內重新連接其目標肌肉，以達致功能上的完全復原。因此，從臨床觀點來說，研發不同的醫療策略來加快受損軸再生速度，對改善功能復原是非常有需要的。 微管動態的調節是控制受損神經元軸突再生的關鍵事件。微管蛋白是微管的基本組成單位。微管蛋白的脫乙酰化作用只會在外周神經損傷後引發，而中樞神經系統的視神經損傷並不能引發有關作用。Formin-2 (FMN2) 是Formin蛋白家族的其中一名成員，並擁有兩個具有高度保守性及同源性的FH結構域（FH1 & 2）。愈來愈多的研究表明FH1及FH2結構域均涉及微管動態的調節。雖然FMN2廣泛地在神經系統中表達，但於神經元功能上的認知甚少。透過使用組織蛋白脫乙酰酶以阻斷微管蛋白的脫乙酰化作用使受損神經元軸突的再生速度顯著減慢。有關的研究表明了微管蛋白的脫乙酰化作用於軸突受損後成功再生上起了重要作用。 為了驗證「由FMN2調節的微管動態於神經元受損後軸突再生上起了關鍵角色」這個假設，我們首先顯示外周神經損傷會減低FMN2的信使核糖核酸（mRNA）及蛋白的表達量。所以，我們使用小分子干擾核糖核酸（siRNA），於體外及體內來抑制Fmn2在神經元的表達，並證實此舉能夠顯著提升受損外周神經元的軸突再生速度，以及透過一系列為期一個月的動物行為測試及電生理學研究，反映功能復原於抑制Fmn2的表達後有顯著的提升。 此研究方案旨在定義FMN2於軸突再生的功能作用，並使用現有的FMN2完全敲除 (Fmn2-/-) 小鼠來闡釋其潛在機理。我們將會透過用於研究外周神經系統損傷關鍵時期的動物模型，來研究敲除FMN2對提升功能復原的能力；以及研究敲除FMN2是否能提升中樞神經系統的視網膜神經節細胞的軸突再生能力。我們亦會將活細胞成像技術用於Fmn2-/- 小鼠上，來闡釋微管蛋白聚合及動態的分子機理。最後，我們將會進行高通量基因組研究，用以找出其中涉及調節微管動態的關鍵信號通路和相關基因，從而為研發不同的醫療策略去治療神經系統損傷提供新的見解。

11100417.label: Realisation of objectives
11100417.value: All Objectives were completed. Figures and References are attached in Part C. Section 11 Other Impact. Objective 1.1. To examine the axonal regeneration and sensory functional recovery in Fmn2 knockout mice: This objective was completed and described in the mid-term report in details (Figs. 1-3, 4A, 5-8 and 9A). Objective 1.2. To examine motor function recovery and the temporal dynamic of NMJ formation in animal model of peripheral nerve injury (PNI) (single crush) in Fmn2 knockout mice: This objective was completed and described in the mid-term report in details (Figs. 4B-G, and 9B-G). Objective 1.3. To investigate the role of histone deacetylase (HDAC) in axonal regeneration: Intense immunoreactivity of Fmn2 protein were detected in the NF-200-positive neuronal cell bodies of DRG neurons (Fig. 10A) and adjacent axons in the sciatic nerves (Fig. 10B). In axotomized DRG neurons, Fmn2 were co-localized with βIII-tubulin-rich microtubule (Fig. 10C). Successful axon regeneration required active tubulin deacetylation to promote microtubule dynamics for axonal regrowth, which is tightly associated with the activation of HDAC5 after PNI (1, 2). We performed Western blot analysis to compare the level of phosphorylated HDAC5 (HDAC5 activation) at different distal nerve segments of sciatic nerves from Fmn2-/- mice and littermates (Fig. 11A). Western blot results confirmed that Fmn2 ablation induced an increase in HDAC5 activation, leading to a marked reduction of acetylated α-tubulin at distal axons (Fig. 11B-C). Immunohistochemistry analysis demonstrated an increase in HDAC5 activity (Fig. 12A-B) alongside with the reduced immunoreactivity in acetylated α-tubulin (Fig. 12C-D) at distal nerve. Pharmaceutical blockade of HDAC5 activity using scriptaid (Fig. 13A) limited the extent of axon regeneration from WT mice 3 days after SNC and completely abolished the growth-promoting effects in Fmn2-/- mice (Fig. 13B). Growing evidence suggested that Fmn2 were involved in the DNA repair mechanisms. Loss of Fmn2 led to an increase in DNA double-strand break (DSB) in the cell nuclei (3). Interestingly, PNI induces a mild DNA damage leading to an increase activity of BRCA1, a protein that is essential for effective DSB clearance (4). Loss of BRCA1 impaired axon regeneration. We hypothesized that Fmn2 ablation might induce a higher level of DNA DSB in injured DRG neurons, which might contribute to the growth-promoting effects in Fmn2-/- mice. We performed additional experiment to examine the DNA damage in Fmn2-/- DRG neurons, we observed a significant increase in protein level of γH2AX (marker for DNA DSB) in the nuclear fraction of injured Fmn2-/- DRG neurons compared with WT controls at day 1 after sciatic nerve transection (Fig. 14A-B), and a reduced expression level of its downstream effector 53BP1 (Fig. 14C). We validated our results using immunohistochemistry, and observed an increased number of γH2AX-positive and βIII-tubulin-positive DRG neurons in injured Fmn2-/- DRG neurons (Fig. 15A-C). Next, we asked if an increase in DNA damage in DRG neurons could recapitulate, at least in part, the growth-promoting effects induced by Fmn2 ablation. We treated the cultured axotomized DRG neurons with camptothecin, a pharmaceutical agent to induce DSB, and observed a 62% increase in neurite outgrowth (Fig. 16A-B), with no effects on neuronal survival (Fig. 16C). Moreover, administration of camptothecin on the crushed site (Fig. 16D) also promoted in vivo axon regeneration 3 days after SNC (Fig. 16E), suggesting that inducing a mild DNA damage could effectively promote axon regeneration after PNI in adult mice. Objective 2.1. To investigate the changes of gene expression profiles in Fmn2 knockout mice by microarray and bioinformatics analysis: We performed a whole transcriptome analysis on the injured lumbar 4 and 5 DRG neurons directly supplying the sciatic nerve from both Fmn2-/- mice and littermates 5 days after sciatic nerve transection (5). Hierarchical clustering and principal component analysis (PCA) showed a clear separation between contralateral and ipsilateral DRG neurons regardless of genotypic difference (Fig. 17A-B). The transcriptomic profiles of injured Fmn2-/- DRG neurons largely overlapped with the injured WT controls (Fig. 17B). After injury, there were 563 genes differentially expressed (DE) in injured Fmn2-/- DRGs, which was at a level similar to 636 DE genes in injured WT controls. Of these DE genes, 397 genes were up-regulated and 21 genes were down-regulated in both Fmn2-/- and WT DRG neurons after injury (Fig. 17C). Those up-regulated genes represented core regeneration-associated genes (RAGs) that were critical for successful axon regeneration after sciatic nerve injury, including Atf3, Sprr1a, Jun, Stmn4, Fabp5, Hspb1, Sox11 and Gap43 (5-7). We further validated these transcriptional changes by qPCR analysis (8, 9), and observed similar degrees of up-regulation of these RAGs between injured Fmn2-/- and WT DRG neurons (Fig. 17D). Our whole transcriptome analysis revealed that a total of 145 genes (87 up-regulated and 58 down-regulated) showed expression difference specifically in Fmn2-/- mice (Fig. 17C). We hypothesized that these genes might contribute to the enhanced intrinsic regenerative capacity observed in Fmn2-/- neurons. We first validated the top 10 DE genes by qPCR analysis, and 6 (Mstn, Fam163a, Ildr2, Nnat, Cd1d1 and Rnf183) genes showed significant up-regulation only in injured Fmn2-/- neurons which is consistent with our RNA-seq data (Fig. 17E). To further annotate the functions of these genes, we imported all 145 genes that were differentially expressed solely in Fmn2-/- mice (Fig. 17C) to construct a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network using STRING (Search Tool for Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins) database (10), and expanded the PPI network with maximum of 5 potential interactors from the imported nodes. Since most of these DE genes shared diverse biological functions and involved in distinct signalling pathways, they barely showed any interactions or co-expression with neighbourhood genes, and thus we excluded those disconnected genes from the PPI network. Interestingly, of these 145 genes, 15 (10.3%) genes were involved in inflammatory responses as highlighted in red in Fig. 18A. Our qPCR analysis confirmed the augmented production of anti-inflammatory cytokines including Tgf-β, IL-10 and Igf-1 solely in injured Fmn2-/- DRGs (Fig. 18B). Our whole transcriptome analysis revealed that deletion of Fmn2 in injured DRGs induced a profound activation of neuroprotective anti-inflammatory signalling pathways after injury, with enhanced production of anti-inflammatory cytokines such as Tgf-β, IL-10 and Igf-1. Objective 2.2. To determine if Fmn2 ablation enhances the regenerative capacity of CNS neurons: We performed optic nerve crush in Fmn2-/- mice and quantified axon regeneration and survival of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) 2 weeks after injury. At day 11 post-injury, 1µl of a recombinant cholera toxin subunit B conjugated with Alexa Fluor 555 (2µg/µl) were intravitreally injected to the vitreous to anterograde label the regenerating axons. At day 14 post-injury, the optic nerve and retinae were dissected out for axon quantification and RGC survival assay (11, 12). In line with previous reports (11, 12), only 23.5% of RGCs were able to survive in WT littermates 2 weeks after injury, which was markedly enhanced to 44.6% in Fmn2-/- mice (Fig. 19A-B). Unfortunately, deletion of Fmn2 failed to elicit a robust regenerative response to promote regrowth of RGC axons, although a large number of RGCs were remained intact after injury. The number of CTB-positive regenerating axons were comparable between Fmn2-/- and their age-matched WT controls (Fig. 19C-D), suggesting that the growth-promoting effects of Fmn2 ablation might be PNS-specific only. A distinct transcriptional program might be required to promote axon regeneration after CNS injury (13).

11100417.label: Major findings and research outcome
11100417.value: Current study demonstrated that formin-2 (Fmn2) is an attractive therapeutic target to promote sensory and motor functional recovery after peripheral nerve injury (PNI). We demonstrated for the first time that complete ablation of Fmn2 enhanced the intrinsic regenerative capacity of peripheral neurons. Fmn2-/- mice markedly accelerated the in vivo axonal regrowth after PNI. These Fmn2-/- mice displayed a remarkable functional recovery after sciatic nerve crush (SNC) as assessed by a battery list of animal behavioural assessment for sensory and motor functional recovery. Furthermore, Fmn2-/- mice demonstrated an improved target reinnervation during the recovery phase (7-21 days) after SNC. The CMAP amplitudes were dramatically improved in Fmn2-/- mice compared with their age-matched littermates. Treating the mice with siRNAs specifically targeting Fmn2 transcripts also markedly promoted the sensory and motor functional restoration as we demonstrated in Fmn2-/- mice. Our Western blot results confirmed that Fmn2 ablation promoted tubulin deacetylation via phosphorylation of HDAC5. Pharmaceutical blockade of HDAC5 using scriptaid completely abolished the promoting effects induced by Fmn2 ablation. Additionally, Fmn2 ablation induced an increased level of γH2AX, leading to the reduced levels of 53BP1 in the nuclei of injured DRG neurons. Mild DNA damages by camptothecin enhanced the intrinsic growth capacity of injured DRG neurons, and accelerated in vivo axon regeneration to a similar extent of Fmn2 ablation after SNC. Mechanistically, we sought to dissect the potential molecular mechanisms underlying the promoting effects of Fmn2 ablation using RNA-seq. Specifically, ablation of Fmn2 augmented the anti-inflammatory responses possibly via profound activation of Stat3/IL-10 signaling pathways. Further investigation is required to identify bioactive compounds that recapitulate the transcriptional change in the injured Fmn2-/- DRG neurons. Finally, we examined whether knockout of Fmn2 in retinal ganglion cells could promote axon regeneration and neuronal survival after CNS injuries. While ablation of Fmn2 dramatically improved the survival of injured RGCs, the survived RGCs failed to elongate their injured axons after optic nerve crush injuries. Two papers were published in top Journals in the area of Neuroscience. Two PhD students (Bennett Au and Chine Virendra) are involved and trained in current studies. We presented the work in the largest Neuroscience Meeting in the US for two consecutive years. We also presented the work in our departmental research gala, and our poster was selected as ‘Best Poster Award’. Bennett Au also presented (invited oral presentation) the major findings generated from this study during ‘Symposium on Neuroregeneration and Neuroplasticity’ in 2018.

11100417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11100417.value: Our findings represented an importance advancement to functionally characterize the role of Fmn2 in axon regeneration and regulation of microtubule dynamics. Knowledge obtained in this project will pioneer the use of siRNA-based in vivo silencing of Fmn2 to treat patients with peripheral nerve injury (PNI). Further investigation is required to identify siRNAs that effectively silence human Fmn2 transcripts with minimal off-target effects. In the past decades, viral-based gene delivery system is capable of stable expression of target genes. Several ongoing clinical trials have been taken place to study the efficacy of gene manipulations to treat inherited neurological disorders such as retinitis pigmentosa. Future study should explore the possibility of using viral-based system to deliver short hairpin RNAs targeting human Fmn2 mRNAs to avoid multiple injections of Fmn2-siRNA. Alternatively, our RNA-seq data will certainly spur new investigation into screening of bioactive FDA-approved small molecules that recapitulate the transcriptional change in injured Fmn2-/- neurons using bioinformatic approaches. Repurposing FDA-approved drugs is a cost-effective strategy as Phase I clinical trial is normally skipped. It makes our existing RNA-seq data an attractive tool for drug discovery for patients with PNI.

11100417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11100417.value: Patients with proximal peripheral nerve injury (PNI), which requires long distance axon regeneration to reinnervate their target muscles. Motor functional recovery is extremely limited even after surgical repair due to the slow rate of axon regeneration in the PNS (1 mm/day in human). Here, we aim to address this question by examining a novel role of formin-2 (Fmn2) in regulating microtubule dynamics, an important cellular event for successful axon regeneration and nerve repair. We showed that ablation of Fmn2 dramatically enhanced the intrinsic regenerative capacity of peripheral neurons, and accelerated in vivo axon regeneration and functional recovery after PNI. Treating the mice with short-interfering RNA specifically targeted Fmn2 transcripts recapitulated similar growth-promoting effects induced by Fmn2 ablation. Mechanistically, Fmn2 ablation promoted activation of histone deacetylase 5 (HDAC5), which facilitate rapid microtubule polymerization at distal axons via augmented tubulin deacetylation activity. Blockade of HDAC5 activity by scriptaid completely abolished the growth-promoting effects of Fmn2 ablation. Moreover, Fmn2 ablation also induced an increased level of DNA double-strand break (DSB), associated with increased BRCA1 activity for effective clearance of DSB in the nuclei of injured neurons. Our current study shed new light in the development of novel therapeutic strategy for patients with PNI.

11100617.label: Project Objectives
11100617.value: Sound textures are very common types of sound in the environment. Different sound statistics are characterized by different statistical properties, and processing such statistics is likely to be a key component of auditory scene analysis. Using specially designed, lifelike but synthetic sets of sound textures and electrophysiological recordings, we will test the hypothesis that neurons at successive stages of the auditory pathway are tuned to increasingly complex key statistical features of sound textures. We will also test the hypothesis that, when presented with two sound textures simultaneously, some cortical neurons respond preferentially to only one of the two textures, even when the neurons' frequency tuning suggest that they should respond indiscriminately to the mixture. Using computational modelling and electrophysiological recordings of responses to a set of specially designed “principal component textures”, we will ascertain to what extent preferential responses to one of two simultaneously presented sound textures can be explained by tuning to texture statistics.

11100617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11100617.value: Picture yourself on a sunny weekend afternoon, sitting by the edge of a stream, water rushing over a small weir, geese honking in the background, and a bumble bee buzzing past. All of these sounds are a constant presence, but drift in and out of your consciousness only fleetingly, and none prevent you from enjoying a conversation with friends. Afternoons like those enrich our lives, we accept them gratefully, and few of us wonder how it is possible that we can so effortlessly shift our attention from the conversation to the buzzing bee or the rushing water or the honking geese, given that all these sounds arrive at our eardrum as an impenetrable mish-mash. So how does normal, healthy hearing take in these sounds all separately and yet all at once? We believe that neurons in the brain may be sensitive to key, identifying statistical properties of the various sound sources, and that this will make them respond selectively to only those sound sources that match the statistics they are tuned to. We also believe that two of the most important statistical properties are "sparseness" and "correlation structure". The geese make occasional but relatively loud honks, interspersed with periods of silence. This we would describe as "sparse". Rushing water sound is less sparse because its intensity varies much less over time. If neurons prefer sparse sounds, then these would respond strongly to the sound of geese but not the water, and their responses would thus to an extent separate the sound of the geese from the rest of the auditory scene. To distinguish the gurgling water and the buzzing bee, but those you could separate using "frequency correlations". Water sounds involve countless bubbles gurgling. Large bubbles make deeper sounds, small bubbles make higher sounds, and high and low bubble sounds are not synchronized. In contrast, each wing beat of a bumble bee is a "flap", in which many frequencies all go off together, perfectly correlated. Neurons which require high frequency correlation would hear mostly the bee, neurons requiring weak correlation hear mostly the water. We hypothesize that sensitivity to these key statistical properties emerges gradually along the ascending auditory pathway, and we propose to investigate neural responses from key stages of the ascending pathway, including the inferior colliculus, primary and secondary auditory cortex of rats to synthetic auditory texture sounds with systematically varying statistics, presented in isolation and superposition. 試想像自己在一個周未下午，在和煦日下靜坐溪邊，流水淙淙越過小堤，背景是鵝群嘎嘎的聲音，然後一隻蜜蜂嗡嗡而過。其實這些聲音一直存在，但是它們只是在你的意識中匆匆地進出，而且並沒有阻礙你與友人的對話。這樣的時光豐富了我們的生活，我們亦為此感恩，但很少人會思考我們如何能如此輕易地把注意力從友人的對話轉移到嗡嗡的蜜蜂、嘎嘎的鵝或淙淙的流水，尤其是考慮到這一切聲音到達我們的耳膜時都是混和了的單一訊號。 正常的聽覺是如何分別又同時地理解各種不同的聲音？我們相信大腦內的神經元能夠感應各種音源中有識別性的統計學屬性，從而讓它們選擇性回應吻合它們設定的音源。我們亦相信其中兩個最重要的統計學屬性是「稀疏度」和「頻率相關性」。鵝會發出偶爾但相對大聲的叫聲，穿插寧靜的時間。我們會以「稀疏度高」形容這種聲音。流水因為它的音量隨時間變化的幅度小，所以是「稀疏度低」的聲音。假如神經元偏好稀疏度高的聲音，它們就會對鵝而不是對流水的聲音有高度的反應，而這種反應會某程度上將鵝的叫聲從聽覺場景中的其他聲音分隔開來。要將流水聲和蜜蜂聲分隔，就要用到「頻率相關性」。流水聲包含無數氣泡的聲音：大氣泡會製造低頻率的聲音，而小氣泡會製造高頻率的聲音，高低頻率的聲音不同步。相反，每當蜜蜂拍一下翼，很多不同頻率的聲音會同時出現，而且極為同步。對高神經反應頻率相關性敏感的神經元會主要聽到蜜蜂聲，而對低神經反應頻率相關性敏感的神經元會主要聽到流水聲。 我們假定音源統計學屬性的敏感度存在於上行聽覺神經通路，而我們建議研究大鼠在上行聽覺神經通路重要結構，包括下丘、初級及次要聽覺皮層，對合成而且有不同統計學屬性的音效的反應；音效會以單獨或層疊方式測試。

11101017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11101017.value: 近幾十年來，在生物界藉由高通量測序的技術所提供各樣生理及病理（例如，神經退化性疾病、癌症......等）的轉錄組數據庫已有相當的累積。而因著現今進階蛋白質技術的發展，提供了不僅高品質蛋白質組資訊，同時也對基因表達開啟了另一新的視野，意即轉譯的過程對某些基因表達有著調控的作用；從另一角度來說，轉譯過程調控大多數和人類疾病相關的基因。 據本研究之前的報告指出染色質重塑複合物NuRD在晝夜節律時鐘機制（負回饋抑制圈）的調控扮演重要的角色。哺乳動物的晝夜節律鐘為一固有在大多數的細胞，從腦至周邊各個臟器之內源性的節律原，其所驅動乃日常生物的節律，包括代謝、生理、以及行為。NuRD為一相當特殊的複合物，其包括兩種酶的作用：染色質重塑酶(CHD4)和組蛋白脫乙酰酶(HDAC1／2)。而於本實驗數據指出這兩個酶亞基只有在PER成功的結合在CLOCK－BMAL1才會聚合起來形成一具功能的共抑制複合物；然而於其他的情況下多為分開。值得注意的是，CHD4在晝夜節律鐘激活期有著促進BMAL／CLOCK的轉錄活性。由此可見，此依賴PER重組的NuRD複合物不僅只於傳送一抑制物，它更含括BMAL1／CLOCK的活化因子來形成一整體的抑制物。因此，從這重組複合物標靶的特性指出了上述兩種酶，即便在其仰賴轉錄因子的特性上，如何的來相互作用進而建構晝夜節律鐘的特異性以及其在調控晝夜節律鐘所占有的重要性。 就文獻報告及本研究初步結果顯示，相當大量的轉錄因子可能參與在晝夜節律鐘的調節機制。根據本研究初步結果所進而提出的假說如下：晝夜節律鐘透過核醣體亞基生物發生的調節而作為一分子傳訊者，將轉錄階段的訊息傳遞給在轉譯階段的機制。為驗證此假說，本研究提案將著重在兩個研究目標：1）定義出晝夜節律鐘所調控核內用來合成核醣體亞基的rRNA轉錄調節機制；2）測試晝夜節律鐘是否參與細胞質中轉譯的起始步驟進而控制轉譯的效率。於此，本研究提案將對於晝夜節律鐘於轉錄及轉譯的調節提供一更為清楚的機制聯結並且進一步了解晝夜節律鐘如何精確的調控細胞基因的表達。

11101517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11101517.value: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is aggressive and has a poor prognosis. Currently, chemotherapy is the only treatment option but the clinical benefit is limited to a subset of patients. Therefore there is an unmet need to identify novel therapeutic targets for TNBC. This project is based on the premise that Akt3 is overexpressed in ~30% of TNBC, and our recent discovery that Akt3, but not Akt1 or Akt2, is a critical regulator for TNBC growth. In addition, our studies have revealed a surprising finding that Akt3 is implicated in acquired resistance to pan-Akt inhibitors, many of which are in clinical trials. These findings challenge the dogma of redundant functions of Akt isoforms in tumor growth. Importantly, they point to Akt3 and its downstream substrates as novel and effective targets for breast cancer therapy. The principal goal of this research is to test the hypothesis that Akt3-specific signaling is critical for TNBC growth, and to delineate the mechanisms underlying this specificity, with an emphasis on identifying new targets to treat breast cancer. This application has three specific aims. Aim 1: We propose to identify novel Akt3-specific substrates which regulate TNBC growth using a genome-wide, high-throughput proteomic screen. Aim 2: The role of subcellular localization of Akt3 in tumor spheroid growth will be examined. In particular, we will utilize CRISPR technology to tag endogenous proteins fluorescently. This would allow for the first time visualization of endogenous Akt intracellular dynamics in a real-time manner in live 3D spheroids. Aim 3: We will examine the physiological relevance of Akt3 phosphorylation in TNBC growth and survival using xenograft models, and evaluate the co-relation of Akt3 signaling and clinical outcomes in cancer patients. By collaborating with a team of experts in bioinformatics and molecular profiling of breast cancer, I am confident that these proposed studies will further advance our understanding of Akt3 signaling in breast cancer tumorigenesis at the molecular, cellular and in vivo levels. They will also address the unexplored role of subcellular localization of Akt isoforms in TNBC. Importantly, our studies will identify novel Akt3-specific substrates that could be targeted for effective anti-cancer therapeutics. 三陰性乳腺癌（TNBC）具有侵襲性，預後差。目前，化療是唯一的治療方法，但臨床益處僅限於患者的一小部分。因此，有必要鑑定新型的靶標來治療TNBC。這個項目的前提是，Akt3在約30％的TNBC中過量表達。我們最近發現，Akt3，而不是Akt1或Akt2，是TNBC生長的關鍵調節劑。此外，我們的研究揭示了Akt3涉及癌細胞對臨床試驗中的泛Akt抑製劑的抵抗性。這些發現挑戰了Akt1-3在腫瘤生長中的冗餘功能的傳統觀念。重要的是，Akt3及其下游底物可能是用於治療乳腺癌的新穎有效的靶標。 這項研究的主要目標是測試Akt3特異性信號對TNBC生長至關重要的假說，並描述這種特異性的機制，重點是鑑定治療乳腺癌的新靶點。目的1：我們建議使用全基因組，高通量蛋白質組學篩選鑑定調節TNBC生長的新型Akt3特異性底物。目的2：檢測Akt3亞型在細胞中特定的位置會否於調節腫瘤球狀體生長上有重要的作用。目標3：我們將使用異種移植模型研究Akt3磷酸化在TNBC生長和存活中的生理相關性，並評估Akt3信號與癌症患者臨床結果的共同關係。

11101517.label: Realisation of objectives
11101517.value: All project objectives have been addressed, and we have identified novel cellular functions of Akt3 in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and discovered a specific Akt3 substrate. As set out in Objective 1, to determine if Akt3 regulates cancer stem cell (CSC) properties of TNBC, we utilized a dox-inducible Crispr/Cas9-mediated DNA editing system to knockout Akt3 in a temporal manner. Immunoblotting confirmed that Akt3, but not Akt1 or Akt2, was knockout specifically in the TNBC cells (Fig. 1A). 3D spheroid growth was significantly reduced in Akt3-depleted spheroids (Fig. 1B). Single cell clones were then generated to assess the effect of complete Akt3 depletion on the ability of CSCs to grow and self-renew as mammospheres. Akt3-depleted mammospheres displayed decreased formation capacity over multiple passages (Fig. 2A), indicating that Akt3 plays an important role in promoting self-renewal of TNBC CSCs. Among the eighteen CSC-related molecules that we tested with real-time RT-PCR, we consistently observed downregulation of Slug and Snail mRNA in Akt3-depleted MCF10-DCIS and MDA-MB-231 cells, respectively. Snail and Slug are homologs belonging to the SNAIL family of zinc finger transcriptional regulators. Indeed, protein levels of Slug and Snail were markedly downregulated in Akt3-knockout cells (Fig. 2B). To identify novel Akt3 isoform specific substrates, we performed proteomic screens as well as bioinformatic analysis on clinical datasets of breast cancer to search for co-relations between substrate phosphorylation and Akt isoform expression. Interestingly, expression of Akt3, but not Akt1 or Akt2, corelates positively with YB1 phosphorylation at Ser102 (Fig. 3). On the other hand, none of the Akt isoform positively associates with YB1 protein expression. These observations prompted us to investigate whether YB1 is a substrate of Akt3, and their roles in TNBC CSC phenotypes. To determine whether YB1 is an Akt isoform-specific substrate, we knockout individual Akt isoform in TNBC cells using tet-on Crispr/Cas9 system. Only depleting Akt3 results in a robust reduction of YB1 phosphorylation (Fig. 4A). Akt3 knockout also led to reduced Slug and Snail expression. To investigate if YB1 is a direct substrate of Akt3, purified flag-tagged wild-type (WT) YB1 was incubated with recombinant active Akt isoforms in an in vitro kinase assay. Akt3, but not Akt1 or Akt2, efficiently phosphorylates YB1 (Fig. 4B). We also demonstrated that Akt3 phosphorylates YB1 at Ser102, since a Ser102Ala (S102A) mutant cannot be phosphorylated by recombinant Akt3 (Fig. 4C). These findings demonstrate that YB1 is a direct and specific substrate of Akt3. We next investigated the contribution of YB1 to stemness potential in TNBC cells. Two distinct shRNA sequences specific to YB1 were generated, and efficient knockdown of YB1 was validated with immunoblotting. Silencing YB1 results in reduced mammosphere formation, accompanied by decreased Slug/Snail expression (Fig. 5). We next determined if promotion of stemness by Akt3 is mediated through YB1 phosphorylation. Overexpression of HA-Akt3 in TNBC cells enhances mammosphere formation capacity and Slug/Snail protein expression. Alternatively, YB1 silencing reduces mammosphere numbers. Depletion of YB1 in Akt3-overexpressed cells results in attenuated mammosphere formation in both first and second generations as well as Slug/Snail protein levels (Fig. 6A), supporting a role of YB1 in mediating Akt3’s function in CSCs. To examine the functional significance of YB1 phosphorylation by Akt3, we knockout Akt3 in MCF10-DCIS and MDA-MBS-231 cells and performed rescue studies. Whereas WT and S102D mutant of YB1 effectively reverse the mammosphere formation in Akt3-depleted cells, S102A YB1 mutant does not rescue (Fig. 6B). These data demonstrate that phosphorylation of YB1 at Ser102 is required for Akt3-mediated promotion of TNBC stemness. In Objective 2, we have used Crispr/Cas9 approach to generate a number of tools to investigate if molecular determinants of Akt isoforms define the specificity. We first utilized the CRISPR technology to tag Akt isoforms fluorescently. We have cloned the vectors and generated DNA fragments to be introduced into various breast tumor cells. We also generated and isolated a large number of clones in different breast tumor lines. Fig. 7 shows the expression of fluorescently tagged Akt1 and Akt2 in MDA-MB-231 cells. This novel approach allows us to visualize endogenous Akt intracellular dynamics in 3D in a real-time manner, and determine if subcellular localization of Akt isoforms determines their functions. We have also examined the localization of Akt3 in TNBC cells, and showed that Akt3 is localized in the nucleus and cytoplasm. Using bioinformatics approach, we identified TCOF1, a nucleolar phosphoprotein, as a candidate of Akt3-specific substrate. We have uncovered a putative Akt phosphorylation site (Serine1350) on TCOF1, and this site has been shown to be phosphorylated in breast tumor samples by numerous proteomic studies. The role of TCOF1 in the pathogenesis of cancer is yet to be identified. We showed that TCOF1 is upregulated in TNBC, and overexpression of TCOF1 is a predictor of poor survival in breast cancer patients (Fig. 8A, B). Depletion of TCOF1 in TNBC lines inhibits cell proliferation significantly in 3D cultures (Fig. 8C). However, phosphorylation of TCOF1 was not significantly affected by Akt isoform depletion. Our data suggest that TCOF1 is a novel TNBC gene promoting growth and CSC properties of tumor cells. In Objective 3, we examined the role of Akt3 and its substrates in clinical datasets and in vivo models. We have interrogated clinical datasets and demonstrated that Akt3 expression is positively correlated with expression of Slug and Snail in breast tumor samples (Fig. 9A). The degree to which Akt3 regulates tumor-initiating ability was assessed by limiting dilution assays in female nude mice. Frequency of tumor-initiating cells was significantly lower in mice injected with Akt3-knockout cells (Fig. 9B). In addition, size of Akt3-depleted tumors is much smaller than those in no dox group (Fig. 9C). These data point to an important function of Akt3 in promoting CSC formation and self-renewal. As YB1 was shown to be a candidate of Akt3 substrate, we analyzed the expression of YB1 in different subtypes of breast cancer using the TCGA and Ualcan datasets. YB1 mRNA is upregulated in 24%, 1.5%, 3% and 7% of TNBC, Luminal A, Luminal B and Her2-overexpressing cases, respectively (Fig. 10A). We then conducted Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and showed that breast cancer patients with higher YB1 or Akt3 expression have significantly shorter relapse-free survival compared to those with low YB1 or Akt3 expression (Fig. 10B). Using multivariant Cox regression analysis, high YB1 mRNA expression was also found to be an independent risk factor for shorter survival in breast cancer patients (Hazard ratio, 1.53916; 95% confidence interval, 1.20515-1.96576; Fig. 11A) and basal-like breast cancer patients (Hazard Ratio, 2.18588; 95% confidence interval, 1.0382-4.60228; Fig. 11B). In agree with our in vitro data, YB1 expression levels were found to be corelated with Snail and Slug levels in breast tumor samples (Fig. 11C).

11101517.label: Major findings and research outcome
11101517.value: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype of breast cancer that is enriched in cancer stem cells (CSCs) which confer high malignancy, recurrence and drug resistance. We previously showed that overexpression of Akt3, but not Akt1 or Akt2, plays an essential role in TNBC growth and resistance of breast tumor cells to Akt pathway inhibitors. However, the role of Akt3 in cancer stemness remains unclear. Furthermore, an Akt3-specific substrate is yet to be identified. In this project, we demonstrated a key function of Akt3 in driving self-renewal of CSCs and tumor initiation in TNBC. Knocking out Akt3 suppresses CSC properties accompanied by reduced Snail/Slug expression. Analyses of clinical datasets revealed that Akt3 expression is positively associated with Snail/Slug expression, as well as phosphorylation of YB1 at Ser102. It has been shown that pYB1 is significantly higher in TNBC than other subtypes; however, the functional significance of Ser102 phosphorylation in CSCs has not been determined. Our findings identified YB1 as an Akt3-specific substrate. Importantly, phosphorylation of YB1 at Ser102 by Akt3 plays a critical role in the self-renewal of TNBC CSCs, suggesting that disrupting the Akt3-YB1 signaling axis may provide new therapeutic opportunity for TNBC. The majority of data collected from this study have been summarized and submitted as a manuscript for publication (under review, see attached manuscript in Part C).

11101517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11101517.value: This study has greatly advanced our understanding in the role of Akt3-YB1 signaling axis in breast cancer stemness. The funded work provides the foundation for identifying more Akt3-specific substrates that play critical roles in various processes driving TNBC growth and progression. Targeting Akt3 may be a new therapeutic strategy for TNBC patients.

11101517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11101517.value: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is aggressive and has a poor prognosis. The objective of this project is to decipher the mechanism of TNBC growth and progression, as well as discover novel mechanism-based therapeutic targets with lower toxicity for breast cancer patients. In human cells, Akt exists as a "family" of related proteins, consisting of Akt1, Akt2 and Akt3. These have both overlapping and unique cellular functions. Our previous findings indicate that Akt3 has increased expression in ~30% of TNBC. Importantly, Akt3, but not Akt1 or Akt2, is critical for regulating growth of TNBC. In this funded study, we identified a new function of Akt3 in regulating the stemness of TNBC. We further identified a specific downstream target of Akt3. We showed that Akt3 phosphorylates YB1, which in turn regulates Snail and Slug expression, and modulates stemness properties of breast cancer cells. Our research has provided insights for developing therapeutic agents targeting Akt3 or its downstream targets to treat TNBC.

11101717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11101717.value: The Ca2+-signaling pathway mediated by cyclic adenosine diphosphoribose (cADPR) is ubiquitous and the functions it regulates are equally diverse. Understanding the molecular mechanisms involved in this novel signaling pathway is not only scientifically important but also clinically relevant. The latter has clearly been demonstrated in CD38 knockout mice. CD38 is the dominant enzyme for synthesizing cADPR in mammalian systems and CD38 knockout mice exhibited multiple physiological defects, ranging from impaired immune responses, metabolic disturbances, to social behavioral modifications. Many extracellular stimuli have been shown to induce cADPR production that leads to calcium release or influx, establishing cADPR as a second messenger. Ample evidence indicates that cADPR targets ryanodine receptors (RyRs) on ER in many cell types, yet cADPR does not directly act on the receptor. We hypothesize that a bridging protein is required for the ability of cADPR to induce Ca2+ release via RyRs. We, therefore, synthesized a novel photoaffinity labeling cADPR agonist, PAL-cIDPRE, and subsequently applied it to purify its binding proteins in human Jurkat T cells. We identified glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) as one of cADPR binding protein(s), characterized the binding affinity between cADPR and GAPDH in vitro by SPR assay, and mapped the cADPR’s binding sites in GAPDH. We further demonstrated that cADPR induced the transient interaction between GAPDH and RyRs in vivo, and GAPDH knockdown abolished cADPR-induced Ca2+ release. On the other hand, GAPDH did not catalyze cADPR into any other known or novel compound(s). Our data suggest that GADPH is the long-sought-after cADPR binding protein and is required for cADPR-mediated Ca2+ mobilization from ER via RyRs. Based on the simulated cADPR-GAPDH complex structure, we also performed the structure-based drug screening, identified a number of small chemicals with high docking scores to cADPR’s binding pocket in GAPDH, and found one of these compounds, C244, is a potential cADPR antagonist. Here we propose to (1) mechanistically study how cADPR binds with GAPDH to trigger Ca2+ release from ER via RyRs, and (2) chemically synthesize and pharmacologically characterize novel cADPR agonist(s) or antagonist(s). Given the pivotal role of cADPR-mediated Ca2+ signaling pathway in a wide variety of cellular processes, understanding the molecular mechanisms of this signaling pathways and identifying novel cADPR agonist(s) or antagonist(s) will be fundamentally important for pharmaceutical intervention in treatment of cADPR-related human disorders.

11101717.label: Realisation of objectives
11101717.value: Objective 1: To chemically synthesize and pharmacologically characterize novel cADPR agonist(s) or antagonist(s). (1) Based on the simulated GAPDH-cADPR complex structure, we performed the virtual drug screening to identify potential cADPR agonist(s) or antagonist(s). We showed that two analogs, compound 244 (C244) and 346 (C346), did not affect cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels, but pretreatment of Jurkat cells or RyR3-expressing HEK293 cells with them abrogated NPE-cADPR-mediated Ca2+ release, suggesting that C244 or C346 is a potential cADPR antagonist (Fig. 1). Next, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiments demonstrated that C244 or C346 bound to the recombinant GAPDH protein immobilized on the CM5 chip. Also, C346 did not affect Ca2+ release mediated by ionomycin, histamine, and ATP, nor did it affect store-operated Ca2+ influx (Fig. 2). These data indicate that C346 is a cADPR-specific antagonist. Subsequently, we synthesized more than 20 analogs of C346, and showed that only compound G32 or G42 triggered stronger intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in RyR3-expressing HEK293 cells than in wild-type HEK293 cells. These results suggest that the second peak of intracellular Ca2+ mobilization triggered by G32 or G42 is RyRs-dependent (Fig. 3). We further demonstrated that G42, in addition to its involvement in RYR-mediated intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, also significantly induces lysosomal Ca2+ release (Fig. 4). We showed that G42 did increase lysosomal pH, but it had little effect on the degradation of DQ-BSA. Likewise, G42 had little effect on the maturation of cathepsin B (CTSB) (Fig. 4). These results suggest that G42-induced subtle alkalization of lysosomes does not change the lysosomal degradation function. We showed that G42 significantly increased the expression of LC3-II and p62. In GFP-RFP-LC3-expressing HeLa cells, G42 significantly promoted the accumulation of yellow LC3 puncta. Moreover, in HeLa cells expressing RFP-LC3 and GFP-STX17, G42 markedly induced colocalization of LC3 red puncta with STX17 green puncta (Fig. 5). These results indicate that G42 is a late-stage autophagy inhibitor. Pretreatment of A549 cells with G42 significantly inhibited ZIKV-induced ZIKV envelope protein, and double-stranded RNAs. The IC50 of G42 against ZIKV was around 1.33 uM. Pretreatment of A549 cells with G42 significantly inhibited ZIKV-induced intracellular and extracellular virus titers. Moreover, treatment of A549 cells after ZIKV infection with G42 inhibited ZIKV-induced intracellular and extracellular virus titers as potently as pretreatment of cells with G42 (Fig. 6). These results suggest that G42 inhibits ZIKV infections after virus entry, likely by blocking autophagy. Also, treatment of 17-Cl1 cells with G42 inhibited the MHV-induced NSP9. Likewise, G42 efficiently inhibited the expression of NSP9 induced by different MOI MHV. Moreover, G42 significantly inhibited MHV-induced dsRNA levels in 17-Cl1 cells with IC50 around 1.4 uM (Fig. 7). These results suggest that G42 is an anti-beta-coronavirus agent. In summary, these results suggest that G42 inhibits virus infection, likely by triggering lysosomal Ca2+ mobilization and inhibiting autophagy. All the figures can be found in a preprint 10.1101/2022.06.09.495506 posted on bioRxiv: https://biorxiv.org/cgi/content/short/2022.06.09.495506v1, and is currently under review in Antiviral Research. (2). We found that the bisbenzylisoquinoline alkaloid (e.g., berbamine or its analogs) significantly inhibited TRPML-mediated Ca2+ release from lysosomes. Also, pretreatment of cells with berbamine significantly inhibited ML-SA1-induced Ca2+ influx. These data suggest that berbamine is an antagonist of TRPML. Berbamine or its analogs effectively inhibited SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses (such as Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) and ZIKV), and MERS-CoV infection of host cells. Mechanistically, berbamine disrupts the endosomal-lysosomal trafficking of some viral receptors such as ACE2 (the receptor for SARS-CoV-2) or LDLR (the receptor for JEV) by inhibiting TRPMLs-mediated Ca2+ release from lysosomes. This promoted the extracellular secretion of ACE2 or LDLR through extracellular vesicles (EVs) and resulted in a decrease in the level of ACE2 or LDLR at the plasma membrane. Likewise, knockdown of TRPMLs resulted in decreased levels of ACE2 or LDLR at the plasma membrane and significantly inhibited SARS-CoV-2 or JEV infection of host cells. Furthermore, we assessed the protective effect of berbamine against JEV infection in a mouse model. We showed that berbamine protected mice from lethal JEV challenge, as demonstrated by higher survival rates and better weight recovery. The rate of viral shedding in the spleen of the berbamine-treated group was much lower than that of the control group. Furthermore, berbamine attenuated brain damage caused by JEV infection, compared with controls. These results suggest that berbamine is a potential anti-JEV drug. In conclusion, bisbenzylisoquinoline alkaloids can act as broad-spectrum antiviral drugs. These results have been published in Signal Transduct Target Ther. (2021) 6: 168, and Emerging Microbes & Infections (2021) 10, 1257-1271. In summary, we have completed this objective. Objective 2: To mechanistically study how cADPR binds with GAPDH to trigger Ca2+ release from ER via RyRs. (1). We showed that recombinant GAPDH was predominantly tetrameric in vitro and displayed normal enzymatic activity. Treatment with cADPR and ATP induced GAPDH to produce a dimeric or monomeric form. GAPDH was subsequently incubated with different concentrations of cADPR in the presence or absence of ATP to grow crystals. We have obtained several crystals of cADPR-GAPDH, but we did not find cADPR in the GAPDH crystals. We, thus, optimized protein purification and crystallization conditions and obtained several high-quality crystals. Also, we mutated T227 on GAPDH to Arg, and showed that the recombinant GAPDH-T229K protein existed mainly in a dimeric form in vitro. We have purified the GAPDH-T229K protein, incubated it with cADPR, and obtained good-quality crystals. Due to COVID-19 pandemic, the border between Hong Kong and the mainland has been closed for the past three years, so we were not able to send these crystals to the Shanghai synchrotron radiation facility to collect their diffraction data. Nevertheless, after the reopening of borders, we will go to the Shanghai synchrotron radiation facility to collect diffraction data of these crystals. After receiving the diffraction data, we will analyze the crystal structure by using human GAPDH as a search model or by molecular replacement with the single-wavelength anomalous dispersion method to determine the binding pocket of cADPR in GAPDH. Based on the structure data, we will finally characterize the binding site of cADPR to GAPDH, and vice versa. (2). We established BioID-GAPDH-expressing HeLa cells. In the presence of cADPR, we biotin-labeled HeLa cells expressing BioID or BioID-GAPDH for 24 h, followed by affinity purification and mass spectrometry to identify the biotinylated proteins. A total of 310 potential GAPDH-binding proteins were identified, including many known GAPDH-interacting proteins. By using KOBAS online software, 37 proteins were clustered in the calcium signaling pathway, 24 proteins in the ER and endocytosis signaling pathways, 4 proteins in autophagy, and 8 proteins in the glycolysis pathway. After constructing a protein-protein interaction network from these 310 proteins by String software, several central proteins were identified, including FKBP12, Homer 1, PSEN1, APP, CIB1, TKT, CHERP, etc. We finally assessed whether the knockdown of these genes by shRNAs affects cADPR-RyR-Ca2+ signaling. We showed that knockdown of FKBP12, CHERP, Homer1, or PSEN1 inhibited the intracellular Ca2+ release induced by exogenous cADPR, suggesting that these proteins are potential positive regulatory proteins in the cADPR signaling pathway. We further examined the interaction between GPADH and FKBP12 by immunoprecipitation. We showed that FKBP12 was detected in the immunocomplex of GAPDH. These results indicate that cADPR-GAPDH may indirectly trigger the channel opening of RyRs to release of Ca2+ from ERs through the activation of the aforementioned proteins, especially FKBP12. In summary, we have also completed this objective.

We further synthesized several analogs of C346, and found that its analog, G42, also mobilized Ca2+ release from lysosomes. G42 alkalized lysosomal pH, and inhibited autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Positive-sense single-stranded ((+)ss) RNA viruses are among the leading causes of human and animal infectious diseases in the world, but so far, no effective antiviral agents are available to treat these infections. 11101717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11101717.value: We showed that G42 inhibits ZIKV or MHV infections of host cells, likely by triggering lysosomal Ca2+ mobilization and inhibiting autophagy. It is of interest to further determine the effects of G42 against other RNA viruses, e.g., SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV. Also, modifying G42 structure might further improve its antiviral activity while decreasing its cytotoxicity. It remains to determine the lysosomal Ca2+ channels targeted by G42, and the potential targets include TRPMLs, TPCs, or both. Since G42 inhibited the autophagosome-lysosome fusion, these RNA viruses might hijack autolysosomes as replication sites. Also, the autolysosomes might be the site for the degradation of the synthesized negative-strand viral RNA. Yet, the role of autophagy in viral infection is complicated, depending upon the viral types, host cells, infection duration, and stages of viral cycles. Thus, more efforts are needed to systematically dissect the role of autophagy in viral infections. We showed that cADPR-GAPDH may indirectly trigger the channel opening of RyRs to release of Ca2+ from ERs through the activation of the aforementioned proteins, especially FKBP12. This work provides a new research direction for the mechanism of cADPR. The specific mechanism of these proteins in activating this signaling pathway is worthy of further study.

11101717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11101717.value: We recently identified GAPDH as one of cADPR (an endogenous Ca2+ mobilizer) binding protein(s), and demonstrated that GAPDH participates in cADPR-induced Ca2+ release. Based on the simulated cADPR-GAPDH complex structure, we identified several small chemicals with high docking scores to cADPR’s binding pocket in GAPDH, and found two of these compounds, C244 and C346, are potential cADPR antagonists. We have also synthesized several novel C346 analogs, and found that these small chemicals compromise lysosomal Ca2+ signaling to inhibit autophagy or to reduce the levels of some membrane receptors, including several receptors for positive, single-strand RNAs viruses, on the plasma membrane. In this way, they effectively inhibit the infection of host cells by these RNA viruses, including dengue virus, Zika virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, SARS-CoV-2, and MERS. In addition, we established a protein interaction network of GAPDH by BioID2-mediated biotin proximity labeling. We found that multiple proteins, such as Homer1, FKBP12, CHERP, and PSEN1, were involved in cADPR-RyR-Ca2+ signaling. Given the pivotal role of the Ca2+ signaling pathway in a wide variety of cellular processes, understanding the molecular mechanisms of this signaling pathway and identifying novel Ca2+ modulators will be fundamentally important for pharmaceutical intervention in treatment of human diseases.

11102317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11102317.value: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal diseases among major malignancies, with only six-month overall survival from diagnosis. Due to limited response to adjuvant chemotherapies, surgical excision provides the best chance for longer survival. Local and distal recurrence, however, are found in 80% patients after surgery, precluding curative resection in more advanced disease. At present clinical, radiological, and pathological data are used for decision-making, but these characteristics are insufficient to identify clinically relevant subgroups. Furthermore, genetic analysis of PDAC intertumor heterogeneity has identified many genetic alterations, but relatively few consistent driver genes. How to stratify PDAC patients into molecularly distinct subgroups, in relation to clinical outcomes, is critical for selection of patients for optimized adjuvant therapies and design of targeted agents. Gene expression-based subtyping has been widely accepted as a relevant source of disease stratification. Four major classification systems for PDAC have been reported in the literature, demonstrating that similar to many other types of cancers PDAC is not a single disease. Our recent work on in-house-generated RNA-Seq data for 90 stage II PDAC patients also identified 4 molecularly distinct subtypes (PDACS1-4). More specifically, PDACS1 and PDACS4 are both enriched for diabetes mellitus (DM) as shown by the increased expression of β-cell and insulin secretion signatures. However, PDACS4 shows higher immune activities, which explains its better overall survival than PDACS1. PDACS2 shows dysregulation of various metabolism programs, mitochondrion-related pathways, DNA repair and MYC- and Wnt-pathways. PDACS3, with the poorest overall survival, is characterized by upregulation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, cell migration, TGF-β1 signaling, stroma infiltration, as well as highly expressed PD-L1 and PD-L2 genes. Despite these various molecular subtyping effort, its translational potential is hampered by discrepant results, which are probably due to differences in bioinformatic algorithms, diverse discovery cohorts, sample preparation methods and gene expression platforms. Of utmost importance is to elucidate the interrelations between the five PDAC taxonomies, including ours, and define common disease patterns (or consensus molecular subtypes, CMSs) in a principled, unbiased manner, which is our 1st objective in the proposal. Through integrative analysis of multi-omic data and clinical information for ~1500 PDAC samples, our 2nd objective is to comprehensively characterize identified CMSs. Focusing on the poor prognosis subtype, our 3rd objective is to dissect tumor-intrinsic regulatory mechanism based on network inference from deconvolved gene expression profiles, and subsequently to prioritize master regulators for experimental validation by our collaborators at the University of Amsterdam. 胰腺導管腺癌 （PDAC）確診後病人總體生存期只有半年左右，因而是致死率最高的癌症之一。由於病人對於輔助化療反應有限，手術切除仍然是獲得較長生存期的最佳手段。然而，80%的病人術後出現局部或遠端復發，因此手術無法根治晚期病人。目前，臨床決策主要依賴於臨床、放療和病理數據，但是這些數據特徵不足以區分臨床上相關的病人群體。此外，雖然腫瘤間異質性的遺傳分析已經發現了許多遺傳變異，但是只有少數驅動基因在這些分析中是被一致確定的。如何將胰腺導管腺癌病人分類成不同的、與臨床表型相關的分子亞型對於優化病人的輔助治療和靶向藥物的設計都極為關鍵。 基於基因表達譜的分子分型已經被廣泛地應用到疾病的分類當中。文獻中已有四種胰腺導管腺癌的分型系統，表明和其他主要惡性腫瘤一樣胰腺導管腺癌不是一種單一疾病。我們基於90例II期胰腺導管腺癌的RNA-Seq數據分析發現了四種分子特異的亞型（PDACS1-4）。具體來講，PDACS1和PDACS4富集糖尿病相關的分子特徵，例如，β細胞和胰島素分泌的標記基因顯著上調。然而，PDACS4具有更高的免疫活性，因而能解釋其相對PDACS1更好的生存。 PDACS2亞型表現各種代謝、線粒體、DNA修復、MYC及Wnt信號通路的失調。 PDACS3亞型的患者預後最差，並表現為上調的上皮間質轉化、細胞遷移、TGF-β1信號通路、基質浸潤及顯著上調的PD-L1和PD-L2基因表達。 儘管該領域內已有各種分子分型研究，其臨床轉化潛力仍被不一致的結論所阻礙。這些看似相互矛盾的分子分型結果可能是由於採用了不同的生物信息學算法、樣本隊列、樣本處理方法及基因表達分析平台。本課題的第一個目標，也是當前最為關鍵的難題，是如何闡明包括我們提出的分類系統在內的五個分子分型系統之間的關係，並進一步無偏差地定義普遍適用的共識分子亞型。基於對~1500個PDAC樣本的多組學及臨床數據的綜合分析，我們第二個目標是全面地研究各種共識分子亞型相關的分子及臨床特徵。聚焦預後較差的分子亞型，我們第三個目標是對基因表達數據分解並進行網絡推理來剖析腫瘤細胞內在的調控機制，然後篩選主調控因子並與阿姆斯特丹大學合作進行實驗驗證。

11102317.label: Realisation of objectives
11102317.value: Objective 1: Elucidating the relationships between different classification systems and identifying consensus molecular subtypes of PDAC The first goal of this project was to elucidate the relationships between existing PDAC subtyping systems, including our PDACS taxonomy. To this end, we employed a robust methodology we established before to quantify the statistical associations between subtypes of different classification systems. We first reproduced the classifier used by each subtyping system based on corresponding signature genes and the discovery data set. Subsequently, we performed cross-classifications, i.e. to use each classifier on the discovery data sets of all reported subtyping systems. For each two classification systems, sample enrichment analysis was performed using hypergeometric tests to compare their corresponding classification results. This approach revealed key correlations between the PDAC subtyping system we established with published subtypes. For example, the PDACS1 subtype significantly correlated with subtypes identified in two other studies that share the exo- and endocrine features of the pancreas. PDCAS2 also strongly correlated with subtypes from two other studies that represented classical, epithelial tumors. To further elucidate the interrelations between all PDAC classification systems, we employed a network-based meta-analysis approach that was established by us previously. The network encodes on nodes the information of subtype prevalence and on edges their association calculated by Jaccard similarity coefficient, which is defined by the size of the intersection between two sample sets over the size of their union. To quantify the statistical significance of subtype associations, we performed hypergeometric tests for overrepresentation of samples classified to one subtype in another. Using this approach, we built a network consisting of subtypes defined in all subtyping systems, interconnected by statistically significant (BH-corrected, P < 0.001) edges. This analysis showed that our PDAC subtypes and those previously published are highly interconnected, and four consensus subtypes can be identified from the network. Objective 2: Comprehensive multi-omic molecular and clinical characterization of consensus molecular subtypes of PDAC Our second goal was to comprehensively delineate molecular properties and clinical characteristics associated with each PDAC subtype. Using gene set analysis on the MSigDB database, we found that each of the distinct PDAC subtypes was characterized by specific biological features. PDACS1 was enriched for endocrine and exocrine functions of the pancreas, as indicated by Moffitt’s endocrine and exocrine factors and β-cell and pancreatic secretion signatures. As neuroendocrine transdifferentiation has recently been associated with poor outcomes in PDAC, these enrichments could indicate high lineage plasticity. PDACS2 tumors were characterized by Myc signaling, high expression of mitochondrial components, and ribosome signatures. PDACS4 was enriched for signatures for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and stroma and TGF-β signaling. PDACS3 featured signatures similar to the mesenchymal subtype but with endocrine characteristics. Based on these comprehensive molecular characterizations, we named the identified subtypes PDACS1-secretory, PDCAS2-epithelial, PDACS3-compound pancreatic, and PDACS4-mesenchymal. Overall, clinical parameters, including age and histologic type, were similar among the subtypes. Based on TCGA somatic mutation data and our targeted mutation analysis for common PDAC driver genes (TP53, SMAD4, KRAS), we found no correlation to the PDACS groups. Compared with the other subtypes, PDACS4-mesenchymal tumors had the most differentially expressed miRNAs and proteins. PDACS3-compound tumors had a relatively high prevalence of somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs). Assessments of tumor purity and stromal and immune cell content by ESTIMATE revealed that the epithelial subtype (PDACS2) was relatively enriched in tumor cells. Survival analysis with a 2-year follow-up revealed that the secretory and mesenchymal subtypes were associated with much poorer outcomes (median overall survival (OS) 14.7 and 14.0 months, respectively), compared with the epithelial and compound pancreatic subtypes (median OS 31.8 and 21.5 months). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed that radicality of resection (P = 0.007), lymph node status (P = 0.003) and degree of differentiation (poor vs well P = 0.011; poor vs moderate P = 0.002) also associated with outcome. We performed multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analysis to test the statistical significance of the association of PDACS with OS, adjusting for potential confounders including sex, age at diagnosis, radicality of resection, lymph node metastasis, and differentiation grade. The association of the secretory and mesenchymal subtypes with poor outcomes remained significant (P = 0.018 and P = 0.036, respectively). Using a merged cohort of three published datasets, we validated that the mesenchymal subtype was also associated with poor outcomes (P = 0.017). Objective 3: Dissecting tumor-intrinsic regulatory mechanisms based on deconvolution of bulk-tumor gene expression profiles Our third goal was to incorporate intratumor heterogeneity based on deconvolution of tumor microenvironment to better classify PDAC and dissect tumor-intrinsic regulatory mechanisms by multi-dimensional network inference. Motivated by the recent success of artificial intelligence (AI) applied for dissecting tumor microenvironment, we developed an AI-empowered framework—PDAC-SPA for automated delineation of histology images and quantification of spatial organization features. PDAC-SPA can efficiently and accurately classify image patches tessellated in each H&E slide into eight tissue classes: PDAC epithelium (TUM), cancer-associated stroma (STR), lymphocytes (LYM), normal pancreatic tissue (NORM), smooth muscle (MUS), debris (DEB), adipose tissue (ADI), and background (BACK). PDAC-SPA is available online at: http://144.214.26.35:3837/PDAC-multi-omic-subtyping/. Applying PDAC-SPA to histology images in the TCGA dataset, we calculated spatial diversity indices (SDIs), defined by the Shannon information entropy, to quantify the diversity of tissue types in the tumor microenvironment. Using SDI, we were able to further classify patients within the mesenchymal subtype of PDAC into SDI-high and -low subgroups (termed SDI-H and -L hereafter). Pathway analysis results showed that SDI-L was significantly enriched in gene sets associated with metastasis and poor prognosis, such as cancer-associated fibroblast and migratory signatures. Instead, SDI-H was significantly enriched for activated immune cell signatures, such as T cell and CD8 activation signatures. More interestingly, SDI-H was found to be relatively more enriched in epithelial signatures, compared to the SDI-L subgroup. Next, we inferred transcription factor (TF) regulatory networks for the two subgroups, which differ drastically in the topology and master regulators regulating epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). In the TF regulatory network for SDI-H, we identified BBX, BACH1, and ZNF146 as the master regulators. Instead, for the SDI-L subtype, five TFs, SNAI2, SOX4, TEAD1, KLF6, and PRRX1, were prioritized as master regulators. Using micro-dissected bulk-tumor sequencing data in PDAC, we found ZNF146 is more epithelium-specific while BBX and BACH1 did not show clear specificity in stroma or epithelium. Three master regulators identified in the SDI-L group, SNAI2, TEAD1, and PRRX1, were strongly stroma-specific. When we compared the EMT signature genes regulated in the two TF networks, few overlapping genes were found, suggesting again that the two subgroups differ in the downstream regulatory mechanisms. Survival analysis revealed that BACH1, ZNF146, and SNAI2 were significantly associated with overall survival in the TCGA dataset. Focusing on the master regulatory TFs found in SDI-H, BACH1 has been reported to be a key master regulator for cancer metastasis multiple cancer types. Reanalyzing published RNA-seq data between PDAC cell lines with BACH1 knockdown and controls, we validated the regulon of BACH1 in the SDI-H regulatory network. Taken together, our network analysis revealed different regulatory mechanisms underlying the subgroups of the mesenchymal subtype and identified key master regulator TFs of specific epithelial or stroma origins, showing great potential as novel prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. In addition, we employed multi-dimensional network inference algorithms to dissect the miRNA/long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) regulatory mechanisms specific to the mesenchymal/squamous subtype of PDAC. Our study gained novel insights into the miRNA/lncRNA regulatory mechanisms and provided potential therapeutic targets specifically for the mesenchymal/squamous subtype of PDAC.

11102317.label: Major findings and research outcome
11102317.value: 1. Molecular subtyping of PDAC with comprehensive characterizations (Dijk F et al. Sci Rep 2020). In collaboration with Dr. Maarten F. Bijlsma, we identified four molecular subtypes of PDAC based on unsupervised classification of RNA-seq data for 90 resected specimens. The four PDAC subtypes are associated with distinct biological properties and clinical outcomes, of which the worst-prognosis subtype was characterized by mesenchymal gene signatures. Comparative (network) analysis showed high interconnectivity with previously identified classification schemes and high robustness of the mesenchymal subtype. The classification approach we developed was also applied to study neuropharmacology, leading to the identification of anti-seizure-like drug leads from non-clinical compounds (Lin X et al., Nat Comm 2018). 2. Elucidating the miRNA regulatory mechanism underlying the mesenchymal/squamous subtype of PDAC (Zhang Y et al., Genes 2020). We performed network inference that integrates miRNA expression and gene expression profiles to dissect the miRNA regulatory mechanism specific to the most aggressive squamous subtype of PDAC. Master regulatory analysis revealed that the particular subtype of PDAC is predominantly influenced by miR-29c and miR-192. Our further integrative analysis found miR-29c target genes LOXL2, ADAM12, and SERPINH1, which all showed a strong association with prognosis. The network inference algorithm was also applied to microbiology, which successfully identified virulence-related transcription factors (Huang H et al., Nat Comm 2019). 3. Identification of master regulatory long non-coding RNAs underlying the mesenchymal/squamous subtype of PDAC (Zhu L et al., BIBM 2020). We inferred a lncRNA regulatory network by integrative network analysis and prioritized key lncRNAs as potential master regulators of the squamous subtype including TGFB2-AS1, AL138930.1, LINC01705, AC245041.1, UCA1, and NKILA. We demonstrated that the upregulation of UCA1 and NKILA in the squamous subtype was likely due to promoter hypomethylation. Survival analysis based on multiple independent datasets confirmed the clinical associations of these lncRNAs. 4. Development of an efficient and robust artificial intelligence (AI)-empowered framework for automated delineation of tumor microenvironment based on histopathological images (Qi L et al., Medicine in Omics 2021). We developed an AI-empowered framework for accurate tissue classification and profiling of spatial organization features using histology images. Applying the framework to PDAC, we identified two subgroups within the mesenchymal subtype by spatial diversity index (SDI), which are regulated by different transcription factor regulatory mechanisms. Furthermore, we identified key master regulator TFs of specific epithelial or stroma origins, showing great potential as novel biomarkers for prognosis and therapeutic targets. PDAC-SPA is available online at: http://144.214.26.35:3837/PDAC-multi-omic-subtyping/.

11102317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11102317.value: Several findings in the project have the potential for clinical translation, pending future experimental and clinical validations. (1) We identified miR-29c as one of the master regulator miRNAs, and its downstream targets LOXL2, ADAM12, and SERPINH1 showed strong potential to be prognostic biomarkers and novel therapeutic targets; (2) the mesenchymal subtype-specific master regulatory lncRNAs, UCA1, AC245041.1, AL138930.1, LINC01705, and NKILA, are also potential prognosticators for PDAC; (3) the AI-empowered framework PDAC-SPA we established also has the potential to be implemented for automated delineation of histology images, which may greatly facilitate pathologists’ diagnosis and decision making in the clinic. To eventually translate these findings into the clinic, in-depth mechanistic studies and large-scale cohort studies with a more rigorous experimental design are needed, which are beyond the scope of this project. However, during the project, we have established close collaborations with multiple research institutions and hospitals such as Sun Yat-sen University, the Academic Medical Center at the University of Amsterdam, and the Beckman Research Institute at the City of Hope. We plan to apply for collaborative grants together with these collaborators to support further development of the research, which we believe will eventually benefit patients in the future.

11102317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11102317.value: Pancreatic cancer is the deadliest disease among major malignancies, with a very low five-year survival rate of only ~7%. Among various clinical types of pancreatic cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) accounts for > 85% of all patients. However, the current decision-making for PDAC is mostly based on clinical, radiological, and pathological characteristics, which are insufficient to identify clinically relevant subgroups. In this project, we identified four molecular subtypes of PDAC characterized by distinct biological and clinical features, which are highly interconnected with previously published taxonomies. Focusing on the mesenchymal subtype associated with the poorest survival, we identified key regulatory microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and their downstream targets, which showed strong potential as prognostic biomarkers and novel therapeutic targets. Furthermore, we developed an artificial intelligence-based framework—PDAC-SPA, which can efficiently and accurately delineate tumor microenvironment. Using spatial diversity index (SDI), which quantifies intratumor heterogeneity, we were able to further stratify the mesenchymal subtype into two subgroups that are clinically relevant. Our further network analysis revealed different regulatory mechanisms underlying the two mesenchymal subgroups and identified key master regulator TFs of specific epithelial or stroma origins, showing great potential as novel biomarkers for prognosis and therapeutic targets.

11102417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11102417.value: The entorhinal cortex enables neuroplasticity of the auditory cortex through cholecystokinin (CCK) [1]. With high-frequency stimulation, the thalamocortical and corticothalamic neurons release CCK that enables thalamocortical and corticothalamic long-term potentiation (LTP). We recently found that high-frequency activation is the compulsory condition for glutamatergic CCK neurons to release CCK (Figs. 2-3 and unpublished). The third population of and also mostly-attended cortex-related CCK neurons found over the past few decades are the GABAergic CCK neurons in the neocortex. In the present study, we aim to examine whether: 1) high-frequency activation of GABAergic CCK neurons induces CCK release; and 2) whether the released CCK enhances GABAergic inputs to the pyramidal neurons. In order to facilitate our aim we will generate two transgenic mice - a GABA-CCK-Cre strain in which only GABAergic CCK neurons express the Cre recombinase and a GABA-CCK-CreER strain in which CCK is knocked-out only and the CreER recombinase is inserted into GABAergic CCK neurons. After transfecting the neurons with AAV-DIO-ChR2-eYFP virus we will specifically activate the GABAergic CCK neurons by employing optogenetics. Thereafter, examination of whether CCK is released from GABAergic CCK neurons after high-frequency stimulation will be explored. We will examine whether CCK is released from GABAergic CCK neurons only after high-frequency stimulation. Enhanced inhibition of GABAergic neurons is expected when CCK is released in GABA-CCK-Cre mouse. The enhanced inhibition can be detected by a probe stimulus consisting of single-pulse laser stimulation and an auditory stimulus with an interval in between. Neuronal responses to the auditory stimulus will be inhibited by laser-activated GABAergic neurons. Further confirmation of enhanced inhibition will stem from the increased inhibitory response in the membrane potential of the pyramidal neuron with in vivo intracellular recording on the anesthetized mouse. Before the above mouse lines are generated, examination of the inhibition of GABAergic inputs to pyramidal neurons can be enhanced after high-frequency laser stimulation of GABAergic neurons, using our existing Viaat-Cre, CCK-Cre and CCK-CreER (CCK-/-) mice. For CCK-Cre and CCK-/- mice, we’ll inject a virus into the superficial layers to avoid deep-layer pyramidal CCK neurons. The long-term impacts of the present study are two-fold: 1) potentially unveil the mechanism of neuroplasticity of the inhibitory circuit in the neocortex; and 2) through the linkage of the high-frequency firing of GABAergic CCK neurons with plasticity of inhibitory circuits provide an important angle for drug development to treat epilepsy through enhancement of the inhibition. 內嗅皮層通過誘導膽囊收縮素（CCK）聽覺皮質的神經可塑性[1]。高頻刺激可以引起丘腦皮質和皮質丘腦神經元釋放CCK並誘導皮質和丘腦的長時程增強（LTP）。我們最近發現高頻激活是谷氨酸能CCK神經元釋放CCK的必要條件（圖2-3和未發表）。 在過去幾十年中發現的第三類並最受關注的與皮質相關的CCK神經元是新皮質中的GABA能CCK神經元。在本研究中，我們的目的是檢查：1）GABA能CCK神經元的高頻激活是否可誘導CCK釋放; 2）釋放的CCK是否可增強GABA能輸入到錐體神經元。 為了實現我們的目標，我們將產生兩個轉基因小鼠- 一種GABA-CCK-Cre小鼠，其中只有GABA能CCK神經元表達Cre重組酶，而GABA-CCK-CreER小鼠的CCK是被敲除，CreER重組酶插入GABA能CCK神經元。用AAV-DIO-ChR2-eYFP病毒轉染神經元後，我們將通過使用光遺傳學來特異性激活GABA能CCK神經元。此後，將探討CCK在高頻刺激後是否從GABA能CCK神經元釋放。我們將檢查CCK是否僅在高頻刺激後從GABA能CCK神經元釋放。當在GABA-CCK-Cre小鼠中釋放CCK時，預期GABA能神經元的抑制會被增強。增強的抑制可以通過由單脈衝激光刺激和具有間隔之間的間隔的聽覺刺激組成的探針刺激來檢測。激光激活的GABA能神經元可抑制神經元對聽覺刺激的反應。增強抑制的進一步確認將源自在麻醉的小鼠體內細胞內記錄的錐體神經元的膜電位增加的抑制反應。 在產生上述小鼠品系之前，我們將使用現有的Viaat-Cre，CCK-Cre和CCK-CreER（CCK敲除）檢測GABA能神經元高頻激光刺激可否增強GABA能神經元對錐體神經元的抑製作用。對於CCK-Cre和CCK - / - 小鼠，我們將注入病毒到皮層表層，以避免深層的錐體CCK神經元。 本研究的長期影響是雙重的：1）揭示新皮質中抑制電路神經可塑性的潛在機制; 2）通過GABA能CCK神經元的高頻放電與抑制電路的可塑性的聯繫為藥物開發提供了重要的角度，即通過加強抑制迴路來治療癲癇。

We selected the normalized sound intensity and laser power after measuring the input-output curve for stimulus intensities for each mouse. We examined the kinetics of optogenetics opsin by applying laser pulse trains of different frequencies (1 to 120 Hz) for both groups. We found that the laser activation of the GABAergic neurons caused a lasting inhibition in the spontaneous firing of about 200 ms. We delivered the AS of 100 ms duration at 50 ms after the laser pulse delivery. We adopted the window of AS presentation to exclude the possible effects of the post-inhibitory rebound excitation, recurrent inhibition, and oscillatory activities in our examination of the inhibitory effect by activating GABAergic neurons. Laser-activated GABAergic neurons inhibited neuronal response to the forthcoming AS in Vgat-Cre. We adopted the HFLS protocol (HFLS, 5-pulse bursts in 40 Hz, 10 s of inter-burst-interval, 200 pulses in total). 11102417.label: Major findings and research outcome
11102417.value: During this report period, we unveiled the emerging role of a certain type of neuropeptide, cholecystokinin (CCK), originated from entorhinal cortex (EC) in the modulation of neural plasticity in many brain regions, including auditory cortex, hippocampus (Su et al., 2020) al and lateral amygdala (Feng, 2019). The transgenic CCK-knockout mutant mice show deficits in both electrophysiological and behavioral aspects, including the induction failure corticocortical LTP, thalamocortical LTP hippocampal LTP and the impairment in spatial memory, sound-sound associative memory and fear memory formation (Chen et al., 2019; Feng et al.,2020; Su et al., 2020). On the other hand, we found that the classical LTP induction protocol, theta burst stimulation, or tetanus burst stimulation (TBS), can induce the release of CCK from entorhinal projection terminals; And the endogenous or exogenous application of CCK both can induced LTP without TBS (Chen et al., 2019). In the present study, we hypothesized that CCK released from the GABAergic neurons mediate the strengthening of their inhibition and induce iLTP. We show here HFLS of GABA neurons induced potentiation of inhibition in the cortex of Vgat-Cre mice, but not in Vgat-Cre-CCK-KO mice. HFLS of CCK-GABA, but not PV neurons induced iLTP, in-vitro. LFLS of CCK-GABA neurons induced no iLTP. With the application of CCK8s, LFLS of CCK-GABA neurons generated iLTP. HF stimulation of the corticofugal CCKpositive pathway enables the LTP of ascending acoustic signal transmission in the MGB (Li et al., 2020). From above results, we can infer that HF activation of the corticothalamic pathway exert much more influence on the ascending acoustic signal transmission than itself. It suggested corticofugal fibers enable long-term modulation of ascending signal transmission via its CCK (Li et al., 2020). Our behavioral experiments showed that CCK infusion significantly increased the frequency discrimination ability by facilitating salubrious plastic changes induced by the passive tone exposure in adult animals. CCK induced plasticity may provide a possible treatment plan which can be applied to enhance the function of late cochlear implants in prelingually deaf children. We are developing CCKBR agonists for the purpose (Zhang et al., 2020). Our findings could be generalized in different sensory modalities, including, but not limited to perception, learning, and memory formation (Su et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020)

11102417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11102417.value: Cholecystokinin (CCK) enables long-term potentiation of the excitatory circuit. In this study, we investigated its involvement in the neuroplasticity of inhibitory synapses. CCK is essential in the long-term enhancement of inhibition after the high-frequency firing of GABAergic neurons. Epilepsy, a brain disorder, is a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. There are fewer opinions in epilepsy therapy through glutamate receptors since the antagonists possess undesired side effects. In contrast, new interests in GABAA receptor (GABAAR) emerged in regulating neuronal excitability and treating epilepsy. Many evidence showed the involvement of GABAergic inhibitory circuits in the formation, propagation, and treatment of epilepsy. GABAergic CCK-induced enhancement of inhibitory effect may provide a possible treatment plan which can be applied to suppress epilepsy.

11102417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11102417.value: Here, we investigated its involvement in the neuroplasticity of inhibitory synapses. Activation of GABA neurons suppressed neuronal responses to the forthcoming auditory stimulus (AS) in the neocortex. High-frequency laser stimulation (HFLS) of GABAergic neurons potentiated this suppression in the long term. HFLS of CCK-GABA neurons potentiated inhibitory postsynaptic current in the pyramidal neuron. This potentiation was abolished in CCK-knockout (KO) mice.

11200317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11200317.value: Network controllability and observability are essential and key to guarantee before one can consider how to control or predict a complex dynamical network in any application. This proposal aims to design control inputs by means of characterizing the control input and inner coupling matrices for achieving complete state and/or structural controllability and/or observability of complex dynamical networks. Basic properties of control input matrices and their relationships with the invariant system state-controllability subspace will be precisely characterized. Then, based on that, the inner coupling and control input matrices such that the overall network is completely state and/or structural controllable and/or observable. Finally, for typical fully-connected networks, trees, or cycles, establish some simple and easily-verifiable criteria for designing the inner coupling and control input matrices towards their complete state and/or structural controllability and/or observability. This proposal aims to design control inputs by means of characterizing the control input and inner coupling matrices for achieving complete state and/or structural controllability and/or observability of complex dynamical networks. Basic properties of control input matrices and their relationships with the invariant system state-controllability subspace will be precisely characterized. Then, based on that, the inner coupling and control input matrices are designed such that the overall network is completely state and/or structural controllable and/or observable. 11200317.value: All proposed research objectives have been completed, each with several related journal papers published (see the publication record). After the completion of this project, the relationship of network input-output with the network controllability has been clarified and become well understood. This laid part of a foundation for further studies of different aspects of the complex network controllability.

11200317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11200317.value: Part of the findings had become the initiatives for the following new GRF proposal on the same subject of complex network controllability but on different aspects.

11200317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11200317.value: This project studies the properties of control inputs and their relationships with the complex network controllability, by characterizing the inner coupling and control input matrices such that the overall network is completely controllable and observable. For some fully-connected networks and special types of networks such as trees and cycles, some precise and easily verifiable criteria have been established for designing the inner coupling and control input matrices such that the given complex network is completely controllable and observable. This will be useful for practical network design especially for multiagent dynamical systems, sensor networks and communication networks where some control tasks are required.
