12604517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12604517.value: This study aims to explore the strategies used by older Hong Kong migrants in Britain in handling their care needs and maintaining relationship with their families in Britain and their place of origin. It is built on the PI’s previous work on the concepts of familisation and defamilisation; and culturally sensitive policy and practice for Chinese older people in Britain. The main focuses are: 1) strategies used by older Hong Kong migrants in Britain in maintaining relationship with their Britain-based and overseas families; 2) how such strategies are related to their reliance on the family, the state and the market for the care and support they need; and 3) how such strategies are related to the intergenerational and transnational division of caring and financial responsibilities in their families. The study will draw references from four areas of theoretical debate: defamilisation and familisation, decommodification and commodification, intergenerational division of labour in the family, and culturally sensitive policy and practice. The study will take two stages and be conducted in three cities in Britain (London, Manchester and Sheffield) and Hong Kong. It will explore the views of both older Hong Kong migrants and their families in Britain and Hong Kong. In the first stage, 80 older people in the three British cities with family connections in Hong Kong and of a variety of personal characteristics will be recruited through purposive sampling procedures to attend a semi-structured interview. Respondents will be asked to share their migration history, care arrangements, support networks and connections with their local and overseas families. In the second stage, snowball sampling procedures will be used to recruit 10 family members of the respondents in Britain and 10 overseas family members in Hong Kong to attend a semi-structured interview to provide their views on the issues concerned. A thematic approach will be adopted to analyse the interview data with the aid of Maxqda. The study will enhance the understanding of transnational family relationships by disentangling some complex patterns concerning caring arrangements of older migrants and exploring how policy and practice can be more responsive to their needs and preferences. It will also contribute to the theoretical debate of different types of defamilisation, their relationship with decommodification in the labour and product spheres and how these concepts could be used to analyse models of family division of labour in care and finance. 本研究計劃是關於旅英港僑長者如何處理照顧需要‚和處理居於英國和居於香港的家庭成員之關係。研究焦點在於三方面: 第一是受訪對象喜歡和已落實採用的處理在英和外海家庭成員的關係的方法。 第二是這些處理家庭關係的方法與他們依賴家庭‚ 政府和市場以滿足照顧需要的方式是否相關。如相關的話‚ 這些相關的具體表現是甚麼? 第三是這些處理家庭關係的方法與跨代和跨境家庭在財政上和照顧上的分工是否相關。如相關的話‚這些相關的具體表現是甚麼? 這些焦點是建基於數項學術討論‚包括家庭化和去家庭化‚勞力商品化和勞力非商品化‚跨代家庭分工和跨境的家庭分工。 本研究將分兩階段進行。第一階段將訪問居於倫敦､曼城和雪菲爾的旅英港僑長者。訪問內容包括受訪者的移民歷史‚照顧安排‚支援網絡和與照顧居於當地和海外的家人的連繫。 第二是以滾雪球的抽籤方式‚聯絡和訪問受訪者的十位居英家人和十位居港家人‚從訪問中所得到的資料均以主題為本的方法作出分析。 本研究有助了解長者移民的跨境家庭關係‚相關資料有助發展老人照顧政策和照顧方法‚並可對家庭的概念的討論作出貢獻。

12604517.label: Realisation of objectives
12604517.value: This project focuses on the conceptual and empirical significance of defamilisation/familisation patterns. It builds on previous research studies – a small scale study on how Chinese older people in Britain respond to defamilisation risks and a study of defamilisation typologies. To further develop the accumulated ideas and to meet the project objectives, three study approaches were used to collect and analyse findings - inviting older Hong Kong migrants in Britain and the family members of older Hong Kong migrants to attend in-depth interviews, re-visiting the ideas shared by respondents based on literature review and exploring the international aspects of these ideas through analysing comparative data. The interviews focused on collecting the examples of how respondents handled familisation and defamilisation issues. The further review of literature and comparative data explored the insights provided by the interview findings into the link of the concepts defamilisalisation and familisation with the concepts/policy issues active ageing, the adult worker model, pension measures and work-life reconciliation measures. The ideas generated from this project are discussed in five published paper, one paper under review and one book chapter (under preparation). How the ideas generated from the three study approaches are used to meet the project objectives is shown as follows: Objective 1: The in-depth interviews provide concrete examples of the six strategies used by older people to maintain relationships with their overseas families and families in Britain: a.Decommodified economic defamilisation strategy ( more than half of respondents relied on pension incomes or their saving to maintain a reasonable standard of living and thus did not need to rely on their children living in Britain and Hong Kong). b.Commodified economic defamilisation strategy (12 respondents had properties in Hong Kong. The rents they collected enabled them to maintain a reasonable standard of living and thus did not need to rely on their children living in Britain and/or Hong Kong).c.Decommodified care-focused defamilisation strategy (6 respondents could look after themselves at the time of interviews but they planned to move to the government-subsidized hostels in Britain so that they would not need to rely on their children).d.Commodified care-focused defamilisation strategy (7 respondents explored the possibility of moving back to Hong Kong and living in private care hostels.). e.Commodified care-focused familisation strategy (5 respondents reported that they also wanted to go back to Hong Kong but they expected that their children would hire a domestic maid to look after them). f.Decommodified economic familisation strategy (About one-third respondents received financial supports from their children (in Hong Kong or in Britain). g.Commodified economic familisation strategy (16 respondents had attempted to assist their children and/or grandchildren living in Hong Kong to look for jobs in Britain). h.Decommodified care-focused familisation strategy (38 respondents received distant and proximate care from their children in Hong Kong or Britain) (discussed in the paper under review) . In conducting the flow of resources (such as financial resources and care) with their children in Britain and Hong Kong, some respondents tried to strengthen the ties with their children. In view of this experience, the investigator has developed a new transnational family contact framework based on the concept of tie and the flow. To show the empirical significance of this framework, it has been applied to the analysis of the data collected in the previous research project (discussed in a published paper). Objective 2. Based on the strategies used and/or suggested by respondents, examples of nine inter-generational and transnational divisions of caring and financial responsibilities were identified: a.Older people act as the main provider of financial support/young family member act as a receiver of the financial support (7 respondents used their pension incomes and/saving to regularly support their children living in Hong Kong; 9 respondents from time to time lent money to their children in Hong Kong). b.Universal provider of financial support model of all adults (5 respondents ran family business with their adult children). c.Older people act as the main provider of both care and financial support in the family (4 respondents mentioned that they had flied back to Hong Kong to provide financial support to their children and provided care to their grandchildren for a short period of time). d.Dual provider of financial support and care of all adults in the family (6 respondents mentioned they shared both the financial and caring responsibilities with their adult children in the family in Britain). e.Older people act as the main provider of care and their younger family members act as the main provider of financial support (15 respondents claimed that they took up most of the care responsibilities in the family and they relied on the financial support from their children). f.Older people act as a financial dependent and younger family members act as a provider of financial support in the family (As mentioned above, some respondents received financial support from their children in Britain or in Hong Kong). g.Older people act as a care receiver and young family member act as a care provider in the family (38 older people received different kinds of care from their children living in Hong Kong or in Britain). h.Non-care provider and non-care receiver ( A number of respondents claimed that their caring relationship with their children in Hong Kong or in Britain are non-active). i.Non-provider of financial support and non-receiver of financial support model (A number of respondents claimed that their financial relationship with their children in Hong Kong or in Britain are non-active) (these findings are partly discussed in the paper under review). Objective 3: As shown in the discussion of objectives 1 and 2, respondents participated in three kinds of market (product market, investment market and labour market) to handle family relationships. Respondents made a number of suggestions about how the Hong Kong and the UK governments should help them to handle defamilisation/familisation issues. Examples of these suggestions are: the UK government should provide training classes for helping older people to use the ITC means to contact their family members, the Hong Kong and the UK governments should sign a joint agreement to allow their citizens to use each other’s subsidised public health care services (these suggestions are partly discussed in the paper under review and the book chapter). Objective 4: Based on the interview findings, three types of defamilisation/familisation risks have been identified: the difficulties in having the defamilisation/familisation patterns they preferred; the difficulties in maintaining a reasonable standard of living when changing their attachment from one type of familisation/defamilisation pattern to another; and the governments’ unwillingness to tackle these risks (discussed in the book chapter). Attempts were made to explore why the governments (including not only the Hong Kong and the UK governments but also some European governments) are unwilling to help people tackle these risks through further reviews of literature and analysis of comparative data (please refer to Yu, et al, 2021b; Yu, et al, 2019). Objective 5: In relation to this project, courses sponsored by the Hong Kong Baptist University were developed to train older people in Hong Kong to use mobile phones to contact their family members. Workshops were held in Sheffield to share the experience of running the training courses. As mentioned, respondents were invited to make policy suggestions on how help them tackle defamilisation/familisation issues.

12604517.label: Major findings and research outcome
12604517.value: As mentioned in 5.1, three approaches were used to collect and analyse findings – interviewing older Hong Kong migrants in Britain and the family members of Hong Kong older migrants, reanalysing defamilisation/familisation issues based on literature review and exploring the international dimensions of these issues based on comparative data. Several findings and outcomes are shown as follows: The interview findings show that pension schemes and childcare services affect older people’s chance of choosing the ways of shaping the defamilisation/familisation patterns. Some respondents looked after their young children full time when they were young and thus had no chance to accumulate sufficient pension incomes. Some respondents (especially women) had no pension incomes and thus needed to rely financially on their children; and as a result, they had no choice but to look after their grandchildren regardless of their willingness to do so. Some family members of older migrants especially female members found it difficult to look after older people because they needed to take care of their own children and career. If there were sufficient childcare services, they would have more time to provide care to their older family members and/develop their career. Based on these findings and further review of literature, the project developed an argument that the government should make effective coordination between the provision of pension schemes and those commonly seen as defamilisation/familisation measures (such as child care and care for older people). This argument was presented with the examples of pension policies in Hong Kong and Taiwan in two papers (Yu, et al, 2020; Yu, et al, 2021). Based on literature review, comparative data and the review of the findings, new defamilisation/familisation concepts were developed and their applicability in the analysis of pension schemes and the adult worker model are shown in academic papers (Yu, et al, 2009; Yu, et al, 2021). As shown in 5.1, the interview findings provide empirical examples of defamilisation/familisation strategies. Moreover, a new transnational family contact framework based on the concepts of ‘tie’ and ‘flow’ was created. This framework was illustrated based on the findings of a study, which provides the foundation of this project (Yu, et al, 2020). As also shown in 5.1, the interview findings show the empirical significance of various forms of the inter-generational and transnational division of family care and responsibilities. These are discussed in a paper under review.

12604517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12604517.value: Defamilisation/familisation is an expanding research area with many unexplored areas. The proposer is going to implement these tasks in the near future. -To refine the transnational family contact framework based on the findings of the present project. -So far only some research findings were discussed in one article for academic journal and a book chapter. Two papers will be written to discuss the research findings (these include how male respondents responded to defamilisation/familisation issues, how the ways respondents living in London handled defamilisation/familisation issues were different from those living in Manchester and Sheffield). -One paper will be written to show how comparative data covering East Asian countries can be used to examine the governments’ willingness to tackle defamilisation/familisation risks. -It is worth studying whether and how respondents responded to the ideas of active ageing and the adult worker model through making transnational family contacts. -In writing joint papers with colleagues, I used some of findings from their study about productivism, more research will be implemented on the link between the study of defamilisation/familisation and productivism. As shown in the research findings, through providing care to other family members and making investments, respondents built their life on productivism.

12604517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12604517.value: This project is concerned with defamilisation/familisation patterns. Building on the previous work concerning how Chinese older people in Britain organise their family life based on the focus group interviews and the analysis of policies in Hong Kong and Britain, this project focuses on how older Hong Kong migrants in Britain meet their needs and handle their family relationships through making transnational contacts. The data is interpreted and collected by interviewing older migrants and the family members of older migrants, analysing government policies and examining comparative data. The research project discovers that the respondents attempted to play different roles in families through transnational contacts. These roles include care providers, care receivers, providers of financial support and receivers of financial support. In order to perform these roles, some respondents sought support from the market and the government. However, not all respondents were able to get sufficient support to perform (or not to perform) the roles in the way they preferred. To tackle these issues, it is suggested that both the Hong Kong and the UK governments should make effective coordination between pension schemes and those commonly seen as defamilisation/familisation measures (such as childcare and care for older people).

12605317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12605317.value: Chinese newspapers are responding to declining audiences and falling advertising revenues by developing their digital offerings. The well-established web sites have been joined by Weibo and Wexin presences. These shifts involve more than simply changing the medium through which news is distributed. In particular, the ability of the digital audience directly to generate news items, to comment upon news stories, and to seek out alternative sources, means that newspapers are obliged to rethink their relationship with their audiences. For the managers of both party and commercial newspapers, the loss of revenues leads them to try to develop new relationships with governmental and commercial organizations that can provide financial support to replace the lost advertising. For newspaper editors, the availability of instant feedback on audience behaviour has meant that they have to reconsider the ways in which they allocate journalistic resources and how they prioritise news stories. They now know, more or less in real time, what stories audiences are clicking on, which they are posting comments upon, and which are failing to attract attention. For working journalists, the new outlets sometimes provide opportunities to publish material that is blocked in their newspaper, sometimes provide leads to new stories and sources to back them up, and sometimes represent serious competition for the attention of the news audience. There is widespread international evidence, and some limited material in China, that suggests that the tastes of audience as expressed through their news preferences diverge substantially from the ways in which journalists have, in the past, defined news. Public affairs, both political and economic, look less large in the audience’s preferences and infotainment looks much more important. This project will analyse the ways in which all three levels of news workers are responding to this new situation. It will analyse the ways in which the content of selected newspapers has changed in response to the rise of new media outlets and compare the news agendas as presented in both printed and various digital forms. It will conduct a survey of news workers in the selected newspaper groups and follow up with interviews at different levels of the organizations in order to discover how journalists and editors are thinking about their new relationships with audience and how they are changing their journalistic practices to accommodate these shifts. The findings of this research will provide important contemporary insights in to the changing nature of Chinese media. 中國報業機構目前面臨著讀者減少和廣告收益下滑的現狀，為應對這一狀況，他們開始進行數字化的嘗試，比如上線新聞網站、開設微博、微信等。這一變化，從表面上來理解是新聞傳播的介質發生了改變，但在更深的層次，伴隨數字化媒體而來的是受眾（audience）這一概念的變化：受眾不再是被動地接收新聞，而是直接生產新聞內容、主動評論新聞報道、有目的地搜素信息，這些都使得報業不得不重新思考它們與受眾之間的關係。對於經營和管理人員來說，收益的下降導致他們格外關注受眾群體中的一部分資源佔有者，如政府和商業組織，期待與他們建立新型關係，以獲得經濟上的支持，彌補廣告收益上的損失。對於採編人員而言，數字化媒體的應用使得及時獲得受眾反饋成為可能，哪些報道會吸引讀者去點擊和評論，哪些報道不會吸引讀者，這些信息現在前所未有地便於獲得和一目瞭然，這逼迫編輯記者們必須重新思考新聞操作的方式，以及如何合理分配新聞資源、如何進行優先排序等。國際上很多現有研究都已經表明，讀者喜好的新聞不一定是記者認可的新聞，兩者之間存在著新聞品味的差距，比如，在新聞工作者的定義中，關乎政治、經濟和公共事務的新聞至關重要，但是在讀者眼中並非如此，他們反而更願意閱讀娛樂信息。在此背景下，這項研究將分析三類媒體從業者（管理人員、經營人員、採編人員）應對這一新情況的不同方式，將通過對媒體組織內不同層次的工作者進行訪談，來揭示他們是如何思考與受眾的新型關係的，以及如何改變新聞操作方式來適應這些變化的。同時本研究還將分析所選的報紙在新媒體渠道增加的情況下其內容的變化方式，並比較紙媒和不同形式的數字化媒體的新聞議程的呈現有何不同。本研究的發現將對理解當下中國媒體的轉型提供重要的見解。

12605317.label: Realisation of objectives
12605317.value: 1. A suitable coding frame for content analysis was developed. A guide to semi-structured interviews was constructed. 2. Five coders were recruited and trained for the content analysis. Appropriate data was gathered and entered. An acceptable level of reliability was achieved. 3. Nearly 200 interviews were conducted with journalists, editors and managers. The data derived from these interviews were analysed. The data from the content analysis was analyzed. In addition, data from a period of participant observation by an additional research associate was analysed. 4. Papers were presented at the meeting of the International Communication Association in Prague in 2018. It was scheduled to present a paper at the Gold Coast conference but this was cancelled due to the current situation. A paper was presented at the annual meeting of the International Association for Mass Communication of the IAMCR in Madrid in 2019. Three scholarly papers have so far been published in English and two in Chinese. Two other papers are under review in English and two in Chinese. A contract was secured to publish a monograph and work began but was suspended due to difficulties arising first from the political situation in China and then from the global public health situation. These events made meetings of the research team impossible. The research team will review the possibility of resuming work when the situation improves but since the research team is now disbanded and widely scattered it may not be possible to complete this effort. 5. An interim dissemination workshop involving scholars from HK, the mainland, and the USA was organised, but the developing political and health situations has made any additional meetings unrealistic. 6. It has so far proved impossible to realise online presentation of the data. Concerns with the sensitivity of the interview data were eventually judged to be too serious to allow it to be placed in the public domain. Discussions continue with regard to the possibility of placing the results of the content analysis online.

12605317.label: Major findings and research outcome
12605317.value: The major findings of the project, which are detailed in the major publications, are as follows: 1. That the collapse in advertising funding has provoked a major crisis for the mainland printed press. 2. In response to this crisis, titles have been obliged to seek new sources of revenue. 3. Various aspects of the state machine have become more important sources of revenue, reverting to something similar to the situation prevailing before the phasing out of subsidies after 1992, 4. As a consequence the internal organization of many titles has been reworked to bring journalists into closer contact with the commercial operations of the newspapers, and to oblige them to (a) work directly to raise revenues (b) to produce "service" editorial copy rather than "public" information. 5. The party press have been revived and are emerging as the dominant force in the new media ecology, at the expense of the more commercial titles. 6. The shift towards online dissemination of news has resulted in some changes in the ways in which news has been presented but the substance of journalistic work remains surprisingly constant. Details of these findings are expanded upon in the various published papers arising from the project.

12605317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12605317.value: Since the research team is now disbanded, and the principal investigator is no longer employed in HK, there is very little probability of the work being directly extended. The more general questions raised by the findings, however, do perhaps provide the basis for ongoing research projects undertaken by other researchers. It is extremely unlikely that the underlying economic problems of the press (and increasingly broadcasting) will go away, and indeed are likely to intensify. One obvious question to pursue would be to investigate which kinds of news media, and which journalistic practices, survive the inevtiable reduction of the size of the industry. Another important line of investigation is into the ways in which online journalism differs from that practiced in the past. As we showed, so far these changes have been relatively small, but that situation may alter and it will need careful analysis.

12605317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12605317.value: The major economic crisis for the newspaper press caused by the migration of advertising online has had some major effects upon mainland Chinese journalism. Newspapers have been forced to look for new sources of revenue and to identify new ways of serving their declining audiences. In the Chinese context, this has meant an erosion of the distinction between the news gathering and the commercial aspects of the press. Internal reorganizations have meant that many journalists are now expected not only to produce journalistic material but also to sell advertising, with inevitably bad consequences for editorial independence. News organisations are also re-orienting their reporting away from news reporting of public affairs towards providing service, preferably commercial services, for consumers. At the same time, the fact that the CP is the major source of this new income stream means that the party press, in decline for 30 years, is now prospering and the commercially press is in trouble. The consequences of this are a decline in critical forms of journalism.

12605417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12605417.value: 「瓷相」在照片歷史學的國際討論鮮有提及，本研究計劃識別「瓷相」在中華文化中物質文明和工藝歷史。 瓷相製作方法於現今數碼世代相對「過時」，當中結合多種攝影及版畫製作工藝，包括以紅礬顯影、轉寫（即「移印」）、上粉、高溫燒製定影等，把影像在瓷板上作永久保存。瓷相在中華文化中的應用主要製作黑白肖像，滲透中國文化中的生與死。在墓碑、祭壇、祠堂出現的瓷相以紀念先人為主，而在慈善團體、公共紀念碑及宗親會的瓷相則為捐款者之功德流芳萬世。 本研究計劃以自1950年代中期瓷相在中華文化的應用出發，並討論在數碼影像技術出現後瓷相工藝無以為計的困境。計劃以三個階段進行：第一階段將在香港、深圳、廣州及景德鎮進行田野觀察、探討自二十世紀中葉後瓷相製作工藝及工匠的歷史發展。第二階段將為瓷相作影像活性測試（PAT）、照片穩定測試及照片鑑証識別瓷相的文化特質、物質文明及工藝特性，測試結果有助研究員把瓷相在照片歷史學中作適當分類及識別。第三階段為瓷相的創意應用，以藝術實踐研究方法，探索陶瓷及攝影兩種視覺藝術媒界的可能性及創造潛力。 研究計劃所收集的經驗知識及創意實踐將會在照片歷史學及物質文明的學術期刊出版，並於社交媒體及學術研究網絡中發表。研究成果與學術界、視覺藝術界及社會大眾對話，以展示視覺藝術實踐主導研究方法的多樣性。

12605417.label: Realisation of objectives
12605417.value: The five project objectives, after revision, are addressed and largely achieved. Due to my appointment as the BA (Hons) Visual Arts Programme Director (2017-2020), then COVID outbreak and the Pandemic (since 2019-), fieldwork in China were unfortunately postponed then cancelled. Without the fieldwork in China, several project objectives and research outcomes could not be realised to their full capacities and made public presentation. In what follows, the five project objectives are assessed and addressed, 1 identify key attributes and cultural uniqueness of porcelain photo and its creation through an examination of materials, techniques and material culture; Key attributes and material culture of porcelain photo in the Chinese context are identified and presented in five peer-reviewed scholarly conferences to both Chinese speaking and English speaking audiences in Asia and Europe during the research period. The peer-reviewed book chapter is served as a conclusive statement of the material culture of porcelain photo in the Chinese context, titled (Accepted) ‘Portrait on China: Porcelain Portrait and Photoceramic in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries Chinese Context’ in Lyce JANKOWSKI and Alice BIANCHI (eds), The Social Lives of Chinese Objects, UK: London, Brill (European Studies in Asian Art and Archaeology series in partnership with the European Association for Asian Art and Archaeology), Expected Spring 2022. 2 examine cultural rituals related to porcelain photo in the twentieth century Chinese context; Cultural rituals, in particular funerary practice in China, related to porcelain photo is addressed, examined and presented in a peer-reviewed scholarly presentation titled ‘Image to Worship: Ancestral Portrait Painting and Funerary Portrait on Porcelain from Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) to 21st Century China’ in Visual and Material Culture in the Early Modern Period Workshop, School of Culture and Society, Aarhus University, Denmark, December 12-13, 2018. 3 delineate the historical development and migration of skills and artisans of porcelain photo making through field research across four Chinese cities; The research on historical development and migration of skills and artisans of porcelain photo making in Chinese cities are addressed and realised based on fieldwork in Hong Kong, Macau and Guangzhou, which is addressed and realised in the aforementioned conference presentations and a scholarly book chapter. However, fieldwork in Shanghai and most importantly Jingdezhen is not yet completed due to the constraints listed above. Instead of conducting first-hand field research, I rely on primary research material from libraries. The PI has to confess that not being able to conduct first-hand research in Shanghai and Jingdezhen does create hurdles to the completion of the project for this objective. 4 produce written scholarly research to articulate the cultural and technical uniqueness of porcelain photos in the discourse and history of photograph; The scholarly book chapter titled (Accepted) ‘Portrait on China: Porcelain Portrait and Photoceramic in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries Chinese Context’ in Lyce JANKOWSKI and Alice BIANCHI (eds), The Social Lives of Chinese Objects, UK: London, Brill, Expected Spring 2022 fulfils this project objective. 5 create studio-based research practice of porcelain photo making and disseminate research outcomes in open-access web-based research portal. The studio-based research practice, an educational toolkit on the making of photo porcelain, has been created and yet with the social distancing measure in Hong Kong, the dissemination is limited. The PI is also actively discussing alternative ways of dissemination and collaboration, that is, to contribute the creative output and scholarly research to the Things that Talk platform (https://thingsthattalk.net/) administered by the University of Leiden, the Netherlands in the near future. And yet at the time being, the PI has to confess that the works are being done but not yet disseminated to the public, in-person and/or virtually. As such, 30% of the project funding is unspent and returned to UGC.

12605417.label: Major findings and research outcome
12605417.value: The major research finding of the project is photoceramic was invented by French photographer Lafon de Camarsac in 1855. The technique of photoceramics and its vernacular application gradually spreads to other European countries, North America, South America and the Far East. Often in form of portraiture, the technique and knowledge of photoceramic making arrived at Chinese treaty ports such as Shanghai, Guangdong and Hong Kong in the late nineteenth to early twentieth centuries, and was extensively employed for ancestral, memorial and commemorative portraits in both private and public spheres. The French origin of photoceramic and historical development of photoceramics in twentieth-century China influence and inform ‘pasted portrait,’ a hybrid form of combining painting and photography in portrait making on porcelain plate that highlights the aesthetic and vernacularity of photoceramics in Chinese society and how the introduction of photography in China influenced the Chinese portrait painting tradition. For a list of research outcomes, please refer to Part C. Five peer-reviewed conference presentations, a peer-reviewed scholarly book chapter and an educational toolkit on porcelain photo-making are produced during the research period as research outcome.

12605417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12605417.value: The future development of this research project will focus on the creative application and its dissemination. Fieldwork to Jingdezhen, when the situation permits and travel restriction loosens, will elevate the understanding and depth of knowledge and technique of porcelain photo making in the Chinese context. The documentation of fieldwork in Jingdezhen, Hong Kong and Macau will provide invaluable research material in the material culture of the subject matter. Collaboration with the Things that Talk platform (https://thingsthattalk.net/) administered by the University of Leiden, the Netherlands is initiated yet it is subject to the readiness of material from Jingdezhen. This will be the next course of action in the post-Pandemic time.

12605417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12605417.value: Porcelain photo making, its material culture, and its roles in funerary rituals in the Chinese context have been an under-researched subjects. This research project addresses the importance of porcelain photo in social-cultural rituals in the 20th Century Chinese context by demonstrating its historical importance and uniqueness, as well as the beliefs of immortality of a photo-object, which could be considered the first attempt in the subject matter in the Chinese context informed by rigours scholarly research. Five conference presentations and a scholarly book chapter in an edited volume specialised in Chinese material culture are published. The project also produces artistic artefacts, an educational toolkit, aiming at promoting the making and cultural-unique technique of porcelain photo, and will publish the results on an international collaborative platform in global material culture as the future and sustainable development of the project.

12606017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12606017.value: The major objective of this project is to undertake a thorough study of the custom of chongfeng huazhu 重逢花燭 from the eighteenth century to the mid-twentieth century in China. Huazhu refers to the decorative candles used for traditional weddings. Chongfeng huazhu basically means to light up the wedding candles once again. According to the chongfeng huazhu practice, long-lived couples were asked to run another wedding to celebrate their sixtieth anniversary. With the help of their offspring and family members, old couples put on the traditional wedding costumes once again, and re-performed every part of their original wedding ceremony, including setting up the fancy candles in the bridal chamber. Chongfeng huazhu is also known as chongxie huazhu 重諧花燭, chongxing huazhu 重行花燭, and chongyuan huazhu 重圓花燭. A period of sixty years is considered as a complete cycle in Chinese history, honoring the sexagenary system formed by ten heavenly stems (tiangan 天干) and twelve earthly branches (dizhi 地支). As the ten heavenly stems and the twelve earthly branches have made up sixty terms to reckon time, one cycle of sixty years is completed in the sense that starting from the sixty-first year the stem-branch labels will be repeating. As human lifespan was much shorter in previous centuries, one would have found it a true blessing if one lived long enough to celebrate the sixtieth birthday. Therefore, sixty years of age is beautifully termed as huajia (花甲). However, further luck is necessary for a pair of husband and wife to live long enough to celebrate their sixty years of marriage, meaning that both of them would have to be at least seventy some years old. As such, cases of chongfeng huazhu were rare and if that happened, people found it extremely justified to celebrate. It is commonly perceived that the idea of wedding anniversary celebration is imported from the West. This project, first of its kind, will challenge the assumption that China herself had not developed any wedding anniversary celebration prior to the twentieth-century worldwide popularity of such activities. Chongfeng huazhu is basically a Chinese version of what we understood as a diamond wedding anniversary in the West. This project will provide a comprehensive account of its origins, development, and impact on both the private and public spheres. 本計劃旨在研究十八至二十世紀中葉之“重逢花燭”習俗。“重逢花燭”指重新燃點花燭，再次舉行婚禮；又稱“重諧花燭”、“重行花燭”或“重圓花燭”。 六十年為花甲一周，對古人而言，人生六十已沾福澤，如果一對夫婦能同偕白首六十載，就更加難得。因此成婚六十年往往得到家人、友朋及鄉里熱烈祝賀，可謂羡煞旁人。由於“重逢花燭”的主角起碼年過七十古稀，有幸經歷六十載婚姻的夫婦始終只在少數，這就令人愈益覺得這是必須大事慶祝的喜事，這項習俗由此形成。 或曰慶祝結婚周年為西方文明產物。本計劃將徵引大量原始材料，挑戰中國於二十世紀前並無近似慶祝習俗之説法。其次，“重逢花燭”可否被視爲中國版鑽婚，亦饒有趣味，值得仔細討論。整體而言，本計劃將就“重逢花燭”一習俗之起源、發展及其在公、私領域上之意義，作一通盤研究。

12606517.value: 贏得“第二次機會”：產前基因檢測，個人選擇和國家前途

12606517.label: Project Objectives
12606517.value: To understand Chinese state’s policy of raising population quality through the commercial implementation of biomedical genomics To reveal the impact of two-child policy in two selected Chinese cities To investigate the application of prenatal genetic testing in two contemporary Chinese cities To differentiate authoritative and folk knowledge and to reveal their reproduction in prenatal genetic testing

12606517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12606517.value: The tension between the quantity and the quality of human reproduction has always been apparent in contemporary China. Such tension is created by two factors: first, the state’s extremely visible and powerful control over and penetration into the private space of individual families, and second, the promotion of “healthy births” through the market but with strict regulations and interventions whenever the state feels it is necessary. At the end of 2015, China officially ended its one-child policy and replaced it with a two-child policy. However, the new population control policy may encourage more women over age 35 to have their second child and cause an abrupt increase in the rate of birth defects. Prenatal genetic testing has therefore become a critical site for the state to “control population growth and improve population quality.” The overall objective of this project is to understand the knowledge, power, and agency in relation to China’s two-child policy. It focuses on the tension arising from the encounters among the state, the formation and upsurge of a commercial market for prenatal genetic testing, and the shifting interpretations of “life” among the expectant parents. Based on our former research experience and our preliminary investigations for this project, we find that knowledge production and consumption surrounding “prenatal genetic testing” go beyond the distinction between “normality” and “abnormality.” It is important to differentiate the authoritative biomedical and genomic knowledge and the folk knowledge related to reproductive health. We will explore and reveal (1) how the state, working along with the market, constructs and legitimizes the authoritative knowledge about a “high quality” life, individuals, and populations through biomedicine and genomics; (2) how the expectant parents understand and interpret both the authoritative and the folk knowledge associated with a “high quality” life, individuals, and populations; and (3) how the expectant parents adopt, contend, and incorporate into practice authoritative and folk knowledge in the case of prenatal genetic testing. This is a multi-sited ethnographic research into the knowledge of prenatal genetic testing. It is located at the intersection of anthropology and science studies. Through a 36-month ethnographic research in two Chinese cities — Shanghai and Guiyang, we will conduct interviews with and observations on at least 150 expectant parents of a second child. As the first anthropological study on China’s two-child policy, findings from this project will contribute knowledge to Science and Technology Studies as well as reproductive health policies and services. 在當代中國，人口增長的數量和質量之間一直保持著顯而易見的張力。這種緊張關係是由兩個因素造成的：第一，國家對私人空間和家庭在強力控制的同時進行滲透；第二，在通過市場化手段來鼓勵“優生優育”的同時，國家會在認為必要的時刻對市場進行嚴格的規範和干預。2015年底，中國正式結束了“一孩政策”，並以“二孩政策”取而代之。這一新的人口政策可能會鼓勵更多35歲以上的婦女生育第二個孩子，從而可能會導致出生缺陷率的增加。 因此，產前基因檢測已經成為國家“控制人口數量，提高人口質量”的關鍵。這項研究主要想了解知識、權力和人的主觀能動性與二孩政策之間的關係。其關注點聚焦在國家、市場和父母這三者在面對由於產前基因檢測技術的發展時，對“生命”的解讀所發生的變化，以及他們的解讀之間的碰撞。基於我們此前的研究經驗以及對此項目所進行的初步調查，我們發現圍繞“產前基因檢測”的知識生產和消費超越了“正常”與“異常”的區分。更為重要的是，權威的生物醫學和基因組知識與跟生殖健康有關的民間知識之間有所不同。因此，在這一研究中，我們將探索和揭示：（1）國家是如何與市場一起通過生物醫學和基因組學來構建關於“高質量”生命、個人和人口的權威知識並將其合法化的;（2）父母是如何理解和解釋與之相關的權威及民間知識的;（3）就產前基因檢測而言，父母是如何採納和討論權威和民間知識並將其融入到實踐之中的。本研究將採用多點族民族志的方法來探討產前基因檢測。它位於人類學和科學研究的交叉點。我們將在兩個中國城市 - 上海和貴陽進行36個月的民族志研究，對至少150名將要生育二孩的家長進行採訪和觀察。作為首個針對中國“二孩政策”的人類學研究，該研究將為科學和技術研究以及生殖衛生政策和服務作出貢獻。

12606517.label: Realisation of objectives
12606517.value: The investigators have achieved all four research objectives, despite the unexpected challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. Objective 1: To understand Chinese state’s policy of raising population quality through the commercial implementation of biomedical genomics By reviewing the state and local policies on human reproduction, maternity and infant health, and regulations on the commercial implementation of biomedical genomics, we have created a timeline of the development and change of the State’s overall policy on reproduction technology and attitudes toward population quality control. Empirical data collected from our field observation and interviews provide important evidence on implementations of state and local policies in medical practices, especially how actors from various social domains (patients, geneticists, clinicians, companies, etc.) interpret the policies and improvise their actions by creatively use these policies. Objective 2: To reveal the impact of two-child policy in two selected Chinese cities We conducted a two-year ethnographic study in Shanghai from 2018 to 2020 and a one-year ethnography in Guizhou from 2019 to 2020. The impact of the two-child policy was observed in both cities. Due to the full implementation of a “two-child” policy in China in 2016, women aged above 35, who only had one child under the former “one-child” policy, rushed to have a second child. Many cases that we studied in Shanghai and Guizhou were related to a “second child”. We have also seen expectant parents’ eagerness of having a “healthy” second child. The experts’ reactions toward the “two-child” policy are certainly different. More interestingly, the obstetricians from different medical departments (such as Obstetrics, Fetal Medicine, In vitro fertilization, etc.) interpreted and practiced with the policy in very different ways. These observations were recorded in the manuscript currently being under review. Objective 3: To investigate the application of prenatal genetic testing in two contemporary Chinese cities We took an ethnographic approach to investigate the application of prenatal genetic testing in Shanghai and Guiyang. A team ethnography approach was employed. We formed a research team of five qualitative researchers, including one principal investigator of the project, one archive researcher, and three ethnographers. The fieldwork was very intensive in Shanghai; however, in Guizhou, due to the unexpected challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic, the fieldwork was interrupted after the first six months. After the field site, a hospital in Guizhou, resumed daily operation, we continued our ethnography there. Our partners from the two hospitals fully supported our research. The scope and depth of our investigation into the application of prenatal genetic testing in Shanghai and Guizhou were very comprehensive. Findings from the fieldwork were presented in the manuscript currently being under review. Objective 4: To differentiate authoritative and folk knowledge and to reveal their reproduction in prenatal genetic testing During our fieldwork, we also collaborated with the hospitals working on training sessions provided for genetic counsellors from other hospitals. Our observations on the training sessions and engagement with the counsellors provided us an emic view of how authoritative knowledge was produced within the medical world. We interviewed nearly 100 patients, their families, care experts from clinical and non-clinical settings and we observed more than 100 doctor-patient consultation sessions, all of which helped us understand the difference between authoritative (expert) and folk (layman) knowledge and how they were translated into each other’s language and understood in each other’s way. We found that, the boundaries between these two types of knowledge were truly fluid and unclear, easily shifting from one side to the other. The process of maintaining the boundaries had become a power struggle between the doctors and the patients.

12606517.label: Major findings and research outcome
12606517.value: To promote “Healthy China,” the Chinese government relaxed its decades-long family planning policy, rolling out the two-child policy in 2016. Along with the policy change is the emergence of the discourse of “choice” in facilitating the development of prenatal genetic testing and reducing the risk of birth defects. One major finding of the project is about how the discourse of “choice” has become available in the Chinese clinics and the market (Zhu & Dong, 2018; Zhu & Dong, “Problematizing 'choice’,” under-review). Our ethnographic research shows the complexities of the intertwined forces of the state and the market and how they mutually depend on each other to achieve their respective goals. The commercialization of Non-invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) relies on the Chinese state’s population quality control policies to gain legitimacy in the national health system. Economic interest remains invisible in local clinic settings with the aid of medical paternalism, a hierarchical relationship between doctors and patients as a norm. We further argue that, while choice gradually becomes a powerful and ubiquitous discourse in the field of reproduction nowadays in urban China, such discourse does not initiate a so-called “project of autonomous self.” Rather, we witness that in medical domain, different social actors draw on such discourse to interact with others; people perform “choice” in concrete institutional context to form an interdependent moral relationship and hold others accountable for particular decisions made. In addition, with the commercialization of medical care, the discourse of choice raises ambivalence for both patients and doctors, fracturing the conventional field of medical care. This ambivalent status further provides a ground for the patients to confront and contests the medical authority and for doctors to reflect on their own practices. We also find the efforts paid by medical professionals to “professionalize” and “digitize” their practices of “choice”. In literature, the application of interactive digital decision aids (IDDS) in prenatal screening decision-making is still inadequate (Wong, et al. Dong, “IDDS,” under review). However, during our observation, especially on the training sessions on genetic counselling, the participants had already realized the need to have more professional and technological support to their own daily counselling practices (Dong, et al., Zhu, “Applying and assessing the PEERS model,” under review). The contents and methods of knowledge production and translation within the medical arena and the transference from medical to everyday life therefore are constantly under transformation and need to be further explored.

12606517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12606517.value: After we completed our fieldwork, the Chinese government announced a “third child” policy in May 2021. The discourse of “choice” has been extended to other reproductive technologies, including the Selective Reproductive Technologies (SRTs) and Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ARTs). Such an extension is in line with the Chinese state’s endorsement of a “three-level” prevention and control system for birth defects. Meanwhile an expedited neoliberal shift in governing human reproduction and the commercialization of medical expert knowledge have surfaced as well. To address such new developments, the PI has started preliminary research and submitted another grant application to support further exploration into the topic.

12606517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12606517.value: It seems natural for people to want to have a healthy child. That is why many people choose to use prenatal genetic testing tools to find out whether a foetus is healthy during pregnancy. Our project explores the application of the newest tool of its kind – Non-invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) – in two Chinese cities, Shanghai and Guizhou. This is the first academic attempt to understand the knowledge, power, and autonomy in relation to China’s two-child policy. We particularly focus on the tension arising from the encounters among the state and the upsurge of a commercial market for prenatal testing. We find that, even though NIPT is described as a “choice” for the patients, it is actually not a “choice” at all. Under the pressure of having a perfectly healthy baby, which is also heavily propagated by the state and the market, many Chinese couples have no other “choices" but to pay for NIPT and other prenatal genetic testing tools by themselves, hoping to fulfill the socially constructed need of having healthy babies.

12606717.label: Project Objectives

To explore whether different lexical factors, including semantic transparency, word frequency, word structure, constituent productivity, and morphological boundedness, modulate the storage of Chinese words.

To establish MMN as a valid tool to investigate Chinese language processing.

12606717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12606717.value: In Chinese, character and syllable boundary is much clearer than word boundary. This leads to a debate on whether Chinese words are stored holistically or they are decomposed into the constituent characters and syllables for storage. Previous behavioral experiments that aimed to investigate the issue have produced inconsistent results, some of which are also difficult to interpret because of methodological concerns and uncontrolled confounding factors. Recently, an electrophysiological technique called event-related potential (ERP) recording, which allows monitoring of brain processes with high temporal resolution, has been adopted to investigate the issue of word storage in Indo-European languages. Specifically, holistic and decomposed storage of words have been shown to affect an ERP index called mismatch negativity (MMN) in opposite directions. Therefore, by examining how Chinese words of different properties affect MMN in one or the other direction, it is possible to infer whether the Chinese words are stored holistically or in decomposed forms. Moreover, MMN can be elicited even when participants are not paying attention to the stimuli. MMN is thus typically considered to reflect relatively early language processes that are free from response-bias, which makes it an ideal measure to supplement previous behavioral experiments in Chinese. This proposed study utilizes MMN as a tool to clarify the nature of Chinese word storage. Specifically, five experiments will be conducted to examine how different lexical variables may modulate the balance between holistic and decompositional storage. Affirmative results may help resolve previous discrepancies by identifying potentially uncontrolled confounding factors. The variables tested include 1.) word frequency (high vs. low), 2.) semantic transparency (i.e., whether constituents contribute to word meanings; transparent vs. opaque), 3.) word structure (monomorphemic vs. bimorphemic), 4.) constituent productivity (i.e., how many words can be formed with each constituent; high vs. low), and 5.) morphological boundedness (i.e., whether the constituents can stand alone as individual words; free vs. bound). Results of these experiments will contribute to a better understanding of Chinese word storage and the development of models of Chinese word processing. They also help establish the validity of using MMN to study high level language processing in Chinese, which can be extended to other aspects in future research. 中文的獨特性使學者對中文詞彙如何儲存在腦海中意見分歧, 一說認為中文詞彙是整詞儲存, 另一說則指「詞」要分解成「字」再作儲存, 早期的行為研究結論並不一致, 且多受任務方法和實驗材料質素所限, 難以令人信服。近年, 研究印歐語言的學者發現詞彙的儲存問題, 可以應用事件相關電位(ERP)中的不匹配負向波(MMN)加以探討, 由於MMN在被試的專注力受到干擾時仍然能呈現出來, 使它特別適合研究早期、與專注力無關的自動性語言加工, 也較不受任務策略的影響。 本研究提案旨在進行五個MMN實驗, 以釐清中文詞彙的儲存問題, 每一個實驗負責探討一種詞彙特徵會否影響整詞和分解儲存的平衡, 探討的詞彙特徵包括: 1.) 詞頻 (高與低), 2.) 語義透明度 (透明與不透明), 3.) 構詞結構 (單詞素與雙詞素), 4.) 詞素構詞能力 (高與低), 5.) 詞素種類 (自由與規範)。在理論層面, 此研究的結果將有助理解中文詞彙的儲存, 藉此建立中文詞彙處理的模型, 在方法層面, 此研究亦能證明MMN在中文研究的有用性, 足以在將來的研究廣泛應用。

12606717.label: Realisation of objectives
12606717.value: Four ERP experiments were conducted to investigate whether the storage and processing of Chinese spoken words are holistic or done through combining the constituents. Experiments 1 and 2 tested the processing of disyllabic Chinese words and revealed evidence of holistic storage. However, with an improved experimental design, Experiments 3 and 4 showed that low frequency words and semantically transparent words were decomposed and processed by combining the individual syllables. Evidence for holistic processing was limited to high frequency words and opaque words. Given that Experiments 3 and 4 provided clearer results, they were written into two manuscripts and were submitted to Biological Psychology (titled “Full-form vs. combinatorial processing of Chinese compound words: Evidence from mismatch negativity”) and Neuroscience (titled “Semantic transparency in Chinese compound word processing: Evidence from mismatch negativity). These experiments showed that both holistic and decomposed forms were present in Chinese spoken word processing, which supported fulfillment of Objective 1 “to examine whether the storage of Chinese words is holistic or decompositional” at 100%. The GRF also supported the work of an MPhil student (ZOU Yun), which examined whether monosyllabic Chinese words are mentally represented as a holistic “segment-plus-tone” unit or decompositionally in segments (onset and rime) and tones. An extra Experiment 5 of spoken sentence comprehension was conducted in early 2019, and the results showed that segments and tones have separate representations, which further supported the fulfillment of Objective 1. This experiment was published in Neuropsychologia (titled “The roles of lexical tone and rime during Mandarin sentence comprehension: An event-related potential study”). Achievement of Objective 2 “to explore whether different lexical factors, including semantic transparency, word frequency, word structure, constituent productivity, and morphological boundedness, modulate the storage of Chinese words” was estimated to be 70%. The achievement was lower than 100% because, although Experiments 2, 3, and 4 had been conducted to examine how semantic transparency and word frequency modulate the storage and processing of Chinese words, the experiments for testing word structure, constituent productivity, and morphological boundedness could not be conducted due to the social unrest in late 2019 and the outbreak of COVID-19 in 2020. To be specific, after establishing an experimental protocol that is sensitive enough to examine the effects of different lexical factors (see achievement of Objective 4), one experiment was prepared for testing each of the five factors (i.e., semantic transparency, word frequency, word structure, constituent productivity, and morphological boundedness) that might modulate the storage of Chinese words. These experiments were originally scheduled to be conducted from Oct 2019 to Feb 2020 (after the first request of a 6-month extension of project period to 30 Jun 2020). However, because of the social unrest in late 2019, the university campus was closed from Nov 2019, which prohibited data collection until Jan 2020. Although some additional data could be collected in Jan 2020, the university campus again closed in Feb 2020 due to the outbreak of COVID-19 in Hong Kong. The ERP laboratory reopened in late Mar 2020, but restriction applied that only staffs were allowed to stay in the laboratory. Data collection was practically impossible. In view of this, the PI applied for the second 6-month extension of project period (final project date: 31 Dec 2020). Data collection resumed in Sep 2020. Yet, the process was slow because ERP data collection involved close contact between the experimenter and participants (e.g., when applying electrolytes, putting on equipment, washing hair after experiment), and not many people were willing to participate even when the monetary reward was raised to HK$500 for a three-hour experiment. The team only managed to collect enough ERP data for the experiments that tested word frequency and semantic transparency (Experiments 3 and 4). For the other three experiments (that tested word structure, constituent productivity, and morphological boundedness), the materials and computer programs had been prepared, but the team was unable to collect data (materials are available in Appendix). As a result of this unexpected scenario, the achievement of Objective 2 was below 100%. Currently, the PI is seeking other opportunities to conduct the prepared experiments. To compensate for the slow ERP data collection process, three extra behavioral experiments (Experiments 6-8) that tested written Chinese word storage and processing were conducted. Because ERP data was not collected, each of these experiments could be completed in 15-20 minutes in groups (complying with social distancing policy) in a computer room. These experiments showed that Chinese written words were stored and processed in a decomposed form, which contrasted with Chinese spoken words that both holistic and decomposed forms were present (as shown in Experiments 1-4). A manuscript was prepared based on these behavioral experiments and it had been accepted for publication at The Mental Lexicon (titled “Morphophonological activation in Chinese word recognition: Evidence from heteronymic characters”). The data obtained in Experiments 6-8 allowed the comparison of the ERP results of Chinese spoken word recognition with novel data of Chinese written word recognition. In addition, when the manuscripts reporting Experiments 3 and 4 were prepared, the introduction and discussion also made reference to previous studies on written, inflected, or derived words. Together, these supported the achievement of Objective 3 “to compare the results obtained with spoken, compound words with previous results obtained with written, inflected or derived words” at 85%. The achievement was below 100% because the experiments that tested some factors listed in Objective 2 were not conducted and could not be compared with previous studies. Objective 4 “to establish MMN as a valid tool to investigate Chinese language processing” was achieved at 100%. Indeed, all MMN experiments (Experiments 1-4) showed that MMN was sensitive to language processing. On the other hand, data of Experiments 1 and 2 showed that the original experimental design could detect the differences between real words and non-words (i.e., meaningless combinations of syllables), but it was not sensitive enough to reveal the modulation of different lexical factors like word frequency. The team had tried several modifications and finally established an improved experimental protocol (a reverse-block passive oddball design) that had superior stability and sensitivity over the original design (a simple oddball design). Experiments 3 and 4 (and the other prepared experiments) followed the improved protocol and produced robust results. It was expected that the improved protocol would become the standard for future language research.

12606717.label: Major findings and research outcome
12606717.value: There are 4 major findings of the research project. First, it demonstrated that MMN is a valuable tool in studying Chinese language processing. The research team has also established a standard procedure to make the experimental paradigm sensitive to linguistic factors. This helps future studies to employ a similar experimental design to investigate Chinese processing. Second, it demonstrated that word frequency and semantic transparency would modulate how Chinese spoken words are stored and processed. Specifically, low frequency words and transparent words have their constituents stored separately (i.e., decomposed), while high frequency and opaque words involve both decomposed and holistic storage. Third, it was shown that during spoken sentence comprehension, the segmental information (i.e., syllables) and lexical tone are separately processed, instead of processed as an integrated holistic unit. This contributes to the understanding of tonal language processing. Fourth, it was shown that written Chinese words are processed mainly through combining the decomposed constituents, in contrast to the parallel processing of spoken words in holistic and decomposed forms. Initial findings of Experiments 1, 2, and 5 were presented in oral presentation and poster presentation in The 17th International Conference on the Processing of East Asian Languages held in Taipei (2018). Four manuscripts were also prepared based on the experiments. The manuscript that is related to the third finding (rime and tone processing) has been published in Neuropsychologia (titled “The roles of lexical tone and rime during Mandarin sentence comprehension: An event-related potential study”). This article also formed part of the dissertation of an MPhil student (ZOU Yun). Because of the article published, ZOU Yun obtained three PhD offers in prestige university in US. He has chosen Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at University of Massachusetts Amherst and has begun his study in September 2021. The manuscript that is related to the fourth findings and Experiments 6-8 was submitted to The Mental Lexicon and was accepted in June 2021. It is now in the publication process. The other two manuscripts are related to the effects of word frequency and semantic transparency (Experiments 3 and 4). They were submitted to Biological Psychology (titled “Full-form vs. combinatorial processing of Chinese compound words: Evidence from mismatch negativity”) and Neuroscience (titled “Semantic transparency in Chinese compound word processing: Evidence from mismatch negativity), respectively.

12606717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12606717.value: The research team has established a set of standard procedure of triggering MMN in language processing experiment. The procedure ensures high sensitivity to linguistic factors and will be useful guideline in future experiments that use MMN to examine other aspects of Chinese language processing. Because of the social unrest and COVID-19, the research team cannot collect enough data to examine the effects of several factors (word structure, constituent productivity, and morphological boundedness). However, materials and experimental protocol are ready. The PI is seeking resources to conduct these experiments. Moreover, the context of processing (isolated words in Experiments 3 and 4 vs. sentences in Experiment 5) appears to matter. It will be meaningful to further examine the effect of context in the storage and processing of Chinese words.

12606717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12606717.value: In Chinese psycholinguistic research, it is under debate whether Chinese words are stored and processed holistically (“動物-animal” as a whole) or decompositionally (“動-move” and “物-object” combine to form “動物-animal”). Similarly, it is under debate whether the syllable and lexical tone form holistic unit (syllable-plus-tone /dung6/) or are separate (syllable /dong/ + tone /6/). To examine the debates, event-related potential recording (ERP) is used, which allows continuous monitoring of brain activities and provides good sensitivity to cognitive processing. It is hypothesized that the holistic vs. decompositional processing depends on factors like word frequency and semantic transparency (i.e., whether the constituents are related to word meanings or not; English analogue: departure vs. department). In a series of eight experiments, it is shown that low frequency and opaque spoken words are mostly stored and processed in decomposed constituents, while high frequency and transparent words involves both holistic and decompositional processing. In contrast, written Chinese words are mostly processed through combining the constituent characters. Moreover, syllables and lexical tones are separate, instead of forming holistic representations. These findings advance the understanding of Chinese spoken word processing.

12607217.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12607217.value: 改革時代的中國城市基層黨建

12607217.label: Project Objectives
12607217.value: To construct a database of the Chinese Communist Party’s party building endeavors in urban China in the 2000s to document a variety of PPO building strategies and models. To conduct in-depth case studies from four regions of China (Guangdong, Sichuan, Shanghai, Fujian) in order to assess the actual effects of party building and identify the micro processes and causal chains that have led to different development trajectories. To understand how the party state links party building to institutional restructuring efforts and the development of the non-state sector in contemporary China.
rows: To construct a database of the Chinese Communist Party’s party building endeavors in urban China in the 2000s to document a variety of PPO building strategies and models.

To conduct in-depth case studies from four regions of China (Guangdong, Sichuan, Shanghai, Fujian) in order to assess the actual effects of party building and identify the micro processes and causal chains that have led to different development trajectories.
To understand how the party state links party building to institutional restructuring efforts and the development of the non-state sector in contemporary China.

12607217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607217.value: The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP’s) efforts and strategies in regard to grassroots party building in the past decade have been well documented in scholarly literature, but empirical evidence remains scattered and piecemeal. Little is known about the impact of such endeavors. How are various strategies implemented? How effective are they? Are primary party organizations (PPOs) able to accomplish their intended goals and help strengthen the governing capacity of the CCP in urban China? What is the popular perception and reception of these organizations within target populations? These questions regarding the long-term consequences of several waves of grassroots party building in the reform era are as yet unclear. Through systematically surveying and compiling cases of PPO building in urban China, as well as examining the operation conditions of a variety of PPOs in regard to handling concrete tasks such as social stability maintenance and crisis management, this proposed project aims to provide a broad and in-depth evaluation of the actual effects of intensive and extensive grassroots party building endeavors in urban China. With a focus on PPOs, this project also addresses two distinct yet related themes: the party state’s institutional restructuring efforts and the development of the non-state sector. Altogether, they allow us to tell a story of the evolving micro-foundation of urban governance in contemporary China. Two objectives are expected to have been accomplished at the end of this project: First, a database of grassroots party building since 2000 will have been constructed; second, in-depth case studies from four regions of China will have been conducted, in order to assess the actual effects of party building and identify the micro processes and causal chains that have led to different development trajectories. 已有充分的學術文獻記載了關於中國共產黨在基層黨建的努力和策略，但經驗證據仍然分散和零碎，對於這些努力的實際效果我們仍知之甚少。各種策略如何實施？是否有效？基層黨組織能否實現黨對它們的預期目標並加強中共在城市的管治能力？人們如何看待基層黨組織？這些關於改革時代一輪又一輪基層黨建到底長期效果如何的問題，我們暫時還沒有很好的答案。這個研究項目將通過系統測量和彙編中國城市基層黨建案例、並詳細分析各類基層黨組織在執行諸如維護社會穩定和危機管理等實際任務中的表現，來廣泛深入地評估中國城市基層黨建工作的效果，從而觀察中國城市治理的微觀基礎變化。

12607217.label: Realisation of objectives
12607217.value: The project objectives have been largely achieved through field research, digital data collection and archival research. (Objective 1: To construct a database of the Chinese Communist Party’s party building endeavors in urban China in the 2000s to document a variety of PPO building strategies and models.) The PI hired research assistants to compile information from a wide range of online sources to create a digital map of the CCP’s grassroots Party building endeavors in both urban and rural China in the 2000s. The information sources included mainstream Chinese media, official publications by different levels of party organizations, and cases mentioned in scholarly works. The following information was archived: 1) the different levels of official directives regarding grassroots Party building, and 2) the exemplar cases of grassroots Party building in various regions and their background information. (Objective 2: To conduct in-depth case studies from four regions of China (Guangdong, Sichuan, Shanghai, Fujian) in order to assess the actual effects of party building and identify the micro processes and causal chains that have led to different development trajectories. Objective 3: To understand how the party state links party building to institutional restructuring efforts and the development of the non-state sector in contemporary China.) In 2018 and 2019, the PI conducted multiple field trips in Sichuan (May 2018) and Shanghai (August 2018 and August 2019) to investigate grassroots Party building strategies and patterns in these two regions. In each field trip, the PI visited different sites and conducted interviews and focus group discussions with various informants (e.g., the CCP rank-and-file members, Party cadres, NGO staffs, social workers and volunteers, etc.) on grassroots Party building efforts and their impacts. The PI identified the informants with a snow-balling strategy. In some research sites, the PI also conducted participant observations of government meetings, NGO operations and community activities. In 2019, the PI also conducted interviews with some Hong Kong social workers who had been long engaged in building social work profession and grassroots civil society organizations in mainland China. The PI learnt from them their personal experience of getting involved in grassroots Party building in mainland China. Between 2020-2021, the PI did not manage to leave Hong Kong for field trips in mainland China as planned due to the pandemic situation. The PhD student of the PI, who worked on a topic of “public goods provision and grassroots Party building in contemporary China” for his dissertation, however, got stuck in mainland China and could not return to Hong Kong, which was unfortunate for him but good for the research purpose. Under the supervision by the PI, the PhD student conducted interviews and participant observations in multiple sites in rural Guangdong where he was able to establish some local connections. The PhD student helped the PI collect the data in the following aspects: 1) the Primary Party Organizations’ (PPOs) efforts in advancing territorial consolidation and organizational penetration in rural Guangdong; 2) the relationships between the Party organizations and government agencies at the grassroots level of governance; 3) the relationships and interactive dynamics between the PPOs and the various non-state actors such as NGOs, private enterprises, civil groups like volunteer teams and hobby groups, etc.; and 3) the PPOs’ mobilization strategies and disciplinary measures. In addition, the PI designed a survey to examine the university students’ incentives to join the CCP. However, the survey company in mainland China with which the PI had already signed a contract for this project could not carry out its work as the local Bureau of Statistics did not approve the project. According to the contact person from the survey company, the policy for overseas scholars doing research (especially survey) in mainland China had been increasingly tightened, and my research project which would not have been considered politically sensitive in the past was then seen sensitive by the local Bureau of Statistics. Therefore, the PI had to suspend the process. Unfortunately, until the completion of the current project, the PI could not find alternative solutions, but the PI is seeking collaboration with researchers from a Party School to see the possibility of carrying out the survey in the near future. Throughout the project operation, and especially during the process of data collection, the PI trained the research assistants and the PhD student in basic skills for literature review, media/document content analysis, archival research, and research ethics. The PI provided systematic training to the PhD student in the qualitative research skills and ethics (interview, participant observation, focus group, ethnography) which turned out to be fruitful. The PI also encouraged the RAs to identify their own research interest and offered guidance accordingly.

12607217.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607217.value: This research has produced several pieces of research outputs (published in peer-reviewed journals) which have addressed different questions as following: 1) The interactions between local Party cadres in China and Hong Kong social workers in their sense-making of innovation, indigenization, and professionalism. The cadres exert strenuous efforts to reshape social workers’ understanding to ensure that the introduction of new knowledge by this group of professionals conforms to the government’s prior-set objectives and agenda. The dominance of cadres reduces the uncertainty involved in learning and, thus, enhances their receptivity to new knowledge but simultaneously curtails diversity and elasticity in government knowledge absorption, which decreases the prospect of double loop learning. Moreover, the serious power asymmetry between government cadres and social workers (both overseas and local) is reinforced in the knowledge absorption and reproduction processes. 2) Local cadres’ dispersed clientelist endeavors seeking stable collaboration with NGOs. As local cadres increasingly deploy their informal authority in addition to their extensive institutional power, and as informal networks lubricate the policy process, state dominance over society becomes more pervasive, entrenched and fragmented. 3) A distinct type of electoral intervention, “harmonizing intervention,” by the Chinese local state to achieve the goal of securing the joint post of the Village Party Secretary and the Villagers Committee Director. It involves mediating conflicts through electoral interventions and using elections to create harmony. My research finds that through such interventions, the local state simultaneously accomplishes the legitimization, information collection, elite co-optation, and clout demonstration functions of authoritarian elections. “Harmonizing interventions” have obvious power concentration effects and strengthen local state control rather than village self-governance. 4) A practice of Party-led social capital building (PSCB), which provides a Janus-faced mechanism for sustaining confidence in the local Party-state and hence investment in state–society synergy: the Primary Party Organizations (PPOs) cultivate bonding, bridging, and linking social capital to enhance community engagement while deliberately limiting the democratizing potential of this process by selecting vetted nonstate actors to serve as key nodes in the community networks, who are tasked with gathering information, building trust and reciprocity, and influencing public opinion to ensure that mass participation in community affairs produces the results desired by the local Party-state. The state-vetted key players are mobilized and controlled by the grassroots cadres through well-targeted actions, including Party discipline and various carrot-and-stick incentives in the private and tertiary sectors.

12607217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607217.value: The PI is developing a new line of scholarly inquiry which is related to and inspired by this GRF project and the previous ECS project: the impact of pandemic management policies on individual attitudes towards grassroots organizing in China. It will focus on how the pandemic management policies have affected Chinese citizens’ attitudes towards collective action and participation in local governance, trust in different forms of organizations (Party-state agencies vs. spontaneous organizations), and thus change of behaviors in grassroots organizing.
