12607417.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12607417.value: 夾縫中的邊緣人：殖民時代東亞港口城市中的非精英歐洲社群

12607417.label: Project Objectives
12607417.value: To identify the social, cultural and professional characteristics of non-elite European communities in East Asian port cities. To chart the personal and professional networks that connected together East and Southeast Asian port cities. To elucidate debates about the extent and limits of imperial subjecthood and citizenship in the British empire world. To reassess the usefulness of distinguishing between ‘informal’ and ‘formal’ empire through a study of liminal colonial environments and communities. To produce three journal articles that will enrich understandings of East and Southeast Asian social, political and urban history.
rows: To identify the social, cultural and professional characteristics of non-elite European communities in East Asian port cities.
To chart the personal and professional networks that connected together East and Southeast Asian port cities.
To elucidate debates about the extent and limits of imperial subjecthood and citizenship in the British empire world.
To reassess the usefulness of distinguishing between ‘informal’ and ‘formal’ empire through a study of liminal colonial environments and communities.
To produce three journal articles that will enrich understandings of East and Southeast Asian social, political and urban history.

12607417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607417.value: Through a study of the lives of non-elite ‘foreigners’ with connections to the British world this research redefines the contours of late-nineteenth- and twentieth-century East Asian port city communities, while also exploring the private and public institutions that controlled and supported them. In doing so, it examines assumptions about foreignness and Britishness, categories which were often determined as much by cultural sensibilities as by bona fide credentials. As this research shows, many marginal Europeans in East Asia were not ‘foreign’ at all, but rather had deep, multi-generational roots in the communities of Asian port cities. However, their cosmopolitan connections called into question their Britishness in the eyes of colonial authorities. This project will, therefore, contribute to historical understandings of imperial subjecthood by highlighting the ambivalences in imperial rhetoric and policy that emerged in the pluralistic environment of the port city. As places that bridged the maritime world and the coastal hinterlands, port cities attracted mobile and multi-national populations. This project will emphasise the social interconnectedness of East and Southeast Asian port cities by charting the webs of professional, family and social connections that enabled non-elite Europeans to move between different colonial hubs. Yet, in addition to fostering cross-cultural connections, the liminal character of port cities meant that they could also be perceived as a threat to colonial stability, acting as gateways through which illegal goods, disease and ‘undesirables’ could enter. Marginal European communities, which elites associated with crime, poverty and the transgression of racial boundaries, were often perceived as a threat to colonial order. This project will produce three journal articles, each of which will explore a distinct facet of non-elite European communities: 1. The mobility of non-elite Europeans and the international networks of family, friends, work and education that enabled these movements; 2. The perceived criminality of marginal Europeans and the attempts of colonial and treaty-port authorities to restrain these illicit activities; 3. Public and private philanthropic initiatives to provide aid to destitute Europeans and thereby enhance the status of foreign communities. Non-elite Europeans were the most visible group of sojourners and settlers in East Asia’s port cities, yet their stories have so far been overshadowed by the aristocratic and middle-class projects of conquest, colonial governance and business in Asia. Overall, this project questions the continuing preoccupation of historical biography with ‘great’ men and women by emphasising the importance of marginal people to shaping the social character of the British empire world. 本研究透過探討大英帝國網絡下一眾精英階層以外的「他者」的生命歷程，以及與他們相關的私人與公共組織，重新勾劃19世紀末至20世紀東亞港口城市的社區面貌。「他者」們的「外來性」和「英國性」除了源於自身的實際身份，更取決於他們的文化意識。然而，大量歐洲人的祖先早在東亞港口城市落地生根。這歐洲社群入鄉隨俗，在當地建立了龐大人際網絡，不再是純粹的「他者」，由是被當地的殖民政府質疑他們的英國性。因此，本研究強調帝國修辭和殖民管治在多元文化的港口城市中的矛盾與差異，重新詮釋帝國主體身份。 此外，本研究藉討論精英階層以外的專業人士、家族與社群得以穿梭於各殖民港口的人際網絡，闡述東亞與東南亞港口城市的互聯關係。港口城市連接內陸地區與海洋世界，是各國人口流動和聚集地。它一方面促成了跨文化交流，但另一方面讓非法貨品、疾病和「不法分子」得以進入社區。而且，邊緣歐裔族群大多牽涉罪案、貧窮與種族衝突。這些狀況均威脅了殖民政府的管治秩序。因此，本研究籍強調邊緣族群對建構大英帝國的社會特徵的重要性，重新檢視史學傳記對「偉人」先入為主的觀點。

12607417.label: Realisation of objectives
12607417.value: The PI, with the assistance of an RA during the initial stages of the project, has mostly achieved the project objectives through the collection and consultation of thousands of pages of archival materials. This work has enabled the PI to produce research which at once makes a significant conceptual contribution to the field of colonial history and is richly empirical. Together, the research outputs give voice to the thousands of non-elite Europeans in the colonial port cities of East Asia, who are usually excluded from the historical record. By elucidating the contours of non-elite settler communities and official efforts to support and control them, this research establishes marginal ‘foreigners’ as an important historical force on the China coast and beyond. Objective #5 anticipated that the PI would ‘produce three journal articles that will enrich understandings of East and Southeast Asian social, political and urban history.’ In service of this objective, to date the PI has produced three major outputs resulting directly from this research project, targeted at leading journals in the field of colonial history; an article (12,300 words) currently under review at the Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History; a second article (9,000 words), which has been prepared for inclusion in a special issue in Itinerario; and a journal special issue co-edited by the PI targeted at Itinerario. After an initial positive response from the target journal, Itinerario, the issue editors and contributors are awaiting the results of a formal review of the special issue proposal before making the final manuscript submission. Due to a pandemic related backlog, this review process is taking significantly longer than anticipated. A third journal article is in preparation and will be submitted for review in Spring 2023 pending the completion of two brief archival research trips, which were postponed due to sustained pandemic travel restrictions. Additionally, the PI has presented the research findings at four international conferences, including three presentations at the Association for Asian Studies annual conference, and two invited talks. Objectives #1-4 promised to make interventions in the history of marginal European settlers and sojourners in the treaty ports of East Asia, bringing in comparative material from Hong Kong and the Straits Settlements. Besides investigating the socio-economic contours of marginal communities on the edges of empire and charting the cross-colonial journeys of non-elite settlers and sojourners, these objectives promised to elucidate important conceptual questions, such as the utility of distinguishing between ‘formal’ and ‘informal’ empire and the significance of debates about Britishness on the colonial periphery. These objectives have been thoroughly addressed in the research outputs produced from this project. The first journal article, currently under review at the Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History, demonstrates how distinctive forms of child welfare work emerged on the colonial periphery, where the colonial state was remote and ‘cosmopolitan’ forms of colonialism prevailed. This article contends that a perception of childhood itinerancy as culturally and politically dangerous increasingly shaped approaches to settler child welfare, which often sought to support children and families to become productive members of the International Settlement’s foreign communities. A second article on crime and criminality among European settlers, which has been prepared for submission to a journal special issue co-edited by the PI on marginal and understudied communities in East and Southeast Asian port cities, demonstrates how, contrary to the prevailing assumption that foreigners could act with impunity in the extraterritorialised environments of the treaty ports, consular authorities on the China coast saw managing the misbehaviour of Europeans and Americans as crucial to maintaining colonial social order and political prestige. A third article in preparation, progress on which was delayed due to pandemic-related restrictions, demonstrates how distinctive types of regional and multi-nodal mobility emerged among marginal settlers on the edges of empire. This mobility was embedded in patterns of casual work and facilitated by extended family networks which spanned East and Southeast Asian colonial port cities. Challenges to achieving the project objectives During the first half of the project timeline, the project team made good progress, completing two major source acquisition trips to overseas archives. The PI completed a research trip to London, focusing on materials in the UK National Archives, while the RA consulted the records of the International Settlement in the Shanghai Municipal Archives, with the expectation that the PI would be able to follow-up on this work at a later date. From 2020 onwards, however, Hong Kong’s COVID-19 control measures, particularly travel restrictions and extended school closures, obstructed the PI’s ability to fully realise all objectives within the timeframe of the project. Restrictions aimed at discouraging international travel made visiting overseas archives at times impossible, due to flight bans, and always a matter involving significant logistical difficulties and great personal risk. These difficulties were compounded by pandemic-related archives closures and the imposition of severe restrictions on inbound travel in two of the countries, Mainland China and Australia, in which the PI had intended to conduct research. These unforeseen circumstances had an indisputable impact upon the ability of the PI to complete source acquisition trips to Australia, Singapore, and the UK in the second half of the project term and thus conduct the empirical research necessary to fully achieve the original project objectives. As a result of inability to conduct these trips and the cancellation of most in-person conferences in 2020 and 2021, the PI returned an unspent balance of approximately $79,000 to the RGC after the closure of the project account. Despite these setbacks, most of the project objectives were achieved. After initially extending the project duration in anticipation of travel restrictions being lifted, the PI contracted and supervised an independent researcher to undertake archival research for two weeks in London. The resulting materials facilitated the preparation of a journal article on European criminality on the peripheries of empire. At the same time, the PI conducted extensive research using primary source databases, Hong Kong based archives (when pandemic control measures allowed), and partially digitized repositories of materials overseas, such as the historical newspapers available through the Singapore National Archives. While these measures provided sufficient empirical data to write two journal articles and to facilitate the planning of a special issue, the third manuscript on marginal mobility on the peripheries of empire is in preparation and requires further materials. Using alternative funding sources, the PI will undertake brief research trips to Singapore and London to acquire the necessary sources to complete this manuscript, with the aim of submitting it to a journal in late Spring 2023.

12607417.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607417.value: Using a rich collection of archival sources, this project has explored the lives of non-elite Europeans and Americans with connections to the British empire in the treaty ports of China, with additional comparative material from Hong Kong, the Straits Settlements, and Japan. By elucidating the contours of non-elite settler communities in East Asia and official efforts to support and control them, this research establishes marginal ‘foreigners’ as an important historical force on the China coast and beyond. 1. This work centres the colonial periphery as an important site for research on imperial history. Distinctive forms of welfare and police work emerged on the peripheries of empire, where the colonial state was remote and ‘cosmopolitan’ forms of colonialism prevailed (outputs 1 & 2). 2. Non-elite settlers in East Asia exhibited patterns of mobility that were most often regional and cross-colonial in character. Their relocations for reasons of education, family, and work drew upon a network of extended family connections embedded in the port cities of East Asia. This mobility provides a corrective to ‘networked’ treatments of empire, which tend to focus on the long-distance circulations of elite men and women, or else the migrations and organized transportations of colonised subjects (outputs 1-3). 3. Marginal mobility was an increasing source of official anxiety as it placed impoverished people beyond the scope of colonial control and, in the case of children, raised the spectre of a decracinated generation of itinerant settlers who lacked proper national, imperial, and cultural loyalties. Accordingly, colonial elites sought to control this mobility through child and family welfare initiatives, the provision of education, and the criminal prosecutions of ‘vagrants.’ Paradoxically, however, colonial and consular authorities in part propelled these circulations through systems of transcolonial deportation (outputs 1-3). 4. Settler children and youth were a locus of colonial anxiety about the vitality of foreign communities and political regimes in East Asia. This was pronounced in the port cities of East Asia, where childhood itinerancy placed children beyond the reach of colonial welfare institutions and sometimes demonstrated parental neglect that undermined European claims to moral authority (research output 1) 5. Contrary to the popular belief that ‘white’ men and women were able to misbehave with impunity in the colonial world, this research shows that managing and criminalizing the misbehaviour of Europeans and Americans was seen as crucial to maintaining social order and political authority on the colonial periphery (output 2).

12607417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607417.value: This research highlighted two major directions for further research. 1. Investigating project objective number three, ‘to elucidate debates about the extent and limits of imperial subjecthood and citizenship in the British empire world,’ brought to light the legislative conundrums and complex personal ramifications caused by the uneven implementation of British nationality on the edges of empire. A second GRF-funded project (currently in progress) aims to provide further elucidation on these problems. 2. Secondly, this project highlighted the need for further research in the history of childhood and youth on the peripheries of empire. The PI will plan a research project on childhood cross-colonial journeys, focusing on the experiences and official treatment of children on the move.

12607417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12607417.value: Using a rich collection of archival and newspaper sources, this project gives voice to the thousands of non-elite Europeans in the colonial port cities of East Asia. By elucidating the contours of non-elite settler communities and official efforts to support and control them, this research establishes marginal ‘foreigners’ as an important historical force on the China coast and beyond. This research has made several key findings: 1. Non-elite settlers in East Asia exhibited patterns of mobility that were most often regional, cross-colonial, and embedded in the port cities of East Asia, thereby calling into question the oft-used categories of ‘foreigner’ and ‘Chinese’ on the China coast. 2. Poor settler children on the move around the edges of empire were an increasing cause of official concern in the early twentieth century, giving rise to distinctive forms of child welfare work which aimed to prevent childhood itinerancy as well as alleviate poverty. 3. Contrary to the popular belief that ‘white’ men and women were able to misbehave with impunity in the colonial world, this research shows that managing and criminalizing the misbehaviour of Europeans and Americans was seen as crucial to maintaining social order and political authority on the colonial periphery.

12610917.label: Realisation of objectives
12610917.value: To a great extent the project objectives have been achieved. This is largely due to the design of an academically rigorous and effective methodology. This project departs from conventional approaches to calligraphy as a pure and exclusive art form. Conventional studies treat calligraphy as a self-contained art form produced, transmitted and consumed by a small circle of literati elites. Therefore, traditional approach emphasizes the study of Chinese calligraphy’s refined aesthetic taste and skill. In stark contrast, this project broadens the study of calligraphy to a public art form, and contributes to the reconstruction of modern civic culture, where a strong sense of vitality of city life is embodied in the coexistence of humanistic, religious, and local cultures. This project carefully selected various works of publicly displayed calligraphy, and investigated how these works have been transformed from a literati-oriented, elitist form of art with a restricted audience into a more accessible form of visual culture that reaches wider audiences, acts as an appealing type of decoration, and forms an integral part of Hong Kong’s public venues. The study treated Chinese calligraphy as a rejuvenated form of public art in the modern world, which intriguingly constructs social and cultural discourses in wider communities. Unlike the PI’s last GRF project, in which he studied calligraphy in traditional materials and formats (such ink on paper or silk and portable hanging scrolls), and the meanings given to these works within limited literati circles, in this proposed project the PI examined the broader social and cultural implications of 60 calligraphic works that are embedded in public venues around Hong Kong. This specific type of calligraphy exists as engraved couplets and tablets, for example, as signs highlighting the cultural, historical or religious significance of ancestral shrines, schools, charity organisations, public parks, historic sites, temples or Christian churches. Other examples of calligraphic art serve to express vernacular culture in various public venues for daily activities such as shops, restaurants or MTR train stations. The calligraphic works under examination were examined as public art, instead of the products on private display in artists’ studios or circulated among relatively small elite circles that were examined in work by other researchers and the PI’s previous GRF project. In the calligraphic works examined in this project, matters of aesthetic choice are obviously intermingled with consideration for the various functions of public venues and for the social, cultural and historical contexts involved. This research therefore elucidated important aspects of the social and cultural developments that are reflected in these calligraphic works with their specialised formats. As for the methodology of this research, the PI drew on eclectic adaptations of Craig Clunas’s approach to the social history of art, and on Cary Liu’s effective methods for analysing the symbology of buildings. These approaches were combined in an integrated methodology for examining and interpreting the relationships and the synergistic effects between 1) the intrinsic elements of calligraphy (i.e., the relationships between the literary contents and the aesthetic or stylistic choices), 2) the architectural symbology (i.e., the interpretation of the systems of symbols used, including the integral elements of calligraphy, decoration, name, numerology, geomancy, ritual layout and design models) and 3) the social and cultural contexts involved in the production of the calligraphic works under examination. Calligraphic works embedded in the public venues of Hong Kong will be analysed, compared and interpreted with reference to the PI’s newly developed methodological framework. This framework was applied to examine five major elements of calligraphic expression, namely 1) village clan culture, 2) charitable and civic culture, 3) revolutionary culture, 4) pluralistic religious culture and 5) vernacular culture. Moreover, field trips to various sites were taken to conduct on-site investigations of the physical conditions of the calligraphic works. Textual and pictorial research materials were collected, analysed, interpreted and used to form pertinent archives. To a great extent the project objectives have been achieved through the major research outputs, including 2 academic papers for presentation at international conferences, a journal article and a book manuscript titled “Geocalligraphy: Publicly-Emplaced-Calligraphy in Hong Kong as Discourse about the City,” submitted to Asia Center Publications Program, Harvard University Asia Center, under review. Lastly, through a mobile application, the new knowledge can be widely accessed to inform and educate many people, transforming their way to perceive culture and life in Hong Kong. On the other hand, the GPS-enabled interactive map can guide users to locate and visit places embedded with calligraphy. With high-quality photos and relevant textual information related to the background and significance of calligraphic works, the mobile application contributes to inspire the app users to explore and immerse themselves in the cultural landscapes in an engaging, experiential way, which could become a strongly appealing item of attraction that favours the future development of cultural tourism for both local and international communities. This mobile app included 524 works of Chinese calligraphy (total images: 1387) in various public venues in Hong Kong. Sorted into 5 main categories: i) village clan culture, ii) charitable and civic culture, iii) pluralistic religious culture, iv) revolutionary culture, and v) vernacular culture, the app additionally offers 10 ‘Recommended Itineraries of Appreciating Public Calligraphy’ :1.) One-day cultural and calligraphy tour of New Territories Clans, 2.) Chinese calligraphy in Tung Wah, 3.) Traditional Chinese temple trip, 4.) Protestantism pilgrimage, 5.) Dr Sun Yat-sen Historical Trail, 6.) ‘King of Kowloon’ graffiti-calligraphy trip, 7.) MTR calligraphy trip, 8.) Kowloon City cuisine and calligraphy journey, 9.) Temple Street night market calligraphy journey, 10.) Neon lights on Nathan Road. This mobile app has great pedagogic value because its design will essentially engage students in multi-domain active learning. On the other hand, it is open to the general public. Hence, the mobile app enhances students’ and the general public’s appreciation and understanding of these important works as artistic, historical and cultural heritage of Hong Kong. In this light, the beneficiaries include the general public, university students and scholars across the fields of digital humanities, visual arts, art history, Chinese language, human geography, the history, culture, sociology of Hong Kong.

12610917.label: Major findings and research outcome
12610917.value: The research moved away from the conventional study in aesthetics of calligraphy, and ventures into social aesthetics to reveal the processes involved in the production and reception of public calligraphy. More specifically, the PI’s new approach of investigating calligraphic works’ wider discursive space, social value and significance in contemporary life and culture offers a new and inspirational paradigm of research that has immense vitality and long-term impact on any future academic research in Chinese art. The PI combined an intrinsic, stylistic sensibility with a broader socially symbolic or cultural semiotics method. This new, integrated method led to the discernment of calligraphy's way of generating meanings, appreciation, sensibility, thoughts and sentiments in a pluralistic public and communal settings in the following 5 major elements of calligraphic expression featured in the 5 chapters of the PI’s book manuscript titled “Geocalligraphy: Publicly-Emplaced-Calligraphy in Hong Kong as Discourse about the City,” submitted to Asia Center Publications Program, Harvard University Asia Center, under review. 1. Village Clan Culture Clan history and culture are an important aspect of identity for the village inhabitants in Hong Kong’s ‘New Territories’. For instance, ancestral achievements in the civil service examinations have been glorified by placing achievement tablets in communal buildings, such as ancestral shrines. Thereby, calligraphy serves as an emblem of familial pride. Many other works express social and cultural ideals pertinent to the development of local customs. Hence, calligraphic works are integral elements of venues used for the performance of rituals or for the traditional practices of ancestral worship, local cults, and weddings. Research on this category of calligraphy will shed light on a broader local cultural legacy that vividly constructs a strong sense of local clan identity. 2. Charitable and Civic Culture The Confucian virtue of benevolent caring and a strong sense of civic culture were identified in calligraphic works displayed by charity organisations formed by community leaders. These works bear witness to the local gentry’s civic participation in altruistic caring for socially disadvantaged groups. 3. Pluralistic Religious Culture Hong Kong’s multifaceted religious culture is embodied in the calligraphy housed in the temples and churches of Buddhists, Daoists, Christians, and followers of other religions. For instance, Rao Zongyi’s calligraphic expression of the Heart Sutra was carved on huge wooden pillars standing on Lantau Island. In contrast, calligraphic expressions of Christian doctrines are inseparable from religious and building rites at the Tao Fong Shan Christian Centre, founded by a Norwegian missionary in 1930. 4. Revolutionary Culture Calligraphic works of major political figures in public venues that reflect revolutionary culture serve to reconstruct the past and express pride in Hong Kong. 5. Vernacular Culture Much more down-to-earth, vernacular calligraphy is embedded in the common aspects of daily life, such as shopping, entertainment, and food. Signs in various styles of Chinese calligraphy are widely used by shops associated with traditional Chinese culture. These signs promote not only the brand names, but also a strong sense of cultural identity.

12610917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12610917.value: This project identified five major elements of calligraphic expression: i) village clan culture, ii) charitable and civic culture, iii) pluralistic religious culture, iv) revolutionary culture, and v) vernacular culture. However, the PI discovered an overwhelming number of additional calligraphic works at other sites that cannot be categorised with these five elements of local culture. Therefore, future research will expand the current project’s scope by identifying and examining more than 150 other calligraphic works that will be categorised according to five other elements of calligraphic expression: 1) educational culture, 2) park culture, 3) festival culture, 4) funerary culture, and 5) alternative modes of expression and cyberspace. The new sites to be examined include parks, schools, festival venues, cemeteries, websites, and social media platforms. Inspiring calligraphic expressions in these sites will signify a wide spectrum of traditional cultures, contemporary thoughts and city life. On the other hand, the invaluable experience of establishing a data archive, designing and developing a mobile app will shed light on the PI’s current GRF application’s proposed development of a website and mobile application for holding online exhibition of other types of calligraphy in Hong Kong. Moreover, item no. 2 listed under 11 (Other Impact) is a creative output that extended the research impact in the form of socially engaged activity that brought the research to wider recipients and communities, suggesting potential future development into an interdisciplinary research that will integrate art-historical research with creative outputs.

12610917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12610917.value: This research made a substantial contribution to the advancement of new knowledge concerning calligraphy’s pivotal role in enriching and shaping Hong Kong’ multifaceted cultural landscapes through the creation of new meaning and symbolism. Its findings pertaining to the formation of local culture and identity will inform and inspire academic and educational developments in the fields of Hong Kong art, Hong Kong studies, cultural studies, sociology, anthropology and any future scholarly researches on local cultures and identities elsewhere. More importantly perhaps, studying Hong Kong’s cultural landscapes is a refreshing way for us – Hong Kong people – to better understand ourselves. The study examined calligraphy in the physical public domain and yielded new or deeper insights into the contextual artistic expression of Hong Kong’s multifaceted socio-cultural development. This offered new perspectives and experiences to Hong Kong people and go a long way towards enhancing our sense of heritage, identity, and belonging particularly among our future generations. This is amenably facilitated by the establishment of research data archive, where original pictorial data and textual materials about calligraphy in public venues in Hong Kong were collected, stored and made available to the public inside and outside Hong Kong, thus contributing to future academic and educational developments.

12611717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12611717.value: In translation and interpreting studies, there is a lack of adequate indicators of learners’ competence levels, which creates great difficulty for systematic assessment. In addition, although translators and interpreters are expected to possess different competences, previous research provides not many measurable differences between the two. Among the different components of translation/interpreting competence, linguistic competence has been regarded as an essential one, yet one whose development has rarely been measured in translator/interpreter training. In this regard, lexical cohesion, which concerns the relatedness of semantic meaning in a text, has been identified as an important indicator of one’s linguistic competence, not only of a foreign language, but also of a native language. Although professional translators and interpreters are supposed to be more resourceful than learners in using lexical cohesive devices, i.e. words in a text tying related meaning together, not many studies have been performed to provide evidence on how and where their use differences of such devices may lie. This project, employing a corpus-based approach, aims to identify the professional developmental path of student translators and interpreters working between Chinese and English, using lexical cohesive devices as an indicator. The study will first develop two learner corpora: a translation one and an interpreting one. The learner corpora include works of learners at the beginning, intermediate, advanced, and semi- professional levels. In addition, two reference corpora will be developed consisting of works of professional translators and interpreters, respectively. Then comparison will be made between learners and professionals on the use of lexical cohesive devices, including reiteration (repetition, synonymy, hyponymy and meronymy) and collocation. The similarity and difference in competence development between student translators and interpreters will be analysed in the aspect of lexical cohesion. The project will contribute to the study of translation/interpreting competence at large. Findings of the study will shed light on the roles of lexical cohesion in differentiating quality levels of translation and interpreting outputs and serve as a basis for further development of quantitative variables applicable to testing and accreditation in translation and interpreting. The learner and reference corpora compiled will become useful resources for investigation of other linguistic features in the works of student translators/interpreters. 在口筆譯研究中，缺少對學生能力水平指標的探索，這對系統性評估造成極大困難。此外，儘管口筆譯員需要具備不同能力，前人研究並未能指出兩者之間足夠的可量化區別。 語言能力是口筆譯能力的基本要素。然而，於口筆譯員的訓練中，語言能力的發展量化卻鮮有量度。在這一方面，詞彙銜接涉及篇章中語義的關連性，已被確認是衡量語言能力（包括母語與外語）的重要指標。儘管職業口筆譯員理應比學生更善於使用詞彙銜接手段（語篇中聯繫相關意思的字眼），有關職業譯員與學生譯員使用詞彙銜接手段方式異同的實證研究卻寥寥無幾。 本項目基於語料庫研究方法，以詞彙銜接手段為指標，旨在了解以中英文為工作語言的學生口筆譯員的能力發展路線。研究將建立兩個學生語料庫（口譯及筆譯），包括不同學習階段學生的譯文（初級、中級、高級和半職業階段）；另將建立兩個對應的參考語料庫（口譯及筆譯），包括職業口筆譯員的譯文。本研究將比較學生與職業譯員詞彙銜接手段的使用，包括復現（同一詞、同義詞、上位詞和概括詞）和搭配；並分析學生口筆譯能力發展在詞彙銜接方面的異同。 本項目將有助於口筆譯能力的研究。研究結果將顯示詞彙銜接的使用如何分辨口筆譯譯文的質量，並有助於發展口筆譯測試和認證的相關量化指標。項目建立的學生口筆譯語料庫和參考語料庫可作為學生口筆譯譯文其他語言特征研究的有用資源。

12611717.label: Realisation of objectives
12611717.value: The project aims to achieve seven objectives, all of which have been fully realised. The general use features and patterns have been identified in the employment of different lexical cohesive devices by student translators and interpreters, and professional translators and interpreters respectively, among which, repetition was found to be a most often employed device by all four groups (Objective 1; Pan & Wang, 2018a; Pan, 2019a, 2019b; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review). A number of lexical cohesive devices, including repetition, synonym, superordinate/collocation, etc. were found to differ significantly between different learners (Objective 2; Pan, 2019b; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review), and also between students and professional translators and interpreters (Objective 3; Pan & Wang, 2018a; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review). In addition, translation and interpreting outputs show different patterns of lexical devices (Objective 4; Pan, 2018; 2019a; 2020b, Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review). The findings mostly fall in line with previous research on the differences between written and spoken languages, but at the same time support the application of reformative tactics recommended for interpreting practices (also see Pan, 2019a, 2020a; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review). The project also provides empirical evidence that leads to possible measurable criteria of lexical competence of student translators and interpreters (Objective 5; Pan, 2019b; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review), and professional translators and interpreters (Objective 6; Pan & Wang, 2018a; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review). In addition, the corpora developed for the project constitute useful resources for further works on student and professional translators and interpreters, as well as a practical reference repository for the teaching and learning of translation and interpreting (Objective 7; Pan, 2018, 2019b, 2020a, 2020b; Pan, Wong, & Wang, under review).

12611717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12611717.value: This project, employing a corpus-based approach, aims to identify the professional developmental path of student translators and interpreters working between Chinese and English, using lexical cohesive devices – words in a text tying related meaning together – as an indicator. The study collected translation and interpreting works of students at different learning stages, as well as professional translators and interpreters. Comparison was made between learners and professionals on the use of lexical cohesive devices. The project identified the general use features and patterns by student translators and interpreters, and professional translators and interpreters respectively. It also identified a number of lexical cohesive devices which differed significantly between different learners, and also between students and professional translators and interpreters. Findings of the study shed light on the study of translation/interpreting competence and serve as a basis for further development of quantitative variables applicable to testing and accreditation in translation and interpreting. The project website (https://sites.google.com/hkbu.edu.hk/cetilc), featuring access to the corpora developed in the project, constitutes valuable resources for investigation of other linguistic features in the works of student translators/interpreters, as well as a practical reference repository for the teaching and learning of translation and interpreting.

12612217.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12612217.value: 專名如何指稱 - 因果描述論是否正確?

12612217.label: Project Objectives
12612217.value: To collect and analyse empirical linguistic data on the use of names, in particular about the initiation, transmission and changes of proper names. To construct a casual theory of proper names and argue for causal descriptivism. To reflect on methods used in philosophy.
rows: To collect and analyse empirical linguistic data on the use of names, in particular about the initiation, transmission and changes of proper names.
To construct a casual theory of proper names and argue for causal descriptivism.
To reflect on methods used in philosophy.

12612217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12612217.value: In philosophy of names, most studies focus on the question of to what a proper name refers rather than how it refers. The what-question centres on reference determination – whether the semantic function of a name is exhausted by its having a bearer, or that something else, such as sense or descriptions, are responsible for its semantic behaviours. The how-question asks about intentionality, namely how a term comes to be associated with an object and be about it. It probes whether reference-determining processes are purely causal or some normative elements are involved. The usual strategy is to take care of the former but leave the latter unanswered. This project fills the research niche by working backward to examine the latter and use the result to challenge the dominant view of the former. The eventual aim is to motivate a causal descriptive theory of names against the current orthodoxy of direct referentialism. To achieve the aims, this research adopts two methodologies. First, it employs the traditional method of philosophical argumentation, literature review, conceptual analysis, etc. to clarify, refute and establish philosophical theses. Second, it sets up empirical research to: (i) gather linguistic data about reference shifts and other anomalous uses of names; and (ii) detect and vindicate our complex intuition to correct name uses. It is relatively unusual for philosophers to employ empirical research in philosophical enquiry. However, empirical data are relevant here because the research concerns how the mind actually works, particularly on a collective level involving the institution of language. Literature in linguistics, psychology and cognitive sciences will be consulted. Cases and stories will be invited in open formats. A survey questionnaire will also be designed and circulated to examine people’s linguistic intuitions and cross-test them across geographical and cultural factors. It is expected that the outcome would be more varied and complex than it is thought to be. A hybrid model will be built to accommodate the results. This project will argue how both causal and descriptive elements are present and necessary at every stage of a name-use practice, including initiation and transmission. Descriptive elements play essential roles in the individuation of names and constitute normative criteria for correct name use. Hence, their roles are semantic, rather than merely meta-semantic. The usual distinctions between semantics and meta-semantics and reference-fixing versus meaning-giving are challenged. Causal descriptivism, in being a viable account for the how-question, is also a viable option for the what-question. 當代有關專名的哲學討論, 一般都把焦點設定於專名指稱什麼, 而非專名如何指稱。「指稱什麼」的問題中心是專名的語意由它擁有指稱對象這事實所完全涵蓋, 抑或其語意表現也需由意涵或相關聯的摹狀詞來解釋。「如何指稱」的問題則與意向性有關, 追問名詞如何與個別對象連結起來, 指稱的決定是否只牽涉因果關係, 還是必須介入一些規範性的元素。一般策略是先解決「什麼」的問題, 而忽視「如何」的問題。本項目填補這個研究漏洞, 認為從探索後者, 反過來會協助解決前者, 並且可能挑戰有關前者的主流意見。本項目即期望透過建構因果描述論, 挑戰目前主流的直接指稱論。 這項目採納兩種研究方法來達成以上目的。首先, 它採取傳統的哲學論辯方法, 包括文獻回顧、概念分析等, 來議論及建立哲學論旨。其次, 它進行經驗研究, 目的在: (1)搜集指稱轉移及其他有關專名的不正常使用的語言學資料, (2)偵測及組織關於名稱的正確使用的複雜的語言直覺, 最後探索什麼哲學論旨最能符合和解釋這些直覺。當今哲學探索中, 一般較少哲學家進行經驗研究; 這項目關注心靈特別是語言作為集體制度的實際運作, 故經驗資料十分重要和相關。此項目探索哲學、語言學、心理學、認知科學的相關文獻, 以開放形式擷取個案和故事, 並使用問卷調查, 研究人們的語言直覺及交叉測試受訪者的地緣和文化背景。預期實際結果將比一般理論構想中的複雜和多變, 需要建構混合方案來容納結果。 此研究將試圖論證, 因果的和描述的因素同時存在於每個名稱使用的階段(包括開始和傳遞), 並成為決定指稱對象的準則。描述的因素在區分名稱和決定正確語言使用上扮演重要功能, 因此, 其角色是語意的, 而非只是後設的。傳統語意與後設語意、固定指稱與給予意義的區分應受到挑戰。因果描述論在回答「如何指稱」問題的同時, 也對「指稱什麼」問題提供了有效答案。

12612817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12612817.value: This research aims to study poetry on post-1997 Hong Kong written in both Chinese and English. It focuses on their representations of Hong Kong as city or urban timespace, and examines their concerns and preoccupations regarding the city. Analyses of the poems will draw out issues of thought and action, subjective emotions and social affect, poetics and politics. The objective of the study is to show how a multi-dimensional and multi-perspectival ‘Hong Kong’ is made visible in the literary imagination. Because both Chinese and English poems will be discussed, a further aim of this study is to offer a bridge between the two languages, often seen and studied as two separate and discrete domains. I will ask questions such as: How can the Hong Kong portrayed in English and Chinese poetry be discussed on the same scholarly platform? How does such a discussion enable their similarities and differences to be apprehended? And how does this discussion help deepen understanding of the creativity of English and Chinese in Hong Kong literature and culture? Hong Kong’s historical and political backgrounds constitute its bilingual reality, which is reflected in representations of the city in English and Chinese poetry. This reality unfortunately leads to what I call a ‘separatist bilingualism’, as there is little contact between works portraying the city written in the two languages, as if Hong Kong existed in two linguistic and cultural universes. In 2014, the Umbrella Movement provided a glimpse at the poetic and interlingual possibilities for bridging this gap. The movement sparked an unprecedented cross-pollination of exchange between the two languages. Publications such as CURA, Drunken Boat and The Margins published Chinese poems about the socio-political situation in Hong Kong translated into English, while the local Hong Kong poetry journal Voice and Verse published English poems about the Umbrella Movement translated into Chinese. This linguistic and cultural exchange demonstrated that there is room and demand for interlingual discussion of poetry written about the city. These two groups of texts emerging from a single historical moment will be the starting point of this study which will expand into a broader investigation of post-1997 poetic perspectives on Hong Kong. 此研究旨在探討以97年後香港為題創作的中英文詩詞。研究集中討論詩詞如何展現香港作為一個城市或「都市時空」（urban timespace）的處境，同時討論詩詞對香港整體走向所流露的關注及思慮。分析將呈現行動與想法之間的矛盾、各種主觀感情、社會情緒，以及詩學與政治之間的關係。是次研究將展示文學創作的想像如何呈現出一個「多面向」（multi-dimensional）、「多角度」（multi-perspectival）的香港。由於中英詩詞皆為研究的對象，此研究亦希望為兩種語言提供一道橋樑，帶動並結合中英詩學的討論，打破過往中英詩詞研究的鴻溝。我亦將提出以下問題：如何在同一學術平台上討論中英詩詞中描述的香港？這項討論將如何幫助我們去理解中英詩詞的異同？又如何令我們加深香港文學及文化裡中英文創作的認識？香港的歷史及政治背景造就了城市的雙語文化，此文化亦可見於中英詩詞中的香港。與此同時，雙語的處境卻造成了我提出的「分離雙語現象」（separatist bilingualism）。以香港為創作主題的中英文學作品往往未有任何交流，猶如香港處於兩個平行的語言及文化世界。然而，2014年的雨傘運動卻提供了一個跨語言及詩學體制的研究機會，並開展了前所未見的雙語交流，有望進一步拉近中英創作的距離。一系列英語刊物，其中包括《CURA》、《Drunken Boat》及《The Margins》等皆出版了講述香港社會政治處境的英譯中文詩詞。同時，香港《聲韻詩刊》也刊登了講述雨傘運動的中譯英文詩詞。此雙語文化交流反映跨語言的詩學討論絕對有發展的空間及需求。兩組同樣討論雨傘運動的中英文學作品將成為是次研究的基礎，並藉此進一步探討97後的詩詞對香港所持有的看法。

12612917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12612917.value: This project will produce the first English-language Commentary on Immanuel Kant’s 1783 book, Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics, including a new, improved translation. The Commentary will scrutinize the Prolegomena’s German text, place its arguments within the context of Kant’s overall philosophical system, and provide a translation that accurately reflects distinctions Kant makes that are not reflected in most English translations of Kant’s writings. Kant wrote the Prolegomena in response to misunderstandings of his 1781 magnum opus, Critique of Pure Reason. He intended it as a simpler explanation of the positions of the larger work. Although Kant claimed to be defending the same conclusions, many interpreters have argued that the Prolegomena marks certain changes in his views. Countless commentaries and studies have been written on the Critique, and on Kant’s various moral writings (especially his Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals and Critique of Practical Reason); yet interpreters rarely examine his Prolegomena in its own right, apart from its relation to the Critique and how it supports claims about Kant’s intellectual development. Given the many complex debates over the proper understanding of Kant’s theoretical philosophy, a close textual study of the Prolegomena is long overdue. The translation will thoroughly revise an older English translation (now in the public domain), with footnotes comparing the new translation to the three translations that are most often used today. Careful attention will be given to preserving distinctions Kant makes that are often conflated in English, such as between “Ding” and “Sache” (both typically translated as “thing”) and between “Object” and “Gegenstand” (both typically translated as “object”). To know what Kant actually wrote, readers of most current translations must consult the German. This project’s new translation will remedy this situation for these and numerous other terminological complexities. The Commentary that accompanies the translation will highlight and seek to clarify numerous debates that are relevant to the Prolegomena’s text. For example, many of Kant’s clearest statements on the relationship between philosophy and mathematics come in the Prolegomena. Thus, he distinguishes the method of philosophy from the method of mathematics: the former is synthetic; the latter, analytic. However, he also says the Prolegomena itself uses an analytic method. How is this different from mathematical analyticity? These passages have been studied in relation to the Critique; but this Commentary will be the first English book to examine them in relation to the whole text of the Prolegomena itself.

12612917.label: Realisation of objectives
12612917.value: In July 2017, when I first received notice that my application for this GRF had been approved, I immediately knew that the first two objectives would be impossible to achieve. That is because the RGC granted only $100,000, which was just a little over 10% of the amount I had requested. My application stated (accurately) that I would need slightly less than a million dollars to complete the Comprehensive Commentary that was originally envisioned as the primary output of this project. The application explicitly stated why I needed so much: the book was to be CO-AUTHORED, and the Senior Research Assistant who was to be hired full time, for three years, was going to serve as the book's CO-AUTHOR. The application's reviewers unanimously expressed strong support for the plan. However, the panel's brief comment, which was meant to explain the rationale for reducing the grant to nearly 1/10 of the originally requested amount, was that the Principle Investigator does not need an assistant to write this book! Obviously, the member of the RGC panel who wrote that comment must not have read my actual application: the person who had agreed to serve as the co-author for this book NEEDS TO EAT; he also needs to pay rent for a place to live; if he chose to sleep on the street, he would not be able to do good research; and these things (food and accommodation) require money! Since the ridiculously reduced amount of the grant was not enough to hire the person who had agreed to be my co-author, he ended up getting another full time job to support himself and his family. Without the help of the planned co-author, I was not in a position to write the commentary, given my other research commitments. Knowing this was the case, I wrote a detailed letter of appeal to the RGC, asking the RGC to reconsider the unprecedentedly large reduction in my grant amount. The RGC took approximately one year to reply to my appeal, but when the reply finally came, there was no evidence that my letter of appeal had even been read. The appeal was simply rejected, without explanation or rationale. Apparently, the RGC does not take appeals seriously. Decisions are final. RGC panel members do not make mistakes. The above situation meant that, once I actually started work on the project, in mid-2018, I knew I would have to do nearly all of the work alone. While I did hire an assistant, and that assistant did make the research I did on Kant's Prolegomena easier in various ways, the RA's level of input to the project was only a tiny fraction of what my planned co-author would have been able to provide. I knew this would be the case, so for the entire duration of the project, my actual objective was not to write a Comprehensive Commentary at all, but rather, to produce several conference papers and/or journal articles / book chapters, as suggested by the third, fourth, and fifth objectives -- the three objectives that were completely fulfilled. I believe the RGC should accept this result as fully acceptable: given the fact that the first two objectives were rendered impossible by the RGC panel's decision to lower my funding to 1/10th of the requested amount, it should be deemed fully acceptable that the PI completed much MORE than 10% of the material that would have gone into the monograph, if funding had been sufficient for the monograph to have been written. That is, the several papers that I did write for this project (detailed below) were closely related to the content that would have become part of the book, had the book been written. Moving forward, I recommend that RGC panels should acknowledge that, in situations where grant amounts are so greatly reduced, the output expected should also be reduced by a similar percentage of the originally requested amount. As explained below, the REAL project objectives--to write 2 to 3 papers about Kant's Prolegomena--were fully realized.

12612917.label: Major findings and research outcome
12612917.value: The most significant finding, in presenting these papers at various conferences and professional lectures, was that the scholarly community would have greatly benefited from having a full-length commentary on Kant's Prolegomena. It is a great shame that this plan did not come to fruition, due to the RGC's mis-reading of my original proposal, its willingness to ignore the explicit advice of the referees regarding the appropriateness of the requested funding amount, and it's unwillingness to take my appeal seriously. More specific findings can be found in the abstracts for the various publications and conference presentations listed below.

12612917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12612917.value: This PI remains interested in writing a full-length commentary on Kant's Prolegomena. However, last year his university's new P/VC misunderstood the way the university's contracts determine employee ages, resulting in the PI's contract being prematurely concluded in mid-2021, two-years earlier than specified in the contract and in the university's official policy guidelines. (The P/VC had decided to solve a financial crisis by discontinuing all extensions of contract beyond age 65; the PI's extension would have brought him to age 65, not age 66 as the P/VC wrongly assumed; sadly, the university refused to correct this error when it was pointed out.) Any further development of this GRF's research will therefore not occur as a UGC-funded project, unless the intended SRA for the project (i.e., the book's intended co-author) eventually gets a full time position at a UGC institution that would give him enough free time to engage in scholarly research once again.

12612917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12612917.value: Understanding the nature of science and how it might develop in the future is one of the most important issues for the well-being of the human race. Kant's Prolegomena tackles this question in a unique way that has never been fully appreciated. Properly understanding his claims would help scholars in many fields to gain a better understanding of the different types of science, of what conditions must be fulfilled in order for science to fulfil its purposes, and in order to avoid the danger of science making claims about matters that go beyond the purview of empirical science. Sadly, the Commentary that would have explained all of this could not be written because the RGC cut the requested funding by 90% and because the PI's university ended his contract under false pretenses.

12613017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12613017.value: This research project aims at completing a book manuscript on the cinematic and other media productions about non-Han ethnic minorities in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) from the 1950s to present. Five draft chapters out of ten are ready, and another 18 months are needed for more research to fill the gaps of the argument, to finish the remaining chapters and to edit the manuscript. The book investigates, with socio-historical contextualization and close textual-visual analysis, how ethnic minorities (which have been classified by the state into 55 nationalities) work within the complex conditions of multiethnic China in its ongoing project of nation-building. Multi-ethnicity can resist the smooth integration of the Chinese state-led system, which is, however, productive to understanding the changing meanings of being Chinese in the modern era. The complicated situation also allows us to seek possibilities for reconfiguring the existing order under the drives for political unification and the impacts of global capitalism. The research critically examines how the state apparatuses appropriate cinema and other media about the ethnic minorities in order to produce the PRC’s designed worlds, values and subjects which are intricately implicated in the processes of nation-building and ecosystem management. However, the multi-ethnic communities who are targeted to be assimilated threaten to topple the system. I reflect on the nature of cinema in terms of the medium’s uniqueness and also its intertwined relations with other media. Being a distinctive genre produced in the PRC, ethnic minority cinema is understood in this project as an integral part of global media culture which can question ethnic-cultural essentialism and Chinese exceptionalism in the world system of the nation-states. The historical transformations of the state ethnic policy, from the legacies of the Qing multinational empire, through the Republic of Five Races and the Soviet model of multinational state-building, to the present depoliticized concept of “diversity in unity”, are scrutinized in order to more thoroughly grasp the mechanisms of ethnic representations and governance. Other than assessing the ideological and aesthetic implications of ethnic minority cinema and inter-medial products, my project studies how the process of modernization monitored by the Chinese state also sets in motion a new conception of liberation and a new desire of the governed to re-appropriate power for themselves. The research also contemplates the possible futures to which angst and crisis in China’s multi-ethnicity may lead.

12613017.label: Realisation of objectives
12613017.value: The book manuscript of 150,000 words on China's ethnic minority cinema has been completed.The book manuscript, first in English on such topic, investigates the convoluted relations between the filmic productions about non-Han ethnic minorities and the project of modern nation-state building in China from the early Republican era of the 1920s through various historical periods of the People’s Republic founded since 1949 to the current authoritarian regime under Xi Jinping at the twenty-first century. It examines how the cinematic depictions of ethnic minorities are tied to the changing meanings of being Chinese under the impacts of political unification throughout the long process of China’s nation-state building project in the global context. The glossy but superficial (moving) ethnic images manufactured and manipulated by the state authorities have penetrated deeply into the Chinese psyche of how an ideal multi-ethnic nation should be like. What is more these representations are entangled with the state policy towards the ethnic minority communities particularly in the aspects of ecological, religious, and biopolitical governance. While adopting the state vocabulary of ethnic minority categories subjected to the visual appropriations by the hegemonic discourse, the book also acknowledges that the peoples, such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongols and Manchus, who are regarded as minority and marginal by modern states, do not necessarily consider themselves as such in their own homeland, a place that has been once a state in its own right. The politics of ethnic cinema, the book argues, is to rethink the assumption of ethnicity and to imagine it as a virtual collectivity of equals that does not yet exist. All the objectives have been achieved.

12613017.label: Major findings and research outcome
12613017.value: The major findings are presented in 6 book chapters as follows: 1 – Offering historical context of Republican China’s craze for ethnic borderlands in the 1930s, this chapter analyzes how the Nationalist state promoted the Northwest development to serve its political conservatism. It focuses on the photographic essays in the Shanghai-based pictorial magazine Liangyou to examine how the images of the northwestern ethnic peoples are integrated. The chapter concludes with a discussion of Zhang Junli’s wartime documentary Long Live the Nations by looking at how ethnic vernacular gestures disrupt their instrumental use for propagating national unity. 2 – The founding years of the PRC have established ethnic minority film as a new genre. Analyzing the major characteristics of China’s ethnic cinema, this chapter discusses how dubbed ethnic musical films function to announce the arrival of a new revolutionary society and the formation of a new multi-ethnic nation. With the Maoist ethnic musical comedy Five Golden Flowers (1959) as the example, it examines how such propagandist genre combines Stalinist musical and Hollywood quality to play to the audiences’ emotions. 3 – This chapter begins with the discussion of how filmmaking constitutes impacts on Inner Mongolia’s ecosystem. Analyzing how different films about Inner Mongolia, especially the works of Mongol directors, engage in ecological politics, this chapter provides a panoramic view of how Chinggis Khan legend has been appropriated by various national cinemas. 4 – Representing Tibetan Buddhism is politically sensitive. It closely analyzes The Serf, the classic film propagating China’s liberation of Tibet, and makes a critical survey of Tibetan Buddhism-related films by Chinese, diasporic Tibetans, and Westerners to understand the roles Tibetan Buddhism plays in these adaptations. Finally, the chapter analyzes the emergence of Pema Tseden-led Tibetan-language cinema. 5 – The first part of this chapter analyzes biopolitical media is an integral part of the surveillance state apparatus and reeducation program in Xinjiang over the Uyghur communities. The second part of the chapter focuses on the Sinicized Hui Muslims who have attempted to merge into the mainstream society but still suffered from oppression. 6 – Non-Han ethnic filmmakers have been facing the assimilation and authenticity pressure in the PRC. This chapter examines how ethnic filmmakers struggle between representing accurately the ethnic reality and pandering the mainstream market tastes. It focuses on Korean Chinese filmmaker Zhang Lu whose border-crossing productions shed light on the discussion of transnationalism and cosmopolitanism in today’s filmmaking.

12613017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12613017.value: The research will be developed into an academic book that may generate further in-depth discussions on China's ethnic minority issues. Once the book manuscript is published, the book launch campaigns can be accompanied with screenings of the related ethnic films and public discussions in order to produce social impacts. Different chapters of the book manuscript can be used as reading materials for organizing related workshops to help participants to understand and discuss China's ethnic issues. The ecological politics discussed in the chapter can be further developed into a new research project to study and analyze the recent situation and development of China's ecological discourses and ecological risks, especially under the campaign of "Ecological Civilization".

12613017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12613017.value: The research project critically examines the visual constructions primarily in the film media (both analogue and digital products) on the ethnic minorities created by Han and non-Han as well as by the state and non-state agencies in order to understand the subtle mechanism of modern Chinese national identity formation in its dynamic relation to the non-Han ethnicity. The less than 10 percent of non-Han ethnic population plays a pivotal role in the construction of modern Chinese nation because of their strategic locations at the regions rich in natural resources and deliberate to military significance, and their political repercussions to China’s own stability, relations with its neighboring countries as well as with the international world. Cinema bears witness to this process of the new nation-building and participates in shaping its ideological representations along the way. The project proposes to develop a notion of global ethnic cinema derived from the experiences of ethnic minorities in China to search for the meanings of how different peoples can live together.

12613117.label: Project Objectives
12613117.value: To investigate how women of different ages experience and deal with their singlehood and creative work in Shanghai; To investigate how the aspirations of women of different ages differ with respect to both their personal and working lives; To compare and synthesize insights gained from 1-2/ for theoretical reflections and policy implications (concerning single populations and creative professionals); To publish three academic articles based on 1-3/; and To use knowledge thus gained for community dissemination and tertiary education.

12613117.label: Realisation of objectives
12613117.value: Two specific developments in our globalized world are of relevance to this project. First, increasingly more people do not subscribe to traditional forms of shared living; they lead a single life, often against stigmatization, inconvenience and discrimination. Second, increasingly more people are attracted to the promises of creative work – autonomy, flexibility, satisfaction – and join the creative workforce, often sacrificing more regulated working hours and stronger job security. Straddling this historical, precarious juncture, this project builds on the PI’s earlier research and a subsequent monograph published in 2019, which covers one particular group of ‘precariat’: single women in Shanghai doing creative work, and their experiences in the often unscrupulous creative work ethos and the (marital) demands of a society configured by Confucian values, heterosexual ideals and global images of womanhood. The proposed project goes further by inserting a perspective largely absent in discussions of precarity: age. It does so by inserting ‘age’ into empirical and theoretical studies on singlehood and creative work. How do women of different ages experience and deal with their singlehood and creative work? What are their survival tactics for the present and their images for the future? In short, how does age impact on precarity? Theoretically, this project fills a research gap by connecting two fields of studies: while studies on the creative class have neglected gender and affective dimensions, studies on single women often privilege the personal and leave behind issues of work. It pushes current debates on precarity beyond the domain of labour towards the domain of life – with its manifestations in different ages. Informed by academic and popular discourses that perceive Chinese populations in distinct generations, the current inquiry focuses on women from three age cohorts: wulinghou, qilinghou and jiulinghou (those born in the 50s, 70s and 90s). The two-year project was designed to investigate the lives of creative work and singlehood of these three sub-groups of single women in Shanghai, focusing on their experiences and survival tactics for the present and their aspirations for the future; to compare and synthesize insights thus gained for theoretical reflection on single women and creative work with specific reference to age and precarity; to publish three academic articles; and to use knowledge thus gained for community dissemination and tertiary education. Shortly after the project started and efforts were made to recruit respondent, the problem of finding single women to talk about aging issues became apparent. While single women born in the 1990s were available and forthcoming, women from the other two age cohorts were more likely to be married and those who remained single seemed to be either invisible, or inaccessible, especially those born in the 1950s. Those rare ones who were known to the PI or his networks of contacts (built up during previous research work in China) often declined invitation to be interviewed. PI will reflect on this particular field experience in connection with possible persistent stigmatization of aging single women in his prospective publications. More immediately, PI reconsidered his project set-up and decided to expand the field from Shanghai to include Beijing, and to relax the comparative paradigm from three clearly-defined age cohorts to how increasing age impacts on issues surrounding single womanhood. In the end, a total of 45 respondents were recruited, aged from 31 (time of interview) to 57 (time of interview), roughly half from Shanghai, half from Beijing. Three rounds of field work were carried out: May – June 2018; February – March 2019; and October – November 2019. In addition to conducting in-depth interviews with the respondents, participant observation was also arranged on sites related to the research themes. The identification of research themes was done in a bottom-up, data-driven manner. After the first round of, primarily sensitizing, interviews were completed, initial analyses were carried out on transcripts prepared from the interviews. They pointed to three major research themes pertinent to these single women’s present and future: retirement plans, cosmetic surgery, and romantic relationship. All respondents indicated their written consent to participate in this inquiry and allowed their real names to be used. PI conducted at least one in-depth semi-structured interview with each respondent (usually about an hour), at the venue(s) preferred by the respondent. PI would typically open the interview with asking them the factual aspects of their (single) lives, followed by questions surrounding their present and future with more elaborate probing in any of the three themes relevant to the respondent concerned. Guided by this rough questioning logic, PI stayed alert to their verbal and non-verbal responses and improvised follow-up questions on potentially illuminating but un- or under-articulated points. Insights drawn from the fieldwork are expected to contribute to three journal articles, respectively on the three research themes. Meanwhile, tentative findings from the project were presented at two international conferences: the Inter-Asia Cultural Studies Conference, Siliman University, Dumaguete City, the Philippines (1-3 August 2019, see: https://iacs2019.weebly.com/program.html); and the Cultural Industries in Aging Asia Conference, Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, Seoul, South Korea (19-20 October 2019, see: https://builder.hufs.ac.kr/common/download.action). Furthermore, they were also incorporated to PI’s teaching on gender studies, and a new course (tentatively on gender and aging in Asia) is under preparation accordingly. It was PI’s plan to finish the write-up of the three journal articles (intended for Inter-Asia Cultural Studies, International Journal of Aging Studies, and China Information, to engage in the respective fields of cultural studies, aging studies, and China studies) and submit them in 2020 after the completion of the project proper. However, the global pandemic surrounding Covid-19 disrupted the plan. On the one hand, PI was required to deal with a number of crisis management tasks. On the other hand, and more importantly, PI believes that the current situation may have impact on the research themes he has been preparing, especially regarding retirement and romantic relationship. Therefore, PI decided to reach out to the respondents for an additional round of data collection, asking if they would like to supplement their earlier interviews with the latest development surrounding the pandemic and their lives. This exercise of data collection is still going on. PI expects to complete it by the end of 2020, and re-dates the article submission to 2021.

12613117.label: Major findings and research outcome
12613117.value: The following summarizes the project inquiries, pending insights from latest round of data collection regarding Covid-19 impact. On cosmetic surgery It addresses the question why aging single women in China decide to transform their bodies through operation. Major findings are: -- They show a sense of knowing what they want, and what they absolutely do not want. They perform themselves as someone who think more, and take pride in such “maturity”. -- Cosmetic surgery is also a social and affective endeavour. These single women have elaborate account that is intricately woven with other women, mostly their age peers and single, exuding a strong sense of single sisterhood. -- They are realistic in what they expect from the bodily interventions. This finding challenges dominant assumption that women who opt for cosmetic surgery are victims of the perfection myth. -- They are striving for the better, and they are better, as single women, in contradistinction to their married contemporaries who have lost the drive to look better. On retirement It seeks to understand Chinese single women’s retirement experience and imagination in the specific context of personal and professional precarity. Major findings are: -- “Financial freedom” is the key term used by the aging single women when they talk about retirement. However, such freedom remains a fantasy for some. -- If financial freedom is their imagination of being relieved of practical concerns, these women are also constructing various scenarios of future. They are not only concerned about freedom from worries; they aspire to be free to do their own things (charity work, start-ups, migrating etc) upon retirement. -- While retirement (tuixiu) is the official term used for a certain phase of one’s work life, these single women mostly prefer: yanglao, roughly translated as “nurturing old age”. -- Integrating all the above, the inquiry concludes with a discussion of the politics of (doing) aging. It proposes a new concept “formative aging” to supplement current notions in aging studies (active aging, successful aging, and positive aging). On romantic relationship It investigates how aging single women envisage their romantic life. Initial analysis underlines persistent stigmatization of female singlehood, while aging, at the same time, opens up more possibilities for them to feel immune from such stigma, and to explore relationships they did not hitherto contemplate, notably non-heteronormative forms of relationships, and relationships with younger men. More needs to be teased out from further analysis.

12613117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12613117.value: Building on this research project, PI can envisage a number of follow-up studies. PI will name three of them. 1/. Single men: This project was conceived with PI’s own research background in single womanhood. While aging single women – given these women’s double marginalization as aging and single – is clearly an urgent topic for investigation, PI also wonders how aging single men’s experience would be, particularly in mainland China where aging single men outnumber aging single women (partly) as an aftermath of one-child policy. 2/ Aging married women: While this project was not designed on a comparative basis, many findings do suggest the need to conduct a more systematic investigation comparing two groups of aging women: single and married. Such investigation may illuminate the impact of marriage and/or cohabitation on aging woman’s life, as well as further our understanding of single living. 3/ Longitudinal: This project was essentially probing what the respondents thought at the moment of investigation. What would their life become in, say, five or ten years’ time? In connection with physical beauty, relationship, and retirement? A longitudinal study on the same group of single women would offer more insights on their long-term experiences.

12613117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12613117.value: This project studies a particular group of Chinese women: aging, single, and creative worker. How do women of different ages experience and deal with their singlehood and creative work? What are their survival tactics for the present and their images for the future? How do they deal with precarities associated with their single womanhood, age, and work? Inspired by the narratives of 45 single women aged between 31 and 57, based in Shanghai or Beijing, analyses were conducted along three research themes: cosmetic surgery, retirement plans, and romantic relationship. While these single women may resort to bodily interventions to maintain or enhance their physical appeal, they are never victims of the perfection myth, demonstrating a strong sense of knowing what they do and single sisterhood. Regarding retirement, they aspire to financial freedom, from pragmatic concerns, and to do their own things, underlining refreshing ways to give form to their own aging. Living in a society where marriage remains the norm, aging single women continue to be stigmatized. Nevertheless, their age also empowers them to imagine and engage in new relationships beyond heteronormativity. Taken as a whole, these inquires call for better understanding and care of aging single women.
