13600717.label: Major findings and research outcome
13600717.value: PUBLISHING STRATEGY About half way into the project I wrote a long essay (approx. 13000 words) on Rebecca West’s political liberalism and sent it the Journal of Politics, based at the University of Notre Dame. More precisely, I wrote it expressly for this journal because it has – or had – an ecumenical attitude towards the study of politics; the journal’s editor is also a feminist (as RW was) and an expert on liberalism (which RW was); and it allows long articles. Within two days of sending it, I was informed by the editor that the article was too “literary” to be published in the Journal of Politics, that the journal did not consider RW to be a political thinker; the editor added that she would not send the article out for refereeing. I then tried the University of Chicago Law Review (for which RW had actually written). I received no reply at all, not even an acknowledgment. I was astonished – but chastened. If the most ecumenical political theory journal could see no place for RW, and if a journal that had once published her could not even be bothered to respond to a submission on RW, then this bode-ill for the prospect of academic journal publications. However, RGC wants deliverables and I want publications. And so I hit on a rather different strategy. RW was a public intellectual, not an academic, and so I decided to re-orient publication to audiences broader than academics. Even before making this decision, I had already published a short piece on RW in Quillette; it was tweeted by Jordan Peterson to his 2 million Twitter followers. Later – following the Journal of Politics and University of Chicago Law Review debacles - I followed this up with articles in National Review, TLS, New Criterion and New English Review. (Note that a convention of the first three is not to include acknowledgments or even an email address; hence RGC is not acknowledged. Quillette did allow an acknowledgment, however, and so did New English Review. I have not yet acknowledged RGC in the Thesis Eleven article; to do so, when the article is under review, would compromise the blind reviewing. ) All these pieces, with the exception of the article for the TLS, were venues of conservative opinion. My choice of venue was deliberate: I wanted to show the conservative aspects of RW’s political liberalism, a dimension that had hitherto been obscured. But it then occurred to me that I should also write on RW for an academic journal with a pronounced left-leaning orientation, and test the waters there. I sent it last month to Thesis Eleven. (I attach the article; a few paragraphs reprise a bit of the Quillette essay.)

13600717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13600717.value: I hit the mandatory retirement age at Lingnan University in 2018 and was extended for another three years. My contract ends in August 2021 and then I will decamp to Canada. When I received my last RGC grant (this was on “the unmasking style”), it took me some time to actually exploit the research. I had open heart surgery and was, for a year afterwards, somewhat shattered. The deliverables I at first gave in were puny. The RGC reviewer was annoyed, dissatisfied, and threatened to give me what amounts essentially to a failing grade. I asked for more time to write up the work. Begrudgingly this time was given. Within three years I had published a book on the topic (The Unmasking Style in Social Theory, Routledge, 2019), had a journal (The American Sociologist) devote a special symposium to the book, had the book reviewed and essay reviewed in another 11 journals, and published 9 articles related to the research. But all that supposed that I had an academic base and a library infrastructure to enable me to continue the work. In August, I will not have that base and my academic career ends. And so, in this case, I imagine that what I send you now will mark the end of this RW project.

13600717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13600717.value: Rebecca West was a twentieth century novelist, literary critic and political writer. As she was also a feminist it is not surprising that a great deal of the secondary literature examines her feminism. I took a different approach, and this I consider to be the chief significance of this GRF research. I was interested in West as a liberal rather than as a feminist. I also approached West as a political writer - whose arguments emerge out of the heat of intellectual battle - rather than as a political theorist or philosopher. In order to get a handle on West's liberalism, I embarked on a study of her opposition to Communism. I did so in a variety of ways. First, I examined her appraisal of ex-Communists, notably Whittaker Chambers and Arthur Koestler. Second, I looked at her analysis of Communist apologetics, as evidenced in the writings of fellow travellers such as Alistair Cooke. Finally, I identified and appraised the several arguments West adduced for the allure of Communism to Western intellectuals. The value of this research is not only that it offers the most detailed account of West's anti-Communism to appear in the Rebecca West literature. It also was an approach that received a great deal of interest in organs of intellectual opinion, such as the TLS, National Review, and the New Criterion.

13600817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600817.value: The proposed research will focus on the opium trade between the Tsarist Empire/Soviet Union and China from the early 1880s to the late 1930s. The trade will be studied at three levels: the borderlands economy and society; state policies toward the illegal (or “grey”) markets; and international relations between China, the Tsarist Empire/Soviet Union, Britain, and the League of Nations. The two regions where opium trade thrived were the borderlands between Tsarist/Soviet Turkestan and Xinjiang and the borderlands between the Tsarist/Soviet Far East and Manchuria. The research will comparatively focus on these two areas. In both regions, the population active in the trade mainly comprised migrants from China (the Hui/Dungans and Taranchis in Turkestan and the Chinese and Koreans in the Far East) who had fled Qing territory during the late nineteenth century. These migrants grew poppies within the Tsarist/Soviet territory and marketed opium back across the border in China. Starting with WWI, the Tsarist and later the Soviet government tried (with mixed results at best) to create a state opium monopoly out of the borderland economies. Opium was also used as an economic base for the local military powers during both the Russian and Chinese civil wars. The proposed research will analyze the connection between the illegal opium markets and the political-military powers in a period of imperial collapse followed by precarious state-building. The proposed research will combine three different scales of analysis: the local communities and their economic activities; the state policies aimed at controlling the borderland society and economy; and the international relations between the states. Its main interpretative aim will be to outline the interactions between political and economic actors at different levels and the role played by their perceptions of the socioeconomic reality of the borderlands. It is only by taking stock of the strategies and events at different scales and how the (often fallacious) perceptions of one scale influenced events at the other two that we can arrive at a convincing picture of this historical phenomenon. The resulting monograph will be both the first systematic study of a completely overlooked historical subject, and a case study at the intersection of local, transnational, and international history. This methodological suggestion could be useful for the study of any case of transnational, cross-border economic ties in which the economic actors are characterized by uncertain and changing subjecthood and the trade enjoys a fuzzy legal status. 是次研究的範圍為1880年代初期至1930年代晚期，沙皇帝國/蘇聯時期與中國的鴉片貿易。研究可分為三個不同層面，邊界經濟與社會、國家對非法(或灰色)市場的政策及中國、沙皇帝國/蘇聯、英國及國際聯盟間的國際關係。 研究會集中、比較沙皇帝國/蘇聯的突厥斯坦和新疆的邊界及沙皇帝國/蘇聯的遠東和滿洲地區這兩個鴉片貿易發展較繁榮的地區。在這兩個地方參與貿易的人口大多是在19世紀末逃離清政府的中國移民(在突厥斯坦的回/東干及塔蘭奇族，遠東的中國和韓國人)。他們在沙皇帝國/蘇聯境內種植罌粟，再跨境售賣鴉片到中國。自第一次世界大戰開始， 沙皇帝國及其後的蘇聯政府嘗試以國家壟斷鴉片貿易所形成的邊界經濟(但兩代政權都不能完全壟斷鴉片貿易，走私和黑市交易仍時有發生)。在中俄內戰時，鴉片更成為當地軍事力量的經濟基礎。研究抽述非法市場和政治軍事力量在帝國瓦解及建國初不穩定之時的關係。 本研究包含三個不同程度的分析: 當地社區及經濟活動、控制邊境社會和經濟的國家政策及國家間的國際關係。解釋有助描述三者的互動、不同邊境對邊界社會經濟現實的扭曲見解和政治家在不同層面下的意向。 研究的主要工作假設為只有在不同程度下觀察事件和見解，和那些(通常是錯誤)的見解如何影響其他兩個程度的行為和結果，我們便能展現歷史，為特定歷史現象提供可信服的畫面。論文將會是第一個具系統俯視歷史事件的研究，以及為本地、跨國和國際歷史交集的案例分析。若實證研究得到證實，這個建議方法將會適用於任何當中的經濟行為具有不確定和改變主題性質及貿易有模糊法律地位的跨國，跨界經濟聯繫的案例。

13600817.label: Realisation of objectives
13600817.value: For my UGC-funded research, I have worked in archives in Russia, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. In Russia, I collected materials in the central state archives of Moscow and St. Petersburg and the regional archives of Khabarovsk and Vladivostok. In Kazakhstan, I collected materials in the central state archives of the Republic of Kazakhstan, the former Communist Party archives (today the archives of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan), and district archives in Zharkent, at the border with Xinjiang. In Kyrgyzstan, I worked in the central state and party archives in Bishkek and the provincial archives in Karakol. My research assistant, Dr. Zhang Deming, has worked in libraries in Beijing in order to provide Chinese-language materials. On the basis of this research, I have published peer-reviewed articles and presented papers at international conferences, and I am completing the manuscript of a monograph, to be submitted shortly to major university presses. The primary sources I have collected, the articles I have already published, and the conference presentations based on this research project show that I have achieved all the objectives listed in the original application. (1) My research has put the Tsarist Empire/Soviet Union on the map of historical studies of the global opium trade. My Modern Asian Studies article, published in 2020, is the only detailed study of the cross-border opium economy between the Tsarist and Qing Empires in Central Asia. The two papers I presented at conferences, in Germany in 2018 and in Russia in 2020 (via Zoom), as well as an invited talk at SciencesPo (Paris) in 2020, focused on the place of the Far Eastern borderlands of the Tsarist Empire and the Soviet Union in the global opium trade during the first half of the twentieth century. (2) My research has highlighted, in an original way, the connection between the emigration from the Qing Empire to Russia and Central Asia and the settler colonization of the borderlands by Cossacks and Russian peasants. (3) By highlighting a crucial economic activity (and a pull factor) in the emigration of the Taranchis, Hui, Koreans, and Han Chinese who migrated from Xinjiang and Manchuria to Tsarist and then Soviet territory, I believe I have also provided a contribution to the connected history of China’s borderlands, as per objective no. 3. (4) As I discussed in my article for Modern Asian Studies, the case studies of borderland migrations from Xinjiang and Manchuria to the Tsarist Empire and the Soviet Union involved borderland populations making active use of the state-border-as-institution. I am expanding this point in my current book manuscript in order to show the agency of the borderlands’ population in creating a cross-border society united by networks of trade, capital, and labor. (5) One of the main objectives of the book manuscript I am completing is to highlight the failures and successes of different state administrations in harnessing the cross-border opium economy. One achievement of my research is that it shows the changes in Tsarist state policies in relation to opium during the First World War, and explains how the cross-border opium economy is a crucial context for understanding the great 1916 Central Asian anti-colonial uprising. I have also shown how the two peripheral regions of the Tsarist Empire and the Soviet Union became more firmly connected during the 1920s, when, under the Bolshevik regime, opium was successfully marketed abroad for the first time in Russian history. (6) In my paper for the Tyumen conference in June 2020 (which was eventually conducted on Zoom due to the Covid-19 pandemic), I analyzed the role of opium as an economic resource for the quasi-states that emerged in both Central Asia and in the Russian Far East after the collapse of the Tsarist Empire. This paper is the draft of one of the chapters of my book manuscript. (7) The history of the way migrants (both settlers from Russia and poppy growers from China) autonomously created a cross-border economy and society that influenced Russian-Chinese international relations is an original contribution to the existing literature. Thus, my research objectives have been largely achieved. I am confident that the publications that arise from the present research will provide an important contribution to the historical literature on the history of Tsarist Empire, the early Soviet Union, relations between empires in Asia, and the global opium trade.

13600817.label: Major findings and research outcome
13600817.value: My research has been the first to show the place of the Tsarist Empire and the Soviet Union in the global opium trade. The research has also shown that opium was a major factor in the creation of a borderland society between China and Russia in the Far East that was shaped by the migration of Han Chinese and Korean peasants into Russian territory. A similar cross-border economy and society was formed by the emigration of Hui and Taranchis from Xinjiang to Russian Turkestan. The creation of this cross-border society was made possible by porous borders that acted as filters, and by the symbiotic economic relations between Russian and Cossack settlers and migrants from China, protecting the migrants from state administrative and fiscal power from the other side of the border and from bandit violence. The research has shown how the Xinjiang/Turkestan and the Manchuria/Russian Far East borderlands between the late nineteenth century and the early twentieth century were important cases of a population making use of the border-as-institution. By showing how the cross-border economy was resistant to state regulation, the research has demonstrated the autonomous agency of borderland populations in influencing inter-imperial relations between the Tsarist Empire/Soviet Union, China, Japan, and Britain. Following the pioneering research of Kyrgyz historian Jamilia Madzhun, my own research has confirmed and deepened the understanding of the role that the cross-border opium economy played in unleashing mass violence during the 1916 Central Asian anti-colonial uprising. Mine is also the first research to show that opium was an important economic resource for Bolshevik and anti-Bolshevik forces during the post-Tsarist civil war, both in Turkestan and the Russian Far East. My research has also demonstrated, for the first time, how the Soviet government created a state company that competed on the legal global opium market during the 1920s, while at the same time the Soviet state was involved in the illegal international opium market in the Far East. By focusing on opium policies, the research then showed how the Soviet Union was influenced by the League of Nations from its creation onwards, even though Moscow only joined the international organization in 1934. The research has also shown how these borderland societies were destroyed by the violent creation of the Stalinist socio-economic system during the 1930s, and then by the forced population movements that connected the Russian Far East and Central Asia in new ways.

13600817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13600817.value: Much more research should be done regarding the Chinese side of the story. Thanks to the collaboration with my research assistant, Dr. Zhang Deming, I was able to cover this aspect partially; however, a much more systematic work needs to be carried out. Given the difficulty of access to provincial archives in Xinjiang and Heilongjiang, research should focus on materials in Archives No. 1 and 2 in Beijing and Nanjing and on the collection of primary sources published by these archives and devoted to borderland regions. Further research could be based on collaborations with historians from China. Hopefully, my own research in former Soviet archives will encourage Chinese historians to devote attention to the cross-border connection.

13600817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13600817.value: So far, the study of the global opium trade in the age of imperialism has mostly focused on the British-Indian-Chinese connection during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and on the Japanese-Chinese connection during the first half of the twentieth century. My research shows that opium was also an important commodity in Russian-Chinese relations. It demonstrates how a peculiar opium economy emerged in the borderlands between the Tsarist and the Qing Empires between the end of the nineteenth century and beginning of the twentieth, both in Central Asia and in the Far East; how it was linked to migrations made possible by porous borders; and how it was entwined with Russian settler colonialism. My research also shows the importance of opium during a period of state collapse: during the Central Asian anti-colonial uprising in 1916 and as an economic resource for Bolshevik and anti-Bolshevik forces during the post-Tsarist Civil War in Central Asia and in the Russian Far East. For the Soviet period, my research demonstrates how the Soviet state sold opium on the international markets, both legal and illegal, during the 1920s; and how Stalinism destroyed the vibrant cross-border society along the Soviet Union’s Asian borderlands during the 1930s.

13601117.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13601117.value: 五六十年代的香港偵探小說與電影

13601117.label: Project Objectives
13601117.value: Given an overview of the detective fiction and film production of Hong Kong during the 1950s-60s, including sections such as censorship policy, authors’ background, detective magazines, distribution channels, audience structure and the types of crimes described in the works. Each section will also compare differences between the 1950s and 60s. I will also examine the dialectal nature of “centre and periphery” through Hong Kong’s replacement of Shanghai as the center of popular literature production and distribution during the post-war era. Explore the formation of urban space in detective fiction and film of the 1950s-60s: to borrow Leung Ping-Kwan’s term “the politics of places,” how Hong Kong authors used the hard-boiled fiction and noir film to formulate a social critique of the city on its own native context, how was the Hong Kong urban culture gradually shaped through these changing city images in fictional and cinematic representations over these two decades, what cultural mentality was explored within the milieu of increasing urbanization and social unrest during 1950s-60s Hong Kong, and how this was achieved. Discuss the issue of female subjectivity in fighting women detective fiction and film: why the formula was so popular in post-war Hong Kong (two different groups of audience: the mainland Chinese immigrants in the 50s and female workers in the 60s), how these heroines were localized through film adaptations and how did the image of female detectives changed from the 50s to 60s. Examine the transculturation in Hong Kong popular culture in the 1950s to 60s through an analysis of cross-culture film adaptations based on serialized detective novels or Western thrillers of the time and how local authors used this genre to localize the Hollywood thriller in these adaptations, representing the old China and building on the established canon of the genre’s classics in new ways.

13601117.label: Realisation of objectives
13601117.value: There are four objectives raised in the original application. 1. Objective 1: Given an overview of the detective fiction of Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s. During my field trip to Singapore, I managed to approach a private collector’s collection on pulp fiction of Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s. Upon his approval, I have his collections about detective fiction magazines and novels scanned. This scanned version of collection will be available for public use in the Database of Hong Kong Literature run by CUHK. Based on these valuable collections, I was able to have a careful check of the different magazines, their characteristic layout designs, contributors and the most popular detective series. In the book chapter of my English book on the history of modern Chinese detective fiction, I gave an overview of the detective fiction of Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s. I have done some of the archive search about the publication policy at the Hong Kong Public Records Building. Because of the social upheaval and Covid-19 eruptions, the government service has been often interrupted. Currently, I am preparing a Chinese-language book manuscript on the development of detective fiction and film of Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s. I still need some more time to check the public records for references and footnotes of the book. I expect this book manuscript could be completed in one year. 2. Objective 2: Explore the formation of urban space in detective fiction and film of the 1950s and 1960s. During the 1950s, many detective stories still took place in Shanghai or Guangzhou areas. They are used to satisfy the cultural nostalgia feelings of new immigrants. But since the beginning of 1960s, more stories and films chose Hong Kong as the central background of the crime events. In these stories and films, the latest urban development, such as the transportation, theme parks, construction sites and shopping malls were quickly adopted into the plots. I wrote an essay titled “The Shape of Hong Kong Noirs during the 1950s and 1960s” on the film noir style in the postwar Hong Kong cinema and the representation of urban space in some representative films. I presented this paper in the Eleventh International Convention of Asia Scholars. The essay was well received and I received many constructive advices for further revision. I expect to include this essay in my forth-coming Chinese manuscript of postwar Hong Kong detective fiction. 3. Objective 3: Discuss the issue of female subjectivity in fighting women detective fiction and film In my published English book, Detecting Chinese Modernities: Rupture and Continuity in Modern Chinese Detective Fiction, I discussed the production and distribution of Female Burglar Huang Ying series and Mulan Hua series. During this project, I also expand my previous studies of Huang Ying stories to more images of female burglars and detectives in Cantonese cinema, including the chivalric tradition, female subjectivity and their connections with 007 films. The draft of this English paper is ready. After I collect comments from my colleagues, I plan to submit it to Journal of Chinese Cinema this summer. 4. Objective 4: Examine the transculturation in Hong Kong popular culture in the 1950s to 1960s. I adopted a case study of the reception and adaption of Hitchcock’s films in Hong Kong to approach this objective. I looked through all the reports about the receptions of Hitchcock’s films in Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s, including the showing period, their popularity, the impact of Hitchcock’s visits to Hong Kong and the representative film reviews by local film critics. Then I focused on three local Cantonese film adaptations. The integrative methodology of the field of film remake studies is adopted to analyze these local remakes from both textual and contextual levels. It argues that two factors have influenced the characterization and solutions in local remakes of Hitchcock’s films: leftist film’s emphasis on the anti-superstition educational role of Cantonese cinema, and audience’s change of aesthetics of the 1950 to the late 1960s. This paper is a pioneer study of Hitchcock in Hong Kong. I have submitted this paper to the international referred journal Adaptation and now is waiting for their review. Overall, this project has been a challenging one because of many unexpected factors appeared during the research. The social upheaval and Covid-19 caused difficulty to do research in the libraries at my desired time. I also had difficulties to check documentary materials overseas, for example, the National Archive of United States has been shup down for a very long time. Covid-19 also made international travel and conference very hard. During this project, I also faced some big career change, which made me not eligible to hire teaching relief as I had planned. These unexpected events caused some delay in the output of this project. But still, I tried my best to manage to complete the objectives as much as I can. I hope my forthcoming Chinese manuscript could contribute to a more comprehensive study of this project.

13601117.label: Major findings and research outcome
13601117.value: 1. Regarding document collection, the first-hand pulp magazines of detective fiction and novels during the 1950s and 1960s have been collected from a private collector of Singapore. The scanned version of these materials will possibly be uploaded to the Database of Hong Kong Literature by CUHK for public use. They will be a very valuable asset for the study of popular literature in Hong Kong. Based on these materials, my essay about the gangster novels by Zhou Baiping, is a pioneer study of this much being neglected field. 2. My output in the production of detective fiction and films in Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s is as follows: 1) Detective Fiction of postwar Hong Kong follows the Republican Mode in the history of Chinese detective fiction. The tradition of Butterfly literature, which had flourished in Republican Shanghai, took on a second life in the postwar popular market of Hong Kong. The images of female detectives and chivalric burglars became very popular in the book market and film adaptations. The Female Burglar Huang Ying stories were first published in Shanghai and continued in Hong Kong. One likely reason for their popularity is that the detailed evocation of Republican Shanghai in these stories aroused the cultural nostalgia of immigrants who came to Hong Kong after 1949. Some other female detective stories also borrowed elements from 007 films. These two findings have been elaborated in the book chapter of my English book Detecting Chinese Modernities (Brill, 2020) 2) Transcultural adaptation of crime films is another feature of postwar Hong Kong cinema. My essay on the adaptation of Hitchcock’s films in Hong Kong is a pioneer study that discussed the reception and remakes of Hitchcock’s films in postwar Hong Kong in great detail. A large body of historical background has been reviewed and I argue that two factors have influenced the characterization and solutions in local remakes of Hitchcock’s films: leftist film’s emphasis on the anti-superstition educational role of Cantonese cinema, and audience’s change of aesthetics of the 1950 to the late 1960s. I have submitted this English paper to the journal Adaptation (Oxford University Press)

13601117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13601117.value: 1. A paper on the subjectivity of female detectives in postwar Hong Kong film will be submitted to MCLC this summer. This leads to a rich area of development of this research, that is, to further discuss the female subjectivity in postwar Hong Kong crime cinema. 2. Based on the pulp materials I have collected and findings of this project, I am currently drafting a Chinese-language book that conducts a comprehensive study of detective/crime stories and films of postwar Hong Kong. More content will be added into this book, including the significances of stories illustrations in these detective pulp magazines, the representations of crimes in the left-wing and right-wing media. I expect this book will be completed in one year. 3. Another further development of the research is to continue to discuss the literature of Hong Kong detective/crime fiction after the 1960s, including contemporary writers such as Chen Haoji and Ma Jiahui.

13601117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13601117.value: This project studies detective fiction and films of Hong Kong during the 1950s and 1960s. It argues that the significance of Hong Kong detective literature at that time is its hybrid nature. Hong Kong played an important and unique role as the distribution center of Sinophone popular literature. The hybrid nature includes that postwar Hong Kong popular literature is developed from the sources of popular literature of both Guangzhou and Shanghai. The uniqueness of its hybrid nature also lies that detective stories published in media with opposite political ideologies co-existed in the postwar Hong Kong book market. Regarding its content, as a British colony, its marginal position in Chinese literature ensured that detective literature in postwar Hong Kong was not much restrained by moral functions. Meanwhile, writers also took a self-censorship attitude to avoid political troubles: all the detectives and criminals were Chinese and the majority of crimes only concerned with emotional or property disputes. This research identifies three particular aspects in postwar Hong Kong detective fiction and films: the material production of detective stories, including the use of the illustrations to attract readers; transcultural adaptations of Hollywood crime films; and the popularity of female detectives and chivalric burglars.

13601717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13601717.value: South and South-East Asian minorities have had a long historical presence in Hong Kong, yet many have been marginalised from mainstream political activities, despite the passing of the Racial Discrimination Bill in 2008, which led to partial recognition of the problems of economic and cultural assimilation of south Asians. The increasing educational and economic opportunities of second/ third generation South Asians, however, have resulted in an increase in recognition of ethnic minority youths gaining recognition, in independent media, in community politics, and in recent social movements, such as the Umbrella Movement. How far has the strategic media use of these ethnic youths enhanced their political agency and bargaining power in social and political affairs? How would their media participation foster a new mode of multi-ethnic participatory democracy in Hong Kong? What are the dynamics and tensions involved in the process of their interaction with local Chinese, other non-Chinese ethnicities, or compatriots who may have different political stances? The goal of this research will be eventually examine the practice and process(es) by which minority groups strategically use media, and the mode of networked/mediated democracy that such tactics help to create. It will aim to i) provide an exhaustive and critical understanding of the forms and rationale of media participation of these communities in Hong Kong; ii) examine whether their increased participation in the media correlates with their participation in community and political activities, and to what extent this increased participation would enhance their public reception and recognition; and iii) delve into their creative tactics of negotiations with diverse ethnic/ political groups in due process. The contribution of this research will be to fill the significant knowledge gap in scholarship on the extent of mediated community participation of South and South East Asians communities in Hong Kong through media use. The research will contribute to local and international scholarship by combining schools of scholarship on minority politics, diaspora, multiculturalism and mediated participation and democracy. The ultimate goal will be to inform our policy of cultural harmony that stems from multi-ethnic partnership, at a troubling time of international migration, ethnic conflicts. Locally, the research is timely, because minority communities as an emerging social and political force are increasingly responding to the changing political, social and economic landscape of a semi-democracy such as Hong Kong.

13601717.label: Realisation of objectives
13601717.value: We have achieved what we have stated in the research plan of the original research proposal to achieve the 4 objectives. We have exhausted relevant literature (both international and local) on ethnic minorities, diaspora or migrants with (political, social and cultural) participation; ethnic/ participatory media, including, their relations with participation, histories of ethnic minorities in Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia and Britain; migration studies, and multiculturalism studies. We have identified the gaps in current research literature which reinforces further the significance of this study. Other literature reviews on the news of mainstream media helped us discover the current representation of ethnic minorities in this platform, and compare this to their representation on ethnic media. Objectives 1 & 2 mainly focused on the relationship between ethnic minorities’ strategic media use and the public perception of south and south-east Asians in Hong Kong. Another dimension was the relationship between these media and the perception and participation in Hong Kong. Benefitting from the PI’s previous research, this research has established the foundations of the mainstream media representation of South Asians, which is believed to have formulated the basis of majority Hong Kong people’s perception of these communities. In the first year of research, we have identified, screened and then conducted textual analyses on 15 selected (social) media texts (the selected media texts are detailed in the progress report). We also did coding analyes to around 30 episodes of 8 Community Integrated Broadcast Scheme (CIBS) radio programmes. The aspects of analyses ranged from narratives and representations, the use of words and tone, and the overall message the production tries to convey to their audiences. Based on the textual analyses findings, we conducted individual interviews to producers of the Facebook and other web pages set up by South Asian minority youths, as well as producers of the selected CIBS radio programmes (please refer to details in the progress report) to understand their rationale, operation, experience and their reflections. These interviews have contributed to our exploration of the degree of these producers gaining definite understanding and changing their viewpoints regarding the social and political issues in Hong Kong with the production of ethnic media, as well as their sense of belonging to Hong Kong. 2 surveys were carried in the first and second year to gauge understanding of the reach of these ethnic media and its impact on public perception of South (South East) Asians in Hong Kong. In the second year of research, we performed a survey on Chinese respondents. A total of 130 questionnaires were returned. We have coded 45x120 categorical variables into numerical data (columns AN-DY on EM exposure and media use). We have created 13 indicators (columns ER-FD) on EM impression, EM acceptance, EM contact, media use, and EM-related opinions. On the other hand, we also conducted 2 surveys among South Asian communities to gauge their access to and extent of ethnic media (websites, facebook pages and CIBS programmes), and how these media affect the ethnic listener’s view of Hong Kong issues. We gathered 55 respondents and the findings show that CIBS ethnic programs are diverse to the point of categorizing them into three types: introducing their cultures, affirming the contributions of ethnic minorities towards Hong, and the critical tone of the programs. In general, there are still very few who are aware of the selected social media pages and CIBS programs, to which the program asserts that not so many people listen to radio nowadays. To triangulate findings from the quantitative surveys, we hosted five focus group interviews (total 8 interviewees) with ethnic minorities to investigate the influence of ethnic media towards their viewpoints on the mainstream social and political affairs. Following the interview, we have conducted a second survey to 167 ethnic minority respondents where we triangulate the factors that affect their identity, sense of belonging, opinions on inclusion and democracy in Hong Kong. In this way, we understood their perception in using media platforms, and the ways the usage influences them and their perceptions. Three more focus group interviews conducted in the second year with 9 Chinese respondents revealed that the influence of mainstream media shapes the image and recognition of ethnic minorities wherein we found that the image and the empathy of Chinese towards EMs are positively changing due to the current movements in Hong Kong. Hence, the representation and participation of EMs in the media increases. The findings from objectives 1 & 2 provide basis for the articulation of objectives 3 & 4. To have a comprehensive understanding of timeline of South Asians’ offline political participation in Hong Kong, we have had to conduct historical data searches on ethnic minorities’ settlement in Hong Kong and their civic and political involvement during the colonial era and in major political events in Hong Kong. This includes the PI going to the UK in March 2019 to visit the British Library and National Archive. We also conducted interviews with 3 federation key figures, and 2 advocates, 3 NGO social workers, 4 legislative councillors. These interviews have offered understandings towards the rationale behind their strategic use of media and organizing offline activities to participate and mobilize ethnic minorities in social and political affairs. As we determined the effects of the use of media in mobilizing offline participation, we had done 7 participatory observations in the whole research period on the range of ethnic minorities’ offline activities, such as sport activities, ethnic talks, cultural tours, fashion shows and social protests. These participant observations achieved multiple objectives. Through interviewing the participants of the offline events, we managed to examine how and to what extent the ethnic media effectively mobilized the participants to attend the events. These interviews also enhanced the researchers’ understanding of respondents’ own experience of ethnic relations in Hong Kong, and their sense of belonging in Hong Kong. Through these participations, we observed the inter-ethnic interaction between ethnic minorities and local Chinese groups. One point worth mentioning was that during the onset of the Anti-ELAB movement especially, we interviewed ethnic minority youths who organized the ‘water giving event’ on Oct 20, 2019. It showed that younger ethnic minority members have a clearer political agenda as they organize more public directed events with articulated motive to enhance public understanding and awareness of minority ethnicities. They are also strategic in using social (ethnic) media to mobilize support for the events. Interviews with the Chinese participants of the event, in contrast to the findings from earlier participant observation, showed quite significant change in the perception of some Chinese on the South Asians. Some of the difficulties we encountered in the study include the initially low response rate of the quantitative surveys, as well as the hesitation and rejection by ethnic minority interviewees. The onset of the Anti-ELAB movement in the second half of 2019 further stalled face to face interviews and participation observations, as many events and activities were forced to be cancelled because of the closure of MTR stations. We tried to overcome such adversaries through arduous planning and persistent efforts to exhaust personal networks for potential respondents and interviewees.

13601717.label: Major findings and research outcome
13601717.value: The major findings of the research in two years have contributed to the fruition of one book manuscript, one journal article, one book chapter, three conference papers, and writing for various other scholarly activities. One major area of findings reveals that South Asian minority youths’ strategic use of social media, radio programmes, and cultural practices such as stand-up comedies and fashion shows (see Part C, 9.3), to protest for belonging, to gain recognition, and others use such for socializing or participating purposes in mainstream society. In the journal article, Closeted Love? Borders of (mediated) Belonging in ‘minority radio broadcasting’, it detailed how radio broadcasting could serve as a particular medium for ethnic minorities to voice out to the general public (see Part C, 8.2, 9.1). In turn, CIBS programs provide ethnic minorities a ‘haven’, albeit a closeted one, as well as a training ground for minority communities to nurture their media production talents. In a similar vein, stand-up comedies become such vehicles for ethnic minorities to struggle for recognition by talking back at the mainstream through using their life stories as materials, but ‘shame’ the mainstream through their laughter. This is detailed in a conference paper ‘Standing up to Racism: Vivek Mabhubani’s Stand-up Comedy as Ethno-resistance in Hong Kong’ (as detailed in Part C, 9.2). However, the research also showed that public access to these ‘ethnic media’ is still low, hence these media has low impact on the perception of the Chinese public of the South Asian community at large. Nevertheless, as the research also revealed, that increasingly South Asian youths are engaging in the above practices to protest for more rights, recognition, as well as desire for membership and inclusion as ‘Hong Konger’. Interviews and participant observations to ethnic minority producers have shown not only their multifarious talents, but their determination to use their voice to enhance awareness in society of the importance of cultural inclusion. The onset of the Anti-ELAB movement has also become a watershed not only demonstrating the ethnic minority youths’ increasing engagement in mainstream social movement as participation, and the transformation of perception and interaction of Chinese public towards these South Asians. Most of the findings in this research have been extensively adopted and analysed in the book manuscript, titled “Ethnic Minorities, Creativity, and Participation: Tactical Belonging in Hong Kong”, which will be published in January 2021 (Part C, 9.1).

13601717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13601717.value: The success of this research confirms the agency and capability of South Asian youths’ to engage in media and cultural practices to struggle for recognition in the mainstream society. However, it also exposes that a deep-seated lack of understanding and stereotype is still prevalent among the general public in Hong Kong, which reveals that policies and measures to ‘listen’ in the mainstream are still lagging behind. Henceforth, further action is necessary in order to explore the ways in developing more appropriate platforms for ethnic minorities to showcase their talents, and enhance their public acceptance. Moreover, the current social and political juncture in Hong Kong will continue to inform ethnic minorities’ participation towards the social activities in mainstream society. The PI will continue to work with NGOs and relevant concern groups to lobby the EOC and the government for more efforts to enforce cultural inclusion. The PI is planning a next stage of research that examines current efforts of ‘cultural inclusion’ in forging cultural citizenship in Hong Kong, as well as a research which delves into the impact of colonization in the formation of racial identities and politics in Hong Kong.

13601717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13601717.value: The research confirmed that second and third generation ethnic minority youths, with their multifaceted talents are capable of, and keen to, strategically use the (social) media and other forms of creative arts and cultural practice to struggle for their deserved rights, as well as to express their nuanced sense of belonging to Hong Kong. These activities also became sites and spaces to foster ethnic minority community building, collective communities of practice, but also inter-ethnic solidarity. On the other hand, the research also shows that these mediated practices still fall short of reaching to the wider general public, as long held racial stereotypes still persist. These stereotypes stem from years of neglect towards the minority communities, and failure of policies to enforce inter-cultural understanding and cultural inclusion. This research also documented how ethnic minorities’ participation in social movements brought to a nuanced change in public reception of the communities, as the minority youths asserted their belonging as ‘Hong Konger. The exhaustive findings from the research would hope to inspire different levels of intervention, from advocacy, policy making, and redistribution/ provision of resources, to contribute to devising genuine measures to cultivating a genuine cultural inclusion and harmony.

13602417.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13602417.value: 全靠我自己？ - 有關兩個中國城市中單身人士狀況的研究

13602417.label: Co - Investigator(s)
13602417.value: Dr Groves, Julian Prof Jiang, Jin

13602417.label: Project Objectives
13602417.value: To analytically compare the trends and characteristics of singles in Shanghai and Hong Kong. To study how singles in Shanghai and Hong Kong perceive their own singlehood and how being single affects their social and work lives. To contribute to scholarship on singles and theoretical discussions in the sociology of personal lives. To provide empirical findings that could inform policy discussions in response to rising singlehood, in relation to areas such as housing, social support, and the socio-psychological well-being of singles.
rows: To analytically compare the trends and characteristics of singles in Shanghai and Hong Kong.
To study how singles in Shanghai and Hong Kong perceive their own singlehood and how being single affects their social and work lives.
To contribute to scholarship on singles and theoretical discussions in the sociology of personal lives.

To provide empirical findings that could inform policy discussions in response to rising singlehood, in relation to areas such as housing, social support, and the socio-psychological well-being of singles.

13602417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13602417.value: Singlehood has been identified as a growing trend that has important social implications. Much of the research on singlehood examines its trends, social impacts, and corresponding policy responses, while relatively little is known about how singles perceive their own single status and how singlehood affects them in everyday life. For instance, what are the levels of satisfaction and permanence that singles attach to their own singlehood? How does being single affect their social and work lives? Do singles develop alternative ways to meet intimacy and interpersonal needs? In particular, there are few studies on the situations of singles (especially single men) in the Chinese urban context. This mixed methods study aims to investigate the situations of singles in the two Chinese cities of Shanghai and Hong Kong. On a macro level we want to identify the trends and characteristics of singlehood, and on an individual level to examine how being single affects the everyday lives of men and women in these two places. Some of the macro-level questions we aim to address include: How have the socio-demographic characteristics of singles in these two cities changed over time, and what are the likely causes for these changes? Which categories of singles are on the increase and which are on the decline? Is it the case, as commonly believed, that well-educated and socio-economically successful women are increasingly without a mate? How do the characteristics of singles in the Chinese context differ from those found in other societies? On an individual level, we aim to address these questions: How do individuals make sense of their singlehood, something that is mostly perceived in a negative way by society-at-large? Do they see their singleness as a temporary state of affairs, or have they rejected more traditional forms of family life? Does the single status affect individuals’ social and work lives, and if so, in what ways? Findings will deepen our understanding of the rising trend of singlehood in the Chinese urban context, contribute to the scholarship on singlehood and theoretical discussions in the field of the sociology of personal lives, provide empirical bases for the discussion of policy responses to the trend of rising singlehood, and lay down groundwork for larger scale studies and cross-cultural comparisons in the future. 單身人士被確定為具有重要社會影響的新趨勢。許多關於單身性的研究都考察了其趨勢，社會影響和相應的政策反應，而較少研究單身人士如何看待自己的單身地位以及單身的身份如何影響他們在日常生活。例如，單身人如何看待自己的單身化的滿足程度和持久性？單身身份如何影響他們的社會和工作生活？單身人士怎樣滿足親密關係和人際需求？有關中國城市單身人士（特別是單身男性）情況的研究很少。本研究採用混合研究方法調查兩個中國城市 - 上海和香港 - 單身人士的情況。在宏觀層面上，我們想要確定單身的趨勢和特徵，並在個人層面上研究它如何影響兩性在這兩個地方的日常生活。我們針對的宏觀層面問題包括：這兩個城市單身人士的社會人口特徵如何隨時間而變化，這些變化背後的原因是什麼？哪些類別的單身人士在增加，哪些是在下降？一般認為，受過良好教育和社會經濟成功的婦女越來越多單身，是否屬實？中國文化中單身人士的特點與其他社會中的單身特徵有何不同？在個人層面上，我們的目標包括：個人如何理解社會大眾普遍認為是負面的單身性？他們把自己的單身視為暫時的狀態，還是因為拒絕更傳統的家庭生活形式而選擇單身？單身人士的地位是否影響個人的社會和工作生活，如果是的話，是如何影響？調查結果將加深我們對中國城市單身人士比例上升趨勢的認識，為社會學中個人生活領域的單身的理論和研究作出貢獻，以及對有關單身人口政策回應提供實證依據，為未來更大規模研究和跨文化比較奠定基礎。

13602417.label: Realisation of objectives
13602417.value: The original proposal was to only compare Hong Kong and Shanghai, but two other cities, Shenzhen and Guangzhou were also included in the eventual execution. We used existing datasets to examine general trends and characteristics of never married persons in these four Chinese cities. The quality of the data varied but in general we found visible differences between the three Mainland cities and Hong Kong. Objective one has been achieved. Qualitative data based on two rounds of in-depth interviews with 71 informants were used to address objective two. The data is very rich and we found again considerable differences but also some common features in how singles in the four research sites make sense of their singlehood. Informants from Hong Kong are evidently under less pressure. Objective two has been achieved. Two articles are in the final stages of preparation at the moment; one on parental matchmaking and another on how male informants experience singlehood. when published these will contribute to scholarship on the sociology of personal lives. Objective three will be 100% when published. One article is in preparation; the topic is related to policy, with a focus on material and psychological well-being. When published, this can inform policy discussions. Objective four will be 100% when published. Objectives three and four have not been 100% achieved in part due to the disruption of Hong Kong's social movement and the COVID-19 pandemic. These two events have affected the progress of data collection.

13602417.label: Major findings and research outcome
13602417.value: Delayed first marriage and increasing percentage of never married persons is a trend in all four research sites, but more prominent in Hong Kong than in the Mainland cities. There is evident gender differences in how singles view their current situation. Men tend to be unaffected by the temporality - they interpret the "waiting" and "searching" time positively while the opposite is true for women (particularly Mainland women). There is also considerable differences in how singlehood is experienced at the workplace and in social lives. The extend of discrimination and negative experiences in general are much higher in Mainland cities than in Hong Kong - but mostly only for women. Another interesting finding is the role of parents and extended family in shaping informants' experiences and perceptions of their singlehood. Chinese familism plays an important role but structural contexts also play an important role. We found that informants use various strategies and tactics to retain their autonomy and manage their well-being in face of familial pressure and intervention, with varying degrees of success. Again we can see evident differences between Hong Kong and the three Mainland cities. State intervention and government policies play an important role in affecting how singles perceive their situation and how they plan their futures. These could be interpreted as "blind spots" resulting from couple- and family-centric models of social and public policy planning, or more critically as discriminatory measures that disadvantage singles. We argue that family-centric models of social policy planning and implementation need to be revisited.

13602417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13602417.value: One shortcoming in this research is that our sample for the three Mainland cities consist mostly of highly educated informants. We had considerable difficulties recruiting informants with lower educational attainment or are employed in working class occupations. These individuals are more likely to be pressured into earlier marriage and also more prone to "accept" marriage as a practical arrangement; as confirmed by the quantitative data, their proportion in the never married population is low. Future research could devote more attention on this population group.

13602417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13602417.value: Delayed marriage is a trend globally as well as in Hong Kong and China, meaning that singlehood is now a common status for many adults. This research found important differences in how singlehood is experienced and understood by never-married men and women in Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Shanghai. Family socialization, workplace cultures and government policies play important roles in affecting the well-being of singles above mean age of first marriage. For singles who want to marry, the tendency to personalise their "failure" to marry and anxiety in finding a partner can negatively affect their well-being. For elective singles, the obstacles and problems they face in everyday life and in planning for their future are considerable. We argue that more attention needs to be given to singlehood as a gendered phenomenon, and that the value of "family-centric" models of policy making requires to be critically evaluated in order to take into account the increasing proportion of singles in Chinese cities.

13603017.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13603017.value: 割裂的成就：國家建設、大學制度與中國社會學的構成，1921-1949

13603017.label: Project Objectives
13603017.value: Schematically, the objectives of this research are four-fold: Historical: to reconstruct the process of knowledge diffusion and appropriation during the period 1921 to 1949 of Chinese sociology’s emergence as a new discipline; Theoretical: to explain the trajectory of Chinese sociology and the development of knowledge in terms of institutional factors, specifically the university system and its relationship to the state; Comparative: to examine the variety of Western traditions on which Chinese sociology drew, and to explain why the American model eventually triumphed; Reflexive: to provide insights into roads taken and not taken in the introduction and adaptation of sociological knowledge in modern China.
rows: Schematically, the objectives of this research are four-fold:
Historical: to reconstruct the process of knowledge diffusion and appropriation during the period 1921 to 1949 of Chinese sociology’s emergence as a new discipline;
Theoretical: to explain the trajectory of Chinese sociology and the development of knowledge in terms of institutional factors, specifically the university system and its relationship to the state;
Comparative: to examine the variety of Western traditions on which Chinese sociology drew, and to explain why the American model eventually triumphed;
Reflexive: to provide insights into roads taken and not taken in the introduction and adaptation of sociological knowledge in modern China.

13603017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13603017.value: How is it possible for an emerging discipline to cease flourishing just at the moment when more institutional support for it suddenly becomes available? This was the curious experience of Chinese sociology during the years 1921 to 1949. Instead of benefiting from the process of state-building, Chinese sociology suffered from it. Throughout the 1920’s, an early generation of Chinese sociologists invested considerable efforts in building the intellectual and organizational basis of their discipline. Professional associations and academic journals were founded, notable advances were made in the collection of survey data, and practical solutions were recommended to social problems. The Nationalist government’s expansion and consolidation of the university system in 1927 gave further impetus to the standardization of a sociology curriculum and the codification of sociological knowledge. Yet, paradoxically, the growth of Chinese sociology began to waver precisely at this point. Theoretical synthesis came to a standstill and was increasingly decoupled from empirical research. While individual sociologists produced impressive works and garnered recognition from the international academic community during the wartime period, the discipline as a whole failed to articulate a coherent basis of knowledge production and accumulation. Why did Chinese sociologists fail to sustain the steady growth of their discipline, despite the nationalization of the university system and the flow of resources it brought about? The research will describe and explain this anomalous pattern of disciplinary development. Tackling the relationship between knowledge processes and institutional structures, it will chart the ways in which Chinese sociology, from the 1920’s to the 1940’s, was shaped by the changing relationships between universities and the state. As one of the first major Asian attempts at a systematic introduction of Western concepts and methods, the prewar development of Chinese sociology constitutes an early and significant chapter in the global diffusion of social scientific knowledge. It also sheds light on an additional puzzle. Although American sociology came to be the dominant influence on its Chinese counterpart, several other national traditions – notably, French, German and British – competed for influence; all were tested, employed, and adapted by Chinese scholars. Explaining why the American model triumphed, this research can clarify the intellectual choices and priorities of Chinese sociology during a fateful period of its development. The research also addresses the theoretical question of how institutional conditions, particularly the modernization initiatives of the state, shape the selection of globally-circulated knowledge in local contexts. 1921 至 1949 年期間，中國社會學經歷了一段獨特的發展過程。在國民政府推動的國家建設計劃下，大學系統正在迅速擴張和整合，其中社會學獲得了更多的資源及制度性支持。社會學家利用這個機會，建立了專業團體和學術期刋，並開展了關於社會學課程標準化、社會學知識系統化等學科建設工作。然而從 1930 年代後期開始，中國社會學的發展開始出現停滯的情況。理論的探索和綜合面臨樽頸，並逐漸跟社會調查、實證研究脫節。雖然在二次大戰期間，個別社會學家取得了可觀的硏究成果，甚至獲得了國際學術界的肯定，但整體而言中國社會學仍未能建立具一致性的學科基礎。 本研究嘗試描述和解釋戰前中國社會學的異常發展模式。為什麼社會學在成功取得國家支持的有利條件下，其學科發展卻愈發停滯不前？藉著釐清知識生產與制度架構之間的關係，本硏究試圖重構由 1920 年代至 1940 年代，中國社會學如何受到國家建設措施，與及大學制度改革過程的影響。作為將西方社會學概念和方法引人亞洲的一個早期案例，對戰前中國社會學的分析，可以使我們加深了解全球流通的知識體系，在本土化過程中如何受制度因素，特別是國家的現代化政策和取態所模塑。

13603017.label: Realisation of objectives
13603017.value: The project objectives have been realized as follows: 1) Historical: In the course of research, I recognize that a preliminary but necessary step in reconstructing the intellectual and institutional history of Chinese sociology is to address the problem of indigenization. As the key concern and “master problem” of Chinese sociology, indigenization entails the diffusion and adaptation of Western sociological knowledge in modern China. In a paper, I attempt to revisit the history of Chinese sociology by situating it in the broader contexts and ramifications of the indigenization or “sinicization” movement. I trace the rise of Chinese sociology to the 1920s, when social survey was promulgated by foreign scholars as the dominant mode of knowledge production. The moment of indigenization came with the return of Chinese sociologists from overseas studies in the 1930s. Sun Benwen founded the Chinese Sociological Society and made the first attempt at theoretical synthesis. Wu Wenzao articulated a research programme of “community studies” that employed field investigation to study and compare urban, rural, ethnic, and overseas Chinese communities. Wu’s program was taken up by Fei Xiaotong, whose research focus was largely confined to rural social structure and culture given the prevalent interest of the government, international foundations, and Anglo-American scholars in China’s rural question. The development of Chinese sociology before 1949 thus set the stage for the community studies that were subsequently revived in post-war Taiwan and Hong Kong. Some inherent problems in Wu’s and Fei’s community studies, such as the relationship of a community with outside social forces, continued to manifest in the sinological anthropology of Maurice Freedman and the sociological theorizing of C.K. Yang. 2) Theoretical Similar to the historical analysis outlined above, a preliminary effort is made in the theoretical discussion pertaining to Chinese sociology. A paper on the “history of social theory” is published to furnish the groundwork for explaining the trajectory of Chinese sociology. The paper reviews the major works and changing approaches in the historical studies of sociological theory. Among the works discussed, Charles Camic’s celebrated studies of Talcott Parsons are most relevant for understanding the role of academic institutions, particularly the university system, in shaping intellectual choice and the direction of theorizing. On the other hand, the debates on classicality, canonization, and the decentering of Western social thought shed a new light on disciplinary history. The history of social theory thus supplements my earlier reading of the sociology of knowledge and science and technology studies, which focused more on the general dynamics of knowledge production than the specific contours of sociological theorizing. Based on these new insights, my major thesis that Chinese sociology had been caught in a situation of “achievement without coherence” can be more precisely formulated in terms of the sociology of theorizing. In the Chinese case, theorizing involved the successive, though not successful, efforts on the part of Sun Benwen, Wu Wenzao and Fei Xiaotong to give coherence to the works of their own and other contemporaries. While Sun adopted a strategy of “assimilation” in incorporating social survey findings and engaging established scholars (such as Wu Jingchao) in his theoretical synthesis, Wu’s strategy was one of “allocation,” in which young and aspiring students were assigned to conduct fieldwork in various sites and pursue doctoral degrees in different overseas institutions. Compared to the two, Fei was able to adopt a flexible strategy of “articulation” as he moved from one research topic to another. While Fei himself saw all his works as belonging to a broadly defined “functionalism,” they were in fact tailored to a wide variety of audiences and interests. How these major strategies of theorizing failed to lend coherence to Chinese sociology will be fully documented in a paper to be submitted to a top-tiered journal in early 2022. 3) Comparative On top of my previous conference presentation on the culture concept in interwar American sociology and its appropriation in Chinese sociology, and an article on the British and American influences in Chinese sociology, some additional observations regarding Sino-American sociological exchange are made upon my closer reading of Sun Benwen, Wu Wenzao and Fei Xiaotong. In all three cases, the primary reference remained American sociology and anthropology. While some attention was paid to European social thinkers, they were largely mediated through the introduction by American scholars. In the case of Sun Benwen, he was mainly influenced by the works of William Ogburn on social change and W.I. Thomas on social psychology. Occupying an authoritative position at the National Central University, Sun was not too keen to branch out from his synthesis of American ideas and Chinese works. Wu Wenzao once wrote articles introducing French sociology and ethnology as well as German systematic sociology as viable theoretical alternatives to the dominant American paradigms. But this soon gave way to British functionalist anthropology when Wu set forth his programme of community studies. Finally, the American influence on Fei had been largely underestimated thanks to his discipleship under Malinowski. It involved not only Fei’s early exposure to Robert Park, but also his exchange with Margaret Mead during his visit to the United States in 1946-47. In line with the institutional focus of this research project, I observe that the Columbia University was a common training ground for Chinese sociologists before 1949, including Sun and Wu and also Chen Da and Pan Guangdan. These observations will be brought together in a special issue of The American Sociologist, a journal for which I served as an editorial board member. 4) Reflexive This aspect leads back to the problem of indigenization, on which I published another paper following a conference on the history of sociology in Asia that I organized and hosted at Lingnan University. While the aforementioned paper on community studies treated indigenization from the perspective of research practice, in this paper I aim to pinpoint the circulation of indigenization discourse in Greater China since the 1980s. Instead of following the “Yanjing School” of Wu Wenzao and Fei Xiaotong to spell out the cultural distinctiveness of Chinese society, most indigenization discourses in contemporary Chinese sociology conceived positivist research as the surest path of building disciplinary autonomy. Notwithstanding the current pledge for augmenting and reaffirming Chinese culture in social sciences, academic sociology in China is still marked by “amnesia” and tends to put aside its indigenous intellectual resources. This paper and more generally this research project represent my modest attempt to strengthen the reflexive awareness of our discipline through detailed studies of its past, particularly those forgotten works and ideas that were worthy of reconsideration. Limitation and future research An original plan of this research project was to conduct archival research in Nanjing and Boston, and in-depth interview at Beijing with some senior scholars in the history of Chinese sociology. Unfortunately, the pandemic situation has made field trips difficult and costly. It is hoped that with the resumption of travel between Hong Kong, mainland China and elsewhere, I will be able to collect original data that can supplement my close reading of primary texts and other materials for this and other related researches. My next GRF project on C.K. Yang and the transnational history of Chinese sociology will continue my research on the major figures in the discipline and the broader and changing contexts in which they set forth distinctive ideas and perspectives.

13603017.label: Major findings and research outcome
13603017.value: The purpose of this project is to describe and explain the trajectory of Chinese sociology in 1919-1949. A notable feature of this formative period was the spectacular achievement of Chinese sociologists in knowledge reception and production. While Anglo-American social survey and sociological theory had long served as the model, in the 1930s Chinese sociologists were increasingly preoccupied with the indigenization or sinicization of Western knowledge. Three laudable attempts were made to integrate the existing knowledge of Chinese society and build Chinese sociology on a distinctive and coherent theoretical basis. Here the three strategies of theorizing can be characterized as assimilation, allocation, and articulation. Thanks to his dominant position in the national university system, Sun Benwen could enlist the established sociologists of his time as representatives of various theoretical schools. In this way, he was able to assimilate and synthesize their works in an encompassing system. A major problem, however, was Sun’s dependence on state supports, which were fluctuating because of political and ideological reasons. On the other hand, Wu Wenzao aimed to contest this dominant position by exploring how anthropological method could be applied to the sociological study of China. Wu’s strategy was to let his students to study with leading Western scholars and conduct field studies of different kinds of community in China. While this strategy succeeded in training up distinguished students such as Fei Xiaotong, the latter soon developed their own agendas that were difficult to subsume under Wu’s original research programme. Finally, Fei Xiaotong had been conducting field studies of Chinese villages that could capture the attention of Western scholars. Apart from overseas connections, Fei’s success owed no less to the quickening circulation of academic elites during the Sino-Japanese War. In the late 1940s, Fei set out to synthesize his works in a project on “Chinese social structure”. Yet remarkable inconsistencies could be discerned in Fei’s works, as they were tailored to a wide range of intellectual and practical interests, both local and overseas. Taken together, the three strategies of theorizing were successful in producing quality works but failed to provide overall coherence to Chinese sociology. Part of these research findings have been published or accepted for publication in several papers listed and uploaded along with this final report. A manuscript on the the strategies and outcomes of theorizing in the Chinese context is under preparation, and will be ready for submission to top-tiered journal in early 2022.

13603017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13603017.value: The American influences on Chinese sociology will receive further treatment in a special issue in the journal "The American Sociologist". Besides, this research will be followed by another GRF project “Yenching, Lingnan, Pittsburgh: C.K. Yang and the Transnational History of Chinese Sociology” (Project Number: 13604821). The new project is a continuation of the present effort to embark upon a systematic and historical study of Chinese sociology. It will focus on the life and works of C.K. Yang (aka Yang Qingkun), an influential albeit oft-neglected figure in the history of Chinese sociology. As Fei Xiaotong’s classmate at the Yanjing University, C.K. Yang exhibited a profoundly different, if not diametrically opposed, sociological orientation. Unlike Fei’s abiding interest in rural China, Yang began his academic career with a creative adaptation of urban sociology to the Chinese context. While Fei’s functionalist anthropology was eclectic, Yang’s structural-functional approach has a more determinate source of influence in the works of Talcott Parsons. Finally, Yang’s preference for quantitative analysis proved to be more influential than Fei’s field investigation in shaping the long-term development of Chinese sociology. The new project will draw upon the findings of the present research to compare Fei and Yang as sociological “alter egos”.

13603017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13603017.value: The 1930s-40s was often regarded as the golden era of Chinese sociology, when an impressive array of empirical studies and sociological discourses were produced. Despite these remarkable achievements, there was no theoretical framework that could serve to integrate these works into a relatively coherent body of knowledge. In this research project, three major attempts at theoretical synthesis were scrutinized and compared. The first was Sun Benwen, an official sociologist seeking to assimilate the works of established scholars by composing authoritative texts. Another attempt was made by Wu Wenzao, who assigned his students with the task of conducting anthropological fieldwork in various regions and communities. Fei Xiaotong adopted yet another strategy in articulating between different approaches as he moved from one research topic to another. While these strategies were equally tenable, wartime conditions served to speed up academic succession from Sun and Wu to Fei. But as Fei’s success was conditional upon the recognition from various parties and institutions, it failed to lend more coherence to the discipline. By probing into the conditions of sociological theorizing and the dynamics of knowledge production, this project offers a new perspective for reconsidering the legacies and limitations of Chinese sociology in its formative period.

13603117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13603117.value: My research project, “Visions of Progress in African American Literature: The Nation, Pan-Africanism, and Social Reform,” explores the way in which novels, poetry and essays can contribute to national solidarity. I plan to engage with contemporary social issues such as the Black Lives Matter movement and the debate over reparations for slavery. Much contemporary scholarship on African American literature, and in American Studies and Race Studies more generally, emphasizes a radical critique of the USA’s status quo. This radical critique accompanies a critical fascination with transnationalism that has resulted in a certain animus toward the nation-state. My book will argue that African American writers have been the major contributors to a left/liberal tradition of American letters. In my approach, black American literary intellectuals become rationalist builders of a post-racial society, as opposed to exponents of an integral Folk or diasporan subjects of an Atlantic countermodernity. The study builds on an article that I am currently submitting to journals, “The Global Du Bois: A Revisionist View,” which argues that the twentieth century’s preeminent black American intellectual could himself be imperialistic when he thought globally. The next chapter argues that Du Bois’s classic revisionist history Black Reconstruction (1935) not only imagines a more racially just New Deal for America, but also makes a major contribution to social contract theory, anticipating in particular the work of John Rawls. The midsection discusses the concept of “black power” at both a national and global level, relating Richard Wright’s travel book about decolonizing Ghana, Black Power (1954), to Stokely Carmichael and Charles V. Hamilton’s more famous work of Sixties radicalism, Black Power (1967). I argue that the writers draw on mainstream American modernization theory, even as they advance theories of decolonization and racial liberation. I may also add a chapter on Alice Walker to accompany the final chapter, “Does W. E. B. Du Bois Speak to the Souls of South African Black Folk?,” which analyzes my experience at a decolonizing African university. The outcome of this project will be at least two refereed journal articles, and a book of approximately 100,000 words from a respected university press. I think that the Du Bois/Rawls chapter is worthy of presentation at a major international conference. In order to complete this project, I will need significant teaching relief, as well as funding for conference travel and visits to the Du Bois and Wright archives in the United States. 專著項目： 非裔美國文學中的進步圖景 中文摘要（Chinese Abstract） 我的研究項目“非裔美國文學中的進步圖景：國家，泛非主義和社會改革”探討了小說，詩歌和散文促進民族團結的方式。就此，我打算探討壹些當代社會議題，如“黑命不賤”運動（Black Lives Matter movement）和關於奴隸制賠償的辯論。 在許多關於非裔美國文學的當代批評、以及美國研究和種族研究中，學者們普遍集中在對美國現狀的激進批評上。這種激進的批判伴隨著對跨國主義——它導致了人們對民族國家的某種敵意——的批判性迷戀。本書認為，非裔美國作家壹直是美國文學中左派或自由主義傳統的主要貢獻者。在我看來，美國黑人文學知識分子成為壹個後種族社會的理性主義建造者，而不是大西洋反現代性浪潮中鼓吹天下壹家親或流散主題的倡導者。 這項研究基於我目前正在向期刊提交的壹篇文章，名叫“全球化的杜波依斯：壹個修訂主義的觀點”。該論文認為，當這位二十世紀傑出的美國黑人知識分子站在全球化的角度思考時，他本人可能就是帝國主義的擁護者。在接下來的壹章裡我認為，杜波依斯（Du Bois）經典的修正主義歷史壹書《黑人的重建》（1935）不僅想像出壹個種族上更加平等的美國新政，而且對社會契約理論作出了重大貢獻，特別是預兆了約翰•羅爾斯的理論。接下來的幾個章節將討論國家和全球層面的“黑人權力”概念，將理查德•賴特關於加納去殖民化的遊記《黑人權利》（1954）”與斯托克•卡米克爾和查爾斯•漢密爾頓關於六十年代激進主義的最著名的《黑人權力》（1967）壹書聯系起來。我認為，這些作家在推動了去殖民化和種族解放理論的發展的同時，也借鑒了美國的主流現代化理論。最後壹章是關於愛麗絲•沃克的，即“W. E. B.杜波伊斯能讓南非黑人民族產生共鳴嗎？”。此章也会分析我在壹所去殖民化非洲大學的經歷。 這個項目的產出將包括至少兩篇同行評審學術期刊的文章，以及壹本由知名大學出版社出版的約十萬字的專著。我認為關於杜布伊斯或羅爾斯的章節值得在重要的國際會議上與同行討論。為了完成這個項目，我可能需要大幅度削減教學任務，並申請會議旅行和訪問位於美國的杜布斯和賴特檔案館所需的項目資金。

13603117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13603117.value: I am grateful to the RGC for funding this research. The initial proposal was for a book called "Visions of Progress in African American Literature," but the project has become more complex. Too often when we discuss racial inequality, we neglect the part that government can play in addressing racism, and how poets, essayists, and novelists can aid in this effort. Research into the racial attitudes of the poet Elizabeth Bishop, and the novelist Richard Wright's relationship to activist government, have seen journal publication, and form part of the completed book manuscript, "White Flight: Travel Narratives, Globalization, and the American Middle Class." When the University of Iowa Press publishes the book, I think it will make a major impact, reminding Americans about the legacy of their activist government during the 1930s "New Deal" era. "The Black New Deal: African Americans Rewrite the Welfare State" is a logical follow-up to this first book. I hope to have it under review with Oxford UP by the summer of 2022. The articles and conference presentations on my CV attest to the value of this research that the RGC has generously helped to fund.
