14165217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14165217.value: 世界上大多數國家正在發生人口老齡化問題。到2050年，60歲以上的老年人數將達到20億，約佔總人口的20-30％。在香港，老齡化正在成為一個重大問題。二十年後，每四名香港居民中有一人年齡將在65歲以上。證據表明，組織幹細胞的衰老在生物體衰老中起關鍵作用。細胞衰老是細胞逐漸失去增殖和分化潛能，最終導致生理功能衰退。 成人間充質幹細胞（MSC）對組織穩態，再生和修復非常重要。 MSC對年齡改變非常敏感，老年人MSC的再生能力下降。相反，MSC衰老與衰老相關疾病如骨質疏鬆症和骨關節炎的發生也密切相關。然而，我們對調控MSC衰老的分子機制知之甚少。有研究表明，細胞衰老伴隨著異染色質廣泛的空間重組。然而， MSC衰老是否也伴隨異染色質重組？異染色質重組所涉及的機制又是什麼？這些科學問題的解決對衰老疾病的控制和提供幹細胞治療效果至關重要。 我們的前期工作發現MSC衰老伴隨著異染色質的動態重組過程。我們還發現H3K9脫甲基酶Jmjd1a和Jmjd2c在衰老的MSC中高度表達。 Jmjd1a或Jmjd2c的過表達加速細胞衰老。此外，Jmjd1a和Jmjd2c與染色質組分蛋白相互作用和調控。基於這些結果，我們假設Jmjd1a和Jmjd2c在異染色質重組中起關鍵作用，並在MSC衰老中扮演重要角色。該項目的研究目標是解析關於去甲基化酶在細胞衰老中的作用，並為衰老幹預提供潛在的表觀遺傳靶點。我們提出三個研究內容：1）澄清Jmjd1a和Jmjd2c在hMSC衰老中的作用; 2）闡明Jmjd1a和Jmjd2c介導的異染色質重組調控的分子機制;和3）通過比較Jmjd1a敲除與野生型小鼠來評估Jmjd1a在體內衰老過程中的作用。 該研究將揭示組蛋白脫甲基酶控制MSC衰老的作用機制。我們研究的結果將為控制干細胞衰老和衰老過程中染色質重組的生理功能提供新的見解，並為老年性疾病的干預和基於幹細胞的治療手段提供新的靶點。

14165217.label: Realisation of objectives
14165217.value: AIM1: To further clarify the functional role of Jmjd1a/Jmjd2c in hMSC senescence. The Aim 1 proposed in the original proposal has been fully investigated and achieved. By using the lentiviral backbone as shown in Figure 1A, we established stable Jmjd1a- and Jmjd2c-knockdown hESCs (Figure 1A). On the other hand, we have validated our differentiation protocol to differentiate hMSCs from hESCs or hiPSCs, and achieved 97-99% induction efficiency (Figure 1B-E). Interestingly, despite being morphologically and phenotypically similar to adult hMSCs, at the molecular level, hESC-MSCs clustered more closely with human umbilical cord-derived MSCs (hUC-MSCs) than hBMSCs, indicating that hESC-MSCs represent a more primitive stage compared to hBMSCs (Figure 1F). To induce acute knockdown, we added Dox to the culture media on p3, 8 or 10 along with serial passaging. Our results showed that at passage 3, knockdown of Jmjd1a did not have detectable effect on cell proliferation and cell cycle. However, when the stable cell lines reached to passage 8-9, acute knockdown of Jmjd1a significantly reduced cell proliferation rate (Figure 2B). No change was found in the CD marker expression (Figure 2A). In addition, the expression levels of p16 and p21 were significantly increased in the knockdown cells. Suppression of Jmjd1a mitigated the osteogenic differentiation potential, whereas promoted the adipogenic differentiation potential (Figure 2C). We also observed increased number of -Gal positive cells in the knockdown population (Figure 2D). Similarly, suppression of Jmjd2c showed significant effects on cell proliferation and differentiation. We also determined the expression levels of histone marks in the knockdown cells and found that the expression levels of H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 were significantly reduced. In contrast, no detectable change in H3K4me3 was found (Figure 2E). Altogether, these results clearly indicate that Jmjd1a regulates MSC senescence and heterochromatin organization. AIM 2: To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying Jmjd1a/Jmjd2c-mediated regulation of heterochromatin reorganization The Aim 2 proposed in the original proposal has been fully investigated and achieved. To elucidate the mechanisms underlying Jmjd1a/Jmjd2c-mediated regulation of heterochromatin reorganization, we used global gene expression analyses. Our RNA-seq data revealed that manipulation of Jmjd1a or Jmjd2c led to a consistent change in chromosome organization genes, in particular chromosome condensation genes (Figure 3). Interestingly, among the chromosome condensation genes, we have identified that various components of the condensin complex I and II are consistently downregulated in either Jmjd1a- or Jmjd2c- knockdown hUCMSCs, or upregulated in either Jmjd1a or Jmjd2c-overexpressing hUCMSCs (Figure 4A&B). We decided to focus on Ncapd2 and Ncapg2, the major components of condensin I and condensin II respectively which are unanimously regulated by Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c. Our Western blot showed that knockdown of either Jmjd1a or Jmjd2c reduced the expression levels of both Ncapd2 and Ncapg2(Figure 4A&B). ChIP-qPCR result revealed that the binding of Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c on the promoter of Ncapd2 was significantly downregulated while the occupancy of corresponding H3K9me3 and H3K9me2 was significantly upregulated in knockdown hUCMSCs (Figure 4C). Consistently, the ChIP-seq analysis showed increased enrichment of Jmjd2c along with decreased binding of H3K9me2/3 on both Ncapd2 and Ncapg2 genes in Jmjd2c overexpressing-hUCMSCs. In addition, inhibition of H3K9 demethylase activity by IOX1 reduced the expression levels of Ncapd2 and Ncapg2. The regulatory effect of IOX1 was attributed to the enzyme inhibitory function, as IOX1 increased the enrichment of H3K9 methylation on Ncapd2 promoter (Figure 5). Furthermore, Jmjd1a physically interacts with Ncapd2 but not Ncapg2 in MSCs (Figure 6). Taken together, these data clearly indicate that Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c function as positive transcriptional regulators of condensin components via their H3K9 demethylase activity. AIM 3: To evaluate the role of Jmjd1a in the aging process using Jmjd1a knockout mice The Aim 3 proposed in the original proposal has been fully investigated. We took advantage of Jmjd1a knockout mice to evaluate the effect of Jmjd1a deficiency on bone aging. We collected bone tissues from WT and KO mice at different ages and found that while mild difference exists between WT and KO young mice (2 month), KO mice at 6 month-old exhibited evident bone aging phenotype (Figure 7A). The expression levels of senescence markers p53, p21 and p16 were dramatically increased whereas the expression of PCNA was significantly decreased in KO bones. In addition, the expression levels of senescence nuclear markers such as Lamin B1, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 and condensin components were dramatically reduced in KO bones, indicating the correlation between bone aging and heterochromatin destruction in vivo (Figure 7B). Of note, the expression of Suv39h1 was slightly increased in KO mice. We also collected WT and KO mice at PN1 and found no significant difference in bone development (Figure 8). To further correlate these changes with BMSCs, we isolated primary BMSCs from WT and KO mice. Our results showed that the expression levels of condensin components were significantly reduced in KO BMSCs compared to WT BMSCs. In contrast, the expression levels of senescence genes such as p53, p21 and Gadd34 were significantly increased in KO BMSCs (Figure 9A). Moreover, when challenged with DOX, KO BMSCs elicited a much enhanced DDR as illustrated by increased expression of 53BP1 and p21. In addition, overexpression of Ncapd2 alleviated the DOX-induced cellular senescence and DDR in KO BMSCs (Figure 9B&C). Taken together, these results strongly indicate that Jmjd1a correlates with bone aging, and Jmjd1a deficiency aggravates DNA damage and cellular senescence in BMSCs, which eventually contributes to the bone aging phenotype in mice. However, it should be noted that we found Jmjd1a inhibitor IOX1 could note rescue the aging phenotype in hMSCs derived from hESCs. In order to identify a potential drug that can target on Jmjd1a, we screened for our natural product library. Interestingly, we found quercetin which was recently recognized as an anti-ageing compound, upregulated the expression of Jmjd1a. Moreover, while quercetin promoted osteogenesis of mBMSCs isolated from the WT mice, this effect was largely mitigated in the KO mBMSCs (Figure 10).

14165217.label: Major findings and research outcome
14165217.value: Cellular senescence is accompanied by an extensive spatial rearrangement of heterochromatin, whereas the mechanisms involved in initiating and maintaining this unique epigenetic state remain unclear. In this study, we show that MSC senescence is accompanied by a stage-dependent heterochromatin dynamics involving both heterochromatin condensation at the early stage and heterochromatin decomposition at the late stage. Using hESC-induced MSC model and knockout mouse model, we have found H3K9 demethylases Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c regulate heterochromatin condensation via transcriptionally activating condensin components Ncapd2 and Ncapg2 in aging MSCs. Suppression of Jmjd1a or Jmjd2c by either genetic or biochemical approaches leads to a robust DNA damage response and aggravates cellular senescence. By contrast, overexpression of Jmjd1a or Jmjd2c or Ncapd2 alleviates Doxorubicin-induced DNA damage response and MSC senescence. In addition, MSCs derived from Jmjd1a-/- mice exhibit compromised heterochromatin condensation machinery and are more susceptible to genotoxic damage, which are associated with augmented bone aging. Importantly, a marked downregulation of Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c associated with a decrease in H3K9me3/2, HP1 and chromosome condensation genes is found in MSCs derived from old human individuals. In conclusion, our study has revealed a previously unrecognized role of histone demethylases in modulating condensin-mediated heterochromatin condensation, which functions as a surveillance mechanism to restrain DNA damage during stem cell aging. These results have been published in iScience 2019. Apart from that, with the captured funding, we have also found that stress-induced MSC senescence is accompanied by heterochromatin organization. Using two different senescence models, we find that disruption of heterochromatin organization leads to robust DNA damage response and aggravated cellular senescence. Suppression of mTORC1/p70S6K pathway promotes heterochromatin organization and ameliorates Dox- or H2O2-induced DNA damage and senescence. In contrast, direct activation of mTORC1 impairs heterochromatin organization and aggravates stress-induced senescence. Moreover, concomitant activation of mTORC1 pathway and heterochromatin organization is found in D-galactose-induced osteoporosis model in rats. Importantly, Rapamycin alleviates cellular senescence and promotes heterochromatin organization in BMSCs derived from D-galactose-treated rats. These results have been published in Stem Cell Research and Therapy 2020. A review article on MSC aging has also been published based on our work and others’ work (Cell Death and Disease, 2021). We have presented our research findings in two ISSCR (International Society of Stem Cell Research) annual meeting and Cold Spring Harbor Asia meeting in aging. In addition, three students who had been working on the project completed phD studies during the funding period.

14165217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14165217.value: MSCs are well-studied adult stem cells, which are broadly distributed in different tissues. Undoubtedly, a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying MSC senescence will not only provide important guidance for how to maintain the natural physiological function of stem cells and delay the aging process, but also offer new strategies for stem cell-based therapies. We have found that along with bone aging, the expression level of Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c is dramatically decreased in BM-MSCs. We will try to identify small molecules that are able to increase the activity of these histone demethylases, aiming to intervene bone geriatric diseases, such as osteoporosis and bone fracture, and improve MSC-based therapy. On the other hand, we find that the association of Jmjd1a, Jmjd2c and chromosome organization genes with stem cell aging is demonstrated in other types of adult stem cells as well. For instance, during brain aging, Jmjd1a is dramatically downregulated in brain and NSPCs. Of particular interest, Jmjd1a regulates PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway and mitochondrial function in NSPCs. Thus, we will further study whether Jmjd1a regulates mitochondrial function and energy metabolism of NSPCs via PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which is highly related to brain aging in future.

14165217.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14165217.value: MSCs are extremely important adult stem cells for tissue homeostasis, regeneration and repair. However, the regenerative capacity of MSCs declines in aged people and their exhaustion is recognized as an important hallmark of aging. Reciprocally, MSC senescence is correlated with age-related diseases, such as osteoporosis and osteoarthritis. Given that the senescence-induced loss of adult stem cell function results in the impairment of homeostatic maintenance and the regenerative potential of tissues, it is important to understand the mechanisms that underlie MSC senescence. In this project, we aim to gain novel insights into the role of Jmjd1a and Jmjd2c in heterochromatin reorganization during MSC senescence, and provide potential epigenetic targets for senescence intervention. Our findings have revealed a previously unrecognized role of histone demethylases in modulating condensin-mediated heterochromatin condensation, which functions as a surveillance mechanism to restrain DNA damage during stem cell aging. In addition, we have also found Jmjd1and Jmjd2c can be used as indicators and therapeutic targets for stem cell aging, which are valuable for us to develop novel therapeutic targets for intervening geriatric diseases and improve stem cell-based therapy.

14165817.label: Project Objectives
14165817.value: Estimating the strength and statistical significance of associations between population mortality rates and various small area urban design characteristics, including urban heat island intensity, green space coverage, wind penetration, proximity to large open areas, and population density. Identifying population subgroups that may be more likely to suffer health consequences when living in unfavourable urban conditions. Explore differences in associations between urban characteristics and mortality from different causes as a way to better understand the mechanisms by which urban design characteristics may influence population health. For example, cardiovascular mortality is influenced by several mechanisms relevant to urban design, including extreme temperatures, stress, and physical activity levels, while colorectal cancer mortality is likely only influenced by physical activity levels, and lung cancer mortality is not strongly influenced by any of these factors. Thus for example finding negative associations of similar strength between green space and both cardiovascular and colorectal cancer mortality would suggest that opportunity for exercise is an important mechanism by which green spaces affect health, while finding a negative association for cardiovascular, but not colorectal cancer, mortality might imply that stress reduction and/or urban heat island mitigation are more important.

Thus for example finding negative associations of similar strength between green space and both cardiovascular and colorectal cancer mortality would suggest that opportunity for exercise is an important mechanism by which green spaces affect health, while finding a negative association for cardiovascular, but not colorectal cancer, mortality might imply that stress reduction and/or urban heat island mitigation are more important.

14165817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14165817.value: Recent years have seen worldwide increases in temperatures, the proportion of populations living in urban areas, and ageing populations, with the latter occurring particularly in developed countries. As all three of these trends are expected to continue for the foreseeable future, evidence-based urban design strategies are needed to mitigate the potential negative health impacts of urban living, such as urban heat islands, stress due to lack of greenery, and environmental noise and pollution. Previous studies have found evidence that access to green space can improve health, and that mortality among people living in urban heat island areas increases more during periods of extreme high temperatures. However a comprehensive, multivariable, assessment of the long term association between urban characteristics and mortality has not been done in a densely populated Asian city. Although Hong Kong is among the most densely populated areas in the world it’s urban geography is highly variable, with some areas dominated by compact high rise buildings, and other consisting of village houses, farmland, and country parks. In the proposed study we plan to examine the association between several small area urban design characteristics, including urban heat island intensity (UHII), green space, open space, population density, and frontal area density, with the mortality of area residents, while controlling for area level socioeconomic characteristics, age, and gender. We will obtain data on all deaths in Hong Kong from 2009-2013, both all-cause and cause-specific for common causes of death, and the corresponding populations counts from the 2011 census, by age, gender, and tertiary planning unit (TPU), and TPU level measurements of socioeconomic status, including median household income, and percentage of the adult population with various education levels, from the Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department. Data on urban design characteristics will be obtained from the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Architecture Department. Negative binomial regression models with age and gender specific mortality counts as the outcome, and TPU level urban design and socioeconomic status variables as predictors, will be used to assess the association between area level variables and mortality. Planned subgroup analyses include examining premature mortality, elderly mortality, gender-specific mortality, cause-specific mortality, and seasonal mortality (hot season: May-October, and cool season: November-April). The results of this study will provide evidence to inform policy makers on how to better perform urban planning in order to reduce the potential negative health impacts of global warming, stress, lack of exercise, and pollution.

14165817.label: Realisation of objectives
14165817.value: We have accomplished the objectives of this project despite some complications. We obtained TPU level data on mortality and population from the Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department (HKCSD), and TPU level urban design characteristics from colleagues in the School of Architecture of CUHK. Some complications emerged during the project. One of these was TPU boundary changes, which was solved by merging some TPUs together so that the population remained consistent throughout the analysis period. Another was that some of the urban design parameters were very highly correlated with each other so that including them in the same model was problematic. We chose to fit separate models including only one of these parameters and seeing which variable was more significant in the model, and then choosing the more significant variable as the one to be retained. From the HKCSD data we created mortality counts for 2008-2014 for each TPU by 5-year age group (20-24, 25-29, ..., 85+) and gender. Similarly, population counts by TPU, 5-year age group, and gender, and TPU level SES status variables, including median monthly household income, percentage of population over 15 years old with a tertiary education, and percentage of unmarried population over 15 years old, were also obtained from the HKCSD. The School of Architecture obtained urban morphological data were obtained from the Planning Department, including land use information, building shapefiles with footprint and height, road network. These data were calculated into various urban morphological parameters in order to characterize the built environment of each TPU. Analyses were restricted to adults > 15 years old. Negative binomial regression models were used to regress mortality counts for each age (5-year groups), gender, and TPU group, on the area level characteristics, with generalized estimating equations (GEE) employed to account for the correlations among mortality counts from the same TPUs. The model equation is: Log(E(Dijk)) = β0 + β1I(age = 20-24) + ... + β14I(age = 85+) + β15 I(female) + log(Popijk) + β16x1k + ... + βm+15xmk where Dijk and POPijk are the number of deaths and person-years, respectively, from 2008-2014 in the ith gender, jth age group, and kth TPU, x1k, ...,xmk are TPU level covariates, I(female) is an indicator variable that the counts are for females (reference = males), and I(age = ..) is an indicator that the counts are for a particular age group (reference = 15-19). Relative risks (RR) associated with a given change in a TPU level covariate Δx were calculated as RR = Exp[β*(Δx)], and 95% confidence intervals and p-values testing the statistical significance of covariates were calculated using the GEE approach. The following outcomes were separately analyzed: all non-external deaths, deaths due to all cardiorespiratory deaths (ICD-10: I00-I99 and J00-J99), all cardiovascular diseases (ICD-10: I00-I99)with subgroup analysis including ischemic heart disease (ICD-10: I20-I25), acute myocardial infarction (ICD-10: I21), heart failure (ICD-10: I50), and cerebrovascular disease (ICD-10: I60-I69)), all respiratory diseases (J00-J99) with subgroup analyses including pneumonia and influenza (ICD-10: J09-J18), chronic respiratory diseases (including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (ICD-10: J40-J44, J47) and asthma (ICD-10: J45-J46)), breast cancer (ICD-10: C50), colorectal cancer (ICD-10: C18-C20), lung cancer (ICD-10: C34), lymphoma and hematologic malignancies (ICD-10: C81-C96), diabetes mellitus (ICD-10: E10-E14), renal failure (ICD-10: N17-N19), and dementia (ICD-10:F01-F03). These specific causes of death were chosen a priori, as is discussed in the objectives above. We also analyzed suicide mortality although that was not part of the original proposal. We did this because we realized that urban design characteristics could affect mental health as well as physical health.

14165817.label: Major findings and research outcome
14165817.value: Our most important finding was that frontal area density (FAD) a measure of urban air ventilation, with higher FAD meaning lower ventilation (due to the inability of prevailing winds to penetrate into the area due to compact high-rise buildings) was the urban design characteristic most strongly associated with higher all-cause mortality rates. A one interquartile range (IQR) increase in FAD was associated with a statistically significant a 10% (95% confidence interval (CI): 2% to 19%, P = .019) increase in all-cause mortality. In subgroup analysis an IQR increase in FAD was associated with a 9% (95% CI: -1%, 19%) for cardiorespiratory deaths. For cardiovascular deaths an increase of 7% (95% CI 0.97-1.18) in the risk of all cardiovascular deaths was found, with similar magnitude of associations identified for disease subgroups investigated. For respiratory deaths, an IQR increase in FAD was associated with a 7% (95% CI 0.95-1.20) increase in the risk of pneumonia and influenza mortality while it was associated with 2% (95% CI 0.90-1.14) and 21% (95% CI 1.02-1.45) risk increase in COPD and asthma deaths, respectively. Regarding cancer mortality, 3% (95% CI 0.94-1.12) and 2% (95% CI 0.94-1.11) increase in the risk of deaths due to lung cancer and lymphoma and hematologic malignancies were found respectively for an IQR increase in FAD whereas it was associated with a significant 10% (95% CI 1.01-1.22) increase in the risk of breast cancer-caused deaths. Overall FAD was not found to be significantly associated with suicide mortality but it was found to be significantly associated for suicides among those less than 70 years old. Surprisingly more green space was found to be positively, but non-significantly associated with suicide mortality. Most of our findings were consistent with expectations as poorer urban ventilation would be expected to lead to higher pollutant concentrations and higher temperatures, due to the inability of winds to disperse pollutants and moderate temperatures. We did not expect to find strong association between urban design and cancer and we didn’t except for breast cancer, which was a surprise. This could be a random finding or it could be that breast cancer risk is increased with air pollutants. Once other urban design characteristics were controlled for more green space was only significantly associated with low diabetes mortality, and was non-significantly protective for most other causes of mortality. This finding is not surprising as green space is expected to encourage exercise.

14165817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14165817.value: I will continue to work on various aspects of the relationship between urban design and health. I am a co-PI on a project (RGC Research Impact Fund (RIF) No. R4046-18) entitled 'Increasing the resilience to the health impacts of extreme weather on elderly people under future climate change'. Urban design and health outcomes is one of the topics covered by this multi-disciplinary project, and we will be looking at the associations between hospitalizations and local climatic zones which are formed in part by urban design.

14165817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14165817.value: This project aimed to examine whether neighborhood level characteristics, including urban air ventilation and amount of green space, had any association with death rates in those neighborhoods. This project is significant because Hong Kong is very densely populated with large areas that have compact high rise buildings with poor outdoor air ventilation and little green space. Due to the housing shortages and growing population choices need to be made regarding space utilization. Our study found that areas with poorer air ventilation, i.e. those with densely packed high buildings on average had higher death rates than those with better ventilation. This evidence could be used to encourage policy makers to promote urban design principals that allow better urban ventilation, either through putting more space between buildings or orienting the buildings to not block prevailing winds.

14165917.label: Realisation of objectives
14165917.value: We have successfully achieved all the objectives of the proposal 1. To resolve the cryoEM structure of bacterial transcription complex consisting of RNAP and NusA to subnanometer resolution. To resolve the structure of RNA polymerase in a complex with NusA, the two proteins have to be purified to a sufficient amount in high purity. Unexpected difficulties were encountered when obtaining B. subtilis RNAP. The initial plan was made to purify RNAP from previously established B. subtilis strain BS200, in which the beta prime subunit was tagged with 6x His to facilitate affinity purification. However, despite multiple attempts, very little RNAP could be obtained due to the poor binding of RNAP with Ni-NTA column (data not shown). It may be because of poor recovery of the original BS200 strain. Then a previously established dual plasmid system was employed to overproduced all the subunits of B. subtilis RNAP in E. coli host. Sufficient amount of RNAP could be obtained by this method. However, after ion change and gel filtration columns, there were still slight impurity proteins carried out from E. coli (data not shown). We managed to obtain a B. subtilis strain MH5636 in which the C-terminal of beta prime subunit was fused to 10x His tag. Sufficient amount of RNAP with high purity was achieved, which is suitable for further structural studies. The quality of the RNAP preparation was assessed by negative stain EM, which showed homogeneity and mono-dispersal of the particles. CryoEM data collection was taken place, followed by single particle analysis. An initial model of RNAP elongation complex was achieved to 4.3 angstrom. 2. To construct a pseudo-atomic model of the bacterial RNAP-NusA complex. A pseudo-atomic model of B. subtilis RNAP-NusA complex were made with UCSF Chimera. In the model, NusA binds to the FTH fragment of RNAP and positioned itself near the RNA exit channel, which is consistent with our previous far-Western blot and affinity gel data. Flexibilities observed around the FTH region made room for accommodation of RNA hairpin formed by the transcript. NusA NTD and CTD interacts with the newly transcribed RNA to regulate transcription elongation, which is consistent with our previous biochemical data. A number of cryoEM structure of E. coli RNAP transcription elongation complexes have also been published. The structural information from the electron density maps showed high degree of agreement to our B. subtilis RNAP and NusA homology model. 3. To optimise the current pharmacophore model and inhibitors targeting RNAP-NusA interaction. Based on the model generated from Objective 2, modifications of the current pharmacophore were carried out using molecular docking software BIOVIA Discovery Studio. The key amino acids of RNAP FTH that are involved in NusA binding were used to refine the previous pharmacophore model. Using the Binding Site Analysis tool in Discovery Studio, the key amino acids were represented by spheres with appropriate radius. Hydrogen bond donors and hydrophobes were identified to add as features in the pharmacophore model using the Add Query Feature Tool. The improved pharmacophore model were used to optimisation of previously discovered small molecule inhibitor targeting RNAP-NusA interaction by target based de novo design. The inhibitor with best activity were docked into the pharmacophore model as the molecular core using the built-in module LUDI in Discovery Studio. Small functional fragments will be positioned according to the pharmacophore model so that hydrogen bonds/hydrophobic interactions can be formed with the targeting region of NusA. Based on the new pharmacophore model, a chemical modification plan was made. Up to the reporting period, 109 chemical compounds were chemically synthesized by co-I Ma and then subjected to the following mechanistic/antimicrobial activity testing. 4. To assess the mechanism and antimicrobial activities of the optimised RNAP-NusA inhibitors. A vector system has been design and developed to study in vitro protein-protein interaction (PPI) as well as to screen for PPI inhibitors using a split-luciferase system as opposed to ELISA-based assay in the original proposal. The split-luciferase system offers much quicker and simplified process for high-throughput screening of PPI inhibitors. PPI inhibitors could be screened and/or characterized independent of cell-associated barriers exampled by compound permeability, efflux, and metabolic enzymes to facilitate the drug discovery process. This work has been published as a supplementary cover article in ACS Infectious Diseases. A series of vectors were designed and constructed to obtain fusion PPI pairs with the luciferase complementation fragments. A small monomeric luciferase, NanoLuc (Promega), was chosen as the reporter enzyme, which emits a bright stable light than traditional luciferases. The NanoLuc PCA system involves splitting the luciferase into two peptide fragments called SmBiT (11 amino acids) and LgBiT (18 kDa), which has previously been used for studying PPIs in live cells. In our system, each of the PPI partners was tagged with one of the NanoLuc complementation fragments and overproduced in Escherichia coli. The lgbit/smbit fragments were cloned to create plasmids for tagging to the PPI partners at both N- and C-terminals, which will allow optimization of the NanoLuc PCA system for particular PPIs of interest. These vectors were used for the production of N- and C-terminal His-tagged recombinant proteins for affinity chromatography purification. Once proteins purified, the interaction between the PPI partners or the presence of the PPI inhibitors will be measured by luminescence released from the reformation of native NanoLuc in vitro. The system was first validated using two pairs of previously characterized PPI in bacterial transcription machinery, RNAP-SigA and NusB-NusE. Then NusA and FTH was then cloned into the vectors to generate the luciferase compartmentation pairs. Six different clones were made and after optimization with the PPI pairs, a specific positive luminescence signal could be generated from the combination between NusA-LgBiT and FTH-SmBiT. The in vitro antimicrobial activities of the anti-NusA inhibitors were first assessed by the microdilution assay. The aim of this assay was to determine the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of a certain compound. The assay was performed according to the Clinical & Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines. Six bacterial species from the most recent “WHO priority pathogens list for guiding R&D of new antibiotics” were chosen for this assay, consisting of Gram-positive Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus. aureus, Streptococcus. pneumoniae, and Gram-negative Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.. As an initial attempt, the lead compound CUHK430 showed antimicrobial activities against all the Gram positive pathogens. Extensive structural modification of CUHK430 was carried out. 109 novel chemical compounds were made in total, with their antimicrobial activities tested using microdilution assay. The results yielded some chemical derivatives with good range of effectiveness against Gram-positives, particularly in staphylococcal type strains ATCC® 25923 and 29213. Interestingly, there were recurring instances of compounds showing certain degree of antimicrobial activity against the Gram-negative pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC® 19606, which may complement prospects for their use in modern clinical settings. The compound(s) with best antimicrobial activity showed MIC 4 microgram/ml against Gram-positive pathogens, which has high potential to be further developed as antimicrobial drug candidate.

14165917.label: Major findings and research outcome
14165917.value: Upon completion of this proposed research, we managed to achieve all of the objectives. A sufficient amount of RNA polymerase was purified from Gram-positive model organism Bacillus subtilis and subject to cryoEM structural analysis. After single particle analysis, an initial model of RNA polymerase elongation complex was obtained at subnanometer resolution. A B. subtilis RNAP-NusA complex psedo-atomic model was made based on the cryoEM structure, and the model was in good agreement with published E. coli transcription complex structures. A pharmacophore model was updated using the structural information and was used for structural-based rational design for RNAP-NusA protein-protein interaction inhibitors. We designed and constructed a vector system for in vitro screening and characterization of protein-protein interaction inhibitors. In total 109 chemical compounds were made in this study, and their antimicrobial activity tested against a panel of Gram-postive and Gram-negative pathogens. A few of the compounds showed promising antimicrobial activities. Two conference posters and three journal articles were published based on the findings of this project, including a supplementary journal cover article in ACS Infectious Diseases. Another manuscript is in preparation. One student, Tsz Fung TSANG was graduated with an MPhil degree in September 2020. He was subsequently registered for further PhD studies.

14165917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14165917.value: In this research, novel bacterial transcription inhibitors were discovered by our group by structural-based rational design. The inhibitors showed promising antimicrobial activities against a panel of Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. After completion of this project, the optimal compounds will be subjected to investigations further down the stages of drug development, such as pharmacological and antimicrobial activity evaluations including the animal model studies. From this research, we expect to develop viable candidates for novel classes of antibiotics and contribute to a new era of antibiotic development. Techniques strengthened in this research proposal will contribute to the construction of a platform for antibiotic discovery targeting bacterial transcription.

14165917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14165917.value: The presence of “superbugs” (antibiotic-resistant bacteria) is causing re-emerging epidemics, which becomes a crisis both socially and economically worldwide. Therefore, antimicrobials with novel mode-of-action are in urgent need to combat infections resulted from the multi-drug resistant bacteria. In this research, small molecule inhibitors of bacterial transcription were discovered. The compounds have high potential for further development as novel antmicrobial agents. The information obtained from this proposal will provide the basis for the discovery and development of new classes of antimicrobial drugs with a unique mechanism of action. This will impact the society by providing exclusive therapeutic potentials against bacterial infectious diseases. The whole pack of research methodologies and expertise will foster a comprehensive platform for novel antimicrobial drug discovery.

14166017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14166017.value: In the management of patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding from non-variceal causes, endoscopic treatment and acid suppression are now the standard of care. Current endoscopic treatment in the form of either thermo-coagulation or clipping to the bleeding arteries is highly efficacious in the stopping bleeding. Unfortunately in 5 to 10% of patients, bleeding cannot be controlled during index endoscopy or recurs after initial hemostasis. These patients are often elderly with significant co-morbidities. Their bleeding lesions are large eroding into major sub-serosal arteries. In the few who need surgical salvage, mortality increases to around 30%. The Over-the-scope-Clip (OTSC) is a device, which allows endoscopists to capture a large amount of tissue and compress on the bleeding artery. The OTSC also has a high retention rate. Recurrent bleeding with the use of standard hemo-clips can occur because of their low retention rate. We reported the use of OTSC with a high success rate in a case series of patients with refractory bleeding after standard endoscopic treatment. We have also used OTSC in the treatment of bleeding from pseudo-aneurysm arising from large eroded arteries in ulcer base. A multicenter randomized controlled trial that compares OTSC to standard endoscopic treatment in the endoscopic treatment of refractory bleeding lesions has just been completed. The use of OTSC has been shown to be superior in achieving hemostatic control and reducing further bleeding. 14166017.label: Major findings and research outcome
14166017.value: We did a multicenter RCT that compared OTSC to standard endoscopic treatment in patients with non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The primary outcome was a 30-day bleeding free probability. 190 patients were randomized (OTSC 93, standard treatment 97). Analysis was by intention-to-treat. The 30-day bleeding free probability in OTSC group and standard treatment group was (90 of 93, 96.8%) and (83 of 97,85.4%) respectively (HR, 0.21; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.73; P=0.006) . Failure to control bleeding at first endoscopy (1 vs.6; OR, 0.16, 95%CI 0.02 to 1.4) and 30-day recurrent bleeding (2 vs.8; OR, 0.23, 95%CI 0.05 to 1.12) were lower in the OTSC group. In ulcers ≥10mm in size, OTSC reduced the rate of further bleeding (1 of 48 vs. 8 of 46; OR, 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.84). The 30-day re-intervention (2 vs. 8; p=0.138) and death did not differ significantly between the two groups (2 vs.4; p=0.438). The cost to avert further bleeds was cheaper with the use of OTSC. ICER was - USD$647 dollar. OTSC treatment can be considered as the first-line treatment for larger peptic ulcers and is cost-saving.

14166017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14166017.value: The trial findings will inform clinical practice and become treatment guidelines. In this RCT, further bleeds were observed in only 3 of 93 patients. The rate is the lowest seen among all endoscopic hemostatic methods. With an accompanying cost analysis, the OTSC was associated with cost-saving when compared to conventional methods. Given the limitation that the cost calculation was based on the Hong Kong Hospital Authority Gazette, the superiority in the control of bleeding and the reduced cost would suggest that OTSC should be used as the primary treatment in acute non-variceal bleeding causes. We used stratified randomization categorizing ulcers into several sizes. The larger benefit with the use of OTSC was observed in patients with ulcers 10 mm or greater in size. At least in these ulcers, OTSC should be used as the first treatment.

14167017.label: Realisation of objectives
14167017.value: Objective #1: To Investigate whether the interaction between integrin and Kindlin-2 is involved in mesoderm formation. We examined the expression pattern of kindlin2 throughout embryogenesis in X. laevis embryos and found strong kindlin2 staining in the neural crest (NC) at the mid-neurula stages and late-neurula stages. We found that depletion of kindlin2 by either morpholino antisense oligonucleotides (MOs) or the CRISPR/Cas9 technique inhibited the expression of NC specifier genes. Consistent with the observations in whole embryos, kindlin2 MOs inhibited NC formation induced by wnt3a and chordin in the animal cap assay. We also found that the neural plate border specification is affected by MO-mediated knockdown of kindlin2. The expression of pax3, one of the specifiers of the neural plate border, in kindlin2 morphant was decreased. As Kindlin2 is renowned for its ability to activate integrins, we next examined whether the role of Kindlin2 in NC formation is dependent on its integrin-activating ability. A previous report has revealed that the substitution of human kindlin-2 QW amino acids by AA amino acids mutant (kindlin-2 QW/AA mutant) failed to bind integrin. We generated the integrin-binding deficient mutant of Xenopus kindlin2 using PCR-based mutagenesis. We injected one dorsal blastomere of X. laevis embryos at the four-cell stage with kindlin2 MO, or kindlin2 MO1 combined with mRNA of either Xenopus kindlin2 QW/AA or mRNA of the mouse kindlin2 L675E mutant, which also fails to localize to focal adhesion and activate integrins. Whole-mount in situ hybridization showed that, similar to the kindlin2 WT, both Xenopus kindlin2 QW/AA and mouse kindlin2 L675E partially rescued the kindlin2 MO-induced decreased expression of the NC marker genes foxd3 and snail2. Taken together, these results suggest that the role of Kindlin2 in NC specification is independent of its integrin-activating ability. Furthermore, this function seems to be conserved across species, as the mouse integrin-binding-defective mutant reversed the kindlin2 deficiency-induced NC defects in Xenopus embryos. Kindlin2 deficiency inhibits NC induction and interrupts the FGF signaling pathway in animal cap explants. We found that the knockdown of kindlin2 suppressed the paraxial mesodermal marker gene myod. The animal caps were microinjected with efgf mRNA, which induced the expression of the FGF signaling target genes xbra, egr1, and myod. The expression of these target genes was significantly decreased in the animal caps microinjected with efgf and kindlin2 MOs. Moreover, the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) induced by the injection of efgf mRNA into animal caps was also suppressed in the presence of kindlin2 MOs. Collectively, these results suggest that the knockdown of kindlin2 interrupts FGF signaling during NC specification. Notably, the expression of FGFR1-FLAG was enhanced in HEK293T cells co-transfected with kindlin2-Myc compared to that in HEK293 cells transfected with FGFR1-FLAG alone. We measured FGFR1 protein stability following inhibition of protein synthesis by cycloheximide (CHX). Western blotting revealed that the FGFR1-FLAG protein level was markedly increased when kindlin2-Myc was overexpressed in HEK293T cells treated with CHX, suggesting that Kindlin2 plays a role in stabilizing FGFR1. Furthermore, we found that the FGF signaling pathway was interrupted by kindlin2 MOs in animal cap explants and that Kindlin2 can enhance the level of FGFR1 protein. In addition, integrin activation-deficient kindlin2 mutants also increased the FGFR1 protein level and rescued the phenotypes induced by kindlin2 MOs in Xenopus embryos. Furthermore, overexpression of kindlin2 QW/AA, like that of wild-type Kindlin2, enhanced the level of both exogenous and endogenous FGFR1 protein in Xenopus embryos, suggesting that the integrin-activating ability of Kindlin2 is not involved in the Kindlin2-mediated regulation of FGFR1 Objective #2: To investigate the regulatory mechanism by which Kindlin-2 mediates the Nodal signaling pathway during embryonic development. Kindlin2 mediates the Nodal signaling transduction and interacts with Smad3. To investigate how Kindlin2 mediates the Nodal signaling transduction. The mRNA of either kindlin2, nr1, and the mixture of both was injected into the animal pole of two blastomeres at the two-cell stage. Animal caps were dissected at stage 9. After culture in the medium at room temperature for four hours, ten animal caps from each experimental group were dissected for qPCR. Brachyury (Xbra), chordin (chd), Goosecoid (gsc), vegT and sox17 β are target genes of the Nodal signal. The co-injection of kindlin2 and nr1 can enhance the expression of the aforementioned gene induced by xnr1 mRNA, suggesting kindlin2 potentiates nodal signal transduction. The initial step of the Nodal signaling activation involves four proteins: type I receptor, type II receptor, smad2, and smad3. Thus, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) to examine whether Kindlin2 interacts with the major components of Nodal signaling. HEK293T cells were transiently transfected with the plasmids. After 48 hours post-transfection, proteins were extracted for Co-IP assay and analyzed by western blot. The results showed that exogenous kindlin2 doesn’t bind with Nodal type I, Nodal type II receptor, and Smad2, but physically interacts with Smad3. Objective #3: To identify downstream target genes regulated by Kindlin-2 during embryonic development. We utilized the CRISPR/Cas9 technique to disrupt kindlin2 in X. tropicalis. A kindlin2 mutant X. tropicalis line with 10-bp deletion was established. This mutation introduces a premature stop codon to the kindlin2 open reading frame, leading to a truncated form of kindlin2 missing most of the functional domains. After being raised to adults, two heterozygous kindlin2 mutant frogs were crossed to obtain the homozygous k2−/− embryos. When the offspring developed to around stage 16, two batches of RNA samples prepared separately from wild-type and kindlin2−/− embryos were employed for RNA-seq. A total of 203 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) have been identified and among which several candidates of interest will be selected for further investigation, of which 110 genes were downregulated, and 93 were upregulated. Among them, 140 transcripts have their functions known/predicted, allowing further categorizing and interpretation. Knockout of Kindlin2 affects the expression of genes related to extracellular matrix modification or adhesion. It is noteworthy that both col6a1 and col6a2 are downregulated in K2-/- mutant embryos, which encodes for alpha1 (VI) and alpha2 (VI) structural units of Collagen VI, respectively. Knockout of kindlin2 also resulted in the expression alteration of several matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs); for example, matrix metallopeptidase 21(mmp21), a Xenopus-specific paralog, was downregulated. The Not gene is downregulated in kindlin2 mutant embryos. Not is activated by the Nodal signaling pathway. In zebrafish, Xenopus, and mouse embryos, Not is expressed in the Spemann-Mangold organizer at gastrula stages and in the notochord at neurula stages. Another gene we detected that interferes with axial determination is growth differentiation factor 11 (gdf11). GDF11 has been implicated in inducing mesoderm in early development and anterior-posterior patterning of the axial skeleton.

14167017.label: Major findings and research outcome
14167017.value: Kindlin2 is widely expressed in mouse embryos, and its absence causes lethality at the peri-implantation stage due to the failure to trigger integrin activation. In our previous study, we suggested that Kindlin2 regulates nodal signaling. In line with this observation. The physical interaction between Kindlin2 with Smad2, but not Smad3, was detected by co-immunoprecipitation. We used clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 to disrupt the kindlin2 gene and establish the mutant line in X. tropicalis. RNA-Seq analysis using RNA extracts from kindlin2 mutant embryo and wild type embryos at stage 16 (neurula stage). A total of 203 DEGs were identified in this study. Among them, 140 transcripts have their functions known/predicted, allowing further categorizing and interpretation. A considerable number of genes have been found to be associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) modification or cell-ECM/cell-cell adhesion. Additionally, another group of target genes was found to be associated with notochord/spinal cord development, e.g., the tmod2 and the not gene. This provided new evidence for the regulatory role of Kindlin2 to Nodal signaling during embryonic development. In addition, we found Kindlin2 is essential for neural crest (NC) formation in Xenopus embryos. Loss-of-function assays performed with kindlin2-specific morpholino antisense oligos (MOs) or CRISPR/Cas9 in Xenopus embryos severely inhibit the specification of NC. Moreover, integrin-binding deficient mutants of Kindlin2 rescued the phenotype caused by the loss of kindlin2, suggesting that the function of kindlin2 during NC specification is independent of integrins. Mechanistically, we found that Kindlin2 regulates the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) pathway and promotes the stability of FGF receptor 1. Our study reveals a novel function of Kindlin2 in regulating FGF signaling pathway and provides mechanistic insights into the function of Kindlin2 during NC specification.

14167017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14167017.value: We found that Kindlin2 is required for both Nodal and FGF signaling, yet it is not unknown how the two signaling pathways interacted by kindlin2. In Xenopus embryo, Kindlin2 physically interacts with Smad3, but not Smad2. It is worthwhile to investigate the mechanism of how Kindlin2 differentiates the two Smad proteins. The Kindlin2 is required for maintaining the stability of FGFR1, however, Kindlin2 does not physically interact with FGFR1. We intend to further delineate the underlying mechanism as to how Kindlin2 regulates the ubiquitination of FGFR1. When all preliminary data are ready, we will apply for a GRF grant to extend our understanding of the regulation of FGFR1 by Kindlin2.

14167017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14167017.value: Kindlin2 is an essential focal adhesion protein required for integrin activation. Loss of Kindlin2 results in peri-implantation lethality in mice. The neural crest (NC) comprises a transient cell population induced at the neural plate border that is unique to vertebrate embryos. NC cells are multipotent stem cells. that give rise to a large variety of cell types, and the cranial NC cells preferentially contribute to mesenchymal cell types of facial cartilage and bone. We found that Kindlin2 is required for NC formation. It mediates the FGFR1 stability during this process. To delineate Kindlin2 function during embryonic development, we established the kindlin2 mutant X. tropicalis line and performed RNA Sequencing analysis in kindlin2 mutant embryos and wild type of Xenopus tropicalis. Total 203 genes showing differential gene expression were identified in kindlin2 mutant X. tropicalis embryos that represent a useful resource for understanding the function of Kindlin2 from a developmental view. Collectively our study uncovered a novel function of Kindlin2 in NC formation via regulating the FGF signaling pathway during embryogenesis. This study extends our understanding of how cell-ECM adhesions control early embryonic development.

14167817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14167817.value: Motor control is one of the most important functions of the nervous system, and is critical for the daily lives. Understanding the neurobiological basis of motor skill and its acquisition is not only a fundamental question in neuroscience but also has significant clinical implications, as many nervous system diseases result in motor deficits that highly incapacitate the sufferers. In recent years, the motor cortex has emerged not only as a brain area that directly controls motor execution, but could also play an active role in learning new motor skills, as well as manifestation of motor symptoms in some brain diseases. Past efforts in understanding the cortical mechanism of motor learning has focused exclusively on the recruitment of neurons and the changes of their spatiotemporal dynamical properties during the process. However, with substantial evidence in recent years suggesting that astrocytes can participate and play a critical role in regulating synaptic transmission as well as plasticity, we have obtained convincing empirical evidence strongly supporting that astrocytes in the motor cortex are functionally involved in the process of motor skill acquisition. To fully elucidate the relationship between astrocyte, neuronal plasticity and motor learning, we propose to examine in a comprehensive manner the functions of astrocytes during motor learning, and also the effects of inhibiting their function during the process. We will first examine the structural plasticity of astrocytes and their calcium activities during motor learning. We will then investigate the role of astrocytic activities on neuronal plasticity during motor learning, This will be achieved by determining the casual relationship between astrocytic activity and neuronal activity and the role of astrocytic activity on reorganization of motor representation in motor cortex after skill learning. To achieve these objectives, we will utilise a custom-designed multi-photon microscope along with a lever manipulation system that can train and assess their forelimb motor skill. Furthermore, we will test the hypothesis that cortical dopamine plays a role in modulating the activities of astrocytes critical for motor learning. To address this question, we will make use of a dopamine receptor gene knockdown strategy. 14167817.label: Realisation of objectives
14167817.value: There are three major objectives of the present proposal. To realise these objectives, we established the necessary imaging platform as well as viral tools. Results of the experiments help confirm or refute the hypotheses put forward. Overall, the results support the hypothesis that astrocytes in the motor cortex play a critical role in facilitating motor learning. At the same time, our results implicate that dopamine's facilitatory action on motor learning is not via its action on astrocytes but rather on neurons directly. Objective 1:To investigate the structural and functional plasticity of astrocytes during motor learning. Under this objective, two series of experiments were conducted. First, we performed histological assessment on mice brain tissues following motor learning. Our results demonstrated that astrocytes in the primary motor cortex (M1) area exhibit structural plasticity after motor learning, manifested by increased astrocytic volume, enhanced tripartite formation, and elevated expression of specific glutamate transporters. In addition, we revealed differences in astrocyte-specific glutamate transporter expression between superficial layer 1 and layer 2/3 after motor training. Moreover, morphological changes of astrocytes are not limited to major branches of astrocytes but have also been found in secondary branchlets and arborized leaflets. To provide more detailed quantitative measures of the fine structural changes of astrocytes, we conducted electron microscopy to quantify tripartite astrocytic volume and mitochondrial morphology, and our results confirmed the increased astrocyte volume and enlarged mitochondrial architecture within the peri-synaptic astrocyte processes. Together, the results in this part have revealed that astrocytes in M1 undergo abundant structural changes following motor learning, supporting their active roles during the process. In the second set of experiments, we established a 2-photon imaging platform suitable for studying astrocytic calcium activities in head-fixed mice. By expressing calcium reporter (GCaMP) in astrocytes specifically, we revealed a great amount of astrocytic Ca2+ events extracted, indicating vigorous Ca2+ activities within M1 during motor learning process. We also found that the total number of Ca2+ events which represents the overall level of Ca2+ activity among different training sessions were changing dynamically, manifested as a significant increase during the early stage of task training and then gradually decreased in the following sessions. By examining the spatiotemporal distributions of these Ca2+ signals, we further demonstrated that although the number of astrocytic Ca2+ events decreased in the later stage of motor learning, these events have formed a temporal pattern more centring around the movement window along with training progress. These results confirm functional plasticity of the astrocytes during motor learning process. Objective 2: To investigate the role of astrocytic activity during motor learning Under this objective, we employed the Gi-coupled and Gq-coupled DREADDs, both of which could evoke Ca2+ elevations in astrocytes, to manipulate astrocytic activity in the forelimb regions of M1. Our results demonstrated that both Gi- and Gq- DREADDs led to impairments in the early stage of motor learning. The average response time of mice was not affected by these manipulations indicating that disturbance in M1 astrocytes did not influence either the process of cognition-motor transition or the initiation of movement during motor learning. By more detailed examination of the lever trajectories during task training, we further revealed that Gi-DREADD hindered the effective suppression of unnecessary movements during trial intervals, while Gq- DREADD had a more general influence on the optimization of motor strategy both during movement and after movement. Since the optimization of motor strategy during motor learning was accompanied by the reorganization of reproducible neuronal firing patterns within motor cortex, we hypothesized that astrocytes may participate in the internal connections within neural circuits which drive movements. Consistently, our imaging results from M1 neurons under astrocytic DREADD manipulations have shown a deceleration in the refinement process of movement related neurons especially during the early stage of motor learning. Together we have provided evidence that cortical astrocyte activities are essential for the normal functioning of skill acquisition during motor learning. Objective 3: To investigate the role of cortical dopamine on astrocyte activity and plasticity In this objective, we aim to test the hypothesis that dopamine receptors expressed by astrocytes participate in the function of astrocytes in motor learning. To this end, we have constructed astrocyte-specific known down viruses with respect to dopamine D1 and D2 receptors. However, although in vitro experiments confirmed the efficacy of the viruses in knocking down dopamine receptors in astrocytes, administration of the viruses in vivo did not significantly affect the performance of the animals in the lever-pushing learning task. This result suggests that the critical role of astrocytes during motor learning may be independent of the modulation by dopamine, which may contribute to other functions of the M1.

14167817.label: Major findings and research outcome
14167817.value: There are several major findings related to the 3 major objectives of the proposal. First, concerning the structural and functional plasticity of astrocytes during motor learning, we confirmed by histological and calcium imaging techniques of the presence of significant changes in astrocyte morphology and calcium activities during early stages of motor skill acquisition. We demonstrated increased astrocytic volume, enhanced tripartite formation, and elevated expression of specific glutamate transporters. Also, imaging results reveal that the total number of Ca2+ events which represents the overall level of Ca2+ activity among different training sessions were changing dynamically, manifested as a significant increase during the early stage of task training. Second, with respect to the role of astrocytes in motor learning, we intervened the functions of the astrocytes via chemogenetic approach and confirmed impairment of motor learning ability in the early stage of motor learning following the intervention. This result confirms a critical role of astrocyte activities in initial stage of motor learning. Finally, to test the hypothesis that dopamine receptors expressed by astrocytes participate in the function of astrocytes in motor learning, we constructed astrocyte-specific knock down viruses with respect to dopamine receptors. Administration of the viruses in vivo did not significantly affect the performance of the animals in the lever-pushing learning task. This result suggests that the critical role of astrocytes during motor learning may be independent of the modulation by dopamine, which may contribute to other functions of the M1. On the other hand, dopamine may act directly on principal neurons in the motor cortex in facilitating motor learning. Taken all together, our results support an important role of astrocytes in motor learning which is largely independent of the action of dopamine on these cells.

14167817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14167817.value: The present project lays a good foundation for further exploring the mechanisms underlying motor learning, an important question not only in basic neuroscience but also has clinical implications. To this end, there are further questions that could be asked. For example, how do activities of astrocytes affect the plasticity of principal pyramidal neurons? What is the exact role of dopamine in facilitating motor learning? These are questions that will be addressed by the research team in future studies and grant applications.

14167817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14167817.value: Motor control is one of the most important functions of the nervous system, and is critical for the daily lives. Understanding the neurobiological basis of motor skill and its acquisition is not only a fundamental question in neuroscience but also has significant clinical implications, as many nervous system diseases result in motor deficits that highly incapacitate the sufferers. Past efforts in understanding the cortical mechanism of motor learning has focused exclusively on the recruitment of neurons and the changes of their spatiotemporal dynamical properties during the process. Our study reveals that astrocytes, the long believed supporting cells of the brain, also participate and play a critical role in the process of motor skill acquisition. Our results not only ascertain the importance of astrocytes in motor learning and significantly advance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms, but also have clinical implications in the search of better treatment for different motor disorders.

14168417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14168417.value: Advance care planning (ACP) has been widely advocated to empower patients to plan for end-of-life care before they lose their decisional capacity. The purpose of ACP is to prepare patients for the anticipated difficult decisions, and to this end, a number of ACP programmes have been developed. The findings showed that these programmes have positive yet limited effects in increasing the uptake of ACP behaviours, such as clarifying their care preferences, communicating their care preferences with family carers, and signing advance directives. Evidence suggests that patients often remain hesitant and skeptical about planning ahead for end-of-life care. Nevertheless, little attention has been given to strategies for promoting patients’ readiness to participate in ACP. This proposed study is designed to test the effects of motivational interviewing (MI) in increasing the uptake of ACP behaviours among patients with palliative care needs. MI is a person-centered counselling approach to work with patients through ambivalence that impedes behavioural changes. A randomised controlled trial with repeated blinded outcome assessment will be conducted to assess the effects of a MI-tailored ACP (MI–ACP) programme on palliative care patients in two hospitals. A total of 204 patients will be recruited from two palliative care teams and randomly assigned to experimental and control groups. The patients in the experimental group will receive a MI–ACP programme facilitated by a trained nurse, whereas the patients in the control group will receive usual care. Primary outcome is the behavioural changes in ACP. Secondary outcomes are perceived stress, decisional conflict and quality of life. Study outcomes will be measured at baseline, 1 month and 3 months after enrolment. Intention to treat principle will be applied in all quantitative analyses. In addition to t-test and chi-square test for the comparison of outcome variables between the groups, generalized linear mixed models will be used to examine intra-correlated repeated measures data by comparing the outcome variables. Individual semi-structured interviews will be conducted with a purposive sample of patients to understand their experiences with the intervention and the perceived impacts. This study is the first to test the effects of MI to motivate patients to participate in end-of-life care planning. This innovative approach will potentially provide significant practical implications in communication strategies and mechanism that improve readiness of patients to adopt ACP behaviours.

14168417.label: Realisation of objectives
14168417.value: Objectives 1 and 2 were achieved through a randomised controlled trial. Up till December 2019, a total of 204 patients were recruited from palliative care units of two hospitals in Hong Kong. The participation rate was 77.9% and the attrition rate was 28.9%. Their mean age was 74.9 ± 10.8 years. Two thirds were male (68.0%). Most of them were living with family (82.0%), had primary education (70.1%) and were diagnosed with cancer (79.6%). A specific motivational interviewing advance care planning protocol was developed to ensure consistency in intervention delivery. The intervention was delivered an experienced counselor. The intervention effects were evaluated in terms of readiness for advance care planning behaviours, decisional conflict, stress and health-related quality of life. Objective 3 was achieved by individual qualitative interviews with 20 participants with different demographic characteristics and responses to the intervention in the experimental group.

14168417.label: Major findings and research outcome
14168417.value: Advance care planning aims to empower patients with skills and knowledge necessary in end-of-life planning. In this study, motivational interviewing was a strategy to support individual through ambivalence and resistance across different stages of change. Through motivational interviewing-tailored advance care planning, significant improvements were noted in patients’ readiness for advance care planning behaviours, including “assigning a proxy”, “communicating end-of-life care preferences with family members”, “communicating end-of-life care preferences with healthcare providers” and “signing an advance directives” in the intervention group between baseline and one month after intervention, and between baseline and three months after intervention. There was no significant group difference in stress and quality of life at the follow up assessments, meaning that the conversation would not result in adverse outcomes. Qualitative findings suggested that some patients were unaware of the concept of advance care planning and thus were resistant to think about end-of-life care issues initially. The underlying principle of advance care planning is to respect individual’s right to self-determination in future care. This situation leads to a question whether it is ethical to motivate people to engage in end-of-life care conversation if they adopt avoidance as a coping strategy. Some patients may not want to have such conversation although literature and guidelines generally suggest the importance of early initiation of advance care planning. The discrepancy between patients’ and clinicians’ values towards advance care planning result in a tension between autonomy and beneficence. Therefore, this study demonstrated the effects of motivational interviewing -tailored for increasing patients’ readiness for advance care planning. Despite the positive outcomes, it remained challenging to initiate the conversation if the patients had limited awareness towards advance care planning. The experience of the study suggested that merely an intervention is inadequate to cultivate a culture for advance care planning in the community.

14168417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14168417.value: An advance care planning programme driven by motivational interviewing was developed to support individual to identify ambivalence and resistance in end-of-life care planning. Motivational interviewing is a counseling approach derived from the Transtheoretical Model for behavioural change. Motivational interviewing enables the clinician and patients work together to resolve ambivalence though several techniques, including reflection, support autonomy and open-ended questions, enable them to realize their ambivalence. A specific protocol developed for this study can be disseminated for wider use in other patient populations. The quantitative and qualitative findings have been presented in international conferences. Research proposals on engaging people with early dementia and their family members was submitted and developing a game for motivating older adults to participate in advance care planning was submitted for HMRF 2018 and the British Council Social Innovation Research Collaboration Platform 2019 respectively.

14168417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14168417.value: Advance care planning is an ongoing communication process for patients to share their end-of-life care preferences with their significant others and health professionals. However, patients usually would like to avoid such discussion due to its sensitive nature. This study aims to promote advance care planning in palliative care patients using motivational interviewing, a counselling skill which has been widely applied to support people to identify ambivalence to behavior changes in chronic disease self-management. In this study, around 200 palliative care patients were randomly allocated to either intervention group to receive the advance care planning programme conducted by a trained counsellor or control group to receive usual care. Findings showed that patients in the intervention group reported a significantly higher level of readiness to engage in various ACP behaviours one-month and three-month after the intervention, whereas such changes were not noted in the control group. On the other hand, the stress level and quality of life reported by both groups were comparable in the follow up assessments. This study provides evidence that motivational interviewing can help to prompt patients to contemplate end-of-life care issues, without inducing negative impacts.
