14173917.label: Major findings and research outcome
14173917.value: Bisphosphonates (BPs)-associated atypical femoral fractures (AFFs) present with impaired fracture healing, yet the underlying mechanism is unclear, which prevents the development of effective therapy. Peripheral sensory nerve has been shown to regulate fracture healing via releasing neuropeptides. Here we show that long-term BPs pre-treatment leads to fracture non-union in rats characterized by reduced expression of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP, a predominant type of neuropeptides) and abundant fibrous tissues in the non-bridged fracture gap, mimicking clinical AFFs. By using single cell mRNA-sequence, long-term BPs treatment was identified to promote transition of progenitor cells into a specific cluster of fibroblasts that actively deposit dense extracellular matrix (ECM) to prevent fracture callus bridging. Administration of exogenous CGRP at early stages of fracture repair, in contrast, eliminates the ECM-secreting fibroblast cluster, attenuates fibrogenesis, and facilitates callus bridging, suggesting CGRP is a promising agent to facilitate AFF repair. Accordingly, we have developed an innovative magnesium (Mg) containing hybrid intramedullary nail fixation system (Mg-IMN) that effectively stimulates rat fracture healing via elevating CGRP synthesis and release. Such device optimizes the fracture healing in BPs-pretreated rats, comparable to direct administration of CGRP. These findings address the indispensable role of CGRP in advancing the healing of AFFs and develop translational strategies to accelerate AFF healing by taking advantage of the CGRP-stimulating effect of Mg-based biodegradable orthopedic implant. The study also indicates fibrosis could be targeted by augmenting CGRP expression to accelerate fracture healing even under challenging scenarios where fibroblasts are aberrantly activated.

14173917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14173917.value: 1. The angiogenic effect of CGRP in bone regeneration needs to be further studied. 2. The counteractive effect of Mg ions on the inhibitory effect of BPs on CGRP expression in DRG is worth further investigation. 3. The role of aberrant fibrosis as a universal factor impending bone regeneration is to be elucidated. 4. The clinical translational value of Mg-IMN in treating AFF patients. Points 1-3 will be addressed experimentally; point 4 will be implemented as clinical trials in Hong Kong and mainland China.

14173917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14173917.value: Bisphosphonates (BPs)-associated atypical femoral fractures (AFFs) show impaired fracture healing. The present study reveals that BPs treatment suppresses nerve fiber growth in the fracture callus, resulting in reduced neuropeptide CGRP expression and impairs fracture union by generating aberrant fibrous tissues at the fracture gap. A translational fracture fixation device, i.e. magnesium containing intramedullary nail (Mg-IMN), was developed to promote AFF healing in rats by stimulating endogenous CGRP expression in the fracture callus, resulting in reduced fibrosis. Such previously un-recognized anti-fibrotic effect of CGRP holds promise for translating Mg-IMN into clinical scenario to treat AFF patients. In addition, eliminating fibroblasts by magnesium-based bimetal could be a novel therapeutic approach to accelerate fracture healing/bone regeneration where over-activated fibroblasts are involved.

14174017.label: Realisation of objectives
14174017.value: Problems encountered: progress of this project was severely interrupted and delayed due to the following events: 1) In Nov 2019, due to “social movement”, CUHK was suddenly shut down. Ongoing animal experiments were abruptly terminated. Several batches of diabetic mice lined up for experiments had to be culled. 2) In Jan 2020, the PhD student responsible for this project went to Hubei during Chinese New Year. Due to outbreak of COVID-19, Hubei province was lockdown. The graduate student did not return to CUHK until late May 2020. 3) From Jan to May 2020, in response to COVID-19 epidemic, CUHK implemented work-from-home arrangement, and our School imposed tight restriction on the number of people and working hours in the laboratory, thus it was infeasible to induce diabetic mice and conducted timed mating for embryo collection. 4) In July 2020, there was an outbreak of Mouse Hepatitis Virus (MHV) in the Animal Holding Core (AHC) of our School. AHC requested us to immediately suspend all breeding and culled all our mouse stock, which included several batches of streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice and mice fed with special diet for type 2 diabetic embryopathy study. Due to a delay in complete eradication of MHV in AHC, we could not get access to a “clean” (certified MHV-free) room to restart our animal experiments until Feb 2021. 5) After eradication of MHV, AHC has imposed new regulations that mice used for breeding have to be housed in individually ventilated cage (IVC) instead of open top cage. Unexpectedly, with this change in housing conditions, over 95% diabetic mice exhibited early pregnancy loss before embryo implantation, and the diet-induced type 2 diabetic mice exhibited very poor pregnancy rate. Thus, collection of embryonic kidney samples had spanned over a long period, which greatly limited the number and type of experiments that we could conduct. Despite the above-mentioned difficulties and challenges, we have achieved the project objectives as follow: Objective 1: To determine whether a decrease in RA concentration in the kidney plays a primary role in impaired nephrogenesis in embryos exposed to diabetes, we first employed an in vitro approach to replenish the kidney with RA, with the prediction that this would rescue nephrogenesis. Kidney rudiments explanted from non-diabetic mice at gestational day (GD) 11.5 were cultured in medium containing 30 mM D-glucose (high glucose) or 5 mM D-glucose (normal glucose) supplemented with varying dosages (10-8 and 10-7 M) of RA. Two days after culture, mRNA levels of downstream targets of RA signaling Ret and Wnt4, which are key regulators of ureteric bud (UB) branching morphogenesis and early nephrogenesis respectively, were determined by real-time qRT-PCR. Six days after culture, explants were subjected to staining of ureteric epithelium and nephric tubules to assess the number of UB branch tips and nephrons being generated. RA signaling is mediated via nuclear RA receptors (RAR). To decipher whether the rescue effect of exogenously applied RA was mediated via RA signaling, RA was replaced by varying dosages (10-6 and 10-5 M) of TTNPB, a potent pan-RAR agonist. After 2 and 6 days of culture, kidney explants were subjected to analysis of expression of RA target genes, and quantification of UB branch tips and nephric tubules. Next, we investigated the effect of in vivo replenishment of RA via oral feeding of streptozotocin-induced type 1 diabetic and non-diabetic ICR pregnant mice with 20 mg/kg bodyweight of RA at GD12 and GD13, which covered the period of RA deficiency found in embryonic kidneys from diabetic mice. Embryos were collected 3 hours post-injection for measurement of RA concentrations and expression of RA target genes. Glomerular number in kidneys of near-term fetuses at GD18 was counted to determine whether replenishment of RA could correct nephron deficit in fetuses of diabetic mice. Objective 2: To investigate the effect of alleviation of oxidative stress on RA homeostasis in the embryonic kidney, streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice were subjected to dietary supplementation with 0.15% (wt/wt) vitamin E succinate (VitE diet) or without supplementation (Con diet) starting from first day of pregnancy. At GD12, embryos were collected for measurement of 8-isoprostane, an oxidative stress biomarker. Kidneys were subjected to analysis of mRNA levels of antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 2 (Sod2). RA homeostasis in the kidney was assessed in terms of RA synthesizing activity by the enzyme retinal dehydrogenase (Raldh), and endogenous RA concentrations, which was measured by using a highly sensitive RA-reporter cell line (please refer to Section 8 No. 1). Expression levels of RA target genes were measured to determine whether RA signaling could be restored after alleviation of oxidative stress. As proposed, we tested whether antioxidants other than vitamin E could exert similar rescue effects. To overcome the difficulties in conducting studies using diabetic mice as mentioned earlier, we changed to use an vitro approach by culturing kidney explants in high glucose (30 mM D-glucose) and normal glucose (5 mM D-glucose) conditions supplemented with or without 10-7 M antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Using similar methods of analysis, 2 days after culture, explants were collected for measurement of RA concentrations, RA synthesizing activity by Raldh enzyme and mRNA levels of genes related to oxidative stress and RA target genes. Furthermore, 6 days after culture, explants were collected for staining of ureteric and nephric tubules epithelium to assess extent of ureteric branching and nephron generation. Objective 3: To determine whether there are similar RA-related changes in the developing kidney exposed to type 2 diabetes, we employed a mouse model of obese type 2 diabetes by feeding female ICR mice with a high-fat diet containing 60kcal% fat starting from 5 weeks of age for 15 weeks, while mice fed a matched control diet containing 10kcal% fat served as control. Prior to mating, mice were subjected to insulin tolerance test (ITT) and glucose tolerance test (GTT) to confirm that they exhibited elevated fasting blood glucose levels, and had developed insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance, which are characteristic features of type 2 diabetes. Pregnancies were obtained by mating with normal male mice. The original plan was to conduct a range of studies including measurement of oxidative stress, RA homeostasis and nephrogenesis in the kidney. However, due to limited availability of embryos as mentioned, we had to narrow the scope of study, and focused on determining the retinol concentrations in the kidney, and studying the expression of a panel of genes related to RA synthesis and catabolism, signal transduction, cellular bioavailability, downstream targets of RA signaling crucial for kidney development, oxidative stress and apoptosis. Objective 4: To determine whether findings from animal studies can be translated to humans, we examined human fetal kidney tissues obtained from Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in Prince of Wales Hospital. Seven pairs of gestational week-matched samples from pregnancies complicated by pregestational type 1 (n=4) or type 2 diabetes (n=3) and normal uncomplicated pregnancies (n=7) were available for the study. These kidney samples from 8-14 gestational week were at early stage of nephrogenesis, similar to mouse kidney development at around GD12-14. Since these samples were not protected from light when collected, they were not suitable for measurement of RA concentrations as RA is highly light-sensitive. As the quantity of tissue in some samples was not sufficient for conducting multiple analyses, we focused on studying expressions of a panel of RA-, oxidative stress- and apoptosis-related genes using real-time qRT-PCR.

Previous studies show that oxidative stress can suppress embryonic RA synthesis. To determine whether an increase in oxidative stress leads to inhibition of RA synthesis and a decrease in RA concentration in the kidney of embryos of diabetic mice, our second objective is to test whether alleviating oxidative stress via maternal supplementation with antioxidant can normalize RA synthesis, restore RA concentration and enhance nephrogenesis in the kidney of embryos of diabetic mice.

To determine whether there are RA-related changes in the kidney of embryos of type 2 diabetic pregnancy similar to that in type 1 diabetic pregnancy, our third objective is to employ a diet-induced mouse model of type 2 diabetes for examining vitamin A and RA concentrations in the maternal serum; and oxidative stress, RA homeostasis and nephrogenesis in the embryonic kidneys.

To determine whether our findings obtained from animal studies may similarly occur in humans, our fourth objective is to compare RA concentrations and the expression of genes associated with RA signalling and oxidative stress between kidneys of human embryos of type 1 or type 2 diabetic and non-diabetic pregnancies.

14174017.label: Major findings and research outcome
14174017.value: Results are shown in Figures 1-7 in Section 8 No 2. Objective 1: RA added to kidney explants cultured in high glucose upregulated Ret and Wnt4 [Fig. 1A], and increased ureteric branching [Fig. 1B, 1C] and nephric tubules generation [Fig. 1B, 1D]. Addition of pan-RAR agonist TTNPB had similar effects [Fig. 2A-D]. Maternal supplementation with RA could raise RA levels [Fig. 3A], and upregulated Ret and Wnt4 expressions in embryonic kidneys [Fig. 3C] without changing blood glucose levels of mother mice [Fig. 3B]. Notably, in near-term fetuses of diabetic mice, glomerular number was markedly increased [Fig. 3D, 3E], such that nephron deficit caused by maternal diabetes was corrected. Objective 2: Maternal dietary supplementation with vitamin E significantly alleviated oxidative stress [Fig. 4A] and upregulated antioxidant enzyme expression in embryonic kidneys of diabetic mice at GD12 [Fig. 4B], without affecting maternal blood glucose levels [Fig. 4C]. Concomitantly, there was a significant increase in RA synthesizing activity [Fig. 4D] and RA concentrations [Fig. 4E], and upregulation of Ret and Wnt4 [Fig. 4F]. Glomerular number was markedly increased [Fig. 4G]. Addition of antioxidant NAC to alleviate oxidative stress in kidney explants cultured under high glucose conditions [Fig. 5A] similarly restored RA homeostasis [Fig. 5B, 5C] and signaling [Fig. 5D], and increased ureteric branching [Fig. 5E, 5G] and nephron generation [Fig. 5F, 5G]. Objective 3: Mice fed with high-fat diet for 15 weeks showed marked bodyweight gain [Fig. 6A] and characteristic features of type 2 diabetes, including insulin resistance [Fig. 6C], impaired glucose tolerance [Fig. 6E] and significant elevation in blood glucose [Fig. 6B, 6D]. While there was no difference in maternal serum retinol levels [Fig. 6F], the findings of prominent reduction in retinol concentrations [Fig. 6G] and obvious changes in a panel of RA-related genes [Fig. 6H-M] suggest that RA-associated pathways are dysregulated in kidneys of embryos of type 2 diabetic pregnancy. Oxidative stress is probably increased [Fig. 6N, 6O]. Objective 4: Human fetal kidney tissues from diabetic pregnancies showed significantly lower levels of expression in RA synthesizing enzymes [Fig. 7A], but higher levels of RA catabolic enzymes [Fig. 7B] in comparison to non-diabetic pregnancies at the same gestational week. The trend of changes in a panel of RA- [Fig. 7C-F], oxidative stress- [Fig. 7G] and apoptosis-related genes [Fig. 7H] is similar to that found in embryonic kidneys of diabetic mice [Fig. 6], which suggests that dysregulation of RA-associated pathways and increase in oxidative stress similarly occur in humans.

14174017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14174017.value: Findings of this project have unraveled a causal link between dysregulation of retinoic acid (RA) homeostasis and signaling, and reduced nephron generation in kidneys of embryos exposed to maternal diabetes. This link not only shed light on a possible mechanism of fetal origin of chronic kidney disease in offspring of diabetic pregnancies, but has much wider implications. Babies born to diabetic mothers are more prone to develop various diseases such as diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular disease, hypertension and chronic kidney disease in adulthood. However, the mechanism underlying prenatal programming of these adult diseases remains poorly understood. In particular, the offspring frequently develop several of these diseases, which suggests that a common denominator may be disturbed in the embryo exposed to diabetes in utero. RA is a master regulator in many developmental processes, such as differentiation of pancreatic islets for insulin secretion and the brown adipose tissue for energy balance. Further studies should be conducted to determine whether dysregulation of RA is a fundamental mechanism that affects development of various organs and thereby predisposes offspring of diabetic pregnancies to multiple disorders. These findings can pave the way for the development of in utero therapeutic interventions to reduce risk of diseases in adulthood.

14174017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14174017.value: Babies born to mothers with pregestational diabetes have reduced number of filtrating units (nephrons) in their kidneys at birth, which render them more prone to chronic kidney disease in adulthood. Vitamin A, via its metabolite retinoic acid (RA), plays crucial roles in regulating nephron generation during embryo development. This project aims to use mouse models to test a novel hypothesis that a diabetic uterine environment perturbs RA homeostasis and thereby adversely affects nephron generation in embryo’s kidneys. Indeed, we found that maternal diabetes impairs RA synthesis and signaling in the developing kidney. Direct replenishment of RA could correct such defects and increased nephron generation. We further demonstrated that alleviation of oxidative stress via dietary supplementation to diabetic pregnant mice with antioxidants, such as vitamin E, could raise RA levels and promote nephron generation in embryonic kidneys. Notably, we find that RA-associated changes and increased oxidative stress similarly occur in human fetal kidneys from diabetic pregnancies. The unravel of this previously unrecognized linkage of increased oxidative stress, RA imbalance and reduced nephron endowment has pave way for developing therapeutic strategies to enhance nephron generation before birth, thereby reducing the risk of offspring of diabetic mothers to chronic kidney disease in adulthood.

14174517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14174517.value: This study investigates if calcium(Ca) plus Vitamin D(Vit-D) supplementation can prevent curve progression and improve bone health in early Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis(AIS) during pubertal growth. AIS is a prevalent three-dimensional spinal deformity mainly affecting girls at puberty. It can lead to serious complications including spine degeneration, cardiopulmonary compromise, grossly deformed torso and psychosocial disorders. Current treatments are far from being satisfactory, with bracing being lengthy and physically demanding and surgery being a major invasive procedure. There is an association between AIS and low bone mass which has been reported to be a significant prognostic factor for curve progression. Given that dietary calcium intake and serum Vit-D levels were also low in AIS, we have completed an award-winning randomized double-blinded placebo-controlled trial showing Ca+Vit-D can prevent curve progression and improve bone health in immature AIS girls having Cobb angle mainly above 20 degrees and Z-score of areal bone mineral density(aBMD)<0. Results showed for those with low baseline serum 25(OH)Vit-D, 16.2% with treatment had curve progression≥6 degrees as compared with 48.6% in the Placebo Group(p=0.003). To translate research findings into clinical practice, it is mandatory to fill in the gap in knowledge on whether Ca+Vit-D is also effective for early AIS having Cobb angle between 10-20 degrees in preventing disease progression and preventing the need for bracing. We therefore propose a randomized double-blinded placebo-controlled trial to evaluate if daily 600mgCa+800IUVit-D can improve bone health and prevent curve progression. Immature AIS girls with Cobb angle 10-20 degrees will be randomized either to the Treatment or Placebo group with 3-year of treatment. The main outcome measures for evaluation at skeletal maturity and 2 years afterwards include: (1)percentage of patients with increase in Cobb angle≥6 degrees and (2)percentage of patients who require bracing. Bone measurements using advanced image acquisition technology(HR-pQCT) to assess bone health will also be evaluated. This proposal will cover the first phase of the study when subjects who have reached skeletal maturity at the end of 3-year treatment will be evaluated. In the second phase beyond the current proposal, subjects will be followed so that the curve status for the entire cohort separately at skeletal maturity and 2 years afterwards will be scientifically examined. The study will carry significant impacts in that if Ca+Vit-D supplementation is proven to be useful, it can be prescribed for early AIS for preventing disease progression to avoid the need for lengthy and physically demanding bracing treatment. 本研究調查鈣加維生素D(Vit-D)補充治療能否預防早期青少年特發性脊柱側凸(AIS)病情惡化和改善骨骼健康。 AIS是一種常見之三維脊柱畸形，主要影響青春期女孩。AIS可導致嚴重倂發症，包括脊柱退化，心肺功能減退，軀體扭曲變形及嚴重心理困擾。目前治療方法不令人滿意:支架治療每日需時冗長及配帶困難，手術治療則富侵入性及風險高。 AIS和低骨量之間存在關聯。據報導，低骨量是脊柱側凸病情惡化的重要預後因素。鑑於AIS患者膳食鈣攝入量和血清25(OH)Vit-D水平偏低，我們成功進行獲獎的隨機雙盲安慰劑對照研究，顯示鈣加維生素D可以預防AIS女孩脊柱側凸病情惡化和改善骨骼健康。值得注意是受試者之脊柱側凸Cobb角度主要在20度以上及骨質密度(aBMD)Z-指數少於零。結果顯示，對於基線血清25(OH)Vit-D偏低患者，鈣加維生素D治療组有16.2％脊柱側凸Cobb角度惡化高於6度，安慰劑組則為48.6％（p = 0.003）。 為了將研究轉化為臨床實踐，資料不足處必須填補, 特別對Cobb角度在10-20度之早期病患者,進一步驗証鈣加維生素D能否防止脊柱側凸病情惡化和避免使用支架治療十分重要。我們因此提出一項隨機雙盲安慰劑對照研究，以評估每日600mgCa + 800IUVit-D能否改善骨骼健康並預防脊柱側凸惡化。未成年脊柱側凸Cobb角度在10-20度之女孩將被邀請隨機分配至治療組或安慰劑組，治療為期3年。評估時間為骨骼發育完成時和2年後, 研究指標包括：（1）Cobb角度增加≥6度之患者百分比和（2）需要支架治療之患者百分比。研究亦包括運用先進圖像採集技術（HR-pQCT）評估骨骼健康狀態。 是項提案將涵蓋研究的第一階段，即對3年治療結束時達到骨骼成熟之受試者進行評估。在超越現行提案的第二階段，硏究範圍包括科學化評估整個隊列在骨骼發育成熟和2年後之脊柱側凸狀態。 是項研究意義重大。若鈣加維生素D補充治療確實有效，將來可運用鈣加維生素D治療早期脊柱側凸患者以預防病情惡化及避免長時間配帶矯形支撐。

14174617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14174617.value: During skeletal development, repair or remodeling osteogenic progenitors or mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are readily located at a hypoxia and calcium rich microenvironment. In the bone forming environment, MSCs or osteogenic cells sense oxygen fluctuations mediated by key transcription factor hypoxia inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). These cells are suggested to response to calcium level changes mediated by calcium sensing receptor (CaSR) during proliferation and differentiation. Our recent data show that conditional inactivation of HIF-1α in the developing mesenchyme in mouse impairs bone formation which is accompanied by down-regulation of CaSR levels. Knockdown of CaSR abolishes the increase of HIF-1α activity in MSCs stimulated by extracellular Ca2+ treatment, suggesting that Ca2+/CaSR might involve in the regulation of HIF-1α. p300 is shown to regulate HIF-1α activity and transcriptionally controls CaSR expression. HIF-1α and CaSR interact to regulate proliferation and osteogenic differentiation of MSCs. Based on the above information and our preliminary data we hypothesize that a crosstalk exists between the HIF-1α and CaSR signaling in regulation of MSCs self-renewal and lineage differentiation. The proposal has the following three specific aims: Aim 1: To examine the roles of HIF-1α in modulating CaSR expression and the involvement of Ca2+/CaSR signaling in regulation of HIF-1α activity in MSCs. Aim 2: To determine the roles of the interplay between HIF-1α and Ca2+/CaSR signaling in regulation of MSCs self-renewal and mesenchymal lineage differentiation. Aim 3: To evaluate the effects of pharmacologic intervention through targeting HIF-1α and/or Ca2+/CaSR signaling on skeletal repair. We expect that the results will facilitate the understanding of molecular regulation between the HIF-1α and CaSR signaling pathways in MSCs function, and lead to novel therapies for patients with impaired skeletal repair, bone defect or metabolic bone diseases.

14174617.label: Realisation of objectives
14174617.value: For Aim 1, to determine the role of HIF-1α in bone formation during skeletal regeneration, we generated mice lacking HIF-1α in MSCs (∆HIF-1α mice) by cross breeding the Prx-1-CreERT and HIF-1α fl/fl mouse strains. The offspring ∆HIF-1α mice were subjected to DO model followed by tamoxifen (400 mg/Kg) induction at day 3 post distraction for consecutive 4 doses (one dose per day). Micro-CT analysis showed impaired bone repair in the ∆HIF-1α mice, indexed by significantly decreased ratio of bone volume, bone volume to total volume, and trabecular number at day 28 post-surgery compared with the controls. At day 14 post-surgery, real-time PCR revealed that the mRNA levels of HIF-1α, CaSR, Runx2, Osx and OCN were significantly reduced in ∆HIF-1α mice relative to the controls. Moreover, immunostaining showed that the level of osterix was significantly downregulated in ∆HIF-1α mice than the controls. Compared to the controls, ∆HIF-1α mice showed a reduction in the number of BrdU-positive cells in the DO gap. These results indicate that deletion of HIF-1α in MSCs attenuates MSCs proliferation and osteogenic differentiation, which subsequently impairs bone regeneration in the DO model. We next performed a hypoxia response element (HRE)-luciferase reporter assay in C2C12 cells. C2C12 cells were transfected with HRE-luciferase reporter construct followed by incubating with calcium chloride at different concentrations under normoxia. [Ca2+]e treatment increased HRE transcriptional activity, as indicated by HRE-luciferase activity. HRE transcriptional activity was also dramatically induced by hypoxia but was substantially inhibited by either extracellular or intracellular Ca2+ chelation with 10mM of EGTA or 20 uM of Bapta, respectively. We observed a Ca2+ dose-dependent elevation in HIF-1α and CaSR protein levels. Knockdown of CaSR inhibited the expression of HIF-1α and P300 or decreased Ca2+-induced elevated HIF-1α and P300 expression in MSCs with CaSR knockdown. Addition of NPS 2390 or NPS 2143 decreased Ca2+-induced elevated HIF-1α and P300 expression in MSCs. These data suggest that CaSR might play an important role in Ca2+ induced HIF-1α and P300 upregulation in MSCs. To further determine the molecular mechanisms, we searched the promoter region of CaSR and found that there was a binding site for p300 (at the transcription initiation start site -564). Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay confirmed the occupancy of the CaSR promoter region by p300. To determine whether p300 can actually affect the promoter activity of CaSR and whether [Ca2+]e treatment could enhance it, we sub-cloned the mouse CaSR gene promoter region containing p300 binding site into a promoter-less luciferase reporter vector, pGL3-basic, to form a pGL-CaSR reporter construct. siRNA knockdown of p300 significantly reduced the relative luciferase activity in the transfected MSCs while [Ca2+]e treatment dramatically increased it. Our data imply the exist of a [Ca2+]e-CaSR-p300 positive feedback loop to contribute to [Ca2+]e-activated HIF-1α transcriptional activity. Accumulation of HIF-1α upon hypoxia was accompanied by increased CaSR mRNA and protein levels while deletion of either HIF-1α or p300 significantly reduced the CaSR mRNA and protein levels, which were more prominent under hypoxia. Interestingly, the expression of HIF-1α and P300 were found to be associated with each other with both decreasing after each other’s deletion and increasing under hypoxia. Like hypoxia, [Ca2+]e treatment also increased the HIF-1α accumulation and translocation, and in the meantime up-regulated the p300 and CaSR protein expression, which was also jeopardized by the deletion of HIF-1α. These data indicate that complex interactions exist among HIF-1α, p300 and CaSR in MSCs. In addition, it was interesting to note that L-VDCC blocker and TRPCs blocker further decreased HIF-1α mRNA level in MSCs following siRNA mediated CaSR knockdown under both normoxia and hypoxic conditions. This was associated with decreased [Ca2+]i level in MSCs. We also showed that Ca2+ activates HIF-1α associated with upregulation of PI3K/AKT, PKA and PKC signals, while the enhanced MSCs self-renewal by Ca2+ is associated with activation of p-CREB mediated by CaSR. For Aim 2, to examine the cell-autonomous effect of HIF-1α in MSCs, we performed Adenovirus (Ad)-Cre mediated deletion of HIF-1α in MSCs isolated from the bone marrow of HIF-1α flox/flox mice. HIF-1α flox/flox MSCs expressed CD29, Sca-1 and CD44, while lacking expression of CD45, CD31 or CD11b surface molecules. It formed Alizarin Red S-positive bone nodules, developed Oil Red O-positive lipids and synthesized Alcian Blue-positive proteoglycans respectively upon osteogenic, adipogenic and chondrogenic induction. Ad-Cre mediated deletion of Hif-1α MSCs, resulted in a significant decrease in HIF-1α protein level in cells cultured under normoxia and a compromised accumulation of HIF-1α protein in cells cultured under hypoxia. Hif-1α deletion in MSCs also abolished the hypoxia-induced increase of colony formation efficiency of MSCs cultured under hypoxia and brought it down to a level even lower than that of the Hif-1α-deleted MSCs cultured under normoxia, highlighting the important role of HIF-1α in MSCs’ slef-renewal in low oxygen environment. Interestingly, following the Hif-1α deletion was the downregulation of CaSR mRNA and protein expression in cells under normoxia. Hif-1α-deleted MSCs exhibited compromised proliferative capacity and osteoblastic differentiation and mineralization ability. On the other hand, we found a significant reduction in HIF-1α mRNA and protein levels in MSCs under normoxia following CaSR knockdown. CaSR knockdown leads to decreased MSCs colonies and osteoblastic differentiation. These data suggest that deletion of either Hif-1α or CaSR in MSCs down-regulated each other’s expression and impairs MSCs self-renewal and osteoblast differentiation. We also show that [Ca2+]e-induced cyclin D1 up-regulation is due to the increase of p300 expression following [Ca2+]e-induced HIF-1α up-regulation. For Aim 3, histomorphometric analysis and immunostaining showed that the calvaria of mice receiving [Ca2+]e injection group were thicker than that of the control group at one month old, and also contained more PCNA positive osteoblasts on the bone surface. Blockage of CaSR eliminated the [Ca2+]e-induced increase in the thickness and the proliferating osteoblasts numbers in calvaria. We further studied the effect of local delivery of [Ca2+]e on skeletal regeneration in the DO model. MicroCT analysis showed that the tibiae from the [Ca2+]e injection group exhibited more bone volume and thicker trabecular bones than that from the vehicle control group. The increased bone mass and the enhanced new bone formation due to [Ca2+]e injection was eliminated by CaSR inhibitor. We observed more colonies in the cultures of [Ca2+]e injection group as compared with the other two groups. This was accompanied by upregulation of mRNA levels of CaSR, HIF-1α, Glut1 and VEGF. Local injection of methylene blue in the DO gap indicated the retention of injected molecules in the repair region. ELISA analysis for PTH showed that local delivery of [Ca2+]e did not affect the serum levels of PTH. We further examined the effect of [Ca2+]e and another CaSR agonist Gd3+ in skeletal regeneration in a critical sized bone defect model in the SCID mice. Similar as that of the mouse MSCs, hUC-MSCs exhibited increased colony formation in response to [Ca2+]e treatment. Transplantation of hUC-MSCs in the femoral critical-size bone defect model in mice, local administration of [Ca2+]e enhanced bone formation during skeletal regeneration as indexed by increased bone volume, bone volume/total volume and trabecular number than that of the control group. This provides proof of principle that [Ca2+] or other CaSR agonist may serve as a potent candidate molecule for promoting skeletal regeneration through targeting the crosstalk of the HIF-1α and CaSR pathways.

14174617.label: Major findings and research outcome
14174617.value: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) that give rise to osteoblasts during skeletal development and regeneration are located in the bone marrow microenvironment, an orchestrated compartment with low oxygen tension and rich in calcium. The fluctuations of oxygen and extracelluar calcium ([Ca2+]e) levels are considered as important regulators controlling the fate or functions of MSCs mediated by hypoxia inducible factor-1alpha (HIF-1α) and calcium sensing receptor (CaSR), respectively. However, how the HIF-1α and CaSR signaling pathways interact to control the fate of MSCs during skeletal development and regeneration remains unknown. In this study, taking advantage of genetic and pharmacological approaches, we identify that the crosstalk between the HIF-1α and Ca2+/CaSR signaling pathways plays an important role in controlling the self-renewal and osteoblast differentiation of MSCs during skeletal development and repair. Conditional deletion of HIF-1α in MSCs impairs bone formation accompanied by down-regulation of CaSR. Knockdown of CaSR in MSCs impairs proliferation and osteoblast differentiation associated with down-regulation of HIF-1α. Interestingly, [Ca2+]e activates HIF-1α in MSCs mediated by a positive feed-back loop of the p300-CaSR axis. [Ca2+]e enhances MSCs proliferation through modulation of cyclin D1 by HIF-1α. [Ca2+]e upregulates osterix expression through transcriptional control by HIF-1α in CaSR-dependent manner. In a distraction osteogenesis or critical-size bone defect model in mice, [Ca2+]e or CaSR agonist Gd3+ increases MSCs pool size and promotes skeletal regeneration. This provides proof of principle that [Ca2+]e or other CaSR agonist may serve as a potential therapeutic approach for promoting skeletal regeneration through targeting the crosstalk of the HIF-1α and CaSR pathways. Based on the research work of this project, 2 international and 2 regional conference oral or poster presentations were given by the PI and team members. One manuscript was prepared under submission for publication. One review paper related with chondrocyte fate control was published. A PhD student was trained when performing the project, during which the student was trained to develop novel fabrication methods for engineering musculoskeletal tissue using MSCs based 3D bioprinting or organ-on-a-chip technology, thus facilitated the potential application of the results in the treatment of difficulty musculoskeletal diseases. The information on the meetings, abstracts, and publications is enclosed in the report.

14174617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14174617.value: Our data suggest that the crosstalk between the HIF-1α and CaSR pathways plays important roles in regulation of MSCs self-renewal and osteoblast lineage differentiation. The p300-CaSR axis is identified as a key mediator to be involved in the regulation of the crosstalk between HIF-1α and CaSR pathways. The study provides novel insights into the understanding of the regulation of HIF-1α and CaSR pathways in bone formation during skeletal development and regeneration. [Ca2+]e functions as a potent HIF-1α and CaSR activator to exert beneficial effect on promoting bone formation in the distraction osteogenesis (DO) and large bone defect mouse models. This may facilitate discovery of novel therapies for patients with large bone defect or impaired bone repair. We propose to continue to determine the pharmacological efficacy and mechanisms of the candidate molecules activating HIF-1α and CaSR in the future work. We aim to an output with knowledge transfer to benefit patients with large bone defect or impaired bone healing through developing collaborations with colleagues in the clinical department and industry to facilitate the translation of the research results.

14175017.label: Realisation of objectives
14175017.value: Objective one: To expand and characterize skin-derived precursors (SKPs) in vitro This objective has been fully achieved with the following experimental strategies: 1. Establishment of mouse lines: We have established three mouse lines: (a) Wnt1-Cre/Rosa26-GFP compound transgenic mice by cross-mating homozygous B6.129(Cg)-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm4(ACTB-tdTomoto,-EGFP)Luo/J male mice with heterozygous Tg(Wnt1-cre)11Rth Tg(Wnt1-GAL4)11Rth/J female mice for labelling all neural crest cells (NCCs) and their progeny including SKPs; (b) B6/EGFP transgenic mice where EGFP is expressed in all nucleated cells; and (c) Dominant megacolon (Dom) mutant line with a frame-shift Sox10 mutation. 2. Isolation, characterization and expansion of SKPs: A microdissection method was developed to isolate SKPs from the bulge region of hair follicles with minimal contamination with surrounding tissues. More than 95% of isolated SKPs expressed GFP and neural crest stem cell/NCC (NCSC) markers Sox10, Sox2, p75, Ednrb, nestin and AP2α by multiple immunofluorescence staining and qPCR. They possessed high migration ability in wound healing and Boyden transwell assays and showed multipotency when induced in specific differentiation media to form neurons, glial cells and muscle cells. These observations suggested that SKPs from the hair bulge were phenotypically similar to NCSCs/NCCs, and therefore also termed hair follicle-derived neural crest stem cells (HF-NCSCs). SKPs isolated from Dom mice also possessed similar migration ability, expressed NCSC/NCC markers, and exhibited multipotency, suggesting that Dom SKPs were phenotypically similar to those from normal mice. We spent much time and efforts to test different expansion culture media with various components using the final cell number and expression of various NCSC/NCC markers as the outcome measurements. Eight expansion media including proliferation medium, expansion medium (EP), XP1, EPα, EPα-DMEM/F12, EPα-DMEM/F12+GDNF, NeuroCultTM+retinoic acid and modified NCC medium were examined, and the modified NCC medium was found to the best expansion medium for SKPs, in which SKPs could be cultured up to 18 passages without reduction of the expression of NCSC/NCC and stem cell markers. 3. Transcriptome analysis of expanded SKPs: Total RNAs were extracted from (a) expanded SKPs, (b) vagal and sacral neural crest cells (vNCCs and sNCCs) emigrated from E8.5-E9.5 mouse neural tubes, and (3) enteric neural crest stem cells (ENCSCs) which have been shown to be able to form enteric neurons after transplanted to the mouse gut, for genome-wide transcriptome profiling with RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). All samples were triplicated. Based on the logarithm of fragments per kilobase of transcript per million fragments mapped (FPKM) of transcribed genes, significant correlations of SKPs with vagal NCCs (R=0.8242 at p<0.001) and sacral NCCs (R=0.8128 at p<0.001) were found. Similarly when SKPs and ENCSCs were compared for the expression of genes associated with different biological functions of the enteric nervous system (ENS) using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients, moderate to high correlations between SKPs and ENCSCs were found (R=0.70 to 0.75). These observations implicated that SKPs cultured in vitro exhibited properties of early NCCs in embryos and ENCSCs. Objective two: To correct the gene mutation in SKPs isolated from an animal model of congenital gastrointestinal motility disorder This objective has been fully achieved after an alternative approach was used. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology coupled with homology directed repair (HDR) was used to correct the frame-shift mutation in Sox10 in Dom SKPs. The targeted gene modification included three steps: (1) In silico design of both the guide sequences targeting the mutation site and the donor template for gene editing; (2) Construction of pSpCas9-sgRNA plasmids and donor plasmids; and (3) Transfection of the constructed pSpCas9-sgRNA plasmids and the donor plasmids into Dom SKPs. Three selected Cas9-sgRNAs-GFP and the donor plasmids were transfected into Dom SKPs. 48 hours after transfection, 18.7% of SKPs were shown to have transfected with the plasmids containing CRISPR/Cas9 and became GFP positive. The sorted cells were re-seeded onto the collagen type I-coated culture surface. Unfortunately, most of the sorted cells died 48 hours later, and only a few surviving cells adhered to the culture surface. This massive cell death was possibly induced by the expression of mutated Sox10 which has been known to induce cell death. Hence we decided to correct the Sox10 mutation before Sox10 was expressed. We reprogrammed Dom skin fibroblasts into iPSCs with 4 Yamanaka factors (Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) and used the same CRISPR/Cas9 method to edit the Sox10 gene. We eventually obtained 3 homozygous corrected lines which did not show meaningful off-targets. Then we used a three-step protocol to induce gene-corrected Dom iPSCs into SKP-like cells which expressed nestin, p75 and Ednrb. Hence we were able to use CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing to correct the Sox10 mutation in skin fibroblast-derived iPSCs which were then induced to form SKP-like cells. Objective three: To determine the ability of SKPs to form enteric neurons ex vivo and in vivo This objective has also been fully achieved with the following experimental strategies: 1. Transplantation of SKPs to hindgut explants cultured ex vivo: We first established an organ culture system for the growth of hindgut explants from E11.5 to E13.5 mouse embryos for up to 7 days ex vivo, and then developed a technically demanding technique to transplant cells by microinjection to the outer wall of the explants. SKPs were found to be able to gradually engraft and differentiate into enteric neurons which were closely integrated into the endogenous enteric neural network of the recipient explant. They exhibited neuronal differentiation, initially expressed markers of enteric neural crest cells (Sox10, p75 and Ednrb) and then expressed markers of enteric neurons (TuJ1, PGP9.5 and HuC/D) and glia (BFABP only but no S100β and GFAP immunoreactivities). Wild-type SKPs were also transplanted to E11.5 aneural hindgut segments (a model of aganglionosis), and found to be able to form neural cells. They expressed neuronal and glial cell markers but their neural network was abnormal, indicating that the network formation of enteric neurons was also regulated by niche factors. When Dom SKPs were transplanted, massive cell death was observed, whereas the gene-corrected SKP-like cells were able to form enteric neurons similar to those formed by wild-type SKPs. Sample number for each experiment was greater than 5. 2. Transplantation of SKPs to the descending colon of adult mice after laparotomy: SKPs were transplanted to the descending colon of normal and Dom adult mice under deep anesthesia. At designated time points (0 to 20 days post-transplantation), mice were sacrificed, and the gut segments carrying the transplanted SKPs were isolated for immunofluorescence staining. The engrafted SKPs gradually spread from the transplantation site to the myenteric plexus and expressed markers of both neurons (TuJ1, PGP9.5 and HuC/D) and glial cells (BFABP, S100β and GFAP) 14-20 days post-transplantation. They formed subtype neurons (ChAT+, NOS+ or calretinin+) and ganglion-like aggregations along the neural network of the endogenous enteric nervous system. When transplanted to the hypoganglionic or aganglionic region of the descending colon in Dom mice, SKPs formed similar subtype neurons, glial cells and ganglion-like structures, but their network was abnormal and disorganized, whereas transplanted Dom SKPs underwent massive cell death immediately after transplantation, and gene-corrected SKP-like cells formed abnormal neural networks. Immune rejection, excessive cell proliferation and tumor-like aggregations were not observed even at 20 days post-transplantation. All sample numbers were greater than 5. This part of study was particularly difficult because it relied heavily on the uninterrupted supply of experimental animals, which was however severely affected during the period of social movements in 2019 and after the outbreak of covid-19.

14175017.label: Major findings and research outcome
14175017.value: During early embryonic development, neural crest cells (NCCs)/neural crest stem cells (NCSCs) migrate to the developing gut to form enteric neurons. Some NCSCs migrate to the bulge region of hair follicles, reside there and persist into adulthood. The main goal of the present study was to determine whether skin-derived precursors (SKPs) from the hair bulge form enteric neurons. We first successfully identified and isolated SKPs from hair bulges in vitro, and then established a specific culture medium to expand the SKP population without affecting their original biological properties. These expanded SKPs expressed NCSC markers, possessed migration ability and exhibited multipotency in vitro, indicating that SKPs were phenotypically similar to NCSCs. Comparisons of the transcriptomes from SKPs, vagal NCCs, sacral NCCs and enteric neural crest stem cells (ENCSCs) demonstrated that the expression profile of SKPs was largely similar to those of embryonic NCCs and ENCSCs, all of which are already known to be able to form enteric neurons in the gut. To explore the possibility of using SKPs as a cell source in the cell therapy for Hirschsprung’s disease, we used CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to successfully correct the Sox10 mutation in iPSCs derived from skin fibroblasts of the Dominant megacolon (Dom) mutant, a mouse model of Hirschsprung’s disease. We then transplanted SKPs to the hindgut segments explanted from E11.5 to E13.5 mouse embryos and cultured the hindgut explants ex vivo. Seven days following transplantation, SKPs formed TuJ1 immunoreactive neurons with long processes, which were closely integrated into the neural network of the recipient explant. However, when transplanted to aneural hindgut explants, the SKP neural network became deranged and abnormal despite that SKPs could still form enteric neurons. Finally we transplanted SKPs to the descending colon of adult mice and allowed SKPs to develop in vivo for up to 20 days. Engrafted SKPs formed TuJ1 immunoreactive neurons, subtype neurons immunoreactive to ChAT, NOS and calretinin, and glial cells. They formed an interconnected neural network closely associated with the recipient enteric nervous system. When transplanted to the aganglionic or hypoganglionic region of the Dom colon, the formation of neural network by the engrafted SKPs was abnormal although SKPs still formed subtype neurons and glial cells. Our results showed that SKPs were able to form enteric neurons in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo, but the formation of neural network from engrafted SKPs in the gut was affected by the endogenous enteric nervous system.

14175017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14175017.value: Before cell therapy can be used to cure neuropathies related to the deficiency of enteric neurons, the following research areas should be explored: 1. How does the microenvironment of the recipient gut affect the differentiation of engrafted SKPs: Our results showed that the presence of the endogenous enteric nervous system was essential to the formation of the normal neural network from transplanted SKPs. Hence further studies should be performed on the extracellular matrix (ECM) using appropriate animal models to determine how cell-ECM and cell-cell interactions affect the formation of the neural network. 2. How does the engrafted SKPs help restore normal peristalsis: The enteric neurons derived from engrafted SKPs will have to be functionally integrated with Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICC) and muscle cells to re-establish the normal peristalsis/motility of the gut. Hence, the electrophysiological properties of SKP-derived neurons and their physiological interactions with various cell types within the gut should be studied. 3. How are the engrafted SKPs induced to form different subtype neurons with a proper proportion within the gut: Engrafted SKPs will have to be induced to form the full complement of different subtype neurons and glial cells in cell therapy. This induction process needs further studies.

14175017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14175017.value: Congenital gastrointestinal motility disorders with deficiency in enteric neurons are common paediatric problems. Current treatments include palliative relief and surgical removal of the affected gut segment. To avoid long-term complications resulting from surgical removal, cell-based transplantation therapy has been proposed, and appropriate cell sources are required for the therapy. The present study aimed to determine whether skin-derived precursors (SKPs) from hair follicles, which are easily accessible from the skin, are a potential cell source for cell transplantation therapy with minimal risk of immune rejection and tumor formation. We successfully identified, isolated and expanded SKPs from mouse hair follicles, and found that they were able to migrate and form different cell types in vitro. When transplanted to the mouse gut explant which was then cultured ex vivo for up to 7 days, SKPs formed enteric neurons. SKPs were also able to form an interconnected network of neurons and glial cells 20 days following transplantation to the mouse descending colon in vivo. Immune rejection, uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumor formation were not observed. Our results thus demonstrate that SKPs are progenitors of enteric neurons that can potentially serve as a cell source in the cell therapy for congenital gastrointestinal motility disorders.

14175617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14175617.value: 在香港，中國學童的哮喘患病率超過百分之十，在過去二十年中增加了三至四倍。塵蟎過敏是過敏反應的常見原因，通常高達百分之八十五的哮喘病者是塵蟎過敏。大多數地理區域的塵蟎主要種類是屋塵蟎和粉塵蟎，分別喜歡溫帶/熱帶沿海地區和大陸氣候。若特應性患者暴露於塵蟎過敏原可引發炎性疾病，包括過敏性哮喘，終年的鼻炎和特應性皮炎。基於研究資助委員會一般研究基金之前的支持，我們已經建立了兩種塵蟎物種的基因組草圖，以及轉錄組和微生物組，大大有助全球的過敏研究。目前，基於序列和功能同源性已定義了三十多個過敏原組。然而，由於不能獲得完整的塵蟎基因組，其他過敏原組以及已知過敏原組的成員仍有待確定。這些基因組信息的缺失也可能阻礙未來對涉及人類過敏性疾病的過敏原的研究。隨著單分子實時測序技術的進步，測序序列的平均長度大大增加，從而增加構建相對較小的完整基因組的機會。此外，可以通過使用單分子實時測序技術的RNA測序來闡明過敏原基因的交替拼接同種型。本研究將會使用單分子實時測序技術技術分析屋塵蟎和粉塵蟎的完整基因組和轉錄組。我們也會用以前資助項目中製定研究方案來確定新的過敏原。此外，我們將使用新構建的基因組和轉錄組數據分析塵蟎過敏原的基因調控機制。本研究的成果將為今後分析塵蟎過敏原提供重要的資源，還將揭示塵蟎引起的過敏性疾病的發病機制。

14175617.label: Realisation of objectives
14175617.value: Objective 1 - To determine the complete genomes and transcriptomes of Dermatophagoides (D.) pteronyssinus and D. farinae using SMRT sequencing technology. Genes in two complete genomes will be predicted and annotated using data generated in this study, as well as data accumulated in our previously funded project. Using the SMRT sequencing technology, we generated a 62.4 Mb assembly of the D. farinae genome with 241 contigs and a contig N50 of 302 kb. Short-read sequence data from published database were mapped to reduce indel errors and improve the accuracy of the final assembly. After scaffolding and gap filling, we were able to obtain a 62.6 Mb genome with 57 scaffolds. The assembly represents a 9-fold improvement in contiguity with respect to the published genome assembly in 2015. Genome quality assessment with Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) indicated 90.8% genome completeness based on the 1,066 arthropoda ancestral protein set. Evidence-driven prediction using MAKER predicted a total of 17,563 putative protein-coding genes and 18,087 transcripts. Among these transcripts, 8,518 (47.1%) had unknown functions and 9,569 (52.9%) were annotated to be known proteins. Regarding the D. pteronyssinus genome, we obtained the 66.8 Mb final assembly with 1,390 contigs and 634 scaffolds, with scaffold N50 being 194 Kb and contig N50 being 80 Kb. To assess the genome completeness, we have analysed the genome using BUSCOs. Results showed that our hybrid-assembled D. pteronyssinus genome contains 90.4% of the examined BUSCOs, of which 949 (89.1%) are complete BUSCOs and 14 (1.3%) are fragmented BUSCOs. After combining the ab initio predicted genes and evidence-driven predicted genes, we predicted a total of 16,805 protein-coding genes. In conclusion, we have generated two high-quality reference genomes for the two most common house dust mites and these deliverables will certainly benefit future research on dust mite-related allergic diseases. Objective 2 - To identify additional allergen groups as well as members of known allergen groups by immunoblotting and mass spectrometry. From the WHO/IUIS Allergen Nomenclature database, we obtained D. pteronyssinus’ known canonical allergen genes’ complete sequences from Der p 1 to Der p 24, as well as their gene structures. Specifically, there was no Der p 12, Der p 16, Der p 17, Der p 19 and Der p 22 in the database. However, we could find putative Der p 16 and Der p 22 in our high-quality genome by inferring homology from Der f 16 and Der f 22 which are known allergens in D. farinae. Moreover, we got the Der p 25 to Der p 33 gene sequences and gene structures. We were able to locate the Der p 34 gene on the genome from Der f 34, an enamine/imine deaminase protein. Besides, the translated Der p 34 only had 76 amino acid residues aligned to Der f 34 with a low sequence identity of 27%. Since Der p 35 reference protein sequence cannot be found in D. farinae, we retrieved the Tyr p 35 sequence from Tyrophagus putrescentiae (storage mite) (NCBI Accession Number: AOD75396.1). The protein could align to aldehyde dehydrogenase-like protein located in scaffold66 with length 297 amino acids and identity 69.7%. However, both Der p 34 and Der p 35 did not have RNA expression evidence to support. To extend the search of non-canonical allergens, we also screened the genome with all of the allergens from both WHO/IUIS Allergen Nomenclature and AllergenOnline allergen databases. Finally, we predicted that there are 59 protein sequences that are highly similar with other species’ allergens. This number of predicted non-canonical allergens is significantly larger than that from the draft genome of D. farinae, of which the number is only 7. This is another evidence supporting the completeness of the D. pteronyssinus genome reported in this study. By using Coomassie Blue stained 2D gel, we successfully separated the house dust mite proteins. Their molecular weights ranged from 15 kDa to 100 kDa. The results of immunoblotting from the 2D gel showed that there were 64 protein spots in the total protein of the HDM bound by specific IgE in the sera of patients with HDM allergy, numbered 1-64 in the 2D gel. All 64 proteins underwent de novo peptide sequencing by MALDI-ToF MS, then the sequenced peptides were searched against our predicted genes. Among them, 55 allergens could be supported by RNA-Seq data. The recombinant proteins of Der p 25 to 33 were successfully expressed in Orgami-expressing bacteria and then purified by Ni2+ affinity chromatography with fast protein liquid chromatography. The allergenicity of the non-canonical allergens of Der p 25, 26, 28, 32, and 33 was detected by ELISA using 26 sera of HDM allergy patients and 4 normal human sera as negative control. The results showed that the IgE binding rates of Der p 25, 26, 28, 32, and 33 were 53.8%, 61.5%, 38.5%, 46.2%, and 65.3% respectively. Therefore, Der p 33 had the highest allergenicity among the novel canonical D. pteronyssinus allergens. Objective 3 - To study the allergen gene regulation mechanism based on the generated genome and transcriptome data. Expression levels of allergens of D. farinae and D. pteronyssinus were compared and normalized by Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase. Results showed that the expression levels of allergens in D. pteronyssinus and D. farinae were quite distinct. The top five expressed allergens in D. pteronyssinus were Der p 1, 5, 10, 21 and 24, while in D. farinae were Der f 10, 13, 21, 26 and 31. Since the genomes of D. pteronyssinus and D. farinae are now available, this enables us to find common transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) between their allergen homologs. Using bioinformatics tools and existing pipelines in the Hong Kong Bioinformatics Centre of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, we have identified the longest common TFBS pattern in each pair of allergen homologs in the two species. The frequency distribution of the individual TFBS elements were also elucidated. Furthermore, we have searched the corresponding transcription factors (TFs) in D. farinae and D. pteronyssinus genomes and 39 out of 71 TFs have the same conserved domains as the reference TFs. This provides strong evidence that the TFBSs in the common patterns are indeed used in the allergen regulation in D. pteronyssinus and D. farinae.

14175617.label: Major findings and research outcome
14175617.value: In this project, we have generated high-quality genomes for D. pteronyssinus and D. farinae using the SMRT sequencing technology. Based on the annotation of the genomes, novel allergens have been identified and characterized. We have also compared the differential expression of allergens in these two house dust mite species using the genomes and transcriptomes data delivered in this study. Findings in this study have been published in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology, the top journal in the area of allergy (Liu et al., 2018 in Part C). The findings in this project also benefited an international study on preventive sublingual immunotherapy published in the journal Allergy (Ponce et al., 2019 in Part C), a prestigious journal in allergy, as well as the discovery of dust mite enolase as an important protein contribute to neutrophilic airway inflammation published in European Respiratory Journal (Lin et al., 2020 in Part C), a prestigious journal in the respiratory medicine. Finally, our genomes generated by the SMRT technology had also facilitated the analysis of miRNA in D. pteronyssinus and our work has been also published in the journal Allergy (Yang et al., 2020 in Part C), thereby open a new avenue for dust mite allergy research. Taken together, we can anticipate that the deliverables of this project have significantly contributed to the research community of dust mite allergy.

14175617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14175617.value: Because of our excellent deliverables and supreme research platform generated from the last General Research Fund (GRF) project (Project Ref. No.: 475113) and this project, two more GRF projects titled “Allergen profile and metabolic characteristics analysis of the storage mite Tyrophagus putrescentiae using single molecule real-time sequencing and bioinformatics tools” (Project Ref. No.: 14119219; Fund Amount: HK$ 1,010,437; Duration: November 2019 – October 2021) and “Investigating the allergen profile and metabolic characteristics of Procambarus clarkii using the single molecule real-time sequencing and bioinformatics tools” (Project Ref. No.: 14119420; Fund Amount: HK$ 1,055,025; Duration: January 2021 – December 2022) has been recently supported by the Research Grants Council. With these resources, we plan to extend our work from house dust mites to storage mites and food allergy causing species. Moreover, based on our analysis on the miRNA in D. pteronyssinus, we will further study the functional significance of such mite miRNA in human allergic diseases. Finally, using the mite genomes we generated as well as the genomes of other mites and ticks in the public domain, comparative genomics will be performed to study the evolution of mites in parallel with the emergence of human household.

14175617.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14175617.value: In Hong Kong, the prevalence of asthma as well as other allergic diseases in Chinese school children is very high. Among numerous environmental factors, house dust mite (HDM) is a major cause of allergic responses. The predominant species of HDM in most geographical regions are Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus and Dermatophagoides farinae and exposure to HDM allergens in atopic patients triggers inflammatory diseases including allergic asthma, perennial rhinitis and atopic dermatitis. In this study, high-quality reference genomes of these two important dust mite species have been constructed and annotated using the recently developed single molecule real-time sequencing technology. Many putative novel allergens identified by bioinformatics tools have been characterized by immunoblotting, mass spectrometry and other immunological techniques. Moreover, the regulation and differential expression of allergens in these two HDM species have been explored by transcriptome and bioinformatics analysis. In conclusion, the resources generated in this study will provide tools for further identification and characterization of HDM allergens and development of diagnostics and immunotherapeutic vaccines.

14176017.label: Project Objectives
14176017.value: Specific Aim 1: Structural determination of a functionally active Cry5Ba. While a truncated form of Cry5Ba(112-698) has been previously reported, this construct lacked regions critical for nematicidal activity. We have crystallized and obtained preliminary data for an active truncation, Cry5Ba(1-772). We plan to improve the quality of the crystals and complete the structure solution of this Cry5Ba(1-772) protein. Specific Aim 2: Probing the mechanism of Cry5Ba activation and oligomerization. Previous studies have demonstrated the ability to purify the glycolipid linked to Cry5Ba toxicity directly from C. elegans. We plan to repeat this purification, and then attempt to obtain the structure of active Cry5B bound to this glycolipid. At the same time, we will explore evaluate whether the tetrameric state observed in the Cry5Ba(1-772) structure is functionally relevant. Specific Aim 3: Towards the structure of Cry6Aa in its pore-forming conformation. Recently the structure of Cry6Aa has been determined confirming its distinct fold from other previously characterized Cry proteins. The structure has revealed its homology to the other bacterial toxins including hemolysin E (HlyE) from E. coli. Notably, for HlyE it was possible to obtain its pore forming conformation by crystallization in the presence of detergent and DTT. Given their homology, a similar strategy might be possible for Cry6Aa as well. We plan to work to explore this possibility.

14176017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14176017.value: The Cry proteins produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis are used as natural biopesticides to protect crops due to their specific toxicity against different insect species. Despite intensive study, the mechanism of activation and insertion of these Cry toxins remains largely unresolved. To address this issue, we propose to perform structural studies on two families of Cry proteins known to act on nematodes. We hope that our structural studies will lead to new insights into the conformational changes that occur upon Cry toxin activation and provide better understanding regarding the origins of their species-specific toxicity. 蘇雲金芽胞桿菌產生的Cry蛋白，作為一種天然的殺蟲劑，被廣泛用於農作物蟲害的防治。不同種類的Cry蛋白對昆蟲的毒性具有選擇性和特異性。儘管已經有了眾多的研究，Cry蛋白毒性的激活及其插入昆蟲細胞膜的機制仍不明確。為了解決這個問題，我們計劃對兩個對線蟲具有特異毒性的Cry蛋白家族進行結構研究。我們希望通過相應的結構研究，能夠為了解Cry毒性蛋白激活時發生的結構變化和Cry蛋白昆蟲毒性的特異性提供新的視野。

14176017.label: Realisation of objectives
14176017.value: Specific Aim 1: Structural determination of a functionally active Cry5B. We previously obtained crystals of Cry5B(1-772) and were able to collect a 4.5 Å dataset. Following molecular replacement, we found that the protein adopted a distinct quaternary structure from that of a Cry5B(112-698) fragment determined previously. While the previous Cry5B(112-698) structure formed a trimer, our Cry5B(1-772) structure was a tetramer with 4-fold symmetry. At the time, we could fit residues 112-698 based on the molecular replacement, but there was a region with significant positive density that we could not assign. Our plan was to obtain more crystals and then use them to get a higher resolution structure to resolve the structural details. We have had difficulty producing improved crystals of Cry5B(1-772) tetramer, but in the meantime made progress on the existing structure. We initially built a polyalanine model of 80 residues into the previously unfit density. This was achieved by first taking advantage of the two independent copies of the molecule in the asymmetric unit and using 2-fold averaging of the electron density to improve the map. From the improved 2-fold averaged map, we were able to discern several long regions of electron density that could fit to α-helices, and built the polyalanine model into this density. However, due to the lower resolution of our data, we were not able to make specific residue assignments directly. Recently we were able to find a solution. We used Robetta to predict the structure of the five helices in the N-terminal extension. The first four helices of the structural model predicted by Robetta fit our polyalanine model quite well, and using this information coupled with the strong peaks in the side chain electron density, we were able to make the side chain assignments and build the final model consisting of residues Cry5B(27-698). The details of this structure are provided in the manuscript that is included in this report. Thus for this aim while we were not able improve the quality of the crystals, we were able to complete the structure and are submitting a manuscript on this structure for publication. Specific Aim 2: Probing the mechanism of Cry5B activation and oligomerization. One aspect of this aim was to try and understand the role of the glycolipid on Cry5B, by cocrystallizing Cry5B and the glycolipid in bicelle-containing solutions. These experiments were performed and completed. On the positive, we were able to obtain crystals of Cry5B(1-772) from bicelles and glycolipid. The crystals diffracted to 4.5 Å resolution, and the unit cell while similar to that of the Cry5B(112-698) trimer determined previously (Hui et al. Biochemistry (2012) 51, 9911-22), had a c-axis that was significantly shorter (Table 1). Analysis of the structure, however, reveals that the structure determined by molecular replacement is similar to the previously determined Cry5B(112-698), with the primary difference being the packing between the Cry5B(112-698) trimers. Unfortunately, the glycolipid could not be observed at the resolution of the data. Another aspect of this aim was to evaluate whether the tetrameric state observed in the Cry5B(1-772) structure is functionally relevant. The significance of this effort has been subsequently enhanced by the recent report by Sun and coworkers (Peng et al. App Microbio Biotech, (2018), 102(8), 3663-3673) who showed that C. elegans cadherin CDH-8 contributes to the internalization of Cry5B into nematode cells, in part by promoting the oligomerization of Cry5B. Westerns of wild type C. elegans fed Cry5B showed the presence of both a ~70 kDa and ~280 kDa Cry5B bands which presumably correspond to monomeric and tetrameric forms of the Cry5B protein. When a C. elegans cdh-8 knockout was fed Cry5B, only a band (~70 kDa) corresponding to the monomeric form was observed. The similar oligomeric state observed in these studies and in our crystal structure, opens the possibility that they might be linked. If so, CDH-8 could be potentially used to promote formation and stabilization of our tetramer in solution. Towards this end, we have developed a vector for co-expressing Cry5B and cadherin proteins in E. coli. Notably, co-expression of reveals the production of a Cry5B oligomer. We are working to try and isolate and crystallize this Cry5B oligomer. In the meantime, we have started to examine the residues at the interface of the tetramer by site directed mutagenesis. The most important of the residues identified was Tyr495 at the apex of the tetramer whose hydroxyl forms a hydrogen bond to the main chain carbonyl of Leu496 from a neighboring subunit. Because of the 4-fold symmetry, these interactions link the 4 subunits of the tetramer together, and thus our prediction was that mutation of the Tyr residue to Phe might impact the toxicity. Site-directed mutagenesis coupled with C. elegans toxicity studies show, however, that while the residue is important, it is not the hydrogen bond, but rather the aromaticity of Tyr495 that seems to be critical to toxicity. One of the observations made from comparing the tetrameric Cry5B(27-698) and previous trimeric Cry5B(112-698) structures, was the presence of two different conformations for residues 112-140. In the trimeric Cry5B(112-698) structure, this region formed an extended helix, while in the tetrameric Cry5B(27-698) structure, this region was partially unfolded into a random coil. We prepared a computational model of the tetrameric Cry5B(27-698), but with residues 112-140 as an extended helix. This model put the N-terminal extension adjacent to the glycan binding site on domain II suggesting a possible role for the N-terminal extension in glycolipid binding. Thus for this aim, we were able to purify the glycolipid and grow crystals in the presence of glycolipid, but could not see the glycolipid in the crystals. We have made progress in the oligomerization, and have confirmed the results of Peng et al. that the cadherin repeats of CDH8 can promote the oligomerization of Cry5B. We have also developed a computational model that suggests a role for the N-terminal extension that can be experimentally tested. Specific Aim 3: Towards the structure of Cry6Aa in its pore-forming conformation. We screened multiple detergent conditions for their ability to promote oligomerization of Cry6Aa, but were unable to identify any promising conditions. However, we were able to identify a heat dependent conformational change in DDM detergent. We attempted to use this step to produce an oligomeric species, but were not able to obtain negative-stain images that were promising. We are also working to use the SapA lipid nanodisc system (Chien et al., JACS (2017) 139, 14829-32) to promote the Cry6Aa membrane insertion and oligomerization. We are working to explore the structure determination of the membrane-inserted Cry6Aa by either protein crystallography or cryo-EM (with Academia Sinica). For this aim, the main hurdle has been our inability to produce an oligomer that we can get either a crystal or cryo-EM structure of.

14176017.label: Major findings and research outcome
14176017.value: We have determined the structure of Cry5B containing an N-terminal extension that is critical for its functional activity. This structure has provided several new insights. (1) The structure reveals a new quaternary arrangement for the protein. While the previous structure of 'elastase-activated' Cry5B which lacked the N-terminal extension was found to assemble into a trimer, the new structure was found to form a tetramer with 4-fold symmetry. (2) The structure revealed that the structural features of the N-terminal extension adopts a motif comprised of 5 alpha-helices. Additionally, an extended helix associated with trimer formation in the 'elastase-activated' structure adopts a random coil in the new Cry5B structure presumably due its connection to the N-terminal motif. (3) We have shown that co-expression of Cry5B with cadherin CDH-8 results in Cry5B oligomerization. While the experiments are distinct, the net result is alignment with the findings of Peng et al. Appl Microbiol Biotechnol, 2018, 102(8):3663-3673. (4) We have developed a computational model assuming the random coil in our structure adopts the helical secondary structure in the 'elastase-activated; structure. This computational model positions the helical N-terminal motif adjacent to the carbohydrate binding site on domain II of Cry5B suggesting its possible role in glycolipid binding.

14176017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14176017.value: There are several directions that can be explored based on the Cry5B structure. (1) One direction is to test the hypothesis that the N-terminal motif aids in binding glycolipid ligand. We will perform N-terminal truncation of Cry5B and evaluate its impact on sugar binding to Cry5B. (2) We are working to determine the structure of Cry5B coexpressed with cadherin CDH-8 to see if we can determine the structure of their complex.

14176017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14176017.value: The Cry proteins produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis are used as natural biopesticides to protect crops due to their specific toxicity against different insect species. Despite intensive study, the mechanism of activation and insertion of these Cry toxins remains largely unresolved. This project focused on performing structural studies on two families of Cry proteins known to act on nematodes. We have determined the structure of one of these Cry5B proteins containing an extra extension required for its functional activity. This new Cry5B structure reveals a distinct quaternary conformation, and insight into the structural features of this N-terminal extension. A role for the N-terminal motif is suggested based on computational modeling. These findings can help in developing an understanding of the mechanism of Cry5B activation and pore formation, insights that could lead to Cry proteins with higher specificity and toxicity.
