14609717.label: Realisation of objectives
14609717.value: All the objectives have been 100% realized through this two-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT). In this RCT, a total of 288 overweight Chinese post-menopausal women were recruited from district centers of women associations in Hong Kong and randomly allocated into intervention (n = 144) or control group (n = 144). Participants in the control group received an established cardiovascular health information website (http://cvhealth.nur.cuhk.edu.hk/) or a self-developed information booklet, contents similar to the website, depending on participants’ preference. The website/booklet provided basic knowledge on menopause and its association with cardiovascular health and recommendations on physical activity (e.g., at least 60 minutes/day of moderate-intensity physical activity for most of the days per week) and diet (e.g., food with low saturated fat, high-fiber, rich in vitamin and mineral contents). One co-investigator provided a didactic lecture (20-30 participants/session, 30-minute/session) to introduce the website/booklet. Participants in the intervention group received the three-month theory-based educational program. Underpinning by the theories of Health Literacy Model and Constructivist School of Leaning, this educational lifestyle intervention focusing on multiple levels of interactions and health literacy was developed to promote enduring behavioral changes and cardiovascular health. This program comprised one individual introduction session of the webpage/booklet (30-minute), three 2-hour group meetings, and five individual telephone contacts (20-minute/time). The individual session was delivered by a trained research nurse to introduce the website/booklet (the same as that for the control group). It involved both learner-content and learner-instructor interactions and emphasized practical and specific information for healthy lifestyles. Then, two bi-weekly group discussion sessions (10-15 participants/group) and one individual telephone follow-up (Call-1) were conducted to enhance participants’ skills in maintaining a healthy lifestyle. The group sessions focused on preparation of individualized action plan and skills in incorporating dietary modification and physical activity into daily life and were conducted by a trained dietitian and a trained physiotherapist, respectively. Another telephone follow-up (Call-2) was made between the group meetings to provide support and enhance participants’ problem-solving abilities. Three bi-weekly telephone calls (Call-3, 4, 5) were made to provide support for adherence to their plan and to discuss strategies for solving the encountered problems. The last group meeting was held by the end of the third month to acknowledge the achievement of the participants and provide further advice on plan modification if necessary. Study outcomes included cardiovascular health knowledge, self-efficacy in physical activity and diet, physical activity and dietary behavior, and cardiovascular health outcomes. Cardiovascular health knowledge was measured using the Modified Chinese version of the Knowledge Inventory: a Measure of Knowledge of Important Factors in Cardiac Rehabilitation (Cheung, 2009). The inventory includes 32 multiple-choice questions. The total score ranges from 0 to 32 with a higher score reflecting better cardiovascular health knowledge. Self-efficacy in physical activity was assessed using the Chinese version of Self-Efficacy for Exercise scale (SEE) (Resnick & Jenkins, 2000). SEE comprises nine items that test individuals’ confidence to continue exercising when facing barriers. Each item is rated on a 11-point Likert scale (0 = not confident to 10 = very confident). The total score ranges from 0 to 90, and a higher score indicating a higher level of self-efficacy in physical activity. Self-efficacy in diet was measured using the Chinese version of the Cardiac Diet Self-Efficacy scale (CDSE) (Hickey et al., 1992). CDSE comprises 16 items assessing individuals’ confidence in coping with the behavior change in diet. Each item is responded on a five-point Likert scale (1= not at all to 5 = totally). The total score ranges from 16 to 80 with a higher score suggesting a higher level of self-efficacy in diet. Cardiovascular health outcomes included body weight, body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, body fat mass percentage, blood pressure, blood glucose, blood lipids, and Framingham cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk score. In addition, C-reactive protein (CRP), adiponectin, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) were measured. Physical activity level was measured using the Chinese version of the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form (IPAQ-SF) (Craig et al., 2003; Deng et al., 2008). IPAQ-SF consists of seven items measuring the self-reported frequency and duration of vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity, walking, and sedentary behavior in the last seven days. Responses to the three types of physical activity (i.e., vigorous-intensity, moderate-intensity, and walking) are converted to Metabolic Equivalent Task minutes per week (MET min/week). A total physical activity score is computed by the sum of the MET scores of each type of physical activity. Dietary behavior was assessed by the Diet subscale of the Chinese version of the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile-II (D-HPLP) (Walker et al., 1987). The diet subscale of HPLP-II consists of nine items, and each item is rated on a four-point Likert scale (1 = never to 4 = routinely). The total score ranges from 9 to 36. A higher total score indicates a healthier dietary behavior. All study outcomes were measured at baseline (T0), three-month (T1), six-month (T2), and 12-month (T3), except for cardiovascular health knowledge that was measured at T0 and T1, as well as blood tests which were measured at T0 and T3 only. Follow-up data collections for the participants were hindered by the pandemic of COVID-19. The average data collection time points for the outcomes were at 0 month (T0), 3.4 months (T1), 7.9 months (T2), and 14.0 months (T3). The generalized estimating equation (GEE) model was used to compare the differential changes of each outcome at T1, T2, and T3 with respect to T0 between the intervention and control groups to address the objective 1: to examine the effects of a theory-based educational intervention on knowledge of cardiovascular health, self-efficacy in diet and exercise, and physical activity and dietary pattern among overweight Chinese post-menopausal women in Hong Kong. Mediation analysis was conducted to address the objective 2: to examine if the effects of the theory-based educational intervention on physical activity and dietary pattern are mediated through knowledge of CV health, and self-efficacy in diet and exercise. Multivariable regressions were used to address the objective 3: to examine if a positive change in physical activity and dietary pattern can result in improvements on cardiovascular health outcomes, sleep quality and vasomotor symptoms References: Cheung, Y. 14609717.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609717.value: From March 2018 to August 2019, a total of 438 women were screened for eligibility. Amongst them, 138 individuals were excluded for not meeting the eligibility criteria and 12 individuals were eligible but declined to participate. Finally, 288 postmenopausal women consented to participate, completed the baseline assessment, and were randomly assigned to either the intervention (n = 144) or control (n = 144) group. The mean age of the participants was 59.1 (SD = 3.9, range: 44 to 65) years. The average year since menopause was 7.92 (SD = 5.05) years. 46.9% of the participants had a family history of CVDs. The GEE model found: The intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in physical activity level, dietary behavior, self-efficacy in physical activity and diet, and several cardiovascular health outcomes (body weight, body mass index [BMI], waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and Framingham risk score) at post-intervention (T1) compared with the control group (all p<0.05). These significant effects maintained at T2, and the effects on dietary behavior, self-efficacy in physical activity and diet also maintained at T3. Cardiovascular health knowledge improved in both intervention and control groups at post-intervention, but the between-group difference was not significant (p=0.051). The mediation analysis found: The effects of this educational intervention on physical activity level could be partly mediated through self-efficacy in exercise; additionally, the effects of the intervention on dietary pattern could be partly mediated through self-efficacy in exercise and knowledge of CV health. The multivariable regression found: In this study, the positive change in dietary pattern can result in improvements on body weight, BMI, waist circumference and diastolic blood pressure (all p<0.05). Based on the baseline data, this study revealed that vasomotor symptoms were significantly correlated with several cardiovascular risk factors including LDL-C, TC, and IGF-1. Moreover, SBP, LDL-C, and TG were significantly and independently associated with 10-year CVD risk. However, there is no significant association between vasomotor symptoms and 10-year CVD risk. Two manuscripts “Effects of a theory-based educational program on health behaviors and cardiovascular health outcomes among Chinese postmenopausal women: A randomized controlled trial”, “Vasomotor symptoms, cardiovascular risk factors, and cardiovascular disease risk among Chinese postmenopausal women in Hong Kong” arise from this project and submitted to peer-reviewed academic journal. A manuscript “Effects of exercise therapy for adults with coronary heart disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials” also arises from this project and has been published though acknowledgements has not been made.

14609717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609717.value: The following recommendations are provided for further development of the research: 1. This study was conducted among Chinese postmenopausal women in a metropolis in southern China. Thus, the findings may only be generalizable to this select group of postmenopausal women. Further research is needed to examine this program across different racial/ethnic groups and in more diverse settings to strengthen the generalizability of the findings. 2. Future studies require further strategies to improve the sustainability of the effects of such educational program on health behavior and cardiovascular health outcomes. Moreover, the current study provides valuable implication for clinical practice. Findings from this study can inform the development of practical, evidence-based recommendations to promote health behavior change and cardiovascular health of postmenopausal women. 1. A theory-based educational program is effective in improving physical activity, dietary behavior, self-efficacy in physical activity and diet, and several cardiovascular health outcomes. Therefore, such educational intervention could be incorporated into routine nursing practice to improve the cardiovascular health for Chinese postmenopausal women. 2. The Health Literacy Model and Constructivist School of Learning could also be used as practical models for nurses to apply in clinical practice and education.

14609717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609717.value: With the natural cessation of estrogen, postmenopausal women are at high risk for CVD. Diet control and adequate physical activity are recommended as the essence of promoting cardiovascular health for postmenopausal women. The present study examined the effects of a three-month theory-based educational program in a powered sample of Chinese postmenopausal women over a 12-month duration. This study provides evidence that the application of interactive education focusing on physical activity and dietary behavior can lead to favorable changes in physical activity, dietary behavior, self-efficacy in physical activity and diet, and several cardiovascular health outcomes (body weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, and Framingham risk score) and the positive effects can maintain for a short-term period. These findings provide further information on the public health impact of interactive educational intervention on lifestyle changes and cardiovascular health, as well as insights into the potential mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects. Yet, further strategies are required to enhance the sustainability of the effects on health behavior and cardiovascular health outcomes.

14610317.label: Realisation of objectives
14610317.value: The two project objectives were fully achieved. Subject recruitment Subject recruitment took place from Jan 2018 to Dec 2020. Of 469 eligible family caregivers of persons with dementia (PwD) from a geriatric clinic and three elderly community center, 390 participants consented to participate [mean age (SD) = 56.2, SD=12.2; female = 77.4%; children caregiver: 73.9%; caregiving for > 3 years = 59.6%]. The care recipients were older in age [mean (SD) = 84.5 (7.3)], with 60.8% being diagnosed as having moderate or severe dementia. Data collection and analysis Baseline data collection by face-to-face interview went smoothly, and the 6-month follow-up assessment for PAC was done through telephone interview. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, only 325 participants completed the reassessment on positive aspects of caregiving (PAC) at the 6-month endpoint. We over-recruited 20 participants to cover the under-estimated attrition rate (16.7%). Among the participants, 30 of them were interviewed to explore how and why the model factors influence the PAC. Little’s Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) test indicated the data were missing at random [chi-square=1127.22, p =0.99]. Regression methods were used to impute missing data. For objective 1, we hypothesized that PAC was evolved from the process of active coping and meaning-making. PAC refers to feeling of role gratification, increased mutuality with the PwD, enhanced family cohesiveness and personal growth in the caregiving process. For active coping, it was postulated that the use of active dementia management strategy (named as “active coping’ thereafter) would induce a sense of performance success (i.e. self-efficacy) among the caregivers, leading to role gratification. As social support is a source of social affirmation on their success, the model postulated the moderating role of social support for the relationship between active coping and self-efficacy in intensifying PAC. As for meaning-focus coping, it refers to a repertoire of appraisal-based coping such as cognitive reframing and benefit findings, and goal reprioritizing to change the meaning attached to the stressful encounters. This coping method renders caregiver to refocus their thoughts on pleasant rather than undesirable issue arising from the caregiving process, so that they are more likely to experience other PAC domains including increased mutuality with PwD, improved dynamic with family members and even personal growth. The model also hypothesized that good dyadic relationship, intrinsic motivation to caregiving and high religiously are associated with increased use of meaning-focus coping, and would indirectly increase PAC. By using path analysis, modification was made to the hypothesized model to fit the collected data. Basically, PAC was found to be evolved from the two major paradigms of active coping and meaning-making. Conforming to the key postulation, increased use of active coping and meaning-focused coping was related to an increased PAC, and the effects of active coping is mediated through an increased self-efficacy. However, social support did not moderate the relationship between active copings and self-efficacy. Instead, caregivers using more active or meaning-focused coping tended to reported better social support, which might, in turn, intensity PAC through increase the caregivers’ self-efficacy. The role of social affirmation from the social network in increasing the caregiving performance success may still be valid in explaining the evolvement of PAC. As for the use of meaning-focused coping, it was more common among caregivers who had higher intrinsic motivation towards caregiving and good dyadic relationship. However, only good dyadic relationship had an indirect effect on PAC which mediated though meaning-focused coping and an increased self-efficacy. Higher religiosity was not related to meaning-focused coping but was associated with greater self-efficacy. Figure 2 is the identified model with estimated parameters (Section C, item xx). The qualitative findings provides more precise explanation on the path analysis model. Conforming to the literature, the reported PAC covers the four key domains of feelings of role gratification, increased in mutuality in the dyadic relationship, personal growth and increased family cohesiveness. Using active coping and meaning-focus coping are the key conditions leading to PAC. For active coping, it involved a wide range of strategies including optimized social engagement, distraction, developing regular life routine, optomized person-centered choices, and uptake of dementia service to manage the care needs of PwD. Positive outcomes in terms of better symptom control, improved functional status and delay institutionalization enhanced the caregivers’ self-efficacy and led to a strong sense of role gratification. Such rewarding experience, in turn, motivated the caregivers to be more active and deterministic in trying out more active coping strategies. It appeared that self-efficacy was the key psychological attribute to spin out the active coping-role gratification cycle, and intensify PAC. As for meaning-focus coping, appraisal-based actions including reframing the caregiving situation as: i) fateful and offering chance for them to reciprocate past attention and love from the PwD; ii) enduring the companionship of PwD, iii) intensify the intimate and social interactional encounters within the dyads, and re-prioritizing the life goals. All these coping renders the caregivers to perceive the process as rewarding in a way to enhance the mutuality in the dyadic relationship. Some of them reported personal growth in terms of becoming more altruistic and caring to the others, has higher resilience to the future adversities, and be more thoughtful and has higher problem-solving ability. Two informants consistently indicated that the caregiving enabled them to have more self-reflection, and they realized the sentence in the bible of Taoism that “the truth can be known but it may be not the well-known to you.” They described themselves as becoming more flexible and accommodating in living a life. Whereas self-efficacy was the key drive for the continuous use of active coping, maintaining a good dyadic relationship motivated the caregivers to exercise various meaning-focused coping strategies. More specifically, good dyadic relationship was most commonly characterized by high appreciation from the caregivers on the contribution, support and love from the PwD in the past. Such long-standing interpersonal relationship renders to caregivers to reframe the caregiving situation in a positive schemata and to find benefits in the challenging process. As for intrinsic motivation towards caregiving, this attribute was mainly evolved from the value system and cultural context of the caregivers including Karma, familism, caring character and sympathetic attitude. However, different from the identified path model, even intrinsic motivation secured the caregivers’ commitment in role engagement, PAC was only reported among those who use active and meaning-focused coping to fulfill the commitement. We also explored the role of social support in the evolvement of PAC. Although family, friends and neighbors are key sources of social affirmation to validate the caregivers’ contribution, the caregivers did not highlight its influence on their perceived caregiving success. Instead, caregivers who used active coping and received tangible and informational support from family were more confident in their role fulfilment, and were more likely to perceive the advantage of dementia caregiving in improving the family cohesiveness (i.e. another domain of PAC). This explained the path model about why social support plays a mediating rather than a moderating role between active coping and self-efficacy in increasing PAC. As for religiosity, its role in the caregiving process was only limited to reinforce the social norm of family caregiving, religious coping (e.g. praying) was sometimes used but did not contribute to PAC. This explains why religiosity was related to higher self-efficacy in the path analysis model.

14610317.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610317.value: Table 1 summarizes the participants’ characteristics (Section C8(No.6) p.22). The hypothesized model predicting the 6-month PAC showed insufficient model fit with RMSEA=0.14, SRMR=0.13, CFI=0.55, TFI=0.31. Guided by modification indices, with considerations given to the theoretical plausibility of the suggested paths, the final model was showed in Table 4 and Figure 3 (Section C8(No.6) p.25&28; RMSEA=0.09, SRMR=0.04 CFI=0.95, TFI=0.79). Conforming to the theoretical postulation, PAC was evolved from the integrative stress and coping, existentialism, and cognitive psychology paradigms, and was predicted by active coping and the meaning-focused coping. The effects of active coping on PAC was mediated through an increased self-efficacy. Active coping also had a direct positive effect on social support which, in turn, mediated its effect on PAC through enhanced self-efficacy. [Total effect: β(SE)=0.24(0.07), p<001]. On the other hand, social support did not moderate the relationship between active coping and self-efficacy, but it increases PAC through a positive mediating effect on self-efficacy [β(SE) =0.07(0.03), p=0.04]. As for meaning-focused coping, it has a direct effect on PAC and an indirect effect mediated through increased social support and self-efficacy [total effect: β(SE)=0.25(0.08), p<0.01]. Conforming to the postulation, good dyadic relationship and intrinsic motivation toward caregiving were positively associated with meaning-focused coping, but only the former has an indirect effect on PAC. Nevertheless, religiosity was not related to meaning-focus coping. It was only associated with increased self-efficacy but its indirect effect on PAC is not significant. The qualitative data provides more precise explanation on the PAC evolvement. Thematic analysis identified two major themes: i) evolvement of PAC from stress and coping paradigm and ii) evolvement of PAC from the meaning-making process. The first theme highlights the importance of active coping in bringing about role gratification. In this process, improved symptom control and behavioral responses of PwDs are crucial, as this strengthened the caregivers’ self-efficacy and, in turn, motivated more active coping to intensify PAC. Family involvement further strengthened PAC through increase family cohesiveness. For the second theme, good dyadic relationship is most crucial to engage the caregivers in the meaning-making process. Finding benefits and cognitively reframing the caregiving process as fateful, grateful and inspiring brings about mutuality in the dyadic relationship and sense of personal growth. Although strong cultural beliefs of Karma and familism among the Chinese enhances the intrinsic motivation towards caregiving, it only strengthens the care commitment, and PAC does not evolve without the use of active and meaning-focused coping.

14610317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610317.value: This project has generated a theory-driven and evidence-based predictive model to explain the manifestation of PAC in dementia caregiving. It enriches the conceptualisation of the adaptation process of family caregivers by adding the manifestation of positive experience to the journey of coping with the stressors in the challenging caregiving endeavours. The findings call for a paradigm shift from ‘directing attention to reducing caregivers’ stressful experience’ to ‘empowering family caregivers to create a meaningful, positive and fulfilling caregiving adventure’. Based on the current findings, the PI has developed a dyadic exercise program for PwD-caregiver dyads. The program optimized predictive factors of PAC, which characterized by optimized mutual support, collaborative goal-setting, caregiver-directed exercise training, and fun-making atmosphere, for the dyads. A pilot-testing of the program among 30 dyads in a seed-fund project (Ref: 1040005942) has identified its positive effects on PAC, a full-scale proposal has been submitted for seeking support from the General Research Fund. As the findings also reinforce the importance of dyadic relationship and caregivers’ self-efficacy in determining the evolvement of PAC, the investigators is planning a mixed-method study to map out the changes and typology of these psychological and interpersonal attributes in the caregiving journey.

14610317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610317.value: Family caregiving is a valuable resource to buffer the dementia disease burden. Research in this field focuses on ameliorating the caregiver burden, least attention is placed on how to promote their positive aspects of caregiving (PAC). This mixed-method study explored how PAC evolves from the coping and meaning-making processes of family caregivers. From Jan 2018 to Dec 2020, 390 dementia family caregivers completed a survey at baseline and 6 months thereafter. Data analysis indicated that those who used active dementia management strategies and meaning-focused coping reported greater PAC. A higher self-efficacy in caregiving, better relationship with PwD and greater social support determined greater use of these coping strategies. In-depth interviews with 30 family caregivers further indicated that the successful use of active coping increased the caregivers’ self-efficacy, which reinforced more active coping to intensify sense of role gratification. Maintaining a good relationship with PwD is crucial to render the caregivers to find benefits and reframe the caregiving in a fateful and grateful perspectives. Although Chinese values increased intrinsic motivation towards caregiving, the concomitant use of active and meaning-focused coping is needed to strengthen PAC. The findings inform the development of innovative care to promote a positive and fulfilling caregiving journey.

14610717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14610717.value: Air pollution is a major problem in high-density cities in Asia (Schwela, Haq et al. 2012). There are two ways to solve the problem: control pollution emission or enhance pollution dispersion. A well-planned urban form helps with the dispersion of pollutants (Robins and Macdonald 1999). Therefore, optimizing urban planning schemes at early stages is an effective way to enhance pollution dispersion. Using PM2.5, a commonly-used proxy to investigate pollution dispersion (Chan and Kwok 2000), this study focuses on optimizing urban planning for better pollution dispersion in compact urban environment. Recent studies have proved that the densely built urban form of Hong Kong is not optimized for pollution dispersion (Yuan, Ng et al. 2014, Shi, Lau et al. 2016). Most current methods on pollution dispersion in urban environments are based on complex numerical simulations (Kakosimos, Hertel et al. 2010, ANSYS 2014, CERC 2016). However, they are too complicated and time-consuming to help planners optimize the planning scheme at early stages efficiently. Planners need straightforward information of reasonable accuracy and quick methods during the initial strategic planning stage of urban renewal and new development areas (NDAs) plan. To address the gap, this study aims to develop scientifically correct and straightforward optimization strategies for planners in Hong Kong. This will allow considerations of pollution dispersion to be incorporated in early-stage planning practices. The objectives of this study are: (A) to study and select suitable and representative sites based on the morphological understanding of Hong Kong’s urban context; (B) to conduct PM2.5 field measurements in sites selected in Task A under designated weather conditions for sampling in-situ data; (C) to collate in-situ data sets and with the collated data to develop spatial-temporal PM2.5 multistage geostatistical models and mappings; (D) based on the findings of Task C, to draw up urban planning optimization strategies for planners and decision-makers. The study output will directly inform the existing Air Ventilation Assessment (AVA) system and Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines (HKPSG) chapter 11 by providing another consideration of pollution dispersion for planning decision-making. This study will also substantially enrich the government effort of “A Clean Air Plan for Hong Kong” by providing practical action plans for policy-makers. Moreover, the study method will be readily applicable beyond Hong Kong to other heavily polluted high-density cities in Asia. 空氣污染是亞洲高密度城市的主要環境問題。解決此問題有兩種途徑：控制污染排放或加強污染擴散。 規劃良好的城市形態有助於污染物的擴散。 因此，在早期階段優化城市規劃方案是加強污染物擴散的有效途徑。 採用PM2.5作爲調查污染物擴散的代表，本研究旨在優化城市規劃，在緊湊的城市環境中實現更有效的污染物擴散。 近期研究證明，香港密集建成的城市形態並沒有基於污染物擴散的考慮進行優化。城市環境污染物擴散的現有研究方法大都基於復雜的數值模擬。 然而，數值模擬太過複雜和耗時，無法有效地幫助規劃師在早期階段優化規劃方案。 規劃師在市區重建和新發展區（NDAs）計劃的初步戰略規劃階段需要具有合理準確性並且能快速提供直觀信息的高效方法。 為了解決這個問題，本研究旨在為香港規劃師制定科學可靠但快速直接的優化策略，以便將基於污染物擴散的考慮納入早期城市規劃設計實踐。 這項研究的目的是：（A）根據香港城市情況的形態理解，研究並選擇合適及有代表性的場地; （B）在指定天氣條件下在任務A中選定的場地進行PM2.5實地測量，以獲取實測數據; （C）整理實測數據集，並基於實測數據在不同空間尺度上開發空間 - 時間PM2.5地理統計模型與分佈繪圖; （D）根據任務C的研究結果，為城市規劃師和決策者制定城市規劃優化策略。 研究成果將為規劃決策提供基於空氣污染物擴散的考量，直接豐富現有的「空氣流通評估（AVA）體系」以及「香港規劃標準與準則」的第十一章。 這項研究亦會大力促進政府為香港「清潔空氣計劃」所作的努力，為決策者提供切實的行動計劃。 此外，研究方法將也適用於香港以外亞洲其他空氣污染嚴重的高密度城市。

14610717.label: Realisation of objectives
14610717.value: All the study objectives have been realized during the project period. Based on the four study objectives, the PI and Co-I completed a four-step research plan which consists of four major research tasks (A-D) corresponding to the four objectives. Details on the objectives’ realization are documented in six publications (five published, one under-review, see Part C). The present GRF funding is acknowledged in all six publications. The corresponding research task of Objective 1 is Task A. It consists of two parts, which are (A1) Data preparation and (A2) Site selection. In Task A1, the land utilization map and road network data of Hong Kong have been collected. For Task A1, the project further improved the plan by introducing more data, which greatly helps to achieve more robust analytic results (over-achievement). Specifically, instead of solely using land utilization from local authorities, we also introduced a more advanced urban dataset - World Urban Database and Access Portal Tools (WUDAPT) and ran a series of land use pattern analyses (technical details documented in the publication entitled "Investigating the influence of urban land use and landscape pattern on PM2.5 spatial variation using mobile monitoring and WUDAPT" which has been attached to this completion report as a part of outcomes). Then, the project team collated the data mentioned above together with building morphological analytic layers in an open-source GIS system (QGIS). Based on the processed data from A1, parametrization was conducted for urban morphology using GIS to complete Task A2. 30 measurement sites reflecting various urban morphological characteristics were identified as suitable for measurement. These sites cover a wide range of land-use types and various road network, thus, are ideal for Task B2. Details are included in the journal publication entitled "Improving satellite aerosol optical Depth-PM2.5 correlations using land use regression with microscale geographic predictors in a high-density urban context". Another part of Task A1 is collecting and pre-processing aerosol optical depth (AOD). We overfulfilled the task. We not only examined the MODIS level 2 3km aerosol optical depth (AOD) data as planned but also tested the 1-km AOD data from the advanced MAIAC algorithm. By conducting additional cross-comparison and sensitivity tests, the MAIAC 1-km AOD is used. Task B (PM2.5 field measurement) was conducted to realize Objective 2. It consists of three parts, which are (B1) Equipment preparation, (B2) PM2.5 measurement in multiple sites, (B3) Measurement time and weather selection. In Task B1, portable instrumentation - PM2.5 and meteorological sensors were prepared and calibrated. The equipment preparation is documented in two publications, one aforementioned journal paper (entitled "Investigating…") and another paper (entitled "A multiscale land use regression approach for estimating intraurban spatial variability of PM2.5 concentration by integrating multi-source datasets". It is under review for publication in the Special Issue "Urban Microclimate Design: Pollutant Dispersion and Ventilation" of the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Expected to be online at the end of 2021). In Task B2, three elements were measured (PM2.5 concentration level, air temperature, relative humidity). In order to increase the measurement efficiency, we were employed not only personal portable equipment sets but also a vehicle-based sampling platform. This multi-method combined mobile observation not only guarantees the amount of data, but also reduces the impact of background concentration changes. Specifically, the 30 selected sites were divided into two groups for field measurement. Among all selected sites, ten high-density urban sites with complex architectural forms and mixed land use were separately measured. This allows capturing the fine-scale variability in PM2.5 concentration of these sites. The relevant information is documented in the paper entitled "A multiscale…". For the measurement using the vehicle-based sampling platform, two mobile monitoring routes (a total length of approximately 90 kilometers) were developed to connect the other 20 measurement sites identified in Task A2. Connecting these selected sites improves the measurement efficiency and reduces the uncertainties introduced by background concentration changes without compromising data spatial coverage. As planned in Task B3, only the data measured under the designated weather conditions were used for further research tasks. Objective 3 was realized by completing Task C. Task C involves four parts of work: Task C1-C4 as described in the project proposal. As planned in Task C1, humidity correction and temporal correction were conducted for in-situ PM2.5 measurement data quality control. Semivariogram modelling was also performed to identify the optimal spatial scale of measured data for spatial aggregation. In Task C2, correlation analysis between measured PM2.5 data and morphological parameters at neighborhood scale was performed. To estimate the neighborhood-scale spatial variability of PM2.5 concentration, we developed the LUR model using the data from in-situ sampling in the ten sites. During the model development, 12 urban morphological parameters were calculated using ten buffer radiuses. As a result, 120 candidate variables were examined. Six influential parameters (Sky view factor, Point-based FAI, Normalized betweenness, Normalized closeness, Control value, Global integration) were identified. The technical workflow and modeling results have been included in the paper entitled "A multiscale…". In Task C3, the correlation was investigated between AOD data, weather data, and ground-level PM2.5 data from the local monitoring network and measurement at the city scale. First, the pattern in the correlation between weather data and ground-level PM2.5 was investigated. This is a part of fundamental, which not only provides a better understanding of how the meteorological condition and regional scale transport of air pollution alter the ground-level PM2.5 but also helps with eliminating other non-local influential factors. The analytic method and results are documented in a journal publication entitled "Characteristics of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) over Urban, Suburban, and Rural Areas of Hong Kong". Then, the correlation between AOD data and ground-level PM2.5 data from the local monitoring network was calibrated by incorporating with microscale geographic predictors (details documented in the paper entitled "Improving…"). Finally, the city-scale LUR spatiotemporal models were developed by four seasons. The model development process consists of three steps, which are variable selection, regression modelling, and spatial mapping. 159 candidate variables (133 spatial variables and 26 temporal variables) were examined by variable importance. GTWR technique were employed. The workflow and results are documented in two aforementioned papers (entitled "Investigating…" and "A multiscale…"). The models at multiple scales were integrated into a final PM2.5 map over the entire city. To realize Objective 4, urban planning optimization strategies were drawn up for planners and decision-makers based on the findings from Task C. Spatiotemporal models developed in Task C2-C4 provides quantitative evidence which helped us to identify the influential morphological parameters decisive to pollution dispersion. These influential parameters were extracted and summarized in Task D1. By extracting quantitative relationships between influential parameters and pollution concentration from the resultant geostatistical models (Task D2) and combining the quantitative relationship with the planning development parameters used by planners in Hong Kong in their daily practice (Task D3), the project provides a readily applicable reference for evidence-based urban planning and design process (Task D4). The above quantitative reference for evidence-based urban planning and design are described in the discussion and conclusion of three publications mentioned earlier (entitled "Improving…", "Investigating…", and "A multiscale…").

14610717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610717.value: In the project, the data collected by Task A can be used for further advanced data analysis. The data quantity and quality are in compliance with and fulfill the requirement of more advanced algorithms used in the geospatial data science field (machine learning, AI etc.). The equipment prepared by Task B are usable for any future works relevant to urban air quality and human exposure to air pollution. Based on such collaborative research and international research impacts, this research will be further developed to be more interdisciplinary and cross-regional.

14610717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610717.value: Urban planners need straightforward information of reasonable accuracy and quick methods to support evidence-based decision-making in the initial strategic planning stage. However, such information is usually not available to planners as there are knowledge and practical barriers between scientific research and real-world practice. There is a lack of practically usable methodology and translatable workflow between scientists and planners. This is caused by the mismatch of information, knowledge and needs between the two. Therefore, traditional methods did not work well to break the barrier. To address this gap, we take urban air pollution diffusion optimization as a starting point. The project develops urban planning optimization strategies for improving air quality in compact cities. From a scientific point of view, using geospatial modelling based on in-situ data, this research has maintained its scientificity and rigor. From data collection instrument calibration to formal analysis and quantitative modeling, each step of the research has undergone careful quality control to ensure the correctness and robustness of the research findings. From a practical point of view, this project develops a feasible workflow that translates complicated scientific findings to fit-for-purpose and straightforward information, which could directly inform the urban planning practice.

14610917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14610917.value: The present project studies the use of witchcraft in court politics and the social and religious environment that encouraged the practice of and belief in witchcraft in early and medieval China, from the Han to the Tang Dynasties. By witchcraft we mean the kind of cultic actions performed by people with the intention to harm a certain targeted person(s). In the context of Chinese history, the term witchcraft can include two kinds of actions. The first is represented by the term “wugu 巫蠱,” that is, employing poisonous vermin with the help of a wu-shaman to harm people; the second is represented by the term “zhuzu 祝詛,” that is, casting curses upon someone. There was, therefore, a certain similarity between the two actions, as both resorted to harming people by using malicious and supernatural methods. From a cross-cultural point of view, Chinese witchcraft shared some fundamental similarities with witchcraft and sorcery in other parts of the world. What is interesting, however, is the different use of witchcraft in each society. This is because witchcraft, just as religion, was a cultural specific phenomenon that could reflect the characteristics of each culture in question. In the present research, we are not merely concerned with finding out if or how witchcraft worked in a technical sense in Chinese society, but more importantly the social, cultural, medical, and religious environment that nurtured or encouraged the practice of and belief in the efficacy of witchcraft. We are particularly interested in the practices of witchcraft in court politics and palace intrigues. A preliminary survey shows that, from the Han to the end of Tang Dynasty (130 BEC-987 CE), there were at least fifty cases of witchcraft recorded in the official histories that involved serious accusations and persecutions of queens, princes, princesses, high officials, and their family members. Through a detailed analysis of these cases, and by placing them in the socio-cultural context, this project wishes to conduct a multidisciplinary research that considers the cases from various angles: court politics, religious mentality, health and medicine, and social psychology. A comparison of the finding with the European witchcraft, although necessarily only a cursory one in this project, may lead us to a better understanding of both societies in the aspects of the interaction between belief, politics, and popular mentality. 本計畫之目標乃針對中國自漢至唐代的巫蠱祝詛現象做一全面之研究。所謂巫蠱與祝詛是兩件事。巫蠱又原為二事，巫是巫術，蠱是病痛或病毒，以巫術之施行而令人中蠱毒，則為巫蠱。祝詛之術，則是以呪術之施行達到令人生病或死亡或遭禍之目的，其中不一定有蠱毒。然而巫蠱祝詛合而觀之，均為以巫術手段以達到加害他人之目的，可以黑巫術一詞統括之。巫蠱祝詛之現象，為世界各文明中常見，其根基部分為人生理和疫病之自然因素，部分則為宗教中有關鬼神力量之信仰因素。此現象之所以值得吾人研究，並非為了要瞭解蠱毒之是否真正存在，或者祝詛是否真正有效，而在其一旦成為社會中普遍相信之事實，則具有重大之文化及政治意義。中國之巫術與世界其他地區的巫術有一些基本的相似性。但有趣的是不同社會中巫術的作用。因為，如同宗教一樣，巫術是一種文化現象，可以反映各個文化的特性。本研究不止要研究巫術是以何種方式在中國社會中運作，重要的是要找出滋養或促成巫術行為及信仰的社會，文化，醫學，以及宗教環境。本研究特別重視的是巫術在宮庭政治中的角色。初步觀察顯示，由漢至唐，在官方正史紀錄中，至少有五十次巫蠱事件發生在宮庭之中，牽涉到對后妃，王子，公主，高官及其家庭的迫害。本研究希望透過祥細的分析，以跨學科的角度，從政治，宗教心態，健康及醫藥，以及社會心理等方面來考量這些巫蠱事件的意義。同時，中古中國的巫術與中古、近代歐洲巫術的異同之處為何？此雖非本研究的重點，但藉由兩者的比較來看待在中國與歐洲同樣被視為異端實踐的巫術，當時所有人與環境是如何創造出巫術的形象，並利用之，能讓我們對於這兩個社會的本質有更深入的瞭解。

14610917.label: Realisation of objectives
14610917.value: The project has been completed according to plan. All four objectives have been achieved. A book has been accepted for publication, and is in the process of typesetting. Please see the attached pdf file. Individual objectives are described below. 1. "To collect and analyze all the cases involved witchcraft and sorcery in court politics from the Han to the Tang Dynasties": The cases of witchcraft in court politics have been collected and studied in chapters 3 and 4. This provides the main body of the study what allows us to see the workings of the origin, the development, and the intrigues behind the cases involving witchcraft in court politics. 2. "To study the socio-cultural, medical, and religious factors that constituted the context in which the belief in witchcraft flourished": This objective has been achieved in Chapters 1, 2, 4 as the social and religious origins of wugu are discussed, and the reasons why the belief of wugu could have persisted in society are explained. 3. "To map out the pattern of the cases of witchcraft: what was the status of the people accused of witchcraft, what was the status of the victims of witchcraft, and what was the general outcome of the persecution": This objective has been achieved in chapter 5, in which the personal backgrounds and relationships of the victims and the villains of wugu-witchcraft are analyzed, and the social and religious mentality of the society that was reflected by these cases are discussed. 4. "To compare the pattern and cultural factors contributed to witchcraft found in the Chinese sources with the findings of witch hunt in the European context": Chapter 6 provides a comparison of the witchcraft cases in Chinese history with the witch hunt craze of early modern Europe, and finds out not only some interesting similarities in how people reacted to the rumors of witchcraft, but also some difference as to the origin and prevalence of witchcraft cases, which reveals the different social and religious realities of China and Europe.

14610917.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610917.value: In the span of over one thousand years, from the Han to the Tang Dynasty, Wugu played a special role in the context of court politics. The idea of gu could have been simply a description of diseases related to food poison. Yet as it developed into something like an invisible evil spirit, it was associated with witchcraft, and became part of the technique that the wu-shaman could perform or control to do harm to people. The reason for this association of disease with witchcraft was often explained as due to the lack of precise medical knowledge about the causes of diseases and the treatments, which is not unique in many pre-modern societies. The fact that wugu-witchcraft in particular was singled out as a most hideous crime against the emperor or the royal family members, must be understood from the combination of wu-shaman and gu-poison. As previous studies have shown, the wu-shaman had been in existence in society as early as the Shang Dynasty, and its function as part of the state ritual system was generally recognized. Yet it is also a fact that in society at large the wu-shamans were the kind of special agents that could communicate with ghosts and spirits, and they could perform certain ritual acts and recite certain spells to either help or harm people. Regardless if particular individuals might not have believed in the reality of wugu-witchcraft, there could not have been resistance against the general social atmosphere. All subsequent political or personal struggles that were conducted under the pretext of wugu-witchcraft were based on the belief that wugu might be effective. It was difficult to deny the charge of witchcraft, since by definition it was a secret action that was hidden away from people’s knowledge. The transmitted “common sense” in society makes it difficult to deny the effectiveness of witchcraft since the general psychology was that “although I did not do it, but I believe many people could indeed perform witchcraft.” Thus wugu-witchcraft was not only a folk belief or an excuse that was deliberately used to persecute others. We need also to consider the psychological, social, and medical factors that all congealed to form the larger environment that makes the idea persuasive: fear of unknown illness, the psychological pressure due to the belief in the gu-poison, or half-heartedly following the crowd and accuse someone not belonging to one’s associates, etc.

14610917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610917.value: This project dealt with wugu-witchcraft in Chinese history, mainly from the Han to the Tang Dynasties and in the context of court politics. However, in order to study this, we need to study the social and religious mentality in society throughout the period, so that what happened in the court could be better understood. The further development of this project would be an investigation into the wugu cases in Chinese society from the Tang to the Qing Dynasties. Because of the availability of more historical sources, such an investigation should concentrate more on the wugu cases in the larger society, so that a more complete picture could be gained, and the impressions and results of the present project could be further examined and compared.

14611017.label: Project Objectives
14611017.value: To survey existing social and spatial structures of nine Dong Minority villages along the Pingtan River valley, Tongdao County, Hunan Province. To position the social spaces and their associated architecture of the Dong Minority settlements as a unique typology of village public space, distinct from other rural communities in China and instrumental in developing a strategic regeneration plan. To implement three innovative architectural prototypes, focusing on regenerating and adapting existing structures of the Dong Minority village of Gaobu, Hunan Province, China. To generate an incremental adaptive planning framework, in the form of a masterplan and associated handbook for the village of Gaobu, outlining alternative development strategies of regeneration that aim to better rural living for the whole Dong community for years to come.

14611017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611017.value: The aim of this project is to develop an alternative sustainable strategy to regenerate Dong Minority villages in China via new architectural prototypes that respond to contemporary rural developments and foster minimum impact to the existing fabric of the village. The Dong ethnic minority people are one of China’s 56 ethnic groups, who live in the region delimited by southwest Hunan, southeast Guizhou and north Guangxi. With a population of almost three million and a long history of more than 1,000 years dating back to the Tang Dynasty, the Dong communities are today, in a similar manner to many other Chinese rural settlements, deeply affected by the phenomenon of “Village Hollowing”. This unprecedented exodus of rural populations to expanding urban areas, has resulted in almost vacant villages inhabited by struggling communities of mostly elderly people and children. The complex relationship between daily life, rituals and buildings is a vital part of how the Dong community dwell within their environment. Dong culture is essentially a material culture, they possess no written language, where their most important means of self-identification derives from an inherent relationship between the inhabitants and their artifacts, rituals and their architecture. Public structures such as the “Wind-and-Rain Bridge” and “Drum Tower” are at the heart of all social activity, supporting an elaborate public space system anchored in daily practice. This social structure which results from the habitus of acquired and settled dispositions of its individuals, represents Dong’s greatest asset to stem the exodus. Using the Dong Minority village of Gaobu, located along the Pingtan River in Hunan Province, China as a pilot project, the aim is to generate an integrated masterplan that will act as a guideline to both national and regional policy makers working on the regeneration of Chinese Minority villages. Following preparatory prior research into the region, we have identified four specific issues that address the complexity of the present Dong settlement, namely: Waste Management, Degradation of the Built Environment, Tourism and Education that will allow us to propose a series of innovative architectural prototypes that can contribute to the village becoming a socially and ecologically sustainable model in the future. Collectively the prototypes and the masterplan aim to develop a handbook of practical recommendations for sustainable adaptive regeneration of the Dong villages, allowing communities to modernize through contemporary interventions which do not compete with tradition, rather complement integration with existing culture. 這個項目的目的是製定一個替代可持續發展的策略，通過新的建築原型在中國重新生成東部少數民族村莊，這些建築原型可以應對當代農村發展，並對現有的村莊結構產生最小的影響。東少數民族是中國56個民族之一，居住在湖南西南，貴州東南，廣西北部劃定的地區。東方社區人口近三百萬，歷史悠久，歷時可追溯至唐代，今天，東方社區與中國許多其他定居點類似，受到“村寨”現象的深刻影響， 。農村人口急劇擴大，擴大了城市地區，導致幾乎空置的村莊居住著大部分老年人和兒童的掙扎社區。 日常生活，儀式和建築之間的複雜關係，是東部社區居住在環境中的重要組成部分。東文化本質上是一種物質文化，它們沒有書面語言，其最重要的自我認同手段來源於居民及其文物，儀式及其建築之間的固有關係。諸如“風雨大橋”和“鼓樓”等公共建築是所有社會活動的核心，支持日常實踐中精心製作的公共空間系統。這種社會結構是由於其個人獲得和解決的處置的習慣而產生的，代表著董事會遏制流亡的最大的財富。 利用位於湖南省平潭河的高布鎮少尉村作為試點項目，旨在製定綜合總體規劃，作為國家和地區決策者在中國再生中的指導方針少數民族村莊在對本地區進行的事前研究之前，我們確定了四個具體問題，解決了目前東沉沉的複雜性，即廢物管理，建築環境退化，旅遊與教育，使我們能夠提出一系列創新的建築原型這將有助於未來村莊成為社會和生態可持續發展的模式。集體原型和總體規劃旨在為東村村莊的可持續適應性再生建立實用建議手冊，使社區能夠通過不與傳統競爭的現代干預措施進行現代化改造，而與現有文化融為一體。

14611017.label: Realisation of objectives
14611017.value: OBJECTIVE 1 The team visited 9 villages along the Pingtan river: Gaobu, Gaotuan, Yanglan, Pingtan, Pingri, Hengling, Shangdutian, Huangdu and Yutou. The fieldwork was structured into three parts; 1) Consultations with Heritage Officials and local stakeholders to understand the key issues affecting the community, 2) Photographic Survey of key public spaces within each village, 3) Architectural Survey in the form of drawings recording the status and public engagement of the village’s civic spaces. Social spaces in Dong culture are linked to two specific village building typologies, namely the “Wind and Rain” bridge and “Drum” Tower. These two types of social space, which have evolved over centuries, are the focal point of all public life within the village. Their location is at the core of the village’s DNA, carefully situated according to longstanding traditions related to land and Fengshui thinking. During this objective, we also conducted two educational workshops associated with a Masters of Architecture at CUHK that assisted our research. The first in 2018, a workshop in conjunction with Guangzhou University where Prof. Cai (CoI) and I, taught 40 students from CUHK and GZU, where students spent 2 weeks creating an architectural and sociological map of Gaobu. The investigation addressed issues relating to public habitation such as Furniture, Children, Water, River, Abandonment, Waste, Events, Food, In-between, Boundary. The second workshop that took place during the summer of 2019, explored how to reactivate residual public spaces within the village. Again students from the same universities, aided by the assistant of two additional professors from the Polytechnic of Milan (Prof. Francesco Augelli) and Hunan University (Prof. LU, Jiangsong), designed and built 9 timber prototypes. From this exercise not only did we help villagers addressed pressing public issues but we also gained intangible knowledge about dong timber construction methods and local craftsmanship. In parallel with these events, several other research activities took place. Together with the CoI, we presented an academic paper at the “Southwest Settlement” conference, Hunan University (2018/05). We conducted a comparative trip to several minority rural areas within China, including Hexinwu (Guangdong) and Chengyang (Hunan). The graphic material associated with this objective is included as a PDF titled “Survey” attached to this report. OBJECTIVE 2 During this objective the team created a detailed typological study of the three main categories of public space in the Pingtan Valley; the “Wind & Rain” Bridge, the “Drum” Tower and associated Public Spaces. For the Drum Tower, we surveyed 20 structures, catalogued them according to their square or hexagonal plans. Generated a detailed survey for two Drum Towers within the village of Gaobu, Longxing and Gaosheng, for which we developed a detailed 3D study analysing the tectonic structure. While for the Wind and Rain Bridges we surveyed two Gaobu bridges analysing: social activities, the timber structure and construction system. For the Public Social Spaces, we investigated 20 different types (gates, squares, rest areas, public stages, etc…) carefully considering the construction materials, associated programme and purpose, type and times of activities. We also catalogued new types of public amenities that today focus around small commercial shops as well as new interventions within the public sphere, such as street lighting, public toilets, new embankments to the river edges, signage and public banners, new tourist centre, parking and social government buildings. In preparation to the 3 design and build prototypes, we carried out detailed evaluations of three ecosystems: The waste disposal system for the entire village (indexing the different types of waste); The village’s educational amenities that centre around the local primary school and finally a comprehensive survey over 300 lived in dwellings and 70 abandoned houses. OBJECTIVE 3 Objective 3 is the core of the research, where the prototype becomes the primary research source. Having identified the 3 key areas of investigation, namely Waste Management, Sustainable Tourism and New Educational Facilities the team embarked on translating the findings into prepositional architectural solutions. Given the time and resources, each prototype varied in degree of resolution achieved. Two prototypes were advanced to the schematic design stage (Waste and Tourism) while the Educational prototype was designed and built thanks to a donation of 500,000 HKD from the One University, One Village charity. Waste is a concept foreign to Dong people, the word doesn’t even exist in their language, as they have always lived in an autonomous ecosystem, where everything is returned to nature. With the advent of modernization, this condition has drastically changed and the village is today ill-equipped to cope with the disposal of modern materials such as detergents that are eliminating the indigenous fish, construction materials which are dumped by the side of the road or plastics which are burnt adjacent to dwellings. For this reason, we designed a small “Recyclable Centre”, strategically located along the main road where people could recycle materials such as plastic, aluminium and other inorganic waste. The centre also acted as a social gathering space with a stand overlooking the river for people to gather. The sustainable tourism residence prototype was the result of conversations held with a local family who owned an abandoned traditional Dong timber dwelling that had long been abandoned. The grandmother, who has been living alone since her family moved to the city, was keen to transform the house into a source of income. The proposed prototype transforms and adjusts the existing structure into a “Carpentry Hostel” aimed at the high school and university students where they could stay and learn about traditional timber construction. The third prototype was the Gabou “Book House” a community library for children designed and built adjacent to the village’s primary school. The project started as an idea presented to the villagers as a means of reviving village culture. Developed over several iterative schemes in close collaboration with local inhabitants and carpenters, the aim was to use the design a building that contained the DNA of traditional Dong architecture, used local timber sources but translated the Dong timber typology into a contemporary design where social gatherings were encouraged through the introduction of natural light. OBJECTIVE 4 The Dong village of Gaobu became the testing ground for a new form of rural regeneration that calibrates how villages can modernize gradually without neglecting their tangible and intangible cultural assets. By working directly with “active” prototypes the team was able to generate innovative proposals that became primary sources of research knowledge. “Adapting Villages” in this regards established an operative framework that responds to direct needs, employing strategic local tools that would allow this transition to happen without destabilizing the fragile cultural and environmental balance developed over time. This strategic knowledge was disseminated by a series of events: 1) International Workshop titled “Adapting Villages” held at CUHK School of Architecture. 2) Several Public Exhibitions including Hong Kong Inspire and the Seoul International Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism. 3) Conference Presentations such as Ted Talk at Lingnan University Hong Kong, I Care Library Talk at CUHK and the PLEA Conference. 4) Journal Papers in the Journal of Architecture. 5) Press articles in leading architectural websites such as Domus and Archdaily, Local Press such as South China Morning Post. 6) International Awards for Architecture recognition including World Architecture Festival, Design for Asia Award, Taipei International Design Awards.

14611017.label: Major findings and research outcome
14611017.value: MAJOR FINDINGS 1) Taxonomy of “Public Spaces” within the 9 villages along the Pingtan river valley, mapping how these spaces are embedded in Dong culture and everyday customs. 2) Detailed survey of Dong minority village of Gaobu, the first document of its kind, analysing how the village works as an ecosystem tightly connected to its environment. 3) Comprehensive catalogue of all domestic dwellings within Gaobu, outlining how houses are used or in the most case not used (abandoned). 4) Recording of local traditional carpentry construction techniques and how this knowledge is still used to build timber structures today. 5) Understanding of rural village family structures and how households adapt to everyday realities. 6) Study of how children behave within the village and the educational amenities available to them. RESEARCH OUTCOMES 1) Built Prototypes Gabou Book House, Public Children’s library. The 200m² two-story Gaobu Book House adopts the traditional Dong house “Ganlan” typology as the creative starting point, where local timber is used for the framing. By working with-in the system, rather than against the system, materiality and craftsmanship inject new life back into the village. 2) Designed Prototypes Waste Management Centre Sustainable Tourist Residence 3) Educational Workshops 2 Summer Elective Courses done in collaboration with Guangzhou University School of Architecture, 2018 and 2019. 80 students participated. 4) Journal Papers The Journal of Architecture Volume 25, 2020, Issue 1 “Villages Prototypes: A Survival Strategy for Chinese Minority Rural Villages” published with CoI Prof. Ling CAI. 4) Exhibitions Design Inspire, HKTDC (2018) Seoul Architecture Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism (2019) 5) Conferences Adapting Villages, International Conference at CUHK (2019) PLEA Conference Hong Kong (2019) TED Talk x Lingnan University (2019) World Architecture Festival, Amsterdam (2019) 6) Press Articles Press articles in leading architectural websites such as Domus and Archdaily, Local Press such as South China Morning Post. 7) Awards International Awards for Architecture recognition including World Architecture Festival, Design for Asia Award, Taipei International Design Awards.

14611017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14611017.value: Adaptive Villages was the starting point for our research into traditional Dong rural villages. To date, the work has already started a series of parallel research projects related to our findings. Firstly, in 2019 we were awarded another GRF grant titled “Mutation Houses: Prototype Solutions for a Prefabricated Self-build Timber House in Rural China” that looks at generating an alternative design for the traditional 3 storey timber Dong house aiming to incorporate modern materials and appliances. Secondly, we are looking to export the Adaptive villages model generated in Gaobu to other Dong areas, specifically in Northern Dong, Guizhou Province. Another related project where we are translating our findings relates to a Knowledge Transfer Grant we have been awarded titles “Forgotten Villages of Hong Kong” where the prototype models of activating abandoned villages are being implemented. For this project, we are working in collaboration with the Environmental Protection Department of the Hong Kong Government.

14611017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14611017.value: Chinese rural villages are rapidly disappearing. This project investigated a specific type of rural minority village in Hunan Province that still survives but is struggling to cope with the advent of rapid modernization. Over the course of two years, working closely with local villagers we gained their trust and support to implement several projects that focused on the realization of community architectural prototypes. Through these projects, we were able to understand how Dong traditional culture survives and is still an integral part of their everyday life. The prototypes were also the vehicle to impact both socially, with the local children making use of the Gaobu Book House and professionally with the building being awarded several prestigious prizes. Through this research project “Adapting Villages” has become a model for rural village regeneration, a model that allows villages to adapt to contemporary life without losing their traditional DNA. The project has also been a success with local government officials who have requested the team to generate similar research prototype projects for nearby village schools.

14611217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611217.value: Ethnic economy refers to high ethnic representation in an industrial sector. It has been a key subject in understanding the economic attainment of racial and ethnic group as the ethnic economy environment is conducive to better economic returns for co-ethnic members working there. While ethnic businesses are embedded in an ethnic economy, the ethnic economy is embedded in a larger industrial environment. The latter relationship has not well discussed in the literature. The proposal takes on this task and concentrate on two aspects of embeddedness of ethnic economy in larger industrial environment that may have strong relationship with economic returns of individuals participating in ethnic economy. First, we explore how the nestedness of ethnic economy in the larger industrial context is related to earnings. To be specific, we will explore how the proportion of co-ethnic representation in an industrial sub-sector and its larger context (i.e., the larger industrial sector in which a sub-sector is situated) are related to the earnings of co-ethnic members working there (e.g. ethnic representation in chemical manufacturing industry and the general manufacturing industry). In addition, we will study how the proportion of co-ethnic representation in industrial sub-sectors and the co-ethnic proportion of other industrial sub-sectors in the same larger industrial sector are related to the earnings of co-ethnic workers (e.g. ethnic representation in chemical manufacturing vs. clothing manufacturing and wood manufacturing). Second, we explore the ethnic enclosure of the ethnic business environment. In other words, we understand the relationship of territoriality of the embedded environment and earnings of those participating in ethnic economy. We suggest that the larger the proportion of ethnic businesses in an industrial sector and sub-sector use of ethnic language is more enclosed to own ethnic group. We examine how the proportion of people using ethnic language at work, the proportion of people using ethnic language among co-ethnic members in an industrial sub-sector, and the proportion of people in other industrial sub-sectors within a larger industrial sector are related to the earnings of those working in the ethnic economy. Our analysis draws on the 2011 Canadian National Household Survey. We will look specifically at the labor force activity of Chinese aged 18 to 64, focusing on the earnings of employers and paid workers in 15 largest census metropolitan areas (CMAs) in Canada. These cities vary in size, have the largest numbers of Chinese, and represent over 93% of Chinese in Canada. 族裔經濟與其背後的工業大環境 族裔經濟是指一工業擁有比例較高的族裔成員。族裔經濟已經成為了理解種族經濟狀況的一個重要課題。一個族裔的小生意有時候嵌入在整個族裔經濟中，而族裔經濟又嵌入在一個更大的工業環境里。我們發現，在已有的文獻中，族裔經濟與大工業環境的關係很少被談及，因此本研究將集中在這一個議題上。我們計劃從兩個方面研究族裔經濟在大工業環境中的嵌入。首先，我們會去探索族裔在其所屬的工業(例如：餐飲業)的族裔分佈和其整體的工業環境（例如：服務業）如何影響參與工作的本族裔工人的收入。同時，我們還會研究，在相同的大工業環境下，同族裔在不同的工業在其整體的工業環境的族裔分佈如何影響工人收入。第二，我們探究在族裔經濟環境和其整體的工業環境中的族裔封閉對個人收入的影響。本研究使用了2011年加拿大國家家庭調查數據，研究群體以在18-64歲間處在勞工活躍期的華裔為目標，集中探究了在15個加拿大的大都會區域，僱主以及員工的收入。這些城市中的華人代表了全加拿大超過93%的華裔。

14611217.label: Realisation of objectives
14611217.value: This is the completion report of the funded project. The project has realized all objectives as stated. Objective 1: To develop a theoretical linkage connecting the levels of embeddedness of ethnic economy to a larger industrial environment in the study of ethnic economy The objective has been achieved. We identified three sets of literature -- human ecology, social network, and organizational ecology -- that help us specify how the earnings of co-ethnic employees and employers are related to the level of co-ethnic representation in the larger industrial cluster. We focused on developing a framework to understand how co-ethnic representation in the industrial cluster shapes the earnings of co-ethnic members and narrowing the income gap between co-ethnic members and others. We developed specific hypotheses to test the relationship derived from the literature. Objective 2: To explore the relationship between co-ethnic representation in an industrial sub-sector and in its larger industrial sector and its implication to earnings of employers and employees working in ethnic businesses. The objective was achieved. Drawing from 2011 Canadian Household Survey, our findings show that earning of ethnic employers and employees is related to the larger industrial cluster with greater co-ethnic representation. However, the relationship is different for employers and employees, and sometimes opposite. Specifically, a larger portion of Chinese ethnic economies in an industry cluster is negatively related to the earnings of Chinese employers, but is not related to the earnings of Chinese employees. A larger portion of employment niches in an industry cluster is negatively related to the earnings of Chinese employers, but positively related to the earnings of Chinese employees. For the relationship of ethnic representation in larger industrial cluster and narrowing income difference between co-ethnic members and others, we find that the percentage of co-ethnic ethnic economies among all related industrial sectors in an industry cluster reduces the differences in earnings of ethnic and non-ethnic members working there. The findings further show that the relationship is significant for co-ethnic employees, but not for co-ethnic employers. Objective 3: To explore how the use of ethnic languages in a workplace, the proportion of workers using ethnic languages in the ethnic economy, and the lager industrial environment are related to the earnings of employers and employees working in ethnic businesses. The objective has been achieved. Using the 2011 Canadian Household Survey, we found that (1) the percentage of workers knowing English or French in the workplace is related to the earnings of co-ethnic employers only and (2) the percentage of immigrants in the workplace is not related to the earnings of both co-ethnic employers and employees. However, on the income gap between co-ethnic members and others, we found that the percentage of workers knowing English or French and the percentage of immigrants are related to co-ethnic employees and others, but not to employers. Objective 4: To explore the relative importance of the level of nestedness and ethnic enclosure of the business and its larger industrial environment on earnings of employers and employees. The objective was achieved. First, the findings show clearly that ethnic embeddedness in an industry cluster is significantly related to the earnings of co-ethnic members working in the industry. Nestedness refers to the representation of ethnic economies (over-representation of co-ethnic employers and employees), co-ethnic entrepreneurial niches (over-representation of co-ethnic employers), and co-ethnic employment niches (over-representation of co-ethnic employees) are nested in larger industrial cluster. This finding leads to an extension of the concept of ethnic embeddedness in the labor market to include the dimension of co-ethnic representation in an industry cluster. Our findings suggest that the evaluation of the earnings of ethnic members should focus not only on the industrial sectors involved, but also on the co-ethnic composition of the larger industry cluster. It is important to consider the co-ethnic dynamics suggested in the original discussion of participation in ethnic economy. However, according to our findings, the co-ethnic composition of the industry cluster containing the industrial sector in which ethnic members participate can have a significant relationship to the earnings of individuals working in ethnic economy. Objective 5: To evaluate the relative importance of socio-demographic backgrounds of employers with and without controlling for the level of nestedness and ethnic enclosure of the business and its industrial environment. The objective has been achieved. The results show that both socio-demographic backgrounds of employers and the co-ethnic representation in the industry cluster have an independent and significant relationship with the earnings of employers. In addition, the relationship remains significant even when the larger industrial cluster is over-represented by co-ethnic employers, employees or both. Yet, the degree to which socio-demographic background is related to reduced earnings gap with others is weaker for co-ethnic employers compared to that for co-ethnic employees and others. Objective 6: To use the Canadian National Household Survey to understand how the level of embeddedness and enclosure is related to earnings of Chinese ethnic entrepreneurs in Canada, which has large numbers of immigrants from Hong Kong and mainland China. The objective was achieved. All analyses are based on Canadian National Household Survey and is to explore how the level of embeddedness and enclosure is related to earnings of co-ethnic employers and employees and narrowing earning gap between co-ethnic and other members. We also used the data to understand how the likelihood of being an entrepreneur is related to the diverse education experience of immigrants.

14611217.label: Major findings and research outcome
14611217.value: We have three sets of major findings. First, the study expands the understanding of the ways that ethnic embeddedness is related to the earnings of co-ethnic members by exploring the relationship between ethnic representation in an industry cluster and the earnings of co-ethnic employers and employees working there. Drawing from the 2011 Canadian Household Survey, our findings confirm the relationship. However, the relationship is different for employers and employees, and sometimes opposite. Specifically, a larger portion of Chinese ethnic economies in an industry cluster is negatively related to the earnings of Chinese employers, but is not related to the earnings of Chinese employees. A larger portion of employment niches in an industry cluster is negatively related to the earnings of Chinese employers, but positively related to the earnings of Chinese employees. Second, we examine how earning differences between co-ethnic members and others not only is related to whether they participate in ethnic economy and also is related to the percentage of ethnic economies among related industrial sectors in a larger industry cluster. The study envisages ethnic economy is embedded in larger industry cluster and its operation is shaped by the larger industrial context. Drawing from the 2011 Canadian National Survey, we find that the percentage of co-ethnic ethnic economies among all related industrial sectors in an industry cluster reduces the differences in earnings of ethnic and non-ethnic members working there. The findings further show that the relationship is significant for co-ethnic employees, but not for co-ethnic employers. Third, we explore how being entrepreneurs of immigrants, with large proportion of Chinese, is related to their diverse educational experiences: studying overseas, receiving STEM education, completing master or doctoral training. Drawing from the 2016 Canadian census, we found that despite the small differences between native-born and immigrant populations in the percentages of entrepreneurs, there are considerable differences in location of study, STEM education, and completion of master or doctoral education.

14611217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14611217.value: There may be differences in social and economic behavior among Chinese sub-ethnic groups in Canada (i.e., Chinese immigrants from Taiwan, Hong Kong, and other parts of East and Southeast Asia), which may suggest that different groups occupy different industrial sectors. Future research should explore the topic with survey data or qualitative interviews to understand the dynamics among Chinese sub-groups. Besides, it is important to disentangle how different university education experiences are related to the short and long term impact on the survival and growth of businesses for both groups. Finally, it is important to understand how specific city context interacts with diverse university education experiences to shape the likelihood of native-born and immigrant graduates becoming entrepreneurs.

14611217.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14611217.value: Instead of focusing only on co-ethnic representations in a particular industrial sector, which has been well researched and documented, we focused on co-ethnic representations in the larger industrial cluster. Using the 2011 Canadian National Survey, we found that the ethnic representation in an industry cluster is related to the earnings of co-ethnic employers and employees working there. Furthermore, we also found that the ethnic representation in an industry cluster is related to the differences in earnings for ethnic and non-ethnic members working there.
