14611417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611417.value: Background: In response to the heavy global burden of disease attributable to alcohol and the increasing drinking rates in traditionally-low consumption regions, the World Health Organization (WHO) has adopted a global strategy to combat the harmful use of alcohol. The WHO has outlined highly cost-effective, evidence-based recommendations ("Best Buys") for reducing the harmful use of alcohol. These "Best Buys" call for: 1) increasing alcohol price through taxation or minimum unit price legislation, 2) restricting availability of alcohol in retail and on-premise establishments and 3) a comprehensive ban of alcohol marketing strategies including event sponsorship. However, in contradiction to these recommendations, Hong Kong has eliminated its duties on beer and wine since 2008. Despite rapid increases in drinking levels, there exist few restrictions on alcohol availability and almost no regulation of marketing. Objectives: This objectives are to examine the public attitudes and expert opinions on a wide range of alcohol harms reduction strategies in order to inform future policy. A stepwise alcohol harms reduction strategy for Hong Kong would ideally prioritize the Best Buy interventions with wide public support that are deemed feasible by experts. Methods: This mixed methods study will consist of two phases. In Phase I, a population-based, telephone survey will be conducted that will update information on current drinking patterns, provide baseline data on the level of harms from alcohol use and assess the public acceptability of a wide spectrum of "Best Buy" recommendations (e.g. restricting hours of alcohol sales) and perceived consequences of these strategies. Drinkers will be asked which interventions would be likely reduce their own drinking levels to gauge potential impact. Qualitative interviews with expert stakeholders (e.g. hospitality and alcohol industry workers, alcohol retailers) will be done in Phase II to obtain their views on the feasibility and likely consequences of WHO Best Buys with particular emphasis on alcohol harms reduction interventions identified in Phase I as having wide popular support. A focus group on regular drinkers will obtain views on the potential consequences of the WHO strategies. Main Outcomes: Acceptability of various alcohol policies will be assessed by rankings of endorsement by the survey respondents . The perceived effect of various strategies on the respondent's own drinking behaviors can provide insight on the likely relative impact of various policies on drinking levels on various demographic subgroups. That qualitative data provides expert views on feasibility and in-depth information about the likely positive/negative consequences of WHO-recommended strategies. 世界衞生組織之“最佳購買”策略減少香港酒精使用危害的可行性和接受度：公眾態度與持份者意見的比較 背景：為應對酒精引起的全球重大疾病負擔以及傳統低酒精消費地區日益上升的飲酒率，世界衞生組織（WHO）實施了一項打擊有害使用酒精的全球戰略。世衞組織概述了降低有害使用酒精的高性價比且基於證據的建議（“最佳購買”）。這些“最佳購買”策略要求：1）通過稅收或最低單價立法提高酒精價格，2）限制零售和特許營業場所的酒精供應，3）全面禁止酒精飲品的營銷策略，包括活動贊助。不過，與這些建議相違背的是，自2008年以來，香港已對啤酒和葡萄酒免稅。儘管酒精的消費迅速上升，但少有對酒精飲品的購買限制，且幾乎沒有對酒精飲品營銷的規管條例。 目標：研究公眾對各種減少酒精危害策略的態度和專家意見，以為今後的政策提供信息。專家預見逐步降低酒精危害的策略將獲得廣泛的公眾支持，這將使得“最佳購買”的干預策略列為香港的優先事項。 方法：這項混合方法研究將由兩個階段組成。在第一階段，將進行電話普查，以便更新目前有關飲酒模式的信息，提供酒精使用危害程度的基本數據，並評估公眾對一系列“最佳購買”建議的接受性（例如限製酒精銷售時間）和他們認為這些建議所帶來的結果。將詢問飲酒者哪些干預措施可能會降低自己的飲酒量以衡量其潛在影響。在第二階段，將對專家持份者進行定性訪談（例如酒店和酒精行業工作人員，酒類飲品零售商），以了解他們對世衞組織“最佳購買”策略的可行性和可能後果的意見，同時在訪談時特別強調第一階段所發現的廣受歡迎的減少酒精危害的干預措施。針對規律飲酒者的焦點小組訪談，將獲得他們對干預策略潛在後果的意見。 主要結果：受訪對象對各類酒精政策接受度的排名。透過瞭解各種干預策略對受訪者自評的飲酒行為的影響，可以瞭解該政策對不同亞人群飲酒水平的影響。定性數據將提供世衞組織推薦的干預策略可能帶來的積極/消極後果的詳細專家意見。

14611417.label: Major findings and research outcome
14611417.value: Nearly half (45.7%) of the study sample reported ever drinking a full serving of alcohol in their life, while 35.5% did so in the past year. The prevalence of past-month binge drinking and weekly drinking were 7.2% and 6.5%, respectively. The most common harms from others’ drinking were inconveniences (10%) (e.g. kept up at night by drinkers), followed by psychosocial problems (5.5%) (e.g. verbally abused, experienced anxiety). Drinkers were most likely to report inconveniences (11.1%) (e.g. unable to get home easily) and work/school-related harms (5.6%) (e.g. productivity loss) from own drinking. Relatively severe harms such as injury and assaults due to drinking of others (3.2%) or their own (0.8%) were uncommon. Among the various strategies recommended by the World Health Organization, more than half of the respondents supported drinking age verification at stores (83.6%) and restaurants/bars (81.4%), moderate alcohol taxes (68.7%), and restricting alcohol retail hours (51.9%). In contrast, restricting alcohol advertising (32.9-34.9%) and sponsorship (17.7-19.5%) showed very low public acceptability. The various alcohol control strategies were more supported by women, older adults, and past-year abstainers. Restriction on alcohol availability (36.0%) and drinking age verification (36.0%) were perceived to be the most effective in reducing own drinking among binge drinkers, whereas advertising (12.6%) and sponsorship (8.0%) regulations were perceived to be the least effective. Scepticism toward alcohol policy effectiveness and the widespread belief that “Best Buys” strategies would substantially hurt the local economy presented the major barriers in increasing public support for greater regulation. While expert stakeholders viewed drinking age verification to be highly feasible, its enforcement was perceived to reduce its real-world effectiveness. Although moderate taxation and retail hour restrictions were publicly supported, stakeholders noted that the lack of advocacy and limited local research in the face of continual alcohol industry lobbying impedes the adoption of such alcohol policies in Hong Kong. Given the low alcohol consumption culture and low prevalence of alcohol-related harms, the impact of implementing these policies was thought to be modest on reducing alcohol-related problems but substantial on hurting the local economy. A manuscript on public acceptability and perceived consequences is currently under review by the International Journal of Drug Policy (Impact Factor=5.0, JIF Q1). The results of qualitative interviews have been incorporated into a manuscript which is being submitted to Social Science & Medicine (Impact Factor=4.6, JIF Q1). Information on the publication of two manuscripts will be forwarded to RGC upon acceptance.

14611417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14611417.value: We feel the results of the current study are interesting enough to be published in good journals. Currently, one manuscript based on the quantitative results is under review and another manuscript based on qualitative results will be submitted for publication shortly. An extension of the study could be to include additional stakeholder groups that could play a role in alcohol policy-making process in the qualitative interviews. For example, non-government organizations, academics, health professionals, social welfare departments, and law enforcement actors. The inclusion of additional stakeholder groups may provide a broader view which allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the potential barriers and impacts of alcohol policy implementation.

14611417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14611417.value: This project was designed to assess whether the World Health Organization-recommended alcohol policies are applicable in the Hong Kong context using a telephone survey on the general population and interviews with key stakeholders. In order to be successfully implemented, policies require broad public acceptability and be feasible in the local context. Past studies have been conducted in Western countries with heavy alcohol consumption levels and high levels of alcohol-related harms. In Hong Kong it was found that checking IDs when purchasing alcohol is highly supported by the public and perceived by expert stakeholders as being highly feasible, and this policy should be strictly enforced to ensure the real-life effectiveness. Unlike Western countries, taxation and alcohol availability restrictions received a fair level of public support but face various barriers in adoption. Younger aged drinkers perceived reductions in alcohol availability to be an infringement of their lifestyles. The general public perceived regulations limiting alcohol availability and bans on alcohol marketing to be harmful to the local economy and Hong Kong’s reputation as a vibrant world city. More locally tailored strategies such as targeted intervention for young people and problem drinkers may be more appropriate for Hong Kong at the current stage.

14611517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611517.value: 未來氣候變化將會出現更加頻繁和激烈的極端炎熱天氣（IPCC，2012）。熱島效應影響下，高密度城市的夏季則會加劇（WMO＆WHO，2015）城市熱環境，導致與熱相關的健康風險，特別是針對窮人和老年人的健康風險也將增加。因此迫切需要在社區開展對與熱相關的健康風險空間評估，以便制定更加適應氣候變化的設計和策略。 本研究借鑒“Crichton風險三角（RT）”風險評估方法來探索和量化極端炎熱天氣的熱暴露，脆弱性及其風險之間的關係。香港是高密度城市，其炎熱的亞熱帶氣候在未來氣候變化影響下，將會增加極端炎熱天氣事件的持續時間，頻率和強度（HKO，2015）。此外，由於密度不均勻的城市形態，导致城市內部的溫差較大。因此，在極端炎熱的天氣下，需要獲取對空間和定量的熱暴露及其脆弱性的分析。 擬議的項目旨在通過以下方式：（i）收集和整理各地區的社會，經濟和環境信息; （ii）調查極端炎熱天氣（白天和夜間）下城市內部溫度的變化，量化極端炎熱天氣的情況; （iii）採用統計方法繪製社區的熱暴露及其脆弱性地圖; （iv）根據上述調查結果，制定具有熱風險水平及相關的風險地圖; （v）制定對氣候響應設計的行動名單，並為規劃者和政府人員在日後製定土地利用，景觀規劃和發展強度時提供參考。 該項目將提供一種更全面評估亞熱帶高密度城市極端熱天氣狀況下熱健康風險的方法。它將討論呼應來自世界氣象組織（WMO）和世界衛生組織（WHO）有關熱風險和響應的號召。同時也對香港政府規劃署制定的“城市氣候規劃建議圖”填補有關熱健康風險的空白，並將在極端炎熱天氣下更全面地分析公共衛生健康的影響。

14611517.label: Major findings and research outcome
14611517.value: 1. Assessing spatial variability of extreme hot weather conditions in Hong Kong In this study, using the very hot day hours (VHDHs) and hot night hours (HNHs) at the locations of the 40 WSs as the outcome variables, land use regression (LUR) models are developed to achieve a spatial understanding of the extreme hot weather conditions in Hong Kong. The mapping results illustrate a significant spatial variation in the extreme hot weather conditions of Hong Kong in both the daytime and nighttime, which indicates that the spatial variation of land use configurations must be considered in the risk assessment and corresponding public health management associated with the extreme hot weather. The results were published in Environmental Research in 2019. Please refer to No.1 of Section 8 of Part C Research Output. 2. Understanding and investigating the urban heat and cool island effects during extreme heat events in Hong Kong In this study, warm periods (May to September) of 2000–2018 were examined to acquire a comprehensive understanding of the UHI and UCI characteristics for the case study of Hong Kong, China. Results show that both the UHI and UCI effects are exacerbated during extreme heat events. Using the concept of the UHI degree hours (UHIdh) and UCI degree hours (UCIdh), their spatial patterns in Hong Kong during extreme heat and non-extreme heat situations were mapped based on multiple linear regression models. The results were published in the International Journal of Climatology in 2019. Please refer to No. 2 of Section 8 of Part C Research Output. 3. Conducting a spatiotemporal assessment of extreme heat risk for Hong Kong This study developed a spatiotemporal hazard-exposure-vulnerability assessment of the extreme heat risk in Hong Kong for 2006, 2011, and 2016 integrating cumulative very hot day hours and hot night hours in summer, population density and a principal component analysis (PCA) of demo-socioeconomic characteristics. The risk was found spatially variant, and high-risk spots were identified at the community scale for both daytime and nighttime with underlying determinants behind. In both the daytime and the nighttime, high risk mainly occurred in the core urban areas. Please refer to No. 3 of Section 8 of Part C Research Output. 4. Further applications in Guangdong Province and Cooling Energy demand in Hong Kong, please refer to No. 4 & 5 of Section 8 of Part C Research Output.

14611517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14611517.value: In this project, we adopted mapping technique to illustrate heat hazards and conducted a spatial assessment of heat risk, so the mapping resulting could maps not only enhance our understanding of the spatial pattern and characteristics of the heat hazards and heat risks in Hong Kong but could also serve as a useful reference in climate change adaptation, heat-health risk detection, cooling-energy estimation and policymaking. The project team would like to explore these related topics based on the current findings. Apart from this, the currently funded project focuses on extreme hot events in Hong Kong. Given changing climate, the project team would like to extend their interests into the study of compound extremes in Hong Kong in near future.

14611517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14611517.value: The study (Shi, et al., 2019) adopted the land use regression mapping technique to illustrate a significant spatial variation in the extreme hot weather conditions of Hong Kong in both the daytime and nighttime, which indicates that the spatial variation of land use configurations must be considered in the risk assessment and corresponding public health management associated with the extreme hot weather. Furthermore, Ren, et al., (2021) found that the urban heat island is exacerbated during extreme heat events. It means downtown areas during heatwaves could be hotter than we expected. Based on our heat risk findings in Hua, et al., (2021) it shows several old communities in Kowloon stayed at high risk from 2006 to 2016. Some new towns in the New Territories turned to be at higher risk in 2016 compared to 2006 and 2011, and this result showed signs to be emerging hot-spots in the near future. This study would be a useful reference for community-scale heat risk assessment and mitigation for the development of healthy and sustainable high-density cities.

14611817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611817.value: This project will investigate the “naocao” (鬧漕 tribute-grain riots) that occurred in the provinces along the Yangzi Valley (where most of them took place) from the late eighteenth century onwards. The project will collect all the instances of tribute-grain riots as recorded in private and government documents from 1700 to 1850, and then analyze their temporal and spatial distribution, and present a theoretical explanation for their occurrence. The “naocao” were the result of disputes between taxpayers and their county magistrates over the payment of tribute grain (caoliang漕糧), a tax levied on the rice-producing provinces to be paid in rice. The tribute grain was transported to the Capital to feed imperial families, officials, and the military troops stationed there. As preliminary research, I investigated cases of “naocao” in the eighteenth century and found that they suddenly became widespread in the last decade of the eighteenth century. I also found that they always followed a pattern: A taxpayer brought his rice to a granary; the granary clerk refused the rice, citing its poor quality, and demanded the tax payment in money, supposedly to buy a better quality rice from the shops himself. The clerk quoted the official prices of tax rice, both in silver tael and copper cash. The taxpayer did not accept these prices, accused the county magistrate of commuting the tribute grain tax, which was forbidden, and protested by rioting. This is an innovative project both empirically and theoretically. Empirically, the project is the first systemic research on the tribute-grain riots in the Qing dynasty. When analyzing the rising number of cases of “naocao” in the nineteenth century, I shall attempt to link them with the drastic changes in currency prices of the time. On theoretical grounds this project may shed light on the reasons for local riots in the Qing empire. Rioters were not rebels. Their aim was not to overthrow the state, but to create local disturbances serious enough to attract the attention of the imperial government. Therefore local riots were usually sparked by a legitimate grievance against local officials – in this case, their illegal and avaricious commutation of the grain tax for money. 這個研究計劃是探討十八世紀後期長江流域的“鬧漕”事件。計劃將從清朝的檔案中收集鬧漕例子，在時間和空間分佈的前提下，提供一個解釋。所謂“鬧漕”，亦即漕糧繳納者與知縣的爭執。漕糧是清朝的主要穀物稅，是清政府從長江流域的省份徵來的大米，再送到北京首都去支持皇室、官員和軍隊的食用。筆者的初步研究中，已經發現“鬧漕”在十八世紀最後十年間特別普遍。它通常是這樣發生的：一個交稅者，帶了漕糧到達倉儲，但負責收漕的胥吏卻以米質不佳拒絕收納。胥吏要求折成白銀或銅錢，好讓他們到附近的糧店購買適合的漕糧。繳稅者不接受折價安排，於是控告縣衙門私折漕糧。本研究課題是嶄新的，它不單有系統地探討清朝漕亂，更嘗試將漕亂與貨幣價格連成關係去作分析。在理論層面上，這計劃有助於我們進一步了解清朝城市暴動的起因。從“鬧漕“的例子，可以發現動亂者不是要推翻清朝，而是希望透過製造動亂來引起中央政府的注意，從而給予地方政府壓力，因此動亂的爆發點往往是從地方官員的非法行為，而在這個例子中，則是“折漕”。

14611817.label: Realisation of objectives
14611817.value: Both objectives 1 and 2 are background for understanding the tribute-grain riots in the Qing dynasty. I achieved them by collecting data from several archival documents such as Qingshi, Qing shilu, Gongzhongdang, DaQing huidian shili, Caoyun quanshu, local gazetteers, and contemporaneous scholarly essays. I discovered that in addition to wanting the grain tribute tax to operate independently of the market, the Qing government intended that the grain tax, like the silver tax on private land holdings, be a matter between the state and individual landlords, without involving intermediaries. There were at least three basic regulations for collecting the grain tax, and they were all prohibitions--against tax farming (baolan), against taking extra grain, and against commutating the tax from grain to silver. These prohibitions showed that the Qing state wanted to collect its exact quota of tax grain directly from individual farmers, without intermediaries. The whole process was set up to operate independently of the market, to assure soldiers and officials of their grain stipend despite price changes. Objective 3 was achieved and shown in two peer-reviewed journal articles. In one article (in press), I investigated the nature of the job as boatmen, who made lots of trouble in the grain tribute tax collection and transportation, and how they survived in a discriminative society in the Qing Dynasty. I argued that the term of “working class” was a modern invention, so it is not so usually used to refer traditional Chinese society before the Opium War. Nevertheless, it does not necessarily mean that working class did not exist at that time. This article showed how these labourers organized themselves and sometimes organized gang fights. This article has been accepted, reviewed, and will be punished in the Yunhe xue yanjiu (Journal of Canal Studies). My second article, which was published in the Quyushi yanjiu (Journal of Regional Studies), used Fu'ning county in northern Jiangs province as a case study, explored the grain tribute tax and riots in the lower Yangzi valley in the nineteenth century. It showed that from the eighteenth to nineteenth centuries, the item of the tribute-grain tax collection changed firstly from grain to silver and then from silver to copper coins, and in this process, how the villagers seized opportunity to evade the tax which occasionally caused tribute riots. With regard to objectives 4 and 5, I took a research trip to the Number One Archival Library in Beijing. I collected price of silver taels in the Yangzi province. In the Qing it was a major duty of local officials to report prevailing economic and social conditions, especially grain prices. These reports were compiled on the basis of prices gathered regularly from the market of the county capital, and submitted to the emperor. There were abundant reports of grain prices in silver in Qing documents. I achieved objective 4 without problem. However, since silver, not copper cash, was the unit of account in the Qing's government finances, there was not much information of the price of copper cash at the Number One Archival Library. To solve the problem, I searched the local gazetteers, and used the information there to complete my article on the grain tribute riots.

14611817.label: Major findings and research outcome
14611817.value: The project generated two articles published in peer-reviewed journals in which two major findings were found. 1. The project contributed to the literature by indicating changing mode of tribute-grain riot. In the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, these riots usually followed a pattern: A taxpayer brought his rice to a granary; the granary clerk refused the rice, citing its poor quality, and demanded the tax payment in money, supposed to buy a better quality rice from the shops himself. The clerk quoted the official prices of tax rice, both in silver and copper cash. The taxpayer did not accept these prices, accused the county magistrate of commutating the tribute grain tax, which was forbidden, and protested by rioting. In this light, the riots seemed to be caused by unreasonable commutation rate. This project showed that tax evasion was the major reason for the riots. As shown in my article, tribute-grain riots continued to occur even though the tax had been commuted to money. What different from the past was the fact that poor harvest replaced unreasonable commutation rate became the new excuse for the villagers to demand tax exemption and make local disturbances. 2. My second article contributed to the literature the organization of tribute-grain boatmen in the eighteenth century. Historians have shown that these boatmen built Luo sect temples as their community centres. I discovered that the Luo sect, though having a religious overcoat, was a pre-modern labour association in essence. The sect provided a personal network where a man could find recommendation for being a boatman on a grain tribute junk on the Grand Canal, and this network was very important for migrant workers who were looking for jobs. In my article, I also showed that temple was one of the two centres of Luo sect associations. On their journey, the boatmen gathered and discussed their affairs on one of the junks in the fleet.

14611817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14611817.value: I am planning to write a book of six chapters on the grain tribute collection and transport in the Qing dynasty, and these two articles could be the two chapters of this book. I think I could finish the draft of the whole book in 2022. In addition to these two chapters, I have also completed one on the Construction of Grand Canal, and another on the choice of rice consumption.

14611817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14611817.value: This was an innovative project both empirically and theoretically. Empirically, the project was the first systemic research on the tribute-grain riots in the Qing dynasty. I linked them with the drastic changes in currency prices of the time. On theoretical grounds this project shed light on the reasons for local riots in the Qing empire. Rioters were not rebels. There were two kinds of rioters. The aim of the farming population was to create local disturbances serious enough to attract the attention of the imperial government, and the aim of the grain boatmen was to secure their jobs under the protection of their Luo sects.

14612417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612417.value: 世界各國的政府每天都製造並蒐集大量的資料，資料的生產是政府的重要功能之一。基於不同的政策考量，開放政府資料近年來已成為一個全球性運動。開放資料，或稱為開放公部門資訊，代表公部門推動開放數碼資訊的政策或作為，用以協助公眾以免費或極低的成本，取得、使用或散布公部門資訊。論者有時會將開放政府資料運動的討論連結到其他鼓吹運用數碼科技或互連網廣為傳播資訊的類似運動，如開放期刊近用、開放教育資源、開放標準及開放原始碼運動等。 據估計，目前全球已經有超過50個國家的250個中央或地方政府開始推動開放政府資料運動，許多政府計畫以開放資料政策提升政府透明度並促進經濟成長，不少商業組織也針對開放政府資料發展出創新的產品或服務。然而，在此同時，開放政府資料的推動也面臨了一些法律問題，而其中資料相關知識產權的特許及政府資料釋出的最佳方式為何，一直是ㄧ個懸而未解難題。 香港政府近年來推出開放政府資料的「使用條款及條件」，並致力建構一個對創業新者友善的環境，本研究以香港作為一個了解政府設計並執行政府資料特許條款的個案，首先探討香港開放政府資料的政策目的為何，及政府資料「使用條款及條件」的設計原因與目的，以「使用條款及條件」的具體內容分析開放政府資料的不同政策面向及其與特許條款之關連；本研究亦將分析民間如何以商業或非商業方式運用政府釋出的資料，研析這些運用方式與前述「使用條款及條件」的關連為何，以及「使用條款及條件」如何型塑新的數碼經營模式。研究成果預期對於知識產權相關議題、政府資料的治理模式及政府資訊政策均可產生相當貢獻，亦可協助政府評估其開放資料政策之具體成效。

14612417.label: Realisation of objectives
14612417.value: I have carefully studied and analyzed the open data policy in Hong Kong and internationally, relevant literature, and various business applications with my research assistants in this project. I also talked to various stakeholders that include but not limited to Mr. Donald Mak (Assistant Government Chief Information Officer, Office of the Government Chief Information Officer, OGCIO), Mr. Charles Mok (Legislative Councillor), Mr. Bastien Douglas, Mr. Scott Edmunds of Open Data Hong Kong (ODHK), Mr. Ben Cheng of Internet Society Hong Chapter (ISOCHK), etc. Based on my study of the open data licences and policies in Hong Kong, I also advised ISOCHK on their proposed Open Data Index. Moreover, I was invited by Mr. Charles Mok’s office to attend OGCIO’s Briefing on Government Open Data Plan to provide my advice on the open data policy on 24 January 2019. To further find out how business developed various data business models and strategies and relevant technologies, I invited Professor Man-Ho Au (Hong Kong Polytechnic University), Ms. Ryanne Lai (Zegal), Mr. Henry Pau (CiSystem Solutions), Dr. Wai Shun Lo (DL Capitals), and Mr. Winfred Fan (Anywhere Networks) to the IP conferences I organized at CUHK LAW in 2018, 2020, and 2021. The sharing of these experts had greatly helped me understand both policy and business implications of open data and to achieve the project objectives, which were sufficiently reflected in the research output listed in Part C. I shared my preliminary findings in an international conference “The Sharing Economy in China: Regulation or De-regulation for Innovation?” held by the KoGuan School of Law at Shanghai Jiao Tong University on March 27, 2018. Experts from Asia, Europe, and North America in the conference provided very helpful suggestions to this project, which lead to a series of relevant publications in Part C.

14612417.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612417.value: The project led to five publications with major findings as below: 1. Hacking into China’s Cybersecurity Law, 53 WAKE FOREST LAW REVIEW 57 (2018) Open data policy often raises security and privacy concerns, which are the focus of this paper. This paper provides a thorough analysis of cybersecurity laws and their policy implications pertaining to national security, human right, and the effectiveness of law enforcement. More importantly, this paper discusses data localization policy, a policy closely related to the limitation concerning the exploitation of open government data. 2. Open Government Data Licenses in the Greater China Region, in MAKING COPYRIGHT WORK FOR THE ASIAN PACIFIC? JUXTAPOSING HARMONISATION WITH FLEXIBILITY 197 (Susan Corbett & Jessica Lai eds., Australian National University Press, 2018) This chapter focuses on legal issues associated with open government data (OGD) licences in the Greater China region, namely Hong Kong, Mainland China and Taiwan. This study argues that the choice and design of an open data licence forms an important element of a government’s information policy. 3. Tripartite Perspective on the Copyright-Sharing Economy in China, 35 COMPUTER LAW & SECURITY REVIEW 434 (2019) This paper observes open government data policies from the perspective of Internet sharing economy. It provides a novel framework by categorizing the sharing economy into unauthorized sharing, altruistic sharing, and freemium sharing. This paper argues that government platforms with excessively restrictive licensing terms may fail to achieve the OGD policy goal of unlocking the value of data by sharing, and such restrictions reflect the political reality of stringent government control of information and market activities. 4. Domain Name Dispute Resolution in Mainland China and Hong Kong, in CAMBRIDGE HANDBOOK ON INTERNATIONAL AND COMPARATIVE TRADEMARK LAW 398 (Irene Calboli & Jane Ginsburg eds., Cambridge University Press, 2020) Just like government data, the control, use and allocation of domain names have been quite controversial. Using the domain name dispute resolution as an example, this chapter illustrates the convergence and divergence of the civil law and common law approaches to the governance of data and intangible resources. 5. Computer-Generated Works under the CDPA 1988, in ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY 177 (Jyh-An Lee, Reto M. Hilty, Kung-Chung Liu eds., Oxford University Press, 2021) This chapter is an extension of my previous study of the exploitation of data in the digitally networked environment. It discusses whether the copyright of an AI-generated work should be assigned to the programmer, trainer, data provider, or machine operators.

14612417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612417.value: I have effectively used the GRF to complete a series of research and publications on open government data licenses as mentioned above. This line of research has formed a solid foundation for future research as below: 1. Open data has become a key component in the design of smart city. Therefore, the research outputs informed other research ideas relevant to legal implications of smart city, such as legal issues surrounding Internet of things (IoT) and autonomous vehicles. 2. The focus of data in this research project has opened another window for me concerning various data governance model and their legal implications. Specifically, some of the rationale in my analysis of OGD can be applied to other types of government control over data flow, such as data localization regulations. 3. Moreover, according to the finding of this research, the major use of OGD is to train AI machines for a variety of commercial purposes. There are various legal issues coming from AI algorithm’s processing of data, such as the ownership of intellectual property, personal data protection, algorithmic bias, etc. All these issues deserve more scholarly attention.

14612417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612417.value: This study first investigates policy considerations for the design of OGD licences by studying government documents in Hong Kong. This study uses the design and implementation of OGD licence terms as a lens through which the different policy priorities and values underpinning OGD policies could be interpreted. The project investigates the relationship between OGD licences and the commercial reuse of OGD. By observing innovative businesses built upon OGD, this study illustrates how the restrictions in licensing terms shape new data business models. This study identifies the primary policy goals of OGD, which include the enhancement of governmental transparency, accountability, public participation, the improvement of democracy and public service quality and the advancement of innovation and economic development. These policy goals should be the deciding factors in the design and choice of licence. This study argues that the choice and design of an open data licence forms an important element of a government’s information policy.

14612517.label: Project Objectives
14612517.value: To design and implement a theoretically grounded intervention program to enhance students’ CC reading development. Building on SRL theories and empirical studies on the relations between instructional practices and SRL development, the PI has developed the “TSAE” framework (elaborated in Section 2) to guide the instructional design of CL teaching. The study will integrate effective instructional practices as proposed by CL scholars and previous reading research into this framework to design a comprehensive intervention program to holistically enhance students’ motivation, strategy use, prior knowledge, and comprehension in CC reading. To evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention program using a rigorous research design. By contrast with existing CC reading literature, which is mainly based on CL scholars’ observations or survey methods, the study will adopt a quasi-experimental design to provide more reliable data to evaluate whether SRL-based instruction is an effective approach to teaching CC reading. To examine the applicability of SRL-based instruction in a Chinese cultural context. Although the importance of SRL has been demonstrated in many studies as well as in HK curriculum reform, it is originally derived from Western theories and studies. It cannot therefore be assumed to have the same effectiveness in CC reading instruction, which is deeply influenced by the traditional Confucian culture. With the combined use of quantitative and qualitative methods, the study will explore which different principles of SRL-based instruction may facilitate or inhibit students’ development in their CC reading ability and motivation, and how.

14612717.label: Project Objectives
14612717.value: To develop a tractable model of repeated games with general timing structure. To identify each player’s effective minmax payoff level in such a game using the recursive backward induction method. To provide a unified folk theorem for standard repeated games and repeated games with asynchronous moves. To gain insights on how to deal with stochastic games with absorbing states in general.
rows: To develop a tractable model of repeated games with general timing structure.
To identify each player’s effective minmax payoff level in such a game using the recursive backward induction method.

14612717.label: Realisation of objectives
14612717.value: The first objective is to develop a tractable model of repeated games with a general timing structure. Towards this goal, we first developed a general model of repeated games with asynchronous moves. In each period of the repeated game, a subset of players are active, that is, they can revise their actions in the current period, while each inactive player sticks to the same action as in the previous period. A crucial element of the model is a stationary stochastic process governing the transition from one set of active players in the current period to another set in the following period. The assumption of stationarity can be properly justified and it accommodates a tractable equilibrium characterization. We further developed a model of two-player infinitely repeated games, in which the players can alter their continuation strategies, in the form of automata with finitely many states, in each period. At the end of each period, there is a chance for each player to become permanently committed to the prevailing automaton. Both aforementioned models can be viewed as stochastic games, thus in our analysis, we can combine the techniques from both the stochastic game literature and the repeated game literature. Our models are tractable and the assumptions are realistic. The first objective has been fully achieved. The second objective is to identify each player’s effective minmax payoff level in such a game using the recursive backward induction method. For two-player games, using a self-generating approach, we can characterize players’ effective minimax payoffs in the repeated game, rather than by their effective minmax values in the underlying stage game. We tried to extend the characterization to the general case with N-player stage game, but did not completely succeed. There are some challenging technical issues which we had not been able to solve. Nevertheless, we are confident that our current analysis points to the right direction. Thus this objective is only partially achieved (80%). The third objective is to provide a unified folk theorem for standard repeated games and repeated games with asynchronous moves. With a two-player stage game, we establish an unconventional Folk Theorem in the sense that the limiting set of subgame perfect equilibrium payoffs in a repeated game is bounded below by players’ effective minimax payoffs. Our main result asserts that when players become sufficiently patient, any feasible payoff vector that strictly dominates players’ effective minimax values can be approximated by subgame perfect equilibrium in the repeated game. As we had not been able to characterize player’s effective minimax payoff for a general N-player stage game, accordingly the extension of the folk theorem result had not been accomplished and this objective is also partially achieved (80%). The fourth objective is to gain insights on how to deal with stochastic games with absorbing states in general. We studied models in which players may become permanently committed to their current stage actions or continuation strategies in the form of finite automata. These models can be viewed as stochastic games in which a permanent commitment can be equivalently viewed as an absorbing state. Through our analysis, we learned that in the context of repeated strategic interactions, the existence of absorbing states has important implications on players’ equilibrium behavior. In particular, through conflicts and compromises at the early stage of the interaction, players can gradually coordinate on a certain pattern of play which is equivalent in terms of payoff to a bargaining agreement. This insight has led us to think further about the connections between repeated games and noncooperative bargaining, which we will explore in future research. This objective has also been fully achieved. Finally, it should be mentioned that our work had been slowed down by the social unrest in 2019 and the pandemic after that. The PI and the Co-I had planned to visit each other from late 2019 to early 2020 to work together on the remaining technical problems. We also planned to attend several international conferences to present our working papers to get feedback and suggestions. These plans were seriously disrupted.

14612717.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612717.value: In this project, we study different models of repeated games with stochastic commitment. By identifying the set of equilibrium payoff of each model, we investigate how timing structure, specifying when each player can revise his choice of action or continuation strategy, determines the bounds of equilibrium payoff. We also explore the deep connection between repeated games and noncooperative bargaining. Our main theoretical findings have been packaged into two working papers. In the working paper, A Closed-Form Folk Theorem for Repeated Games with Asynchronous Moves, we study repeated games with asynchronous moves, in which not all players may revise their actions in every period. Using a self-generating approach, we derive the infimum of a player’s subgame perfect equilibrium payoff, namely, the effective minimax value, in the repeated game. A player’s effective minimax value depends on the timing structure of players’ asynchronous moves. We establish an unconventional folk theorem: as players become sufficiently patient, any feasible payoff vector that strictly dominates the effective minimax values can be approximated by a subgame perfect equilibrium in the repeated game. This result also implies a number of Folk Theorems and Anti-Folk Theorems in the current repeated game literature. In another working paper, Commitment and Compromise in Repeated Games, we study two-player infinitely repeated games in which the players choose automata with finitely many states instead of actions at each stage. At the end of each period, there is a chance for each player to be committed to the prevailing automaton. We analyze the subgame perfect equilibrium in this repeated automaton game with commitment. It is shown that the well-known folk theorem generally does not hold. We characterize the set of subgame perfect equilibrium payoffs under the conditions that the players are sufficiently patient and the probability of commitment is sufficiently small. In particular, we show that for a special class of stage games, provided that a small enough probability of commitment is fixed, the equilibrium payoff vector will be located in a small neighborhood of the symmetric Pareto efficient payoff vector. Such an equilibrium outcome can be interpreted as an implicit bargaining agreement between the two players. In another work in progress, we study a sequential bargaining model in which two players, under budget constraints, compete for the proposing right via a second-price auction in each period. We establish the uniqueness of Markov perfect equilibrium and show that the equilibrium outcome is determined by the initial endowment.

14612717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612717.value: During our study of repeated games with stochastic commitment, we realized that there are deep connections between repeated games and noncooperative bargaining. An infinitely repeated interaction can be viewed as a bargain problem among agents. Although players cannot specify an explicit binding agreement as in bargaining, through conflicts and compromises, they may gradually coordinate on a pattern of play that is equivalent, in terms of payoffs, to a bargaining agreement. While this insight has been partially developed in our working paper, Commitment and Compromise in Repeated Games, it is desirable to explore it in a more general framework in future research. We also developed a sequential bargaining model in which two players, under budget constraints, compete for the proposing right via second-price auction. It is an interesting model, but unfortunately, we were unable to spend much effort on it. While we have established the uniqueness of Markov perfect equilibrium, it remains unclear whether the uniqueness result holds for subgame perfect equilibrium. Both the PI and the Co-I have done closely related research in the past, thus it would be feasible and desirable for us to eventually complete this analysis.

14612717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612717.value: Strategic interaction in real life often repeats itself indefinitely among a fixed group of agents, who care about their long term welfare. Moreover, it is also common that agents in the repeated interactions cannot revise their choices of actions at any time; instead, the opportunities of action revision often arrive stochastically. To put it alternatively, agents may commit to certain actions and their commitments may last for certain periods of time, and then, expire stochastically at last. Our main goal in this project is to investigate what can happen in equilibrium in such repeated strategic interactions with stochastic commitments. We develop a unified model of repeated games with a general timing structure specifying when each agent can revise his action. Combining techniques in both the repeated game literature and the stochastic game literature, we characterize the entire set of equilibrium outcomes by drawing a clear line between what can happen and what cannot happen in equilibrium, provided that agents are sufficiently patient. The key insight is that the timing structure plays a critical role in determining the lower bound of equilibrium payoff. In some situations, durable commitments lead to a much sharper prediction than that of the classic folk theorem.

14613417.label: Project Objectives
14613417.value: To clear up the conceptual confusion surrounding Greek rhythm. Narrowly defined, Greek rhythm belongs exclusively to antiquity and is thus caught in a time warp. More broadly defined, it remains a fluid concept, understood differently by philologists and musicologists, as well as by composers. I aim to clarify its ontological status, which is an historical variable. To trace the evolution of both philological and musicological studies of Greek rhythm, and to bridge the gap between the findings of these two disciplines. The musicological study of Greek rhythm is primarily, though not exclusively, a French story taking us from the sixteenth-century poet Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589) and the composer Claude Le Jeune (1530–1600), who worked on the revival of Greek rhythm in their creative works under the auspice of the Academy of Music and Poetry, to the writings of Fétis, Gevaert, Bourgault-Ducoudray, Laloy, Emmanuel and Messiaen. To locate studies of Greek rhythm within the context of theorising about rhythm more generally. The range of reference here is from German theorists such as Kirnberger, Hauptmann and Riemann to North American theorists such as van den Toorn and Hasty. For the most part, the more sophisticated general theories of rhythm make no reference to ancient Greek theory. To advance independent theory on the basis of my own analysis of relevant works by, inter alia, Wagner, Stravinsky, Debussy, Ravel and Messiaen. While research is currently at an early stage, the preliminary findings of some close-to-the-text analysis of Stravinsky in particular suggests that existing theories of rhythm may be usefully inflected or even transformed by my findings and that a new synthesis may be possible.

14613417.label: Realisation of objectives
14613417.value: All four objectives have been satisfactorily achieved. The following narrative gives an overview of the main points and also the pathways mapped out for further enquiries. Nineteenth-century German philologists researched into ancient Greek rhythm with reference to the cognitive modalities of modern languages. They drew on a distinction between stressed and unstressed syllables, rather than between short and long syllables, and rendered ancient Greek rhythm in accentual terms. A paradigm shift came in the late nineteenth-century when classical philologists rethought and ultimately discarded the establishment of isochronism (equal measure length) as an axiom. Leading classical philologists in the nineteenth century were predominantly German-speaking. Influential musicologists who wrote about ancient Greek rhythms, on the other hand, were mostly French. Fétis and Gevaert referenced their contemporary German philologists without really critiquing them. With Laloy, Emmanuel, and Messiaen, however, there was a remarkable change of orientation. All of them discussed what Nietzsche the philologist described as an “error.” This change is noteworthy, for it is remarkably close in timing to the paradigm shift initiated by Nietzsche. Laloy, Emmanuel, and Messiaen all read as if they had somehow become aware of Nietzsche’s discovery. Yet none of them make any mention of him whatsoever. Even within the field of classical philology, Nietzsche’s contribution to the paradigm shift was slow in gaining recognition. Most philologists today still credit Paul Mass, Wilamowitz’s pupil, who published the highly influential monograph Griechische Rhythmik (1923) and plagiarized Nietzsche (as argued by Porter), with having initiated the paradigm shift. Indeed, Nietzsche’s discovery in the 1870s of an “error” committed by a long line of distinguished German philologists went unnoticed until Bornmann edited the manuscripts of the “four notebooks” for Nietzsche Werke Kritische Gestamtausgabe in the 1980s. Within the field of musicology, Paris had become established as a center of rhythmic research and innovation by the time of the 1913 première of Stravinsky’s Le sacre du printemps. The Paris Conservatoire was a powerhouse of rhythmic theory, with an impressive lineage from Fétis and Gevaert through Laloy and Emmanuel to Messiaen and beyond. In his doctoral thesis on ancient Greek rhythms, Laloy refuted “the principle of equidistance between downbeats” and remarked that the juxtaposition of different meters, though rarely heard in classical music, was beginning to gain currency. Fétis had expressed a similar view in “Du développement futur de la musqiue: Dans le domaine de rhythme” (1852), notwithstanding his derogatory note on the irregular alternation of duple and triple times as typical of “barbaric” peoples. Musical rhythm, according to Fétis, evolves over time, and will one day attain “the immense and new musical realm in which various rhythms and different metric systems can follow one another and be connected naturally to produce effects unknown at this [his] time.” Fétis was not alone in this prophetic insight, for there were similar ideas in circulation in Paris at the time, ideas that came to fruition in Le sacre. Music by composers such as Debussy, Ravel, and Stravinsky suggests that Nietzsche’s insights might very well have percolated down into their compositional praxes. During the long nineteenth century, the ictus theory, and hence the axiom of equal measure lengths, espoused by numerous eminent German philologists, waxed and waned. Despite the fact that the ontological status of Greek rhythm remains a historical variable, the initiation of a dialogue between the philological and musicological studies of Greek rhythm, which traditionally trace distinct paths, has unravelled facets of modernist compositional praxes where meter and rhythm are concerned. Stravinsky’s rhythmic inventions in Le sacre prompt us to question the conventional dichotomy between the metric and the ametric. Do they constitute antithetical poles that defy any mediation? Or perhaps a continuum of multiple gradations? Can they overlap to some extent? And can the metric accommodate the ametric and vice versa? There is evidently more to the metric-ametric dichotomy than has hitherto been explored. To advance further the existing metric and rhythmic theoretical models, however, a longer-term research commitment and closer collaboration with researchers in the European (and not just the Anglo-American) academic circles need to be duly prioritized.

14613417.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613417.value: Based on compelling evidence unearthed when working on this GRF project, I postulate the theory that Wagner had appropriated ancient Greek rhythms in Tristan (Cheong 2018). The appropriation of choriamb (Greek rhythm associated with tragedy) in the “desire” motive, which is heard pervasively throughout Tristan, is a particularly striking example. My theory also throws light on an obscure link between Tristan and Nietzsche’s philological research, which dates back to the 1870s, the time he worked as a professor of classical philology at Basel University. Due to the century-long delay in the publication of Nietzsche’s notebooks, the impacts of Nietzsche’s groundbreaking philological research in the music-theoretical sphere have escaped commentators’ critical attention. A scrutiny of the impacts is carried out by bringing the latest scholarship on Nietzshe’s philological studies to bear on related research conducted by distinguished musicologists at Paris Conservatoire, including Messiaen’s analytical discovery of a plethora of Greek rhythms in Stravinsky’s “Sacrificial Dance” (Cheong 2019a). By way of such an interdisciplinary approach, I revealed the interrelationship between Wagner’s and Stravinsky’s quest for musical modernism (through the adaptation of archaic rhythms) and the paradigm shift in classical philology in the late nineteenth century, to which Nietzsche had yet to be more properly attributed (Cheong 2019b).

14613417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613417.value: The existing theoretical studies on meter and rhythm in Western art music is highly compartmentalized. There is no lack of metric and rhythmic theories about early music or, alternatively, tonal and post-tonal music, but they seldom inform one another. The problem of compartmentalization becomes acute when we come to address the research question of how composers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries appropriated ancient Greek rhythms in their quest for musical modernism. Fortunately, it lays bare for us a research pathway that have hitherto been under-explored. A few attempts (for example, Maurice Emmanuel’s Histoire de la langue musicale) have been undertaken to make sense of the many changes in the conceptions and perceptions of meters and rhythms over a vast time span. Nevertheless, they are surveys and do not zoom in to tackle any theoretical issue in details. Apart from treating the compartmentalization problem where metric and rhythmic studies are concerned, the proposed course of action also includes liaising with fellow investigators to foster collaborative research between, inter alia, music theorists and classical philologists.

14613417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613417.value: Nature Central to the project is a music-theoretical inquiry into the under-researched problem of how European composers of art music had since the mid-nineteenth century capitalized on the unknowability of ancient Greek meters in their quest for music modernism. Apart from reexamining the historiography of pertinent rhythmic and metric theories, where ancient Greek meters are hardly present, the project also necessitates a delve into the discipline of classical philology and, more specifically, the theories of a long line of distinguished German metricians and French rhythmicians vis-à-vis ancient Greek rhythms. Significance and Value Due to its interdisciplinary in nature, this project has opened up new research pathways with a distinct collaborative edge. The impacts of this undertaking also radiate from: (1) the analytical discoveries of ancient Greek meters in Wagner’s Tristan and Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, two epoch-marking works set up as case studies; and (2) a critique of Nietzsche’s classical philological works, including his analysis of Tristan, and the writings on ancient Greek rhythms by Messiaen, one of the most influential art music composers in the twentieth century.

14613717.value: 香港會於未來的某些節點陷入資本管制方面的困境,而這種困境將會在以下兩組義務發生衝突碰撞時產生：香港簽訂的國際貿易協定和國際投資協定中規定的義務，和香港對中國和（或）國際貨幣基金組織的義務。 然而香港該採取何種措施來應對這一問題仍不明晰；同樣，香港的投資者在其他國家實施資本管制的背景下享有怎樣的權利也不明朗。 此次項目旨在解決這種困難而惱人的法律狀況，以期澄清歧義、為香港及投資者指明方向。 具體而言，此次專案將會研究貨幣流動方面的制度規則, 以期達到下述目標：第一，闡明在何種情況下，資本管制會和基於國際貿易協定、國際投資協定產生的國家義務相衝突；第二，研究含有保障措施條款的國際貿易協定和國際投資協定在多大程度上允許政府於發生危機時或在其他狀況下採取措施、保障穩定；第三，探析如果香港採取資本管制措施，其將承擔何種責任( 然而，這一情況發生概率很小) ，以及作為人民幣交易港，香港是否會因為其所採取的、中國的資本管制而必然導致的措施而需承擔違反國際貿易協定和國際投資協定的責任。 跨境貨幣流動對於國際金融，以及幫助世界各國壯大、發展、繁榮都至關重要，如今的問題在於，這一方面的制度既不統一，也不和任何組織的職責範圍完全契合。國際貨幣基金組織在過去年間逐漸掌握了維護全球金融市場穩定的權威，並大力支援開放及貨幣自由流動；但同時可能也催生了資本泡沫，幣值波動，以及突發的貨幣流入流出激增，而這些正是導致亞洲、俄羅斯、巴西、土耳其和阿根廷金融危機（1997-2001），以及全球金融危機（2008）的原因。 現在,國際貨幣基金組織意識到了貨幣自由流動的危害，並且在“機構觀點” （2012）中合法化了資本管制措施的使用， 將其稱之為“有用”及合法的對抗不穩定的工具，並且將其納入貸款和穩定項目。 然而這也造成了國際經濟法中金融、貿易和投資規則之間的緊張。 國際貨幣基金組織的要求可能會與國際貿易組織、自由貿易協定和（或）國際投資協定中的規則產生衝突。 國際貨幣基金組織意識到了其與現有法律制度的緊張與衝突，但令人震驚的是，它並未對之加以處理，而僅僅是呼籲其他組織和成員在未來起草協定時“考慮國際貨幣基金組織的觀點和立場”。這一建議對未來的協定有所裨益，但是並不能解決國際貨幣基金組織、國際貿易組織和其他超過3200份的協定之間的衝突。 此次專案會通過調查研究，來界定這一問題，並專注於香港由於其在人民幣貿易中扮演的獨特角色和與中國的特殊關係，而可能面臨的責任。

14613717.label: Realisation of objectives
14613717.value: The project met all of the objectives set out in the revised proposal. The first three published works dealt with Objectives 1-3. The first, ‘Towards Convergence of Trade and Investment Law? A Right to take Prudential measures for the Preservation of Financial Stability’, laid the groundwork for the project. While existing literature debates whether and to what extent States should be allowed to take “prudential” regulatory measures in order to safeguard their financial systemic interests from serious threats of financial crisis, and more critically the conditions, necessity, timing, and length of such measures, there has been virtually no case law applicable to the subject matter. This article, and the second publication, ‘Regulating Tax Havens: Insights from the WTO Appellate Body Decision in Argentina – Financial Services’, evaluated and reviewed the only dispute involving financial services at the WTO. This case provided an opportunity to contribute to the doctrinal debate on prudential measures by drawing a parallel between trade and investment perspectives on the matter. Prior to these publications, no article had discussed the potential convergence between WTO case law and investment arbitral law on the issue of measures taken for prudential reasons relating to economic duress. Another output, entitled, ‘Liberalization Commitments, Financial Stability Safeguards and Capital Controls: The Evolution from GATS to TPP and Megaregional Trade Agreements’, traces and places the capital control debate into perspective by evaluating how the drafters of the most recent Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) managed the issue of necessary regulatory interference in times of economic, financial and monetary instability. More specifically, the article reviews the market access provisions of several FTAs relating to foreign financial service suppliers and focuses on the regulatory prudential safeguards or ‘carve-outs’ included in liberalization agreements to ensure that partner countries/members retain a certain freedom to regulate on financial stability matters, comparing an FTA provision to the GATS. The article also contributes to the literature in discussing the carve-out from a political perspective with a view to consider whether prudential measures will be relied upon in order to preserve financial stability or whether such provisions will in practice be ignored or untrusted. While at least one prominent political economist suggests that FTAs leave no room for capital controls aimed at preventing and mitigating financial crisis, this article reaches the opposite conclusion, finding that modern trade agreements leave significant room for regulatory exceptions, particularly in times of financial instability. Taken together these three articles largely fulfil Objectives 1 and 3, and touch upon Objective 2. Post-mid-term reporting period, two additional articles were published. The first, ‘The Legitimacy of Controlling Capital Flows Under International Economic Law During a Retreat from Globalization’, contributed to the fulfilment of Objectives 1-4 as it dealt with the right of governments to take capital controls to maintain financial stability and prevent or mitigate the effects of economic crises. The article serves as somewhat of an outline to the later monograph in that it directly engaged with IMF policy and the use of short-term and long-term controls implemented in Chile, Malaysia, Iceland and China before examining the consistency of selected controls with international rules. Ultimately, as with the earlier publications, the findings are that treaty language is a critical factor in determining the legality of a particular capital control under a trade or investment agreement. Having started to look to the fulfilment of Objective 4 in the previous article, the second article ‘Do Beijing’s Capital Controls Restrict Hong Kong?: Reality or Illusion’ fulfils Objective 4 by directly assesses Hong Kong’s potential liability as an RMB trading hub for the imposition of capital controls in China. The article provides an overview of Hong Kong’s policy on capital flows, its commitment to capital transfers in related trade and investment agreements, and its financial positioning in relation to the BRI. It then traces China’s gradual and steady policy of liberalizing its capital markets in recent years and after thorough examination concludes that although there is some risk it may be theoretical in nature and is unlikely that China’s capital controls will legally bind Hong Kong and affect its legal commitments. Indeed, Hong Kong stands to benefit from China’s continued liberalization, especially with increased regional unity stemming from the GBA, and can continue to capitalize on its unique advantages to connect China with other regions. Finally, and most importantly, work continued researching and drafting the monograph, Capital Controls and International Economic Law (CUP, forthcoming 2022). The book brings the existing work together and fulfils the first three project objectives (Objectives 1-3). The first 4 chapters introduce the concept of financial movements and capital controls before mobbing on to explore the legal foundation for the IMF’s mandate over capital controls. Here, and in accordance with Objectives 1 and 2, the research finds that while the Fund grounded its mandate shift and expansion on the text and wording of the Articles of Agreement, it did so by using a “byroad” which allowed the Fund to interpret its constitutive instrument and creatively use its legal instruments to escape the historical distinction between “capital movements” and “current international transactions”. The book then explores whether the Fund’s expansion in mandate is legally valid and legitimate. By looking at hard and soft law, the book concludes that the mandate expansion was in line with the standards of international law applicable to international organizations and thus the Fund can legally monitor and discipline capital movements. These chapters fulfil Objective 1 and set the stage for the fulfilment of Objectives 2 and 3 in the later chapters. Chapters 5-7 determine whether the Fund’s approach to capital controls conflicts with international economic law, namely the disciplines of trade and investment law. Through the negotiation of trade and investment agreements, countries agree to certain obligations and make specific market access commitments. While such agreements contain safeguards and exception clauses, the scope and depth of such clauses varies between agreements. This research found modern agreements negotiated included deep obligations but also broad safeguards and exceptions. In contrast, older treaties and those negotiated by numerous developing countries lack adequate safeguards and exceptions. For this reason, the Fund’s approach to capital controls may run afoul of the obligations and commitments undertaken in certain agreements. These chapters, in addition to the conclusions developed in Chapter 8, fulfil Objectives 2-3. The project also produced two short pieces for public dissemination, one was published by East Asia Forum and one by the Oxford Business Law Blog. These discussed various aspects of the research, most notably the potential for regime conflict between the IMF and various other strains of international economic law in line with Objectives 1-3. The project hosted a Workshop (covering Objectives 1-4) in November 2019. The workshop was held at the height of the Hong Kong protests and as several speakers were unable to travel to due to disruption at the airport the event was smaller than originally planned. The project was mainly doctrinal, desk based, but interviews were conducted with a range of officials and stakeholders in the North America, Europe and Asia.

14613717.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613717.value: The major findings and research outcomes are as follows: (1) The IMF was not only to demonstrate how the IMF shifted its mandate to include authority over capital movements, but why it was legally entitled to do so. (2) The WTO’s GATS Agreement does not serve as an impediment to the implementation of capital controls, especially when supported by the IMF. (3) Modern properly drafted FTAs and international investment agreements are not an impediment to the implementation of CFMs, but that some risks remains due to older generation treaties and for countries continuing to negotiate without appropriate safeguards and exceptions. (4) The WTO and investment tribunals have interpreted exception clauses broadly, fairly and reasonably (5) There seems to be a convergence between WTO and International Investment law in this area of the law (6) Capital controls taken in accordance with IMF recommendations or guidance are unlikely to conflict with modern trade and investment agreements The main conclusion coming from this analysis is that the risk of international economic law instruments constraining governments from using capital controls as part of their policy toolkit has been overstated. Not only can modern treaties be drafted in such a manner so as to restrict investor protections and governmental obligations through targeted treaty language and the use of safeguards and exceptions, but both investment tribunals and the WTO panel/Appellate Body have demonstrated an awareness and appreciation of broader, societal interests and in the main avoided interpreting the relevant treaties in a narrow and constricting manner. The main risk lies with free trade agreements and international investment agreements that do not incorporate modern drafting techniques which limit or condition State obligations and provide for a wide range of safeguards and exclusions to ensure that legitimate capital controls do not run afoul of treaty obligations. In this regard, I agree with the IMF that “the limited flexibility afforded by some [trade and investment agreements] in respect to liberalization obligations may create challenges for the management of capital flows”, and call upon governments not only to be mindful of the issues discussed in this book when negotiating new agreements but also to seek to revise older agreements to provide for more and better protection as a safeguard should they desire or need to employ controls in the face of financial turmoil and crisis.

14613717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613717.value: Research in this area remains ongoing, and trade and investment tribunals should be carefully watched to see if the trend of interpreting obligations fairly narrowly and exceptions broadly continues. Moreover, there is scope to improve the treaty practice of numerous countries, most of which are developing countries, that have not incorporated modern safeguards and exceptions into their trade and investment agreements. Finally, further development and impact could be gained by presenting this information to governments and having them re-evaluate older generation treaties with a view to updating them in a manner which better protects governments that may seek to maintain and preserve financial stability in times of financial crisis.

14613717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613717.value: This project addresses the regulation of capital movements and has three aims: (i) determine under what circumstances capital controls conflict with state obligations under trade and/or investment agreements; (ii) consider the extent trade/investment agreements include safeguards enabling governments to preserve stability in times of crisis or otherwise; and (iii) assess Hong Kong’s liability should it initiate capital controls and whether it might be liable under trade/investment agreements for China's controls. The main conclusion is that the risk of international economic law instruments constraining governments from using capital controls as part of their policy toolkit has been overstated. While capital controls conflict with state obligations under trade and/or investment agreements, modern drafting techniques can restrict investor protections and governmental obligations through targeted treaty language and the use of safeguards and exceptions. That being said, numerous trade and investment agreements do not incorporate modern drafting techniques. Hong Kong's treaties are modern, and its risks from the issuance of capital controls locally or in Beijing are minimal. As financial crisis is a recurring feature of the modern economy, and as more countries are agreeing to the liberalisation of trade and investment, the findings are significant and could help shape the future generation of treaties.

14614217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14614217.value: This research aims to identify how different generations record and communicate their memories of mass protests through the use of changing communication technologies. In addition to uncovering how personal and autobiographical memories are stored and recalled, the study also examines the social and cultural dimensions of memories. It posits that collective memories of major social events can be analyzed through the lens of “interpretive communities”. It argues that the interpretive strategies different social groups adopt in acts of remembering and forgetting contribute to the formation of Hong Kong identities that are constantly in flux. In short, the project describes, discusses and evaluates the intricate and dynamic relationships among mediated memories, interpretive communities and cultural identities with four particular case studies. The four mass protests in study are the riots in 1967, the Tiananmen Square Incident in 1989, mass rally in 2003 and Umbrella Movement in 2014. All four are recognized as significant events in Hong Kong history. Coincidentally, each of these protests happened at a time with the absence or presence of a major media. The 1967 riots preceded the arrival of free-to-air television, while in 1989, the Tiananmen Square Incident was broadcast on television around the clock. Social media had not yet made their entry when the 2003 mass rally took place in Hong Kong, yet by 2014, social media was found playing a significant role in protest mobilization. The four cases provide meaningful comparison and contrast in the use of communication technologies in memory practices. The study collects two sets of data. Textual materials including official documents, anniversary news reports and major archival publications are identified. Content and textual analysis will shed light on how these events are framed to be remembered. The second set of data will be from interviews and focus group interviews. Mass protests are often times of turmoil that are characterized by intense debates and participants have stronger desires to communicate what they remember about the protests. Through individual interviews, autobiographical accounts allow more personalized expressions of memory. Focus group interviews recruit different social groups to share their memories with other members from similar background. They will not only recount what actually happened but also engage in face-to-face discussion in which meanings need to be clarified, elaborated and/or debated. Findings will show the co-production and co-evolution of media and memory. Retrospective and prospective memories will offer new perspectives about the often controversial “Hong Kong identities”. 過去數十年，傳播科技發展迅速，不但改變了人們傳意、溝通、獲取資訊、娛樂和教育等方式，作為記憶的載體，傳播科技亦影響了個人如何儲存和召喚記憶，不同年代的人因著當時當地的科技條件，為各自的時代留下記錄，固然有其私密性，亦能反映特定時空的社會和文化面向。本研究藉媒體化記憶、詮釋社群和文化身份建構等理論視角，以香港五十年來四場大型社會運動為案例，試圖整理和描述不同年代參與者的媒體記憶，從中討論媒體在個人及集體記憶的角色，因技術轉變帶來的可能性或相關限制。 研究選取四場社會運動為案例，包括六七暴動，八九年天安門事件，2003年大遊行及2014年雨傘運動。這四件事發生時，都巧合地遇上媒體環境出現大變動的時機。1967年11月，無線電視廣播啟播，此前大眾主要倚賴報章及電台；1989年，電視實時轉播方興未艾，家家戶戶安坐家中卻如置身示威現場；2003年五十萬人遊行，雖然互聯網已很普及，但標榜社交功能的臉書仍未面世；2014年，各種社交媒體大行其道，有論者甚至形容雨傘運動為社交媒體革命。上述各個案正好為我們了解媒體和記憶之間的關係，提供了不少比較角度，預期可豐富我們對相關事件及其記憶的了解。 本研究會產生兩大類資料。通過文本和內容分析，我們會檢視大眾媒體的周年回顧專題，整理媒體在重覆的敘述中，記住甚麼，又遺忘甚麼。相關結果亦會與其他文獻，包括官方紀錄和歷史研究參照對比。研究會進行大量一手訪問，與經歷過四場運動的人深入探討主題，亦組織集合不同背景參與者的焦點小組訪談，探討香港身份的形塑和流變。

14614217.label: Realisation of objectives
14614217.value: The project aimed to discuss the roles of media in shaping, circulating, and sustaining the collective memory of four mass protests in Hong Kong. It proposed to examine the notion of “mediated memories” through the lens of media technologies, interpretive communities, and generational perspectives. Overall speaking, the first four stated objectives have been addressed to a large extent, yet the fifth objective needs much further work. While this underachievement suggests that the principal investigator had underestimated the scope of the subject under study, the research did lead to a much clearer, broader, and deeper understanding of the relationships between media and memory. The principal investigator continues to work on studies about protest memory in legacy media and digital media. More research output is expected in addition to those reported in Part C. How the research objectives were addressed and realised are reported as follows. Mediated memories “Mediated memories” is the core concern of the study. The research was first inspired by an observation of a “coincidence” regarding the arrival of certain “new media” and the outbreak of mass protests. During the turbulent months in 1967, newspapers and radio were the two major media. Free-to-air television was launched in mid-November that year, which helped to explain why there was a lack of moving images about the events. In 1989, however, television had already become the dominant medium in ordinary household. News footage were broadcast and delivered to living rooms around the clock. Moving on to 2003, social media like Facebook were not yet born. By the time when the Umbrella Movement happened in 2014, social media were commonplace in everyday lives. In hindsight, the four mass protests could be divided into two groups, with the 1967 and 1989 as one group differentiated by the absence and presence of television; while the 2003 and 2014 as another group characterized by the influence of social media. This initial hunch led to the exploration of the roles of media technologies in capturing, representing and storing memory (objective 3). Through analysis of media history and relevant media texts, as well as in-depth interviews with individuals who have stakes in the events, this aspect of mediated memory was addressed. Media representation is another key dimension of mediated memory. Collective memory is certainly about the past, yet it has been generally agreed that its representation and interpretation is based on the needs of the present. Media are considered to be important mnemonic agents because of their power to select, present, and interpret certain historical events. They exercise cultural authority through repeating particular narratives and hence reinforcing certain ideologies. This aspect of mediated memory was examined through a case study of the news coverage of the annual candle light vigil in Victoria Park. News editions of June 5th from 1990 to 2019 of a local newspaper were collected and analysed. Recurring themes were identified, dominant news values and assumptions were noted. This case study of anniversary journalism indicated how collective memory was brought to the fore and reinterpreted in regular in conventional journalistic practices. Despite the cultural authority in mobilising and representing collective memory, media as agents of memory are subject to other influence that would affect the (re)making of memory. To probe into the dynamic and unpredictable nature of collective memory, and to account for the transmission of particular narratives, the research interviewed young journalists who have participated in covering commemorative activities related to the protests in 1967 and 1989. Their works were also analysed as background reference. Through these two studies, one of anniversary journalism and one of young journalists covering old news, the idea of “interpretive communities” and cultural identities was further explicated. Objective 1 and 4 were addressed. History and identities A dominant theme has emerged in the research process. Although the four protests in question were regarded as significant historical episodes in Hong Kong, they received rather different treatments and public attention in collective memory. The roles of media in upholding and reinforcing certain narratives were compared. The findings pointed to the presence of subtle sentiments and emotions in both individual and collective remembrance. It was stated in objective 2 that the research should update and innovate research about Hong Kong history and identities through the use of mediated memories. While both history and cultural identities are huge subjects that can hardly be fully addressed in one single study, this research did show that mediated protest memories provided a valuable venue for reviewing various historical events and their impact on identities. In this regard, objective 2 was also to a large extent addressed. Generational perspectives The research proposed to examine and discuss generational perspectives in terms of the production, storage, transmission, and consumption of memory. The emphasis is placed on how and why certain personal memory is shared and become part of the collective memory. The plan was to conduct in-depth interviews with individuals related to each of the four protests, supplemented with focus group interviews targeting at intergenerational exchanges. Due to the wide time span covering the four protests, the principal investigator could eventually manage to focus on two earlier protests in 1967 and 1989. For the two protests related to the Internet and social media, digital media materials abounded which posed serious challenges in data collection and ensuing analysis. Notwithstanding, more than 60 in-depth interviews were conducted for the two protests in study, which provided rich data for addressing the first four objectives. During the research, the outbreak of Covid-19 brought tremendous challenges for organizing focus group meetings. To overcome the problem, generational perspectives were mainly identified and interpreted through individual interviews. Objective 5 was only partly addressed in this regard.
