14614217.label: Major findings and research outcome
14614217.value: The project contributes to the existing research literature about collective memory and social movement studies, with an emphasis on the roles of media. It has clarified and deepened the understanding of the concept of “mediated memories”. Three aspects of mediated memories have been analysed, which findings are reported in four articles as listed in Part C. First, through content and textual analysis of news, the study identified recurring themes and examined ideological packages in memory construction. It showed how anniversary journalism represented historical events while responding to the changing needs of the present. It also highlighted how journalistic conventions and practices, for example, a preference of visual presentation and certain news values, led to the selection and production of memory content. Second, the study scrutinized the assumed cultural authority of journalists as mnemonic agents. In addition to shedding light on the mnemonic socialization young journalists went through, the research traced how journalists did initial research and completed their news assignments in anniversary journalism. The findings noted the impact of memory traditions on memory construction, contestation, and transmission. While recognizing the “power” of journalists to shape memory through their narratives, the findings also suggested various constraints that could lead to discounted account of historical events. On a different note, such limitations might contribute to some “distilled” versions of collective memory, hence favouring the continuous circulation of specific memory discourses. The third aspect was concerned with the roles of technologies. It was found that newspapers, radio, television, and social media formed different “backdrops” for individuals to form and retain memory. Print, broadcast and digital media allowed varying technological affordances and affected how individuals remembered the past and recalled such remembrance in the present. This part of finding was also closely related to generational perspectives and helped to refine the concept of “media generations”. In summary, this research facilitated a comprehensive review of the increasingly popular notion of mediated memory. The three sets of findings offered new perspectives in analysing interpretive communities and cultural identities. The research has focused on protest memory, yet the findings laid solid groundwork for the exploration of other emergent memory phenomena. Further studies about the relationships between digital media and digital memory are being conducted.

14614217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14614217.value: In the present research, the objective related to the roles of social media in two more recent protests was only partly addressed. It remains to be an important and worthwhile topic for deepening understanding of mediated memories. The subject matter aligns with a growing enthusiasm in digital memory. It is now widely recognized that digital technologies have fundamentally changed how information is generated, stored, distributed, and consumed. Digitization has enabled the production of massive amounts of information in various forms of data. Some of these data are digital records of personal activities and they have acquired properties of memory. The principal investigator proposed to evaluate the digital memory phenomenon not only in terms of protest memory, but also as a general digital media trend. The research reported has mainly tackled legacy media. With a fuller consideration of the roles of Internet and social media in memory making, the functions, power and limitations of modern media will be articulated and inform relevant theories in media, memory studies and communication technologies.

14614217.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14614217.value: The project is concerned about the roles of media in collective memory. Collective memory is about history, but it is not “history”. It is about how members of a community recall and remember about the past. It is a product of a social group which tells much about the cultural values and identities a community share. Collective memory is unpredictable and can be subject to disputes. Interpretations about the past are related to the present and can influence future events. Like personal memory, collective memory is fluid and non-representational. It needs a social framework through which the past can be represented. This research asked why different historical events, despite that they were of similar significance, were remembered rather differently in our society. It found that media affected the making of collective memory in three ways. Firstly, media technologies conditioned how memory was captured, stored, and transmitted. Secondly, news institutions participate in the (re)construction and maintenance of certain narratives and exert subtle influence in memory transmission. Thirdly, journalistic practices impose constraints in the selection and presentation of memory content. The research enriched our understanding about the power and limits of media in memory matters.

14614917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14614917.value: How do social networks evolve over time and affect individual economic activity? This is the question set out to study in this project. To provide an adequate empirical tool for answering this question, we propose a new modeling approach for longitudinal data of networks and activity outcomes. The key feature of this model is the use of latent variables to capture unobserved individual traits in the processes of network formation and activity interactions, and more particularly, these unobserved traits are assumed to vary over time. The proposed model naturally combines two well-known models in the field: latent space model for network formation and spatial dynamic panel data model for network interactions. This combination reflects real situations that network links and activity outcomes are interdependent and jointly influenced by unobserved individual traits. Moreover, this combination allows us to (i) handle the endogenous selection issue inherited in network interaction studies, and (ii) investigate the effect of homophily in terms of activity in network formation. We propose a tractable Bayesian MCMC approach to estimate this model. We will conduct two empirical studies using the new modeling approach in this project. In the first one we study students' friendship networks and their influences on students' school outcomes, e.g., academic achievement, unhealthy and risky behaviors (including smoking, drinking, and using drugs), and delinquent behavior. We will exploit three high school student datasets from U.S., Dutch, and Taiwan to conduct the analysis and compare empirical findings from different countries and cultures. In the second one we study the world trade network (WTN) and its effect on a country's economic growth. Our goal in these two applications is to provide a comprehensive analysis on every determinant of activity outcome -- contemporaneous peer effect, persistency of outcome, temporal peer effect, own and contextual effects, and correlated effects. Meanwhile, we will tailor the network formation model in different applications to capture unique features in each network data, for example, the geographical dependence on trade flow. 社會網絡如何隨著時間的推移而發生變化且影響個人經濟活動？這是我們在這個計畫中研究的問題。為了提供一個合適的實證工具來回答這個問題，我們提出了一種新的模型方法，以用於網絡和經濟活動結果的長期觀察數據。該模型的關鍵特徵是使用潛在變量來捕獲網絡形成和活動相互作用過程中未觀察到的個體特徵，詳細來說，這些不可觀察的特徵會隨時間而變化。我們所提出的模型自然地結合了現有的兩個模型：網絡形成的潛在空間模型和網絡交互的空間動態面板數據模型。這種組合反映了在現實上，網絡形成和相互作用結果彼此依賴，共同受到不可觀察的個體特徵影響。此外，這種組合使我們能夠（i）處理在網絡相互作用研究中的內生性選擇問題，以及（ii）研究在網絡形成中受活動結果相似性的影響。我們提出了一種可操作的貝氏MCMC方法來估計該模型。我們將使用新的建模方法進行兩項實證研究。第一，朋友網絡以及學生的學校行為，例如學業成就，危害健康行為（包括吸煙，飲酒，使用藥物）和違法行為。我們將利用美國，荷蘭和台灣的三個高中學生數據進行分析，比較不同國家和不同文化的實證結果。第二，我們研究世界貿易網絡（WTN）及其對一國經濟增長的影響。我們在這兩個應用程序中的目標是對每個活動結果決定因素 - 同時期的同儕效應，持續性的結果，跨時間同儕效應，自身和情境效應以及相關效應進行綜合分析。同時，我們將在不同的應用中定製網絡形成模型，以捕獲每個網絡數據中的獨特功能，例如貿易流量中的地理相關性。

14615317.label: Project Objectives
14615317.value: To write the history of France's militias and citizen-soldiers, a story which has never been told in English and has barely been told even in French. To examine the role of civic republicanism in the French context, during the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, and to give France a more prominent role in the history of eighteenth-century republicanism. To bring the question of physical force to the center of the French Revolution, in a way that highlights the organized force of France's militias over disorganized "mob" violence. To use France's National Guards to reexamine Weber's narrative of a modern states gaining a monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a territory. To use France's National Guards as a way of reconciling a Marxist analysis of the French Revolution (focusing on class struggles and abrupt transformations) with a Tocquevillian analysis (focusing on state formation and long-term continuities). To place France's 1793 order of mass conscription into a larger perspective of arming citizens during the eighteenth century. To provide a broader analysis of eighteenth-century militias and citizen-soldiers throughout the Northern Atlantic World.

14615317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14615317.value: This project studies militias and citizen-soldiers in France during the early modern era (1550-1800), a story with five distinct phases. In the first phase, the private armies of medieval France gave way to France's royal army, creating a sharper distinction between civilians and soldiers than had previously existed. In the second phase, while France's royal army grew, its bourgeois militias deteriorated, and the provincial militia became a new (and unpopular) institution. In the third phase, eighteenth-century Enlightenment writers presented myriad proposals for reshaping France's army, many based on the ideal of recreating the citizens' armies of the ancient Roman Republic. In the fourth phase, following the outbreak of the French Revolution, well-off citizens formed bourgeois militias throughout France and used them to police poorer citizens. In the final phase, while at war against most of Europe, France instituted a citizens' army in which all adult men theoretically were soldiers. Telling this story helps explain several key phenomena, including the rise of the centralized state, the place of violence in the French Revolution, and the centrality of social class in French history. It will also help reexamine the role of civic republicanism in France's Revolution. Throughout this period there were citizens who performed part-time military duty during peacetime and who were called up to full-time duty during wartime. At first glance the heterogeneity of their roles and the different militias make these seem like separate phenomena, but they warrant being treated together in one research project as part of France's search for a way to maintain its "monopoly on the legitimate use of force" in a way that combined public order with the attachment of inhabitants to the regime. The transformation of men from being "subjects" during the monarchy to being "citizens" of the republic should not obscure the continuity of a centralizing state trying to maximize control over its population while minimizing the costs of its military. The difficulty of this task meant that France never did establish a stable peacetime system of integrating civil society and the military. The history of French militias will be a welcome point of comparison for historians of militias and citizen soldiers elsewhere, especially in other parts of the eighteenth-century Atlantic World. 本項目研究近代早期(1550-1800)法國「民兵」(militias)和「公民兵」(citizen-soldiers)的五階段演變過程。在第一階段，中世紀法國的私人武裝被皇家軍隊所取代，公民與士兵的分別前所未有地擴大了。在第二階段，隨著法國的皇家軍隊日益擴張，城市民兵衰落，農村民兵崛起，成為一種嶄新但不受歡迎的建制。在第三階段，十八世紀啟蒙運動諸子提出花樣百出的改革法國軍隊方案，其中許多方案都以古羅馬共和國時期的市民軍隊為理想。在第四階段，隨著法國大革命的爆發，不少富裕的市民組織城市民兵來彈壓窮人。在最後階段，由於法國要與歐洲大部分國家交戰，法國建立了全公民皆兵的制度，在此制度下，所有成年男子理論上都是士兵。 研究此一演變過程，能夠解釋法國歷史上的幾個主要現象，包括中央集權政府的誕生，法國大革命的暴力現象，以及法國歷史上社會階級的重要性。本項目還將重新檢視法國大革命時期的「公民共和主義」。在大革命期間，不少市民在和平時期擔任兼職的軍事任務，在戰爭時期則被征召為全職軍人。驟眼看，軍人角色不一，民兵五花八門，似乎風馬牛不相及，但是，本項目抓住了其中的主要脈絡：法國近代早期民兵和公民兵的演變過程，也就是法國建立對於合法使用暴力的壟斷制度的過程。這個壟斷制度，一方面要維持公共秩序，一方面要維持人民對於政權的支持。法國帝制時代的「臣民」，雖然轉變為共和國時代的「公民」，但奉行中央集權的政府，卻一直嘗試盡量強化統治，同時盡量降低軍費。此目標自相矛盾，導致法國一直無法建立一套適用於和平時期的協調軍民關係的穩定制度。把法國的民兵與和其他地區的民兵作比較，尤其是與十八世紀大西洋兩岸地區的民兵作比較，將會是極為有趣的研究。

14615317.label: Realisation of objectives
14615317.value: The three years since I applied for this grant have been productive ones, though – as often happens in academia – in ways that I had not foreseen when I wrote this proposal. I am pleased that my initial instincts were correct: there is an important story to be told about France’s history of citizen-soldiers and militias; it does tie in with the broader history of citizen-soldiers and militias in the Early Modern Atlantic World; and it does provide a new way of examining the French Revolution that puts violence back at the center of the story. It also provides a new way of rethinking Max Weber’s views on the relationship between the state and violence. Its relevance for the debates about Marxism and Tocquevillian analysis are perhaps less salient than I had thought, but those debates have also lost much of their salience in recent years. My hubris in the original proposal was to think that one work would be enough to tell this whole story, at least one told by someone who is not themselves based in France. I’ve broken up the work into several different pieces, while also taking advantage of its ability to complement other work I am doing on the history of the Second Amendment to the US Constitution. I have detailed in 6.1 my research outputs. Overall, I have been able to produce a significant amount of research on this topic, both in what I have written and in the archival and library research I have done and out of which I plan to produce more writing. During this time, I have also published a book that dealt with the history of militias in the Early Modern Atlantic World, but which does not focus on France, but rather on the prehistory of the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution. This book grew in part out of my earlier GRF, and was an opportunity which, when I applied for this grant, I did not think would be possible. Completing that book and including material from this research in that book was a better approach than concentrating all of the research on France into one book. It also became clear to me that trying to write on book that included everything from the provincial militia of the seventeenth century to the mass conscription that began in 1793 would not be feasible. Early Modern France – and especially the second half of the eighteenth century – has been the subject of a disproportionately large amount of historical research, but very little of it was about the history of citizen-soldiers or militias. So it was good to see that such a vast subject was relatively unexplored. The history of citizen-soldiers in English history was relatively well studied, and the history of citizen-soldiers in Colonial America and the American Revolution has had an enormous amount of work done. The GRF allowed me to spend two weeks in Paris doing research at the National Archives, the Prefecture of Paris Police Archives, and the National Library. I concentrated there on doing research from the Revolutionary period, which has become key to the work in one article I have since published and another I expect to submit in the coming weeks. That research has turned out to be especially important given the difficulties of doing archival work since the pandemic began. (I would also like to point here to the research I have been able to do during this time at the University of Pennsylvania’s Van Pelt Library, while visiting family in the area, though not explicitly part of this grant; Hong Kong libraries are not yet capable of matching US libraries for their resources in Western History, and I am not sure that the digitalization process will ever reach the kind of largely obscure secondary works that I find are vastly underutilized, especially in European history). Civic Republicanism, meanwhile, has played a more complicated role in the history of militias than I had expected; and, as someone who finds the subject relevant but tired, I was pleased to see that it had less impact than its advocates might have claimed. One of my real breakthroughs during my research was realizing just how different the intellectual history of the militias was from its institutional history. The intellectual history was very much a part of the larger history of civic republicanism, and this can be seen in the influence that a Scottish writer I studied, Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun, had on the much better known Swiss writer Jean-Jacques Rousseau. And Rousseau’s role in the republican tradition is a complicated one, but also one which has received significant attention from scholars. Yet neither Rousseau nor Fletcher – nor Machiavelli, nor any of the other writers – did much to influence the actually existing militias. Where they existed, they were there out of institutional inertia or economic necessity (or both). The one exception was the creation of France’s National Guard in 1789, but there I think the role of ideology was limited and of Civic Republicanism – a largely Anglophone phenomenon – even less so. What studying France’s National Guard does let me do, though, is to put violence at the center of the story of France’s Revolution, as I had hoped. This is my goal in the article I’m currently completing, “The Somewhat Organized Violence of the French Revolution.” There I argue that “Throughout the Revolution, the forces of order were less organized than their titles would indicate, while insurgent forces were more organized and better trained than they portrayed themselves to be.” The common portrayals today tend to portray a government vs people Revolution, but the key role played by the National Guard, including its citizen-soldiers, makes that kind of approach inaccurate. France’s Revolutionary governments rarely had a “monopoly on the legitimate use of force,” to use Weber’s definition of the state. Instead they had to rely on an assortment of different forces that were at times professional, at times hybrid, and at times volunteer; the “legitimacy” of those forces of violence, which were more or less organized at different times, could only be established after the fact, and even then, that legitimacy was often contested. The coexistence of different state, quasi-state, and non-state armed groups meant that even during smooth times the legitimate forces of violence were often under unclear and largely ad-hoc administrative hierarchies meant that the allegiance of those groups could be quite mercurial – one of the major reasons for the consistent upheavals of the early Revolution. These factors together show, I believe, that there is a lot to say about the history of citizen-soldiers and militias in France and, moreover, that that history is key to the broader history of France. It also helps establish that that history is a key part of a broader Atlantic history of militias and citizen-soldiers, one which has been much better studied in the Anglophone context. One of the main areas for future study – whether by myself, or by other scholars – is how much France’s history fits into a broader colonial history, one that includes the slave societies of the West Indies.

14615317.label: Major findings and research outcome
14615317.value: My research has resulted in the following publications: -Shusterman, Noah. « La seule loi « qui soit toujours sûre d’être obéie » : Robespierre, les milices et le débat sur l’armée permanente », Annales historiques de la Révolution française, vol. 398, no. 4, 2019, pp. 25-46. It has also been a significant part of my book, Shusterman, Noah. Armed Citizens: The Road from Ancient Rome to the Second Amendment. University of Virginia Press, 2020. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv13842t6. Although this book is not primarily about France, the research on France was central for Chapter 3: The Fall of La Rochelle, 1628; and for key parts of Chapter 4: England Debates the Militia Act, 1642, and Chapter 6: Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun Publishes A Discourse of Government with Relation to Militias, 1698. Those two chapters both put the rise of militias in England into the context of the growth of France’s professional army. -I will also point to Noah Shusterman, The Strange History of the Right to Bear Arms in the French Revolution, Journal of Social History, Volume 54, Issue 2, Winter 2020, Pages 453–479, https://doi.org/10.1093/jsh/shz029 which is mostly based on research from my earlier GRF but overlaps with the issues I talk about in this one. In the coming weeks, I also plan to submit my manuscript, “The Somewhat Organized Violence of Revolutionary Paris, 1789-1792,” which examines the role of France’s National Guard and other armed formations in shaping the first years of France’s Revolution. These works have seemed to be far more productive in terms of sharing knowledge about France’s history of citizens and citizen-soldiers during the eighteenth century than the book which I had first planned, given both the amount of information available and the paucity of works already existing on the subject.

14615317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14615317.value: There is an enormous amount of potential here, both in France, and in the broader Atlantic World, especially in the West Indies. The militias and citizen-soldiers in the Atlantic Empires of England and France were major institutions of society, both in the metropole and, even more so, in the colonial territories. While the militias of Colonial America have been well studied, the various forms of non-professional soldier in France have not been, and my research has only begun to cover it. The Provincial Militias of seventeenth-century France are woefully understudied, as is the Revolution’s National Guard. Meanwhile, French Colonial history is expanding, so hopefully that can include more detailed studies of the militias there.

14615317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14615317.value: At the start of the early modern era, France had very few men who could be called professional soldiers, and nothing that could be called a national army. By the start of the eighteenth century, France had a large professional army of full-time soldiers. But France also continued to have various institutions that blurred the distinction between soldier and subject, much to the dismay of those men required to participate. During the eighteenth century, though, various writers began proposing ideas which would eliminate France’s need for a professional army, and do away with the vices perceived to have been caused by relying on professional soldiers. When the Revolution began in 1789, France declared the French men were citizens, rather than subjects, and began to explore ways of combining the status of citizen and of soldier. These attempts included both the formation of a “National Guard” of citizen-soldiers which acted as a domestic police force and, eventually, universal male conscription aimed at creating a citizens’ army.

14615817.label: Project Objectives
14615817.value: Data analysis. First analyze the publicly available part of the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) and provide some descriptive statistics on parental time allocation, child time allocation, usage of different modes of child care, cognitive and noncognitive skill measures. Next, apply for the restricted access Geocode data. The Geocode data provides the geographic residence of each LSAC respondent and can be merged with a child care center data set that contains all child care centers (including preschool) in the neighborhood. This will allow us to analyze the quality and prices of each type of child care service available to respondents in their neighborhood. Estimate the production function of cognitive and noncognitive skills from age 0 to 5. Inputs of the production function include previous period's cognitive and noncognitive skills, investment, and family environment. Investments include parental quality and non-quality time, time and quality of each type of child care, and goods investment. We will deal with the endogenous investments using a control function approach. Develop a household optimization model that explicitly captures parents’ investment choices. Parents make labor supply decision, and divide their non-working time into leisure, quality time with children, and non-quality time with children. Parents also make child care choices by deciding whether to use preschool, formal care, or informal care, and also choose the quality of these three types of care. Lastly, parents can also spend on goods investment. We will start from estimating a simple static model, focusing on children aged 4-5. We will then extend it to a dynamic model and estimate the model for children from 0 to 5 years old. Evaluate the effectiveness of policies that aim to improve children outcomes. In particular, we will study the Child Care Rebate Reform in 2008, which increased the rebate rate from 30% to 50% of the out-of-pocket expenditure. We will also conduct counterfactual experiments, including designing a new child care subsidy system, lowering the costs of day care and preschool, or providing a direct transfer to parents. We will analyze the impact on child cognitive and noncognitive skill development, as well as the impact on parent time allocation and child care choice.

Lastly, parents can also spend on goods investment. We will start from estimating a simple static model, focusing on children aged 4-5. We will then extend it to a dynamic model and estimate the model for children from 0 to 5 years old.

Evaluate the effectiveness of policies that aim to improve children outcomes. In particular, we will study the Child Care Rebate Reform in 2008, which increased the rebate rate from 30% to 50% of the out-of-pocket expenditure. We will also conduct counterfactual experiments, including designing a new child care subsidy system, lowering the costs of day care and preschool, or providing a direct transfer to parents. We will analyze the impact on child cognitive and noncognitive skill development, as well as the impact on parent time allocation and child care choice.

14615817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14615817.value: 目標 該項目旨在了解父母的時間投入和學前教育投入對幼兒認知和非認知技能發展的影響。該項目建立了一個模型來捕捉父母在兒童投資方面的決定，包括選擇工作時間，高質量和低質量 的兒童陪伴時間以及休閒時間，以及每個學前教育模式的時間和質量。該模型可為改善兒童成果和家庭福利提供政策指導。 背景 近些年來，兒童早期發展的經濟學研究逐漸增加。許多實證研究，包括Perry學前教育計劃，Abecedarian計劃，Head Start和護士家庭夥伴計劃，均發現投資於從初生到五歲兒童的人力資本具有重要的社會價值。這些研究提供證據表明，兒童早期的表現可以對個人終身福利產生深遠的影響。然而，目前還不清楚父母如何為子女作出投資決定，特別是選擇花時間陪孩子，還是將孩子送到學前教育機構，或兩者兼而有之。父母時間投入與學前教育投入之間的互補性對政策設計有重要影響。例如，如果父母的時間投入和學前教育投入是替代關係，提供免費的學前服務可能不利於兒童發展，因為這將擠出父母的時間投入。因此，該項目通過估計父母時間，學前教育和消費品投入對認知和非認知技能發展的影響，並對家庭優化問題進行建模，了解不同投資選擇之間的相互作用，對了解該問題作出了重要貢獻。 項目介紹 該項目將使用一個追踪了10,000名澳大利亞各地兒童和家庭的澳大利亞兒童面板數據。該數據從2004年開始，追踪兩組兒童，一組是嬰兒（2004年0-1歲），一組是幼兒（2004年3-4歲），每兩年訪問一次。這個獨特的面板數據庫收集了關於兒童發展成果，學前教育的使用，和兒童時間日記的豐富信息。該項目將首先估計不同年齡的認知和非認知技能的生產公式，同時考慮到投入選擇的內生性。然後，它將估計一個擴展的動態模型，以了解父母如何決定他們的勞動力供應，分配非工作時間在不同質量的親子互動活動，購買兒童消費品，並選擇每種類型的學前教育的時間和質量。估計該模型使我們能夠進行模擬試驗來評估潛在的政府政策對兒童發展和家庭福利的影響，例如設計新的學前教育補貼制度，降低日托和幼兒園的費用，或直接提供轉移支付給家長。 項目意義 這個項目將對兒童早期研究產生重大影響。之前的研究並未考察過父母的時間投入與學前教育投入之間的關係，以及他們如何共同影響孩子的發展。它還將提供實用的信息幫助政策制定者充分利用公共資源以提高學齡前兒童的認知和非認知技能。這將對這些孩子的一生的福祉產生深遠的影響。

14615817.label: Realisation of objectives
14615817.value: We have finished the first objective, data analysis. We analyze the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) that is available to the public (General Release) and provide some descriptive statistics on parental time allocation, child time allocation, usage of different modes of child care, cognitive and noncognitive skill measures. We have collaborated with Kailing Shen, an associate professor at the Australian National University, to get access to restricted access data of LSAC (Restricted Release), which contains the geocode and birth date information, as it is only available to researchers in Australia. We also hope that Prof. Shen can get us the child care census that provides the child care prices at the neighborhood level. However, due to the covid-19, the application process is quite slow and we still have not yet got the two data sets. We have completed the second objective, estimating the production function of cognitive and noncognitive skills from age 0 to 5. We consider various types of inputs, including the previous period's cognitive and non-cognitive skills, parental inputs (parental quality and non-quality time, parenting style, goods investment), school inputs (time in and quality of daycare center and preschool), and family background. We find that lagged skills, parent’s quality time, parenting style, time in preschool, and family background are the most important determinants of cognitive and non-cognitive skills. We have completed the third objective. We develop and estimate a household optimization model. The model describes parent’s choices in their time input, good input, as well as school input. In particular, we model how parents allocate their time to work, taking care of children, and leisure. We also model how parents choose whether to and how long do they send their children to daycare centers or preschool. We also completed the last objective, evaluating the effectiveness of the Child Care Rebate Reform in 2008. We conduct a difference-in-differences analysis by comparing cohorts born before and after the CCR reform and children living in regions with high and low child care prices. We find that a decline in the child care price increases the cognitive skills at age 4-5 for both boys and girls, but the advantage disappears after age 6, when children enter primary school. We also find that the reform has a long-run effect on the non-cognitive skills (up to age 11) for boys but not for girls. An examination of the channels suggests that boys tend to delay their school entry when child care becomes cheaper, but not for girls. In addition, boys tend to enter primary schools with higher quality and enjoy more non-quality time input from parents at age 4-5.

14615817.label: Major findings and research outcome
14615817.value: We examine the effects of a reduction in child care prices on children’s cognitive and non-cognitive skills in the short- and long-run. We also explore the potential mechanisms by analyzing the effect of child care prices on school starting age, school quality, and parental time input. In addition, we analyze the heterogeneous effects by sex. We make use of a universal Child Care Rebate (CCR) reform in Australia, which started to provide a 30% child care rebate to all families using approved care services in 2004, and conduct a difference-in-differences analysis by comparing cohorts born before and after the CCR reform and children living in regions with high and low child care prices. Using the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) data, we ﬁnd that a decline in the child care price increases the cognitive skills at age 4-5 for both boys and girls, but the advantage disappears after age 6 when children enter primary school. We also ﬁnd that the reform has a long-run effect on the non-cognitive skills (up to age 11) for boys but not for girls. An examination of the channels suggests that boys tend to delay their school entry when child care becomes cheaper, but not for girls. In addition, boys tend to enter primary schools with higher quality and enjoy more non-quality time input from parents at age 4-5. We further provide a supplementary study on the effect of school entry age on cognitive and non-cognitive skill outcomes. We conduct a regression discontinuity analysis using the school entry age cutoffs that differ across states. We ﬁnd that children born right before the cutoff enter school at a younger age and they have lower non-cognitive skills in the long-run.

14615817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14615817.value: In the future, we will continue collaborating with Prof. Kailing Shen to obtain the restricted access LSAC data and child census data. We will use the restricted data to take a closer look at how Child Care Rebate (CCR) reform affects children living in different places with different pre-reform child care prices. We will also make use of the exact birth date of the children to examine how children born before or after school entry cutoff date perform differently in the long run.

14615817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14615817.value: This project adds greatly to early childhood studies. Researchers have never before examined the relationship between parental time input and child care input and how they together affect children’s outcomes. It also generates policy implications that help policymakers make the best use of public resources to improve children’s cognitive and noncognitive skills before primary school. Previous studies have shown that early childhood development can have a life-long effect on the education, labor market, and welfare of individuals.

14615917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14615917.value: This study aims to examine the key questions of how social media affect political participation of the youth and its implications on policymaking by using Hong Kong as an in-depth case study. In many countries, there is a general increase in the level of political participation among the youth, often in the form of non-institutional and contentious means such as protests and social movements, with heavy utilization of the Internet and social media. Theories of the Internet technology emphasize its capabilities in political communication and mobilization to significantly transform policymaking and governance by redistributing power among political actors and influencing their values and behaviors. However, many research questions on this topic remain unanswered and little is known about the situation in Hong Kong. This project should fill some important gaps in the previous studies which are often confined to a binary approach. Discussion is usually shifted between the optimistic view that social media would alleviate the problem of democratic deficit to lead to a rise of youth engagement and the pessimistic view that it would convert them into disaffected insurgents. It is unsure how social media will affect their mode and nature of participation (e.g., online vs. offline, civic vs. political), who are being mobilized, why and how. Does social media serves mainly as an enabler to reinforce the already engaged youth or as a new stimulus to mobilize a new group of youth who is not engaged before? Is it possible, if so, how the youth may be transformed via social media into a group who distrusts political institutions, representative politics, and mainstream media, and engage mainly in non-traditional, leaderless, individualized forms of participation? Are similar effects observed in other age groups? Many previous studies focus mainly on the one-way Web 1.0 rather than the more interactive and user-centered Web 2.0 of social media. Most studies are also conducted in the Western context so that effects of variation in historical, political and social contexts are not fully understood. With an integrated and multiple-method research design including survey, focus group, interview, content analysis, and case study, this project allows a comprehensive testing of major hypotheses based on the above competing views. As an international city with a high level of penetration of social media among the youth which has witnessed a major social movement, the Umbrella Movement of 2014, Hong Kong provides a good setting for addressing these research questions. 這個研究的目標是探討社交媒體如何影響青年人的政治參與，和對政策制定的啟示，並用香港作為深入分析的案例。在世界多國，青年人的整體政治參與均有所增加，並經常是透過制度外的抗爭方式，例如遊行和示威來進行，而且在過程中大量使用互聯網及社交媒體。有關互聯網科技的理論指出，互聯網可以透過重新分配政治行動者的權力，以及影響他們的價值和行為，在政治溝通和動員上，有重大的威力，足以嚴重地改變政策制定及管治。不過，很多相關的研究問題仍然未被解答，而對香港的情況的所知亦很少。這研究會對由過往因兩極二元的研究取向，所做成的知識洪溝作出填補。過往的相關討論過於兩極化，不是過份樂觀地認為社交媒體可減低民主倒退，增加青年人的政治參與，就是悲觀地認為，社交媒體會把青年人轉化為不滿的抗爭者。目前的研究仍未清楚，青年人是如何及為何被轉化和動員，與及他們的參與模式，如網上及網下，及公民性與政治性的參與，是如何被影響。社交媒體可以只扮演一個擴大器的角式，加強政治活躍者的參與度，但亦有可能是動員從未參與政治的青年人的新因素。亦有可能，社交媒體有份造成青年人不信任政治制度，代議政治，主流媒體的現象，及鼓勵他們追求非傳統，無領袖和個人化的參與。同樣的情況，亦有機會在不同的年齡層中發生。很多過往的研究只集中於單向的網絡1.0，而非互動和用者主導的網絡2.0。由於很多研究也集中於西方國家身上，對於歴史，文化及社會等因素變化的影響的所知亦甚少。有見及此，這研究運用整合和多元方法的設計，包括了問卷調查，聚焦小組，訪談，內容分析，個案研究，來全面地測試以上互相競爭的觀點下的假設。香港，作為一個社交媒體滲透率極高的國際城市，同時剛剛在2014年見証了一場主要的社會運動「雨傘運動」，是一個探索以上研究問題的好埸所。

14615917.label: Realisation of objectives
14615917.value: This project would like to make a contribution in filling some important gaps in the study of the impact of social media and political participation of the youth by examining the major issues which are not fully addressed in its current research. In this regard, this project has a total of five objectives which are listed below. They are fully realized in the project and their attainment are elaborated in the paragraphs below. 1. To conduct a comprehensive survey of the youth and general citizens in Hong Kong on social media and political participation 2. To conduct statistical analysis of the survey findings to examine the relationships among key variables and hypothesis testing 3. To conduct interviews, focus groups, content analysis, and case studies to collect more in-depth and contextual information for answering the research questions 4. To address the major debates and research puzzles in the literature, particularly under the historical, social and political contexts of Hong Kong and Asia 5. To examine the policy implications of the project findings For the first objective, a comprehensive survey of the youth and general citizens in Hong Kong on social media and political participation has been conducted. It is implemented by the Center for Communication and Public Opinion Survey of the School of Journalism and Communication in the Chinese University of Hong Kong. This citizen survey is the first major research task of our project is to conduct a comprehensive citizen telephone survey on the use of the Internet and social media by the youth and general citizens and their political participation. The inclusion of citizens other than the youth would allow comparison of findings with the general population and across different age groups. In the citizen survey, it collects detailed information of the characteristics of the youth who participate and do not participate, their use of the Internet and the social media, the extent and type of their participation, including both online and offline. It would enable us to address the issue of what type of youth would be influenced by the Internet and social media and what type of participation they are being engaged in. It breaks through constraints set by the binary approach and go more deeply and carefully to understand what factors affect youth participation in the era of social media and Web 2.0. In the survey, political participation is defined broadly which include major forms of civic participation. This enables us to have a wider range of conception and observation about participation. Civic participation includes many major forms of participation in social and civic life, including membership of and volunteering in civic, social and non-profit organizations. The measure of participation would be based on a revised and expanded political activism index adopted by Norris (2005), which is a 21-point index divided into four major dimensions: voting, campaign-oriented, cause-oriented, and civic oriented. For the second objective, mainly based on the data collected from the citizen survey, statistical analysis of the survey findings to examine the relationships among key variables and hypothesis testing. A total of three set of hypotheses are tested which are shown below. Hypothesis Set 1: Web 2.0 (Social Media) and Youth Participation The first set of hypotheses tests the core of the theory which is the impact of the Internet on youth participation, including the individual effect of Web 1.0 (website) and Web 2.0 (social media). If the Internet does have an effect on youth participation, the effect of Web 2.0, which significantly magnifies the impact of the Internet, should have an even bigger effect on the political participation of the youth. The echo chamber effect is also tested here by the variable of political tolerance. Political attitude is also introduced as a dependent variable. 1a. The effect of Web 1.0 on the level of political participation is larger than that of Web 2.0. (social media effect hypothesis). 1b. The use of social media is negatively related to the level of political tolerance (the echo chamber hypothesis). 1c. The use of social media is negatively related to the trust / support of the government (the insurgent hypothesis). 1d. The effect of social media on political participation in the youth is higher than the general citizen / other age groups. (The youth effect hypothesis). Hypotheses Set 2. Mode of Participation The second set of hypotheses assess whether social media would only affect online participation or both online and offline participation. It verify if there can be a substitution effect under which an increase in on-line participation may result in a corresponding decline in off-line participation, leading to a zero-sum game in political participation of the youth. It also examines whether social media will affect all modes and forms of participation uniformly. 2a. The use of social media is positively related to online participation (online participation hypothesis). 2b. The use of social media is positively related to offline participation (offline participation hypothesis). 2c. Online participation and offline participation is negatively related (substitution hypothesis). 2d. The use of social media is positively related to civic participation, but not political participation (civic vs. political participation hypothesis). 2e. The use of social media is positively related to individual-based and non-institutional participation but not group-based and institutionalized participation (individual vs. group hypothesis / institutional vs. non-institutional hypothesis / leaderless and organizationless hypothesis). Hypothesis Set 3: Group and Effects of Participation The third set of hypotheses assess whether social media would activate all groups of youth (mobilization effect) or only empower those who have been engaged in politics (reinforcement effect). The existence of digital divide is also one of the issues which is examined in the analysis. 3a. The use of social media is positively related to level of political participation of only those youth who are already engaged in politics. (reinforcement vs. mobilization hypothesis) 3b. Political participation of the youth is positively related to key socio-economic and demographic variables (e.g., education, income, economic status, class, etc). (digital divide hypothesis) 3c. Level of political participation of youth can sustain over time (sustainability hypothesis) In the third objective, interviews, focus groups, content analysis, and case studies are conducted for collecting more in-depth and contextual information for answering the research questions. These methods in the third objective contribute to the mixed method design of this project for overcoming a blind spot in the previous research, which is also a weakness of quantitative research, is the limited knowledge collected on how and why (or why not) the youth chooses to participate. Some of the interviewees are recruited from the citizen surveys to maintain consistency and reliability for the study. Among the cases analysis, the anti-extradition movement of Hong Kong in 2019 becomes a major case for further testing the hypotheses in this project and contribute significantly to the theory building. In the fourth objective, we have addressed the major debates and research puzzles in the literature, particularly under the historical, social and political contexts of Hong Kong and Asia by comparing the cases of Hong Kong with other Asian countries and Western contexts. Finally, in the fifth objective, the policy implications and significance of the project findings are highlighted in all the completed and ongoing research outputs of the project.

14615917.label: Major findings and research outcome
14615917.value: This project aims to go beyond the binary approach in addressing the key questions of how social media affects the political participation of the youth and its implications on policymaking. With its multi-method research design combining both qualitative and quantitative analysis, the key components in this project which integrate quantitative and qualitative analysis include citizen survey, focus group, interview, content analysis and case study. Three sets of competing perspectives and hypotheses are examined in the analysis. The first set focuses on Web 2.0 (social media) and youth participation which tests the core of the theory which is the impact of the Internet on youth participation. It is found that the effect of Web 2.0 on the level of political participation is larger than that of Web 1.0. In addition, to a considerable extent and with moderating effects from some key variables such as network, the use of social media is negatively related to the level of political tolerance (the echo chamber hypothesis). The use of social media is also negatively related to the trust / support of the government (the insurgent hypothesis). The effect of social media on political participation in the youth is higher than the general citizen (the youth effect hypothesis). In the second set of hypotheses, it tests the theories of the mode of participation to find out whether social media would only affect online participation or both online and offline participation. It is found that the use of social media is positively related to online participation (online participation hypothesis). To some extent though with a smaller effect, the use of social media is positively related to offline participation (offline participation hypothesis). Online participation and offline participation is not mutually exclusive and can be closely linked together within the context of a social movement, rejecting the substitution hypothesis which is oversimplified. In general, no major conflict is found between the civic participation hypothesis and the political participation hypothesis. The use of social media is more related to individual-based and non-institutional participation than group-based and institutionalized participation. With regard to the third and also final set of hypothesis on groups and effects of participation, the use of social media is not only limited to those youth who are already engaged in politics so that both reinforcement and mobilization effects can co-exist. Political participation of the youth can cut across socio-economic background and can sustain over time.

14615917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14615917.value: The project findings have implications for both further development of the research and policy advice. It aims to help scholars and policymakers to understand the core issues involved in this topic more thoroughly and at a more discerning and in-depth level. Building on but also looking beyond the project, there are still many questions which can be enlightened and answered in the future research and policy discussion such as the implications and impact on policymaking. More knowledge about the situation in Hong Kong and the effect and outcomes in a comparative context are also necessary for enhancing the policy knowledge and research frontier of this topic. More specifically, since the integration of online and offline participation are an universal phenomenon with the rise of social media around the world and its active engagement with the youth, future research can use mixed methods particularly in-depth comparative case study to examine the policy learning and diffusion of the new mode of participation in different countries. Another important question which should be addressed by both research and policy is how to integrate the new mode of participation into the normal functioning of governance system to strike a balance between change and stability.

14615917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14615917.value: This study aims to examine the key questions of how social media affect political participation of the youth and its implications on policymaking by using Hong Kong as an in-depth case study. In many countries, there is a general increase in the level of political participation among the youth, often in the form of non-institutional and contentious means such as protests and social movements. Theories of the Internet technology emphasize its capabilities in political communication and mobilization to significantly transform policymaking and governance by redistributing power among political actors and influencing their values and behaviors. This project fills some important gaps in the previous studies which are often confined to a binary approach. With an integrated and multiple-method research design including survey, focus group, interview, content analysis, and case study, this project allows a comprehensive testing of major hypotheses. It finds online and offline participation of the youth is closely integrated and the new digital community with democratic and competitive participation has replaced many functions of traditional leaders and institutions. The findings help to explain the rise of organizationless and leaderless movements and highlight the importance of traditional political institutions to adapt to this new mode of participation.

14616117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14616117.value: 體力活動對學童身、心健康都極為重要。研究顯示，活躍的學童到了成年的階段亦會做較多的體力活動。因此，我們應培養學童自幼養成做運動的習慣。然而，現時很多家長郤沒有為子女提供足夠及適切的支援，故要有效提升學童的體力活動習慣，就必須同時干預學童及其家長。 是次研究乃根據自我決定理論(self-determination theory)為基礎設計。參加者（262名學童及每名學童的一名家長）將被隨機分配到實驗組及對照組，實驗組的參加者將於計劃第一階段接受干預，對照組的則只會於第二階段接受相同之內容。干預的主要部份為一個為家庭而設計之體力活動班，通過理論和實踐部份去增加家長和子女一起做體力活動的動機及時間，亦讓家長能夠更於課外為子女提供更充足及合適的支援。透過比較兩組於基線、干預後的運動量數據增減，及與參加者的訪談，研究將能夠評估是項干預的效用及可行性，並審視將干預大規模進行之可能性。

14616117.label: Realisation of objectives
14616117.value: Our study delivered a family-based physical activity intervention aiming to improve children and their parents’ physical activity behaviours. A total of 171 families from seven local primary schools were recruited and completed all data collection at baseline (Time 1; September 2018), at the end of the intervention period (Time 2; approximately 6 months after Time 1), and 1 year after baseline (Time 3; September 2019). Specifically, during the intervention, children and their parents were administered accelerometers and were asked to fasten them to their waist on five consecutive days, except during water-based activities, to record their physical activity behaviours (moderate and vigorous physical activity [MVPA], children and parents’ co-physical-activity [co-PA]). All participants’ performances in four fundamental movement skills (FMS; overhead throw, forehand strike, catch, and kick) in two trials were video-recorded and rated by the same research assistant. In addition, children completed self-report questionnaires including measures for perceived autonomy support from parents, perceived control from parents, basic need satisfaction/frustration, and health-related quality of life. Parents reported their degree of autonomy support provided, controlling behaviours, need satisfaction and need frustration, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). All the objectives stated in the proposal were realised. Further details are provided below. Nonetheless, implementation of the intervention to one cohort of participants was not completed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and resultant cancellation of school activities. Interventions for the wait-list control in the first cohort was also heavily affected. In turn, there was a significant reduction in expenses, including coaching fees and participant subsidies. As a result, the funded project concluded with an unspent balance of 9.81%. Objective 1: To evaluate the effectiveness of a family-based physical activity intervention in terms of changes in children’s objectively measured physical activity behaviours. (100% achieved) Objective 2: To evaluate the effectiveness of a family-based physical activity intervention in terms of changes in fathers’ and mothers’ objectively measured physical activity behaviours. (100% achieved) As stated above, the MVPA of children and their parents (including mothers and fathers) were measured before and after the intervention. The effectiveness of the intervention in terms of accelerometer-measured physical activity was examined using linear mixed models. Participants in the experimental group showed higher levels of physical activity at the end of the intervention. However, they also had higher baseline values. As a result, a significant intervention effect was not found. Objective 3: To test the mediating effects of perceived parental autonomy support and controlling behaviours on children's psychological need satisfaction/thwarting, and in turn their activity behaviours. (100% achieved) We examined the mediating effects of perceived parental autonomy support and controlling behaviours on children's psychological need satisfaction/thwarting, and in turn their activity behaviours. We found a positive association between perceived support and need satisfaction, and between perceived control and need frustration, respectively. Need frustration, but not need satisfaction, was significant associated with children's physical activity. Mediation effects were examined using structural equation models. Results suggested there was a significant indirect effect from need frustration to children's MVPA. However, the indirect effect from autonomy support to children's MVPA was not significant. 4. To examine how the intervention was perceived by participants and whether it successfully initiated behaviour changes through qualitative interviews. (100% achieved) At the end of the intervention, children and parents were invited to take part in focus groups. Forty parent-child dyads from seven schools (three to five dyads per school) were interviewed. Facilitators, children and parents perceived the theory-driven intervention to be effective in increasing family’s leisure-time co-PA and basic psychological need satisfaction.

14616117.label: Major findings and research outcome
14616117.value: The present study collected data from 171 families for quantitative analyses. In terms of qualitative data, 5 semi-structured interviews with facilitators, and focus groups with 40 families were conducted and transcribed. Quantitative analyses of MVPA and ratings of fundamental movement skills (FMS) showed that, in terms of children’s FMS, a significant Time*Group interaction (B = 0.52, 95% CI [0.07, 0.96] for Times 1 to 2; B = 0.24, 95% CI [0.01, 0.48] for Times 1 to 3) in favour of the experimental group was found. No significant intervention effects were found for children’s and parents’ accelerometer-measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, or their co-physical activity. co-PA between parent and children was positively associated with children’s perceived autonomy support (r = .15), need satisfaction (r = .11), and negatively with BMI (r = -.09). We also found that it was related to parent outcomes, including autonomy support (r = .17), need satisfaction (r = .18), need frustration (negatively, r = -.18), and well-being (r = .16). The above findings are presented in the following published paper: Ha, AS, Lonsdale, C, Lubans, DR, Ng, FF, & Ng, JYY. (2021). Improving children's fundamental movement skills through a family-based physical activity program: Results from the "Active 1+FUN" randomized controlled trial. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, 18:99. Thematic analysis of focus groups with parents and children showed that parents and children perceived more competence, motivation and engagement in PA, as well as improved parent-child relationships. Semi-structured interviews with facilitators showed that facilitators perceived the theory-driven intervention was feasible to deliver to families and observed participants’ improvement of PA behaviours engagement and relations. The above findings are presented in a manuscript currently under review.

14616117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14616117.value: Results of the study provided support for the application of family-based approaches to promote physical activity and fundamental movement skills in primary school children and their parents. We found that children who took part in the study had weak fundamental movement skills and general knowledge regarding physical activity. This suggests that intervention may be needed at a younger age. Therefore, the intervention will be further developed and modified for younger, kindergarten-aged children. A proposal for the continuation and extension of the study to younger participants will be submitted in the upcoming GRF exercise.

14616117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14616117.value: Our study shows the effectiveness of a family-based program in improving children’s fundamental movement skills and physical activity behaviours. It also shows that co-PA between parents and children is positively associated with psychosocial outcomes. It also provides a comprehensive evaluation of the intervention by collecting and analysing the facilitators and participants’ perceptions. This study highlights the value of family-based PA intervention programs for families and the intervention components developed under the study may serve as a blueprint for future physical activity promotion initiatives using a family-based approach.

14616317.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14616317.value: 任務驅動式詞語聯想：跨語言詞彙網在英漢翻譯中的運用

14616317.label: Project Objectives
14616317.value: To demonstrate the difference between bilingual and cross-lingual word webs with examples from dictionaries, free association norms, corpora, and computational modeling. To test and use statistical natural language processing methods to address various problems anticipated in corpus-based modeling of cross-lingual word associations for computer-aided translation.
rows: To demonstrate the difference between bilingual and cross-lingual word webs with examples from dictionaries, free association norms, corpora, and computational modeling.
To test and use statistical natural language processing methods to address various problems anticipated in corpus-based modeling of cross-lingual word associations for computer-aided translation.

14616317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14616317.value: Motivated by a real-world problem, this project aims at exploring the possibility of enhancing bilingual lexical resources by better modeling cross-linguistic differences and considering the information demand of specific language tasks. Various types of lexical associations, typically including paradigmatic and syntagmatic relations, can be statistically modeled from large corpora to a certain extent and have been used to facilitate lexical information retrieval in electronic dictionaries and thesauri. Notwithstanding this, it is observed that the way bilingual lexicons are built may not have sufficiently taken into account the cognitive aspects of bilingual lexical access. Especially for language pairs like English and Chinese, with so much cross-linguistic difference, many conceptual or translation equivalents are not really completely equivalent. Hence dictionary users can often only access the pre-defined translation equivalents and the corresponding word associations, and may not be shown adequately the range of potentially possible usages in real contexts. The information demand of particular language applications has not been thoroughly considered either, and the more relevant lexical associations are not always distinguished from and more often hidden among the less relevant ones for a specific user request. The current project thus proposes a task-driven approach for more guided utilization of lexical associations modeled from large corpora. We focus on the possible lexical information demand of English-Chinese translators, and thus the following research questions: What are the similarities and differences between bilingual word associations (obtained from one language and translated to another) and cross-lingual word associations (obtained separately from the two languages directly) for English and Chinese? How can we filter or re-prioritize statistically modeled lexical associations in response to specific information demand in a particular language task? They are to be probed by analyzing and comparing empirical data from dictionaries, free association norms, and corpora, and by testing different ways of statistical modeling of lexical associations within the distributional semantics framework, respectively. With the prototype system to be developed, and empirical evidence to be found, the project is expected to open a new path in computational lexicography and computer-aided translation with genuine cross-lingual lexical resources, and to inform further research on bilingual lexical access models. 本研究從實際問題出發，考慮特定語言任務的信息需求和所涉語言差異，以構建適用的雙語詞彙資源。目前利用統計模型，可從大型語料庫中提取多種詞彙關聯信息，此技術已應用於提升電子詞典的檢索功能。然而一般雙語詞彙的設計和構建，並未充分考慮到雙語詞彙提取的認知層面，尤其是在中文與英文般差異較大的語言中，概念或詞彙間的對應多半不是完全對等，用戶只能查閱預設的翻譯對等詞和相關詞彙，未必就能聯想到其他在實際語境中可用的字詞。至於一般靠統計得出的詞語關聯程度，也不會照顧個別用戶的信息需求，以致關聯的強弱與預期不符的情況屢有發生，檢索結果不如理想。本研究聚焦於英漢翻譯的詞彙需求，提出以任務驅動的方式，運用大型語料庫蘊含的詞語關聯信息：先從詞典、自由詞語聯想常模、語料庫等提取詞語關聯的實證，分析比較，探討英漢之間基於翻譯對等的雙語詞彙網跟基於個別語言生成的跨語言詞彙網有何異同；再參考分佈式語義模型，測試不同方法，以因應特定語言任務的信息需求將詞語關聯的統計數據過濾或重新訂定優次。本研究並計劃開發雛型系統供教學實驗，期望為計算詞典學和電腦輔助翻譯開闢新資源，同時為雙語詞彙提取模型的研究帶來新啟示。

14616317.label: Realisation of objectives
14616317.value: The difficult times during 2019 and 2020 had inevitably hindered the progress of the project. There were four objectives in the original project proposal. The first two objectives have been achieved as planned. The other two have been partially addressed but have become unfeasible due to unforeseen circumstances in the final year, and had to be put on hold eventually. For Objective 1, based on the evidence gathered from free word association norms (including the Birkbeck Word Association Norms and the University of South Florida Association Norms for English, and the Hong Kong Chinese Association Norms compiled by the PI) and different ways of corpus modeling of free word associations (with the Word Sketch and Thesaurus functions in the Sketch Engine), the difference between English and Chinese word associations had been empirically established. The analysis was continued with examples from electronic dictionaries and lexicons, particularly the Princeton WordNet and the Chinese Open Wordnet, which link up words in a network according to various lexical semantic relations. The cross-linguistic differences and thus the potential pitfalls of creating bilingual wordnets with simple translation equivalents were discussed. In addition to general lexical items, domain-specific glossaries were also examined. In particular, we analyzed English-Chinese financial term pairs with respect to word classes, constituent compatibility, syntactic structures and compositionality, to obtain a clearer picture of the cross-linguistic lexical correspondence as far as terminology is concerned. For Objectives 1 and 2, we examined the lexical usages in three contexts of translation, namely simultaneous interpreting, domain-specific practical translation, as well as general and literary translation. We have compared the lexical choices of translators and interpreters based on the Hong Kong Hansard and the corresponding transcriptions of the Cantonese interpreted speeches, and found quite strong evidence of different lexical access between interpreters and translators. We have compared terminology translation in bilingual financial texts, and proposed a user-driven standard for assessing commercial term extraction systems, to help users make the most of such computer-aided translation tools. We have also highlighted the need for context-sensitive translation in literary translation, and proposed ways to enhance the navigational means in existing dictionaries, considering the cognitive aspects of the lexicon. Altogether we have managed to demonstrate the similarities and differences of English-Chinese bilingual word associations as manifested in dictionaries, free association norms, corpora, and computational modeling. More importantly, by considering their applicability and usefulness in various contexts of translation, we have been able to showcase that the most relevant word associations are somewhat task-driven, thus strengthening our proposal for task-driven word associations to enhance lexical access to facilitate translators’ work. For Objective 2, we have proposed two natural language processing methods using neural network models and deep learning to enhance bilingual lexical access beyond simple translation equivalents. One method tries to use neural machine translation to rank translation examples along the free/literal translation distinction to show users the many possible context-sensitive expressions in addition to the context-free equivalents typically provided in bilingual dictionaries. A preliminary version of a prototype system for this was implemented. Another method targets at the translation of collocations. Starting with a given collocation in one language, it uses word embedding for measuring word similarities, as a means to re-order related words according to the requirements of the specific task and to reveal less seen combinations not covered in dictionaries, thus allowing translators to access a wider variety of lexical choices, to think more comprehensively about fidelity and fluency, and to be more aware of context-sensitive translation which is especially salient for literary translation. Since the end of the last reporting period (mid-2019), the project has been unexpectedly and considerably disrupted for reasons beyond the PI’s control. First it was the aftermath of the abrupt early termination of 2019-20 Term 1 due to local challenges, followed by the global pandemic lasting throughout 2020. On the one hand, the PI had to spend much extra time and effort on online class preparation and re-designing her courses, given the inaccessibility of campus facilities for usual class activities. In particular, the courses on Computer-aided Translation which relied on licensed software installed in the computer lab had to switch to web-based tools, meaning that most course materials had to be done anew and the usual face-to-face practical workshops had to be completely revamped to be operable for Zoom classes. On the other hand, working from home had been a normal practice, at least for some time last year. In fact, the research assistant for the project who lives across the border in Shenzhen could not even come to the office for a prolonged period; and without the necessary computing equipment, the experiments and system testing had to be delayed. Understanding that most projects faced similar adversity, originally the PI had planned to apply for an extension of the project completion date. However, it turned out that she would leave her academic position by the end of December 2020. As a result, some of the project objectives became unfeasible and unachievable within the remaining project period. Hence, a revision of the project objectives, keeping two of the four original items, was requested and was approved by RGC in November 2020. Thus the limited time and effort during the second half of the project had been concentrated on achieving the two more important objectives satisfactorily, which had led to one workshop proceedings paper, one book chapter and one journal paper, during 2020 and 2021. Despite the necessary change in the final stage, the two objectives that have been forgone were already mildly addressed in the project, as documented in the mid-term progress report. This would leave a good foundation for future work, for completing the two tasks and for further development of the research.

14616317.label: Major findings and research outcome
14616317.value: 1. Based on the Princeton WordNet, subsequent development of wordnets in other languages has followed either the Merge Model or the Expand Model. The Open Chinese Wordnet follows the latter, adding translations found in authoritative bilingual dictionaries to the existing synsets. Examining its adjective database, it was found that despite the increased coverage, the resulting Chinese synsets often deviate from the basic infrastructure and synonymy relation of WordNet, showing the inadequacy of creating cross-lingual word webs with simple translation equivalents. (See paper in Proceedings of GWC 2018) 2. Analysis of bilingual financial terminology revealed various linguistic differences between the English and Chinese equivalents. They may not have the same word classes and constituency; and for multi-word expressions, the equivalents may not be compositionally formed. For the same English terms, different Chinese equivalents may be used by different organizations. Competence and experience may also affect the way they are associated in translators’ minds. Users of commercial term extractors thus need more objective means to assess such computer-aided translation tools to benefit from them. (See paper in Proceedings of FNP 2018 and paper to appear in Terminology) 3. The lexical choices of translators and interpreters were compared to further showcase that the most relevant word associations are task-driven. It was found that where a different lexical item was used in the translation and the interpretation respectively, interpreters tend to use words of higher frequency, and the difference in the mean word frequency is statistically significant. This provides strong empirical evidence for previous interpreting models suggesting that under the time pressure, interpreters can only access their active vocabulary which often contains words that are more frequent. It also supports our argument for task-driven modeling of cross-lingual word associations. (See book chapter to appear in New Perspectives on Corpus Translation Studies, Springer) 4. For general and literary translation, the need for task-driven word associations is particularly evident. Translators should be aware of the many context-sensitive translation possibilities in addition to context-free equivalents. We have proposed a method making innovative use of the attention scores in neural machine translation for distinguishing between free translation and literal translation, in a relative sense, for bilingual sentence pairs. We have also tried using word embedding to enhance the navigational means in existing dictionaries for users to access associated words to facilitate collocation translation. (See papers in Proceedings of NLPTEA 2018, Proceedings of PACLIC 32 and Proceedings of CogALex 2020)

14616317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14616317.value: The preliminarily designed and implemented prototype system providing translators with examples of literal and free translation could be better built into a usable tool, upon more comprehensive development and testing of the algorithm for determining the relative degree of literalness of sentence translation, as well as rendition of fragments within sentences. More features including options for highlighting specific parts in the sentence pairs, grouping examples demonstrating a similar translation strategy, and filtering the examples by various criteria could be added. The method for enhancing the navigational means and lexical access of dictionaries with word embedding, to be tested at a larger scale, has great potential to be developed into an application software that assists translators in dictionary lookup and lexical suggestions during translation. Collaboration with dictionary publishers would be a satisfactory option, which would not only promote dictionary usage among different kinds of language users but also enable the research to make more far-reaching impact.

14616317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14616317.value: Words are inter-connected in the human mind, and when we see or hear a word, we quickly think of words related in one way or another. Bilinguals can even connect words from two languages. Psychologists use free word associations to demonstrate the massive network in the mental lexicon. In specific language tasks, however, the activation triggered in the network could be quite different. For instance, translators often need access to words and expressions beyond simple translation equivalents. This project thus proposes task-driven word associations. With more guided utilization of lexical associations, we hope to enhance the navigational means in existing dictionaries and thus the lexical access needed by English-Chinese translators. To demonstrate the need for task-driven word associations and the inadequacy of existing dictionaries in this regard, we had compared data from dictionaries, free association norms, corpora and computational modeling, and examined the lexical usages and choices in three contexts of translation: simultaneous interpreting, domain-specific practical translation and literary translation. Two natural language processing methods using neural network models and deep learning to enhance bilingual lexical access beyond simple translation equivalents have been proposed and shown to have great potential to be developed into useful computer-aided translation applications.
