15101517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15101517.value: Beclin 1是Beclin 1-Vps34复合体中一个关键的支架蛋白。该复合体对于细胞自噬和内溶体系转运至关重要，因为这两个过程都依赖Vps34的活性将细胞溶质材料运输至溶酶体进行降解。Beclin 1在多种生理过程中起着重要作用，包括调制胰岛素敏感性，激发先天免疫力和抑制肿瘤发生。 Beclin 1与许多“一级”和“次级”的调节因子如Atg14L，UVRAG，Bcl-2，Rubicon和Ambra1相互作用，以形成具有不同生化活性的Beclin1-Vps34亚复合物，从而使依赖Vps34的细胞自噬和内溶体系转运过程可以根据不同的细胞信号来精准地调控。 Beclin 2是最近新发现的Beclin 1在哺乳动物中的直向同源物。 Beclin 2可以形成Beclin 2-Vps34复合体来执行和Beclin1相似的功能。同时Beclin 2与Beclin 1有多处显着区别。首先， Beclin 2具有与Beclin 1不同的遗传位点和组织表达谱。其次，Beclin 2与“一级”和“次级”调节因子的作用方式也有别于Beclin 1。更重要的是，Beclin 2通过与GASP1的特异性相互作用在G蛋白偶联受体（GPCRs）的溶酶体降解中发挥独特的作用，GASP1是一种与GPCRs亚类（如大脑异丙型肝炎1受体（CN1R））相关的支架分子。此功能仅与Beclin 2有关，但与Vps34或Beclin 1无关。 Beclin 2基因敲除小鼠不仅出现自噬缺陷，而且脑中的CN1R表达水平上升，对胰岛素产生耐受性并导致肥胖。 我们计划用竞争模式来阐述Beclin 2如何协调其介导的自噬和GPCR转运两个过程。我们猜测与自噬相关的Beclin2-Atg14L / UVRAG蛋白作用以及与GPCR转运相关的Beclin 2-GASP1蛋白作用两者直接竞争，将内源Beclin 2招募到不同功能的复合物群体以协调这两个过程。同时我们也注意到Beclin 2与 “一级”调节因子Atg14L和UVRAG的结合亲和力模式有别于Beclin 1，这或许是Beclin 与Beclin1功能区别的另一原因。 在本项目中我们将对Beclin 2进行综合的生化和结构研究，以证实我们的假设。 我们计划对Beclin 2-Atg14L / UVRAG / GASP1蛋白相互作用进行生化表征，并用实验和计算方法解析Beclin 2卷曲螺旋结构域以及Beclin 2-Atg14L / UVRAG复合体的结构。我们还将进行基于细胞的功能研究来确认我们的生化和结构数据。本项目的成果将不仅提升我们对Beclin直系同源物在自噬过程中的功能和机理的认识，还将提供关于Beclin 2介导的GPCR转运过程的新信息，有助于我们更好地了解与GPCR信号通路有关的重要生理和疾病过程如饮食调节，止痛反应和精神病治疗。

15101517.label: Realisation of objectives
15101517.value: The project has progressed very well through the 30-month period with all objectives realized to 100%. We would like to report our activities and results obtained according to the four proposed objectives. Objective 1. Biochemical and structural study of the Beclin 2 CC domain to confirm its oligomeric state and metastability for Atg14L/UVRAG interaction We confirmed the homodimeric state of Beclin 2 CC domain by Size Exclusion Chromatography-Light Scattering (SEC-LS) profile. The temperature-dependent circular dichroism (CD) profile of the Beclin 2 CC domain reveals an estimated melting temperature (Tm) of ~40 degrees. Additionally, the dissociation constant (Kd) of Beclin 2 CC domain was ~100 μM as measured by Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) assay. These results suggest that Beclin 2 CC domain is indeed metastable. We determined the crystal structure of the Beclin 2 CC domain. It adopts an anti-parallel coiled coil homodimer similar to Beclin 1, with multiple “imperfect” a-d’ pairings at its dimer interface. The Beclin 2 dimer interface has 2 fewer canonical hydrophobic pairings than Beclin 1, thus likely leading to its lower stability. In summary, Objective 1 is 100% accomplished with the Beclin2 CC domain confirmed to be a metastable homodimer similar to Beclin 1. Beclin 2 CC domain is less stable than Beclin 1 due to fewer hydrophobic pairings at the dimer interface. Objective 2. Comparison of the Beclin 2-Atg14L and Beclin 2-UVRAG interactions through biochemical and structural characterizations to delineate their distinct binding modes We measured the binding affinities of the Beclin 2-Atg14L and Beclin 2-UVRAG interactions by ITC. Our data shows that Beclin 2 CC domain binds to Atg14L significantly stronger than UVRAG (Kd of 0.55 μM vs. 14 μM). This binding pattern is in distinct contrast to Beclin 1 as our previous study has shown that Beclin 1 CC domain binds to UVRAG stronger than Atg14L. We determined the crystal structure of the Beclin 2-Atg14L coiled coil complex using a construct that tethered the critical Beclin 2 and Atg14L fragments together via a flexible (GS)5 linker. The structure reveals a parallel heterodimeric coiled coil assembly consisting of only the N-terminal 4 heptad repeats of Beclin 2 CC domain on one helix and the matching N-terminal portion of Atg14L coiled coil segment on the other. This short Beclin 2-Atg14L complex is highly stable, as 6 out of the 8 a-a’ and d-d’ pairings at the coiled coil interface are the canonical hydrophobic type. Additionally, we also generated a homology model of the Beclin 2-UVRAG complex using our previous Beclin 1-UVRAG structure as template. Comparison of the Beclin 2-Atg14L and Beclin 2-UVRAG coiled coil interfaces shows that Atg14L-R119 forms electrostatically favorable interaction with Beclin 2-E173 but UVRAG does not. In summary, Objective 2 is 100% accomplished. We have determined the crystal structure of the Beclin 2-Atg14L coiled coil complex and generated a homology model of the Beclin 2-UVRAG coiled coil complex. Careful comparison of these two structures reveals that subtle sequence differences between Atg14L and UVRAG lead to differential pairing to Beclin 2, resulting in Atg14L being a stronger binding partner for Beclin 2 than UVRAG. Objective 3. Biochemical mapping of the GASP1-binding motif within Beclin 2 The Beclin 2-GASP1 interaction is critical for endolysosomal trafficking and degradation of a subset of GASP1-associated GPCRs such as the delta opioid receptor (DOR), cannabinoid 1 receptor (CB1R) and dopamine D2 receptor (D2R). We have carried out extensive biochemical studies to map the binding sites for GASP1 within the N-terminal region of Beclin 2. However, three in vitro assays, including GST pull-down experiments, ITC and peptide microarray, all failed to detect direct and specific interaction between Beclin 2 and GASP1. We then reasoned that the Beclin 2-GASP1 interaction might require additional binding partners. To test this hypothesis, we used mass spectroscopy to analyze protein components in the cell lysate after tandem pull down by GFP-tagged Beclin 2 and FLAG-tagged GASP1. After a few trials, we detected >20 potential candidates that co-eluted with Beclin 2 and GASP1. In summary, Objective 3 is 100% accomplished with our in vitro biochemical studies suggesting that the Beclin 2-GASP1 interaction is likely to be indirect and requires some additional binding partners. While our proteomic studies have yielded many potential candidates, further studies to validate these findings are beyond the scope of the current project and will be pursued in the future. Objective 4. Structure-based functional study on how competitive recruitment of Beclin 2 by Atg14L or GASP1 coordinates Beclin 2-mediated autophagy and GPCR trafficking In the initial proposal, we suggested that there could be delicate coordination between Beclin 2-mediated autophagy and GPCR trafficking via a competitive recruitment model, i.e. partition of Beclin 2 to the pro-autophagic Beclin 2-Vps34 complex would reduce the amount available for the Beclin 2-GASP1 interaction, leading to less degradation of GPCR and sustained GPCR signaling. To test this hypothesis, we set out to generate three types of Beclin 2 mutants, including “Atg14L-Loss”, “Atg14L-Gain” and “GASP1-Loss”. Based on our competitive model, we reasoned that “Atg14L-Loss” mutants would show reduced autophagic activity but more efficient degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs. In contrast, “Atg14L-Gain” and “GASP1-Loss” mutants would be expected to show higher autophagic activity but impaired degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs. Guided by the Beclin 2-Atg14L structure in Objective 2, we first generated Beclin 2 mutants with two, four or five Leu residues critical for Atg14L binding mutated to Glu. These mutants, termed 2E, 4E and 5E, were confirmed to be the “Atg14L-Loss” type because they lost binding to Atg14L as assessed by in vitro ITC experiments and in vivo Co-IP studies. Transient over-expression of Beclin 2 wild-type as well as 2E, 4E and 5E mutants in Beclin 2 knockout HEK293 cells had little effect on cellular autophagic activity. Similarly, in non-small-cell lung cancer cell line A54, these constructs did not promote the endolysosomal degradation of oncogenic cell surface receptor EGFR. Intriguingly, in HEK293 cells stabling expressing GASP1-associated D2R, transient over-expression of Beclin 2 wild-type led to enhanced D2R degradation. In contrast, the “Atg14L-Loss” mutants did not show any effect. We also generated a Beclin 2 mutant of the “GASP1-Loss” type by deleting the N-terminal putative GASP1-binding region. This “GASP1-Loss” mutant showed similar phenotype as “Atg14L-Loss” mutants and exerted little impact on autophagy or endolysosomal degradation of EGFR. Additionally, the “GASP1-Loss” mutant also failed to promote D2R degradation in comparison to Beclin 2 wild-type. We attempted to generate Beclin 2 mutants of the “Atg14L-Gain” type by mutating the “imperfect” polar or charged residues at the Beclin 2-Atg14L interface to Leu. However, these mutations stabilized the functionally inactive Beclin 2 homodimer instead of promoting the Beclin 2-Atg14L interaction. As a result, these “Atg14L-Gain” mutants showed little in vitro or in vivo effect. Overall, Objective 4 is 100% accomplished with two important mechanistic findings. First of all, Beclin 2 is functionally distinct from Beclin 1 by exerting dominant role only in degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs but not canonical autophagy or endolysosomal trafficking. Secondly, the initially proposed competitive binding model may not apply because the Beclin 2-Atg14L interaction did not promote autophagy at the expense of slowing down the degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs or vice versa. Instead, this interaction had dominant effect on degradation of GASP1-associated GPCR but showed little effect on autophagy.

15101517.label: Major findings and research outcome
15101517.value: During this project period, we solved the crystal structure of the Beclin 2 coiled coil domain and showed that it formed a metastable homodimer similar to Beclin 1. We also solved the crystal structure of the Beclin 2-Atg14L coiled coil complex and revealed that the heterodimer interface was strengthened by extra hydrophobic pairings and electrostatically complementary interactions. Our cell-based studies reveal that Beclin 2 is functionally distinct from Beclin 1 because it only exerts dominant effect on degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs but has no similar effect on autophagy or endolysosomal degradation of cell surface receptors like EGFR, both of which were dominantly regulated by Beclin 1. Guided by our structural findings, we designed Beclin 2-targeting stapled peptides that promoted degradation of GASP1-associated D2R but did not affect autophagy or EGFR degradation. A manuscript reporting these findings is under review in Cell Research (Part C, item 8[6]). A link to this manuscript is attached in this report, which contains all the data referred to in this completion report. As part of our on-going research on Beclin 1 and Beclin 2, we also determined the crystal structure of Beclin 1-UVRAG coiled coil complex and designed Beclin 1-targeting stapled peptides that increased autophagic flux and enhanced endolysosomal degradation of EGFR. A manuscript reporting these findings have been published in PNAS in 2018 (Part C, item 8[1]). A US patent for our designed peptides was awarded in April 2021 (Part C, item 11[*]). In collaboration with Dr. Congcong He in School of Medicine, Northwestern University (Chicago, U.S.A.), we investigated the role of Beclin 2 in cocaine reward behavior and drug addiction. A manuscript reporting our findings has been published in Science Advances in 2021 (Part C, item 8[3]). In collaboration with Prof. Renxiao Wang in School of Pharmacy, Fudan University (Shanghai, P.R.China), we optimized the Beclin 1-targeting stapled peptides by staple scanning and enhanced their binding affinity to Beclin 1 by ~10-30 fold. These newly designed peptides showed potent anti-proliferative efficacy in multiple cancer cells. A manuscript reporting these findings is under minor revision in J. Med. Chem. (Part C, item 8[4]). A patent application for these newly designed peptides has been filed in China (Part C, item 11[2]). Two more research output items, including one manuscript published in Sci. Rep. in 2020 (Part C, item 8[2]) and one manuscript under review (Part C, item 8[5]), are also included in this completion report.

15101517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15101517.value: Our research team is interested in pursuing the following two initiatives in our future study. First of all, we plan to identify the additional factors involved in mediating the Beclin 2-GASP1 interaction. Our proteomic analysis of cell lysate after tandem pull-down by Beclin 2 and GASP1 revealed more than 20 potential candidates that co-eluted with Beclin 2 and GASP1. For further studies to validate these candidates, we plan to first use siRNA screening to assess if knockdown of a candidate molecule would lead to impairment in D2R degradation. For those positive hits, we would further confirm their association with Beclin 2 or GASP1 by Co-IP and biochemical assays. The second initiative we plan to pursue is the optimization of Beclin 2-targeting stapled peptides through staple scanning and sequence permutation to enhance its binding affinity to Beclin 2, similar to what we did for Beclin 1-binding stapled peptides. We also plan to develop new stapled peptides that serve as Beclin 2 inhibitors by blocking its binding to Atg14L. These Beclin 2-targeting peptides may have translational potential in Beclin 2-mediated pathological conditions such as obesity, insulin resistance and cocaine addiction.

15101517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15101517.value: Beclin 2 is a mammalian gene that acts as a scaffolding member of the Class III phosphoinositol-3-kinase (PI3KC3) complex. Similar to its close homolog Beclin 1, Beclin 2 is essential for PI3KC3-mediated cellular processes including autophagy. But Beclin 2 is not functionally redundant with Beclin 1 because it facilitates the endolysosomal degradation of some unique targets including GASP1-associated GPCRs like the delta opioid receptor (DOR), cannabinoid 1 receptor (CB1R) and dopamine D2 receptor (D2R. Beclin 2 has been functionally implicated in obesity, insulin resistance, tumorigenesis and innate immunity. Here we report the biochemical and structural studies of the Beclin 2 coiled coil domain and the Beclin 2-Atg14L complex. Our studies reveal that Beclin 2 coiled coil domain is metastable and biochemically distinct from Beclin 1 with higher binding affinity to Atg14L than UVRAG. The potent Beclin 2-Atg14L interaction is essential for promoting the endolysosomal degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs. Guided by our structures, we also designed Beclin 2-targeting stapled peptides that specifically enhanced endolysosomal degradation of GASP1-associated GPCR without affecting autophagy. These results suggest that the coiled coil domain of Beclin 2 is functionally distinct from Beclin 1 and can be targeted by designed peptides to promote degradation of GASP1-associated GPCRs.

15102417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15102417.value: 記憶是生物體根據學習經驗獲得、存儲和檢索信息的能力。當印跡細胞存儲記憶時，它們的興奮性會暫時性的提高，從而增加了參與後續存儲記憶的可能性。為了提供如何在提高的興奮性下分配印跡細胞的因果關係，需要一種非侵入性地操縱特定神經元興奮性的工具。 超聲腦刺激是一種非侵入性的方式，在探索人類大腦功能和治愈腦部疾病领域具有重大前景。目前的研究顯示超声能夠有效地刺激特定腦區域的神經元而不損傷腦組織。由於超声能夠非侵入性投过颅骨，精确聚焦在一个小脑区中，它被被認為是現有刺激策略（例如深部腦刺激，光遺傳學，經顱磁刺激和經顱直流刺激）之外的令人鼓舞的手段和良好的替代方案。此外，理論和我們最近的研究表明，超聲刺激可以增加神經元的興奮性。這些對神經興奮性的有趣影響使超聲波成為探索記憶編碼和檢索神經迴路的潛在工具。迄今為止，超聲調製對神經興奮性的潛在機制仍然未知，因此，迫切需要進一步的研究，使其成為操縱記憶分配的可控工具。 在此提案中，我們計劃探索超聲波刺激對神經興奮性的生物效應，並了解可能的機制。為了使這種方法成為探測記憶分配的有用工具，我們計劃研究超聲誘導的神經興奮性升高與其周圍的自然提示相結合以引起記憶。秀麗隱桿線蟲作為模型生物體，在自然提示下具有明確的行為，將用於測試我們的假設。我們計劃從行為、單一神經元功能、到分子水平研究超聲波刺激，以了解可能的功能。預先訓練的線蟲將通過超聲波刺激下的趨溫和趨化測定進行測試。響應時間將用於神經興奮性進行評估，從而影響學習和記憶。此外，將進行體內鈣成像和CREB活性成像，以測試趨化性和熱變態期間的單一神經元功能。由成像數據確定的反應溫度和鹽濃度將被用於確認影響並揭示單神經元功能水平的機制。最後，將使用具有特定神經元突變體中某些機械敏感離子通道的野生型和轉基因秀麗隱桿線蟲來測試這些離子通道如何介導神經興奮性。 這項研究預計將為腦刺激研究做出突破性創新，增加研究記憶如何儲存在大腦中的關鍵方法。考虑到这是一项非侵入性，高穿透深度，不需要基因改造的技术，這項研究的成功可能為研究記憶分配和增強學習記憶提供了寶貴的工具.

15102417.label: Realisation of objectives
15102417.value: 1. Instrument an ultrasound stimulation and optical imaging system We developed a customized in vitro ultrasound stimulation system incorporated with a calcium imaging system. Briefly, the calcium imaging system consisted of a modified upright epifluorescence microscope. The excitation light was generated by a dual-color LED, filtered and delivered to the sample to illuminate the calcium sensor. Signals from the cells were collected by a water immersion objective, passed through a dual-filter wheel, and captured by a camera. To minimize phototoxic effects, the LEDs were triggered at 1 Hz and synchronized with sCMOS time-lapse imaging. Ultrasound was delivered through a triangle waveguide attached to the transducer placed below the culture dish at a 45-degree angle. The waveguide was also attached to an acoustic absorber to minimize acoustic reverberation. This design helped us to minimize the generation of standing waves and created a strong water-air interface on the bottom of the dish. This results in a controllable ultrasound field, as measured by an acoustic pressure mapping system consisting of a needle hydrophone and high-precision 3D motor. The obtained acoustic pressure map was measured. Each stimulus was composed of 200 tone burst pulses at a center frequency of 500 kHz with a duty cycle of 40% at a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 1 kHz, at low acoustic intensities. These parameters corresponded to very short bursts of ultrasound stimulation, helping to minimize any resultant thermal effects. 2. Perform molecular and functional study of neural excitability under ultrasound modulation To confirm that ultrasound could activate Piezo1 using our customized setup, we overexpressed mouse Piezo1 heterologously in HEK293T cells, known to show minimal response to mechanical stimulation. For this, we transfected cells with a pcDNA3.1-mPiezo1-IRES-GFP plasmid or a vector control, and treated them with a Piezo1-specific agonist, Yoda1. We verified the overexpression using qRT-PCT and Western blotting for Piezo1, and calcium imaging revealed that 1 µM Yoda1 induced significantly more Ca2+ influx in the Piezo1-transfected cells, compared to the control. This confirmed the presence and functionality of transfected mouse Piezo1 channels in HEK293T cells. We proceeded to perform Ca2+ using ultrasound at acoustic pressures corresponding to a range previously reported to have elicited responses. We found that increasing ultrasound intensity on Piezo1-transfected cells resulted in increasing Ca2+ influx into cells, with 0.3 MPa ultrasound showing a significant increase, while the control remained largely unchanged. To exclude the possibility that the fluorescence changes were due to cells being out-of-focus due to ultrasound perturbation, we also performed ratiometric Ca2+ imaging. We observed that the fluorescence ratio (340/380) of control cells showed no response while the Piezo1-expressing cells showed a robust and large response to 0.1 MPa ultrasound. Pre-treating the Piezo1-expressing cells with a Piezo1-specific inhibitor, GsMTx-4 at 40 µM reduced the cells’ response to the same level as the control cells. This finding confirmed that the elevated cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels seen upon ultrasound stimulation were not experimental artifacts. Thus, our ultrasound stimulation setup could successfully activate Piezo1 to allow Ca2+ influx at low, physiologically relevant intensities. 3. Examine the role of mechano-sensitive ion channel in ultrasound mediated neural excitability We next tested the effects of ultrasound on primary cortical neurons harvested from embryonic mice to test the feasibility of stimulating live neurons with ultrasound. We first probed whether primary neurons cultured using our protocol could express any functional Piezo1. Treating primary neurons at DIV 10 with 10 µM Yoda1 stimulated Ca2+ influx, while pre-treatment with 40 µM GsMTx-4 significantly reduced it. The inhibitory effect of GsMTx-4 upon Yoda1-induced Ca2+ influx was consistent with the known mechanism of its action as a Piezo1 gating modifier. Immunofluorescent staining revealed that primary neurons at day in vitro (DIV) 10 expressed Piezo1 endogenously. Thus, primary neurons at DIV 10 expressed some functional Piezo1, and we proceeded to evaluate the effects of ultrasound on these cells. We also acutely isolated mouse cortical neurons from mouse pups at P3, to evaluate in in vivo expression of Piezo1 in neurons of approximately equal maturity. These neurons could be made to influx Ca2+ when stimulated with Yoda1, but not this effect was almost completely abrogated in presence of the mechanosensitive ion channel antagonist Ruthenium red. We thus found that mature neurons, both in vitro and in vivo expressed functional Piezo1 with detectable effects. Ultrasound stimulation resulted in dose-dependent Ca2+ influx into the neurons, and this influx was abrogated when the cells were pre-treated with 40 µM GsMTx-4. Ultrasound at 0.3 MPa and above was able to induce significant Ca2+ influx, so we evaluated the effects of ultrasound on neuron activation by immunofluorescent staining of c-Fos, a well-established molecular marker of neuronal activation that is responsive to Ca2+ influx. Untreated cells, cells treated with 0.3 MPa ultrasound for 20 minutes inside a standard cell culture incubator, and cells pre-treated with 20 µM GsMTx-4 before ultrasound were compared. We found that c-Fos expression in the nuclei of neurons (identified by MAP2 staining) significantly increased upon US treatment compared to the untreated control and reduced significantly when GsMTx-4 pre-treatment was applied. Hence, low-intensity ultrasound could activate primary neurons in vitro by opening the Piezo1 channel to allow Ca2+ influx. We were interested in exploring the signaling implications of Piezo1-mediated ultrasound effects on neurons in greater depth, to help elucidate the possible downstream effects of Ca2+ influx through ultrasound-activated Piezo1 channels. We chose the mouse hippocampal cell line mHippoE-18 (CLU199) as an in vitro representation of normal (non-cancerous) neuronal cells to enable better quantification of these effects. Expression of Piezo1 in CLU199 cells was confirmed through semi-quantitative RT-PCR, with HeLa cells as a positive control and Western blot. To evaluate the treatment’s effects on downstream cell signaling, we investigated levels of the phosphorylated (activated) forms of the Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase type II (p-CaMKII), and the transcription factor CREB (p-CREB), both of which are crucial players in Ca2+ signaling. CaMKII and is directly regulated by calmodulin, a good indicator of the level of Ca2+ inside the cell, and both it and CREB are involved in critical neuronal functions like neurotransmitter secretion, plasticity, transcription regulation, learning and memory. We observed the levels of these activated proteins, along with c-Fos, by Western blot to gauge whether ultrasound might affect aspects of neuronal function and activation downstream of Ca2+ influx. Ultrasound treatment inside an incubator for 20 minutes increased the levels of p-CaMKII, p-CREB and c-Fos in a dose-dependent manner, with 0.3 and 0.5 MPa inducing significant increases. We then evaluated Piezo1’s contribution to these effects by siRNA knockdown. We were able to achieve over 50% knockdown of Piezo1 and found that this significantly reduced the 1 µM Yoda1-induced Ca2+ influx compared to cells treated with non-targeting siRNA (‘Ctrl’). CLU199 cells with Piezo1 knockdown also displayed no significant upregulation of p-CaMKII, p-CREB and c-Fos than the control when treated with 0.3 MPa ultrasound compared to the control. Thus, we determined that ultrasound stimulation significantly affects the levels of important proteins in CLU199 neuronal cells, and these effects were dependent upon Piezo1.

15102417.label: Major findings and research outcome
15102417.value: Our results demonstrate that ultrasound can exert effects on cells in vitro through activation of the Piezo1 channel. We observed that heterologous Piezo1 expression in cells could enable them to respond to ultrasound (HEK293T). We showed that mouse neuronal cells express Piezo1 endogenously and that ultrasound alone can open these channels, allowing Ca2+ influx into them. We also demonstrated that activation of primary neurons by ultrasound in vitro can be significantly reduced by inhibiting Piezo1’s activity. Our experiments used low-intensity low-frequency ultrasound, without microbubbles, allowing us to minimize the thermal and cavitation effects of ultrasound. We manipulated endogenous Piezo1 on a functional level, using an inhibitor drug, and at the expression level, using siRNA, and found that the effects of ultrasound on proteins crucially involved in neuronal activation and calcium signaling were significantly reduced in both cases. Blocking the activity of heterologous Piezo1 could also suppress ultrasound-induced Ca2+ influx. Thus, we see an important role played by Piezo1 activation in enabling neurons to respond to ultrasound stimulation. In addition to increased c-Fos expression in primary neurons, our results in a neuronal cell line also showed that the expression of the activated forms of CaMKII and CREB can be increased by ultrasound stimulation, along with increasing c-Fos expression. These proteins are involved in complex neuronal functions such as neuronal plasticity, learning and memory. While results from a cell line must not be overinterpreted, previous studies of ultrasound have also shown increases of calmodulin-dependent kinases in primary neurons (Liu et al., 2017) and increases in the crucial neuroprotective protein BDNF in mouse and rat brains treated with ultrasound (Chen et al., 2018; Su et al., 2017; Tufail et al., 2010). The observed Piezo1-dependence of these effects in our experiments also help to pinpoint their source to the ultrasound stimulation. Such results at the cellular level also provide evidence of the basis for non-auditory effects of ultrasound. Our results help to bolster the idea that ultrasound treatment can have therapeutic effects in the brain, and could contribute to identifying which conditions could benefit most from such a treatment.

15102417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15102417.value: The obvious next step would be to demonstrate Piezo1-dependence of ultrasound effects in vivo, by upregulating or downregulating it in rodent brains. It will likely be challenging to upregulate Piezo1 in vivo, due to its size and complexity, but also to downregulate it, as knocking it out totally in mice embryos can be lethal. However, delivering a Piezo1 inhibitor or Piezo1 knockdown reagents in rodents is feasible and are a promising approach for further understanding the effects of ultrasound. Transgenic mice with conditional knockout of Piezo1 in the brain are also a viable option. Concurrently, research about the Piezo1 molecule itself could contribute to both evaluating and enhancing the role of brain-based Piezo1 in mediating ultrasound’s effects. Studies comparing the different segments show some domains to be more mechanosensitive than other. This raises the possibility that studying the effects of ultrasound on such domains could be studied instead of the entire molecule, making it easier to tailor ultrasound parameters to activate Piezo1 more efficiently. Thus, understanding ultrasound’s mechanism of action on Piezo1 could have implications for usefully modulating neuronal activity, as well as that of a host of other cell types.

15102417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15102417.value: Ultrasound brain stimulation is a promising modality for probing brain function and treating brain disease non-invasively and with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, the mechanism underlying its effects remains unclear. Here, we examine the role that the mouse piezo-type mechanosensitive ion channel component 1 (Piezo1) plays in mediating the in vitro effects of ultrasound in mouse primary cortical neurons and a neuronal cell line. We show that ultrasound alone could activate heterologous and endogenous Piezo1, initiating calcium influx and increased nuclear c-Fos expression in primary neurons, but not when pre-treated with a Piezo1 inhibitor. We also found that ultrasound significantly increased the expression of the important proteins phospho-CaMKII, phospho-CREB and c-Fos in a neuronal cell line, but knocking down Piezo1 significantly reduced this effect. Our findings demonstrate that the activity of mechanosensitive ion channels like Piezo1 stimulated by ultrasound is an important contributor to its ability to stimulate cells in vitro.

15102717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15102717.value: 在過往的研究中顯示, 柏金遜症(PD) 會影響患者的視覺功能及眼球運動能力。但大多數的研究僅針對固定，追踪和快速跳視的眼動行為及特征，忽略了PD對眼睛聚焦在不同遠近的物體上的輻奏眼動的影響。為了卜土進一步探討眼動特徵對動態視覺功能的影響，我們的第一個實驗將詳細分析PD患者的動態視覺功能及眼球運動的轉變及其相互的關係。然而，基於眼球活動能力受阻，PD患者在日常生活中可能難以追踪和觀察快速移動的物件，影響其日常生活。近年，一些臨床的眼動訓練已証實能有效地增強由神經性疾病引起的眼球運動障礙患者的功能表現，但這些訓練是否可以提升PD患者的相關功能和表現？我們的第二個實驗將使用安慰劑對照設計的探索性臨床試驗來確定眼動訓練對PD患者的動態視覺和功能表現的有效性。在這項試驗中，32名PD參與者將被隨機分配到眼動訓練或安慰劑訓練組。參與眼動訓練組的人士將接受為期12次的訓練（2次×6週），而安慰劑組的參加者將獲得12次的（安慰劑）休閒活動。干預措施的效果將以4個時段進行：干預前，6至12次的干預後，以及在完成所有干預的8週後。主要結果測量是動態視覺功能；輔助措施包括眼動特徵，閱讀表現和生活質量。 此項研究將測試以下假設： 1）與年齡相似的健康對照組相比，PD患者的眼運動功能（跳視，追求和聚焦）和動態視覺功能受損; 2）眼運動訓練將改善PD患者眼動運動和動態視力。

15102717.label: Realisation of objectives
15102717.value: This study involved two main experiments to achieve our project’s objectives. Our first objective was to examine the oculomotor functions and dynamic visual function in patients with Parkinson’s Disease (PD) and age-matched healthy controls (HC). Two aspects of experimental settings were established to measure participants’ oculomotor and dynamic visual functions. Research methods for measuring 4 types of oculomotor functions were developed: 1) fixational eye movements; 2) saccadic eye movements; 3) pursuit eye movements; and 4) vergence eye movements. For the first 3 types of eye movements, a commercially available eye tracking system (table-mounted Tobii eye tracker) was used although protocols of the visual stimuli and data collection had to redevelop because the built-in software did not include the analysis of our required oculomotor characteristics. Regarding the vergence eye movement, Tobii eye tracker could not provide reliable measure although several modifications of the table-mounted eye tracking system had been attempted. Poor quality of eye tracking could be related to the droopy lid during vergence (i.e. people tend to drop their eye when tracking a moving object from distance to near, covering part of the pupil tracked by the system) and the design of the system. Given that PD patients always had some difficulty to maintain their eyelids open, Tobii eye tracker were not suitable for vergence eye movement measure. After studying different types of eye trackers available in the market, a head-mounted eye tracker (Pupil lab) could fulfil our needs, where an eye camera of the system was set below the participants’ eye, allowing better capture of their eye movement when the target moved towards the subject. However, this eye tracking system was not designed for measuring vergence eye movements, so substantial redevelopment of the hardware and software of this measure was required such that the vergence task could synchronize with this new eye tracking device to provide reliable vergence eye movement measure. A small pilot testing was conducted to confirm the reliability of this new system with new analytical protocols and programme. Due to tight timing of this project and commitment with the eligible participants, our data collection of this experiment was started while we were redesigning the vergence eye movement measures. Hence, some of the participants (~15%) joined the project at the early stage did not have the vergence eye movement measures. Instead, other 3 aspects of eye movement measures and functional measures were completed. For the dynamic visual function, before data collection of the main experiment, a pilot study was conducted to examine the dynamic visual functions for a range of target moving speeds (1, 2, 4 and 8 deg/sec). Practically, to measure dynamic visual acuity (i.e. the smallest size of a target moving at different speeds), visual stimuli of sinusoidal gratings of 100% contrast and different spatial frequencies were generated by OpenGL-based software package computer programme (Psykinematix version 2.0) and displayed on a flat cathode-ray-tube (CRT) monitor screen (357.4 mm (width) x 268.1 mm (height)) located 6 m away. However, with this experimental setting, participants could only track the target moving across a small visual angle of 3.5 degrees instead of a wide visual angle. Results of our pilot study did not show any significant differences in dynamic visual function between PD and HC. We believed that the insignificant findings in the dynamic visual function might be due to the insufficient amount of eye movements triggered by the current experimental design. Although an alternative measure for dynamic visual function was explored through collaboration with University of Waterloo, the experimental setting could not reach our requirement. Even using a large high-resolution monitor and a high-powered computing system, quality of the presented target remained sub-optimal although the target could be moved in a much wider area across the monitor, ensuring that more effort in eye movement was required to track the target. After several rounds of pilot testing, results illustrated a strong ceiling effect, which might impose a strong limitation to reveal the differences of dynamic visual functions between PD and HC groups. Due to the time constrains for further developing a reliable dynamic visual function measure, this measure was removed from our project for both main experiments. Our second objective was to examine the effectiveness of oculomotor training on functional performances for PD patients, in which participants were randomly assigned into an intervention group (receiving oculomotor training) or a placebo group (receiving leisure activities). Based on the preliminary results from the first experiment, in which PD patients had much stronger deficits in the vergence eye movements than other types of eye movements, our training protocol had been modified to address the specific needs for PD patients. For the intervention group, training on improving saccadic and vergence eye movements instead of all types of eye movements was adopted and pilot tested. In addition, a combination of in-office and home-based training which is a common clinical practice in vision therapy was adopted, in which participants received 10 sessions of 45 mins in-office training and 10 sessions of 10-20 mins home based training per week (3 sessions/ week). For the placebo group, participants received 10 sessions of 45 mins in-office leisure activities and 10 sessions of 10-20 mins home-based video watching p(3 sessions/ week). Due to the several waves of pandemic, number of patients attended their follow up medical appointments at our collaborating hospitals (Queens Elizabeth Hospital, Prince of Wales, and Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital) dropped substantially, largely increasing the difficulty of patient recruitments. In addition to smaller patient pools, very few PD patients were willing to participate in research projects because of their difficulties for independent travel (as some required family members/ caregivers’ accompany) and huge concerns of contracting the virus. Even if some PD patients agreed to participate in this project, some of them withdrew at the beginning or during the training due to physical/ medical issues or difficulties to commit further. This imposed some impacts on unbiased sampling of PD patients to participate in this project, which might slightly limit the generalization of our findings. In our original proposal, a sample size of 36 PD patients was proposed for this pilot randomized clinical trial. Despite extensive efforts made by our collaborating clinicians at hospitals, subject recruitment remained extremely difficult. In addition to the 3 collaborating hospitals, we further expanded our recruitment site to Kwong Wah Hospital (by inviting Dr Helen Yip) and posted our recruitment advertisement through different social medias. However, the recruitment rate remained very challenging. Given that our project had exceeded the maximum project period, we had to stop our recruitment in June 2022 and completed all data collection in Nov 2022. Due to the unprecedented events (social unrest and pandemic in the past 3.5 years), the work had been slowed down substantially and interrupted many times. Months have been wasted and we were not able to complete the experiment on progress. We managed to collect all the data in Nov 2022 and completed the data analyses recently. Two manuscripts (one for each experiment) are in preparation. We plan to publish our manuscripts within the next six months. We would be grateful if the review committee of GRF would kindly consider assessing the project in light of all the experimental hurdles and unexpected happenings.

15102717.label: Major findings and research outcome
15102717.value: In our first project, 36 adults with Parkinson’s Disease (PD) aged from 40 to 70 year-old and 23 age-matched healthy controls (HC) who fulfilled our criteria were recruited. In general, patients with PD exhibited impaired oculomotor behaviors in different extents. In fixational eye movements (EM), PD patients made significantly more fixations along the vertical than the horizontal meridian. However, this discrepancy became insignificant when an overall fixation area in terms of bivariate contour ellipse area was compared (p=0.09). This implied that only mild deficits of fixational EMs were exhibited in the PD (ref #1). In saccadic EMs, PD patients had significantly reduced saccadic gain in the prosaccade (15.7%, p<0.01), anti-saccade (38.3%, p=0.001) and self-paced saccade tasks (10.2%, p<0.001). They showed more hypometric primary saccades, indicating that additional saccades and effort were required in executing reflexive, anti-reflexive and repetitive EMs. This implied that PD patients had no deficits to initiate a saccade, but underestimated the range of required EM for accurate positioning onto the new target (ref #1). In pursuit EMs, PD patients had significantly smaller pursuit gain (i.e. eyes moved slower than the target, p=0.01). Pursuit gains decreased exponentially when the target’s moving speeds increased (p<0.001). Compared with the fast-moving targets, pursuit gains for tracking slow-moving targets were significantly better. Despite compromised smooth pursuit EMs in the PD patients, the average difference of pursuit gain was only 6% (ref #2). In vergence EMs, PD patients had significantly poorer binocular functions. In smooth vergence, PD patients required targets positioned much further away to maintain their binocularity (34.1%, p=0.037, ref #3). In jump vergence, PD patients could only complete 36.5% of presented trials compared with 62.8% in the HC (p=0.04). This implied significant deficits in vergence EMs in PD. In our second project, 25 adults with PD who fulfilled our criteria were recruited and randomly assigned to either intervention (n=13) or placebo group (n=12). Vergence EMs improved after receiving the office-and-home intervention, but the improvement did not reach statistical significance (p=0.08). In smooth vergence, their near point of convergence improved by 12% to 16% when tracking a target moving at different speeds towards them. In contrast, no significant training effect was found in the saccadic EMs. A larger scale clinical trial would be warranted to confirm the effectiveness of this training paradigm and explore the transfer effect to daily functional performances such as visual search or eye-hand coordination tasks.

15102717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15102717.value: Emerging evidence has demonstrated the remarkable neuroplasticity of adult brain, allowing us to learn and adapt to our environment throughout the lifespan. Recent studies have revealed the potential therapeutic effect of non-invasive brain stimulation on vision enhancement including eye movements. For example, our recent finding revealed improved reading performance after receiving 20 mins transcranial direct current electrical stimulation (tDCS) at visual cortex (Silva et al. 2022). Similar strategy can also apply to improve oculomotor functions in PD patients, by receiving 20-30 mins tDCS at frontal eye field (a cortical area for controlling eye movements) before receiving oculomotor training. We hypothesize that this combined intervention will provide optimal therapeutic effect. Eye movement analysis was very tedious and time-consuming, remarkably limiting its clinical application. During our data analysis, it was not surprising that most eye data were quite noisy because of the compromised eye movements in patients. After discussing with collaborators from data science, we are establishing different machine learning models to analyze the pursuit eye movements. We aim to develop an algorithm for more automated analysis of eye movement and provide reliable indicators to identify patients with eye movement deficits.

15102717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15102717.value: Parkinson’s Disease is a common age-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by both motor and non-motor symptoms. Eye movement deficits and visual changes in PD may result in functional impairment. Our findings confirmed that PD patients had remarkable deficits to track or fixate at a target approaching them at close distance. This kind of eye movement problem may exacerbate the effects of motor deficits of PD on patients’ ability to carry out activities of daily living which require manipulation of objects close to them. Further, we found PD patients having mild to moderate impairment in pursuit and saccadic eye movements, which might hinder their ability to track a moving object or fixate a suddenly presented object. To address PD patients’ eye movement issues, they were randomly assigned to either an intervention (receiving oculomotor training) or a placebo group (receiving leisure activities). Results from our pilot randomized clinical trial revealed some improvement in the vergence eye movement after receiving intervention, although it remained statistically non-significant. A larger scale clinical trial will be warranted to confirm the effectiveness of this training paradigm and explore the transfer effect to daily functional performances such as visual search or eye-hand coordination tasks.

15103217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15103217.value: 視網膜感光細胞進行性功能障礙和死亡是視網膜變性疾病，如視網膜色素變性（RP）的主要病因 。 RP是由各種基因突變引發的，但是感光細胞死亡的分子機制尚不清楚。目前，RP在臨床上是無法治療的。我們的研究小組以及世界其他研究小組過去的研究表明， 神經炎症在RP發展進展中起關鍵作用。然而，神經炎症的誘發機制目前仍然不清楚。 以前的研究已表明，小膠質細胞中的轉化生長因子-β激活酶1（TAK1）在中樞神經系統的自身免疫性炎症的發病機制中起著關鍵作用。不過，TAK1在調節RP神經炎症反應以及感光細胞凋亡方面的作用仍然不明。為了研究TAK1在RP中的作用，我們將首先採用TAK1抑製劑治療RP的小鼠模型rd10。其後，我們將敲除rd10小鼠中小膠質細胞裡的TAK1基因。所得小鼠將用於研究小膠質細胞內源性TAK1對RP中神經炎症發展的特異性貢獻， 了解TAK1缺失是否會抑制小膠質細胞介導的炎症反應，同時提高視網膜感光細胞成活率。 本研究將有助於了解TAK1對RP疾病發展的影響，並探討在臨床建立利用抑製TAK1來治療視網膜色素變性的患者可能性。

15103217.label: Realisation of objectives
15103217.value: For objective #1, we examined TAK1 cellular expression pattern and protein expressions of TAK1 and its downstream targets including phospho-JNK, IL-1β, TNF-α, phospho-NF-BP65, and phospho-ERK1/2 in the rd10 mouse model of RP by using western blot, RT-qPCR and immunofluorescent staining. We found that TAK1 was especially expressed in activated microglia, which migrated to the outer nuclear layer, where the degenerating photoreceptors resided. Similarly, we observed that upregulation of TAK1 at both RNA and protein levels in the rd10 retina. These findings indicate the potential involvement of TAK1 in regulating microglia activation in the rd10 retina. For objective #2, we investigated the potential involvement of TAK1 in regulating microglia activation in the rd10 retina. To this end, we treated rd10 mice with 5Z-7-oxozeaenol, a TAK1-specific inhibitor, and investigated the impact of TAK1 inhibition on inflammation and photoreceptor apoptosis in the rd10 retina using immunocytochemistry and confocal microscopy and ELISA analysis. After 5Z-7-oxozeaenol treatment, we observed downregulation of inflammatory responses in rd10 retina, and suppression of TAK1-mediated neuroinflammation resulted in the preservation of retinal morphology and function using immunocytochemistry and confocal microscopy, electroretinograms and optokinetic tracking. Meanwhile, we used flow cytometry and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to purify primary microglial cells from CX3CR1+/GFP/rd10 treated with or without 5Z-7-oxozeaenol, and verify TAK1 expression changes in sorted microglial cells by qPCR. Indeed, qPCR analysis confirmed downregulation of TAK1transcripts in the microglia of CX3CR1+/GFP/rd10 mouse retinas treated with 5Z-7-oxozeaenol relative to those in CX3CR1+/GFP/rd10 control mouse retinas. Similarly, we found that transcripts for both IL-1β and TNF-α in sorted primary microglial cells were downregulated in the rd10 retina after 5Z-7-oxozeaenol treatment, confirming the inhibition of inflammatory responses in microglial cells after the drug treatment. Taken together, our results confirmed that TAK1 was a key regulator in pro-inflammatory cytokine-driven signaling pathways in RP. For objective #3, we generated a new line of CX3CR1CreER/+/rd10/TAK1fl/fl mice by backcrossing CX3CR1CreER/+ with TAK1fl/fl and with rd10 mice for more than 9 generations and investigated the effect of microglia-specific TAK1 deletion on inflammatory cytokine production and photoreceptor morphology and function in the resulting mice. Immunocytochemistry, confocal microscopy and animal behavioral tests demonstrated that microglia-specific TAK1 was involved in regulating inflammatory responses, which contributed to photoreceptor degeneration in rd10 mouse retinas. We found that conditional deletion of microglia-specific TAK1 results in a reduction in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and subsequent decreased photoreceptor apoptosis in the rd10 retina. Together, our results confirmed that microglia-specific TAK1 plays a major role in modulating inflammatory response in RP. For objective #4, we investigated the mechanisms of TAK1 activation in rd10 mice. To this end, we applied a data-independent acquisition-based mass spectrometry (SWATH-MS) -based proteomics and bioinformatics analysis. We revealed a total of 115 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) (47 upregulated and 68 downregulated) in the retina between rd10 mice and rd10 :Cx3cr1CreER/+ :TAK1fl/fl mice treated with tamoxifen (TAM). After performing gene ontology (GO) terms based on biological process (BP), cell component (CC) and molecular function (MF) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis, we identified calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), LIM kinase 2 (Limk2) and transcription factor specificity proteins 2 (SP2) as the top significantly enriched proteins among the DEPs. We then validated CaMKII expression in the rd10 retina by qPCR and western blot analysis. We found that the both mRNA and protein expression levels of CaMKII were elevated in the rd10 retina relative to rd10 mice and CX3CR1CreER/+/TAK1fl/fl/rd10 mice treated with TAM. To confirm the role of CaMKII, we treated rd10 mice with either the CaMKII-specific inhibitor KN93 or CaMKII-specific siRNA via intravitreal injection. We found that CaMKII inhibition or knockdown inhibited microglia activation and preserved photoreceptor morphology and retinal function using immunocytochemistry and confocal microscopy, electroretinograms and optokinetic tracking. Our data suggest that CaMKII is a critical downstream effector of TAK1-mediated neurotoxicity in rd10 mice. Unexpectedly, we found that TAK1-deficiency resulted in microglia cell death in the retina of both rd10 mice and wild type mice, suggesting that microglia cell death was induced by TAK1-deficiency. However, our finding is contradictory to previous observation that TAK1-deficiency does not cause microglial cell death in the central nervous system (CNS) including brainstem and spinal cord. Consistently, we did not observe any microglial cell death in the brainstem of rd10 mice after microglia-specific TAK1 deletion. Taken together, we demonstrated that TAK1 is potentially required for microglial survival in the retina. To understand underlying microglial cell death in the retina, we performed in vitro experiments. We found that receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) and caspase 3 were upregulated in BV2 cells, a microglia cell line, after TAK1 blockage by drug manipulation. Conversely, RIPK1 blockage by using Necrostatin-1, a specific small molecule inhibitor of RIPK1, showed a rescue effect on BV2 microglia after TAK1 blockage. Our data confirm that RIPK1’s upregulation contributed to BV2 microglia apoptosis after TAK1 blockage.

15103217.label: Major findings and research outcome
15103217.value: In this project, we investigated the role of TAK1 in microglia during photoreceptor degeneration in rd10 mice model of human retinitis pigmentosa. We found that TAK1 was upregulated in the retina of rd10 mice and TAK1 was especially expressed by activated microglia, which migrated to the outer nuclear layer where the degenerating photoreceptors resided. We found that pharmacological inhibition of TAK1 by 5Z-7-oxozeaenol and specific genetic ablation of TAK1 in microglia alleviated neuroinflammation and subsequently preserved retinal photoreceptor and function and visual performance in rd10 mice. By using data-independent acquisition-based mass spectrometry (SWATH-MS)-based proteomics and bioinformatics analysis, we identified calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) as the top upregulated protein. We then validated that both mRNA and protein expression levels of CaMKII were elevated in the rd10 retina. Moreover, we found that CaMKII inhibition or knockdown inhibited microglia activation and preserved photoreceptor morphology and retinal function. Our data suggest that CaMKII is a critical regulator of TAK1-mediated neurotoxicity in rd10 mice. Furthermore, we found that TAK1-deficiency resulted in microglia cell death in the retina of both rd10 mice and wild type mice, which is contradictory to previous observation that TAK1-deficiency does not cause microglial cell death in the central nervous system (CNS). Consistently, we did not observe any microglial cell death in the brainstem of rd10 mice after microglia-specific TAK1 deletion. Taken together, we demonstrated that TAK1 is potentially required for microglial survival in the retina. To explore underlying microglial cell death in the retina, we performed in vitro experiments. We found that receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) and caspase 3 were upregulated in BV2 cells, a microglia cell line, after TAK1 blockage by drug manipulation. Conversely, RIPK1 blockage by using Necrostatin-1, a specific small molecule inhibitor of RIPK1, showed a rescue effect on BV2 microglia after TAK1 blockage. Our data confirm that RIPK1’s upregulation contributed to BV2 microglia apoptosis after TAK1 blockage. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that TAK1 supports microglia survival in the retina and that TAK1’s upregulation in microglia contributes to the activation of microglia and subsequently contributes to neuroinflammation and photoreceptor degeneration in rd10 mice retina. Our study provides evidence that TAK1 could be a potential target for RP treatment.

15103217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15103217.value: To our surprise, we observed that TAK1-deficiency resulted in microglia cell death in the rd10 retina. We found that more than 90% of microglia were ablated at P25 rd10 mouse retina 15 days after TAM administration. Meanwhile, we found that microglia remained intact in the hippocampus and visual cortex of P25 rd10 mice 15 days after TAM administration. We will continue to investigate the mechanisms underlying the differential effects of TAK1 on microglia in the retina and hippocampus of rd10 mice through single-cell RNA sequencing, SWATH-MS-based proteomics and bioinformatics analysis.

15103217.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15103217.value: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) is a group of inherited retinal degeneration diseases, which can cause gradual death of photoreceptors. Although various genetic mutations have been identified in RP patients, the mechanisms underlying photoreceptor death are not yet well known, and RP is currently untreatable. Transforming growth factor-β-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) is reported to be involved in regulating proinflammatory responses. However, the essential function of TAK1 in RP remains unknown. We found that that TAK1 was upregulated in the retina of rd10 mice and TAK1 was especially expressed by activated microglia. We found that TAK1 inhibition or deletion reduced neuroinflammation and preserved retinal photoreceptor and function and visual performance in rd10 mice. Moreover, we identified calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) as the top upregulated protein, and CaMKII inhibition or knockdown inhibited microglia activation and preserved photoreceptor morphology and retinal function. Our data suggest that CaMKII is a critical regulator of TAK1-mediated neurotoxicity in rd10 mice. In summary, we demonstrate the involvement of TAK1 in RP progression. Our study provides evidence for establishing the translational potential of TAK1 inhibition for treating the patients who suffer from retinal degeneration.

15103617.label: Project Objectives
15103617.value: The objective of this study is to increase our scientific understanding of the effects and mechanisms of rTMS on gait performance in individuals with PD. To address this objective, we propose the following three aims: To determine if 1Hz and 25Hz rTMS are more effective than sham TMS in augmenting treadmill training on gait performance in individuals with PD at 1 month and 3 months after treatment. To determine if any improvement in the gait performance produced by active rTMS treatment is mediated by a normalization in corticomotor excitability. To explore the relative efficacy of 1Hz and 25Hz rTMS on augmenting treadmill training on long-term gait performance in people with PD. To address these aims, we propose to test the following specific two specific hypotheses and perform one exploratory analysis: Hypothesis 1: Participants who receive treadmill training preceded by either 1Hz and 25Hz rTMS will demonstrate more improvements in gait performance at 1 month and 3 months after treatment than participants who receive treadmill training alone. Hypothesis 2: The improvements in the gait performance found in participants who receive 1Hz and 25Hz rTMS will be mediated by a normalization in intracortical inhibition and cortico-motor excitation Exploratory analyses: We will also compare the benefits in gait performance between those who receive 1Hz and 25Hz stimulation to determine if these two interventions result in differences in improvement in gait performance. Sixty individuals with PD will be recruited and randomly allocated into one of the 3 groups: 1Hz, 25Hz and sham. Each subject will receive rTMS followed by treadmill training for 12 sessions in 3 weeks. Outcome measures will include spatio-temporal gait characteristics (i.e., self-selected and fastest gait speed) and neurophysiological changes (i.e., corticomotor excitability and intracortical inhibition). To address the first and third objectives, the effects of combined rTMS and treadmill training will be compared among the 3 subject groups at post-treatment, 1-month and 3-month follow-ups after treatment completion. To address the second objective, there will be regression analysis between the spatio-temporal gait characteristics, cortico-motor excitability and intracortical inhibition.

15103617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15103617.value: Gait disorder is one of the most incapacitating symptoms of Parkinson’s disease (PD) that leads to loss of independence and quality of life. Treadmill training has been found to be effective in enhancing walking performance in PD patients [1,2]. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non-invasive brain stimulation that has also been shown to have therapeutic benefits in patients with PD. High-frequency rTMS (5Hz-25Hz) has been found to up-regulate corticomotor activity while low-frequency (≤1Hz) rTMS down-regulate the corticomotor activity [3,4]. Yang et al. [5] reported that combined high-frequency rTMS and treadmill training was more effective than treadmill training alone in enhancing walking performance immediately post-training in patients with PD. Although this preliminary finding is promising, the long-term beneficial effects of treadmill training with rTMS versus treadmill training alone is not known, and the mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects of this approach is limited. Neurophysiological research has found that PD individuals have inadequate facilitation of the direct cortico-striatal-cortical pathway and/or inadequate inhibition of the indirect cortico-striatal-cortical pathway, leading to reduced cortical output and impaired movement execution [6]. One way to boost motor learning is to transiently increase the cortical excitability, e.g., by high-frequency rTMS precedes the training [7]. Paradoxically, low-frequency rTMS may also lead to better motor learning, either by restoring inhibitory control or priming the brain for improved learning through homeostatic principles [8]. To address the knowledge gaps, the present study aims to examine the long-term benefits of combined rTMS-treadmill training and increase our understanding of the mechanisms that enhance motor learning and neuroplastic changes with this treatment. Sixty individuals with PD will be randomly allocated into one of 3 groups: low-frequency of 1Hz, high-frequency of 25Hz and sham rTMS. All subjects will receive treadmill training four times per week for 3 weeks. Outcome measures will include spatio-temporal gait characteristics and electrophysiological changes, i.e., corticomotor excitation and intracortical inhibition. If combined 25Hz rTMS-treadmill training produces more beneficial effects on gait, then we can conclude that motor learning facilitated by an increase in the motor cortical excitation. On the other hand, if combined 1Hz rTMS-Treadmill training produces more long-term improvements in behavioural and electrophysiological outcomes than the other training groups, then inhibition of cortical activity is beneficial for subsequent motor learning. Findings from the present study will provide scientific evidence that underpin the appropriate rTMS stimulation protocol that can maximize motor learning and practice-dependent plasticity in PD patients 眾所周知，柏金遜患者會出現行走困難，從而導致功能受限並降低生活質量。已有研究發現用重複經顱磁刺激與跑步機步行訓練一起可改善柏金遜患者的步行能力及大腦的興奮度。然而，為了能夠優化治療方法，需要更多地瞭解其改善效果的生理機制。此研究是為了探索重複經顱磁刺激與跑步機步行訓練聯合治療後的柏金遜患者的運動學習及神經可塑性的改變。對運動學習的機制瞭解可以為柏金遜患者制定出最好的改善步行能力且產生神經可塑性的變化的訓練方法提供科學依據。 參與者將會接受經顱磁刺激適合性刪查, 刪查合格後才能參加此研究. 60名柏金遜參與者將隨機分為3組：低頻1Hz，高頻25Hz和假重複經顱磁刺激。然後在跑步機上進行20-30分鐘的步行訓練。在這個研究中，所有參與者都會接收重複經顱磁刺激和跑步機3週, 每週訓練4次。除了訓練以外，參與者將會參與4 次評估：訓練前，期訓練後，訓練結束後1個月及3個月時。每次評估包括步行能力測試及運動皮層興奮度檢查。研究成果將提供支持適當重複經顱磁刺激的科學證據, 可以最大限度地提高柏金遜患者運動學習和神經可塑性的變化, 為這些患者找出最佳治療方法。

15103617.label: Realisation of objectives
15103617.value: The study has one objective and three aims. All the objective and aims have been fulfilled (100%). The project resulted in a number of conference presentations and one journal publication. After recruitment and screening, sixty participants with Parkinson’s disease (PD) were randomized to receive 12 sessions of rTMS at 25 Hz, 1 Hz or sham followed by treadmill training. All participants were assessed at baseline, post-intervention and three-month post-intervention. The behavioural outcomes included fastest walking speed, timed up-and-go test (TUG), dual-task TUG (DT-TUG), and motor section of the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS-III). The electrophysiological outcomes included cortical silent period and short-interval intracortical inhibition for evaluating cortical excitability. The results showed that the active rTMS were more effective than sham rTMS in augmenting treadmill training in people with PD. The normalization of cortical excitability by rTMS could lead to the motor improvement.

15103617.label: Major findings and research outcome
15103617.value: The findings revealed that 1 Hz and 25 Hz rTMS groups produced a greater improvement in fastest walking speed at one-day and three-month post-intervention than the sham group. Only 1 and 25 Hz rTMS groups sustained the improvements in TUG, and had a significant improvement in DT-TUG and MDS-UPDRS-III for up to three months. Behavioral improvements correlated with increased cortical silent period and short-interval intracortical inhibition in both groups receiving real rTMS. Priming with either 1 Hz or 25 Hz rTMS has similar effect on augmenting the benefits of treadmill training and led to long-term motor improvement up to three-month post-intervention. The motor improvement at follow-up was associated with a normalization of cortical excitability, which in turn suggests rebalancing cortical excitability by rTMS is critical for plasticity induction.

15103617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15103617.value: Future studies could employ structural MRI of the brain and a computational model to give more information about the stimulated site, and to simulate the resulting electrical field in the stimulated brain region for establishing the rTMS dose-response relationship. Additional imaging studies or magnetic resonance spectroscopy may assist in confirming the changes in connectivity in the network and change in neural activity of relevant neurotransmitters. We plan to submit a GRF research grant to assess these theoretical concepts. The priming effect of rTMS on gait training has potential for implementation in clinical settings that offer rehabilitation for PD. We have started to discuss its implication in a few hospitals.

15103617.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15103617.value: Walking difficulty is one of the most incapacitating symptoms of Parkinson’s disease (PD) that leads to loss of independence and quality of life. There is a need to find out new treatment approaches and to explore the possible changes in the brain. This study combined non-invasive brain stimulation, rTMS together with treadmill training and aimed to find out whether priming with rTMS augmented the effect of walking training with treadmill. We further explored whether the changes in functional performance was associated with physiological changes of the brain. Our results showed priming walking training with rTMS was more effective than walking training with treadmill alone on walking performance, functional mobility and PD-specific symptoms. These effects could be maintained up to three-month post-intervention. The motor improvement at follow-up was associated with a normalization of cortical excitability. Rebalancing cortical excitability by rTMS appears critical for long-term plasticity induction.

15103817.label: Realisation of objectives
15103817.value: 1.To functionally characterize the potential tumor-initiating effects and sorafenib resistance of EPHB2 in HCC (100%) a) EPHB2 exhibited upregulated expression in sorafenib-resistant HCC cells In an attempt to identify critical kinases involved in sorafenib resistance, we developed two sorafenib-resistant HCC cell lines from two PDTXs (PDTX#1 and PDTX#5). By RNA-sequencing analysis, EPHB2 was found to be the most significantly upregulated kinase, which was confirmed by Quantitative PCR analysis. Consistently, similar upregulation of EPHB2 expression in sorafenib-resistant Huh7, PLC/PRF/5 and MHCC-97L cells. b) EPHB2 regulates the cancer stemness and drug resistance of HCC cells We performed EPHB2-knockdown and EPHB2-overexpression experiments using lentiviral-based overexpression and knockdown approaches. In a sphere formation assay performed with PLC/PRF/5 or MHCC-97L cells, knockdown of EPHB2 expression significantly reduced the number and size of primary spheres and their second passages. Accordingly, EPHB2 overexpression was shown to enhance the sphere-forming ability of Huh7 cells. Similar findings were observed in limiting dilution assay. In line with this finding, alterations of EPHB2 expression changed tumorigenicity, expression of liver cancer stem cell (CSC) markers including CD47 and CD90, and sensitivity towards doxorubicin or sorafenib treatment. To further confirm the role of EPHB2 knockdown in chemosensitization, we employed lentiviral-based doxycycline-inducible knockdown of EPHB2 expression in PLC/PRF/5 cells. Consistently, inducible suppression of EPHB2 led to sensitization of the PLC/PRF/5 cells to sorafenib treatment. Next, we examined whether EPHB2High HCC populations possess enhanced liver CSC properties by separating MHCC-97L cells into EPHB2High and EPHB2Low populations by a cell sorting approach. We found that EPHB2High HCC cells showed higher CSC properties including sphere formation, tumorigenicity, drug resistance and expression of CSC markers. To further investigate the effect of endogenous knockout of EPHB2 in an immunocompetent mouse model, we have employed hydrodynamic tail vein injection (HTVI) delivery approach using a combination of activated forms of myr-AKT and N-RasV12 proto-oncogenes and SB transposase. Endogenous EPHB2 knockout significantly attenuated the size and number of tumor nodules compared to sgNTC treatment. This finding supports a key role for EPHB2 in promoting HCC growth. C) Intravenous administration of rAAV-8-shEPHB2 sensitized HCC cells to sorafenib treatment in an immunocompetent mouse model We examined the therapeutic targeting of EPHB2 by intravenous injection of rAAV-8-EPHB2 alone or in combination with sorafenib in an NRAS/AKT-induced HCC mouse model. Two weeks after hydrodynamic injection of plasmids encoding the activated forms of NRAS and AKT, we intravenously injected the mice with either rAAV8-shEPHB2 or rAAV8-NTC. After one week, we started to treat the mice with sorafenib at 30 mg/kg for 21 days. We found that rAAV8-shEPHB2/sorafenib produced significantly maximal suppression of tumor growth, indicating that shEPHB2 treatment can synergize with sorafenib treatment and is effective against liver tumors in vivo. 2. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which EPHB2 functionally contributes to tumor initiation, self-renewal, and drug resistance (100%) a) Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is the downstream effect of EPHB2 mediated CSC functions To determine the major downstream effector of EPHB2, we employed RNA-sequencing analysis to compare the gene expression profiles of shEPHB2 and nontarget control (NTC)-transfected cells derived from the PLC/PRF/5 cell line. By gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), we found several pathways to be downregulated, with over 60% of genes related to the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway being significantly altered. A TOP/FOP reporter assay showed that the transactivation activity of β-catenin was suppressed when EPHB2 was repressed, while this activity was elevated in EPHB2-overexpressing cells. Consistent with the results for the transactivation activity of β-catenin, the expression of known downstream targets of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, including Cyclin D1 and CMYC, showed similar trends in response to alterations in EPHB2 expression. Consistently, higher β-catenin transactivation activity was observed in EPHB2High Huh7 cells than in EPHB2Low cells. By immunoprecipitation analysis, we found that EPHB2 physically interacted with SRC. Upon interaction, EPHB2 was able to phosphorylate SRC, as evidenced by the corresponding changes in phosphorylation at Y416 upon suppression or overexpression of EPHB2, which subsequently led to changes in the AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin signaling pathway. b) β-catenin/TCF-1 pathway regulates the expression of EPHB2, forming a Wnt/β-catenin positive feedback loop To examine whether Wnt/β-catenin alterations affect EPHB2 expression, we analyzed the impact of introducing constitutively active β‐catenin (Δ45β‐cat) into Huh7 cells. Upon activation of β‐catenin transactivation activity, we found that both the mRNA and protein levels of EPHB2 were upregulated. To further confirm this finding, we administered Wnt3a-supplemented medium to activate the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and EPHB2 mRNA and protein levels were consistently upregulated. Based on the in vitro observation, we postulated that Wnt/β-catenin transcriptionally activates EPHB2 expression. In silico analysis (PROMO 3.0) identified one putative TCF1 binding site (CTGTTAATGATG) at the position of -1014bp to -1003bp upstream of the TSS of the EPHB2 gene. Upon suppression of TCF1 in EPHB2-knockdown HCC cells, we found that there was a significant decrease in the fold enrichment of TCF1 binding relative to that in NTC cells, suggesting that TCF1 physically binds to and activates the promoter of EPHB2, which forms a Wnt/β-catenin positive feedback loop. 3. To evaluate the clinico-pathological relevance and prognostic significance of EPHB2 expression in human HCC (90%) a) EPHB2 was sporadically expressed in human HCC specimens with clinical significance In an analysis of dataset (GSE25097), EPHB2 expression was significantly upregulated in tumor specimens, with stepwise upregulation from normal to cirrhotic to tumor tissues, suggesting an oncogenic role for EPHB2 in liver carcinogenesis. Similarly, we found stepwise increases in the mRNA expression of EPHB2 from normal to fibrotic to HCC tissues in the STAMTM nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) HCC mouse mode. Interestingly, along with EPHB2 overexpression, a similar stepwise increase in the expression of liver CSC markers, including CD133, CD90 and CD24, was previously reported upon fibrosis and subsequent HCC development. Next, we examined the prognostic significance of EPHB2 expression in HCC patients. The cutoff value of T/N > 6 was used to divide HCC patients according to their EPHB2 expression. Patients with high EPHB2 expression were significantly correlated with poor disease-free survival (p=0.041). b) EPHB2 formed a Wnt/β-catenin positive feedback loop in a cohort of HCC patient samples In a TCGA cohort analysis, Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway was the only pathway that was significantly enriched in HCC patients with high EPHB2 expression. Intriguingly, high EPHB2 expression significantly co‐occurred with beta‐catenin (CTNNB1) driver mutations, which further confirms the role of Wnt/β-catenin in driving EPHB2 expression in HCC clinical samples. Collectively, these data suggest that EPHB2 overexpression may be associated with liver carcinogenesis and sorafenib resistance via regulation of a Wnt/β-catenin positive feedback loop. We have not performed the IHC staining on EPHB2 expression in the tissue microarray of 90 HCCs from patients administrated with sorafenib after resection, as we could not go to Guangzhou to perform this IHC staining due to COVID-19. 15103817.label: Major findings and research outcome
15103817.value: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ranks the 6th most commonly diagnosed cancer with a poor prognosis. The first-line treatments for HCC are liver transplantation and surgical resection. However, most HCCs are inoperable, as patients typically are diagnosed at advanced stages. HCC treatment recently entered a new era with the development of molecular-targeted therapies, as sorafenib improved survival in advanced HCC patients. However, the survival benefit of sorafenib is modest, with median survival times 2.8 and 2.3 months longer than those of the placebo arm found in two large-scale trials. Therefore, studies on the mechanism underlying sorafenib resistance are urgently needed. Targeting cancer stem cells (CSC) is a possible way to reverse drug resistance; however, inhibitors that specifically target liver CSCs are limited. In this study, we established two sorafenib-resistant, patient-derived tumor xenografts (PDX) that mimicked development of acquired resistance to sorafenib in HCC patients. RNA-sequencing analysis of sorafenib-resistant PDXs and their corresponding mock controls identified EPHB2 as the most significantly upregulated kinase. EPHB2 expression increased stepwise from normal liver tissue to fibrotic liver tissue to HCC tissue and correlated with poor prognosis. Endogenous EPHB2 knockout showed attenuation of tumor development in mice. EPHB2 regulated the traits of liver CSCs; similarly, sorted EPHB2High HCC cells were endowed with enhanced CSC properties when compared with their EPHB2Low counterparts. Mechanistically, EPHB2 regulated cancer stemness and drug resistance by driving the SRC/AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin signaling cascade, and EPHB2 expression was regulated by TCF1 via promoter activation, forming a positive Wnt/β-catenin feedback loop. Intravenous administration of rAAV-8-shEPHB2 suppressed HCC tumor growth and significantly sensitized HCC cells to sorafenib in an NRAS/AKT-driven HCC immunocompetent mouse model. Our findings are scientifically important and clinically relevant and will definitely appeal to the readership in different scientific research field. Our finding will convey several important messages to the readers: (1) EPHB2 mRNA and protein levels is strikingly increased during liver carcinogenesis and correlated with aggressive tumor phenotypes and patients’ survival; (2) EPHB2 plays a crucial role in regulation of liver CSCs and sorafenib resistance; (3) identifies a EPHB2/β-catenin/TCF1 positive feedback loop that augments cancer stemness and sorafenib resistance in HCC. Our data suggest that targeting a positive feedback loop involving the EPHB2/β-catenin axis may be an attractive therapeutic target for HCC.

15103817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15103817.value: Thus far, there is no EPHB2 inhibitor which is commercially available for research purpose. Based on the 3D crystal structure of EPHB2 and is catalytic domain, I am currently collaborating with Dr. Ma Cong (ABCT, PolyU) and synthesized several EPHB2 specific inhibitors with the similar potency as dasatinib, the FDA approved Src inhibitor (P0035357, Project of Strategic Importance, PolyU). We have synthesized different peptides which potentially target the ATP binding pocket of EPHB2. Our pilot study showed that two compounds (KM07489 and JFD0218) are potent to suppress the growth of HCC cells, accompanied with the decrease in ATP activity of EPHB2. Based on this encouraging data, we will further modify the structure of compounds. amine its biological effect on suppression of liver CSCs using various in vitro CSC assays, and ultimately explore the therapeutic potential of EPHB2 inhibitor in vivo. Ultimately, we would like to synthesize the novel EPHB2 inhibitor with high specificity and hope to translate the results generated in this grant proposal.

15103817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15103817.value: Liver cancer (HCC) is the fifth most common cancer worldwide. The 5 year-survival for this disease is not satisfactory due to tumor relapse and refractory to the current targeted therapy including sorafenib. Therefore, it is of great importance to identify the factors leading to these tumor behaviors. Recently, cancer stem cells (CSCs) is regarded as the root of tumor relapse and therapeutic resistance. Thus, targeting these cells may be a novel therapeutic strategy against HCC. In the current proposal, findings presented in this study not only provide evidence to show the clinical relevance of and functional role of nuclear factor EPH Receptor B2 (EPHB2) in liver cancer but also demonstrated its pivotal role and mechanistic action in regulation of liver CSCs and resistance to sorafenib treatment. Specifically, EPHB2 regulates the liver CSCs and drug resistance by directly turning on Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway, a well-known pathway in stem cells. Targeting this signaling pathway may be a promising approach for cancer treatment.
