17613417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17613417.value: The last decade has seen the gradual incorporation of the concept of cultural security into the national security discourses of both China and Saudi Arabia. It has emerged as a constitutive non-traditional element of how these non-Western authoritarian polities understand their comprehensive national security and is increasingly deployed in many spheres of concern to the state. The concept of cultural security can be understood to refer to the state’s attempt to insulate society against a broad range of ideational influences or threats of an ideological, value-based, and/or cultural nature. Of particular interest to this study are those influences or threats that the state has deemed to carry negative political consequences if left unchecked, including those that risk undermining the legitimacy of the prevailing order by altering or eroding dominant societal values, weakening national cohesion, or harming the image of the regime through the spread of presumably foreign and/or problematic lifestyles and behavior antithetical to the moral order implicit in its mandate to rule. These threats are ambivalently depicted as being either generated by natural processes of globalization or as part of a wider strategy of destabilization and/or “regime-change” pursued by outside actors via the dissemination of political/religious propaganda or, alternatively, through cultural imperialism exploiting globalization as such. The Chinese and Saudi discourses and the state practices of cultural security of the past two decades’ exhibit differences in their points of emphasis and even in the manner in which the outcome of said threats are articulated. Notwithstanding these differences however, the past few years have seen a relative convergence in how cultural security is conceptualized and practiced in China and Saudi Arabia, with similar threats being identified and responded to. This study has three major objectives. First, it aims to explore the discourse of cultural security with an eye towards explaining its emergence, evolution, as well as its near simultaneous adoption by these wholly dissimilar politically and culturally non-Western authoritarian regimes. Second, through a comparative lens, this project seeks to understand how a state goes about “practicing” cultural security. Third, this project attempts to reconsider existing regime typologies and offer an explanation as to why China, a Leninist-Marxist party-state and Saudi Arabia, a dynastic monarchy are perceiving similar threats and responding to them in comparable ways. 過去十幾年間，在中國和沙特阿拉伯的政治話語中，文化安全逐漸成為一個重要概念。文化安全逐漸成為非西方威權主義政體綜合國家安全觀的關鍵組成部分，也在諸多領域成為國家政治日常實踐的核心環節。本研究著眼於該等政權防範被國家視作有可能產生負面政治後果的文化威脅的實踐：這些威脅往往包括不同內外力量通過散播外國生活方式和有悖於制度內涵的道德規訓的行為準則以侵蝕社會價值觀、顛覆政權合法性、削弱國家凝聚力或醜化制度形象，等等。 在國家政治實踐中，上述文化威脅有時被描述成全球化過程中的自然產物，而有時則被歸結為境外勢力通過政治、宗教宣傳或文化帝國主義來顛覆既有政權的政治圖謀。在過去二十年間，中國和沙特阿拉伯兩國關於文化安全的話語和行為在關註的重點以及應對威脅的方式等很多方面存在差異；然而，近年來，隨著兩國所面臨的文化威脅的變得日漸相似，兩國政府在理解和處理文化安全問題的方式也開始逐漸靠攏。 本研究主要有三個目標：第一，研究文化安全話語的產生及流變，進而比較中國和沙特阿拉伯兩國政府文化安全戰略的異同。第二，通過比較視角來理解不同類型的政治國家如何運作文化安全戰略。第三，通過反思現存制度主義理論文獻，解釋形成中國和沙特阿拉伯在文化安全戰略上不同政治實踐的導因。

17613417.label: Realisation of objectives
17613417.value: The research project has successfully and completely achieved its three proposed objectives in the form of a series of edited volume, book chapter, journal articles and manuscripts under review. The research project charted out the genealogies of cultural security discourses among epistemic and academic communities in China and Saudi Arabia, explained their evolution in light of changing domestic and international trends relevant to each country, and analysed the dynamics underlying the state’s adoption of this discourse. It also shed light on how states practice cultural security through a number of case studies, which showcased the multiple types of cultural security threats confronting such regimes as a result of their legitimacy matrixes, the coherence and common logic of regime responses across these disparate case studies, and the contradictory pressures facing such regimes in both protecting regime legitimacy on the one hand and upholding their modernisation projects in the other. The research project has successfully explained how the conceptualisation and practice of cultural security in these two states emanates as a response to the dialogic interaction between the regime types of China and Saudi Arabia and the international conditions they face. In “Guarding Against the Threat of a Westernising Education: A Comparative Study of Chinese and Saudi Cultural Security Discourses and Practices towards Overseas Study” (co-authored by Yan Xiaojun and Mohammed Al-Sudairi, forthcoming in Journal of Contemporary China), the authors traced the genealogy of cultural security in China and Saudi Arabia. It reveals that cultural security has become a major watchword in the national security discourses of both the People’s Republic of China and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Within this discourse, overseas study has been imagined as a conduit for cultural and ideological subversion threatening the authority of the prevailing regimes. At the same time, overseas study has been actively encouraged by both the Chinese and Saudi states as an important element in their modernization projects. In the past two decades, the Chinese and Saudi overseas student populations have been some of the largest in the world—which indeed caused concerns of increasing western influence in domestic socio-political spheres. The article explored these tensions by examining the conceptualisation and practice of cultural security in China and Saudi Arabia through their management of overseas study. The volume Ruling by Other Means: State-Mobilised Movements (co-edited by Elizabeth J. Perry and Grzegorz Ekiert and Yan Xiaojun, published by Cambridge University Press), provided a plethora of cases to understand how states practice cultural security, and how cultural security is related to the security of the regime in general. Particularly, this volume studies the state’s mobilisation and (often covert) mobilisation of collective actions and social movements to advance state interests. It offers a comparative perspective on the state’s mobilisation of cultural and symbolic resources to protect regime legitimacy on the one hand and uphold their political goals on the other. The book chapter “Suppressing Students in the People’s Republic of China: Proletarian State-Mobilized Movements in 1968 and 1989” (co-authored by Elizabeth J. Perry and Yan Xiaojun in Ruling by Other Means) further zoomed in to the Chinese state’s mobilisation of social forces to defend its legitimacy and security. Instead of resorting to military or police force, the Chinese state deployed cultural and symbolic means for the mass mobilisation of pro-state collective actions based on the working proletariat. Unlike repression by the police or military, proletarian action has the advantage of political correctness. Relying on squadrons of workers to neutralize other social forces also promises more pragmatic advantages, especially when the social movement in question is composed largely of students. In responding to contention on the part of idealistic students, whose movements typically generate widespread sympathy among urban residents, intervention by unarmed workers is less apt to alienate the populace than naked military suppression. The PRC has tapped the proletariat for crucial support at several critical junctures in its tumultuous history. Demobilizing student Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution and demobilizing student democracy activists in the Tiananmen Uprising both involved state sponsorship of large-scale proletarian countermovements. Although previous scholarship on these suppression efforts has focused on the Chinese state’s bold deployment of the People’s Liberation Army, in both cases proletarian state-mobilised movements played a key role in the battle to win over public opinion and to secure the regime through cultural means. The manuscript “Greasing the Wheels of Abrupt Political Reversal: Discursive Engineering and Public Opinion Management in the Relaxation of China’s Family Planning Policy” (by Yan Xiaojun and Li La, under review) provides another case study of how the Chinese state uses propaganda and political discourses to manipulate public opinion at the high time of neck-breaking policy turn. It showcases how the state legitimises its policy choice and maintain regime stability through flexible and strategical deployment of symbolic and propagandistic means. The research article “Is the Chinese ‘Entrepreneurial Welfare State’ an Industrial Policy in Disguise” (co-authored by Yan Xiaojun, Chen Hanyu and Li La on Third World Quarterly) further highlighted the discursive power of the state in securing its legitimacy and achieving its political goals. Drew on extensive field research in a prefecture-level district in southwest China, the authors argue that local governments in China provide welfare housing programmes as a veil for developmentalist industrial policies aimed at industrial upgrading and the improvement of dynamic efficiency. In this way, the state manoeuvres the symbolic discourse of social welfare to justify its own developmental goals whilst preventing grievances against social inequality. The manuscript “Propaganda beyond State Borders: The Deployment of Symbolic Resources to Mobilize Political Support Among the Chinese Diaspora” (by Yan Xiaojun and Li La, under review), reveals that the Chinese party-state engages its diasporic populations residing overseas and courting for their economic, political and ideological support with external propaganda. It argues that the Chinese state extended its reach beyond the territorial boundaries with the help of cultural and symbolic forces. Extra-territorial propaganda helps autocratic regimes to amass integrative capacity by dispersing carefully tailored discourses, sanctioning opposing voices, promoting a unified interpretive framework for conceptualizing socio-political reality, forming a standard meaning system for diasporic communities, coordinating collective action, and forging an integrated patriotic identity through the repetition of codified communications. This type of extra-territorial state project aims to construct a stable, exclusive, and institutionalized diasporic network of influence within host societies. It shows that cultural security takes not only a defensive and domestic pathway, but also permeating and out-reaching manner.

17613417.label: Major findings and research outcome
17613417.value: This research project traced the origin and evolution of cultural security discourse in China and Saudi Arabia in both domestic and international arenas. It also reaches beyond the two authoritarian countries and extended the investigation of the concept and practice of cultural security with a broader comparative lens by conducting case studies from other—authoritarian and democratic—countries in the world. It reveals how the states, through dogged defence and deft deployment of their cultural, symbolic and ideological values, securitised legitimacy and stability, meanwhile advanced their political goals. The research further discovers that the practice and pursuit of cultural security is not only domestically relevant, but also internationally conditioned. In other words, the securitisation of domestic cultural security is to a large extent influenced by the transnational political forces such as diaspora, overseas students, and foreign relations. The research project yielded a range of deliverables, including edited volume, book chapter, journal articles and manuscripts under review. (see Part C)

17613417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17613417.value: The research could be further developed in three fronts. First, upon the clarification of the genealogy of cultural security, future research could further investigate the relations between cultural security and other aspects of national securities, so as to yield a more systematic and holistic understanding of political security in general. Second, the study of China and Saudi Arabia on cultural security could be further compared with democratic regimes so as to construct a valid general theory. Our edited volume Ruling by Other Means paved the way for this exploration, whereby further explorations could be extended. Third, as our manuscript under review “Propaganda State beyond Borders” indicates, the securitisation of culture is not only defensive. It could also take a proactive and outreaching path by courting support from diaspora, forming overseas alliances, and engaging in external propaganda. This connection between culture security and transnational propaganda (often conceptualised as “sharp power”) is to be further probed.

17613417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17613417.value: This research project studies how countries protect and defend their culture, ideology and value from the infiltration of that of the foreign countries. This is called “cultural security”. This research project traces the origin and development of the concept of “cultural security” in China and Saudi Arabia with a comparative perspective. It demonstrates through case studies how the countries maintained their cultural and ideological value, and used these values to justify their ruling, secure social and political stability, and achieve their political goals. The research project also reveals that the cultural security of a country is very much subject to the international context, particularly how well the countries deal with the overseas populations. This research is very significant because it broadens our understanding of national security and introduced the dimension of culture as a crucial factor of political stability.

17614217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17614217.value: The proposed project aims to investigate risk communication vis-à-vis uncertainty management and decision-making in genetic counselling for inherited conditions that may occur within an individual’s lifespan (namely, in prenatal, postnatal, adolescent and adult stages of one’s life). The notion of risk of occurrence of a genetic condition at the individual level is extended to consider the family perspective as there are risks associated with i) the process of genetic testing which invariably involves other family members, and ii) disclosure of genetic test results to at-risk family members. Interpersonal and sociocultural issues assume significance in how risk is communicated and perceived as a basis for decision-making. Since the same clients and family members attend more than one consultation, our interest lies in how professionals include family members in the testing process and whether (and how) the clients’ and the family members’ understanding of risk changes over the course of the consultations. The project consolidates the team’s previous work in Hong Kong with regard to prenatal (Down’s syndrome) and postnatal (G6PD deficiency) genetic counselling, and examines a novel context for adolescent and adult genetic counselling for Sudden Arrhythmia Death Syndrome (SADS). SADS includes genetic cardiovascular conditions that may cause death in young and seemingly healthy people. While over the last decade risk communication-oriented research has been undertaken, especially in the UK, the USA and also in Hong Kong, the nature and scope of risk communication in SADS have not been studied empirically. To investigate risk communication, the project proposes an innovative research design that: (a) integrates the insights from a range of disciplines; (b) draws on a large corpus of primary data of real-life genetic counselling consultations supplemented by interviews and focus groups with clients and family members; (c) employs a theme-oriented discourse analytic framework (Roberts and Sarangi, 2005); and (d) examines the interpersonal and sociocultural dimensions of risk perceptions. In addition to analysing the SADS dataset of 50 video-recorded consultations, meta-analysis will be undertaken of previously gathered data corpora concerning Down’s syndrome and G6PD deficiency to draw general conclusions about genetic risk communication, and about counselling diverse client populations. The meta-analysis will focus on the communication strategies that facilitate decision-making in the face of uncertainties and risks. The findings will be directly translatable to everyday clinical practice and public understanding of genetic risk inheritance. The project will add to the emerging healthcare communication practice and policy in South East Asia. 本項目旨在研究遺傳諮詢中風險溝通與不確定性管理及决策的互動機制。遺傳諮詢針對可能在個人生命周期內（即産前、産後、青少年和成年階段）發生的遺傳疾病。鑒于以下兩類風險的存在，基于對家庭視角的考量，我們擴展個體層面的遺傳疾病風險。這兩類風險爲：1）與家庭成員遺傳檢測相關的風險，2）將測試結果透漏給家庭成員的風險。在决策過程中，人際和社會文化因素在風險溝通和理解方面具有重要意義。由于同樣的病人及其家庭成員參加多次遺傳諮詢，我們的關注點在于醫務人員如何將家庭成員納入測試過程，以及病人和家庭成員對風險的理解在諮詢過程中是否（以及如何）發生變化。 該項目鞏固團隊已在香港完成的産前（唐氏綜合征）和産後（G6PD缺乏症）遺傳諮詢研究，幷探索遺傳諮詢新情境，即針對青少年和成人的突發性心律失常死亡綜合征（SADS）。 SADS包括可能導致青年人和表面看似健康的人死亡的遺傳性心血管疾病。雖然在過去十年中，以風險溝通爲導向的研究已經實施，特別是在英國、美國和香港，但SADS風險溝通的性質和範圍尚未得到實證究。 爲了研究風險溝通，該項目提出了一個創新的研究設計，具體特點爲：（1）整合多學科視角；（2）以真實遺傳諮詢爲主要數據，建立大型語料庫，輔以病人及家庭成員焦點小組訪談；（3）采用主題化話語分析框架（Roberts and Sarangi, 2005）； （4）研究風險認知的人際和社會文化層面。除了分析50個SADS遺傳諮詢錄影外，本項目還將對先前收集的唐氏綜合征和G6PD缺乏症語料庫進行薈萃分析，得出關于遺傳風險溝通的普遍結論，以及向不同病人群體提供諮詢的經驗。薈萃分析將側重于在面臨不確定性和風險的情况下，那些促成决策的溝通策略。 本項目的研究結果可直接轉化爲臨床實踐，提供關于公衆對遺傳風險理解的信息。該項目將擴展東南亞地區逐漸興起的健康傳播實踐和政策討論。

17614217.label: Realisation of objectives
17614217.value: All the objectives of the project have been achieved successfully. Objective 1: The project has resulted in building an extensive unique database of genetic counselling consultations in Hong Kong. The database includes (a) new data of genetic counselling consultations for Sudden Arrhythmic Death Syndrome (SADS), and (b) consolidates the data from the previous projects on counselling for Down’s syndrome and G6PD deficiency. The database covers genetic conditions that may occur within an individual’s lifespan (prenatal, childhood, adolescent, and adult). It includes consultations with patients and family members from over 25 countries who speak English or Chinese (both Cantonese and Mandarin) as their first language in the consultations. As it was planned at the onset of the project, the database has been used for the purposes of research, professional training and education. It is expected that the data set will serve as a resource for future investigations of other aspects of genetic counselling communication in Hong Kong after the completion of the project. Objective 2: To investigate risk communication in genetic counselling the team has employed an innovative research design that draws on interdisciplinary insights that reflects the research team’s professional backgrounds; builds on examination of authentic interactional data of genetic counselling consultations; employs an integrated discourse analytic framework; pays particular attention to the sociocultural dimensions of communication; and draws on secondary data (e.g. interviews) that provides further contextual information and facilitates data interpretation. This research design has been employed in the project and is described in the publications that have resulted from this project (see Objective 5 for details). Objective 3: Family, family kinships and dynamics have comprised one of the main foci of investigation in the project. Specifically, the MPhil thesis that was completed as part of the project (by Mr. LC Hui “Children’s participation in genetic counselling: A theme-oriented discourse analytic investigation” focused on children and the role of family members in genetic counselling. Several publications that have resulted from the project specifically focus on family kinship and dynamics in genetic counselling. Objective 4: The focus on the sociocultural context of Hong Kong has comprised the novelty and the main contribution of the project. Much of the previous research on genetic counselling communication has been conducted in Anglo-dominant contexts. The project has specifically focused on how communication is dependent on the context where participants may not share linguistic and cultural backgrounds. This objective is reflected in three major publications in the project (in Journal of Genetic Counseling and American Journal of Medical Genetics), which align with one of the aims of the project to contribute to professional practice and training. Specifically, by disseminating the project findings through professional journals the team have aimed to raise the awareness among the genetic counselling professionals how risk and uncertainty pertinent to genetic counselling could be communicated to clients whose backgrounds require the use of lingua franca in an interaction, and whose cultural backgrounds call for specific interactional strategies to ensure that informed decision-making is achieved. Two major findings of the project with regards to this objective relate to (a) the importance of considering the backgrounds of genetic professionals, particularly when English (their second language) is used in the interactions; (b) understanding that language and culture (even when the participants do not share the same backgrounds) may not necessarily have an impact on the interactions. In other words, the project has highlighted the importance of context, and considering different contextual variables (e.g. socioeconomic backgrounds that impact clients’ decisions whether they opt for testing or not). Objective 5: The project has contributed to professional training, education, and policy-making by identifying and disseminating effective practices of genetic counselling for SADS and other genetic conditions. This has been achieved through presentations at multiple interdisciplinary and professional conferences. The PI has presented the project at the World Congress on Genetic Counselling at the University of Cambridge in 2019 (see project outputs for further details). The project outputs include publications in top international journals for genetic and genetic counselling professionals. In addition, the interdisciplinary project has built on close collaboration between linguists and genetic counselling professionals who have actively implemented the findings of the project in their ongoing practice and have actively participated in expert appraisal meetings. The PI has chaired a major international event, 3rd International E-Symposium on Health Communication in March, 2021 that has included a session on genetic counselling and genetic testing (featuring internationally renowned speakers and leading genetic professionals in Hong Kong). Objective 6: The online platform that the team have used to disseminate the project findings among the general public have been re-designed to make it more user friendly. Since the start of the project, the research team have set up Research and Impact Initiative for Communication in Healthcare (HKU RIICH, www.hkuriich.org; and @hkuriich on Twitter). The team has been actively publicizing its ongoing activities and published research through these online platforms that allow reaching a larger number of project beneficiaries. This work will continue after the completion of the project. The resource developed by the team on one of the conditions (G6PD deficiency) that is featured on the website of Clinical Genetic Services of Hong Kong and is used by hospitals has served as an example of developing a methodological communication-oriented framework that could be applied to other health resources. In subsequent projects the team will aim to publish this framework.

17614217.label: Major findings and research outcome
17614217.value: The project has consolidated the research team’s work on genetic counselling in Hong Kong by building on previous projects and the data collected in those projects and investigating a novel context of counselling for Sudden Arrhythmic Death Syndromes (SADS). Effective communication is particularly crucial in SADS contexts, as SADS conditions are potentially fetal but preventable if certain measures and lifestyle changes are implemented. The collected data in the project involves interactions with minors (i.e. children and adolescents under 18 years old) and their cognitive and decision-making abilities may make it particularly difficult for genetic professionals to communicate complex genetic information. The project has demonstrated that in interactions professionals typically orient to parents, as the children’s age increases there is an expectation of the children’s increased cognitive abilities and genetic literacy, which, however, do not impact the extent to which children are involved in decision-making. In genetic counselling literature there is an increasing interest to children’s assent/ consent, and the findings of the projects provide empirical evidence of existing practices and make suggestion on how children’s participation could be improved (see Hui et al. output submitted to Journal of Genetic Counseling). Major research findings of the project relate to the impact of language and culture on genetic counseling interactions (see Zayts et al., 2019; Zayts et al., 2021). Contrary to popular beliefs about communicative difficulties that arise in intercultural interactions, the differences in sociocultural backgrounds may not necessarily impact examined clinical interactions. In their work, the team have foregrounded the importance of other contextual factors, such as clients’ socioeconomic backgrounds, that impact decision about whether to take or to opt out of testing. This aligns with broader genetic counselling literature and the increasing call to consider factors, such as clients’ genetic literacy, sex, gender, occupation, mental health status, etc. that impact decision-making. A finding concerning sociocultural backgrounds of professionals is important for professional practice. In particular, the project has demonstrated that lower language proficiency of professionals may impact practices of informed consent (Zayts, 2021; Zayts and Hui, fc). The major findings of the project are based on empirical evidence that provides invaluable resources for training genetic counselling professionals in specific communication strategies to ensure that complex risk information and uncertainty are communicative clearly. These empirical findings are particularly valuable as to our knowledge this is the only work in the Region that is based on real-life interactions in the examined context.

17614217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17614217.value: The project offers ample opportunities for further development. The collected empirical database of authentic interactions between genetic counselling professionals, patients and family members will be used in the PI’s next project (Humanities and Social Sciences Prestigious Fellowship, HSSPF) “Talking Genetics: Intersections of Language, Culture and Genetic Literacy in Intercultural Genetic Testing and Counselling Contexts” that will involve completing a book-length manuscript. The project will focus on intercultural dimensions of communication, more specifically the interactions that involve at least one non-native speaker of English or Chinese. Another future development of the project that the PI would like to explore is how COVID-19 has impacted communication practices in genetic counselling, for example, the increased need for tele-genetic counselling (i.e. provision of services by distance using phones or computers). This will also be included in the HSSPF project. Several publications are at the stage of preparation at the moment in line with the dissemination activity to academic and professional communities. The project database of clinical interactions in genetic counselling will continue to be used for training purposes of future genetic counselling professionals in Hong Kong (MSc programme at HKU that is being revised at the time of submission of this report).

17614217.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17614217.value: The project focused on how risk and uncertainty are communicated in genetic counselling. Three genetic conditions that may occur within an individual’s lifespan (in prenatal, childhood, adolescent and adult stages of one’s life) were examined. The project drew on real-life audio- and video-recorded consultations between genetic professionals, patients, and family members, and resulted in the creation of a unique empirical database of genetic counselling interactions. Two specific foci of the project were family kinship and dynamics, and sociocultural aspects of communication. Family dynamics of communication carry prominence in genetic counselling because of the inherited nature of genetic conditions. The focus on the sociocultural aspects of communication is significant as the research team has pioneered this research outside of the English-dominant contexts. The project’s interdisciplinary team of genetic counselling professionals and linguists has allowed to produce findings and outputs relevant to both professional and academic communities. Among the main outputs of the project are publications in top peer-reviewed international journals for professionals, lectures/ seminars at professional events. Findings will form part of training of genetic counselling professionals in Hong Kong (MSc programme at HKU). One MPhil dissertation on communicating with children in genetic counselling was completed as part of the project.

17614717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17614717.value: Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS), or developmental verbal dyspraxia (DVD), is a lifelong condition where the individuals experience great difficulty learning to produce new sounds and using the acquired sounds consistently. In many of these cases, the etiology is unknown. Despite the consensus on existence of CAS among clinicians, there are no satisfactory gold standard diagnostic criteria. Clinicians have to rely on their own perceptions to construct a model for diagnosing the disorder. Researchers also encounter the problem of circularity - there are no unambiguously diagnosed clients because of the non-specific diagnostic markers. The best available markers are still the opinions of expert clinicians. CAS is assumed to be a disorder affecting populations speaking different languages. The signs described by experts are based on English-speaking children and not all can be directly applicable to the Chinese population whose speech sound system is markedly different from English. However, the pathology that underlies CAS is assumed to be the programming/planning of speech movement sequences. Theoretically-driven interventions are based on this assumption. High-level evidence attesting to the efficacy of intervention is emerging. Given the availability of effective treatment, the present study proposes a new way of approaching the disorder in general and in Chinese, so as to breach the problem of circularity; that is, to use participants’ response-to-treatment as an indicator for diagnosis. Individuals who respond positively to a specific treatment are likely to be prototypical of the disorders. Thirty-four Cantonese-speaking children with suspected CAS will be recruited after screening and eligibility assessment. Eligible participants will then receive the intervention of Rapid Syllable Transition (ReST) which is effective for English-speaking children (Murray, McCabe, & Ballard, 2014). Response-to-treatment measured using effect size will be examined case by case. The characteristic speech profile of the children with the most observable progress would assist in establishing the diagnostic criteria. At a clinical level, establishing a “valid” diagnosis can improve clinicians’ prediction of the prognosis and selection of appropriate treatment that is of best benefits to clients. Informative and uniform diagnostic criteria can also facilitate communication among clinicians and researchers. From the perspective of public health surveillance, the current study can provide new data about the characteristics of CAS in an unexplored language. This could enable refinement of the existing criteria for a more accurate case identification. 兒童期言語失用症（Childhood Apraxia of Speech, CAS）亦稱為發展性口語失用症（Developmental Verbal Dyspraxia），是一種較難根治的構音障礙。患有這種障礙的兒童會很難習得新的語音，而且亦未能有規率或有效地使用已獲得的語音。許多個案的病因都是未知的。儘管在臨床領域中，專業人員對CAS的存在已達至共識，但仍缺乏一套令人滿意的金標準作診斷依據。臨床的專業人員必須依靠自己的認知和經驗去建立診斷障礙的指標。同樣地, 研究人員也遇到循環的問題: 由於CAS臨床表現與一般的構音障礙的兒童有部份雷同，欠缺特異性的診斷標記，所以沒有完全肯定以CAS為名的確診個案。目前最好的指標仍然是臨床專家的意見。理論上CAS這種障礙會影響到不同語言和國籍的人。專家學者在文獻中所闡述的標記大都以英文為母語的兒童為基礎而建立的。由於中文語音系統與英文截然不同，所提出的標記並不是全部都可以直接適用於中文兒童身上。然而，CAS發生的病理被認為是缺乏言語動作控制的能力。以理論為導向的干預治療是基於這個一假設的。本研究提出了一種全新方法，避過循環問題， 制定一套客觀和有效診斷CAS的標記。也就是說，我們通過患者對治療的反應制定診斷的指標。對治療作出正面反應的兒童便很可能是典型個案。 我們在篩選和評估後，將招募三十名有疑似CAS的粵語兒童。然後，符合條件的參與者將接受對英語兒童有效的音節快速轉換（ReST）的干預（Murray，McCabe，＆Ballard，2014）。干預效果將逐案評估。進展最明顯的兒童的表徵將有助於確定診斷標準。在臨床層面，建立“有效度”的診斷有助於提高臨床專業人員對預後的預測和挑選對患者最有利的治療方案。有效和一致的診斷標準也可以促進臨床專業人員和研究人員之間的溝通。從公共衛生監督的角度來看，此項研究可以提供有關中文CAS特徵的新數據。這可以使現有的標準得到改進，從而更準確地進行個案識別。

17614717.label: Realisation of objectives
17614717.value: The project mainly included two board objectives. Objective 1: To examine the response-to-treatment of Cantonese-speaking children with suspected CAS to the ReST treatment programme. This objective was generally achieved. To achieve the first objective, the following research-related tasks have been conducted: (1) construction of an assessment protocol, (2) recruitment of children with suspected CAS, and (3) implementation of ReST intervention, and (4) evaluation of their progress. Construction of assessment protocol: The assessment protocol consisted of two main parts, oral motor examination and a speech probe list based on Cantonese phonology. The oral motor examination protocol was developed based on Robins and Klee (1987) and was normed on 50 typically-developing Cantonese-speaking pre-schoolers. A list of 102 single words that include all Cantonese syllable structures and all Cantonese initial consonants, vowels and final consonants was devised. Recruitment of children with suspected CAS: Given the lack of consensus regarding the diagnostic criteria of CAS, the inclusion criteria of the participants were: (1) having at least 50 expressive vocabulary, (2) multiple speech sound errors, (3) minimal progress after at least a block of traditional therapy on speech sound production, (4) no reported hearing loss, (5) speak Cantonese as the native language, and (6) no frank delay in cognitive ability and organic deficit in oral motor structures. Flyers and a website http://www.fe.hku.hk/ewcounts/zh/our_research.php were developed for public education and participant recruitment. A total of 18 preschool and school age children were initially recruited. Among them, only 10 met the above criteria and completed the intervention phase. Seven of these 10 children were at age 8 and above and the remaining three were preschool children under age 6. Implementation of ReST intervention: Following the ReST treatment protocol (McCabe et al., 2017), a list of nonwords were devised for each participant following the principles of having four consonants and three long vowels. Consonant and vowel selection was based on the participants’ phonetic inventory. Different consonants with at least 2 manner classes are included. For vowels, three long vowels were chosen. Some adaptations were made when constructing the nonword stimuli for Cantonese. Syllable structures of CV, CVC, and CVV were included in addition to CV as stated in the original protocol, given the large number of the latter two in Cantonese syllabary (Benedict & Bauer, 1997). The Cantonese vowel /ɐ/ was included given its closest position, in terms of vowel height, frontness and lip roundness, to the schwa in the original protocol. Twelve 35-40 minute sessions with two treatment sessions per week over six to nine weeks, subject to individual scheduling, were provided to each participant. Treatment sessions typically consisted of two parts following the PML, namely pre-practice and practice. Pre-practice involved the provision of maximal cueing strategies (e.g., imitation, phonetic placement, blending, etc.) as well as specific feedback of KP (e.g. "the lips should be rounded"). In practice trials, no additional cueing support will be given, and feedback of KR (e.g., “this is right/wrong”) would be given in 50% of the trials. 100 trials were conducted with a target of 80% accuracy. All treatment was given face-to-face, except for one participant (CCW_03). 75% of his sessions was conducted through telepractice via zoom. Evaluation of treatment progress The progress of the six school-age children were examined in details (see separate manuscript to be submitted). Outcome measures based on the (perceptual) accuracy of non-treated real words probes was quantitatively documented and then analysed using Tau-U statistics. Results showed that all participants have significant treatment gains in at least one speech parameter. Objective 2: To provide a set of measurable criteria that characterize the speech of Cantonese-speaking children with CAS based on the profile of children who show significant progress after the treatment. The objective was only partially achieved. To achieve this objective, we have to identify the children who show the most robust progress after treatment. However, based on the perceptual judgement about the accuracy in the speech probe list, all children showed some degree of progress but in different dimensions. We did not yet have strong justification of selecting other unexamined dimension as the outcomes. Data mining with different acoustic measures is on-going. It may be possible that duration of syllables and pauses at conversation level. Remarks: The study was conducted during the social unrest and pandemic. Participant recruitment was affected resulting in a small number of participants recruited. Based on the data from a small number of participants, only robust observation can be conclusive. Data mining has to be continued to identify rigorous measures in addition to the planned perceptual measures.

17614717.label: Major findings and research outcome
17614717.value: The current study indicated positive intervention effect of the ReST program on Cantonese-speaking children with suspected childhood apraxia of speech. The progress of the 6 school-age children was documented in details in form of a case study series. The report will be submitted to journal (Journal of Communication Disorders) for review (see Part C). For the construction of the assessment protocol, the part of the oromotor mechanism examination was normed on typically development children. The report was written up and is under review in Clinical Linguistic and Phonetics (see Part C). However, as mentioned above, all children showed certain degree of significant improvement and stronger evidence was needed to support which children showed the most robust growth when compared to others. We have been working on various acoustic measures such as duration of intra-syllable, inter-syllable, and inter-utterances pauses, as well as PVI (pairwise variability index) which is a measure of rhythm.

17614717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17614717.value: By the end of the intervention, all the school-age children still demonstrated reduced speech intelligibility and unresolved speech sound errors in conversational speech. These children have a clear profile of persistent speech sound disorders and represent the phenotype of severe speech sound disorders. Genetic study on these children and new probands with persistent speech difficulty may be possible. A recent study on English-speaking children identified new genes linked to severe childhood speech disorder (Hildebrand et al., 2020). It is of great theoretical interest to examine if these genes can be identified in ethnic Chinese speakers. This could be a CRF project involving experts on genetics.

17614717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17614717.value: Childhood Apraxia of Speech (CAS) is a motor speech disorder that severely affect speech intelligibility in children. This study investigated the effectiveness of Rapid Syllable Transitions (ReST) treatment for CAS in Cantonese context. ReST is currently one of the English CAS treatment with highest evidence, which emphasizes the principle of motor learning in improving segmental accuracy, transition within and among syllables, and prosodic accuracy in speech. In this study, a multiple-baseline across participants design was used to examine treatment efficacy for six school-aged children with CAS, aged eight to 11 years, who received ReST treatment twice a week for six to nine weeks. Outcome measures from non-treated real words probes was quantitatively documented and then analysed using Tau-U statistics. Results showed that all participants have significant treatment gains in at least one speech parameter with large effect sizes. This study provided preliminary evidence that ReST is effective in generalizing segmental accuracy and syllable transition to real words. Severity may have played a role in responsiveness towards this approach. Clinical applications and limitations were further discussed.

17615217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17615217.value: Feedback is central to student learning in undergraduate education: students improve when comments and critique connect with them and help to advance their learning. Without effective feedback, it is difficult for students to reach their maximum potential and attain the kinds of learning outcomes to which contemporary universities aspire. Feedback processes are, however, challenging to implement effectively. They are generally rated by students as one of the least satisfactory aspects of their undergraduate experience; and viewed by university teachers as frequently frustrating. Developing effective feedback processes is thus a high-profile and crucial research topic which goes to the heart of the improvement of student learning. The research strategy involves using the principles and processes of constructivist grounded theory to understand and theorize feedback processes. Using a grounded approach is particularly suitable when studying complex educational processes which involve interaction between participants. Our theorizations are to be grounded in data but use our prior knowledge of relevant literature to inform them. Main research methods include semi-structured interviews with teachers to probe conceptions of feedback; supplemented by observations and documentary analysis to understand how feedback processes are implemented. To capture the important student voice, focus group and individual interviews are conducted. Data are collected across disciplines from 16 teachers and their students, spread across four subjects, one each from hard pure, hard applied, soft pure and soft applied disciplines at a research-intensive English medium university: the University of Hong Kong. Data are analyzed through coding, categorizing, theory generation and theory verification. Feedback in higher education is a very important topic and much related research has been undertaken but feedback processes are somewhat under-theorized. The project explores feedback in the context of different disciplines as a means to interrogate existing conceptualizations of feedback and develop further theorizations. By theorizing, important understandings of issues, challenges and conceptualizations can be generated. These provide the basis for both new theorizations of feedback and ways forward for its practice in the context of different disciplines. The research addresses the challenge of how to facilitate effective feedback processes for undergraduate students. Its intended outcomes are: • To understand how university teachers in different disciplines manage feedback processes in context, and how students respond to them; • To interrogate existing theorizations of feedback and develop new theorizations; • To derive implications for effective feedback practice contextualized within different disciplines, including critiquing existing models and strategies.

17615217.label: Realisation of objectives
17615217.value: 1. To investigate how university teachers in different disciplines manage feedback processes in context and how students respond to them; Our project focused on how university teachers in four disciplines (architecture, education, engineering and medicine) managed feedback processes and how students responded to these practices. The three objectives are fully achieved, for example, by three publications appearing in prestigious internationally refereed journals. In architecture, a major feature of design studios is a series of critical reviews or crits where students receive feedback on work in progress, culminating in a final public review carried out in front of a jury of teachers and practitioners. Teachers and students expressed the view that feedback was most useful when it was during the process of production in providing comments on work in progress that could then be revised. From our observations we noted that feedback often occurred at an early planning stage in the design cycle and enabled students to clarify the requirements of the particular project. The design studio seems to evidence a productive feedback culture where feedback exchanges are planned and designed within the curriculum to inform student appreciation of disciplinary ways of thinking and doing. Feedback processes are built into the signature pedagogies of the discipline and there are plentiful opportunities to review and clarify feedback. The main feedback strategies in Engineering were collective feedback and peer interactions of different forms. Collective feedback is a practical and manageable strategy that is relatively workload-friendly for the teacher and can be carried out with large classes. Its drawback lies in being somewhat impersonal and non-specific to individual needs, so students may not perceive that it is applicable to them even if it is. Peer learning in engineering included vertical peer tutoring across year groups and horizontal peer learning amongst classmates. Peer tutors learn communication skills, reinforce their own subject knowledge and may be perceived as more approachable, although perhaps less credible or authoritative, than teachers. In education, teachers were a bit more familiar with principles and practices of feedback designs as outlined in educational literature. Students expressed appreciation of feedback designs that enabled them to use comments so that they could improve their grades, including teacher comments on work in progress, such as outlines or drafts; or when commentary on the first assessment task could be used in the second task of the module. Summative comments which occur after a grade is awarded were deemed to be not useful because there was no time or space for acting on the feedback. Pockets of audio and video feedback practice were also salient in the data, and represented good examples of technology-enabled feedback. These were particularly effective when they prompted students to respond or follow-up on feedback inputs from teachers so as to develop shared responsibilities in the enactment of feedback. In medicine, productive feedback opportunities in the data emerged mainly from Problem-based learning (PBL) tutorials and even more significantly from feedback exchanges during clinical clerkships. With groups of 10-12 students, PBL tutorials can be used to establish the supportive relationships for feedback dialogues to thrive. Clinical clerkships conducted in the hospital context provide an environment for authentic feedback where students can receive personalized feedback and hands-on guidance. The authentic workplace context also enables educators to demonstrate alternative ways of examining patients in the real-life bedside context. Student e-portfolios documenting progress in their clerkships encourage students to take some responsibility for their ongoing progress by reflecting on what they have learnt, establishing further learning goals for themselves in relation to their further learning, and consider ways to improve. Feedback in the clinical setting was conceptualized as signature feedback practices. 2. To interrogate existing theorizations of feedback and develop new theorizations; The research interrogated existing theorizations of feedback and developed new theorizations relevant to feedback literacy, signature feedback practices and authentic feedback. Some of the existing theorizations of feedback focus on generic principles of good feedback, and whilst these are useful, they fail to account fully for the disciplinary nature of feedback exchanges. Our new theoretical contribution of signature feedback practices emphasizes the disciplinary nature of feedback processes. In this way, our research asserts the disciplinary nature of feedback practices to add to, and contrast with, promising insights on good generic practice. Crits in architecture and clinical bedside rounds in medicine are compelling examples in our data of signature feedback practices in that they are well-established disciplinary-specific practices. Signature feedback practices carry potential to be authentic and motivating for students because they are rooted in the social practices of the discipline. A key implication is that focused research and development work on a single signature feedback theme might represent a more promising way forward than general attempts at improving feedback, such as more detailed comments or faster turnaround times (Carless et al. 2020). A second theoretical contribution of our research lies in the concept of authentic feedback. By building on and extending the concept of authentic assessment in terms of realism, cognitive and affective challenge, we have conceptualized authentic feedback processes as resembling the feedback practices of the discipline, profession or workplace. Our framework for authentic feedback can be applied to feedback designs as a way of identifying their authenticity and enabling their adjustment in a more authentic direction (Dawson, Carless & Lee, 2020). Both signature feedback practices and authentic feedback are rendered more feasible when teachers and students develop shared responsibilities in developing feedback literacy. The notion of feedback literacy: the capacities of teachers and students to involve themselves productively in feedback exchanges (Carless & Boud, 2018) underpins the conceptualization of the research and its outcomes. 3. To uncover implications for effective feedback contextualized within different disciplines, including critiquing existing models and strategies. For feedback potential to be realized, learning activities needed to be organized in ways which enable sufficient time and space for productive feedback encounters to emerge. Our critique of previous models and strategies lies in emphasizing the crucial disciplinary nature of these learning activities. Implications for practice suggest that promising feedback processes involve the mutual development of feedback literacy, and a focus on student uptake of feedback messages contextualized within the study of disciplinary content and skills. The mutual development of feedback literacy occurs in Architecture when students and teachers accept shared responsibilities to design, generate and respond to feedback of different forms. In these ways, Architecture teachers and students engage in feedback dialogues focused on both the improvement of work in progress as well as sharing braider thinking about the nature of quality work within design fields. Feedback literacy is enhanced when teachers attend to how students are responding to feedback messages, and students recognize that they need to engage with feedback inputs. The uptake of feedback information is facilitated when teachers design opportunities within curriculum and assessment for students to make use of feedback in their ongoing work; and when students summon the will power to respond positively to critical feedback. Both teachers and students need to take responsibilities for different aspects of feedback processes: teachers are responsible for equipping students with strategies for taking productive action on feedback information, whereas students carry responsibilities to engage with and use feedback. The most effective disciplinary feedback practices in architecture, education, engineering and medicine evidenced these kinds of shared responsibilities between teachers and students.

17615217.label: Major findings and research outcome
17615217.value: This research investigated feedback practices in four different applied disciplines (architecture, education, engineering and medicine) through observations, interviews with teachers and students, and document analysis. The main finding was the identification of what we called signature feedback practices: the characteristic ways feedback processes are enacted in specific disciplines (Carless et al., 2020). Critical reviews or crits in architecture and bedside rounds in medicine were examples in our data of signature feedback practices in that they are well-established disciplinary-specific practices that integrate pedagogy and feedback. Through crits, architecture students collect iterative cycles of feedback from teachers, classmates and practitioners in the industry to inform the further development of their design work. During bedside rounds in medicine, medical students collect insights from patients, guardians, their university teachers and other medical professionals. A further major finding was the interplay between disciplinary-specific feedback practices and generic recommendations for good feedback practice in the literature. In our data from education, the more promising practices resonated with key literature: skilful feedback designs; audio and video feedback practice; and attempts at developing shared responsibilities between teachers and students in feedback processes. In engineering, the main identified feedback strategies were collective feedback, peer interactions of different forms and the design of an automated feedback system. In architecture, cycles of feedback enabled students to make use of feedback in revising design work – this is significant because it speaks to the issue of student uptake of feedback. In medicine, productive feedback opportunities in the data also emerged from problem-based learning tutorials where the space for dialogic interaction contrasted with the impersonal nature of large class lectures. The successful enactment of these feedback practices was enhanced when teachers and students evidenced feedback literacy: the capacities to participate in meaningful feedback exchanges in which shared responsibilities between teachers and students are salient. We have also proposed the concept of authentic feedback building on the more familiar concept of authentic assessment (Dawson, Carless and Lee 2021). Authentic feedback is defined as feedback processes that resemble the feedback practices of the discipline, profession or workplace. Enhancing the authenticity of feedback could be a useful means of making it more engaging for students and carries potential to contribute to the development of student feedback literacy. Learners need to develop feedback literacy strategies that are useable in relation to university feedback practices, transferrable to the workplace and valuable for lifelong learning.

17615217.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17615217.value: The key concepts of signature feedback practices, authentic feedback and feedback literacy all carry potential for further development. Disciplinary feedback processes seem to be influenced by local social, cultural and contextual factors, generic feedback practices and discipline-specific features. Building on how feedback is typically enacted in the discipline could carry potential for the enhancement of signature feedback practices resonating with authentic real-life applications. Further research and development work on signature feedback practices in different disciplines, including pure disciplines, would be helpful in advancing the concept. I have some work in progress, based on data collected by Dr Edd Pitt in the UK which examines signature feedback practices in creative arts disciplines: Film, Drama, Comedy and Music. There is also further work to be done on feedback literacy: the capacities of teachers and students to maximize the potential benefits derived from feedback processes (Carless and Boud 2018). What are the capacities that teachers need in different disciplines to design and implement productive feedback processes? What are the relationships between authentic disciplinary-based feedback practices and the capacities of students to make the most of signature feedback possibilities? There is also an urgent need to conceptualize and investigate, teacher feedback literacy more deeply. It is clear from the research (and other literature) that effective feedback processes are dependent on the capacities of teachers to design feedback sequences effectively as well as students to engage themselves productively.

17615217.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17615217.value: Feedback processes involve participants entering into interactions in order to enhance their performance or broader learning. Being able to make the most of feedback opportunities is both a skill for doing well at university and a lifelong learning capacity. These capacities to benefit from feedback comprise feedback literacy. The enactment of feedback takes place in specific disciplinary contexts. The aim of this research was therefore to investigate feedback practices in four different applied disciplines. For purposes of variety the following disciplines were chosen: architecture, education, engineering and medicine. In architecture, students developed designs over periods of several weeks and received multiple different forms of feedback. In education, there was a wide variety of feedback practices, including audio and video modes. In engineering, practices included collective feedback where teachers gave feedback in writing or orally to groups of students; engineering students also appreciated getting feedback or support from peers of the same year group or from seniors. In medicine, clinical clerkships where students examined patients at the Queen Mary Hospital provided opportunities for purposeful real-life feedback exchanges. It seems that when feedback relates to real-life features of the discipline, it is more likely to be useful to students.

17616117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616117.value: For hundreds of years, innovation in the architecture of housing happened without architects. Drawing upon the availability of materials and adapting to changing social structures, what has come to be understood as vernacular architecture evolved with the transformation of livelihoods through indigenous knowledge about the built environment. In rural China, as a result of a dramatic shift to an economy based primarily on migrant labour, the rural is no longer recognizable and has given rise to an urgent problem. In many Chinese villages, a building boom, coupled with a lack of regulation, has led to densities more often found in urban areas. Without planning policies or codes, the informal densification of rural villages has created an unprecedented problem. On one hand, vernacular dwellings are no longer suitable for residents who demand the conveniences of modern life. Uncertainty in rural policy and the expansion of the family (on limited plots of land) has also generated unique demands on vernacular housing, rendering it unviable. At the same time, the prevailing house building model proposes a generic system comprised of a concrete frame and brick infill whose main advantage is speed and cheapness of construction. These units can be built by unskilled labour with ceramic tile used to finish over poor quality construction. This method is so efficient that it is used for all kinds of buildings -- from houses, to schools and hospitals -- rendering these different functions indistinguishable. The tendency is for villagers to abandon their ancestral dwellings for cheaper alternatives, eschewing a rich vernacular tradition. This proposal addresses the tendency toward vernacular obsolescence in rural China by looking at those vernacular dwellings that have been informally adapted and transformed by villagers themselves. Through this documentation -- a close reading of how villagers transform their homes -- we hope to compile an understanding of how renovation might expand the possibilities and long term viability of vernacular dwellings. In our preliminary research, we discovered intelligent and surprising solutions conceived by villagers. Often these changes were environmentally sustainable and contained spatial nuances related to deep rooted social structures of their respective region. A systematic documentation of these cases will produce a design manual, or toolbox, containing strategies for adaptation, while also providing architectural evidence for the social, economic and cultural imperatives motivating transformations of the rural environment, thus making it possible to assemble a comprehensive design program for contemporary rural dwelling. Renovation toolbox: Strategies for adapting vernacular architecture in rural China 改造工具箱：中國農村鄉土建築的適應策略 幾百年來，住宅建築的創新在沒有建築師干預的情況下自發進行著。基於可以獲得的材料和適應不斷變化的社會結構，“鄉土建築”隨著生活方式的轉變和人們對建築環境的認知的改變而不斷發展進化。 隨著中國經濟轉型，大量農民走出農村進城務工，農村的面目改變了，並產生了一系列緊迫的問題。在許多中國村莊，建築熱潮加上監管缺位，導致農村出現了在城市地區常見的高密度環境。由於缺乏規劃政策或規範，農村的非正式密度化造成了前所未有的問題。 一方面，鄉土建築不再滿足居住者對便利的現代生活的需求。由於農村政策的不確定性以及在有限土地上的家庭擴張，鄉土建築也不能再滿足當下農村對住房的特殊需求。與此同時，房屋建造的主流方式通常采用混凝土框架結構和轉砌墻填充的系統，其主要優點是施工快速和造價低廉。這些單位可以使用低技術含量的勞動建成，然後在劣質的建成品表面貼上瓷磚。這種方法非常高效，它被用于各種建築物 —— 從房屋到學校到醫院，讓這些不同功能的房屋類型也變得難以區分了。這種趨勢使得村民放棄他們的祖傳住宅而采用更廉價的替代品，抛棄了豐富的鄉土傳統。 這一計劃針對中國鄉土建築逐漸廢棄的趨勢， 考察了村民們對鄉土民居的自發的非正式改造。通過解讀和紀錄村民們對傢宅的改造，我們希望理解改造的方法可以怎樣拓展鄉土民居的可能性和可行性。在初步研究中，我們發現村民們構想了許多令人驚訝的充滿智慧的改造方法。這些改造通常合乎環境的可持續發展，並包含根植于當地深層社會結構的豐富細膩的空間層次。通過對這些案例的系統紀錄，我們可以創造一個包含改造策略的設計手冊或工具箱，同時為農村急需的社會、經濟和文化轉型提供建築方面的依據，使得為當代農村住宅提出全面的設計方案成爲可能。

17616117.label: Realisation of objectives
17616117.value: Find Research Appendix: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/ Objective 1: To identify cases where villagers adapt vernacular dwellings to better suit the realities of their daily lives. ( See Appendix 1 and the link for Appendix 1-6: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/) The team has visited 75 houses in 18 villages in China. The team traveled across the diverse climatic and environmental ranges of China, eventually focusing our attention on four regions where adaptations offered particularly strong lessons: the underground house in a cold climate; wooden houses of multiple minorities in China’s mountainous south-central region; the large communal houses, or tulou, of southeastern China: and the high-altitude dwellings of the Tibetan people in the far west. All 75 houses with photographic documented (See Appendix 1). After rounds of analysis and drawing studies, 15 of them are selected as case studies: five underground houses in Shaanxi Province, five collective houses in Fujian Province and five wooden houses in Guizhou Province. Each case has a completed set of architectural drawings (plan, section and elevation) and a thorough survey of photographs and interviews with residents to investigate how cases are being transformed. Objective 2: To make an objective documentation of this adaptation utilizing photography and drawing. ( See Appendix 2,3,4,5 and the link for Appendix 1-6: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/) After initial analysis and drawing attempts of 75 houses, the team returned to three sites and re-visited 15 cases to complete documentation in detail. The team has produced axonometric drawings (See Appendix 2), plans (See Appendix 3) and photographs (See Appendix 4) for all 15 case studies. Each house has two different scales of axonometric drawings: 1) urban scale (See Appendix 5).: drawings of pre-existing urban fabric to show the different conditions in which each typology is sited; 2) micro scale: drawings of interventions to create a catalogue of the ways in which users have transformed their dwelling and to identify changes in the village house, name these changes and classify them to delineate the logic structuring the modifications. Plans drawings were also produced of each case to analyze what renovations the owner did and how did they use this space (See Appendix 3). The plan drawings show recent design decision linked to program, materials, and construction and the more embedded condition of typology. Objective 3: To create a record of the lived experience of village life within vernacular dwelling by interviewing and narrating the stories of home owners. ( See Appendix 6 and the link for Appendix 1-6: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/) The team has interviewed 25 houses owners in 3 regions and six narratives (See Appendix 6) have been chosen as representative. During fieldwork, the team conducted multiple interviews in each house and discussed with family members from different generations. The recording history of the houses consist history of the family and how inhabitants understand their place in the large community within transformation and typologies. The narratives of the houses were discerned through site visits, photography, and drawings; of the people through discussion and interview. By combining the two, the team has gained an understanding of the architecture of the house and their transformation. There interviews and human histories comprise a text that operates in a reciprocal relation with cultural, social, and economic contexts. Some interviews provide anecdotal support for empirical findings from social science on rural transformation. Other times, those findings explain the material changes that we observed in house construction. Objective 4: To identify best cases that can lead to strategies and prototypes for the renovation and adaptation of vernacular housing. ( See Appendix 2 and the link for Appendix 1-6: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/) Out of 15 case studies, three houses were identified as best cases. Those houses identify examples of innovative, sustainable and efficient renovations that offered strategies for how to render traditional housing forms viable for modern living. - The underground house: Cut Away House When the district government built a new road, they cut away earth on one side of this family’s house, leveling ground that once enclosed rooms. This family took advantage of the change of grade created by the excavation, they built a direct entrance into the sunken courtyard from the new street. This entrance comprised a series of rooms-both private rooms and shop-front spaces open to the street. - The wooden house: House on House The family decided to add a wooden frame and pitched roof on top of their concrete house. The dimensions and spatial organization of both houses follow a traditional spatial diagram: three even bays with an open middle area flanked by four equal rooms. In traditional houses this mean that the main space would often be used for a fire; other rooms had no fixed use and could be adapted to a family’s needs. - The collective house: Plug-in House Over the course of several years, this old tulou was redefined by additions both inside and outside its wall. The families here wanted to remain part of the traditional collective living structure, but also to have bigger, updated houses. Volumes plugged in to the tulou from the exterior, orient their once inward-looking units outward. New openings in the earthen wall link the old spaces to those of the plug-in extension. Objective 5: To develop a design manual, or tool box, that can make the research conclusions available and accessible to diverse actors implicated in the development of rural architecture. ( See Appendix 2 and the link for Appendix 1-6: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/) The toolbox is a set of renovation strategies. These strategies are described as axonometric drawings of the 15 selected cases. They make visible different spatial, constructive and material transformation to the original house. The strategies are also described in general terms which be further copied by others seeking to so the same. The axonometric drawings can be understood by non-architects and a broad audience can be benefited. Objective 6: To assemble a comprehensive program for the design of the modern rural house in China, incorporating the research outputs. ( See Appendix 3 and the link for Appendix 1-6: http://www.rufwork.org/index.php?/research/renovation-toolbox/) The comprehensive program is the list of functions from 15 selected cases. In addition, the design program is illustrated as in 15 plan drawings as well as a list of all functions for each of the selected house. We show programs in plan drawings to better understand the spatial relationship between the functions.

17616117.label: Major findings and research outcome
17616117.value: The documentation, drawing, interviews and analysis of the case study houses led to three major findings: renovations to traditional houses by self-builders, are sometimes informed by a desire to make dwellings more energy efficient and sustainable and deploy non-standard solutions to achieve these goals; second, from an architectural design perspective, our understanding of the traditional house will need to be reconsidered as new building techniques and materials create hybrid vernacular forms; third, these hybrid forms of construction are also having an impact on village fabric, both reflecting larger sale changes within the rural urban economy and necessitating new wakes of thinking about the civic structures that tie villages together. These findings were common to all three case studies, but manifested themselves in varying ways that were explored both in the Research Output As Found Houses, and in the conference presentations in Berlin [Contemporary transformations of Dong houses in rural China] and the proceedings of the Architectural Ethnography program. Energy efficiency and sustainability were a primary factor motivating the renovations of underground houses in Shaanxi, with residents seeking to transition from traditional wood burning stoves to more energy efficient forms of heating to warm their homes without producing the choking smoke that earlier led to respiratory problems. Importantly, solar heating and ventilation systems that transformed the dwellings capacity to welcome contemporary, year-round ways of living. Hybrid forms of construction were found in nearly every typology, with concrete often used in conjunction with traditional forms of wood or earthen building. In Guizhou, hybrid concrete and wooden frame construction has transformed the programmatic use and architectural meaning of elements of the typology, changing traditional understandings codified for hundreds of years. These shifted architectural significations, demand new methods of looking at the traditional house, that we begin to propose in the book. Finally, in Fujian, tulou housed marketplace or schools in central courtyard. A proto-urban condition emerged where collective spaces were not only used privately but as shared public institution in an increasingly densifying region. This makes it necessary to reassess the larger community structures and institutions that support village life, particularly in relation to the larger shifts in population, migration, birthrates and aging. Where before, the village was organized a specific support system of family, clan and village council, itself supported by an architecture, the research suggests that new civic and community institutions may need to develop to address the village of today.

17616117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17616117.value: The further development of the research will take place in following directions: - Renovation Toolbox 2: Assessing the sustainability of modern vernacular houses The team will continue the research of sustainability in rural China and apply effective sustainability assessment for vernacular houses in Tibetan area. This new proposed GRF project will focus on establishing methodology of measuring social, cultural and environmental measurement in local and modern houses. - Un-Modern Houses: Renovation strategies for traditional homes This is a research proposal which is a companion to As Found House. After documenting and studying the innovative house strategies, this research intends to consider design and possible contributions to vernacular house from trained architects. - Integrating Tradition: a modern housing prototype for rural development in China The proposal tests a strategy for delivering meaningful impact to the development of sustainable housing in rural China through the conception, fabrication and promulgation of demonstrator houses that integrate traditional housing forms with modern innovations.

17616117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17616117.value: In rural China, an informal wave of building jump started by economic and social transformations over the past 40 years has rendered some villages unrecognizable. The resulting building boom, taking place in a context with very few regulations, has created densities more often found in urban areas. At the same time, the sudden availability of new materials and industrial methods of construction have enabled some remarkable hybrid experiments where rural self-builders adapt, modify, graft, cleave and wrap traditional building types. Unconstrained by notions of good taste or formal consideration, these unexpected and innovative solutions are reflections on some of the most pertinent issues of contemporary dwelling, whether on the issue of living with seasons or modernizing tradition. This research argues that the manifold evolution of the vernacular is part of the every-day practice of the villagers’ lives, and that architecture for them is very much still a home. It is a guide to the surprising design decisions found in the domestic architecture of rural China and a resource for thinking about new ways of living today.

17616217.label: Project Objectives

17616217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616217.value: This project will examine how institutions shape the dynamics of public policy agenda-setting in the government of China. A major puzzle in the literature of the public policy process in China and elsewhere is that, as authoritarian regimes are characterized by restriction on political participation and monopoly of policymaking power by governing elites, how do the authoritarian institutions impact on agenda-setting dynamics? We bring together an Information Processing Theory (IPT), and an Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to analyze the impact of China’s authoritarian institutions on policy agenda processes and outcomes. Focusing on post-Mao China (1976-2015), we will construct a novel dataset that captures policy attention to different policy issues across time at the national level. A series of longitudinal case studies will be conducted to examine the nuances of the mechanisms and processes underlying the policy agenda-setting in selected policy domains. Our study will be among the first major theoretical applications of the IPT and IAD framework to policymaking in an authoritarian regime, which will be of major theoretical and practical relevance to the study of the public policy process. 本研究項目檢視制度設計對中國政府政策議題設定的影響。公共政策文獻的其中一個迷思，是針對威權政體的特質--包括限制政治參與及政治權力壟斷--怎樣影響政策議題的設定。本硏究項目應用資訊處理理論及制度分析與發展架構，分析中國的威權制度對政策議題設定的影響。以後毛時代(1976-2015)為重點，本項目將建構一個能描述中國不同政策範疇政策關注程度的數據庫，並進行一系列誇時比較個案分析。作為首次應用資訊處理理論及制度分析與發展架構於威權政體的政策制定研究，本項目將對政策制定的理論及實踐作出貢獻。

17616217.label: Realisation of objectives
17616217.value: The research team managed to build a novel quantitative dataset on policy attention with help from more than 10 student research assistants supervised directly by the PI and Co-Is. The dataset keeps track of policy attention from 2002 to 2018 in four major venues of Chinese policymaking: the National People's Congress, the Political Consultative Conference, the Standing Committee of the Communist Party of China, and the State Council. The database included more than 29,000 observations. The data provided solid empirical evidence for our analysis of how an array of institutional and contextual factors affect the policy agenda setting. Based on the quantitative analysis of policy attention in China, our team has published two articles on top-tier Public Administration journals—one published in Governance and the other in Regulation and Governance. Re the collection of qualitative data and case studies, while Covid travel restrictions across Mainland China made it impossible for the PI and other Hong Kong-based investigators to personally visit the sites, we conducted fieldwork through partners based in mainland China, such as Dr HC Wang at Tsinghua. We managed to conduct in-depth interviews with elite policy actors, including industry leaders, current and former government officials, and other key stakeholders. The fieldwork has allowed us to put together an in-depth case study of policy attention on filmmaking under the leadership of two leaders. Based on the case we have produced an article which is currently under review at Policy Studies Journal.
