18602917.label: Major findings and research outcome
18602917.value: Below is the summary of findings on factors that explained participants’ intervening behavior. Among 581 college students, awareness of cyberbullying, subjective norm, and self-efficacy to intervene, positively explained participants’ intentions to intervene in cyberbullying situations. Also, intention to intervene in cyberbullying positively explained intervening behavior; and intention to intervene partially mediated the relation between a) subjective norm to intervene and intervening behavior; and b) self-efficacy to intervene and intervening behavior. Finally, past experience with of being cyber-victimized also positively predicted intervening behavior. See item 1, part C. A paper currently under review tested a comprehensive model that examined cyber-defending behavior among secondary school students. Results showed that socio-emotio4al factors; beliefs (pro-victim belief, cyberbullying awareness); and experience with victimization and witnessing cyberbullying positively explained cyber-defending (see item 4, part C). These results were reported in a conference paper. We have been working on another paper (manuscript in preparation) analyzing participants’ belief systems and intervening behavior across T1 and T2. In the short training programme, participants in the experimental and control groups completed measures at the outset (T1) and end (T2, 5 weeks after the 3-week-6-session training program), which included: awareness of cyberbullying, intention to help cyberbullied victims, perceived behavioral control about helping cyberbullied victims, self-efficacy to combat cyberbullying, and likelihood of behavioral intervention in cyberbullying. At T1, there were no significant group differences on the measures, then, repeated-measures analyses of covariance revealed significant interaction effects for all 5 measures after the training. Those who received the training had higher scores on the measures than those in the control group. These findings (see item 2, part C) show how the constructivist e-learning program promotes prosocial behavior. Preliminary analysis (manuscript in preparation) of the participants’ tendency to intervene in the experiment using the simulated cyberbullying scenarios, showed that they were most likely to help a victim who was active (actively defending themselves) and not provocative, and the least likely to help a victim who was passive and provocative. We fully utilized part of our datasets and other pilot datasets that contained measures of different online activities and other psychological measures, and published a paper on the association between social media usage and depression (see item 3, part C). This effort also yielded one conference paper on how attitudes toward cyberbullying, experience in witnessing cyberbullying, empathy and cyberbullying were related.

18602917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18602917.value: Over-time, changes in individuals' beliefs are common and are parts of human nature. Therefore, we suggest that a three-time point dataset may be more conducive to understand longitudinal changes. We may seek future funding to collect a three-time-point dataset on understanding cyberbullying (or intervening behavior upon witnessing it) in the future. Moreover, given that our cyberbullying intervention was preliminarily successful, we can realistically consider beginning anti-cyberbullying interventions in schools and educational institutes to reduce the harm of cyberbullying at a local and eventually a societal level. Our major findings also revealed important factors that may explain cyber-bystanders helping behavior. Specifically, the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) appeared to be instrumental in increasing the likelihood of individuals intervening when witnessing cyberbullying. Key aspects of TPB, such as barriers to action and adjusting empirical and normative expectations should be further investigated to develop a behavior change campaign within the community. Future research could also focus on reducing the bystander effect and pluralistic ignorance through direct and indirect means of dealing with the negative effects of cyberbullying, whilst increasing the intervening of cyberbullying instances through mass media campaigns.

18602917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18602917.value: The study examined the phenomenon of cyberbullying and how cyber-bystanders or those who witness cyberbullying can be empowered to stop cyberbullies behavior and respond effectively to help the victims. Using a multiple measure approach, we found that cyber-bystanders' socio-emotional background, their attitudes about cyberbullying, their subjective beliefs about their ability to intervene, perceived social norms to intervene, and their own past involvement in victimization (or cyber-victimization) were significantly related to their intention or behavior to help a cyber-victim. Finally, it is notable that a short, few-week training program focused on anti-bullying can significantly increase individuals' awareness of cyberbullying, their likelihood, and intention to help cyber-victims, and efforts to combat cyberbullying. Therefore, the project contributes to the field by a) providing a clear and concise theoretical framework to explain intervening behavior of cyber-bystanders; b) informing the development of future anti-cyberbullying programmes which aim at promoting the awareness for and knowledge of combating cyberbullying among cyber-bystanders. All of which are key to future educational plans and policies.

18603117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603117.value: This oral history project aims to document the voices of Hong Kong leftist film workers who were active from 1949 to 1966 and to utilize their voices to reconstruct Cold War Hong Kong history. The principal investigator adopts the common usage of the term “leftist” during this era, defining leftist film workers as those who worked for the three major leftist film studios and the sole distributor of films made in the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Until the mid-1960s, leftists controlled a significant share of the Hong Kong film market, produced popular movies and exported their productions and PRC-made films to other Chinese communities. However, their role in Hong Kong history has not yet received adequate attention. David Faure has pointed out that to understand Hong Kong history, it is urgent for scholars to conduct research on local leftist organizations and to interview their veterans (Faure, 2009). This project aims to fill this gap by creating the first oral history archives about Hong Kong leftist film workers. The researcher will interview not only prominent actors/actresses, directors and playwrights, but also technicians, painters and administrators of the leftist organizations. Audio records, transcripts and artifacts will be housed permanently in the Education University of Hong Kong and a database will be created. The creation of the archives will contribute to the addition of firsthand sources to the highly limited pool of materials regarding the Hong Kong left. It will benefit historians and scholars in other disciplines who are interested in the development of the city. The researcher will also write three journal articles using the oral interviews along with untapped archival materials and other written and visual materials to address questions critical to the history of Hong Kong left. These questions include: (1) How did the leftist film workers interact with the colonial government, their Mainland counterparts and the PRC authorities? (2) How did they export Communist revolution to other regions? (3) How did different leftist organizations work with each other for a common cause? By addressing these questions, my articles will contribute to reconstructing the history of Cold War Hong Kong, the role of Hong Kong leftists in disseminating revolutionary ideas in the colony and to other regions, and the institutional history of the leftist organizations. My articles will also use empirical research to contribute to the theoretical discussions about the weaknesses and strengths of oral data as historical sources.

18603617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603617.value: Art museums are places where students learn from original artworks. Previous scholarship on museum education has placed the emphasis either on visitors’ experiences or on outcomes of learning gained from museum visits. There is a lack of empirical research into group dialogue – the most used education strategy in museums and the most basic component of teaching in classrooms. The proposed study will investigate the group dialogues conducted by teachers with students in museums and classrooms. Three modes of dialogue proposed by Hubard (2015) – predetermined, thematic and open – will be tested with primary school teachers and students. ‘Design-based research’, a method to identify improvements systematically from experiments in learning situations, will be the methodology employed. The study will be conducted in three phases. Phase 1 will involve the preparation of teacher participants for leading group dialogues and curriculum plan development. Ten teachers and about 270 sixth-grade students (age 12) from different primary schools will be invited to participate in the study. Five workshops on effective group dialogue strategy will be conducted for the teacher participants. They will develop two five- to six-week curriculum plans with each incorporating one museum visit. Phase 2 will focus on the implementation of the plans with the support of the investigators and the evaluation of teachers’ and students’ performance in the group dialogue. Data will be obtained from the teachers’ reflections, interviews, observations and video recordings of museum visits and classroom teaching before, during and after the implementation of the plans. Phase 3 will be the data analysis stage. Taking the Hong Kong context into consideration, the results of the study will be used to create a pedagogical model that is theoretically and practically sound. The study is particularly meaningful given the increased emphasis that has been placed on learning art criticism in the new Education Bureau Visual Arts (VA) curriculums. In the revised VA curriculum for primary one to secondary three levels, it is explicitly stated that art making should be learned in connection with art criticism. The study will also be a timely response to the development of the West Kowloon Cultural District. In 2019, the Museum+ will be launched and the Hong Kong Museum of Art will be re-opened after renovation. There will be numerous opportunities for students and members of the public to visit these purpose-built museums. In this connection, an educated audience and refined museum practices are much needed. 在展館及教室學習視覺藝術 : 小學師生對話及提問策略研究 藝術館是學生認識藝術原作的地方。過往有關藝術館教育的研究成果不是強調觀者的經驗，便是參觀藝術館於學習上的效用。小組對話 (Group dialogue) 是藝術館裏最常用的教學策略和學校教室中最基本的教學元件。然而，有關小組對話的實証研究卻相當缺乏。本研究將探討於藝術館和課室場景裡展開的師生對話。由Hubard (2015) 倡議的三種對話模式－預定式、主題式和開放式－將於小學教師和學生身上實踐和進行測試。本研究會採用設計研究法 (Design-based Research)，有系統地檢視對話及提問教學方法的成效。 本研究將會分為三個階段實行。第一階段為教師參與者提供訓練，學習帶領小組對話和建立課程計劃。八位教師和約二百二十位小六學生（約十二歲）會受邀自不同小學參與研究計劃。研究中共有五次工作坊，訓練教師帶領小組對話及不同的提問策略。教師會建立兩個為期五至六週的教學單元，每個單元均包含一次藝術館參觀活動。第二階段是教學單元的實施和評估。教師參與者將在研究者的支援下實行各自的單元教學。他們與學生在小組對話的表現將會被紀錄及評估。研究數據會取自教學單元實施前和後的教師教學自省記錄、訪問、教室及藝術館的觀察和錄影。第三階段則為數據分析。結合香港的情境，本研究的結果將能用作建立兼具理論和實踐的小組對話教學模式。 鍳於教育局於新的視覺藝術課程中強調學習藝術評賞的重要性，本研究的義意顯得尤其重大。修訂後的視覺藝術課程（小一至中三），明確指出藝術創作的學習應該與藝術評賞連繫。此外，本研究亦適時響應西九龍文化區的發展。在二零一九年，M+展館將會啟用，而香港藝術館經修葺後亦於同年重新開放。學生與公眾人士將會有大量機會參觀各展館。配合文化區的落成，曾受觀賞教育的觀眾尤為本地所需。

18603617.label: Realisation of objectives
18603617.value: Objective 1: To identify and describe the ways in which teachers translate group dialogue and questioning strategies into practice in the art museum and classroom context. The researcher synthesised Feldman’s (1992) art criticism model, the ‘seven questions’ approach proposed by Bell (2011), the four ‘Ways In’ questioning framework developed by Charman, Rose and Wilson (2006), Wolff and Geahigan’s (1997) inquiry-based art criticism learning, the Visual Thinking Strategies developed by Yenawine (2013), and Rorty’s (2014) interrogating questions and proposed a dialogue and questioning framework which was used as the experimental tool. The framework consists of six domains: Personal Connection, Observation, Visual Analysis, Context, Interpretation and Judgment. Teacher participants learned about and practiced the framework in a two-day workshop. During the development of the framework for each iteration of teaching in schools and museums, the researchers visited the teachers and provided suggestions for improvement, such as the selection of artworks, formulation of questions, and the design of relevant teaching activities. Objective 2: To field test and refine the group dialogue and questioning strategies at the senior primary school level. The study involved teachers, students and independent raters. Eight teacher participants were recruited. After the workshop, each teacher conducted five iterations of experimenting the dialogue and questioning framework in the 2018-19 school year, with three in classrooms and two in museums. Each iteration was between 25 and 40 minutes long. One teacher withdrew for medical reasons and thus only seven teachers and 187 sixth-grade students completed the study. A rubric consisting of six evaluative domains was developed by the researcher to assess the quality of the teacher-student dialogues. The dialogues were given a score from one to six in each domain by independent raters. The teacher participants were interviewed individually before the training and after each of the iterations in schools. The pre-training interview focused on the teachers’ original practice, their expectations of and difficulties with engaging students through questions in their art lessons. The post-iteration interviews focused on the improvements that had taken place after each iteration, the difficulties the teachers had encountered, and the impact they observed on teaching and learning. After all the iterations, a group interview was conducted which focused on the refinement of the dialogue and questioning framework. Objective 3: To develop and propose effective group dialogue and questioning strategies for primary school students learning visual arts. A dialogue and questioning framework has been developed: Personal Connection • Facilitate personal responses to and reflections on artworks • Focus on the connection between viewers’ personal experience, values and emotions related to the work • The main question: How do I participate in this viewing experience? • Curiosity and wonder about the work • Personal connections/views/thoughts and critical reflections on the work Observation • Lead viewers to observe and describe the work in detail • Prepare viewers to collect visual data for further investigation • Focus on the objects/events/matters depicted or presented in the work • The main question: What is happening in the work? What can I observe? • Able to observe and describe the work comprehensively Visual Analysis • Guide viewers to analyse the work from a formalistic/aesthetic/perceptual perspective • Focus on the visual elements and their relationships • The main question: What are the colour, shape, proportion, space, and process of making of the work? • Identification of the use of formal elements and visual organisation • Understanding of the making process and the use of materials Context • Make viewers aware of their incomplete understanding of the work if certain contexts are missing • Assume that the work is a product of culture, reflecting different contexts • The main question: When, where, for whom, and how has the work been created and presented? • Knowledge of relevant contextual information: politics, culture, economy, technology, history, etc. • Understanding of the ways in which the work was created, displayed and appreciated Interpretation • Explore the meanings of the work • Focus on one’s interpretation of the work with explanation and justification • The main question: What are the messages, themes and emotions of the work? • Reasonable, informed and convincing interpretation • Justification of one’s own interpretation Judgment • Guide viewers to rationalise their own judgment • Focus on the critique and judgment of the work • The main question: What is the value of the work? • Argument to support the judgment Objective 4: To investigate the effectiveness of group dialogue and questioning strategies in enhancing student learning of visual arts. A quantitative analysis was conducted on the number of questions asked and the rating of dialogue performance. For the classroom dialogues, the total number of questions asked increased significantly from 395 in the baseline observation to 814 in the third iteration. A series of paired-samples t-tests were conducted to compare the performance of teacher-student dialogues between the baseline teaching and each iteration. In the first iteration, no statistically significant increases were observed in the scores for any of the domains. In the second iteration, there were statistically significant increases in the total score and in the scores for two domains (Personal Connection and Evaluation). In the third iteration, there were statistically significant increases in the total score and in the scores for three domains (Observation, Interpretation and Evaluation). In summary, the overall scores for the classroom dialogues had improved significantly after all except the first iteration. However, the improvements in each domain varied each time. Similar result was found in the number of questions asked in the museum dialogues. There were statistically significant increases in the total score and in the scores of Interpretation and Evaluation in the first iteration and Visual Analysis and Interpretation in the second iteration. Objective 5: To evaluate the impact and outcomes of group dialogue and questioning strategies on student learning of visual arts. Diverse perspectives on the investigation of artworks In the baseline teaching, the teachers had a relatively narrow focus and investigation of artworks was primarily used as a preparation for the ensuing art making activities. However, in the three iterations, the students were exposed to different kinds of information either discovered by themselves or prompted by teachers. These changes had enabled the students to construct more personal, diversified and contextual interpretations of artworks, rather than simply giving superficial responses. Ownership of /involvement in the investigation of a work The dialogue and questioning framework provided students with a learning experience with a greater sense of ownership. It was observed from the baseline teaching that most of the students lacked sufficient skills or knowledge to make visual analyses and were afraid to make mistakes. Questions on personal connections provided a relatively easy and comfortable way for students to enter the dialogue. Instead of being detached from the investigation, they became the ones who were investigating. Change from glancing to examining In the three iterations, when the teachers kept guiding and posed more observation questions, the students were stimulated to observe and to discover what could be found out from the artwork. When more content was revealed, the students became curious about what else they could find out from the work. As a result, students became more willing to examine the work and respond to the teacher’s questions. More conceptual development in art making Some of the teachers reported that after a deep investigation of selected artworks, the students displayed a better conceptual design in their own art creations. Some students were used to copying representations or imitating expressions they learned from artworks. However, after a thorough investigation of the artworks, they used more of their own images, representations or expressions to deliver the messages of their artworks.

18603617.label: Major findings and research outcome
18603617.value: Major Findings A dialogue and questioning framework was developed and tested in schools and museums in five iterations. A quantitative analysis was conducted on the number of questions asked and the rating of dialogue performance. For the teaching in schools, the total number of questions asked increased significantly from 395 in the baseline observation to 814 in the third iteration. A series of paired-samples t-tests were conducted to compare the performance of teacher-student dialogues between the baseline teaching and each iteration. The overall scores for the classroom dialogues improved significantly except in the first iteration. Similar findings were found in the teaching in museums. The results of the study indicated that the dialogue and questioning framework is an effective pedagogy, particularly when teachers were trained to use it. It works well in classroom teaching when the focus was on one or a few artworks. With data collected from teaching observations, rating results and interviews with teacher participants, the followings were observed: Impact on student learning 1. Demonstration of diverse perspectives on the investigation of artworks 2. Ownership of /involvement in the investigation of a work 3. Change from glancing to examining 4. More conceptual development in art making Impact on teaching 1. Concern with students’ ownership of learning and connection to artworks 2. Improved interpretation questioning 3. Introducing judgment questions Research Outcome 1. Publication: Two papers were published in Research in Arts Education (2019) and the Australian Art Education (2019). One paper was submitted to The International Journal of Art & Design Education and under revision. 2. Invited Speech: Three speeches were given at the High School Fine Arts Education Resource Centre, Ministry of Education, Taiwan (04/2019), the National Changhua University of Education (05/2019) and the Virginia Commonwealth University (10/2019). 3. Paper Presentation: Four papers were presented at the InSEA Asia Regional Congress (Hong Kong, 12/2018), the National Visual Art Education Conference (Canberra, 01/2019), the 36th InSEA World Congress (Vancouver, 07/2019), and the International Council of Museums General Conference (Kyoto, 09/2019). 4. Website: 29 dialogue and questioning plans (14 in both English and Chinese and 15 in Chinese) were uploaded to the bilingual website ‘Learning and Teaching Art Criticism’ (www.artcrit.eduhk.hk). As at June 2021, 1,043 teachers and students have registered as members and the website was visited 17,383 times. 5. Workshop: A workshop for the EDB Primary School Visual Arts Professional Learning Community (1/12/2020) and five school workshops (30/10/2018, 30/11/2018, 20/3/2019, 10/11/2020, 19/11/2020) were held for 92 teachers. 6. School Project: A professional development project on dialogue and questioning strategy for four primary schools was initiated by the Christian Alliance S. Y. Yeh Memorial Primary School (8/2020-12/2021).

18603617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18603617.value: Consolidating the findings of the study, a 3-hour mini-MOOC was developed and incorporated in one of the researcher’s undergraduate courses. Students took it as part of the course and were required to design a dialogue and questioning plan. The quality of the plans was very good and some of them were uploaded to the researcher’s art criticism website. The mini-MOOC can be developed into a full MOOC for in-service local and overseas teachers. It has the potential to reach a much wider audience and engage teachers to use the dialogue and questioning framework in authentic teaching situations. In the interviews, teachers showed their concerns about connecting art appreciation to the teaching of art making. In teachers’ mind, many questions asked on artworks are directly related to the follow-up creating activities. Even teachers can engage students in talking about artworks, it is a challenge to connect it to art making. In this connection, I worked on a new GRF proposal on connecting art appreciation to art making using a virtual exhibition. The project “Creating Connections: A Study of the Impact and Effectiveness of a Visual Arts Teacher-curator Pedagogy” was funded for implementation in January 2021 (HK$889,420. GRF, 01/2021 – 06/2023).

18603617.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18603617.value: The present study investigated the dialogues and questions conducted by teachers with students – the most basic component of teaching in classrooms and the most used education strategy in museums. Synthesizing art criticism models, dialogue approaches and questioning strategies reviewed from the literature, a dialogue and questioning framework was developed and used as the experimental tool. The framework consists of six domains: Personal Connection, Observation, Visual Analysis, Context, Interpretation and Judgment. In the school year of 2018-19, seven primary school teachers experimented the framework with 187 sixth-grade students in five iterations in schools and museums. Data were collected through interviews, observations and video recordings of classroom teaching and museum visits before, during and after the implementation of the plans. A quantitative analysis was conducted on the number of questions asked and the rating of dialogue performance. In both schools and museums, the total number of questions asked increased significantly in the final iteration. There were also statistically significant increases in the total score measuring dialogue performance. The findings of the study indicated that the dialogue and questioning framework is an effective pedagogy, particularly when teachers were trained to use it and when the focus was on one or a few artworks.

18603717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603717.value: 就以複雜詞庫而言，詞彙可再細分為詞彙闊度及詞彙深度。詞彙闊度可容易被定義，即是個人可容納的詞彙數量。相反，詞彙深度的概念可從多方面探討。因此，本研究以英語作為第二語言的華人學生為對象，探討中文及英文詞彙深度的概念結構，及探討詞彙深度與詞彙闊度在概念上的差異。研究均指出詞彙對閱讀理解上扮演著很重要的角色。過往研究顯示詞彙的初期程度及增長分別與英語作為母語的學生的閱讀理解能力及英語作為第二語言的學生的閱讀理解能力有獨特的關係。就此研究範圍而言，詞彙深度在英語作為第二語言之學生中所扮演之角色並未曾進行深入了解。因此，本研究旨在探討詞彙深度在排除詞彙闊度的因素後於閱讀理解中所扮演的角色。由於母語及第二語言之間的關係已被廣泛認受，不少研究均提出母語及第二語言之間轉換的議題，但有關不同語言的詞彙及閱讀理解之間的轉換之研究則缺乏。在本研究中，我們將會探討英語作為第二語言之華人學生的跨語言詞彙及閱讀理解之間的轉換。在此追蹤性研究，研究人員將追蹤300位小三 (8歲) 學生，為期2年。一系列中文及英文詞彙及認字測試將會分4次進行，每次相隔6個月。閱讀理解將會在第一次測試、第四次測試及其六個月後進行。詞彙測試的量度模型將會被測試。潛在的成長模型將被用作探討母語及第二語言的詞彙闊度、詞彙深度及認字的發展。這些技巧的初期程度及其發展將會被用作預測閱讀理解的成績。我們特別感興趣探討在詞彙闊度、認字的初期程度及其發展被以統計方式控制的情況下，詞彙深度的初期程度及其發展 (這些潛在變數由量度模型的結果決定) 是否獨特促成閱讀理解能力。同時，我們亦有意探討母語及第二語言之間的轉換。理論層面方面，本次以英語作為第二語言之華人學生為對象的研究將促使詞彙及閱讀理解之間的縱向關係得以從動態發展方面探討。實際層面上，教育工作者及行內專業人士可參考本研究結果，對英語作為第二語言之華人學生提供早期閱讀發展的教育支援。

18604317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18604317.value: This GRF study aims to measure and understand the perception of Hong Kong secondary school teachers on their national identity and National Education after the anti-National Education and Occupy movements. The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government announced the mandatory subject of Moral and National Education (MNE) to replace “moral and civic education” in 2011 for all government and aided primary and secondary schools. But several thousand of people protested against it and the government finally decided to shelve MNE. Civic education has since remained a non-mandatory school-based subject. However, civic education is important for cultivating coming generations who live under the “One Country, Two Systems” principle. The Occupy and Umbrella Movement in 2014 saw a wide participation by youngsters with implications for ideas of localism, calls for self-determination and independence. The District Board and Legislative Council elections in 2015 and 2016 further testified to the need for understanding the perception of identity. All these developments call for teachers to take action on civic education, and thus show the need for an investigation on how civic educators perceive national identity and National Education as they are teaching students about their identity and national orientations. This study will adopt mixed methods (Teddie &Tashakkori, 2009) for triangulation, which include questionnaires for teachers; interviews with purposive samples of teachers, parents and students; non-participant observation and document analysis. This study will measure how teachers’ perceptions influence their understanding of teaching (Fullan, 1989), against the relationship between variables of perception of national identity and National Education. The test will use statistical measurements and structural equation modelling. This study will also interview teachers on what are facilitating and hindering factors of implementing National Education and how it is related to civic education from the perspectives of educators, parents and students. With reference to Chong (2012) and Leung & Print (2002), this study’s validated questionnaire (Leung & Print, 2002) and interview design was informed by a framework based on critical patriot (Fairbrother, 2003, 2004) typologies on National Education; of cosmopolitan, civic, cultural, anti-colonial and totalitarian nationalism; and pedagogies including issue-based critical thinking (Hahn, 1998); participatory and affective approaches (Brown, 2001). Also, a multiple citizenship model (Heater 1990) guides the setting of interview questions for studying the relationships between National Education and civic education. The findings on the relationship between teachers’ perception on their national identity and teaching of National Education will contribute to a conceptual modelling. 本研究計劃旨在瞭解香港中學公民教育教師對國民教育的看法，將邀請教師、家長和學生參與，以瞭解不同公民教育持份者對國民教育的看法，也作為研究資料的互相印證。本研究將邀請全港中學的公民教育老師(每校約三至四位)填寫一份六頁的問卷，以瞭解他們對國民教育的目的、內容及教學方法的意見。其次，本研究將會按老師們在問卷的回應類型，挑選約40位來自不同學校的老師，進行深入個人訪談，以瞭解他們對國民教育的深入看法，並進行公民教育/國民教育的觀課活動。另一方面，本研究將會邀請家長和已成中學階段的學生/大專學生，參加深入焦點小組訪談，以瞭解他們對國民教育的看法。

18606017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18606017.value: Existing literature demonstrates the relevance of both institutional and cultural issues to understanding higher education (HE) governance. On this basis, this research will examine the complexity of the relationship between governance and the institutional and cultural settings in the HE systems of three Chinese societies – Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. The comparative analysis to be developed in this research is guided by an analytical framework which comprises three dimensions. Through a comparison of (1) substantive governance matters, the research seeks to penetrate down to modes of (2) institutional balance of power and patterns of (3) cultural hybridity in the three HE systems. The research employs a mixed-method strategy that consists of semi-structured interviews and a small-scale survey. The research will solicit interview data through a purposive selection of respondents from key system-level governing bodies, and will use case studies to secure data from university-level governing bodies. The primary goal of the interviews is to explain the coordination mechanism in HE governance by examining interactions and relationships among the various actors on governance matters. Evidence collected from the interviews will also be used to construct a taxonomy of institutional balance of power. A series of open-ended descriptions of governance matters will be developed during the interviews. These open-ended descriptions will provide examples of cultural hybridity. Based on the open-ended descriptions, a small-scale survey will be designed and implemented. A total of 450 manager-academics will be asked to rate scenarios of governance matters and cultural hybridity in terms of their realism and acceptableness. A correlation analysis, which takes account of this perception of cultural hybridity and its connection with institutional arrangements, will illustrate the complex relationships between institutional forms and cultural features of HE governance in the three societies. One important contribution this research will make will be to deepen our understanding of the organisational and cultural conditions of academic work in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, three post-colonial societies in proximity to mainland China. Their colonial history and close but complicated relationships with the Chinese mainland justify an exploration of relationships between institutional and cultural issues in academia from a comparative perspective. The research will complement the researchers’ previous work on hybridisation of academic values and briefs, and will enrich both empirical and theoretical knowledge of the nature and consciousness of being Chinese to HE development in Chinese societies. 現有文獻指出研究制度和文化問題對於了解高等教育治理非常重要。在此基礎上，本研究將探討香港、澳門和台灣三個華人社會的高等教育治理與制度和文化情景的複雜關係。是項比較研究以一個三維模型為分析框架，通過比較（1）實質性治理事項，透視三地的高等教育體系中（2）制度的權力平衡模式和（3）文化的糅合方式。 本研究採用混合方法策略，當中包括半結構訪談和小規模問卷調查。本研究將通過立意抽樣方法選擇三地的高等教育體系的主要領導機構成員為受訪者，並以案例研究方法選擇大學管理層為受訪對象。訪談的主要目的是通過審視各個參與者在治理事項上的互動和關係來說明高等教育治理的協調機制。從訪談中獲得的資訊亦將用於構建一個制度權力平衡的分類法。在訪談期間，受訪者同時會對治理事項作開放性描述，為文化糅合方式提供例子。 小規模問卷調查將根據開放性描述的內容設計，並邀請450位擔任管理職務的學者對描述中的治理事項和文化糅合方式的真實性和認同程度評分。透過相關性分析，本研究將審視調查受訪對象對文化糅合方式的觀念與制度模式的聯繫，以說明三地的高等教育治理中制度模式和文化特徵之間的複雜關係。 著眼於香港、澳門和台灣這三個接鄰中國內地的後殖民社會，是項研究將加深我們對三地學術工作的組織和文化狀況的認識。三地的殖民地歷史及其與中國內地密切而複雜的關係解釋了為何我們要從比較角度探索它們學術界的制度與文化之間的關係。本研究將補充研究人員以往關於學術價值與文化糅合的研究，並豐富我們對華人的特質和意識如何影響華人社會的高等教育發展這問題的實證和理論知識。

18606017.label: Realisation of objectives
18606017.value: The four objectives listed in the research proposal have been fully achieved. Objective 1 was to address the roles and capacities of major governing actors in higher education governance in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. This has been achieved through two pathways. The first pathway is through an analysis of relevant documents published by higher education governing bodies in the three systems. The documentary research helped us to understand the similarities and differences between governance structures of universities in the three societies. For example, we recognised that though university autonomy was emphasised in all these higher education systems, it was upheld to different extents and in different ways. The second pathway compared the result of the documentary analysis with data collected from semi-structured interviews. One example of this was to compare the roles of the university steering bodies noted in the documents with those described by our interviewees. We also examined the mechanism of coordination among the internal and external governing actors (Objective 2) and analysed its relationship with institutional balance of power in higher education (the first part of Objective 3) through an empirical investigation of governance matters (i.e. financial governance, staffing matters and substantive issues). As planned, the data was collected mainly through interviews with 58 respondents from higher education governing bodies. These respondents included seven respondents from system-level governing agencies and 51 interviewees from university-level governing bodies in the three societies. As the government agency in Macau declined our interview request, we interviewed a lawmaker who was heavily involved in the making of Macau’s higher education laws as compensation. The findings from the interview data showed how the coordination mechanisms and institutional balance of power in the three higher education systems corresponded to the three major coordination approaches (i.e. state-centred approach, market-oriented approach and academic self-governance) identified in the literature. For example, one set of these findings related to how managerialism has influenced the ethos and practices of universities and thus has substantially undermined the significance of academic self-governance in understanding contemporary university governance in the three societies. Our project also aimed to examine cultural hybridity in higher education governance (the second part of Objective 3). This has been achieved through two pathways. The first pathway was through the development of a set of open-ended descriptions of governance matters in which hybrid elements emerged. These open-ended descriptions, which were collected from the 58 interviews with respondents from governing bodies, illustrated how cultural hybridity characterised the behaviours performed in the governance matters. As planned, 12 situations of cultural hybridity were developed from the open-ended descriptions collected. These situations of cultural hybridity provided evidences for the significance of hybridisation in understanding university governance in the three Chinese societies. The second pathway was a small-scale survey. A seven-point grading scale on hybrid elements was developed based on the open-ended descriptions. A sample of 261 participants, who were academics with managerial role in their universities, rated the 12 scenarios of cultural hybridity in terms of their realism and acceptableness. This survey showed the extent to which cultural hybridity explained the behaviours seen in the governance matters, and captured cultural differences in handling governance matters in the three higher education systems. In general, the findings revealed that Macau had greater acceptance of these cultural scenarios in comparison with Hong Kong and Taiwan. However, the figures also indicated that most of these cultural situations were generally considered unacceptable, though their likelihood varied in the three places. A major purpose of the study was to investigate conceptual implications of the institutional and cultural differences and/or similarities in higher education governance (Objective 4). To achieve this objective, we compared the data on institutional balance of power with the data on cultural hybridity to draw conclusions about the pattern of higher education governance. We also compared the findings from the three systems, and explicitly discussed the relevance of Chinese cultural elements to higher education in these three Chinese societies. While confirming the existence of Chineseness in the three systems, we suggested that, given the strong influences of contemporary managerial discourses, cultural scripts and legacies subtly influenced their institutional development and imperatives.

18606017.label: Major findings and research outcome
18606017.value: This study explored the nature of university governance and its implications for hybridisation (i.e. the integration and competition between different cultural values) of higher education in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. The study’s findings enhance understanding of university governance in the contexts of Chinese societies. It found that, despite emphasising university autonomy in the three systems, different agents (e.g. university leaders, academic staff, students and lay members) understood the concept differently. This finding vividly illustrated the complexity of the coordination mechanism in higher education governance. Following the comments from the mid-term progress report review, we reported this finding by focusing on the interpretation and implementation of university autonomy in Hong Kong in order to provide a timely response to the changing socio-political contexts that substantially influenced the state-university relation in the city (see Outputs 1 and 2). Meanwhile, while data suggested that cultural scripts and legacies influenced higher education governance in a rather implicit manner, our findings identified both similarities and differences in the trajectories of the development of higher education in the three societies. Thus, we have conducted a comparative study that saw higher education development as a complex interacting process in which historical, cultural and political factors interacted with each other (see Output 3) and explained the hybrid and organisational settings of university in the three Chinese societies (see Outputs 4–6). Based on the findings of this comparison, we organised a couple of panel sessions in international conferences, and have secured a special issue in a reputable journal in the field. This special issue includes three articles on Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan respectively for disseminating the findings.

18606017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18606017.value: By examining the nature of higher education governance and its implications for hybridisation of higher education in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, this project comprehensively responded to the question of how cultural scripts and legacies, which are derived from cultural roots of societies, influence institutional development and imperatives in higher education. This GRF project triggered the PI’s interest in further exploring the significance of Chinese cultural elements in higher education governance. A new GRF proposal entitled “From Excellence to Impact: A Comparative Study of Research Assessment in Hong Kong and the United Kingdom” has been submitted to RGC for funding consideration. In this proposed research, Chinese cultural elements are considered as a counter to Anglo-American culture to construct a theoretical framework for comparing how the impact agenda is received in Hong Kong and the UK. Additionally, the special issue generated from this project opens up a discussion about the significance of Chinese cultural elements in higher education governance in other Chinese societies and overseas Chinese communities (i.e. Mainland China, Singapore and Malaysia). Further research will be conducted to explore how cultural scripts and legacies have influenced the trajectory of the higher education systems in Chinese societies and how these created distinct forms of governance.

18606017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18606017.value: Both institutional and cultural issues are significant in understanding higher education governance. This study collected data from interviews with respondents from higher education governing bodies and a small-scale survey to examine the complex relationships between institutional forms and cultural features of higher education governance in three Chinese societies – Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. The study showed how Chinese cultural elements together with other contemporary ideas and discourses have variously influenced the institutional development of higher education in these three systems. Its results also shed light on how the roles and functions of universities were understood within the cultural as well as socio-political contexts of the Chinese societies. Thus, this comparative study has enhanced understanding of the organisational and cultural conditions of academic work in Chinese societies.

18606417.label: Realisation of objectives
18606417.value: The selected book chapter, “A Turning Point in History of Cantonese Writing: City Magazine and its Views on Languages in 1980s Hong Kong”, aims at explaining the importance of Cantonese Writing in the process of identity building. Objective 3 is regarded as the theme of the chapter. In this way, it would be fully realized. The PI, the sole author of the preparing chapter, would introduce five major parts of content to argue that attitudes and choices of written languages of founders and writers of City Magazine in the late 1970s and 1980s, signified a critical change in the relation of identity and written languages of Hong Kong. The five major parts of the contents are as follow: 1. Economic and demographic changes of Hong Kong in the 1970s The “Baby Boom” after WWII signified critical changes in the history, culture, and literature of Hong Kong. In the mid-1970s, some young literati of this baby boomer generation who had studied in America and Europe came back to Hong Kong shortly after finishing their programs. This generation, unlike their parents’ generations, did not have a hometown in Mainland China to return to and Hong Kong has become their hometown. The convergence of the economic take-off and maturity of baby boomers contributed innovative energy and openness of visions to Hong Kong culture which further flourished in the 1980s. There were many significant features in this baby-boomer generation. Their cultural activities and products became milestones of literature, publication, film industry, etc. City Magazine is one of the most representative examples. 2. Background of the founders and writers of City Magazine The major founders, editors, and writers of City Magazine, e.g. Chan Koon Chung (1952-), Joseph Yau Sai Man (1951-1998), and Dunn Siu-Yue (1952-) are all baby-boomers. This generation was born and grown up in a city that no longer a migration place of refugees. From this generation onwards, identity issues of local-born Hongkongers became inevitable. Their childhood and life goals are completely different from their parents who mostly fled from mainland China in the 1950s. In addition, Chan, Yau and Dunn were well-educated elites. They graduated from local famous secondary schools and university, continued their study in America and Europe. The social and educational backgrounds were influential in forming their international visions. Chan and the editorial team cared much about the social and cultural development of Hong Kong rather than the sustainability of tradition in China. Like many baby boomers in other countries in the 1960s and 70s, they were discontent about the reality and believed that they could, at least to a certain extent, changed this reality for a better future. Writings and publications were regarded as useful tools in the period especially Chan and Dunn were further educated Journalism in America. With the contributions of talented editors and writers, City Magazine further developed the local Hong Kong identity by using a kind of written language that contained Standard Chinese, Cantonese, and English. This turned City Magazine into a “trendsetter” in written Cantonese as even educated elites valued the vernacular as a written language. 3. Discussions of written languages in City Magazine By analyzing the views and discussions of choices in written languages, it is clear that the writers of City Magazine advocated an equal and open-minded attitude towards languages. As young intellectuals in the late 1970s and 80s, they strongly objected to the unified and static form of written languages. City Magazine suggested local identity and at the same time worldwide vision in using Cantonese. This is valuable for today’s Hong Kong when the usage of Cantonese writing becomes highly politicalized. As early as 1979, Chan emphasized the important role of “written language” by writing an essay named “City Language”. He stated clearly that Hong Kong had already had its written language. It was the printed media that still hesitated to use the unique language but only the printed media could transform innovative spoken language in daily life into readable words. In Dec 1982, Joseph Yau argued that Chinese intellectuals tried to politicalize languages to protect their social and cultural interests. (“To Purify the Chinese Language”) 4. Language use and Genres in literary works of Joseph Yau The importance of Yau’s literary works and his status in Hong Kong literature would be discussed under the consideration of this project title, i.e. usage of various written language and development of different genres. On a Weekend Bed: narratives in standard Chinese and dialogue in Cantonese, with partial English in vocabularies and sentences. Smart-Ass: in form of authentic Cantonese and “the Quotation”, a creative demonstration of anxiety, collective behavior, and consciousness, style of speaking of Hong Kong people in the 1980s-90s. 5. Conventional attitude towards written Chinese To compare and contrast the views of City Magazine, representative views of other parties would be introduced. Take the column of “Chinese Language Mailbox” (1979.6 – 1981.11) of Overseas Chinese Daily News as an example, a reader of Baptist College suggested that “Because of popularization of social education, there is mixture usage of regional dialects. ‘national language of literature’ and ‘literature of national language’ cannot be implemented. In addition, Chinese writing becomes unclear in the meaning of vocabularies, not understandable in structure, mix with slangs and vulgar sentences…” It was not surprising that editors of City Magazine received complaints when they published essays with hybrid language consists of Standard Chinese, English, and Cantonese. In Part 1 & 2, PI would explain the origin and background of the emergence of written languages of City Magazine and why this is closely related to the identity establishment process in the 1970s and 80s. Part 3 & 4 analyze why and how writers and editors of City Magazine cannot use Standard Chinese only and reveal the important meaning of this choice. As stated above, much persuasive and interesting evidence would be involved. These four parts would fully realize Objectives 1 & 2 and contribute to Objective 3 as the theme of the chapter. Part 5 is indispensable in revealing identity issues in language choice. It is important in providing a convincing comparison to contrast language views of City Magazine is contradictory against major cultural and educational parties. In this way, this part helps to realize Objectives 1 & 2.

18606417.label: Major findings and research outcome
18606417.value: The major findings are as follow: 1. There is imitate relationship between the mother tongue and its people. The value of local languages is irreplaceable and should be regarded as a resource of creativity. This finding seems only common knowledge, however, the pressure of national language upon local languages will never fade. The project emphasizes the importance of local languages in the formation of identity and cultural production. 2. Cantonese writing signifies the uniqueness of Hong Kong history, literature, and culture. Usage of Cantonese in writings serves many purposes and does not necessarily lead to localism in a narrow sense. Although Joseph Yau and City Magazine had not advocated Cantonese writing, the experience in usage of Cantonese in writing is invaluable to Hong Kong nowadays. Joseph Yau, as an important author in the history of Hong Kong literature, involved Cantonese in many different ways. He used Cantonese to represent and also criticize the local culture and characters of common Hong Kong people. The international visions on cultures and dynamic attitude regarding written languages are legacy City Magazine that needs to be reminded and reinforced. 3. Joseph Yau’s contributions to Cantonese writing and Hong Kong literature are unique and irreplaceable. There has been an acknowledgment of the contributions of Joseph Yau in local academia, however, not many specific research outputs delicate to him. This finding supplements this important blank. The representative work of Yau, On a Weekend Bed, has been an important experiment with all dialogue written in Cantonese. The breakthrough in the genre of Smart-Ass is impossible without Cantonese. The research outcome: With the publication of the book chapter, the long-term impact of the research project would exceed what the proposal stated. For the first time, research findings of Cantonese writing in literary studies would be put into the context of international academia and Sinographic Cosmopolis. Under the book title, The Politics of Language: Sinitic Scripts in Asia Since 1900, Cantonese writing in investigating from innovative perspectives like Sinitic scripts, Sinography and modernization of Asia. Brill Publishers in Leiden has been an internationally famous scholarly publisher that focuses on Sinography. Other contributors including senior scholars specialized in Asian studies are from America, Europe, Mainland China, Korea, etc. Moreover, the PI has benefited from communication with other contributors of the book when a series of online workshops were held in early May 2021. By presenting her preliminary outline of the chapter, the PI received constructive comments from scholars in Italy, America, Mainland China, and Hong Kong. (413 words)

18606417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18606417.value: Among many cases of Cantonese writing that have already been studied by the PI, Joseph Yau and City Magazine is especially important as it is closely related to the historical development and identity building of Hong Kong. Therefore, the research would form an important section of PI’s next monograph which focuses on the development of Cantonese writing in post-war Hong Kong. In preparing the book chapter, the PI has further communicated with linguistics. “Written Cantonese” has been a well-developed field in linguistics. The PI has been borrowed concepts and research findings from linguists. However, she finds that it is necessary to state clearly that “Cantonese Writing” is a field in literary studies. Although it can be regarded as interdisciplinary specialization closely related to social linguistics, “Cantonese Writing” is not only concerned with Cantonese as a language in that piece of literary works but also is considered as an organic component. Its literary effects, styles, and its relationship with other languages used are important approaches for analysis. At the same time, “Cantonese Writing” is different from “dialect literature” which does not emphasize very much historical, social and cultural context. In this way, the PI will broaden the boundary of literary studies. This would be another important section of her next monograph. In addition, the PI plans to further consider the possibility of investigating contributions of Cantonese Writing under the context of Asia and Sinographic Cosmopolis. (234 words)

18606417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18606417.value: This is a research project on Cantonese writing in literary studies. Regarding Joseph Yau and City Magazine as a representative case in the late 1970s to 80s, the project reveals the uniqueness of Hong Kong history, literature, and culture. The findings demonstrate the values and significance of local language in writing and publication in process of identity establishment. According to the views of Joseph Yau and City Magazine, choices of written languages should align with living experience and reality. In the late 1970s and 80s when Hong Kong reached its peak in economic and cultural development, the editors and writers of City Magazine found that only a “City Language” can represent the young cosmopolis. The hybridity of languages of this “City Language” symbolizes the diversity of cultures which demonstrates the unique nature and history of Hong Kong. With an in-depth investigation of discussions and literary works of Joseph Yau and City Magazine, the project emphasizes that different written languages should be regarded as creative resources in equal status. By analyzing various texts and genres in City Magazine, the research team would like to remind Hong Kong society with many valuable beliefs of Joseph Yau and City Magazine, e.g. open-minded attitude to language choice, dynamic and innovative creativity, the courage of self-criticism, and international localism. In this way, this project urges for “language awareness in heteroglossia” and “equality of language use”. The project suggests that both concepts are important in the future development of the written languages and culture of Hong Kong. (244 words)

18606717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18606717.value: This proposed study will investigate the obstacles and success factors influencing the enrolment of immigrant, minority and low-income youth in post-secondary education (PSE) in Hong Kong, with reference to educational access, equity and outcomes. Immigrant and ethnic minority populations are among the fastest growing groups around the world and often overlap with the low income class. It remains a significant challenge for each of these categories to gain access to PSE and to be successful. The under-representation of South Asian and mainland Chinese immigrant youth in PSE has raised serious concerns about education access and equity. Many young people in that low-income category say they lack both the confidence to be accepted and the financial means to realise their aspirations. The barriers outlined above are likely to affect the different groups in different ways, and knowing the underlying reasons behind this phenomenon both overall and for each group will help narrow unacceptable disparities in access to education. The proposed study will employ a mixed-method approach to provide the empirical data necessary to shed new light on the complexities of educational decision making for PSE pathways among the young people in these sectors. Cross-sectional survey data will be collected using the modified Factors Influencing Pursuit of Higher Education Questionnaire (Harris & Halpin, 1999; 2002), while qualitative data will be generated through multiple case studies (Yin, 2014) and three rounds of longitudinal tracking and in-depth interviews. The multiple data sets will offer a holistic understanding of the educational pathways and choices of some of the most disadvantaged student groups in an Asian context. The objectives are: (1) to analyse the patterns of the academic and career pathways of immigrant, minority and low-income youth by tracking their graduation from secondary education; (2) to compare the types of PS institutions in which these groups first enrolled with those selected by their more socially advantaged counterparts; (3) to identify the obstacles and success factors of immigrant, minority and low-income youth in the transition from secondary to PSE in Hong Kong; (4) to provide evidence-based recommendations for promoting social equitable policy and enhancing successful PSE preparation programmes for all students; (5) to generate a data-set to understand the strategies in creating human capabilities and economic returns for immigrant, minority and low-income youth in Hong Kong; (6) to advance theory in understanding the complexities of what is a common issue worldwide by engaging in discourse with international scholars.

18607017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18607017.value: As the mechanisms underlying parental control and child aggression both involve the use of manipulation to achieve their desired outcomes in relationships, a growing body of research has focused on the association between types of parental control (e.g. physical coercion and psychological control) and forms of aggression (e.g. physical aggression and relational aggression). But important research questions remain, such as 1) what are Chinese parents’ beliefs on parental control; 2) what are the bidirectional relations between parental control and child aggression; and, 3) does child temperament moderate the links between parental control and child aggression? This study aims to explore Chinese parents’ beliefs on parental control (Study 1) as well as to analyze the bidirectional relations between parental control and child aggression and the parenting-by-temperament interaction effect on child aggression (Study 2) using a two-wave longitudinal, mixed methods, and multi-informant research design with a Hong Kong preschool sample. Stratified random sampling will be used to recruit one kindergarten in each of the three strata (i.e. high, middle and low income) developed based on the median monthly household income of the districts. Within each kindergarten, one class of each grade (a nursery, lower and upper kindergarten class), with children aged three to six years, will be randomly selected, totaling nine classes. A new nursery class will be recruited in each kindergarten in the following academic year (i.e. Study 2) when the upper kindergarten classes from Study 1 have graduated. In Study 1, one parent of a boy and one parent of a girl from each participating class will be randomly selected for individual interviews (N1 = 18). In Study 2, 180 children and their parents will be recruited (20 children X 3 classes X 3 kindergartens). At both Time 1 (i.e. November) and Time 2 (i.e. May), lead teachers in each classroom will provide ratings of physical and relational aggression for each participating child, while the child’s mother and father will be asked to complete a survey to report on their own and their spouse’s parental control, as well as to assess their child's temperament. Research assistants will also visit each kindergarten to conduct child tasks to assess child temperament and aggression. The procedures and measures at Time 1 and Time 2 will be the same, except child temperament will only be assessed at Time 1. 本研究旨在運用混合研究方法探索中國父母對父母控制的信念、分析父母控制與兒童攻擊之間的雙向關係、並探討兒童氣質如何影響父母教養與兒童攻擊之間的關係。 本研究將根據各區每月家庭入息中位數， 從高中低三個收入分層各隨機招募一間幼稚園，並在每間幼稚園內文邀請幼、中及高各一班之學生及家長參與 。 在第一個階段，研究將於每個班別隨機挑選一名男孩和一名女孩的家長進行個人訪談（N1 = 18）。 在第二個階段 ， 共180名兒童及其家長（20名兒童X 3班X 3幼稚園）將會被邀請參與評估及測試。首先，每位班主任將評估每位參與的兒童的攻擊行為，而兒童的母親和父親則會完成一份問卷，報告自己和其配偶的父母控制，以及評估孩子的氣質。最後，研究助理亦將會到訪每間幼稚園，為參與的兒童評估兒童的氣質和攻擊行為。

18607017.label: Realisation of objectives
18607017.value: This study contributed to a theoretical understanding of Chinese parents’ beliefs about coercive parenting as well as the bidirectional relations between coercive parenting and child aggression and the parenting-by-temperament interaction effect on child aggression. The achievement of the objectives lay the foundation upon which further support can be built in the community for facilitating parenting from the early education years, particularly in the Chinese context. Below is the summary of how the project objectives have been fully achieved. Objective 1: To explore Chinese parents’ beliefs on parental control Study 1 was designed to achieve Objective 1 of this project, in which 18 parents (one father and 17 mothers) were invited to participate in individual interviews to share their experience of parenting and respond to questions developed based on a review of the literature, to assess: 1) parents’ beliefs about the acceptance and effectiveness of parental control and 2) parents’ use of controlling parenting behaviors. Specifically, four hypothetical vignettes involving parents’ use of physical coercion and psychological control (2 each) in response to non-desired child behaviors (physical aggression and relational aggression) were developed for this study. After reading each vignette, parents were asked to comment on the parent’s parenting behaviors in each vignette and to describe situations during the past two weeks when they used those controlling parenting behaviors. The incidents and descriptions of parental control described by the parents were also used to modify the two parental control measures in Study 2 for achieving Objectives 2 and 3. The PI and the research assistant (RA) conducted all individual interviews. Training were provided to the RA prior to the beginning of the interviews (e.g. avoiding leading questions, utilizing probing techniques and letting the informant lead). Each interview lasted approximately 30 minutes and were audiotaped for transcription. The constant comparative method of the grounded theory approach was use. The respondents’ responses to each interview question were compared and contrasted to form categories, assign codes to the categories, summarize the content of each category for developing themes, and find negative evidence. Every interview was carefully studied to examine the internal consistency of individual interviews. As soon as more than one interview has been completed, comparisons between interviews were conducted. Five randomly selected transcripts were cross-coded by the PI and the RA to check for inter-coder agreement. The PI and the RA also held discussions to ensure the congruency between the emerging findings and the respondents’ responses. Objectives 2 & 3: To identify the bidirectional relations between parental control and child aggression; To examine whether child temperament moderates the associations between parental control and child aggression In Study 2, 168 Hong Kong Chinese children (88 girls; M = 60.97 months, SD = 5.51 months) and their parents were recruited. The interval between the two waves of data collection was approximately six months. At Time 1, 158 mothers and 154 fathers completed the questionnaires, provided demographic information as well as reported on their own parenting behaviors and that of their spouses. At the same time, the RA and student research assistants (SRA) visited each kindergarten to conduct child tasks to assess child temperament (Time 1 only) and aggression (Time 1 and Time 2). At Time 2 only one boy dropped out of the study because of school transfer, and all participating teachers along with 152 mothers, and 148 fathers reported on children’s aggression. The RA and SRAs received three hours of training prior to administering child tasks. All child assessment sessions were videotaped and later coded by SRAs who were not involved in data collection and were unfamiliar with the children. Trainings were provided to SRAs and consisted of coders watching videotapes of children participating in the child tasks during the pilot study and continued until an acceptable inter-observer reliability criterion (i.e. Intraclass Correlation Coefficient > 0.80) was achieved between the coders. To examine the second objective, the degree to which parents’ parenting and child aggression predicted changes in one another over time, cross-lagged panel analyses were run involving two set of structural equation models. This approach made it possible to examine what predicted changes in both child aggression and parenting over time and provided insights into the possible direction of effects—that is, from parent to child versus from child to parent. Separate analyses were run for each of the two child variables: physical aggression and relational aggression. To address the third objective, a path analysis was conducted to examine the main effects and the interaction effects involving parental variables and child temperament at Time 1 on child physical and relational aggression at Time 2 in one model.

18607017.label: Major findings and research outcome
18607017.value: In Study 1, responses from interviews with parents provided evidences about the beliefs and practices of coercive parenting among Chinese parents. Specifically, most of the participating Chinese parents were found to endorse democratic parenting practices and do not support the use of coercive parenting. For parents who endorse the use of parental control, they expressed that parental control is more likely to be employed when children engage in persistent and serious misconduct. For instance, parents were more likely to report the use of parental control in response to physical aggression than relational aggression, as physical aggression is considered a more serious form of peer conflicts that would harm the harmonious social relationships that Chinese parents value. Among the two types of parental control, Chinese parents perceived psychological control as more acceptable than physical coercion, as it is perceived to be more subtle and does not involve any physical harm on children. In Study 2, results show that there is a bidirectional relation between parental control and child aggression. Results revealed that parental control predicted children’s aggression over time. Parents were also found to use more parental control at Wave 2 when their children demonstrated higher levels of aggression at Wave 1. Lastly, child temperament was found to moderate the effect of parenting on child aggression. Specifically, the findings revealed that mothers’ parental control was associated with child aggression, but these associations were not moderated by child temperament. In contrast, fathers’ parental control was significantly related to child aggression, and the association was moderated by effortful control.

18607017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18607017.value: First, findings from Study 1 offer detailed information on Chinese parents’ practices of parental control in the early years and provide evidence to modify the measure of parental psychological control developed in the West. The measure modified in this study can be widely used in future research of psychological control involving Chinese families. Findings from Study 1 also provide important information on Chinese parents' beliefs for understanding parental control, which has strong translational value for practitioners who work with families of young children. For example, the findings that Chinese parents tend to endorse psychological control suggest that in addition to preventing parents’ use of physical control, Chinese parents should be educated about the detrimental effect of psychological control on parent-child relationships and child development. Second, by showing that the relation between parental control and child aggression is bidirectional in nature, we are able to provide specific advice concerning what parents may do to reduce their children’s aggression, particularly among parents of children who display a high level of aggression. Further, by exploring the role of child characteristics in moderating these parental influences, we are able to provide tailored parenting advice to parents, specifically fathers, of children with difficult temperament.

18607017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18607017.value: Extensive evidence suggests that children of coercive parents and aggressive children are at higher risks for adjustment difficulties, including high levels of psychological distress, low levels of prosocial behavior, and high levels of peer rejection. Findings of this study contributed to the existing literature by informing the parents’ beliefs and practices of coercive parenting and providing insights on how parents may be supported to reduce childhood aggression. In general, this study found that parents tend to perceive psychological control as normative. This study also found that parents engaged in higher levels of coercive parenting over time when their children displayed a high level of aggression. Also, the findings showed that parents’ use of coercive parenting predicted child aggression over time, and that temperament moderated the association between fathers' coercive parenting and child aggression. Our findings suggest that parents, particularly fathers of children with difficult temperament, should be educated about the harmful effect of both parental physical coercion and psychological control as well as the use of effective parenting strategies. Doing so would help parents obtain information about parenting strategies for preventing childhood aggression and for supporting positive child development.

18607717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18607717.value: Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education has become an integral part of educational policies in many countries. In Hong Kong, the promotion of STEM education was repeatedly mentioned in the government policy addresses of 2015 and 2016. With the promotion of STEM education by the government, there have been initiatives and practices by various stakeholders aiming to provide an array of STEM learning experiences for students. These activities are mostly informal learning opportunities, which are co-curricular and/or event-based, with little attention paid to infusing STEM into the formal school curriculum. Besides, there exist few guidelines or models for teachers to follow on implementing STEM education. The real-world STEM scenarios occur as integrated processes. There are advocates that STEM education should involve learning experiences that will engage students in real-world situations in order to nurture their interest (Zeid et al., 2014). As such, STEM lessons need to take on an integrated approach, adopting manipulation and hands-on learning, cooperative learning, inquiry, problem-solving, and technology-enhanced learning (Stohlman et al., 2012). This will help to develop the necessary competencies and practical skills to prepare our students for STEM professions (Hsu, Lin, & Yang, 2016). This research advocates a “School-STEM Professionals Collaboration” to empower primary General Studies (GS) teachers to develop authentic STEM inquiry activities similar to the work of STEM professionals through design-based “STEM-in-GS” teacher professional development (PD) programmes. Such STEM professionals include scientists, engineers, chemists, and doctors. Changes in teachers’ conceptions as they work through the design and implementation of authentic STEM inquiry activities for senior primary students during the PD programme, as well as changes in students’ attitudes towards STEM after engaging in STEM activities will be examined. This will provide useful research-based evidence for a sustainable model to support the development of STEM education in the school curriculum. A three-phase design-based approach will be adopted in the design of authentic STEM inquiry activities with pre-study and post-study comparisons. The investigation of change in teachers’ conceptions of STEM education will involve the use of the drawing of mind maps as well as interviews. Factors influencing the implementation of STEM activities in the classroom will be identified through lesson observations of the instructional approaches. The change in students’ attitudes towards STEM will be studied using pre-lesson and post-lesson surveys and interviews. Last but not least, the STEM professionals involved will be interviewed regarding their possible contribution to STEM education in Hong Kong. STEM (科學,技術,工程和數學)教育已經成為很多國家的教育政策裡不可分割的一部分。在香港，2015年和2016年的行政長官施政報告中屢次提及推行STEM教育。隨著政府對STEM教育的推動，不同的持份者己積極地提出並實踐了為學生提供一系列的STEM學習經歷。這些活動大多是非正式學習機會，基本上是在課程以外和/或個別單一活動，並未着意融入正規的學校課程。除此之外,機乎没有為教師提供指引或可模式以實施STEM教育。 在現實世界中，STEM是一個綜合的過程。有主張STEM教育應為學生提供在真實的情境下培養他們的興趣的學習經歷 (Zeid et al. ， 2014)。因此, STEM課堂需要以一個綜合的模式進行，包括操作和動手、合作、探究、解決問題和以科技促進的學習(Stohlman et al . ，2012)。這將有助學生發展成為STEM專業人員所需的能力和實踐技能 (Hsu, Lin, & Yang, 2016)。本研究主張以“學校-STEM專業人員協作”模式促進常識科(GS)教師基於STEM專業人員的工作而開發真實STEM探究活動，並透過設計為本的“STEM-in-GS”教師專業發展(PD)項目體現。這些STEM專業人員包括科學家、工程師、化驗師和醫生。是項研究希望能在教師於PD中設計STEM探究活動及在高小課堂中實踐過程中檢視教師觀念的轉變。同時亦能檢視學生在參加STEM探究活動後對STEM的態度的改變。這些研究結果將為STEM教育如何在學校課程內持續發展提供研究證據。 研究將採用三階段設計為本的方式來設計真實的STEM探究活動，並透過前測和後測進行對比。教師對STEM教育觀念轉變的調查將使用思維導圖以及訪談的方式進行。同時亦會透過課堂觀察教師的教授模式，以確定影響STEM活動在課堂中實施的因素。學生對STEM態度的轉變會透過收集課前和課後問卷和訪談作分析研究。最後，亦會訪問參與的STEM專業人員，探討他們為香港STEM教育可作出的貢獻。

18607717.label: Realisation of objectives
18607717.value: A total of 15 teachers from four schools participated in the activity design with supports from educators and STEM professionals from different fields including environmental scientist, food scientist, information technologist, and water and drainage engineers. Around 60 lessons were observed and video-recorded. 508 3rd to 6th grade students were provided experiences of working as professionals in different STEM fields. To address the first objective, this study used a qualitative approach with teachers’ pre- and post-concept maps, self-reflections and interviews, to capture changes in the teachers’ STEM conceptions. The teachers’ concept maps were analysed around themes including content, educational advantages and disadvantages of STEM activities, and contributions of STEM education. The interviews and self-reflections were supplementary information for better understanding of the teachers’ conceptions. To achieve the second objective, teachers were encouraged to design authentic STEM inquiry activities with the support of educators and STEM professionals. The teachers were asked to explain the ways in which they engaged students in STEM learning during interviews. How they implemented STEM lessons in the classroom was observed using an observation tool to explore the factors affecting their practices. The interview data of the teachers were analysed according to the theory of concern comprising stages of awareness, informational, personal, management, consequence, collaboration, and refocusing. Data collected through the observation tools were used as supplementary materials for the interview results. To achieve the third objective, we examined the impacts of the “School-STEM Professionals’ Collaboration” on students' interests in STEM careers and their stereotypes of STEM professionals through pre- and post-student drawings and surveys. The students were provided with STEM role models, and were engaged in authentic and hands-on activities to mimic the research work of experts in diverse STEM fields. The students’ drawings were analysed using graphic content analysis. The coding process was based on the coding schemes and categories including appearance of engineers/scientists (e.g., gender, clothes), actions (e.g., fixing, testing), and artefacts (e.g., tools, chemistry). The methods for analysing survey data mainly included: (1) descriptive statistics and one-sample t test via SPSS 24.0 to examine the direction (positive vs. negative) of the student attitudes toward STEM, views about STEM professionals, and interest in STEM careers, and (2) mixed ANOVAs to: (i) assess the changes in students’ attitudes toward and perceptions of STEM professions from pre- to post-survey, and to (ii) detect differences in the impacts of the STEM instruction by student gender and the gender of the introduced STEM professionals. Based on the above data analysis, five journal articles were completed with the following five have been accepted for publication/published. 1. Chen, Y., Chow, S. C. S. & So, W. M. W. (accepted). School-STEM professional collaboration to diversify stereotypes and increase interest in STEM careers among primary school students. Asia Pacific Journal of Education. 2. So, W. M. W., He, Q. W., Chen, Y., & Chow, S. C. F. (2020): School-STEM Professionals’ Collaboration: a case study on teachers’ conceptions, Asia-Pacific Journal of Teacher Education. DOI: 10.1080/1359866X.2020.1774743. 3. So, W. W. M., Chen, Y., & Chow, S. C. F. (2020). Primary school students' interests in STEM careers: How conceptions of STEM professionals and gender moderation influence. International Journal of Technology and Design Education. DOI: 10.1007/s10798-020-09599-6. 4. Cheng, Y. C. & So, W. M. W. (2020). Managing STEM Learning: A Typology & Four Models of Integration.
