18607717.label: Major findings and research outcome
18607717.value: (1) The teachers generally held narrow views of STEM engagement. “School-STEM Professionals’ Collaboration” had a positive impact on teachers’ conceptions of STEM education and STEM professionals. Teachers reported improved understanding of the STEM disciplines, student learning, and the contribution of STEM professionals. (2) It was also found that the teachers mainly perceived STEM education as models of separate disciplines, science or engineering design process as context or real-world problem solving as context. Their views differed with respect to the equivalence in integrating science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. The teachers’ concerns regarding informational, personal adequacy, management, and collaboration issues seemed to impede their implementation of STEM education. (3) Analysis of drawings showed that the students had inadequate understanding of engineers or scientists in some specific areas. Boys were more likely to hold gender-related stereotypes about STEM professionals than girls. Analysis of survey data revealed that students’ views about STEM career implications, STEM professionals’ personal aptitudes, and social relations significantly predicted their STEM career interest. Gender significantly moderated the association of social relations and interest, meaning that compared to boys, girls might express higher STEM career interest when they more strongly believed that STEM professionals are able to build good social relationships with others. (4) “School-STEM Professionals’ Collaboration” diversifying the stereotypes of STEM people can be beneficial to students. Students increased interest in STEM careers, and held more positive perceptions of STEM professionals after they were engaged in STEM activities. In addition, the impacts of “School-STEM Professionals’ Collaboration” were found to be influenced by gender-matching between students and STEM professionals. Girls were more likely to improve their interests and alter stereotypes with exposure to female role models.

18607717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18607717.value: Continued research on enhancing the professional development of teachers, and to strengthening partnerships with community key players such as practitioners who specialise in various science, technology, and engineering and mathematics fields is needed. Follow-up studies may involve more local schools to add more evidence to the causal relationship between the involvement of STEM professionals in STEM education and student outcome measures, and to ensure more reliable and generalized findings. It is also necessary to determine whether engaging students in activities to simulate STEM professionals’ research work would have long-term impacts on students’ aspirations for or perceptions of STEM study or careers through a longitudinal design.

18607717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18607717.value: This research advocated a “School-STEM Professionals Collaboration” in teacher professional development programmes to empower primary General Studies teachers to develop authentic inquiry activities similar to the work of scientists or engineers. To investigate the effectiveness of the “School-STEM Professionals Collaboration”, this research examined (1) changes in teachers’ conceptions using the drawing of mind maps as well as interviews, and (2) changes in students’ attitudes towards STEM and their stereotypes about STEM professionals using pre- and post-surveys and interviews. The findings of this research demonstrate positive outcomes of the “School-STEM Professionals Collaboration” on both teachers and students, providing useful research-based evidence for supporting collaboration with professionals in developing STEM education. Moreover, the findings enable educators, school leaders, policy-makers, or parents to better understand the barriers or concerns teachers believed about STEM education, and in turn, to provide teachers with support that realistically assists them in integrating STEM into the classroom. This research with its findings on the support of involving STEM professionals can be useful for more effective teacher professional development and STEM education.

18610817.label: Project Objectives

• To evaluate the effectiveness of implementing the m-Orchestrate learning system;
• To work out the teacher orchestration pedagogical principles for scaling up collaborative science inquiry practices using the m-Orchestrate learning system.

18610817.label: Realisation of objectives
18610817.value: This study adopted design-based research in three stages with different focuses to address the three objectives from 2018 to 2020. How the objectives have been achieved is presented below: Stage 1: Design and development of the m-Orchestrate system (02 Jan. 2018 - 20 Dec. 2018) Stage 1 aimed to address the first research objective of the GRF project: To design and develop the m- Orchestrate learning system for teacher orchestration in collaborative science inquiry in a mobile learning environment. This stage focused on setting up the infrastructure of the m-Orchestrate system and provided data for addressing Research Q1 about the affordances of the m-Orchestrate learning system in terms of “flexibility, continuity, awareness, curriculum relevance, assessment relevance, and collaboration”. Three cycles were involved in the system design. Cycle 1 focused on the design of Student Module (17 Jan. - 4 Jun. 2018). Researcher-teacher partnership was established for the instructional design of collaborative inquiry activities; the entity relationship diagram (ERD) of the database was also designed for functionalising the m-Orchestrate system. Development of Student Module focused on the functions of “Project” which was evaluated by the usability test and refined after the evaluation. Cycle 2 focused on the design of Teacher Module (5 Jun. - 13 Sep. 2018). This cycle focused on the development of Teacher Module and the usability test and refinement of the Module. Cycle 3 focused on development of advanced Plugins and Assessment Module (4 Sep. - 20 Dec. 2018). This cycle put emphasis on the development of the learning system, focusing on Learning Analytics (assessment) and other plugins in both Student Module and Teacher Module; Usability test and refinement of - “Learning Analytics” in both Student Module and Teacher Module were conducted. In the first year, the research team developed the m-Orchestrate learning system as a web application. After trail use of it, the researchers interviewed student participants and teachers. They provided feedback on their experience of using the first version of the m-Orchestrate learning system. On the one hand, positive comments were received on (1) ease of use, (2) affordance on guiding collaborative inquiry and orchestration practices, and (3) shaping actual impacts on teaching and learning. On the other hand, some participants also reported that the m-Orchestrate learning system lacked clarity and mobility in synchronous co-construction of contents in multimedia. Stage 2: A pilot study of m-orchestrate system and teacher professional development to test the effectiveness of the m-Orchestrate learning system (21 Dec. 2018 - 17 Jul. 2019) Stage 2 focused on evaluation and refinement of the m-Orchestrate learning system. The researchers consulted Prof. Hiroaki Ogata and Prof. Pierre Dillenbourg about the problems identified at the first stage to optimise the performance of the m-Orchestrate learning system. Some major revisions were made by considering their comments and suggestions. Firstly, we transferred the web features with file uploading demands into (1) file transfer portal (FTP) to improve its stability and (2) friendly user interface (UI) for easier interactions on the Unity platform. All previous features are included as web plugins in the application. This mobile app is delivered via iOS and Android devices. Secondly, the researchers created the app with five inquiry-based learning components (WeExplore, WeCollect, WeAnalyse, WeExplain and WeReflect) with specific plugins in the WeEngage (raising inquiry questions) and WeReflect (KWL tables) phase. Although the social events in 2019 caused some disruptions in normal school routines at this stage, fortunately, teachers with their students overcame the difficulties and kept engaging with the researchers to carry out the pilot study on use and evaluate the app. The pilot study comprised three phases below: Phase I (21 Dec. 2018 – 21 Feb. 2019) focused on evaluating the m-Orchestrate learning app; Phase II (22 Feb. 2019 – 17 Jul. 2019) focused on further evaluation of the newly designed app after refinement; and Phase III (10 Jun. 2019 - 19 Jul. 2019) put emphasis on four teacher professional development workshops. The researchers also attempted to identify pedagogical principles for implementing the m-Orchestrate learning app based on the orchestration framework of “flexibility, continuity, awareness, curriculum relevance, assessment relevance and collaboration”. Stage 3: Implementation of the m-Orchestrate learning system (02 Sep. 2019 - 27 Oct. 2020) Stage 3 focused on implementation of the newly designed m-Orchestrate app to scale up teachers’ orchestration practices and students’ collaborative science inquiry in four local primary schools in Hong Kong with three iterative cycles. In Cycle 1, the m-Orchestrate app was implemented to conduct collaborative inquiry activities (09 Sep.-12 Nov. 2019 ). The topics for the inquiry learning were (1) “Protect Our Environment” and (2) “Chinese Herbs”. The first inquiry topic involved four teachers with two classes in a school in the instructional design and implementation of the inquiry learning activities supported by the m-Orchestrate app. The second topic “Chinese Herbs” included 12 teachers in five classes (a few teachers with different subject worked together) in a school in the instructional design and implementation of the inquiry learning activities supported by the m-Orchestrate app. Several issues were identified from three iterative cycles of implementation of the m-orchestrate app for teachers to design and enact collaborative learning activities, and remedial measures were taken to cope with the issues and problems. In Cycle 1, a few bugs of the app and problems were identified. In response to these issues, before Cycle 2’s implementation, (1) we debugged the app; and (2) developed a dashboard on the app in order to support teachers to monitor and facilitate students’ collaborative inquiry activities more conveniently, and increase students’ awareness of the progress of their collaborative learning activities among other groups. In Cycle 2, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the initial plans for enacting the collaborative inquiry activities had to be postponed. Schools, teachers, and students experienced unprecedented challenges due to a sudden transition from face-to-face to online teaching. It was really difficult for schools to conduct this project as they were engaged in many issues from students, teachers, and parents. We felt thankful to collaborate with two teachers from a school to conduct the collaborative learning activities. Their inquiry topic was exploring different types of masks: classification criteria and choice of use. All the data were recorded on the app. The interviews were conducted via Zoom. Finally, in Cycle 3, the inquiry project “Eight Planets in the Solar System” was co-designed by the teachers and researchers based on the school-based curriculum. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the teachers and students conducted the inquiry project on the m-Orchestrate app fully online and at home. The teachers and researchers prepared resources of web resources related to each inquiry phase. They also provided guidance on how to make use of features on the m-Orchestrate app. All in all, although the project encountered the social event and the COVID-19 pandemic, both teacher and student participants overcame the difficulties and collaborated with the researchers in conducting the research online using the newly developed m-Orchestrate app. We appreciated their sustained efforts in making this study a success. We also valued the research assistant and the PhD student great contribution to this project.

18610817.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610817.value: Regarding Q1 – affordances of the m-Orchestrate app: the results show the six affordances of the app: Flexibility, continuity, awareness, curriculum relevance, assessment relevance and collaboration. Regarding Q2.1 - teachers’ orchestration competency: The results show that the teachers found that the m-Orchestrate app was indeed useful for them to manage students’ collaborative inquiry in science across different settings. Without the app, although they could use other learning platforms, they might upload the data they collected in a mess or forget to upload the data they collected. On the other hand, the app could guide the teachers to design collaborative science inquiry learning activities more “scientifically” premised on the pedagogical model and principles. It could also help the teachers to monitor students’ inquiry learning activities with “continuity”, provide feedback with “flexibility” and make formative assessment. Regarding Q2.2 - teacher attitude change over time in using the m-Orchestrate learning system to orchestrate collaborative science inquiry activities, the results show that the teachers attitudes toward adopting the m-Orchestrate app in collaborative inquiry pedagogical practices were statistically significantly different during three cycles. The post hoc analysis with a Bonferroni adjustment revealed that the 16 teachers attitudes were statistically significantly improved from Cycle 2 to Cycle1. Regarding Q2.3 – students’ science knowledge advancement, inquiry skills improvement and their relationships with teacher orchestration: The results show that there was a significant difference between the total scores of pre-domian test and post-domain test, suggesting that the learners’ knowledge advancement significantly improved from using m-Orchestrate in collaborative inquiry in Cycle 3. The students inquiry skills were statistically significantly different during three cycles, with students inquiry skills improving from Cycle 1. In addition, teachers’ orchestration competence was divided into high and low performance groups. Then, a regression analysis was conducted using SPSS version 21 to compare students’ performance with teachers’ orchestration competence. The preliminary data analysis show that students in the teachers’ high performance group outperformed those in both science domain tests and inquiry learning skills significantly. Regarding Q3 – teacher orchestration pedagogical principles: A set of teacher orchestration pedagogical principles was evaluated and developed after refinement in the 3-cycle of study in Stage 3. The principles include the six components in line with the six affordances of the m-Orchestrate app: flexibility, continuity, awareness, curriculum relevance, assessment relevance and collaboration for teachers to use the app to design, implement and orchestrate students’ collaborative learning activities in science learning.

18610817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610817.value: After the three cycles of iterative implementation of the m-Orchestrate app for teacher orchestration of students’ collaborative learning activities, the researchers identified further potential in upgrading the m-Orchestrate app. First, development of co-orchestration dashboard powered by artificial intelligence (AI) technology. The researchers found that students with higher inquiry skills performed highly autonomously in their group activities. They initiated more frequent discussions in the Chat Room. By using the dashboard powered by AI technology, it is more convenient for groups members to (1) follow up the work done by peers, (2) discuss in time whenever needed, and (3) keep working on tasks to achieve their inquiry objectives. It could be regarded as a kind of student’s participation of the class orchestration. Second, teacher-student co-orchestrate the inquiry-based learning activities leveraged by the m-Orchestrate app. Although this research was focused more on teacher orchestration of students’ collaborative inquiry-based learning, students themselves were also orchestrators of their group work. Thus, our research team came up with the idea to assign the student a role of orchestration at a group level using learning analytics and AI technologies. A collaborative scheduler may be designed and developed for micro-level co-orchestration among (1) teachers and students. and (2) group peers in teacher-planned inquiry phases.

18610817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610817.value: The importance of this research lies in six aspects. First, the m-Orchestrate learning app is the first mobile learning app which fully considers design features with a set of affordances for teacher orchestration to improve students collaborative science inquiry in a mobile learning environment. Secondly, practically, the research unfolded the orchestration process in fine-grained details, and developed a set of teacher orchestration pedagogical principles in a mobile learning environment as guidelines for orchestration related research and practice. Thirdly, theoretically, this research conceptualised the teacher orchestration for inquiry-based learning in a mobile learning environment for orchestration practices which fills the gap of the literature. Fourthly, the rigorous empirical study provides valuable information about professional development for teacher orchestration in a technology-rich learning environment. Fifthly, the development and evaluation of the m-Orchestration app lays a useful foundation for future extended research such as developing a learning analytics tool powered by artificial intelligence to allow teachers visualise their learning progress and identify their learning difficulties to inform instructional practices. Finally, the findings provide a comprehensive knowledge base for scaling up the orchestration practices in Hong Kong primary schools and across the broader Hong Kong learning community.

18611117.label: Project Objectives
18611117.value: To develop a preliminary empirically-based understanding of the mechanism and functioning of the teacher learning system in Shanghai; To investigate how leaders-as-expert-teachers perceive and enact their leadership roles in promoting cross-school teacher learning and disseminating instructional expertise and to explore how their role is understood by their peer teachers; To explore the characteristics of the socio-political and education systems that facilitate and inhibit the exercise of leadership roles by these leaders-as-expert-teachers; and To synthesize a set of propositions emerging from the study about the teacher learning system and cross-school leadership strategies that Hong Kong and other societies can learn from the experience of Shanghai.

To investigate how leaders-as-expert-teachers perceive and enact their leadership roles in promoting cross-school teacher learning and disseminating instructional expertise and to explore how their role is understood by their peer teachers;
To explore the characteristics of the socio-political and education systems that facilitate and inhibit the exercise of leadership roles by these leaders-as-expert-teachers; and

18611117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18611117.value: Prompted by Shanghai’s performance on the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), the past few years have witnessed increased interest in education in the city. The crux of this interest is around what Shanghai schools and teachers are doing differently from other education systems. A key focus has been on its unique teacher learning system. This system recognizes, differentiates, and labels teacher expertise at multiple mastery levels. Expert teachers are either granted titles such as Subject Leaders (xueke daitouren) and Special-class Teachers (teji jiaoshi) or promoted to district-level and municipal-level instructional guidance offices to be Teaching-research Officers (jiaoyan yuan). The formal recognition as ‘expert teachers’ comes with increased leadership responsibility to lead cross-school teacher learning and to initiate instructional and pedagogical improvement. In other words, these formally recognized expert teachers are no longer ‘assets’ just of their own schools; their expertise and wisdom needs to be shared across a wider group of teachers. They function as critical professional leaders and ‘influencers’ to other teachers in curriculum and instruction. They are referred as leaders-as-expert-teachers in this study. This study will explore the role of these leaders-as-expert-teachers in promoting cross-school teacher learning and instructional improvement. The study employs a case study design. For the study, 12 leaders-as-expert-teachers and their peers will be selected to participate. Data will be collected through multiple rounds of interviews with the 12 leaders and their peers. Supplementary data will be collected from observing the various collaborative learning activities organized by the leaders, and associated documents such as these teacher leaders’ writings and public talks. This study will provide insights drawn from insiders’ views about one aspect of the success of school education in Shanghai. It will contribute to the knowledge base in three domains: teacher learning and professional development, international understanding of instructional leadership, and educational leadership in China. The research findings will have important implications for teacher learning and instructional improvement practices in Hong Kong and other societies. 近年來上海在“國際學生能力評估計畫”（PISA）中的表現越來越引起外界對上海教育的關注。大家的興趣集中於上海學校和老師與其他教育系統的做法有何差異。其中一個關鍵焦點在其獨特的教師學習體系。該體系在多個專業層面上識別、區分及認可教師的專業知識。專家型教師被授予“學科帶頭人”、“特級教師”等稱號，或晉升為區級乃至市級指導教學的“教研員”。被正式認可的“專家教師”，則需要擔負引領跨學校教師學習及改進課堂教學的領導責任。換言之，這些被正式認可的專家教師不再只是他們自己學校的“資產”，他們的專業知識和智慧需要在更廣大教師群體間共用。他們在課程和教學中扮演專業教學領導者和其他教師“影響者”的關鍵角色。 本研究擬探討這些專家教師領導在促進跨校教師學習和教學改進方面的作用。本研究採用案例研究法，計畫選取12位專家教師領導及其同事參加。通過與12位專家教師領導及其同事的多輪訪談來收集資料，同時觀察12位元專家教師組織的各種合作學習活動，以及收集這些教師領導的著作和公開講話等相關檔來補充資料。 本研究將從局內人的角度對上海學校教育成功的其中一方面提供洞見。這項研究會對三個領域的知識體系有所裨益：教師學習與專業發展，教學領導的國際理解，以及中國的教育領導力。研究結果將對香港和其他社會的教師學習和教學改進實踐產生重要影響。

18611117.label: Realisation of objectives
18611117.value: The four objectives listed in the project proposal have been fully achieved. Objective 1: Since the project began, interest in the importance and uniqueness of Chinese teacher learning systems has increased both internationally and within China. The research team is grateful for the timely RGC funding and believes the outputs generated from this project have enriched the knowledge base of teacher learning systems in China. This has been achieved through three pathways: The first pathway is to explore the cultural and contextual antecedents of successful teacher learning systems in China. For example, there appears to be a high degree of coherence between stated policy and subsequent implementation, partly due to the top-down, centralized government administration. This political condition enables resources to be squarely targeted on improving quality teaching in and across schools. Furthermore, peer support and shared responsibility for collective learning evident in Shanghai schools are congruent with the traditional Chinese values of collectivism. An exploration of these cultural and contextual antecedents has been successfully published (see: Output 1, 2 & 4). We have also traced the development of a specific type of teacher learning strategy – the Master Teacher Studio. A paper on this topic is now under second-round review by International Journal of Educational Management (see: Output 7). The second pathway is through an empirical investigation of teacher learning systems. The work has allowed us to integrate the findings from this project with our previous studies of principal instructional leadership and system leadership. For example, we reported how principals explained their reliance on expert teachers to promote teacher learning and build Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) (see: Output 3). We have also included Networked Teacher PLCs as illustrative cases in a paper discussing system leadership in China (see: Output 2). The third pathway compared the teacher learning system in Shanghai with other education systems. One example of this was to compare Chinese expert teachers with US coaches. This work resulted in a funding application to Spencer Foundation (see: Impact 3). We also explored the teacher learning system in Singapore and juxtaposed this with the Shanghai system (see: Output 8). Objective 2: As planned, the project selected 12 leaders-as-expert-teachers as the major research participants. Data was collected mainly through at least two rounds of interviews with these expert teachers and focus group interviews with their peers. The 12 expert teachers included two special-class teachers, two district-level jiaoyanyuan, and eight district-level backbone teachers. Expert teachers' subject backgrounds included Chinese, English, Mathematics, geography and politics, and information technology. We have generated two sets of findings and written these up (see: Output 5, 9 &10). One set of these findings relate to how these expert teachers acquired and accumulated their human, social and cultural capital from novice teachers to their present standing as influential teacher leaders. Human capital involves their knowledge, skills, and expertise. Social capital mainly refers to the access and mobilization of resources attained from social networks. Cultural capital emphasizes specific interactive styles, a solid commitment to education, and holding a strong sense of purpose for their profession. Their work voyages show that some critical incidents such as receiving an award in a teaching contest marked the capital acquisition and accumulation. In addition, they received strong support from the mentors they worked with at various stages of their careers. Therefore, when they assume the mantle of teacher leaders, they also imitate how their mentors guide them and try to infuse the values they inherit from their mentors to the mentees (see: Output 9). A further set of findings specifically focus on the way the expert leaders exert their leadership. Four significant roles are reported in the international literature: brokering, mediating, participating, and forging. Our project identified similar roles for Chinese expert teachers. However, these roles appeared mediated in context-specific ways, and these were reflected in how they enacted their leadership in at least two ways. First, our data showed that the expert teachers also served as action research advisors to cross-school teacher learning groups. They are expected to produce concrete outputs such as published books or newly designed textbooks. Second, Chinese expert teachers carry out more district-level (or above) initiatives and receive more district-level support to provide instructional guidance. In other words, expert teachers in China generally have broader responsibility. Objective 3: We have committed considerable efforts to decoding the complexities of the education system and the socio-political context in China. The centralized system has both strengths and limitations. On the one hand, the centralized and strong government has framed policy-driven standards, focused resource allocation, and set high expectations for education. Teacher engagement in collaborative activities is highly institutionalized and integrated into teachers' professional lives in China. However, there appears an over-reliance on government policies and mandates. As a result, teacher leaders tend to follow the directions of those above them in the hierarchy. These findings have been reported in a book chapter (see: Output 2). The complexity of the traditional culture was explored and recognized. For example, when school principals or local education bureaus identify and reward senior and competent teachers with high-status titles, such actions usually meet with few arguments because of the traditional respect for seniority in Chinese culture. However, expert teachers are also expected to be loyal and obedient to their mentors and other professional authorities, sometimes stifling teaching innovation. These issues have also been discussed in our publications (see: Output 3). Objective 4: A major purpose of the study was to delineate implications of the teaching-learning system and cross-school leadership strategies in Shanghai for other societies. This has been achieved through these pathways: Pathway one was to summarize the Shanghai practices and explicitly discuss the implications for other societies. For example, we published a paper about expert teachers in Shanghai in The Australian Educational Leader (see: Output 5). In the article, we introduced how the system operates in Shanghai and the necessary enabling system-level conditions required to support expert teachers in meaningfully applying their leadership to professional teacher learning. We suggested that Australia may well be at a critical point in terms of how it values and leverages the expertise of its top teachers. The second pathway was a comparative study between Chinese jiaoyanyuan and US coaches. Although the Spencer Foundation proposal was not funded, the positive comments of the reviewers resulted in a seminar proposal by our US partner Dr. Xiu Cravens (Vanderbilt University). The seminar received financial support from Vanderbilt and was planned for 2020 but was postponed due to the pandemic. The third pathway was to spread the research findings through knowledge transfer activities with local HK leaders. The PI was a director of an EDB leader development program Professional Vision and Growth of School Leaders in 2020-2021, which aimed to introduce to school leaders the latest international and national education developments in China. The PI used this opportunity to introduce both the teaching-learning system in Shanghai and some expert teachers' stories drawn from the project to more than 300 participants. Many program participants commented that the stories of the expert teachers are inspirational and that the program has opened their horizon (see: Impact 2).

18611117.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611117.value: The study explored the role of leaders-as-expert-teachers in promoting cross-school teacher learning and instrumental improvement. The data was collected from 12 expert teachers of different ranks and their peer teachers. The study's findings enhance understanding of the teacher learning system and system reform in the Chinese context. The study found that the teacher learning system as a whole emphasized collective capacity building and sustained improvement through (see: Output 2, 3 & 5): • Combining bottom-up initiatives with top-down support; • Investing heavily in teachers' professional learning and promoting models of collaborative inquiry; • Establishing mechanisms for expert teachers to network and exert leadership beyond their schools; • Taking exceptionally skilled teachers out of their classrooms to spread their influence across classrooms. Some cultural and contextual antecedents are important preconditions for the successful teacher learning systems in China (see: Output 2 & 4) During the expert teachers' professional voyages, they worked closely with different mentors and experienced some 'turning points' in their career development. These contribute to acquiring and accumulating their capital (human, social and cultural) and shaping who they are today (see: Output 9). The expert teachers also play a vital role in forming Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) in their schools (see: Output 3). Compared with teacher leaders in other societies, such as the US coaches, the Shanghai expert teachers have broader responsibility. They need to demonstrate their teaching as role models, coordinate research projects, and carry out more district-level initiatives (see: Impact 4). A more detailed study of their leadership strategies is under preparation. Their leadership will be discussed with reference to boundary spanning and other boundary practices. The study has also found that the expert teachers saw themselves as learners first and as leaders second. Their love of learning provided them with a sense of purpose to help others develop. The paper about expert teachers as learners has been prepared and the abstract submitted (see Output 10). This project contributed empirical data and insights to a chapter in the International Encyclopedia of Education (4th edition) on the topic of leadership in China (see Output 4). In addition, the implications of the Shanghai teacher learning system for other societies have also been discussed and published (see: Output 2 & 5).

18611117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611117.value: Promoting expert teachers as cross-school instructional leaders is a system-wide reform effort. System reform involves collaboration and networking across schools and districts to narrow gaps between schools or enhance teacher capacity on a large scale. The current GRF project triggered the research team's interest in further exploring more system reform initiatives in China. A new GRF proposal entitled An Exploration of the Role of Leadership in Successful Systemic Improvement in China was submitted in 2019 and funded by the RGC in 2020. The research team initiated a collaborative study in 2019 with our US partner, Dr. Xiu Cravens from Vanderbilt University, and applied for the competitive Spencer Foundation Small Grant. The proposal got very positive comments. The research team will continue to adopt the comparative frame to explore the relevance of the Chinese teacher learning system in the international context. The PI has developed deeper interest in understanding the learning trajectory of women expert teachers. She is particularly interested in how female special-class teachers, that is, those who have achieved the apex of their professional career, seek formal and informal avenues to express their leadership. Further research will be conducted.

18611117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611117.value: Professor Cheng Kai-Ming commented recently that teacher learning systems are a real asset to Chinese education. This project collected data from 12 expert teachers and their peers in Shanghai to explore their role in promoting cross-school teacher learning and instructional improvement. The Shanghai system invested heavily in teachers' professional learning and established mechanisms for these expert teachers to network across schools. The expert teachers usually started to gain honorary titles after winning awards in teaching contests and were then selected to join teacher learning schemes and be mentored by outstanding teachers. Throughout this process, the expert teachers enhanced their instructional and pedagogical knowledge and skills, gained access to social network resources, and developed a stronger sense of professional purpose. These then influenced how they acted as mentors, developed mentoring relationships with their mentees, engaged with peers in collaborative activities, and instilled a sense of mission and commitment to education in their fellow professionals. Much more can be learned from teacher learning in Shanghai, especially about system structures and networked PLC practices.

18611717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18611717.value: 越來越多的證據顯示睡眠不足和情緒困擾有關，然而目前為止，人們關於睡眠缺乏對情緒功能的影響的認知仍不完整，其神經基礎很大程度上亦不為人所知。 研究睡眠缺乏對情緒的影響對於了解情緒障礙及睡眠障礙至關重要，對於公共健康政策亦有借鑒意義。 是次研究計劃通過結合電腦測試和腦電圖，讓我們了解睡眠剝奪如何在行為和神經層面上影響情緒功能。 我們的主要假設包括：（1）睡眠剝奪會使參加者在情緒抑制控制、情緒記憶和情緒調節測試中的表現受損；（2）睡眠剝奪會改變與情緒相關的神經活動，如情緒測試中的靜息態腦活動（resting-state EEG）和事件相關電位（event-related potentials, ERPs）；（3）睡眠剝奪後的靜息態腦電指標（腦前額不對稱性活動）可以預測參加者在情緒功能測試中的表現；（4） 慣常的睡眠質量和人格特點（比如外向）會調節睡眠剝奪對情緒功能的影響。 本研究將招募健康的青年人進行睡眠剝奪的實驗。在正式的實驗開始之前，參加者需完成一些慣性睡眠監測包括連續佩戴腕動計、填寫睡眠日記，並在正式實驗前一晚佩戴可攜式多頻道睡眠記錄儀以測量其睡眠模式。在正式實驗的第一晚，所有參加者將會佩戴多頻道睡眠記錄儀進行慣性睡眠。其後，睡眠被剝奪的參加者將被要求保持一晚的清醒狀態。第三日早晨，參加者將於實驗室的電腦上完成有關睏意程度、警覺性、情緒抑制控制、情緒記憶和情緒調節的測試。與此同時，參加者的靜息態腦活動和事件相關電位將會被記錄，以探討在睡眠剝奪狀況下 情緒功能和神經機制的變化。這項實驗的研究結果會為睡眠匱乏和情緒功能在神經和行為指標上提供一個全新的科學視角。此外，研究結果將揭示睡眠紊亂如何影響有情緒或睡眠障礙的病人的情緒處理，以及為睡眠缺乏如何影響大眾情緒功能提供借鑒。

18611717.label: Realisation of objectives
18611717.value: We have conducted three studies, with 51 participants in Study 1 (pilot data), 51 participants in Study 2, and 62 participants in Study 3 to realise all four objectives. For Objective 1, we investigated the effect of one-night sleep deprivation (SD) on an emotional regulation task. For both valence and arousal ratings, there was only the main effect of conditions (neutral-maintain, negative-maintain, negative reappraisal, negative distract and negative suppress) but no main effect of group (SD vs. SC (sleep controls)) for valence and arousal (Output 2). This result was replicated in study 3 . Regarding the impact of SD on the regulation of emotional conflict, results from our factorial model with group × previous-trial congruency (congruent vs. incongruent) × current-trial congruency (congruent vs. incongruent) on accuracy data revealed a significant main effect of condition, but no interaction effect, indicating that participants made more errors in the sleep-deprived condition than in the normal sleep condition There was also a significant main effect of current-trial congruency, and a marginally significant interaction effect of previous-trial congruency × current-trial congruency. Participants made more errors in the SD condition than in the SC condition. They also made less errors for current-congruent trials than current-incongruent trials. On reaction time data, we observed a significant main effect of current-trial congruency, a significant main effect of previous-trial congruency, and a significant interaction effect of previous-trial congruency × current-trial congruency. Results indicated that participants were slower on incongruent trials than on congruent trials, and were slower following incongruent trials than congruent trials. For Objective 2, results suggested that one-night SD impaired emotional functionings to some extent, as suggested by the resting-state EEG and event-related ERPs. Regarding the resting-state EEG, results showed a trend of higher frontal alpha asymmetry score in the SC group than in the SD group. This group difference is significant in a one-tailed t test given the directional prediction. Even controlling for potential effects of habitual sleep quality (PSQI) and chronotype (CSM), an ANCOVA indicated a similar effect of group. In addition, our data showed that the SD group had a larger theta/beta ratio over the frontal area relative to the SC group. Changes/trends in these two EEG indices were in the same direction, indicating compromised emotion functioning after sleep deprivation (Output 1*). However, in study 3, this result was not replicated (Output 7 & 9). To examine the influence of SD on the effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies, we performed a 2 groups × 4 (condition: negative-maintain, negative-distract, negative-reappraise, negative-suppress) repeated-measures ANOVA on postinstruction late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes, which is an ERP index of emotional reactivity. The analysis revealed a main effect of condition and group, and importantly, a significant group by condition interaction. The interaction between group and condition indicated differential effects of emotion regulation strategies in attenuating LPP amplitudes between the SC and SD groups. This finding suggested that SD impaired the effectiveness of distraction and reappraisal in regulating emotions at the neurophysiological level (Output 2). Regarding the P300 component, results from factorial model with group × previous-trial congruency × current-trial congruency on P300 amplitudes at the central-parietal site (CPz) revealed a significant main effects of condition and previous-trial congruency; significant interaction effects of condition × current-trial congruency, previous-trial congruency × current-trial congruency, and condition × previous-trial congruency × current-trial congruency. The main effect of current-trial congruency was only marginally significant. The P300 amplitude evoked under sleep-deprived condition was significantly more positive compared to normal sleep condition, and this appears to be driven by the significantly more positive P300 amplitudes evoked by the incongruent-incongruent trials after sleep deprivation, when compared to incongruent-congruent, congruent-congruent, and congruent-incongruent trials regardless of sleep conditions. Post-instruction LPP has also been found sensitive to emotion regulation strategies and closely related to amygdala activity. Results from factorial model with condition , valence (neutral vs. negative) and strategy (first vs. third) revealed a significant main effect of condition, suggesting that participants in the SD condition in general showed greater LPP amplitudes towards negative stimuli than SC condition (Output 8). Regarding Objective 3, results showed that the EEG indices were significantly related to sleepiness and PVT performance. A lower alpha asymmetry score was correlated with higher sleepiness and more lapses in the vigilance task. The theta/beta ratios at Fz were positively correlated with higher sleepiness and longer RT in the vigilance task. Higher theta/beta ratios at F3 and F4 were also significantly correlated with higher sleepiness level (Output 1*). Regarding Objective 4, we have explored the possible moderators interacting with SD on emotional functioning. In Study 2, SD and depressive symptoms have a significant interaction effect on trust was found in Study 2. Simple slope analysis showed that participants with a higher level of depressive symptoms showed less trust after a night of SD compared to a night of normal sleep. It supported the role of depressive mood in modulating SD effects on social decision-making (Output 3 & 11). To examine the habitual sleep quality as a potential moderator in the relationship between sleep deprivation and emotional regulation using self-talk, we conducted a factorial model with group, valence, strategy and sleep quality (good vs. poor). There was a significant 4-way interaction effect on the mean post-instruction LPP amplitudes at the right-frontal electrode (F8), indicating an effect of SD moderated by habitual sleep quality. While poor sleepers tended to show greater LPP amplitudes overall, SD only increased the LPP for negative picture trials among good sleepers. This pattern may be driven by the elevated LPP in the neutral picture condition when sleep-deprived poor sleepers showed heightened LPP as compared to their own SC baseline. Findings suggested that the experience and the subsequent effects of sleep deprivation on emotional functioning might be moderated by one’s habitual sleep characteristics. (Output 8). We also conducted a 2 (group) X 2 (sleep quality) X 5 (condition) mix-effect ANOVA to examine the effect of SD on emotional regulation strategy and the moderating effect of sleep quality. For both valence rating and arousal rating, there was no significant three-way interaction but a main effect of condition and a significant group by PSQI interaction. It was found that among the good sleepers, the valence and arousal ratings were higher after SD compared to SC groups. We speculated that individuals with poor sleep quality had a higher valence and arousal rating towards negative pictures at the baseline, therefore, the SD effect on emotional regulation reached a ceiling and did not significantly differ between SD and SC groups (Output 2). The above effect of SD on emotional regulation was replicated in Study 3. We found that there was a significant three-way interaction, but no simple two-way interaction in follow-up analyses. *Output 1 was based on preliminary data collected in the pilot phase before the official project start date

18611717.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611717.value: H1: Partially supported. For emotional regulation, sleep-deprived participants rated the valence and arousal level more intensively when viewing negative pictures. The valence and arousal level decreased when participants were instructed to use emotional regulation strategy. Specifically, reappraisal and distraction were found to be effective emotional regulation strategies but not suppression (Output 2). Regarding the impact of SD on the regulation of emotional conflict, which involves attention and inhibition of emotional information, participants showed compromised behavioural performance after SD, as indicated by making more errors after SD condition as compared to the normal sleep condition. However, SD did not affect the speed at which participants resolve emotional conflicts (Output 4 Manuscript under preparation). H2: Partially supported. For resting-state neural correlates, participants did show a marginally compromised emotional regulation ability as indicated by EEG indices (i.e. frontal alpha asymmetry and theta/beta ratio) after one night of SD (Output 1*). However, the effect of one-night SD on resting-state EEG indices was not replicated in the within-subject design (Output 9), which suggested finding on the effect of SD on emotional regulation ability may be due to individual differences. For event-related neural activity (ERPs), we found that the mean P300 amplitude evoked under sleep-deprived conditions was significantly more positive (i.e., larger in amplitude) compared to normal sleep conditions. This appears to be driven by the significantly more positive P300 amplitudes evoked by the incongruent-incongruent trials after sleep deprivation, when compared to other trial types regardless of sleep conditions. P300 component has been considered to index allocation and maintenance of attentional resources, which suggest that more attentional resources were dedicated to successfully resolve emotional conflicts after sleep deprivation. H3: Partially supported. Our results suggested that resting-state EEG indices of higher theta/beta ratio and more left alpha lateralization were significantly correlated with increased sleepiness and lower vigilance level (Output 1*). However, none of the other behavioral performance on the emotional tasks correlate with the ERP neural indices. H4: Partially supported. Our results showed that individuals with better habitual sleep quality showed impairment in their emotional functioning after SD as indicated by both behavioral performance and neural activities; the same effect was not demonstrated in poor sleepers. Moreover, participants with more depressive symptoms were more vulnerable to be affected by SD on their trusting behaviors (Output 3 & 11). However, we did not find any moderating effect of personality traits on SD and emotional functioning as proposed.

18611717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611717.value: Having tested on a total of 164 participants, we noted that a night of SD brings some impairment on emotional functioning, including emotional regulation and emotional inhibition. Moreover, we detected some individual factors that play a role in moderating the effect of SD on emotional function, including habitual sleep quality and mood symptoms. We plan to explore more individual differences in the vulnerability to the effect of SD on emotional and social functioning. Since there are inconsistent findings regarding the effect of SD on emotional regulation as indicated by EEG indices, we plan to analyze other EEG indices for emotional regulation and compare the results. We provided objective evidence of compromised emotional functioning after SD at the behavioural and neural levels with the current funding support. Pending further funding support, we plan to study the effect of sleep extension on neurocognitive and affective functions in emerging adults with habitually restricted sleep, i.e., a protocol to potentially reverse the compromised emotional functioning post sleep deprivation, that is prevalent amongst young people world-wide and especially in busy cities like Hong Kong.

18611717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611717.value: The primary aim of this study is to assess the effect of a sleepless night on emotional functions at both behavioural and neural levels. Our results showed that 24 hours of sleep loss disrupted how we feel, regulate, and control our responses in the face of emotional information. After sleep loss, the brain network of emotion regulation is compromised physiologically during a resting state without direct input or output. It may also impair the effectiveness of applying emotion regulation strategies and potentially hamper our emotional well-being. Poor habitual sleep quality and sleep loss are double trouble when regulating emotions. Besides, more depressed people are more susceptible to the effects of sleep loss on their trusting behaviours. Our findings should act as a wake-up call for people to recognize the mental health risks associated with restricted sleep. The discovery of individual differences on the vulnerability to sleep loss could benefit emergency services to select the right person to work under sleep loss if needed. Our findings also provide further impetus to assess and treat sleep problems and address sleep inadequacy in clinical populations with difficulties in emotional regulation.

18611917.label: Realisation of objectives
18611917.value: The present study utilized a 2-year, 3-wave longitudinal design to examine the impact of experienced discrimination on harsh parenting among parents of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). A total of 441 parents of children with ASD participated in this study. The participants were recruited from 4 autism service centers and 14 special schools in Hong Kong. The findings of this study have been published in 6 journal papers (Chan* & Leung, 2020, Autism Research; Chan* & Leung, 2021, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders; Chan* et al., 2022, Autism; Chan* et al., 2022, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders; Chan* et al., 2022, Mindfulness; Yip & Chan*, 2022 Research in Developmental Disabilities). Realization of Objective 1: The objective – to investigate whether experienced discrimination predicts higher levels of harsh parenting – was well achieved as evidenced by the development of 1 new conceptual model in this project (Chan* et al., 2022, Autism). Our model shows that, when parents are stigmatized and discriminated as a result of their children having ASD, they may perceive a negative influence of their children on themselves and consider their lives to be spoiled by their parental roles. These parents may develop more negative attitudes toward their caregiving responsibilities, experience a greater sense of caregiving burden, and show greater hostility and harshness toward their children. Specifically, the parents may exhibit greater psychological aggression and physical assault in their parent-child interactions. Realization of Objective 2: The objective – to investigate whether affiliate self-stigma mediates the relationship between experienced discrimination and harsh parenting – was well achieved as evidenced by the development of 3 new conceptual models in this project (Chan* & Leung, 2020, Autism Research; Chan* & Leung, 2021, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders; Chan* et al., 2022, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders). Our models show that, when parents of children with ASD face constant disapproval from the public, they may start applying the stigmatizing views toward themselves and developing self-stigmatizing beliefs. Specifically, their experience of interpersonal rejection may increase the degree to which they feel inferior and endorse their self-stigmatizing ideas. Their ruminations and worries about social disapproval may also elevate the extent to which they feel insecure and think about their self-stigmatizing ideas repeatedly and frequently. As parents with self-stigma may feel highly stressed in parenting, they may become so mentally exhausted that they have little energy or desire to exercise positive parenting and demonstrate parental warmth. Also, as these parents may suffer greater caregiving burden and strain, they may become more agitated and irritable and exhibit greater parental hostility. As such, parents with self-stigma may exhibit fewer positive, and more negative, parenting practices. Realization of Objective 3: The objective – to investigate whether psychological flexibility weakens the association between experienced discrimination and harsh parenting – was well achieved as evidenced by the development of 3 sets of conceptual models in this project (Chan* et al., under preparation; Chan* et al., 2022, Mindfulness; Yip & Chan*, 2022 Research in Developmental Disabilities). Our models show that experienced discrimination is longitudinally associated with higher levels of harsh parenting, and that this association is mediated by self-stigma and moderated by psychological flexibility and related constructs, namely mindfulness and nonattachment. Importantly, our findings show that, in the long term, parents who are more psychologically flexible, mindful, and nonattached are less affected, psychologically, by experienced discrimination. In particular, the mindful and nonattached attitudes associated with psychological flexibility may enable parents to acknowledge the presence of external criticisms without developing negative self-perceptions and suffering shame or discomfort. Rather than ruminating and worrying about their experiences of social disapproval, psychologically flexible parents are more likely to take nonjudgmental, accepting, and open standpoints toward their suffering and keep a safe emotional distance from it. As they are able to cope better with discrimination experiences, they are less likely to become demoralized and distressed and are less susceptible to self-stigma and harsh parenting. Theoretical contributions and practical implications: On a theoretical level, our findings reveal how societal stigma (i.e., experienced discrimination) may negatively affect individual self-perceptions (i.e., self-stigma) and thereby family interactions (i.e., harsh parenting). Our findings also demonstrate how these negative effects can be mitigated by such protective factors as psychological flexibility, mindfulness, and nonattachment. On a practical level, our findings point to the importance of developing anti-stigma and anti-self-stigma interventions at societal and individual levels in order to reduce discrimination-related harm and improve parenting practices among parents of children with ASD. Our findings also highlight the potential utility of increasing psychological flexibility, mindfulness, and nonattachment in parents of children with ASD in order to help them cope with community stigma and promote positive parenting.

18611917.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611917.value: Major findings: Many parents of children with ASD are stigmatized and discriminated by the public, as they are thought to “cause” their children’s social and behavioral problems by failing to provide effective parenting and being unable to control and discipline their children. Although these parents are commonly stigmatized and discriminated, few studies have investigated the potential impact of stigma and discrimination on their parenting practices. The present study addressed some of these research gaps by examining the longitudinal association between experienced discrimination and harsh parenting among parents of children with ASD and explored the potential mediating and moderating factors of this association. Our results showed that experienced discrimination was longitudinally associated with higher levels of harsh parenting, and that this association was mediated by self-stigma and moderated by psychological flexibility and related constructs, namely mindfulness and nonattachment. Research outcomes: We have published 6 papers in international peer-refereed journals. In particular, we have published 2 papers in Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2020 impact factor: 4.291; rank: 15/77 in Developmental Psychology). We have also published 1 paper in Autism (2020 impact factor: 5.689; rank: 7/77 in Developmental Psychology), 1 paper in Autism Research (2020 impact factor: 5.216; rank: 4/53 in Behavioral Sciences), 1 paper in Mindfulness (2020 impact factor: 4.684; rank: 22/130 in Clinical Psychology), and 1 paper in Research in Developmental Disabilities (2020 impact factor: 3.230; rank: 4/74 in Rehabilitation). All of these journals are listed as Q1 journals in the Journal Citation Report. We have conducted 2 presentations at international conferences. In particular, we have conducted 1 presentation at the 2019 International Convention of Psychological Science. We have also conducted 1 presentation at the 2021 Association for Psychological Science Virtual Convention. We have secured 2 external competitive research and knowledge transfer grants to develop new projects based on the findings of this study. In particular, we have secured 1 General Research Fund to develop a new intervention program to reduce stigma stress among parents of children with ASD. We have also secured 1 Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Fund to develop a new internet-based intervention program to reduce stigma stress among families of children with neurodevelopmental disorders.

18611917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611917.value: Our study reveals that parents’ discrimination experiences may affect their parenting practices. Building upon our findings, future studies may examine the potential impact of parents’ discrimination experiences on their children’s developmental outcomes. Specifically, future studies may examine whether parents’ discrimination experiences may influence their children’s well-being and functioning through parent-child interactions. Future studies may also examine whether these influences can be moderated and mitigated by parents’ and children’s internal psychological resilience resources and external social support systems. Our study has several important practical implications. Given the damaging effects of discrimination experiences, future practitioners should consider developing effective stigma reduction programs to eradicate public stigma at societal level. Also, given the pivotal role of self-stigma in translating discrimination experiences into negative parenting practices, future practitioners should consider developing evidence-based self-stigma reduction programs to mitigate self-stigma at individual level. Furthermore, given the protective effects of psychological flexibility, mindfulness, and nonattachment against the psychological harm of discrimination experiences, future practitioners should consider developing an intervention program that integrates the elements of acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness intervention, and nonattachment training in order to help parents of children with ASD enhance stigma resistance and promote positive parenting.

18611917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611917.value: Many parents of children with ASD are stigmatized and discriminated by the public, as they are thought to “cause” their children’s social and behavioral problems by failing to provide effective parenting and being unable to control and discipline their children. Although these parents are commonly stigmatized and discriminated, few studies have investigated the potential impact of stigma and discrimination on their parenting practices. The present study utilized a longitudinal design to examine the impact of discrimination experiences on parenting practices among parents of children with ASD (n = 441). Our findings show that, when parents experience constant disapproval from the public, they may internalize the external criticism as self-stigma. Parents with self-stigma may develop negative self-evaluations and feel ashamed of their parental identity. They may also perceive a greater sense of burden in parenting and exhibit increased irritability and harshness toward their children. Importantly, our findings show that the undesirable link between experienced discrimination and harsh parenting can be mitigated by such protective factors as psychological flexibility, mindfulness, and nonattachment. Future practitioners should consider facilitating parents of children with ASD to increase psychological flexibility, mindfulness, and nonattachment in order to enhance stigma resistance, reduce stigma internalization, and promote positive parenting.

18612117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18612117.value: Entrepreneurship is widely regarded as a key driving force of economic development in both global North and global South. The increasing contribution of entrepreneurship to the Chinese economy has recently attracted the attention of economic planners, business practitioners and policy analysts both within and outside China. In spite of its rapid increase over the past decade, China’s entrepreneurial activities are marked by considerable regional disparity. Scattered information from different survey projects suggested a negative association between urban housing price and entrepreneurial rate. To date, however, little research has been done to critically evaluate the multiple mechanisms of housing access on entrepreneurial endeavors in transitional urban China. Existing studies of the determinants of entrepreneurship has tended to emphasize the “wealth effects” of housing price appreciation with little attention paid to the possible “crowding out effect” of housing market change. On the other hand, the extant literature on the social-spatial effects of housing has focused overwhelming on the domestic and family functions of housing and its surrounding neighborhood and has shed little light over the economic and financial function of housing to would-be entrepreneurs. Noticeable gaps and missing links are apparent in the existing literature. This proposed research will work at the interface of two main lines of scholarly inquiry and investigate the relationship between forms of access to housing and transition into entrepreneurship through a comparative study of three China’s globalizing cities. Through quantitative analyses of statistical and questionnaire data as well as qualitative studies of the insightful information to be obtained through in-depth interviews, this research will contribute new knowledge to advance theoretical inquiry into the complex nature and dynamics of entrepreneurship in different housing contexts, shed new light over the ramifications of China’s real estate-led urbanization model, and facilitate better policy making for a healthy urban real estate market and vibrant urban economy in globalizing China. Its findings will be of direct relevance to Mainland China where the government is determined to boost mass entrepreneurship and innovation and to Hong Kong characterized by extremely high property price and dormant entrepreneurial spirit. 企业家精神是发达和发展中国家经济发展的关键动力。近年来中国国内外的学者、政策研究人员和商界人士越来越重视企业家精神对中国经济增长的重要贡献。中国的创业活动不但在过去10多年来呈现快速发展的态势，也表现出显著的区域差异。从不同的调研项目中收集的信息可以发现一个有趣的现象：中国城市的创业比重与住房价格似乎存在负相关关系。但是迄今为止尚未有研究对居住状况如何影响城市居民的创业意愿这一议题进行深入系统的研究。已有的对企业家精神的研究多强调住房价格上涨对创业意愿的“财富”效应，而相对忽视其挤出效应。另一方面，对住房社会空间效应的研究则主要聚焦于住房的家庭和社会功能，很少关注其对潜在创业者的经济功能。本研究计划对北京、杭州和重庆这三个城市的实证研究来弥补这一研究不足。本研究的成果有利于丰富不同住房体系下企业家精神的动力机制研究，阐明中国房地产导向型城市化模式的影响。研究结论对于处在高房价、低创业意愿的香港有借鉴作用。

18612117.label: Realisation of objectives
18612117.value: The three objectives identified in the original proposal have all been accomplished satisfactorily and successfully. A summary of what have been done is provided as follows. Objective 1 has been successfully accomplished through a panel data analysis of the data collected for China’s 230 Chinese cities at or above prefectural level during the period 2003 to 2016. A review of the existing measurement of entrepreneurship has identified the presence of two commonly utilized approaches in empirical studies, namely the occupation choice approach to measure entrepreneurship as urban individuals in self-employment and the business enterprise approach to measure entrepreneurship as new firm formation. Both of these measurements are suitable only for cross-sectional data analysis. So this project has chosen to use the ratio of employment in private firms and individual businesses to total labour force in each city to measure urban entrepreneurial rate in Chinese cities. The result of the spatial dependency analysis has revealed the existence of spatial interactive effects for both urban housing price and entrepreneurial rate. Spatial panel data regression model analysis has identified an inverted U-shape pattern of association between housing price and urban entrepreneurship, which is quite contrary to most of the findings from existing studies. The analysis has further found significant inter-city housing price spillovers in the mega urban agglomerations surrounding the first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen. Objective 2 has been accomplished satisfactorily through the analysis of a sample of urban individuals developed from the 2016 China labor-force dynamics (CLDS) data which provides detailed information on the entrepreneurs’ motives. Through a distinction between opportunity-driven entrepreneurs who are pulled into entrepreneurship by the prospect of opportunity and necessity-driven entrepreneurs who are pushed into starting a business because they could not find jobs in the paid employment sector, this project has examined the uneven impact of housing conditions on urban individuals’ entrepreneurial choices. The two-level probit model analysis finds that the probability of being an opportunity versus a necessity-driven entrepreneur is higher for urban individuals with financial start-up support from their social networks in their residential cities and those with negative attitudes toward public sector employment. A rise in urban housing price is found to exert significantly negative impact on urban individuals’ propensity to engage in necessity-driven entrepreneurship, but exhibiting no significant influence on the location and prevalence of opportunity-driven entrepreneurship. Urban areas with larger and diversified economic sectors are found to confer significantly more advantage on the occurrence of opportunity-driven entrepreneurship than on necessity-driven entrepreneurship. Objective 3 has been satisfactorily achieved with interesting findings. A new sample of homeowners with the inclusion of individual, city and community-level variables has been generated from the 2007 China Income Household Project (CHIP) Survey data. A multi-level probit regression analysis has identified significant role of community housing rent and peer effect in influencing urban individuals’ entrepreneurial entry in Chinese cities. Opportunity and necessity-driven entrepreneurs are found to respond differently to China’s speculative real estate market. Necessity-driven entrepreneurs are more sensitive to the presence of low-cost housing accommodations and peer influence in their residential communities, while opportunity-driven entrepreneurs are more response to the magnitude of city-level agglomeration economies. Overall, we are very pleased with the results of this project as what have been originally planned.

18612117.label: Major findings and research outcome
18612117.value: This project has generated several important findings, some of which have already been published or under review in leading internationally referred journals in the fields of urban studies, housing studies and public policy, while some others are in the pipeline for submission. Major research findings of this project include: 1) There exists an inverted U-shape pattern of association between housing price and entrepreneurship in urban China. When the price of housing is at a low level, a housing price rise brings more opportunities than costs to would-be entrepreneurs and encourages entry into entrepreneurship. But when the price of housing continues to surge above a certain threshold value, the start-up costs associated with further appreciation of the price of housing will outweigh the potential benefits, leading to the dominance of crowding-out effects and discouraging entrepreneurial activities and intentions 2) The entrepreneurial motive of would-be entrepreneurs plays a mediating role in the nexus between urban housing price and individuals’ propensity of engaging in entrepreneurship. Urban housing price appreciation has only significantly negative impact on the possibility of being necessity-driven entrepreneurs. 3) Urbanization economies have significantly positive impact on the occurrence of opportunity-driven entrepreneurship and no significant effect on the possibility of being necessity-driven entrepreneurs. 4) There exists a significant role of community housing rent and peer effect in influencing urban individuals’ entrepreneurial entry in Chinese cities. The two types of entrepreneurship, namely necessity-driven entrepreneurship and opportunity-driven entrepreneurship, are found to be dictated by forces operating at different spatial scales. The probability of engaging in necessity-driven entrepreneurship is heavily shaped by the housing rent level and the location of like-minded, self-employed persons in their surrounding community environment, while the choice of becoming opportunity-driven entrepreneurship is more closely bound up with the degree of diversity in urban economies and industries. 5) housing market’s hard/soft landing may not be beneficial for entrepreneurial activities in some lower-tier cities where housing prices have not exceeded the threshold level. A cautious and balanced attitude towards the development of the real estate market should be adopted to avoid overkilling local entrepreneurship. 6) urban housing price appreciation is detrimental to the positive functioning of community peer influence and urban agglomeration economies. Combating high housing price in the formal housing sector can facilitate the unfolding of urbanization economies, while protecting the supply of low-cost housing units in the informal housing sector can contain the operating costs of small business startups in rapidly growing cities.

18612117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18612117.value: This project has highlighted some knowledge gaps in the existing literature on housing-entrepreneurship nexus. Three important issues arising from this project are believed to have great potentials for further theoretical and methodological advancement. 1 The emerging literature on the nexus between housing and entrepreneurship has focused too much on the differentiation between home owners and renters. This project has clearly identified the mediating role of entrepreneurial motives. How does this distinction interact with the heterogeneity in homeownership status to shape the possibility of urban individuals’ entrepreneurial choices deserves to be investigated in future studies. 2. Most of the prior work on housing-entrepreneurship nexus paid limited attention paid to neighborhoods and communities factors. This project made original attempt to explore the neglected role of community effects in Chinese cities. future research can be done along this line to investigate and distinguish the various ways through which neighborhood/community contexts impact on entrepreneurship and self-employment. 3. The existing quantitative analysis only draws upon traditional panel models . This project partially addresses this methodological deficiency through spatial panel model analysis. More sophisticated spatial interaction model techniques can be experimented in future research to uncover the spatially varying effects of housing conditions on entrepreneurship.

18612117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18612117.value: This project investigates the extent to which Chinese urban individuals’ involvement in different types of entrepreneurial activities can be explained by housing and non-housing factors operating at different spatial scales. The possibility of entrepreneurial entry in a city is found to be influenced by not only local housing price, but also the housing price change in surrounding ‘superstar’ cities. The impact of urban housing price on entrepreneurial entry is mediated by urban individuals’ entrepreneurial motives and the neighborhood and community context in which they live. The decision of becoming necessity-driven entrepreneurs is more likely to be held back by urban housing price appreciation, while the possibility of being opportunity-driven entrepreneurs tends to be enhanced by the magnitude of urban economic diversity. The presence of low-cost housing accommodations and the co-location of like-minded, self-employed persons in the same community environment are crucial to the engagement of small-scale, necessity-driven entrepreneurship. The research calls for bridging entrepreneurship studies, neighborhood studies and the literature on the geography of entrepreneurship to achieve better understanding of the multifarious ways through which housing and entrepreneurship are interconnected
