25602517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25602517.value: This research centers on the state-capital-school relationship in framing student internships in China’s development. Official statistics show that student enrollment in secondary vocational schools doubled from 11.7 million in 2001 to 22.4 million in 2010. The government aims to reach 23.5 million vocational students by 2020, that is, 50% of the total student population at the secondary school level. As vocational education and training programs have expanded across the country, firms have begun recruiting interns for temporary employment. There has been, however, scant attention to student interns as nonstandard, irregular or contingent workers. Interning students, who are classified as part-students, part-employees seeking to fulfill graduation requirements and gain specialized training, occupy an ambiguous position at the intersection of education and work. Drawing insights from labor sociology, education and law, the Principal Investigator asks three research questions: 1. How do the state, vocational schools and enterprises collaborate to run internship programs for a new generation of Chinese youth? 2. Under what circumstances are student interns more likely to receive genuine training to become skilled employees rather than being used as cheap, disposable labor? 3. In what ways do interning students attempt to safeguard their educational and labor rights in the growing intern economy? While the research focus is on China’s working youth, internships are now widespread and the subject of controversy throughout the world. Interestingly, some employers are climbing value chains by upskilling their employees through methods including the recruitment of student interns. But others collaborate with local governments and school administrations to exploit legal loopholes incentivized by the convenience of obtaining interns under short-term employment and by the low cost of young students’ labor, including non-contribution of social security. The informalization of labor, particularly the place of student interns, deserve detailed analysis. This three-year project will generate new data to compare different types of internships, that is, the insourcing and outsourcing of student labor. An insourcing employer invests in a school so that the school will train prospective employees with company-specific skills. Under outsourcing, an employer signs a labor service contract with the agency, which then dispatches student-employees as interns to fill the client’s human resource needs. As a result, the pathways to skill acquisition and decent employment for the interns can be very different. In the context of slowing growth and an ageing population, proper training of vocational students is significant to sustainable development in China and far beyond. 本研究採用國家、資本與學校三者聯動的分析框架，探索中國學生在實習過程中的現況。我國中等職業學校學生的數量從2001年的1170萬已翻倍到2010年的2240萬，而官方的目標是，到2020年，全國中等職業教育在校生將達到2350萬人，佔高中階段教育招生數的50%。企業伴隨國家領導人擴大職業教育和專業培訓的範圍，開始招聘實習生到短期性的工作崗位。然而，即使大批實習生已成為了非正規或不固定的從業人員，卻未受到學界高度重視。職業教育處在教育和就業的交叉點上，學生實習生在勞動過程中佔據了一個介於學生和工人之間的模糊位置，值得廣泛關注。 研究員參考勞動社會學、教育與法律等相關文獻，提出了三個主要的問題︰ 1. 中國政府、職業學校和企業怎樣為新一代的年青人提供實習機會呢？ 2. 學生實習生在甚麼情況下能得到真正的培訓，不致淪為廉價的、用過即棄的勞工？ 3. 實習生如何保障自身的教育及勞工權益呢？ 事實上，實習制度在全球各地、各行各業已相當普遍。本研究聚焦在中國青年，嘗試引發社會上更多的討論。有趣的是，一些僱主投放了不少資源在實習生身上，務求提高競爭力；另一些卻鑽法律的空子去連結地方政府和學校行政人員，使用臨時性實習學生，規避繳納員工社保費等基本責任以減低成本。勞動力非正規化的現象，透過具體的個案分析可突顯出來。 這為期三年的研究著重比較不同類型的實習計劃，目前大致歸納為內包和外包兩大類。內包指企業為學校提供專門的培訓，量身訂造，孕育人才。外包指企業透過勞務派遣的方式，把學生勞動力輸送到所需崗位以滿足用工需求。結果，實習生在獲取職業技能和體面工作的路徑可能大有差別。正當國內經濟增長放緩及人口急劇老化，我們如何適切地培育職校學生，對社會未來的發展將會帶來深遠的影響。

25602517.label: Realisation of objectives
25602517.value: The three objectives of this research project titled “Internships, Informal Labor and Vocational Skills Training in China” have been realized. First, the Principal Investigator aims to understand work and training experiences from the perspective of student interns in China’s changing state-labor-capital relations. The following 4 case studies illustrate the positive training outcomes. The socialist legacy of Chinese state-owned enterprise schools Case study I. PetroCN (a pseudonym) is a centrally-administered state-owned enterprise in the oil and gas sector. It provides apprentices with comprehensive training in management and leadership, occupational safety and health, and elective courses relating to petrochemistry and renewable energies. Following the company’s best practices, a master pairs up with an apprentice to share craft experiences. The company also collaborates with universities (e.g., China University of Petroleum) to build a tech talent pipeline. Cast study II. AutoCN (a pseudonym), a large state-owned enterprise, strives to become a leader in the automobile industry. It has established a corporate university to strengthen research and development in smart manufacturing, global supply chain governance, and customer service. In addition, in collaboration with a college of electronics engineering, the company has trained apprentices in self-driving car technologies, low-carbon energy and logistics systems. Apprentices had some degree of autonomy and employee voice in a work team. Corporate skills training in the private sector Besides the Chinese state sector, foreign-invested and privately-run enterprises have likewise established corporate universities, laboratories, and research centers to enhance staff training and development. They offer awards and prizes to outstanding student interns and apprentices. Case study III. Taiwanese-invested Foxconn Technology Group, the world’s largest electronics manufacturer, operates Foxconn University at its mega-factories across coastal and interior provinces in China. The corporate university boasts extensive partnerships with Stanford University, Tsinghua University and Peking University, among others. High-caliber students with a background in electrical and electronics engineering are prepared to become team or group leaders. They are motivated to join industrial robot technology competitions and promised a stable career upon graduation. Case study IV. Alibaba Group, along with Baidu and Tencent, enjoys an oligopolistic position in China. Alibaba’s business segments have extended from online sales to financial services (through its affiliate Ant Group) and logistics management (such as food and parcel deliveries). Leveraging both material and digital infrastructures, the platform company runs its Hupan Entrepreneurship Research Centre at the company headquarters in Hangzhou city, Zhejiang province. Managers provide trainings to students majoring in marketing, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, and cloud computing. Self-motivated trainees plan to take vocational national exams in their field of expertise. In summary, against the tides of flexibilization and precarization of labor, the institutionalization of skills training and talent retention schemes is very important. But it turns out that, except in a few cases, enforcement of internship regulations has remained highly uneven. The second objective of this research is to inform contemporary analyses of skill upgrading and labor informalization through comprehensive research on student internships in China. As the first-hand research data shows, many student trainees were recruited as low-cost, short-term laborers for the benefit of companies, rather than with the purpose of fulfilling the educational missions. 1. Violations of state regulations. The student interviewees—including sales agents, retail clerks, office assistants, warehouse workers and factory workers—were required to adapt to “flexible schedules” to meet customers’ needs. Repair and maintenance workers, for example, had to attend alternate day and night shifts (each working shift lasts for 10–12 hours), even when the state regulations prohibit overtime and night work in student internships. Worse, the content of assembly-line or manual labor was unrelated to students’ majors or learning plans. 2. Low wages during internship and apprenticeship. The law stipulates that student interns and apprentices shall be paid at least 80 percent of the wages of employees working in the same position. As a norm, cost-conscious employers take it as the maximum pay standard. Moreover, they are not obligated to provide students (who are not legally classified as formal employees) with social insurance benefits. In this sense, student-workers are cheap laborers. As of January 2022, the local statutory minimum wage was 2,280 yuan/month in Hangzhou city and 2,070 yuan/month in Huzhou city, Zhejiang province, and 1,900 yuan/month at Zhongshan and Foshan cities, Guangdong province. At non-technical positions, students were paid just 1,500–2,000 yuan a month, depending on the locality. In comparing to social science and humanities students, science students tended to make a little more, earning a monthly wage ranging from 2,000–2,800 yuan, particularly in large electronics, automobile, and aluminum factories. 3. Limited prospects. A typical comment about a disappointing internship or apprenticeship is the low value added to one’s future prospects. In a parts-processing workshop, two students from the same vocational college were assigned to coating and cleaning machinery. They gained a clearer understanding about the entire process of lens coating, but there would be no chance to get promoted. The local business market was very small. Many others in small workshops (e.g., welders, millers and fitters) shared concerns about limited career advancement. The third objective of this project is to generate information that could contribute to enhancing the quality of China’s vocational education and training and the protection of student interns’ rights. School principals, program leaders and teachers informed the Principal Investigator that they have raised teaching standards to compete for state and industry resources to recruit excellent students. The four researched vocational institutions (renamed to protect the teacher and student interviewees) are based in urban city clusters in Guangdong and Zhejiang provinces: 1. Foshan Vocational Technical School, Guangdong province (founded in 1989; with 2,600 students) 2. Zhongshan Polytechnic, Guangdong province (founded in 2004, with 10,000 students) 3. Hangzhou Technician College, Zhejiang province (founded in 1979; with 2,300 students) 4. Huzhou Technician College, Zhejiang province (founded in 1979, with 3,100 students) The teachers have actively liaised with alumni, enterprises, and trade associations to broaden student training opportunities at home and abroad (e.g., in Japan and Germany). They aspire to become leading vocational universities by professionalizing their faculty, opening new courses, raising funds, and upgrading campus infrastructure. a) Professionalization in teaching. Vocational college teachers of technical subjects are required to possess a master’s degree and at least three years’ relevant working experience. They are also expected to attend workshops at partnering corporations to keep abreast of industry knowledge. b) Development of high-level skills. The teachers aim to promote lifelong learning through deeper engagement with the public and private sectors. They have identified trustworthy enterprises that uphold students’ rights and interests, and develop useful learning resources to enable students to gain new skills and recognized qualifications. Looking ahead, the Beijing government has enforced the expanded Vocational Education Law (2022), which extensively revised the version that first came into force in 1996. The law stipulates that vocational education is equally important as general education, signifying the development of a balanced dual-track educational system in the long run. Meanwhile, the state experiments with an eight-grade system of skill development by sponsoring employers. A good-performing trainee can climb the internal career ladder to become a junior technical worker, mid-level technical worker, high-level technical worker, technician, senior technician, special project technician, and principal technician. The national policy further defines commensurate salaries and benefits by skill levels, thus incentivizing employees to excel and equip themselves.

25602517.label: Major findings and research outcome
25602517.value: China has the world’s largest vocational education and training system. Between 2016 and 2020, the central government expended 129 billion yuan to enhance the quality of vocational education with an annual growth rate averaging 9.8 percent. As of 2021, the total number of vocational school students surpassed 29 million, comprising 13 million teenagers at the upper secondary level (who have already completed nine years’ basic schooling) and 16 million at the tertiary level (aged 18 or above). To facilitate a transition to working life, the Chinese state, school and enterprise play a significant role. The nature of student internship and apprenticeship is pre-employment training. This multi-year research finds that a good program is participatory and reflective in learning. The trainees have a contextual understanding of their work responsibility through the combination of theory and practice. While there are highly successful cases, the Principal Investigator reveals that a non-negligible number of employers have failed to comply with Chinese labor laws and International Labour Organization (ILO) standards, including a ban on forced labor. Drawing on 112 interviews with students, schoolteachers, corporate managers and government officials, supplemented with school and workplace visits in Guangdong and Zhejiang provinces, the research team traces the evolution of vocational education and training models with an eye on student-workers’ well-being. The dual mentorship mode synergizes schoolteachers and corporate managers to provide students with appropriate training. Innovative pedagogies and rigorous assessment rubrics are core components, and there is consensus that one-off examination does not serve to inspire curiosity and nurture growth. In a closer look, while approximately 25 percent of the interviewed students did accomplish meaningful goals at large state-owned enterprises and non-state firms, many employers have arguably taken student interns and apprentices as low-cost temporary workers to meet human resources needs, rather than providing them with useful training, let alone recognizing their right to resign. It is evident that both the national legal framework and transnational corporate social responsibility (CSR) system in the area of student labor governance have to be improved. Moreover, challenges remain on the creation of stable employment and industrial upgrading. Future research on widening access to high-quality training for disadvantaged groups in economically underdeveloped regions is suggested. Vocational education is strategically designed to promote local and national growth. To accumulate human capital—a crucial element of the “Made in China 2025” developmental plan and Belt and Road Initiative—China’s leaders should vastly expand higher education including vocational training.

25602517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25602517.value: This study shows that in-house corporate-administered training programs have yielded high levels of satisfaction among student trainees. Large state-owned and non-state enterprises utilize their own universities or laboratories to train and retrain the workforce. An over-reliance on firm-specific skills (vis-à-vis transferrable skills and knowledge), however, may constrain labor mobility, thus aggravating the looming problem of skilled labor shortage. Employers should be incentivized to foster industry-level innovation and workforce upskilling as a whole. In terms of scope, this research has focused on vocational education and training in developed cities in Guangdong and Zhejiang provinces. Researchers are encouraged to explore new forms of skills training in economically underdeveloped regions. Training providers (including adult-education schools) should extend their programs to support farmers, migrant workers, ethnic minorities and other vulnerable groups. In this way, rural revitalization and urban-rural integration will be advanced. With state subsidies and tax exemption, the use of industrial robots is growing in assembly, packaging, and quality testing. While automation technologies and digitalization can boost output and manufacturing productivity, tensions arise as labor intensive jobs are replaced and industrial relations are changed. Now is the time to introduce appropriate training through curriculum planning and school-business partnerships to co-create a sustainable, post-pandemic future.

25602517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25602517.value: How to analyze the development and effectiveness of internship and apprenticeship programs in China? Drawing on in-depth interviews, supplemented with school and workplace visits, this research project finds that student interns and apprentices’ satisfaction with vocational training varies widely by several factors, namely, (1) training content and pedagogical approach; (2) access to universities, corporate, and external professionals; and (3) technological level and corporate production capacity. Large corporations are well-funded to run a hybrid mode of e-learning and face-to-face teaching, even long before the breakout of the continuing COVID pandemic. They have established their own universities or accredited educational centers to offer comprehensive courses for students and employees. By contrast, in other places, students at low-level posts on factory assembly lines, warehouses, and offices frequently complained that they were compelled to do excessive overtime and nightshifts. The professed ideal of vocational training through the integration of education and industry, especially in micro and small-sized enterprises, has yet to be realized. At a time of slowing economic growth, a shrinking pool of workers and an aging population, vocational school graduates could play a significant role in Chinese industrial and technological upgrading if they were to receive appropriate training leading to better jobs.

25604917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25604917.value: Land-related disputes have become a chief cause of rural resistance in contemporary China and a subject of increasing concern for both academic and policy communities. A majority of conflicts has been associated with the contentious expropriation of collectively-owned rural land by state actors for industrial, commercial and infrastructural development. In south China, local governments and village communities have been experimenting with rural land management and development policies that are based on the retention of collective property. Instead of state-led land expropriation, village communities have retained a portion of collectively-owned land for accommodation and collective economic development. To manage common property, distribute collective revenues and provide public goods, a variety of institutional arrangements and property rights regimes have been introduced including community-based rural shareholding and the establishment of shareholding cooperatives and shareholding companies. These land-based organizations yield managerial control over key rural assets and are playing an increasingly prominent role not only in the governance of China’s urbanizing village communities, but also in state-society dynamics concerning land management and land use control, fiscal arrangements, and the negotiation of rural-urban relations. Despite their centrality in the ongoing transformation of rural China, little systematic effort has been made towards analyzing these policy experimentations and the outcomes obtained. Drawing on the theory of institutional change, this project comparatively examines how interactions and contestations between local state and society actors have produced different institutional forms and property rights reform pathways in three types of territorially-defined communities situated respectively at the rural fringe, urban fringe and urban core of Chinese cities. Based on fieldwork in Guangdong province, it analyzes the structural characteristics and societal functions of land-based organizations, identifies the key actors engaged in land management, shareholding and property rights reform, and assesses the local impact on rural communities and livelihoods. This project is expected to yield theoretical and empirical insights that will be of interest to scholars and policymakers. First, it will generate insights into models of land development and collective asset management in south China and enrich understandings of the institutional dynamics of rural transformation by focusing on collective ownership and property rights reform. Second, it will provide timely research on the urbanization and integration of rural communities and shed light on the functions and operation of land-based collective organizations. Finally, this study will enable theorization of policy-making and institution-building at the level of the local state, and deepen understandings of state-society relations in contemporary China.

25604917.label: Realisation of objectives
25604917.value: This project sets out to explore how local governments and village collectives in contemporary China are addressing land-related disputes through institutional innovation, specifically by establishing rural collective economic organizations and shareholding corporations to manage the conversion of rural land to non-agricultural uses. The PI has successfully achieved all five stated objectives. 1. Objective 1 concerns surveying the land-based collective economic organizations that have emerged in three types of communities in southern China. Through ethnographic fieldwork carried out between 2018 and 2019 in the cities of Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Zhuhai, the PI has completed data collection in all three field sites. The three types of communities surveyed include industrializing rural communities at the rural fringe of metropolitan regions (site in Zhuhai); rural-urban communities situated at the urban fringe of Chinese cities, commonly referred to as “urban villages” (site in Shenzhen); and formerly rural communities that have been completely urbanized and integrated into the urban surrounding through administrative reclassification and neighbourhood redevelopment (site in Guangzhou). The data generated from field study provided important insights into the structural characteristics and societal functions of collective organizations found in the three types of communities, including the organization of political power, the structures of decision-making and popular representation, the allocation of collective revenues, and the role of the collectives in guaranteeing subsistence, providing public goods, and community governance. 2. Objectives 2 and 3 involve identifying the key state and society actors engaged in land management and rural shareholding reforms, and comparing how interactions between local state and society actors have produced variation in property rights arrangements and institutional reform pathways. Interviews and participant observation during field study enabled the PI to achieve these two aims. Specifically, the PI compared the different roles played by local governments, village leaders, as well as informal institutions such as clans and kinship groups in exercising managerial rights over land and instituting property rights reform. It is found that, in the most urbanized rural communities, the presence of strong local social organizations and kinship networks has facilitated the formation of highly organized shareholding corporations that are managed by village leaders. These corporations are effective in negotiating land deals, distributing land rents, and providing welfare to village members, though the unequal distribution of power within these institutions has been a source of bottom-up discontent amongst villagers. In comparison, collective organizations in villages located at the urban-rural fringe are less organized and effective. The function of shareholding in these villages is mainly limited to distributional purposes. 3. Objectives 4 and 5 involve analysing how existing property rights arrangements may entail differential distributional consequences for social groups, and assessing the impact of institutional reform on local communities and state-society relations. It is found that land and shareholding reforms have been a controversial process and engendered unequal relations of distribution in all three types of communities studied. The axes of contention varied however between the three communities. Some villages saw contestations between rural cadres and villagers, while in others there were distributional conflicts between local villagers and non-local residents. 4. Making use of the data collected, the PI published a total of seven papers in Q1, SSCI-indexed peer-review journals. The PI also disseminated the project’s findings through paper presentations at seven international conferences, including conferences organized by the Association for Asian Studies, Urban China Research Network, and Royal Geographical Society.

25604917.label: Major findings and research outcome
25604917.value: This project has several major findings: 1. By analyzing the latest policies and dynamics of land reform, this project shed light on the changing strategies adopted by the Chinese state in managing and developing rural land. It demonstrated a shift in approach from state-led expropriations toward an increasing reliance on market mechanisms in land development. By enlisting rural collectives as corporatist market players and enrolling villagers in speculative rentiership, the reforms pre-empt organized resistance to land takings by giving both rural elites and residents a material stake in land commodification. These findings advance the comparative study of land and property rights reform in transitional economies and contribute to theorizations of territorial transformation in a context where diverse property arrangements – state, collective, and private ownership – coexist. The PI has published these findings in the International Journal of Urban and Regional Research (2019), Geoforum (2020), and Journal of Rural Studies (2021). 2. This study highlighted the role of informal institutions and social forces in land development. By comparing the community dynamics of reform in different field sites, it is found that villages with strong lineage and solidary groups tend to have highly-organized collective economic organizations. The presence of these organizations on the one hand facilitated land development as their leaders represented the village in negotiating land deals and overseeing development projects with the state and private capital. The dominance of certain social groups in these organizations has on the other hand engendered contestations from below. The PI discussed the role of informal institutions in land politics in papers published in the China Quarterly (2019) and Urban Studies (2020). 3. This study also drew attention to the distributional consequences of rural land and shareholding reform. By comparing how the advent of rural land markets and neighbourhood redevelopment affected villagers with different levels of political, economic and social capital, this project demonstrated how power differentials endogenous to communities could create unequal access to land and result in uneven incorporation into land-based accumulation. The findings were published in Cities (2021) and Journal of Agrarian Change (2022).

25604917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25604917.value: Given the evolving dynamics of rural land development in China, there is strong potential for the further development of the research agendas identified in this project. In particular, recent policies of rural land transfer provide a novel context for analyzing the direct circulation of rural land from villagers to commercial users without going through state expropriations. The introduction of land transfer has also given rise to new corporate actors in rural land politics, such as agribusinesses and tourism companies. To pursue these lines of enquiry, the PI submitted and obtained a GRF grant which builds upon the present project while advancing the scope of analysis. Going beyond this project’s focus on the industrialised and urbanising parts of rural China, where land is mostly converted to industrial or commercial use, the GRF examines the dynamics of rural land development for agricultural and recreational purposes. It further extends the regional scope of enquiry by introducing a comparative dimension between Guangdong and Jiangsu provinces. It is expected that the projects will form a comparative framework for analysing land transfers to different types of capital and yield new insights on the evolution of land policies under different local institutional contexts.

25604917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25604917.value: Rural China has been the site of intensive administrative, economic and territorial restructuring in the reform era. As processes of state-led land expropriation became increasingly contested, grassroots experimentation in shareholding based on collective property has been seen as an alternative and more equitable means of achieving the non-agricultural conversion of rural land and the urbanization of rural communities. This project examines these reforms by carrying out field research in three types of communities situated at the rural fringe, urban fringe and urban core of Chinese cities, and analyzes the different property rights and land-based institutions that have emerged in each region. It is found that rural collective economic organizations have played key roles in managing land and providing welfare, but the uneven distributional consequences arising from reforms have also engendered contentious politics from below. The findings point to the need to pay further policy and research attention to addressing relations of extraction and exclusion at the community level. By shedding light on grassroots structures of power and dynamics of land development, this project contributes to current debates on the governance of urbanizing rural communities in China and the integration of rural residents into urban society.

25605317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25605317.value: 批判思維（或稱明辨思維），泛指反思懷疑的傾向與技巧。培育學生批判思維是香港教育的一個核心目標，它是正向成長的關鍵因素，對青年公民參與尤為重要。本研究建議運用青少年媒體實踐作為培育青少年批判思維性情的補充介入方法。青少年媒體實踐泛指各類協助年輕人透過媒體製作表達己見的活動，其目標並非鼓吹或否定特定觀點，而是在表達觀點的過程中促進表達者的批判思維性情。基本原理是協助個人將思維外在化，繼而有更多空間闡明、否定或修改觀點。青少年媒體實踐已非新鮮事，但社會工作文獻是近年才有所討論，有待進一步討論與檢視。建基於青少年媒體實踐的框架，本研究將設計及進行一個以社交媒體為本的照片說故事活動，從而評估該活動能否提高參與者的批判思維性情。 在兩個月內，參與者就“民族身份”為題，在社交媒體分享照片。他們將最少一周兩次在社交媒體組群中上載照片，得悉研究員及研究助理回饋，並進一步發展照片故事。研究員和研究助理將使用特定的反思提問方法與參與者交流。最後，參與者將序列不超過 10 幅標題照片，以總結見解。本研究採用隨機對照試驗 (RCT)方法，透過教師及社工招募 60 位參與者，年齡介乎18-24歲、生於香港、中國籍、並完成新高中通識考試。參與者將隨機被分到介入組和對照組，每組 30 人。評估分三階段： 介入前、介入後、及完成介入後2個月。量度項目包括批判思維性情、民族身份認同、高階思維素質等等。 本研究有助引入一種創新、可重覆及可研究的社會工作方式，啟動學術界討論能否透過發展性活動支援青少年公民教育。

25605317.label: Realisation of objectives
25605317.value: Objective 1. To develop a social media based photo-story intervention model with reference to a youth media practice framework. This project did not merely validate a one-off intervention trial, but it has largely supported the development of a media technology informed psychosocial intervention approach. In the preparation stage and initial stage of this project, I adopted slightly different terms to refer to the practice that I have been researching and developing, due to differences in terminologies used in different academic traditions. After comprehensive reviews and strategic considerations, I started consistently calling this approach “Media-informed Narrative Practice (MNP)”. This is also a name I coined, which is innovative and yet related to existing academic discussions. MNP evolved from Narrative Practice (NP also known as Narrative Therapy; NT) and Digital Storytelling (Digital Storytelling). There are three publications derived from this project that have paved the way for this innovative practice approach: * Chan, C., & Yau, C. (2019). Digital storytelling for social work interventions. In E. Mullen (Ed.), Oxford Bibliographies in Social Work. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/OBO/9780195389678-0273. This encyclopedia article is the first in social work that describes the trend of digital storytelling, which is a storytelling method that is interwoven with digitized images, texts, sounds, and other interactive elements. Such a method can be applied at different levels of practice: i) micro-level: individuals, families, and small groups; ii) meso-macro-level: community, organization, society, and culture; and iii) multiple-level: targeting micro, meso, and macro levels in the same intervention. Digital storytelling practice emerged with the advent of accessible media production hardware, editing software, and media sharing platforms. In addition, there are sustainable organizations that have gradually developed their unique methods and funding models. This growing network has popularized the concept of digital storytelling. Further, there are academic networks studying the phenomenon, which have further positioned the field in scholarly discussion. * Chan, C., & Sage, M. (2019). A narrative review of digital storytelling for social work practice. Journal of Social Work Practice. https://doi.org/10.1080/02650533.2019.1692804. This peer-reviewed journal article is the first in social work that provides an overall review of the use of digital storytelling for social work interventions. It points out that while the term has become more popular, its role in actual social work interventions is not clear. The ambiguity of “digital storytelling” presents a hurdle to further theorization for social work practice and research. This article provides a narrative review and derives a conceptualization that is in line with social work’s psychotherapeutic and systems orientation. The review has derived a two-layer conceptualization. In a broad sense, digital storytelling can be seen as an umbrella term covering different sorts of storytelling activities that use digital communication media. Practitioners and researchers can adopt a set of parameters for describing and comparing different practice designs. More specifically, it can be seen as a kind of narrative practice utilizing digital communication media. This definition offers a conceptual base for such practice, which helps further theorization and research in social work practice. * Chan, C., & Au-yeung, H. (2021, in press). When narrative practice suddenly goes online due to COVID-19…. Qualitative Social Work. https://doi.org/10.1177/1473325020981086. This upcoming article (which will be counted in another GRF research report, but it is largely inspired by this present ECS project) is a reflective consolidation of my practice experience in Hong Kong during the COVID-19 period, in which social work educators and practitioners needed to work online in a prolonged period of social distancing. It illustrates in what ways online practices may denote emerging knowledge and skills that are worth further discussion. These reflections have been consolidated as some knowledge/skill domains, and they have inspired me to comprehend the potential of media technologies more fully, and eventually informed me to consolidate the basic framework of MNP. Objective 2. To evaluate whether the social media based photo-story intervention can enhance participants’ critical thinking disposition, particularly in the context of which they express views on ethnic identities (the heuristic production theme used in the project). This project has validated the initial effectiveness of such a storytelling approach. It is assumed that participants will become more aware of their strengths, alternative voices, and potential solutions to the challenges they face. Therefore, general psychometric outcomes include, such as increased critical openness, decreased closed-mindedness, increased self-esteem, and reduced essentialist views. Detailed outcomes will be reported in section 6.1 of this report. The following paragraphs serve to introduce the two peer-reviewed articles that have reported outcomes of this research project in different stages. * Chan, C., & Holosko, M. (2020). Utilizing youth media practice to influence change: A pretest-posttest study. Research on Social Work Practice, 30, 110-121. https://doi.org/10.1177/1049731519837357. This is the first study that developed and field-tested my MNP-based intervention using a pretest-posttest design. Using “My National/Ethnic Identity” as a heuristic production theme, a pilot study was conducted in Hong Kong in 2018. Participants shared and discussed photos online and conducted face-to-face presentations. The program was evaluated using a one-group pretest-posttest design. Participants included (N= 20) Hong Kong Chinese students aged 18–24. Results indicated that participants’ need for cognitive closure decreased, self-esteem increased, and their essentialist views on ethnic identity decreased. * Chan, C. (2019). Using digital storytelling to facilitate critical thinking disposition in youth civic engagement: A randomized control trial. Children and Youth Services Review, 107, 104522. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.childyouth.2019.104522. This study further field-tested the MNP approach using a more rigorous experimental design. Using civic identity as a heuristic production theme, a Randomized Control Trial (RCT) was conducted in Hong Kong in 2019. Participants were youths in Hong Kong, aged 16–24. They were randomized into a group receiving the intervention (n1=36) and a control group that did not receive the intervention (n2=51). Participants shared photos on social media, chatted online and offline with facilitators, and finally produced their digital photo stories. Participants in the intervention group increased their self-esteem and critical thinking disposition. Their ethnocentric views also declined. Participants in the control group became more closed-minded, but participants in the intervention group remained at a stable level. Objective 3. To open the discussion of using developmental programs to support youth civic engagement. I have shared my idea of MNP on various conference/workshop occasions, including: * A conference presentation “Utilizing Digital Storytelling to Influence Change: An Outcome-based Trial Case Study: on 2019-06-28, at Department of Social Work & Social Administration, HKU, Hong Kong (live, face to face sharing) * A workshop “MNP workshop” (媒介敘事工作坊) on 2020-07-08, at The Hong Kong Council of Social Service, Hong Kong (live, face to face workshop) * An “extended MNP workshop” (媒介敘事延伸工作坊) on 2020-08-12, at The Hong Kong Council of Social Service (via Zoom)

25605317.label: Major findings and research outcome
25605317.value: Intended psychometric outcomes include, such as increased Critical Openness, decreased Need for Cognitive Closure, increased Self Esteem, and reduced Ethnic Essentialism. Results showed that most of these intended outcomes were achieved as planned, lending further support to the potential efficacy of such a storytelling approach. The pretest-posttest pilot (Chan & Holosko, 2020) indicated that almost all participants significantly reduced their Need for Cognitive Closure (NFC) – aversions toward ambiguity – immediately after the program. Average NFC Score reduced from 6.29 at T1 to 5.74 at T2, p < .001. Critical Openness score also increased from 7.34 at T1 to 7.59 at T2; although it did not reach a level of statistical significance, it is close to the statistical significance level (p = .08). Moreover, participants generally felt good about themselves. Their self-esteem Score increased from 6.12 at T1 to 6.45 at T2, p < .05. Also, Essentialist Views on ethnonational identity include beliefs such as one’s ethnic identity is innate and essentially has an unchanged essence. In this study, most participants had reduced their essentialist views on ethnic identity, particularly a deconstruction of extreme nativist nationalism or extreme PRC Chinese-ness. Average Essentialist Views Score reduced from 4.75 at T1 to 4.08 at T2, p < .05. In the RCT (Chan, 2019), the Self Esteem scores of the intervention group increased (+0.50, p < .001, d = .73), while the control group did not indicate significant change. The Critical Openness scores of the intervention group increased (+0.35, p = .02, d = .40), while the control group did not indicate significant change. The Need for Cognitive Closure score of the intervention group did not decrease as predicted, while the control group significantly increased (+0.34, p = .001, d = .47). The scores reflecting ethnic essentialism of the intervention group decreased (-0.83, p = .05, d = -.34), while the control group did not indicate any significant change.

25605317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25605317.value: Riding on the foundations of NP, MNP incorporates new techniques to help human service professionals to improve their practice, and such innovations imply potential for further development of the research. First, and these new knowledge and techniques present potential research areas that can be further developed. For example, how MNP can enable practitioners to: 1) utilize new media communication contexts to engage service users, 2) assess and advance their conversations with service users, 3) utilize different communication-modalities to enhance their conversations with service users, and; 4) promote service users’ voices in a broader circulation network to influence social discourse. Second, a training manual can be published in form of a book. MNP can be used in different fields, including counseling, psychotherapy, interviews, speech, group work, and community education. A manuscript of that book (tentatively called “Media-informed Narrative Practice” 媒介敘事工作手冊) has been drafted, it is expected to be published in 2021 (the Chinese version) and in 2022 (the English version). This book can help provide foundational training for research personnel involved in upcoming research and enhance intervention fidelity

25605317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25605317.value: This study demonstrated in what ways media technology can create space and opportunities for reflective conversations, and it can be used to formulate a change-making strategy for social work practice. Specifically, production-based activities can attract young participants and they can develop their critical openness in civic engagement activities. The trials supported by this project have supported the development and consolidation of a practice approach that I call Media-informed Narrative Practice (MNP). MNP can be used in different fields, including counseling, psychotherapy, interviews, speech, group work, and community education. It assists service users to explore core values, revisit their strengths, and face their challenges more effectively. MNP offers techniques that enable human service professionals to 1) utilize new media communication contexts to engage their service users, 2) assess and advance their conversations with service users, 3) utilize different communication-modalities to enhance their conversations with service users, and; 4) promote service users’ voices in a broader circulation network to influence social discourse.

25606117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25606117.value: 神经语言学的一个大研究问题是词汇和语言声音在脑海里怎么存储；就是说，脑海里的词汇表征是抽象的（只包含一些关键的特征）还是情节的（包含很多关于对这个单词的经历的细节）。中文很适合研究这个问题，因为声调会经历很多种有系统的变化；因此，一个声调的正常形式和特殊情况下的形式有时候会有差别。我们可以用这些差别来测探大脑里是否存储了特殊情况下的声调形式是否，还是只存储了基本的抽象形式。这项研究会关注像 ka2的普通话音节；这些音节不是真正的词（比方说，词典里没有任何发音ka2的字），但是讲普通话的人会经常遇到这些 音（比方说，在“我电脑卡死了”着聚会，卡会发音成ka2，因为上声变调让ka3变成ka2）。我将会使用神经语言学的研究技巧来测试这种音在大脑里的认知表征。如果大脑里只有抽象的表征，那么大脑对像ka2这种音节的加工应该跟对不存在的词的加工似的。而如果大脑里存储了一个人生活中遇到过的每个音，那么这种音节应该像一个真正的词，而大脑对这种音的加工应该跟对真词的加工似的。这个项目会用三种对某个音是否单词的状态很敏感的神经语言范式来测试三种假设：像ka2这些音的表征 甲、像真词的表征；乙、像假词的表征；丙、又不像真词又不像假词。这些研究会帮我们进一步了解语言在大脑里的组织，尤其是在有声调的语言中。而且，这项研究的结果说不定会应用到语言疾病的治疗、二语教学、同语音技术。

25606117.label: Realisation of objectives
25606117.value: The objectives changed because the initial set of experiments revealed that the paradigm we planned to use did not work in the way that was previously understood. Specifically, before we did this project, it was generally believed that the Mismatch Negativity (MMN) brain component is sensitive to whether or not a stimulus is a word, and thus we planned to use that to test whether sandhi accidental gaps behave like words or not. But in the course of our experiments we found that the MMN is actually not reliably sensitive to that. Therefore, we were unable to answer the initial question we set out to answer, but instead we discovered something new -- we discovered a previously unacknowledged challenge to traditional assumptions about what modulates the MMN. We pursued that discovery further in a follow-up experiment; these experiments led to a publication. We also tried using a different paradigm, not originally part of our research plan, to get back to testing the original question we had set out to answer. Anyway, we do not consider this an under-achievement; while we were not able to answer the question we originally set out to answer, we made unexpected discoveries and pursued them.

25606117.label: Major findings and research outcome
25606117.value: Publication: Stephen Politzer-Ahles & Suyeon Im (2020). Mismatch negativity is not always modulated by lexicality. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 14, 459. (we also had a conference presentation of this same work at the 2019 Hanyang International Symposium on Phonetics and Cognitive Science, Seoul, Korea) Conference presentation: Politzer-Ahles, Stephen, Ka Keung Lee, & Julie Siying Chen (2021). A failure to replicate the Ganong effect for tone continua. 2nd Words in the World Conference, Montreal, Canada (online). Overall, the main finding of the project was that the MMN is not always sensitive to lexicality, contrary to what has previously been thought. Our follow-up experiment also found another situation where expected effects of lexicality fail to occur.

25606117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25606117.value: A clear next step is to figure out why some studies find effects of lexicality on the MMN (i.e., words elicit larger MMN than nonwords) whereas others do not. While this project shows that words to not always elicit larger MMN than nonwords, we have not yet discovered why; presumably there is some hidden moderator that determines whether a given experiment gets a lexicality effect or not, and future study needs to figure out what that is. Similarly, in follow-up research we also failed to find a Ganong effect (another situation where words and nonword normally behave differently in a certain experiment context) for Mandarin tone continua. Clearly across this project what we have been finding is that there are constraints on when lexicality effects do and do not emerge -- across different paradigms -- and we need to do more research to figure out what those constraints are.

25606117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25606117.value: Brain activity can be separated into many different components, and these different components represent different mental processes (i.e., when you see a recording of brain activity it looks like a squiggly line, and each of these squiggles [roughly] represents something happening in a person's mind). There is one component of brain activity which has long been assumed to be sensitive to words -- i.e., it was thought that hearing a real word triggered more brain activity (in this particular component) than hearing a made-up word. Our project, however, discovered that this is not necessarily the case. For some situations -- and particularly for Mandarin -- this brain component does not reliably differentiate between real words and made-up words. This finding suggests that there are limitations in our understanding of how this brain component works, and it motivates further research to figure out what exactly are the factor that drive this component. This sort of research is necessary to help us get a better understanding of how the brain functions.

25608817.label: Project Title(Chinese)
25608817.value: 從天台宗看中國十六、十七世紀佛教中的"反律法主義"

25608817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25608817.value: This project examines Mahayana antinomianism in the late Ming Dynasty in China through studying Chuandeng (1554-1628) and his intellectual networks. The term “Mahayana antinomianism” in this project refers to the doctrines and narratives that, being related to Mahayana Buddhism, praise or justify violations of general moral laws or monastic precepts. These doctrines and narratives originally appeared in Mahayana scriptures composed in India or Central Asia and were transmitted to other areas in Asia. This project investigates its interpretations and adaptions in China during the late-Ming period, a very special period in Chinese history known for unconventional, antinomian ideas and behaviors, as well as the attacks against them. In 1621, Chuandeng, a very active Tiantai monk, composed and published "Treatise on the Good and Evil Nature," which includes an unprecedented collection of antinomian stories taken from the Mahayana scriptures. Why did this collection appear at this particular time? The content of this treatise, which centers on discussing antinomianism and human nature, indicates its involvement in the ongoing philosophical debates in the late Ming. While a few scholars have already studied the text, more revealing for the understanding of the Mahayana antinomianism in China at this period is its subtext, which has become covered in history and can only be disclosed by reconstructing its context. To whom was Chuandeng preaching through this treatise, and against whom was he arguing? In addition to its explicit confrontation of Mencius and Zhuxi (1130-1200), how was it situated in the intellectual landscape of its time? How was his stance and hermeneutical strategy related to his Tiantai predecessors, Chan Buddhism and to the Wang Yangming (1472-1529) branch of Neo-Confucianism? These are the questions I aim at answering in this project. The hypothesis to be tested, calibrated and developed is that Chuandeng may have attempted to advocate a middle path between the libertine atmosphere and orthodox Confucianism. While pointing out the limit of orthodox Confucianism, it does not echo Wang Yangming’s words that the essence of the mind/heart is neither good nor evil, which was cherished by many Chan Buddhists. Instead, it emphasizes that antinomian behaviors should be either conducted as skillful means to help others to reach the good or be transformed into the good through fear, remorse, and repentance. He made this point by bring antinomian ideas back to their original narratives, instead of cutting them out from their contexts as some Chan authors had done. 此研究項目圍繞天台宗高僧傳燈（1554-1628）的生平和著作，考察晚明大乘佛教中的“反律法主義”。所謂“大乘佛教中的反律法主義”是指在一些大乘佛教經典中對違反寺院戒律或一般道德規範之行為的辯護。這樣的思想可以追溯到寫於古印度和中亞的佛典。本研究旨在考察此類思想如何在晚明時期的中國被解釋和理解。晚明時期在中國歷史上非常特殊，以“反叛”、“狂狷”的人物知名，同時對這類人物和行為的批判也甚囂塵上。此時期佛教中的“反律法主義”常常會被人以為和“狂禪”同義。然而，中國歷史上最全面地收集了大乘佛經中宣揚“反律法主義”的故事和學說，并加以分析闡釋卻是天台宗僧人傳燈於1621年寫作的《性善惡論》。迄今，此文研究者僅僅集中與文本自身，而對於其所處的社會環境、思想語境尚未深入探討——例如，為何此文會在此時出現？其針對的讀者是誰？又在和誰論辯？除激烈地反對孟子和荀子之外，作者又是如何處理與天台傳統、禪宗和陽明心學之間的關係的？本項目將試圖回答這些問題。 本研究希望檢驗并發展的假設如下：傳燈試圖在狂狷和正統之間找到一條中間道路。一方面他指出正統儒家的局限；另一方面也反對王陽明和許多禪宗追隨者所謂“無善無惡心之體”之說，強調人性中有善也有惡。通過將反律法思想還原到其最初的經文敘事中而非斷章取義，傳燈強調反律法的行為或者是救度他人的方便法門，或者是犯法者本人改悔從善的契機。

25610217.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25610217.value: Based on textual and performance evidence, this study will discuss the history and the development of the performing status of female actors in Beijing’s theatrical circles during the period of 1911-1937, from the perspective of gender. In the early Qing Dynasty, female actors were prohibited from performing in the public. Consequently, until the late Qing Dynasty, Beijing’s theater circles were dominated by male actors. From the Republican period, however, female actors were able to perform on Beijing’s stage legally. Soon afterward, Beijing government implemented a policy to separate the performance of male and female actors, giving rise to the formation of female-only troupes. Thus began a unique history of the female theatre. The female theatre at this time was focused primarily on the performance of Bangzi Opera (梆子Clapper Opera), which, together with Beijing Opera, constituted the two popular theatrical styles in Beijing, with female actors playing mainly Bangzi Opera, and their male peers Bangzi Opera and Beijing Opera. As female theater gained popularity from 1915, male actors began to retreat from Bangzi Opera, focusing instead on Beijing Opera. Taken as a whole, then, with the advent of the female theater, Bangzi Opera was performed primarily by female actors, making them the primary shaping force of the performance styles of Bangzi Opera from 1911 to 1937. This study will explore the situation after the emergence of female actors, how they confronted with the performance system originally established by male actors and how they transformed the male performance model into a performing style unique to female actors. Besides, this study will broaden our understanding of drama texts, reinterpret the roles of female characters in Bangzi Opera, in addition to discussing the particular perspectives and consciousness that female actors injected into scripts written by male actors and male playwrights. This project will not only constructs a conceptual framework for the study of the history of the development of female performing arts from a gender perspective, it will also fill a significant gap in the studies in Beijing theater history that has up to this point decidedly and understandably favored Beijing Opera. 本研究將以性別的角度切入，從表演與文本兩個大方向，論述1911-1937 年間北京地區女性戲劇表演史的發展過程。清代初期禁止女演員公開表演，直至清末，北京劇壇只存在著男演員，進入民國，女演員終於能合法地登上北京劇壇。隨後北京當局施行男女演員分開表演的政策，引發了女戲班興起，開啟一段獨特的女劇發展史。此時的女劇以演出梆子及京劇為主，梆子與京劇在形成初期，並無女演員，全由男性演員開創。本研究將探討女演員出現之後，如何面對原由男演員創立的表演系統，她們如何從繼承男性表演典範進化至建立屬於女性特有的表演風格。 此外，本研究更將視野拓展到文本分析， 論述原由男演員創造的劇本，女演員如何在其中加入女性意識，重新詮釋劇中人物。

25610217.label: Realisation of objectives
25610217.value: By parsing through archival, published documents, newspapers and scripts held by institutions in Taipei, Beijing and Japan, the PI is able to realize all five objectives. Through the study of drama review, the performance of Beijing female theater during 1911-1937 has been confirmed. The dramatic criticism mainly refer to the performance of female theater and female actors, and there are also many dramatic criticisms for Bangzi Opera, which is of great help to understand the situation of the drama field in the early years of the Republic of China. In order to keep track of the development of female theater, this project also compiles a list of the plays performed between 1911 and 1937. These plays are different from those of the male actors, as the female actors have their own special works and also create many new plays. Most of the plays performed by female actors were about contemporary women's lives, which was very different from Beijing Opera and had a unique style. However, due to the social unrest in Beijing after 1930, female theater gradually disappeared. In the past, researchers have not paid much attention to the history of female theater in Beijing because of the lack of information. Through this project we can understand the contribution of female actors and fill the gaps in theatre history. The results of the above studies have been published successively. The first conference paper was delivered at Memorial Symposium: Tsuji Chōka, 150 Years from Birth in Tokyo, Japan. The paper was then expanded, after more through research into magazines and newspapers, into a journal article. It discusses the development of female theater in Beijing and adds more information about how the female actors created their performing styles. This article received the Best Research Paper Award in Honor of Professor Xu Fuguan: the 35th volume of New Asia Journal. The second conference paper was delivered at the Conference on Chinese and East Asia Theater in Fukuoka, Japan. It was extended to a journal article which analyzes how the drama policy affected the development of the female theaters in the early years of the Republic of China.

25610917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25610917.value: This project sets out to broaden the study of East Asian design history by encompassing the vernacular “in the light of Hong Kong neon signs”. It reveals a neglected segment of Hong Kong’s graphic design history, through a historical and empirical inquiry into the city’s renowned but graphically and culturally under-researched neon signs and their vernacular designs. The vernacular has long been acknowledged in Western graphic design history (e.g. Glauber 1993; Lupton 1996). Yet, the relatively small body of work on histories of Asian, specifically Hong Kong and Chinese graphic design, has until today focused mainly on establishing the discipline by taking stock of local adaptations of traditional Chinese arts and crafts into modern graphic design (e.g. Feng 2006; Huppatz 2005; Wong 2001). As Western design studies have dominated the discipline at large, their Asian equivalents have – with the exception of Japanese design research which dates back to the 1950s (Kikuchi 2011) – only recently found scholarly ground when local design came to be narrated as matching “international standards” and remaining unique to the local context(s) (Wong 2001). This has been important in view of the strengthening of design studies in the region, but vernacular forms in graphic design remain unrecognised. One of the oldest neon sign factories in Hong Kong, Nam Wah Neonlight & Electrical Manufactory Ltd (established in 1953), recently donated 1000 of its hand-painted neon sign artworks to the School of Design of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. They allow a first-hand view of half a century of vernacular neon sign design and an entry point into the study of vernacular graphic design in the East Asian region. As the collection is specifically local, the research will substantiate a visual analysis of its forms and styles with insights from an empirical study that is ethnographically influenced and, in part, shaped into a comparative analysis of different East Asian localities. In this way it will devise a visual understanding of the vernacular designs of Hong Kong neon signs and extend the inquiry towards a larger argument about East Asian design history. The proposed research, thus, aims to (1) gain insights into the history of local vernacular graphic design supported by the collection of Hong Kong neon sign designs, (2) broaden the field of East Asian graphic design history through visual, ethnographic and comparative studies, and (3) pace out new directions for the study of graphic design in the region. 此計劃旨在研究香港本地霓虹招牌以拓闊平面設計史在東亞的學術範圍，將透過歷史及實證研究探索香港霓虹招牌及其本土特色。香港霓虹招牌雖聞名於世，卻於設計及文化方面仍未獲得學術關注。在西方的平面設計史上，關於本土風格的論述長久以來都佔一席位（Glauber 1993; Lupton 1992, 1996）。然而，針對亞洲地區，尤其是香港及中國平面設計史的文獻和研究相對較少，反之大多是著重研究本地化的中國傳統工藝所引伸的平面設計。（Feng 2006; Huppatz 2005; Wong 2001, 2011）。除50年代開始的日本設計研究在外（Kikuchi 2011: 274 ），設計學素來受西方主導，本土設計文化直至最近才能夠同時達至「國際標準」及保留本地特色，並得以在亞洲的設計研究立足。（Wong 2001）。雖然這些論述對設計界相當重要，但是當中始終欠缺對本土風格的肯定和研究。 一九五三年開業的南華霓虹燈電器廠為香港歷史最悠久的霓虹招牌製造商之一，早前將一千多張霓虹手稿捐贈予香港理工大學設計學院。這批藏品有助我們窺視過去半個世紀的本土平面設計。霓虹手稿不單提供了二十世紀中後期香港街道上店舖招牌及品牌商號的珍貴紀錄和線索，亦展現了大師級的設計作品和美學，為我們對本土設計的探究提供獨特的切入點。基於藏品的本土性，是次研究將透過民族誌學的實證硏究分析霓虹招牌的視覺形式及風格。研究目標如下： 1）透過香港霓虹招牌設計藏品試圖更深入瞭解香港本地平面設計史，2）從而勾畫及拓闊平面設計史在東亞的學術範圍，3）並在這領域上尋求平面設計史研究當中的新方向。

25610917.label: Realisation of objectives
25610917.value: The objectives of the research project have been achieved satisfactorily and in line with the planned schedule. The following descriptions in response to each objective. 1. In order to fill a knowledge gap in regard to Hong Kong's graphic design culture and research, the team and PI went to the Hong Kong Central Library to search for relevant information in a large number of both Chinese and English microfilm newspapers as well as its online archive system. The team attempted to review all relevant news from the 1900s to 1990s in relation to neon signs and its regulations and socio-cultural-economical aspects. As a result, the team mapped out a chart in which all relevant information is placed on a timeline to plot out an overview of Hong Kong’s neon sign history and graphic design. 2. In order to gain insight into the history of local vernacular graphic design supported by the collection of Hong Kong neon sign designs, the team and PI developed an inventory that recorded a series of visual attributes of neon signs such as colour, pictogram, shape, typography, patterns, orientation, etc. The inventory of visual forms provides an overview of vernacular Hong Kong graphic design from the 1950s to 1990s. In short, all neon signs and their visual forms have been synthesised and analysed from a perspective of visual communication so as to contribute to the visual analysis of graphic design and identify other vernacular forms. 3. In order to identify design wisdom and vernacular design practices, the team interviewed different stakeholders involved in the process of neon sign making and/or vernacular graphic design in Hong Kong. At the end of the project, the team interviewed about 20 interviewees to further understand neon sign craftsmanship, the history of graphic design and cultural-economic aspects of Hong Kong society. Each interview was conducted using a semi-structured approach. The group of interviewees comprised neon sign makers/masters and shop owners. 4. The team attempted to trace the artistic origin of the neon sign artworks. After the interviews with neon sign masters, the team then moved on to exploring the local design context in which the artworks were made. The team broadened its scope and subsequently interviewed a range of graphic designers who were design students in the late 1970s. They shared incredible insight into the ways in which local design knowledge and practices were nurtured. Besides the interviews, the team reviewed literature on graphic design in Hong Kong and East Asia, which helped to understand that little is written about design practices in neon sign making in Hong Kong. The lack of extensive written materials about Hong Kong graphic design subsequently proves the importance of this project on neon signs. Also the historical context in which the designing happened was explored through secondary research. The historical developments of Hong Kong (and its relation to mainland China) and East Asia have influenced how graphics were made. 5. In order to set out new directions for the study of graphic design and its history in Hong Kong, how 1,000 donated neon sign artworks were created was considered. The artworks served as concept designs for clients’ approval. Besides showing particular artistry, they include significant and Hong Kong-specific graphic features, and they present a unique visual history of the defining decades of Hong Kong as a place of and for commerce. The artworks were subsequently digitised for content analysis. The team classified the artworks according to the type of business. They were roughly 18 business types grouped – food & restaurant, hotels, household electrical appliances, jewellery, etc. In sum, the project can be understood as a historical inquiry into ways of thinking and making. It involved design work, sketches and drawings, but most of all it captured a set of design practices. The inquiry was a prelude to this research on Hong Kong neon signs (their history and graphic designs) in that it looked into an under-exposed and under-explored aspect of the process of neon sign making: the making of visual prequels to Hong Kong’s spectacle of signs in the service of potential and comparable future research in the East Asian region. The project did not spend the proposed budget. The following are explanations. 1. No contact information It is a bit unfortunate that there was no way to interview neon sign artwork painters or artists who mainly drew the neon sign artworks during the process. This is because most of them had either passed away or in their late 80s or early 90s when the team contacted the Neon Sign and Light Boxes Advertising Employees Association. The research team attempted to track down these neon sign artwork painters or masters from Shanghai and Taipei. But no further information could be provided by the Association. Due to there being no contact information for Shanghai and Taipei’s neon sign masters, the team had no way to contact them, so the original planned expenses in the General Expenses, including translator (10,000), two people for the Shanghai (35,000) and Taipei trips (37,000), were not incurred. In order to overcome the problem of contacting Shanghai and Taipei’s neon sign painters and masters, the team and PI therefore relied on oral history and interviews with local neon sign masters, graphic designers and content shown on neon sign artworks. In addition, regarding the expenses for the project website’s domain name and server space (5,000) and equipment for hard drives (2,200), the team decided to host all data on the School’s server with the full support of technicians and free hosting that would cut down the major cost of hosting services, server management and maintenance fee if run by a third party. 2. Withdrawal of research staff There is another issue concerning the research staff’s budget balance. In the proposed budget there was 176,400 for research staff for the whole project. But only 94,594 was spent because a senior research staff member withdrew from the project midway through. It was very difficult for the PI to recruit a new research staff member who had the relevant academic background and research experience and could handle the rest of the project. Fortunately, the senior research staff member was willing to be a part-time volunteer to complete the unfinished parts. Meanwhile, other sources from the School of Design and Information Design Lab could support the PI to hire student assistants who helped in data collection and input, interview preparation and transcripts, etc. 3. Significant impact from the social unrest The project was commenced in 2018 and completed in 2019. However, the date of the project has been revised to June 2020 due to the social unrest in 2019 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. In fact, the impact was not just the project’s postponement; it influenced deeply the disruptive progress of the project, such as research staff withdrawal, ceasing the process of neon sign artwork documentation that caused the failure to make a submission to a conference (20,000 for conference expenses) when the whole PolyU was locked down due to the social unrest in 2019. Fortunately, neon sign artworks and computers were found not to have been damaged after the campus was gradually reopened.

25610917.label: Major findings and research outcome
25610917.value: This project has significant research outcomes comprising 3 journal articles, 1 conference paper, 1 international exhibition, 1 website, 1 cultural tour, 7 public seminars and 1 booklet. For the first article, however, I didn’t realise that I needed to include an acknowledgement of RGC/ECS funding in the article which was due to my careless. For the second article, I did include an acknowledgement, but there was mis-communication between the author and the journal. I put the RGC/ECS fund acknowledgement in the field of fund supporter provided in the system of the journal. But it ended up not being show in the final article. By looking at Hong Kong’s neon signs, some unique attributes of Hong Kong’s vernacular design can be summarised in a few points. First, it has a high degree of fluidity and uncertainty, owing to Hong Kong’s rare sociocultural, political and demographic conditions. As a fluid form of vernacular design, it is slowly dying out and being replaced by other, similar design products. Second, it is not based on an indigenous culture refined by its long history. Hong Kong’s neon signs reflect the vernacular of Hong Kong, which is neither entirely Western nor entirely Chinese. While neon signage itself is a Western invention, both Western and Chinese elements were incorporated into sign design when it was introduced to Hong Kong, expressing Hong Kong’s ‘non-East, non-West’ identity. This shows that Hong Kong is a melting pot of cultures in which multiple cultural influences exist and interplay with each other to create cultural hybrids. Third, it is important to take not only graphic dimensions but also urban and spatial conditions into account for the study of vernacular design, particularly in public spaces. As shown in the analysis, neon signs have a close relationship with urban landscape and architecture. Fourth, grassroots forces played an important role in influencing the design of Hong Kong’s neon signs. This bottom-up autonomy reflects the way of life and the quotidian culture and vibrancy of the city. To sum up, Hong Kong's neon signage is not only influenced by Western attributes, but also by various local factors, such as Hong Kong's design history, East-meets-West aesthetics, unique urban environment and bottom-up autonomy. These factors give us a more comprehensive understanding of Hong Kong’s vernacular design.

25610917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25610917.value: The PI received a donation of over 1,000 hand-painted neon sign artworks that constitute a valuable collection for research and preservation. The artworks have currently been categorised and digitised for our archives. They will no doubt be helpful to future research endeavours towards understanding Hong Kong’s histories of visual culture, Chinese typography, graphic design and visual presentation. Using neon signs as a design artifact which has been under-researched offers further possibilities in future analyses of vernacular design and visual culture. Although the European modern framework can definitely serve as a reference in the study of vernacular design, many other factors must be considered when it is applied to places beyond its original scope. Therefore, it is critical to note that the vernacular can indicate something different depending on its locus. It is hoped that this method of looking at vernacular design can contribute to its further study and the design history of neon signs and visual culture. The proposed course of action will be taken to apply for external funding (e.g. GRF and ADC) in order to further examine visual transitions and Hong Kong’s unique visual culture across the years from the visual database of neon sign artworks archive.

25610917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25610917.value: This project set out to establish a long-overdue introduction to an important segment of Hong Kong’s graphic design history through a visual and historic inquiry into the city’s renowned yet graphically and culturally under-researched neon signs. The 1,000 donated neon artworks are not just masterly works of design but also allow both a visual perspective on Hong Kong’s economic development and changing urban life and a unique base for a historic inquiry into Hong Kong’s graphic design. Following the rise of Hong Kong’s consumer culture – as well as the move south of Shanghai’s entertainment industry ensuing from the Chinese Communist Revolution – streetscapes became famously illuminated with signs. Hong Kong’s neon signs portrayed (and still portray) a mixture of Western and Asian symbols, Chinese and Roman typefaces, visual styles that form eclectic blends of art deco and related vogue, and Chinese calligraphy often combined with illuminated interpretations of traditional decorative frames. It invokes further thinking about how the emergence of neon signs fit into Hong Kong’s graphic design history and how this visually and culturally connects with sign design as well as identifying design wisdom and practices by considering the vernacular in the context of Hong Kong’s design history.

26100617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
26100617.value: Although we perceive our visual world as unified and three-dimensional, visual information enters our brains through the two separate and two-dimensional channels of the eyes. Somehow, the brain is able to combine these channels into a perceptual whole, and in the process take advantage of the slightly different perspectives provided by the eyes to calculate the distance to objects in the visual field. The ability to perceive depth in this way is called stereopsis, and it is one of the most important cues that humans use to see their environment in 3D. However, the mechanism by which the brain accomplishes this feat remains mysterious. This project addresses binocular depth perception in a simple visual system, that of the zebrafish larva. These animals use their visual system to hunt prey, which requires precise localization in visual space. In this model organism, we can take advantage of genetic tools to label and manipulate neurons In addition, the larvae are transparent, which facilitates functional imaging in the intact organism. We will first ask how the prey capture behavior uses binocular input, and whether the different perspectives of the two eyes are being used to calculate distance to the prey. We will then use functional imaging to identify neurons that respond to binocular input, and are tuned to stimuli at particular depths, which will give us insight into where in the brain the inputs from the two eyes are combined. Finally, we will determine the anatomy of these neurons at high resolution. Overall, this project will help us understand how the brain combines input from the two eyes, and uses this information to calculate depth. 雖然我們通過視覺系統感知到的世界是三維的、統一的，但視覺信息通過眼睛傳遞進入神經系統時是二維的。大腦可以將來自眼睛的二維信息轉換成三維，並在此過程中，通過比較每個眼睛感知到的細微差別來提取空間深度的信息。這種感知深度的方式叫做立體視覺（英文：stereopsis），它是人類感知三維空間的重要方式。但是大腦如何實現立體視覺的神經生物學機制現在仍然不清楚。 斑馬魚幼魚在捕食過程中需要借助視覺系統來感知空間中獵物的具體位置，本課題便以斑馬魚為模式動物，利用其幼魚較為簡單的視覺系統來研究雙眼立體視覺的神經生物學機制。斑馬魚幼魚是透明的，因此我們可以在活體清醒動物上進行功能成像，同時還可以利用遺傳學工具來標記和操控相關的神經元。 首先我們會驗證斑馬魚的捕食行為是不是通過利用雙眼來感知立體視覺，並探索它是如何利用來自雙眼不同的信息來計算和獵物之間的距離。接下來，再用功能成像去鑒定出來對雙眼視覺輸入有特定反應的神經元，研究它們是否會對某一深度有特異的反應曲線。最後，分析這些感知深度神經元的解剖學功能連接，從而剖析背後的環路機制。綜上，本課題將會幫助我們來理解，大腦是如何整合來自雙眼的視覺輸入，並用此信息來感知空間深度。

26100617.label: Realisation of objectives
26100617.value: The goals of objective 1 were to record and analyze prey capture strikes in freely swimming larvae for comparison with our head fixed larvae. We have successfully carried out this recording and analyzed tail kinematics as well as eye movements and other parameters such as dorsoflexion and have fully achieved this objective. For Objective 2, we have achieved the goal of developing a head-fixed strike preparation. Our initial observation was that the larva’s swim bladder would show a fast forward motion during a strike, and since the swim bladder is relatively easy to track in highspeed video when recording from above, we pursued this avenue initially. We hypothesized that depression of the jaw bone during the strike to expand the mouth cavity could pull the swim bladder forward, as it is connected to the jaw bone. We observed a decrease in the distance between the swim bladder and the centroid between the eyes during putative strikes, and when we plotted this distance the strikes stood out as obvious peaks. However, we felt it was important to validate swim bladder movement as a criterion for strikes by linking it to one of the known characteristics of the strike in free swimming larvae, such as large jaw opening/protrusion or dorsoflexion. We first tried to record jaw protrusion in our head fixed larvae, which required tilting the larvae 20 degrees upward to get the right angle, and comparing the timing of jaw protrusion to the fast swim bladder movements to see if they were correlated. We were able to see a correlation between fast swim bladder movements and jaw protrusion, but the jaw measurement was quite noisy and had significant fish to fish variability due to difficulties controlling the exact angle of embedding. We also tried to correlate tail movements in head fixed fish doing putative strikes with those of free swimming fish doing strikes. This proved problematic due to the differing kinematics of free swimming vs. head fixed tail movements. To solve the problem, we have taken a different approach; using a second high speed camera to monitor another known feature of the strike, dorsoflexion. We found that we can identify this movement in our head fixed fish during the strike. We have developed a quantification method and are now using this for strike identification. The second part of objective 2, to test the role of binocular vision in the strike using our head fixed paradigm, also faced some challenges. We were able to show, using the swim bladder as a strike indicator, that this putative strike occurs only when the prey are within 2 mm of the larva, whereas more distant prey will trigger eye convergence but not strikes. However, this suffered from questions about the validity of the swim bladder movement as a definition of strikes. We are now conducting these experiments using dorsoflexion to identify strikes. Objective 3 required a switch from using natural prey, paramecia, as the stimulus to using artificial prey, or moving dots projected onto a screen, in order to conduct functional imaging experiments. We built a set up with a motorized stage that could be moved to 10, 5 or 2 mm from the larva, to test whether we could see the distance dependence of the strike using artificial stimuli. However, our initial results were not what we expected, as the strike rate was inconsistent and did not show significant distance dependence. We then upgraded to a projector that also includes UV light, which may be important for triggering the strike, and indeed we started to get strikes with much more reliability. Due to difficulties in evoking strikes with artificial stimuli, we switched to a different strategy to use functional imaging to identify binocular neurons. We built a mechanical eyeblocker which allows us to perform behavior and imaging experiments with one eye occluded or both eyes able to view the stimulus. We validated the completeness of the block using imaging experiments. We performed imaging experiments in larvae with the calcium indicator GCaMP6s expressed panneuronally, so we can identify cell bodies in visual areas that are activated by prey stimuli in different configurations of the blocker. We were able to find binocular neurons whose responses are enhanced in the binocular vs. monocular condition, achieving the goal of objective 3.
