27602917.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27602917.value: This project studies the intricate relationship between religion and urban space by focusing on the local history and changing religious landscape of Jiangbeicheng, a river town on the upper Yangtze River, during the imperial, Republican, and socialist periods from the late Qing to the present. Located at the confluence of the Jialing and Yangtze Rivers in Chongqing, an inland megacity in southwest China, Jiangbeicheng was an administrative center and official river port from ancient times (316 BC). Due to increased population and economic activity, it became a Sub-Prefecture of Chongqing during the Qianlong era (1754). The Sub-Prefectural Magistrate Office, tongzhi shu, established in town, existed until the end of the Qing (1754-1912). The cityscape of Jiangbeicheng took shape during this period and many temples were built for the religious activities of local people who made a living in river trade and transportation. The religious landscape expanded in the nineteenth century with churches erected by Roman Catholic and Protestant missionaries. Throughout the twentieth century, different political forces (local warlords, Republican nationalists and municipal communist government) attempted to transform Jiangbeicheng into a modern urban center. Urban space became an arena of contestation in which religious agents had to engage with local state forces under the pressure that religious sites being replaced by public institutions. After a serious decline in the reform era (1980s-90s), Jiangbeicheng was completely demolished in 2003. It has now been rebuilt into a central business district in which Catholic and Protestant churches have been reconstructed. Other religious sites have, however, been erased. The changing cityscape of Jiangbeicheng provides a concrete means for understanding the role of religious competition in the historical process of building urban China. In this study, I will explore how different religions flourished in Jiangbeicheng and how Christian churches and state intervention altered its religious landscape. I will examine the development of temples, churches, and other ritual places across historical periods, with particular focus on the high Qing to 1891 when Chongqing became a treaty port, the heyday of urbanization in the 1920s and 1930s, the early period of socialist construction from 1949 to the 1970s, and the recent new-century urban reform. Focusing on religion in an urban setting, this study will offer a micro-historical perspective of how local experience is shaped by and fits into changing political discourses on religion, society and urban development in modern China. 本課題聚焦江北城內宗教文化和城市景觀的歷史變遷，梳理自明清以來，江北城在帝制晚期、民國、以及1949年之後社會主義建設和當代中國等不同歷史時期所經歷的城市景觀的改變，及其背後宗教、文化、社會和國家不同力量之間的斡旋、衝突、妥協與融合。 江北城位於長江上游長江與嘉陵江匯合處，是一個由水運而發展起來的城市中心，屬於今天的重慶市江北區。自古以來，江北城不但是川江地區重要的商業碼頭，也是長江北岸文化宗教繁衍興盛之地。早在公元前316年，江北城就成為嘉陵江上一個重要的行政中心和官運碼頭。隨著人口的增加和經濟活動的日益頻繁，乾隆十九年（1754），重慶府在江北城設立江北理民府。直到1912年民國始，府衙江北同知署始終位於今天的江北城內。在同知署存在的150多年間，江北城的城市建設逐漸完善。依山臨江，寺廟密集，因水而生的商業活動和宗教活動此起彼伏，形成了江北城特有的城市景觀。到了十九世紀中葉，隨著鴉片戰爭之後國門漸開，尤其是1891年重慶開埠，成為長江上游唯一的通商口岸，西方天主教與基督教傳教士開始進入江北城，在城內修建了天主堂和福音堂。20世紀以來，和中國其他城市一樣，不同的政治力量，包括地方軍閥、國民黨政府和共產黨政府，均在江北城內進行城市建設，力圖把這個歷史碼頭轉變為一個具有現代城市功能的商業中心。建設新的城市設施，常常會侵佔舊有的宗教場所，城市空間也就成為各種政治力量和宗教勢力的角力場。直到20世紀後半葉，隨著1963年第一座嘉陵江大橋建成，經濟中心北移，以及改革開發以來，江北城傳統水運交通產業的落後，使得江北城逐漸衰落。2003年，江北城開始全城拆遷。今天，被夷為平地的江北城已經被完全重建為現在重慶市的核心商業區。拆遷與重建期間，江北城內所有建築，包括各類亭台寺廟屋宇被全部拆除，唯一保留重建的只有天主堂與福音堂。 江北城城市景觀的歷史變遷，為我們提供了一個長時段中具體而微的研究對象，去理解不同宗教在現代中國城市發展過程中所經歷的競爭與妥協。在本課題中，我會去探索不同的中國傳統宗教為何能在江北城內得以發展，而十九世紀晚進的天主教與基督教，及二十世紀以來，不同政治力量主導的城市化進程又是如何改變了江北城內的宗教面貌。我會具體研究江北城內寺廟、教堂和其他宗教場所的歷史變遷，尤其關注1891年重慶開埠，20世紀20年代到30年代，1949年到70年代這幾個歷史時期宗教和國家力量的角逐。通過江北城的個案研究，我希望能提供一個微觀歷史的視角，去探討現代中國城市發展的過程中，宗教、社會、和國家所扮演的不同角色，及其對現代中國發展的影響。

27602917.label: Realisation of objectives
27602917.value: This project is a historical study of an urban district of Chongqing from the late Qing to the present. It examines the intricate relationship between religion and urban development by focusing on the local history and changing religious landscape of Jiangbeicheng, a river town on the upper Yangtze River, during the imperial, republican, and socialist periods from the eighteenth century to the present. From the perspective of social history and religious history, this project aims to illustrate the historical trajectory of the development of an urban district in southwest China, reconstruct the formation of an urban transportation hub in inland China, and examine the changes in the religious landscape in modern Chinese cities. In methodology, this study offers a micro-historical perspective of how local experience is shaped by and fits into changing political discourses on religion, society, and urban development in modern China. During the course of extended 42 months of intensive research and writing, this project has made significant progress and achieved all proposed objectives. So far, this project has resulted in a book manuscript (a monography in progress), an edited book volume (published in 2021 by Brill), 1 book chapter, and 4 international conference papers. The research outcomes listed in Part C will illustrate in detail the contributions this project has made in Chinese history, particularly in the field of religion, state, and local society in late imperial and modern China. In the following part, I will summarize the realization of objectives and project achievements in two categories. Part I: Theoretical and Methodological contributions The first objective of this project is to write a local history of an urban district of Chongqing from the late Qing to the present. The second objective aims to contribute to three fields of scholarship: the study of religion in Chinese local society, the church-state relations, and the history of modern China. The third objective intends to make a methodological contribution by developing a microhistorical approach. And the last objective aims to contribute to the contemporary understanding of the development of Chongqing as the leading inland megacity in the strategy of developing western China and the One Belt One Road initiatives. All these objectives have been achieved in the form of publications. The major scholarly contributions of this project are in the following three interrelated aspects. 1. The local history of an urban district in inland China. This project examines the changing religious landscape in a river town on the upper Yangtze River. It focuses on the negotiation and competition of different religions in this area during different historical periods. The book manuscript I am working on illustrates changing religious landscape in a specific urban locale and highlights the interaction of religions amid a mosaic of political forces operating throughout late imperial and modern China. 2. Religion and its role in the historical process of urban development. Religion, local governance, and church-state relations have been constant negotiations during the long process of building modern China. As shown by this research, the urban development of Jiangbeicheng under different political regimes complicated the interaction of religions, which shaped and was shaped by the local religious culture. This intricate yet largely overlooked relationship between religion and the city contributes to the state-building in modern China. 3. Historical experience and contemporary development. The urban district under study is a unique area in Chongqing and occupies a strategic position in its current development plan. The study provides a much-needed historical background for the new development plan of Chongqing as a leading metropolis in western China and China’s OBOR initiatives. Part II: Archival Research, Data Collection, and Production One significant contribution of this project is the collection of a set of historical documents regarding the local history of Jiangbeicheng. I have been working with the systematic church record and historical archives for over a decade. My research experiences in this field have helped me discover and collect different historical documents in Chinese and Western languages that contribute to reconstructing the lost history of the demolished urban area. The data includes: 1) Local archives and gazetteers. There are two editions of the Gazetteer of Jiangbei District (江北廳志) published in 1844 and 1921, respectively. Other local gazetteers include the Ten-Volume Draft on Jiangbei County (江北縣志稿十卷), Gazetteer of Chongqing Prefecture (重慶府志), and Local Account of Chongqing (重慶鄕土志). Modern reminiscences of local histories are also collected, primarily Cultural and Historical Data on Jiangbei District (江北區文史資料) and Cultural and Historical Data on Chongqing (重慶文史資料), historical maps, river surveys (e.g., 峽江圖考), and local literati writings (e.g., 重慶江北歷代文學作品選). Another critical body of local materials is the well-known Baxian County Archive (巴縣檔案), housed primarily in the Sichuan Provincial Archives in Chengdu and Nanchong Municipal Archives in Chongqing. This archive covers the years 1752 to 1911. It is one of China's most extensive and most valuable county-level archives. I have visited Sichuan Provincial Archives in Chengdu and Municipal Archives in Chongqing and collected all accessible documents concerning Jiangbeicheng during my visits. However, I could not return to work in these archives since 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic. The current records are sufficient for my writing, but future archival research can enhance the diversity. When the situation permits, I'll plan to return to the archives. 2) Church records and Chinese documents on religion. In the nineteenth century, French Catholic and American Protestant missionaries established churches in Jiangbeicheng. They also built hospitals, schools, orphanages, and libraries. Because of the lack of Chinese documents on religion, church records from both the Catholic and Protestant missions are instrumental in reconstructing local religious life. There are also Chinese official documents illustrating religious conflicts. Besides the national collection of the Documents on Religious Affairs (教務教案檔) and Legal Documents on Religious Conflicts at the end of the Qing (清末教案), local religious documents include the Collection of Documents on Religious Conflicts and Boxer Uprising (四川教案與義和團檔案) and Selected Christian Documents in Sichuan during the Boxer Uprising (四川基督教檔案輯要). In addition to Christian records, published collections on popular religions and religious culture include Books Series/Journal of Chinese Ritual, Theater, and Folklore (民俗曲藝叢書/民俗曲藝期刊), Documents on Popular Ritual Collected from Chinese Gazetteers (中國地方志民俗資料彙編), and Collections on Chinese Popular Religions and Popular Culture (中國民間信仰民間文化資料彙編). Luckily, most of these published Chinese documents are accessible from libraries and online datasets. The Covid-19 pandemic did not have a severe impact on collecting these documents. 3) Government papers. Published materials on urban design during the republican period (e.g., 江北建設特镌), local surveys (e.g., 江北縣基本國勢調查總報告), and other historical materials on business, trade, and industry (e.g., 重慶工商史料選集, 西南實業通訊, 海關十年報告1892-1901) are collected. But unpublished local materials on the urban planning of Jiangbeicheng in recent decades are mainly preserved in the urban planning archives in Jiangbei District. Due to the pandemic, I could not visit these local archives. I will maintain this part to be researched in the future when the situation permits. 4) Travel journals and memoirs. Since Chongqing became a treaty port open to the West in 1891, many missionaries and adventurers from other countries have visited Chongqing, leaving many writings about the city. Archibald Little, for example, writes about the city and people in his works, including Through the Yangtze Gorges (1888), Mount Omi and Beyond (1901), The Far East (1905), and Gleanings from Fifty Years in China (1910). All western-language travel journals and memoirs are accessible and collected.

27602917.label: Major findings and research outcome
27602917.value: This project has so far resulted in a book manuscript (a monography in progress), an edited book volume (published in 2021 by Brill), 1 book chapter, and 4 international conference papers. Please refer to Part C for detailed information on these publications. In addition to the publications, this project has made a substantial contribution to the following two fields as mentioned in the project objectives. 1. Local history of Jiangbeicheng. One key issue in modern China is urban development. This project examines China’s urban development from a neglected perspective of religion by focusing on a particular yet representative district in today’s Chongqing, a megacity in southwestern China. It investigates the changing religious landscape at the grassroots level and explores the intricate relationship between religion, urban development, and local power structure. The monograph writes the local history and the edited book volume provides a comprehensive religious context for the monograph. 2. Religion and State Dynamics. China has experienced explosive growth in urban development in the past century. Religion has played a significant role in this historical process as western missionaries and local popular religious societies took an active role in establishing urban and modern institutions such as schools, hospitals, libraries, and charity organizations. However, the religion and state relationship remains controversial and understudied. My study takes a micro-historical approach to examine the competition between religions and their interaction with the modern state apparatus. From a historical perspective, this study contributes to our understanding of the origins of China’s church-state relations at the grassroots level and provides much-needed historical context for contemporary urban development strategies.

27602917.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27602917.value: During the course of this research, I discovered and collected a body of historical materials from both Chinese and Western archives. These materials open up a new window for us to explore the interaction within different religions (world religions such as Christianity and Islam in negotiation and competition with popular Chinese religions), and between religious sectors and the modern Chinese state. Currently, I am working on a book manuscript to illustrate this historical process. I also created a website for this project open to the general public. I’ll continue developing the website to make it a public platform for people to learn about the local history.

27602917.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27602917.value: This project tells a story about religion and the development of urban China by illustrating the changing religious landscape of Jiangbeicheng, an urban district in today’s Chongqing municipal and a water transportation hub on the upper Yangtze River. Rich with religious cultures in the past three centuries, Jiangbeicheng has experienced dramatic changes in the process of urban development from the eighteenth to the twenty-first century. Through an examination of local and international archives, this project examines the construction and transformation of Jiangbeicheng by illustrating the changes in its religious landscape and the interaction of religions amid a mosaic of political forces operating throughout late imperial and modern times. It reveals events and trends of national significance in the history of building urban China as experienced at a local level.

27604417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27604417.value: This project explores the issue of jury comprehension in the unique context of Hong Kong courts, where English-medium trials are argued before Chinese jurors who speak English as a second or even foreign language. The pool of potential jurors is dominated by Hong Kong Chinese who have Cantonese as their first language. While increasing numbers of trials are heard in Chinese (Cantonese), English retains a highly significant role in the criminal justice system in Hong Kong, and there is no prospect of English disappearing as a medium of law in the foreseeable future. Studies in jury comprehension have been largely carried out in monolingual legal systems where jurors speak English as their native language or English operates as a societal lingua franca. These studies have focused on jurors’ ability to understand legalese or to follow and evaluate highly technical and scientific evidence given by expert witnesses. This research project investigates jurors’ ability to understand a foreign language in the bilingual Hong Kong courtroom, where communication between legal professionals and lay participants appearing in court as witnesses and defendants, more often than not, has to be mediated by an interpreter. The interpretation provided in court, however, is not always accessible to the jury because jurors selected for the jury service are held as a matter of principle to be proficient in the language in which the trial is conducted. However, no prior test is administered to determine prospective jurors’ proficiency in the language. This project will be the first empirical study, using authentic courtroom data, of the jury comprehension issue in the context of Hong Kong. It draws primarily on recordings of two jury trials obtained from the High Court of Hong Kong. These will be employed as research data to test the understanding of prospective jurors and those with actual jury experience. Situated in an unusual and dynamically evolving socio-linguistic context, this study will add a new dimension to scholarly research on jury comprehension. It will extend substantially the existing literature on legal-lay or expert-lay communication, but in addition it goes beyond this, to offer an analysis in terms of cross-linguistic and cross-cultural communication in the legal context. This study is also intended to contribute to policy debates concerning the Hong Kong legal system, contributing to much needed reform in the operation of the jury system and the practice of court interpreting in Hong Kong.

27604417.label: Realisation of objectives
27604417.value: Conduct of Experiments To realise the project objectives, experiments to test potential jurors’ listening comprehension ability were conducted, using authentic audio recordings extracted from the court proceedings of two jury trials, one murder case and the other a rape case, both conducted in English. The audio recordings include monologues such as judges’ jury instructions and summings-up, counsel’s opening and closing addresses, as well as witness examination, all without the mediation of the court interpreter in open court. Only whispered simultaneous interpretation was provided to the defendants in the dock in both cases, inaccessible to the jurors or anyone else in the actual court proceedings. The variety in the courtroom discourses and speakers was to enable comparisons and contrasts to be made and the identification of factors inhibiting the potential jurors’ comprehension. For contrastive purposes, a written text excerpted from the transcript of the summing-up of the murder trial was included in the questionnaire to test and compare the subjects' reading comprehension with their listening comprehension. A total of 53 subjects eligible for jury service, recruited from the community through social networking media took part in the experiments. A declaration form in which the participants confirmed their eligibility for jury service and their undertaking not to disclose the contents and the data used in the experiments was also signed and dated by each participant. The experiments were conducted in 6 groups in the language laboratory of the School of Chinese at HKU on three days. Each experiment session lasted approximately 1.5 hours and an honorarium of HK$500 was given to each participant at the conclusion of the experiment as was promised in the invitation flyer. The participants comprised 38 females and 15 males, aged between 21 and 59. Of these participants, 18 had been summoned for jury service, and 7 had actual jury experience. Of the 7 participants with actual jury experience, 5 indicated that the trials in which they had served were conducted in English. In terms of education level, only one participant held an Associate Degree. The rest held a Bachelor’s Degree (35) or a Master’s Degree (14), and 3 of them even had a doctoral degree. Data management and analysis All the completed questionnaires have been scanned and saved in a secure server. The results were later manually inputted into Google Forms for Excel spreadsheets and charts to be generated to facilitate the management and analysis of the responses. A total of 56 gradable questions were designed to test the subjects’ listening and reading comprehension of English courtroom discourse. Each question carries 1 mark and unanswered questions and wrong answers were given zero marks. Overall listening comprehension and reading comprehension were generated for comparative purposes. Average comprehension accuracies of speeches by different speakers were compared to identify the impact of speaker variables such as accents, articulation and delivery rates on the participants’ comprehension. Individual participants’ scores were also analysed against their age, education, occupation as well as experience in jury service, for any possible correlations to be identified. Comparisons were also made between the participants’ self-rated comprehension and their actual comprehension as reflected in their scores. Presentation of research results A paper based on the findings of the research project was presented at the 14th Biennial Conference of the International Association of Forensic Linguists (IAFL14), held at University of RMIT, Melbourne, Australia, on 1–5 July 2019 (details in Part C). This conference attracted Before that, an invited talk on the same topic was given to the Japanese Association of Interpreting and Translation Studies (JAITS), held at Rikkyo University, Tokyo, Japan, on 14 June 2019. A manuscript based on the results of this project is being prepared and will be submitted to the International Journal of Speech, Language and the Law, a top-tier international journal in the field of forensic linguistics. The paper will, among others, report the findings of the study, identify factors contributing to jury comprehension problems, evaluate the effectiveness of the current practice of court interpreting in facilitating Chinese jurors’ access to the trial in its entirety, and make recommendations for improving jury comprehension in the special context of Hong Kong in the light of the findings. It is hoped that the publication of the findings will attract attention from the legal area and result in efforts being made by the Judiciary to address the issue of jury comprehension, for example, by enabling the jury to access the simultaneous interpretation otherwise audible only to the defendant. This will lead to the full achievement of the last two project objectives.

27604417.label: Major findings and research outcome
27604417.value: Overall accuracy The overall comprehension rate is 47.2%, with two scoring only 21.4% at the lowest end. Listening vs reading comprehension The results show that the subjects’ reading comprehension (86.8%) is much higher than their listening comprehension (41.5%). Education It is found that subjects with a postgraduate degree performed slightly better than those with only a Bachelor’s degree, and way better than the only subject with an Associate degree. However, the subject who scored the highest accuracy rate (69.6%) was a Bachelor’s degree holder. Age The results show that those in the 40–49 age group had the best performance (53.6%), while those in the 50–59 age group scored the lowest accuracy rate (42.9%). Occupation In terms of occupations, those working in the media or culture sector or as social workers were found to have performed best (53.9%), and surprisingly, those from the education, translation and editing sector had the lowest average comprehension level (40.5%). Jury experience It is interesting to note that those with actual jury experience in hearing cases in English has shown a comprehension level (44.3%) slightly lower than that of those without jury experience (45.7%). However, those with experience in serving in trials conducted in Chinese show a much higher comprehension rate (54.5%). Speaker accent The participants scored significantly lower on their comprehension when listening to native English speakers, but showed a much higher comprehension level of the Chinese accented speech delivered by a local Chinese lawyer. Speech delivery rate The delivery rates of the speakers chosen for the experiments vary from 86 to 208 words per minute (wpm), and the comprehension levels scored range from 24.3% to 82.5%. Slow speakers were better understood, or perceived to be more comprehensible by the subjects than fast speakers. While the results indicate that delivery rate may not be the only reason for a higher comprehension level, the monologue delivered at 86 wpm did yield the highest comprehension rate at 82.5%. Legal terminology/concepts Most of the subjects had a problem with the comprehension of legal terms and concepts, and most of the questions about the trial procedures were wrongly answered. Self-rated comprehension vs actual comprehension The subjects’ average self-rated listening comprehension level (51.3%) of the courtroom discourse is higher than their actual comprehension of 41.5%. A paper based on the results of this study was presented at IAFL14 (see Part C for details).

27604417.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27604417.value: This study indicates that lay persons eligible for jury service under the law do not possess a sufficient knowledge of the English language to be able to fully understand the court proceedings. Potential factors contributing to the low comprehension levels identified include the legal language used and the manners in which the legal speeches were delivered. In the light of these findings, further research may examine potential jurors’ comprehension of the same legal speeches reworded in ordinary language free from the linguistic features of typical legalese, and delivered in a clearer manner and at a slower rate. The results can be compared with those generated from the present study. On the other hand, further experiments may also be conducted to test potential jurors’ comprehension of the legal speeches with the assistance of an interpreter. It will be an easy way out to improve jury comprehension if interpretation is found to help with potential jurors’ comprehension. Given that interpretation between English and Cantonese is a regular service in court proceedings conducted in English, enabling the jury’s access to the interpretation provided in court otherwise audible only to the defendant would not be too much of a technical issue for the court.

27604417.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27604417.value: This study set out to examine potential jurors’ ability to hear trials conducted in English by using authentic recordings of court proceedings to test their listening comprehension of courtroom discourse. The findings of this study indicate that lay persons eligible for jury service under the law do not possess a sufficient knowledge of the English language to be able to fully understand the proceedings. The results are particularly worrying as jurors are expected to return a verdict at the end of a trial, based on their comprehension of the evidence presented in court, as well as the legal instructions and speeches addressed to them. The findings of this study highlight a compelling need to improve jury’s comprehension to ensure the administration of justice. In the light of the findings, it is recommended that legal discourses should be made more comprehensible to jurors in terms of both the language used and the manner in which the speeches are delivered. It is also recommended that the whispered simultaneous mode of interpreting currently used in court should be replaced with the electronic mode to make the interpretation provided in court accessible to the jury, and anyone in court in need of the service.

27605817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27605817.value: Shared book reading, where an adult reads a storybook with a child and encourages interaction through questioning and discussion about the book, is ideal for fostering oral language and emergent literacy skills. However, young children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD)—with demonstrated weaknesses in social interaction and communication—are often reported to have difficulties engaging in shared reading. These children also have trouble understanding what they read due to impairment in social cognition. Their weak ability to draw inferences from implicit information often predicts poor performance in reading comprehension. The proposed research will investigate whether children with ASD can benefit from a more structured shared reading approach that addresses these core difficulties. Among a range of approaches to shared reading, dialogic reading has been identified as a promising intervention for children with language disorders. It comprises a structured framework of instructional sequence (PEER: prompt, evaluate, expand, and repeat), and specific question prompts (CROWD: completion, recall, open-ended, wh-questions, and distancing). Research on typically-developing children has consistently reported benefits for expressive and receptive language skills following dialogic reading intervention. Nonetheless, no published studies have measured cognitive benefits of dialogic reading beyond the language and literacy domains. Using randomized controlled trial, Study 1 will examine the effects of a 12-week dialogic reading intervention on foundation cognitive skills (attention control and working memory), higher-order thinking skills (inference-making and theory of mind), and their relations with listening comprehension, among typically-developing preschoolers. Moreover, this study will examine whether RECALL, a less demanding version of dialogic reading, benefits young preschoolers even more than the regular dialogic reading approach. The findings will contribute to our theoretical understanding of how dialogic reading in the pre-literacy stage predicts later reading comprehension performance in children. Based on the RECALL model, which incorporates additional instructional support for learners with ASD (e.g., visual cues, interaction prompts, and prompting hierarchy), Study 2 will examine whether this intervention approach helps preschoolers with ASD by enhancing their engagement in shared reading and addressing their core difficulties in joint attention, social reciprocity, and inference-making. A few prior studies have shown positive results, but they involved only very few participants and did not include any control groups. Study 2 will be the first randomized controlled trial testing the effects of dialogic reading on children with ASD. 27605817.label: Realisation of objectives
27605817.value: Young children with ASD are found to enjoy shared book reading less and spend less time on it than their language-matched peers. Difficulties experienced by children with ASD in shared book reading may partly stem from the social and communicative demands of the activity. Moreover, children with ASD may struggle with inference-making and have trouble understanding what they read. We examined the effectiveness of a less demanding paradigm of dialogic reading, known as Reading to Engage Children with Autism in Language and Literacy (RECALL), on enhancing social interaction and communication for preschoolers with ASD (Objective 2). The RECALL intervention comprises a structured framework of instructional sequence (PEER: Prompt, Evaluate, Expand, and Repeat), specific question prompts (CROWD: Completion, Recall, Open-ended questions, Wh-questions, and Distancing), and a four-level prompting hierarchy. We conducted two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 93 preschoolers aged 4.5 to 7 years diagnosed with ASD or suspected of having ASD. They were recruited from Early Education and Training Centers (EETC) and kindergartens along with their caregivers. In both RCTs, the parent-child dyads were randomly assigned to either the experimental group or the control group. The parents in the experimental group attended a 1.5-hour training session on the dialogic reading approach of RECALL. The workshop included demonstrations on the use of the instructional sequence (PEER), followed by small group practice on asking the various types of questioning prompts (CROWD), and employing the steps of PEER and the four-level prompting hierarchy. Reading materials (i.e., storybooks) and visual prompt booklets created by the team were provided to the parents in the experimental group to assist them in conducting RECALL at home. Parents in the control group did not attend any training prior to the intervention, but they were provided with the same reading materials as the experimental group, except without the visual prompt booklets. These parents were asked to read with their children at home as they would normally do using the materials provided during the intervention period. Parent-child reading was conducted at home twice per week, about 10-15 min each time, for 6-8 weeks among the experimental and control groups. A reading log was provided to all parent-child dyads to record the date and duration of reading over the intervention period. Videos on home-reading sessions were sent by parents from both groups to the research team every week for further monitoring of compliance. All parents were contacted by the research team for phone consultation on a biweekly basis to promote treatment integrity. Video-based feedback on the use of RECALL techniques was given to the parents in the experimental group over the phone by the research team, while more general feedback on parent-child reading was offered to those in the control group. In the first RCT (n=31), pretest and immediate posttest data were collected from participants in both the RECALL and control groups to assess the child’s social communication, social reciprocity, story comprehension, inference-making and language ability. Our results indicated that preschoolers in the experimental condition scored significantly higher in the posttest than in the pretest for all the child measures, including receptive vocabulary, emotion situation knowledge, responsiveness in reading, story comprehension, and engagement in reading session. By contrast, only receptive vocabulary was improved in the control group after 6 weeks of parent-child reading, while all other measures did not show significant improvement among children in the control group. Hence, the results revealed training effects on vocabulary, emotion knowledge, reciprocity in verbal communication, and story comprehension for preschoolers with ASD after the 6-week RECALL intervention. We further conducted the second RCT in a larger sample of preschoolers with ASD (n=62) to examine the sustained effects of the RECALL intervention (Objective 2) beyond immediate post-intervention, and to identify the relations between dialogic reading and cognitive skills (Objective 1). Intervention procedures were identical to the first RCT, except that parent-child dyads were asked to conduct home-reading for 8 weeks. Assessments were conducted at two timepoints: 1) prior to the start of the intervention, and 2) 8 weeks after intervention was completed. We examined children’s theory of mind and story comprehension abilities via direct assessment. To examine the effects of the RECALL intervention on parent-child interaction, we invited each parent-child dyad to complete a 15-minute play session (which included 6-min child-directed play, 6-min parent-directed play, and 3-min clean up) at each assessment time point. All play sessions were video-recorded and coded by research interns (undergraduate students majoring in psychology) who were blinded to the experimental condition of the children. Verbal and nonverbal social reciprocity and social spontaneity, as well as joint engagement, were coded based on a standard coding manual. Our results showed that at 8-week post-intervention, verbal and nonverbal social reciprocity, and story comprehension were significantly improved in both the RECALL and control groups. Nonetheless, children’s theory of mind and their verbal spontaneity in parent-child interaction were improved only in the experimental group, but not in the control group, after controlling for children’s age, nonverbal IQ, attention and language ability at baseline. Importantly, mediation analyses showed that children’s theory of mind completely mediated the effects of the RECALL intervention on story comprehension and measures of social reciprocity, social spontaneity, and joint engagement in parent-child play. These findings align with our hypothesis that dialogic reading enhances cognitive skills such as inference-making and theory of mind, which in turn benefit story comprehension. Using a similar research design, we examined the effects of RECALL among typically developing preschoolers (Objective 3). We recruited 120 parent-child dyads to participate in this study. They were typically developing children studying K1 and K2 at local kindergartens. The participating dyads were randomly assigned to the regular reading group (RR), the RECALL group, the math board game group (MB), and the waitlist control group. Parents in the RR group and RECALL group were asked to read with their children twice per week at home for 10 weeks, while the control group was not asked to do parent-child reading over this period. Parents in the MB group were provided with board game materials and asked to play number board games with their children at home twice per week for 10 weeks. By including both a regular reading group and an additional math board game group, we were able to compare the effects of RECALL with interactive parent-child play, as well as with a more typical approach of parent-child reading without implementing the techniques of RECALL. Similar procedures as described for the RCTs in preschoolers with ASD were followed. Pretest and immediate posttest were administered to children in all experimental conditions to assess their expressive language, verbal working memory, inferencing ability, and story comprehension. Our results showed that narrative description of pictures significantly improved in the RECALL group at the posttest, but not in other groups. Inferencing ability and verbal working memory improved in the RECALL and MB groups, but not in the RR and control groups. By contrast, story comprehension was found to improve in all groups, but the increment was most prominent in the RECALL group after controlling for age and nonverbal IQ. Our findings supported that the additional structured support entailed in the RECALL intervention benefited typically developing preschoolers beyond the effects of a regular parent-child reading approach.

27605817.label: Major findings and research outcome
27605817.value: Based on an RCT conducted among preschoolers with ASD, we found that a more structured and less demanding shared reading approach—Reading to Engage Children with Autism in Language and Literacy (RECALL) significantly enhanced story comprehension, emotion knowledge, and reading engagement among preschoolers with ASD. By contrast, children who received similar intensity of parent-child reading not based on RECALL showed significant improvement only in receptive vocabulary. These findings suggested that parent-child reading per se might help young children with ASD understand more vocabulary, but the application of RECALL might generate additional benefits on story comprehension and verbal responsiveness. The instructional sequence and specific prompts emphasized in RECALL provide a scaffold for parents to elicit language from their children and a prompting hierarchy appropriate to the preschoolers’ cognitive level, thus encouraging the children to process the materials more deeply and consequently construct a better mental representation of the text. These findings have been presented in the American Psychological Association Convention 2019, and published in Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (IF: 4.29, 15/78 in Developmental Psychology). In a second RCT involving a larger sample of preschoolers with ASD, we indicated that the effects of RECALL were maintained for at least 2 months after completion of the intervention. Specifically, we found that children’s theory of mind and their verbal spontaneity in parent-child play were improved only in the RECALL group, but not in the control group. Hence, benefits on social interaction reaped from the intervention were generalized to parent-child interaction beyond shared book reading. We found that the effects of RECALL on story comprehension and social reciprocity were completely mediated by improvement in children’s theory of mind. This finding provided a plausible explanation of how dialogic reading in the pre-literacy stage predicts later reading comprehension performance in children (manuscript submitted for publication). In a third RCT among typically developing preschoolers, we demonstrated that both RECALL and interactive parent-child play enhanced the inferencing ability and verbal working memory in non-ASD children. The interactivity in parent-child interaction may underlie the language and cognitive gains resulted from these activities, be they reading or playing. These findings have been presented in the International Convention of Psychological Science 2019, and a manuscript has been submitted for publication. Using a rigorous experimental approach, our studies were amongst the first to identify the relations between dialogic reading and cognitive skills and provided the first evidence on the effectiveness of RECALL intervention on enhancing inferencing ability, theory of mind, and social interaction for preschoolers with ASD. These findings have important implications for educational practices and early intervention for children with and without ASD. Other outputs: Based on the reading materials used in this project, our team created a set of children storybooks with visual prompts and guided questions to support adult-child dialogic reading, which was published by Caritas On-Site Preschool Rehabilitation Services. This set of storybooks and the dialogic reading approach have been adopted by Caritas Rehabilitation Services in their training workshops for social workers and early childhood educators. Moreover, we were awarded a Knowledge Exchange (KE) Impact Project Fund (HKD89,726) by the University of Hong Kong to teach parents and teachers to conduct dialogic reading with preschool children.

27605817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27605817.value: Capitalizing on the knowledge gained from the dialogic reading project, I am collaborating with Dr. Lamei Wang (Shenzhen University) on a project entitled “HK-Shenzhen Collaboration: Early intervention for children with autism spectrum disorder”. We received an external grant of HKD3,800,000 from the Guangdong Key Project in “Development of new tools for diagnosis and treatment of autism”, funded by the Guangdong Science and Technology Department. We aim to develop and validate a training program for Chinese parents of preschoolers with ASD to enhance parent-child interaction. To further extend the impact of this research, we will continue to work with community partners to train more healthcare professionals, early childhood educators, and parents to adopt the dialogic reading approach in their interaction with young children both at school and at home. We believe that quality research-based instructional intervention, when implemented as a Tier 1 support, will help most students meet their learning expectations. Therefore, we plan to explore whether the RECALL approach of adult-child reading can be effectively adopted by preschool teachers as an instructional approach in a regular classroom. This reading strategy may well turn out to be very useful for implementation in the general education classrooms that include mainstreamed children with ASD.

27605817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27605817.value: Young children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD)—with demonstrated weaknesses in social interaction and communication—often have difficulties engaging in shared book reading, and do not spend as much time on this activity as their counterparts. These children also have trouble understanding what they read due to impairment in social cognition. While dialogic reading has been identified as a promising intervention for children with language disorders, few prior studies have measured the effects of dialogic reading on preschoolers with ASD. We conducted three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to investigate the effects of a parent-implemented dialogic reading approach—Reading to Engage Children with Autism in Language and Learning (RECALL)—among preschoolers with and without ASD. Our findings suggested that parent-child reading per se helped children with ASD understand more vocabulary, but the application of RECALL generated additional benefits on story comprehension and verbal responsiveness. These benefits were generalized to parent-child interaction beyond shared book reading. The effects of RECALL on story comprehension and social reciprocity were completely mediated by improvement in children’s theory of mind. Similar effects on inferencing and story comprehension were observed in non-ASD children. Our studies were amongst the earliest RCTs to test the effects of dialogic reading on children with ASD. Our findings have strong practical significance for the development of evidence-based early reading intervention for preschoolers.

27606317.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27606317.value: Anthropogenic climate change is one of the most urgent problems of our time. This is powerfully captured by the notion of the ‘Anthropocene’, a term used to name our current epoch in which human agency – in the form of consumption, production and pollution – has become one of the earth’s most powerful geological forces. In this project I demonstrate how this new reality augurs a confrontation with some of the basic assumptions on which most legal and political theory rest. In particular, I will inquire into the function and form of ‘sovereignty’ in the context of climatic mutation. If the sixteenth century was marked by the West’s ‘discovery’ of new areas of the globe, along with distinct modes of its inhabitation, climatologists today have discovered a new relation that the human has to the earth and its atmosphere. ‘Sovereignty’, a concept that gained particular significance at the onset of modernity in the 17th century, increasingly appears inadequate in the context of this new climatic regime. The classical theorisations of modern sovereignty depend on a constitutive division between ‘societal’ and ‘natural’ forces that today appears increasingly untenable. The ‘environment’, once conceived as a neutral backdrop against which human institutions could be understood, is now pressing to take centre stage. How does anthropogenic climate change affect our existing theories of sovereignty? And in what ways might extant accounts of sovereignty hinder our response to the changed reality signalled by the Anthropocene? Pursuing an interdisciplinary ‘law and humanities’ approach to these questions, I assess the unique ‘aesthetics’ that sovereignty produces, accounting for how it affects our sensory apprehension of the world. The project re-assesses the fictions and figurations that have animated modern theorisations of sovereignty, from the idea of ‘the body politic’ to the abstractions of legal ‘persona’. Through readings of literary fiction published in the wake of events in which the meaning of sovereignty became a particularly pressing or contentious issue, I assess the political aesthetics that sovereignty installs, illustrating the limitations it imposes on our ability to both sense and address the challenges associated with the Anthropocene. With the objective of publishing the first book-length study in the ‘law and humanities’ discipline on the topic, this project will shape on-going debates in legal and political theory but will also impact research in literary, cultural and environmental studies. 人類行爲引起的氣候轉變是現今最為迫切的問題之一。「人類世」(Anthropocene)一詞有力地反映了這個問題。「人類世」充分地表現了現世代人類的消費、生產和污染等行為，如何成為地球上至為有力的地質力量。是次研究將會揭示這個新狀況如何與過去的法律和政治理論互相衝突，特別會探討在氣候突變的視角下，主權的形式和功能是如何的。如果十六世紀被標誌為西方對地球新地域的「大發現」時代，那麽伴隨著不同的居住模式，氣候專家今天已經探究出了人類與地球和環境的新關係。「主權」，一個自十七世紀現代化過程中起著重要影響的概念，在新的氣候變化的背景下已顯得無力解決問題。近代傳統的主權理論建基於「社會」和「自然」力量的區分，這在今日愈來愈站不住腳。然而，曾經被視為中性人類組織的「環境」一詞卻逐漸被重視。人類行爲對氣候帶來的轉變如何影響現有的主權理論? 現有對主權的理解又如何妨礙我們回應人類世改變了的現實? 以「法律」和「人文學」的跨學科視野，本人將會探討由主權產生的獨特「美學」，解釋它如何影響我們對世界的觀感。是次研究將會重新審視一些塑造現代主權理論的小說和畫作，由「政治實體」 以至抽象的「法人」概念均會涉及。通過分析一些和主權爭議相關的文學小説，本人會探討主權背後的政治美學，解釋它給人類能力帶來的限制，以及與人類世相伴隨的挑戰。是次研究以出版第一本跨「法律」和「人文學」的書為目標，將會引領目前法律和政治學界相關討論的方向，亦會為文學、文化和環境等方面的研究帶來影響。

27606317.label: Realisation of objectives
27606317.value: Overview The central research objective (RO1) has now been completed. Through an in period of research and writing, I have examined the various ways in which the prevailing discourse of sovereignty in legal and political theory has failed to address the challenges associated with climate change and the onset of the Anthropocene. In two journal articles and in a monograph (RO3 and RO4), I have outlined the nature of this challenge and assessed possibilities for imagining sovereignty anew in light of the Anthropocene thesis, and its various entailments. My exploration of this problem has been guided by an interest in the aesthetics of sovereignty (RO2), a theme that I have explored at length in the course of this project. My approach to this theme has been elaborated in one of outputs for this project (RO4) and forms the central plank of the argument developed in the monograph (RO3). I have presented my work at international conferences and events (RO5) and incorporated this research into my teaching (RO6). Outputs I achieved the goal of publishing my research in a top tier, generalist law journal (RO4). This piece was published in the Modern Law Review and is entitled, ‘From Global to Anthropocenic Assemblages: Re-Thinking Territory, Authority, Rights’. This is the first piece to develop a sustained engagement with the Anthropocene in this leading UK -based international journal. A second piece entitled, ‘Law and Aesthetics in the Anthropocene: From the Rights of Nature to the Aesthesis of Obligation’ has been published in the leading US-based international journal: The Journal of Law, Culture and the Humanities. This paper has already been engaged with by a number of scholars, receiving 4 citations of already. The key output of a monograph (RO3) is now complete, with the manuscript currently undergoing copyediting at Edinburgh University Press. I presented my research at conferences and workshops at the University of Glasgow, the Birkbeck Institute for the Humanities, and Oxford Brookes University (RO5). I had intended to use funds from this project to fund a trip to Australia to present my work at an international symposium. Unfortunately I fell ill and was unable to attend this event. Education plan I was very pleased to be able to introduce my research on sovereignty and the Anthropocene into an advanced underground option course: ‘Sovereignty in law, theory and culture’ (RO6). I dedicated two weeks of teaching to this topic with a number of students picking up this theme in their end of term assessment. Budget / under-spend As indicated in my previous progress report, my budget overestimated the extent to which I needed to employ a research assistant. This was for two reasons. Firstly, I was fortunate to be offered two visiting research fellowship, firstly at the University of Glasgow and secondly at the Birkbeck Institute for the Humanities, during the period of the project. This made employing a research assistant in Hong Kong impractical whilst I was abroad. Secondly, as the project evolved, it became clear that the thrust of this research was going to be theoretical in nature. This meant that I needed to dedicate my own time to reading the primary sources, synthesising existing approaches and developing original arguments on the topic. For this work an RA is of limited use. I did employ an RA for a spell during the latter stages of the project as I was finalising my manuscript, and this was very helpful. In the end, however, I overestimated the extent to which an RA’s services were going to be needed during this project.

27606317.label: Major findings and research outcome
27606317.value: 1. The issue of climate change (and the broader challenges associated with the Anthropocene) has been systematically ignored within the writing on sovereignty in legal and political theory. 2. This lack of engagement is not simply an oversight but speaks to far deeper presuppositions that structure how sovereignty has been conceived, represented and debated throughout modernity. These deeper conceptual co-ordinates have an aesthetic dimension which means that political subjects are constitutively inured to the challenges associated with the climatic change. In short, this research shows how sovereignty renders subjects insensitive to these challenges because they are ‘framed out’ by the limits of the existing discourse. 3. This research demonstrates that addressing climate change at the level of law reform or state policies must also be accompanied by a deeper, theoretical and aesthetic transformation in which political authority itself is understood new ways which sensitise subjects to material, ecological and geological relations. 4. Finally, this project elaborates three trajectories through which an aesthetic transformation of political authority might be effected: with attention to terrain, ahead of territory; by engaging post-human themes within the discourse of popular sovereignty; and in privileging city institutions, ahead of a predominant state scale.

27606317.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27606317.value: This research raises a number of challenging questions for legal and political theory. The key issues that now need to be addressed are largely historical. Three key moments mark our transition from Holocene stability to the Anthropocene: 1610, 1850 and 1945. These dates coincide with geological and ecological transformations brought about by colonialism in the Americas; the rise of industrialism and fossil capitalism in Europe; and the so-called ‘great acceleration’ of economic growth from the mid-20th century. These moments also coincide with key innovations within Western law and politics: the birth of modern sovereignty and international law; the rise of positivism and modern private law; and the rise of human rights. It is understanding the interwoven histories of these intellectual and ecological transformations that now needs elaboration. I intend to undertake this work over the next decade in a series of funded projects.

27606317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27606317.value: Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Can we address these challenges within the existing conceptual and institutional co-ordinates that define modern legal and political life or are new concepts and approaches required? This project shows how sovereignty, the defining feature of modern law and politics, constitutively inures us to the challenges associated with climatic change and the onset of the Anthropocene epoch. It shows that our existing conception of sovereignty needs to be re-framed in order to accommodate a sensitivity to the forces and relations described by geology and ecology. This, the project contends, involves re-thinking our conception of: territory, in a way that focuses on geophysical, meteorological and atmospheric factors; popular sovereignty, in a way that engages a range of nonhuman actors on which claims to peoplehood ultimate rest; and the predominance of the state scale by foregrounding the extent to which global cities and global city networks might best address the challenges of climate change.

27606517.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27606517.value: With growing economic and social inequality in Hong Kong and globally, addressing the educational needs of diverse and marginalised learners has become a global imperative. Preparing student-teachers to teach diverse learners, critique societal structures that maintain inequality, and practice inclusive education is a challenge for teacher educators in the context of outcomes-based, skill-focussed teacher education. Service-learning, which combines community service and formal study, is increasingly adopted in initial teacher education to develop prospective teachers’ social awareness and civic engagement. This project is one of the first studies of youth mentoring as service-learning in teacher education in Hong Kong. It aims to investigate undergraduate student-teachers’ complex development of dispositions and practices of social justice as they engage in one-to-one mentoring of underprivileged youth from a high-poverty secondary school as part of a credit-bearing service-learning course. While one-to-one mentoring is frequently hailed as an effective way to address youth disaffection, often lurking within the mentoring relationship are conflicting expectations, ambivalent emotions and fragile identities. These are often unconscious as the mentoring relationship is shaped by the mentoring programme, by educational and social policies, and by beliefs about marginalised social groups in the wider society. Likewise, in developing social awareness and advocacy strategies, student-teachers may experience inner conflict as they explore their life histories and confront their own privileges and biases. Employing theories of psychoanalysis, the study also investigates these unconscious tensions and desires experienced by student-teachers, through a detailed, contextualised account of their one-to-one mentoring interactions. The study investigates a new credit-bearing youth mentoring service-learning course as an in-depth case study of fifteen student-teachers’ learning to mentor. The research will analyse course materials, class discussions, students’ reflective writings and tutor field notes. Four undergraduate student-teachers and their mentees are selected as individual cases within the larger case. Audio-recordings of their mentor-mentee meetings and interactions through social media will be analysed. Interviews with mentors, mentees and supporting teachers in the partner secondary school will also be conducted. The findings potentially advance theories of youth mentoring relationships and service-learning within higher education, and will have practical impact on the design of teacher education for social justice. As experiential learning is being institutionalised in higher education around the world and in Hong Kong tertiary institutions, this research is timely and may assist in understanding how best to foster student learning whilst increasing community impact and sustainability. 隨著香港以至全球社會及經濟不平等的深化，滿足多樣和邊緣化學習者的教育需求已成為全球要務。而讓實習教師做好準備以教育多樣化的學習者、批判社會結構所延續的不公義、及實行融合教育，則是師資培訓者在成果為本、技能為主的師資培訓背景下所面臨的一個挑戰。為發展準教師的社會意識和公民參與，越來越多的初期師資培訓已採用服務學習——包括社區服務與正規課堂學習。本計劃是最先研究香港師資培訓中將青少年輔導作為服務學習的項目之一。本計劃研究對象為參與一門服務學習大學課程(學分制)的本科生實習教師，而實習教師與來自一所高度貧困的初中的基層青少年所進行的一對一輔導亦是課程的一部分；其目的在於探究本科生實習教師在此過程中的複雜的性情傾向發展以及對社會公義的實踐。 儘管一對一輔導經常被譽為一種有效應對青少年不滿情緒的方式，然而在輔導雙方的關係之中，卻也常常潛藏著相互衝突的期望、矛盾的情緒、以及脆弱的身份。由於輔導雙方的關係是由輔導計劃、教育和社會政策、以及廣泛社會對邊緣化群體的看法共同塑造的，所以以上所述的問題往往沒有被意識到。同樣地，在發展社會意識和倡議策略時，實習教師也可能在探索個人經歷以及正視自身優勢和偏見的過程中經歷內在衝突。本研究亦讓實習教師細緻和情境化地描述他們的經歷，並通過精神分析理論來分析他們在一對一輔導中的互動，從而探究他們的潛意識中的衝突和願望。研究將一門新的青少年輔導服務學習大學課程(學分制)作為一個深入個案研究，該個案包含15個學習輔導的實習教師。研究將分析課程材料、課堂討論、本科生實習教師的反思寫作、以及輔導筆記。四個本科生實習教師以及他們的輔導對象被選為個案中的個別案例。他們輔導會面時的錄音和社交媒體上的互動都將被分析。導師、輔導對象、以及該中學相關支援教師都將被採訪。研究成果將對青少年輔導雙方關係理論及高等教育中服務學習理論的發展有所貢獻，並對推動師資培訓中的社會公義有實際影響。當體驗學習正被全球高等教育界及香港高等教育機構正式規範時，此研究可適時探究如何在增強社區影響力和可持續性的同時最有效地促進學生學習。

27606517.label: Realisation of objectives
27606517.value: This critical, qualitative case study examined student-teachers’ development of social justice pedagogies during a service-learning course offered within an undergraduate teacher education programme. The service-learning course was entitled, Mentoring for Social Justice and Inclusion. Thirteen undergraduate student-teachers of different majors (English, Science, Social Science) enrolled on the year-long course. During the course, student-teachers took part in a youth mentoring programme in which they mentored, on a one-to-one basis, thirteen Secondary 3 youth for one academic year. The S3 students, the majority of whom were Newly Arrived Students (NAS) from Mainland China, were studying in a Band 3 secondary school in a northern district of Hong Kong. Each mentor-protégé dyad met 7 to 10 times during the year engaging in a range of activities. All 13 mentors (student-teachers) and 13 secondary students (protégés) agreed to participate in this study. Four focal dyads were selected for a close analysis of mentor-dyad interaction. The data collection procedures were well achieved, resulting in the following data set: • Dialogic blog posts written by 13 student-teacher (mentors) • Audio recordings of 7 mentor small-group meetings • Individual interviews with 13 protégés at the start and end of the programme • Post-project interviews with 12 mentors • Group interviews with 9 protégés from previous years’ programmes • Audio recordings of 10 meetings of four focal dyads. • Video recording of 1 whole-group excursion • Archival and documentary data of university-based service-learning course activities • Whatsapp exchanges between 7 mentor-protégé dyads • Field notes and conceptual memos The study aimed to gather approximately 6 audio recordings of four focal dyad interactions. However, only 3 audio recordings were made by 3 dyads and only one recording was gathered from the fourth dyad. There were many factors which led to this reduced number, including the concern by dyads of the disruptive presence of the audio-recorder on their developing relationships, and the relatively few number of meetings involving only talking. Nevertheless, given the dearth of empirical research on youth mentoring conversations, the 10 recordings provided rich, connected examples of the range and nature of mentor-protégé interactions. In addition, these recordings of naturally occurring conversations in public areas were challenging to transcribe as they were often difficult to hear, and sometimes involved three languages (Mandarin, Cantonese and some English). The transcriptions were translated into English and selected segments were subjected to a fine-grained sociolinguistic transcription. Segments of talk were cross checked with the mentor and between research assistants to increase accuracy. The first objective, to understand and theorise the development of social justice pedagogies in student- teachers was well achieved through a critical qualitative analysis of the data. Firstly, the data was examined to identify how ‘social justice’ was conceptualised by student-teachers. The data was further explored to examine how social justice concepts and theories were appropriated by individual mentors in relation their experiences of privilege or disadvantage, the Hong Kong sociocultural and educational context, and in relation to their protégé’s lifeworld and educational opportunities. Mentors’ final reflections and post-project interviews enabled the research team to identify examples of critical consciousness and transformation. Mentor-protégé interactions were analysed as enacted pedagogies. These were reported by student-teachers and observed in the four focal dyad transcriptions. The theorisation process was achieved through comparing the categories derived from the analysis and defining their interrelations with the youth mentoring course, the mentoring programme and individual mentors and protégés. The second objective, to examine the manifestations of inner tensions and challenges in mentor-protégé relationships as they are shaped by programme, institutional and societal discourses, was well achieved through a critical qualititative analysis of the data informed by Lacanian psychoanalytic discourse theory to identify inner tensions, doubts, questions and dilemmas that mentors’ experienced about their roles, their relationships and their mentoring and relational practice as they engaged with issues of social justice and inclusion during the year. Then, selecting critical incidents in the data, a fine-grained analysis was conducted to identify discourses and their influences on mentors’ (and protégés’) subject positions within discourses which gave rise to inner tensions and challenges. These discourses were ideological in nature reflecting assumptions about social justice education, what constitutes ‘service’, and the inherent hierarchical roles and relationships in youth mentoring. Some mentors’ interrogated these discourses in relation to their mentoring practices. For example, when M12 unpacked the social constructedness of her own performance of a “good student” and how this might lead to negative consequences for her protégé, this was analysed as manifestation of critical consciousness. The third objective, ‘to identify practices and structures which sustain both university learning and positive community impact within service-learning in higher education’ was also achieved. The identified ‘practices and structures’ which fostered or hindered student-teachers’ university learning were derived from the findings arising from the analyses conducted for the first two objectives. In particular, the analyses of mentors’ inner tensions around notions of ‘social justice’ enabled the research team to critically review service-learning content and process within the youth mentoring course, with implications for other university-based service-learning courses and projects. To consider community impact, the protégé interview data at two stages of the mentoring programme were closely analysed and compared to mentor self-accounts to examine the nature of the impact of mentoring on protégés. This enabled the research team to determine the features of the mentoring programme, the relationship with the community partner school, and the structures of the youth mentoring service-learning course which facilitated or hindered positive development in protégés. The key implications arising from this analysis include: 1) need for rigorous articulation of learning outcomes connected to university learning (in this study, education and teaching); 2) lengthening the partnerships between university and community partner to 1 year or longer; 3) university-community collaboration in supporting university learning and community growth; 4) critical social approaches to reflection and evaluation to address deficit views of communities. Given the broad nature of this objective, and the project’s view of service-learning as both a philosophy and pedagogy rooted in democratic and justice oriented worldviews, it is recognised that these findings and implications for service-learning and community engagement in higher education are tentative. The final and fourth objective, ‘to develop a framework and model for youth mentoring as service-learning within initial teacher education’ was also realised, albeit with a different perspective than originally planned for. The research team developed this framework drawing on the findings of this study and the PI’s previous youth mentoring research, and by drawing upon the Research team’s observations of implementing the youth mentoring course, engaging in community-engaged work, and initial teacher education for social justice and inclusion in the Hong Kong educational context. The team also returned to the literature on teacher education for social justice to further refine the framework and situate it within international approaches to initial teacher education, and interrogated each iteration of the framework in terms of the institutional and sociocultural contextual factors which might hinder or enhance the adoption of the framework in university-based teacher education programmes. Therefore, rather than a ‘model’ to imitate and adopt, a developmental framework was eventually conceptualised in which youth mentoring as service-learning is embedded within undergraduate initial teacher education, and facilitates curriculum reform towards social justice on multiple levels: staffing and admissions, relationships, curriculum and instruction and longer community engagement with schools.

27606517.label: Major findings and research outcome
27606517.value: The study found that the 13 student-teachers developed relational skills and pedagogies. Mentoring conversations of the four focal dyads revealed a range of interaction from social talk to academic guidance. Mentors developed an ethic of care in their efforts support their protégés and understand their socioaffective and academic needs (ICLS2019 conference). Student-teachers’ critical consciousness was enhanced by examining their own and their protégés’ multiple intersecting identities with regards to social class, linguistic and national identity, economic privilege/disadvantage, and sexuality/gender identity. The experiential process of interacting with their protégés enabled them to challenge stereotypes of Band 3 students in society and gain first-hand understanding of how societal inequality has impacted their protégés’ lives. Although mentors did not take up the task of advocating for their protégé beyond their dyad interactions, they assisted their protégés in navigating social tensions, parental expectations and school-based issues (AERA 2020 conference, manuscript in preparation). The study found that inner tensions in mentors emerged with regards to social class (discomfort around youth of grassroots backgrounds); economic difference (confusion arising from protégé’s financial privilege, or discomfort around own economic privilege); Hong Kong - Mainland identities (prejudice against Mainland Chinese); race and language heritage (pain of racial or linguistic discrimination); and deficit discourses of protégés and marginalized social groups (AERA 2019 conference, manuscript in preparation). These tensions arose within what Lacan calls the discourse of the Master of a ‘good mentor’ and a ‘good student’, which led to ethical self-questioning (of one’s own emotional maturity, of one’s capacity for interpersonal connection). In the case of one mentor, a deeper epistemic questioning of the youth mentoring programme arose (Lo.M.M, forthcoming; AERA 2019 conference). A framework for the development of social justice teacher education involving youth mentoring as service-learning was articulated. The framework recognizes the need for university-based teacher education programmes to develop social justice orientations through its recruitment and staffing, curriculum and instruction, relations and roles, and longer-term community partnerships. An integrative approach is adopted in which a ‘social justice in education’ (SJE) stream within the undergraduate teacher education programme is offered to teacher candidates; partnerships with schools serving grassroots families are sustained through youth mentoring and the teaching practicum; and a community of university teacher educators committed to curriculum reform around social justice and inclusion is built. This gradual, integrative approach can potentially facilitate changes initial teacher education programmes towards a social justice orientation.

27606517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27606517.value: There is a need to investigate the longer term impact of youth mentoring as service-learning on graduates who have entered the teaching profession and on protégés study trajectories and well-being. • The PI will interview former mentors to examine how their mentoring experiences and understandings of social justice pedagogies have shaped their teaching practice and professional identities; and whether and to what extent these impacted upon their response to recent social and political unrest and the COVID19 pandemic in Hong Kong. • The PI will seek to interview former protégés to understand how the mentoring experience has influenced them and to document to their study trajectories and well-being. This will be done through continued collaboration with the partner school and through former mentors who continue to contact their former protégés. The framework for the development of social justice education has been proposed to the PI’s institution’s undergraduate programme in initial teacher education. If implemented, further research into the student-teachers’ appropriation of social justice and inclusive pedagogies, positive youth development, and nature of collaborative community partnerships will be explored.

27606517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27606517.value: With growing economic and social inequality in Hong Kong and globally, preparing teachers to address the educational needs of diverse and marginalised learners has become a global imperative. This study examined how university student-teachers learned to teach for social justice and inclusion by serving as mentors to secondary school youth from low-income families for one year, whilst they learned about social, economic and educational inequality in Hong Kong and reflected on their mentoring practices. The study showed how student-teachers learned to understand, relate to and support someone different from themselves. In the process, student-teachers experienced discomfort and doubt as they became conscious of their own biases and prejudices, and understood how wider messages in society and in schools helped to reinforce these biases and negative messages about youth. The findings of this study suggest that youth mentoring as a form of service-learning helps student-teachers develop both personally and professionally as more compassionate and responsive teachers. The study also suggests that initial teacher education programmes should include service-learning and specifically youth mentoring as an integrated part of their programmes, and that long-term and genuinely collaborative partnerships are needed between universities and schools to address educational inequality in Hong Kong society.
