27606617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27606617.value: Digital forms of money, such as e-payments, online personal finance management tools and virtual currency, have undergone explosive growth in China in the past decade. These technologies represent a fundamental transformation in the mode of everyday exchange for an ever-increasing number of China’s 649 million Internet users. As of December 2014, 361 million of this group had shopped online, and 79 million users had purchased Internet wealth management products, including small loans, stocks and savings accounts (CNNIC 2015). However, far from the use of digital money services in China only being a preserve of populations with wealth or advanced technical skills, increasing numbers of low income people are also finding use for these technologies. The rise of these of these digital money services in turn raises important anthropological questions regarding the effects that such new forms of exchange have upon lives of ordinary Chinese citizens, and their position within the national and global economy. This study will seek to investigate the social effects of these new mobile money services. I will explore how digitised monetary forms are transforming local monetary ecologies; altering the circulation of money, people and goods; reworking how individuals relate to money and its potential effects on inequality. China’s migrant labourer population particularly stand to have their lives significantly altered as a result of their adoption of digital money services. Members of this group frequently face numerous financial challenges: maintaining economic and social connections with their place of origin, barriers to the access of certain financial services (loans, credit cards), and uncertainties over their future livelihoods. This project will use interviews (both group and individual), and participant observation with migrant factory workers in Shenzhen to understand the consequences of digital money for their contemporary lives and imagined prospects, in addition to providing a valuable account of the social implications of digital forms of money in China to a growing body of scholarship working on these themes across the world. 過去十年間，電子貨幣使用—包括流動支付平台、個人網上理財工具與虛擬貨幣等—在中國經歷了爆炸性的增長。這種新科技徹底改變了中國6億4千9百萬互聯網使用者的交易方式。截至2014年12月，3億6千1百萬中國網民曾經於網上購物，其中7千9百萬網民曾經購買網上理財產品，當中包括小額貸款、股票以及儲蓄賬戶。然而，使用電子貨幣的不僅是有錢人及高技術人士；越來越多低收入人士也正在享受著電子貨幣技術所帶來的的效益。 電子貨幣服務之興起同時亦引起了一連串重要的人類學問題，尤其是交易方式之變革如何影響中國普羅大眾的日常生活，以及他們在國家經濟與全球經濟體系中的地位。這項研究將探討電子貨幣在中國所帶來的社會效應。研究者將會探索電子貨幣正如何改造本地金融生態系統；如何改變著貨幣、人與貨物三者之流通；以及其如何影響了人與貨幣之間的關係甚至各種社會不平等狀況。 電子貨幣的普及對中國外省勞工們的生活產生了重大改變。此群體裡的人經常面對財政負擔， 譬如：如何與遠方的家人維繫經濟上和交際上的互動、如何跨越某些金融服務的門檻（如貸款及信用卡申請）、如何面對未來生活中種種不確定因素等等。此項目將會針對在深圳工廠裡的外省勞工， 通過集體或個人採訪以及參與式觀察的硏究方式，深入瞭解電子貨幣對他們日常生活之影響以及其對未來的構想。與此同時，本項目也期望能為在全球各地研究電子貨幣如何影響社會的一眾學者提供一份以中國為例的寶貴參考資料 。

27606617.label: Realisation of objectives
27606617.value: In order to address the objectives, the project implemented four main research methods, as discussed in the original proposal. These were (1) web and media analysis, (2) group interviews, (3) semi-structured interviews with individuals, and (4) participant observation. These four methods were complemented by other approaches iteratively developed during the course of the fieldwork, such as gathering recent transaction histories from participants’ digital money platforms, asking participants to walk us through the features of particular platforms, etc. The process of achieving each of the Research Objectives (RO) is described below. Given that the project’s associated peer-reviewed publications result from—but also act as evidence of—the fulfilment of the Research Objectives, mentions of these publications are accompanied by the Publication Number (PN) as listed in Part C, Section 8. (RO1) FORM, FREQUENCY AND NATURE OF REMITTANCES Participants were asked about their remittance-sending practices during group and individual interviews. Responses generally revealed that remittances have taken on a diminished role in migrant workers’ lives, especially amongst younger workers. This was further confirmed through collection of participants’ transaction histories. The journal article output detailing the emergent infrastructures of digital monetary storage (PN5) outline changes in the frequency and importance attached to remittances that workers send to family members in the countryside, noting that “the emotional intensity of remittances also seemed to have lessened due the increased ease of initiating transfers”. The diminishing importance of remittances is further explained in the output exploring the growing popularity of Ant Credit Pay (PN4), which documents young migrant workers’ strong desire for financial autonomy from family remaining in their hometown, something that shapes both remittances to and borrowing from migrants’ hometowns. The research output documenting workers’ engagement in online thrift activities through digital money platforms (PN3) contributes additional complexity to the picture of remittances. Online thrift activities, which were particularly popular amongst older workers, reveal remittance sending to be interlinked with economic practices. In this instance, online thrift was shown to combine with “earmarking” practices to allow greater amounts of workers’ factory wages to remain untouched, which were then directed towards household economies. (RO2) SAVING, INVESTMENT AND ENTREPRENEURIAL ACTIVITIES Group and individual interviews allowed for enquiry into how digital money platforms are changing how migrants save and invest their money. Participant observation was also vitally important in the context of this research objective, making it possible to contextualise responses against the broader backdrop of the savings and investment opportunities available to migrants in their communities (for example, in comparison to local banks, “folk” credit, etc.). The manuscript concerning the changing infrastructures of monetary storage (PN5) provides perhaps the clearest example of the significant role that digital money is playing in shaping migrants’ savings and investment practices. This paper demonstrates how migrants favour the assured return that digital finance products such as Yu’e bao (Alipay’s interest-bearing savings account) offer in comparison to other riskier investment opportunities available to them (such as starting small businesses or investing in educational training). Yu’e bao is also preferred over savings products offered by state-owned banks, which although trusted by workers, are also felt to be staid, unappealing and discriminatory towards rural migrants. In contrast, Alipay is understood to be more in line with migrants’ own entrepreneurial aspirations. The theme of entrepreneurialism becomes most fully-fledged in the article regarding Alipay’s online loan service, Ant Credit Pay (PN4). Part of the article describes how Jack Ma’s entrepreneurial charisma ends up becoming associated with lending products, leading migrants to believe that Ma is literally “giving away” money with little concern over whether he gets it back. The issue of “saving” of money is a major theme in the article detailing online thrift activities engaged in by participants (PN3). (RO3) EVERYDAY CONSUMPTIVE PRACTICES This project has also delivered fresh insight into how the use of digital money platforms by workers was transforming their everyday consumptive practices. Participant observation played a particularly important role in fulfilling this research objective, showing how consumptive practices interwoven in factory workers’ everyday lives were being reworked as a result of the digitisation of money. The paper detailing the craze for online thrift activities (PN3) built into digital money platforms demonstrates how the desire to save money when making purchases led to a reworking of work and leisure time within the factory environment, challenging hierarchical relations within the factory itself. A separate journal article demonstrates how participants attach different degrees of sociality to different digital money platforms, which becomes especially important in the context of online shopping and transacting with strangers (PN2). (RO4) GENERATIONAL/GENDER VARIABLES Careful selection of the factory that formed the focus of much of the fieldwork allowed the project to fulfil its objective of assessing whether remittance, investment and consumptive practices were experienced differently by migrants according to age and generational variables. The study’s participants were comprised of a heterogenous mix of workers that spanned young and middle age, as well as male and female genders. This resulted in the realisation of a number of different variations in digital money use. The paper describing migrants’ use of Ant Credit Pay (PN4) demonstrated how younger migrant workers, especially those who were male, were much more likely to explore new modes of borrowing, while older workers remained more cautious with regards to debt. The article concerning online thrift (PN3) demonstrates how engagement in thrift activities was particularly pronounced amongst older female workers. The project has also urged for caution against “attributing particular attitudes toward infrastructures solely to variables such as gender, age or marital status” (PN5). Fulfilment of the above four Research Objectives would not have been possible without the help of the project advisory board. Board members were updated on the progress of the research on an annual basis. Several members of the board also provided comments on early drafts of journal articles.

27606617.label: Major findings and research outcome
27606617.value: The five major findings of the research as they correspond to the Publication Numbers (PN) listed in Part C, Section 8 are detailed below. (PN1) The project has found that it is necessary to unpick the multiple and contesting platforms, functions and uses of digital money that are emerging in China in order to see how money is being shaped by market processes to become embedded and disembedded in social relations during specific moments and to varying degrees. (PN2) Scholars of Chinese society have predominantly regarded the region’s money to represent an unusually “social” artefact. However, this study has demonstrated that rather than digital money necessarily being more or less social, different platforms instead extend the possibilities of sociality in varying ways. This in turn can enrich our understanding of the emergence of a new “digital working-class” in China, by revealing how such contemporary working-class subjectivities are shifting, contextual and processual in nature. (PN3) This project has found that digital money platforms allow thrift to be viewed as a kind of “work”. This represents a challenge to established viewpoints which tie thrift to the home, pointing to the need to acknowledge how thrift mediates exchanges across a broad array of social domains and divisions (i.e. home/work, employee/employer, online/offline, platform user/provider) and as such, plays a central role in contemporary social life. (PN4) Scholarly accounts of the global rise of statistical credit scoring technologies have tended to portray these automated, digitised systems as supplanting human involvement in lending. However, by examining Alipay’s novel consumer credit facility, Ant Credit Pay, this study claims that acknowledging the depersonalising/re-personalising qualities of Ant Credit Pay necessitate the productive analysis of digital credit as a human-machine assemblage. (PN5) Scholars studying infrastructural systems have emphasised that such systems generally only become visible upon breakdown. However, this study finds that during the emergence of new infrastructures for monetary storage, existing infrastructures—along with the money stored within them—also become rendered conspicuous to users. We claim it is necessary to acknowledge the shifting visibility of infrastructures during occasions of systemic transformation. Doing so can help to better understand how users navigate such infrastructures in attempts to solve problems of storage, while in the process re-evaluating their relationships with a variety of entities and institutions.

27606617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27606617.value: One of the particularly promising areas for future research has been the realisation that novel digital forms of credit are making it easier for low-income populations to engage in borrowing. This raises multiple questions, including whether this constitutes a ‘safer’ form of credit, how it influences consumptive practice, and how it may reshape personal relationships. I intend to further examine this issue through a concerted study of online borrowing practices amongst another group of low-income persons in China: students. To facilitate this, I have submitted a GRF proposal entitled “The digitisation of credit amongst higher education students in Shenzhen, China” for the 2020/21 General Research Fund exercise. This research has also demonstrated how acts of boundary crossing raise fundamental questions about the role that digital forms of money play in the construction of identity and the navigation of social difference. While the focus of this study has chiefly been on migrants navigating rural-urban divides, I will be further investigating this issue through my newly-funded HKSAR Public Policy Research Funding Scheme project “Facilitating everyday cross-border monetary transactions and the potential of digitisation in the Greater Bay Area” (http://hub.hku.hk/cris/project/hkugrant126132), which commenced 03 February 2020.

27606617.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27606617.value: This study has provided a detailed picture of the digital money platforms that are being adopted by migrant workers in China and how this is changing how they send, store, invest and spend money. It also considered how migrants’ use of digital money differs according to gender and age. This research is of significance because it allows us to understand how the adoption of digital money is shaped by market processes and social relations. It allows for an improved understanding of the importance of thrift, and how new forms of value can be created. It reveals that alongside the role of money, new kinds of credit are being produced, which are challenging the way that lending occurs. New infrastructures of storage are also being developed alongside these new kinds of money, with new meanings being attributed to them. This research is valuable because it provides us with insight into how a particularly vulnerable, low-income group in Chinese society are having their lives affected in multiple ways when their money becomes digital. The study also provides us with an improved understand of what money is, and how this might be changing as a result of its digitisation.

27606817.label: Project Objectives
27606817.value: This project is closely aligned with the RGC’s funding criteria. Its three interrelated objectives and their sub-objectives are: From the perspective of religious tourism, to analyse the descriptions of Haichuang Temple written by local and Western visitors and elaborate upon how the temple’s priests developed different ways of accommodating them. ．To make the first attempt to investigate the importance of the temple in the history of Chinese-Western contacts, with human activity, i.e. that between Westerners and the temple’s priests, rather than writings about the temple itself placed at the study’s core. ．To accurately describe the travel experience of the Westerners visiting the temple, explain the priests’ different ways of satisfying their various needs and demonstrate the temple’s characteristics as a multi-functional venue. From the regional and semi-official perspective, to examine how the temple established local and overseas connections in alignment with the Canton Trade and became the designated venue for accommodating foreign embassies. ．To explore new frontiers for the study of Chinese-Western diplomatic relations in the Qing dynasty and investigate how a local religious organisation assisted the Qing government in handling particular diplomatic affairs. ．To expand the research domain of the Canton Trade and unravel the social network of Haichuang Temple, with temple priests-Hong merchants, local officials-foreign merchants and the community of foreigners-foreign diplomats constituting the main threads of that network. From the perspective of Buddhism in its contacts with Protestantism (including Anglicanism), to examine the temple priests’ exchanges with Western missionaries and the former’s differing attitudes towards Christianity. ．To re-investigate Protestant missionaries’ understanding of Chinese Buddhism, with Robert Morrison serving as a typical example, with emphasis on their observations of Haichuang Temple, reading of the Haichuang literature and exchanges with the temple’s priests as the major factors affecting their views of Buddhism. ．To conduct pioneering research on the Haichuang priests’ reactions to Protestant missionaries’ attempts to tour, stay over, learn and even preach in the temple, and to elucidate the process by which the priests became acquainted with the missionaries’ Christian beliefs and resisted their inflow. The achievement of all of these objectives and sub-objectives will effect a breakthrough in both scholarly understanding of how Haichuang Temple connected China with the world and a new interpretation of 19th century Chinese-Western relations.

27606817.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27606817.value: During the 19th century, Haichuang Buddhist Temple was better known to Westerners than any other similar establishment in Canton (Guangzhou). That familiarity stemmed from the temple’s regular use as a venue for a variety of Chinese-Western contacts. It was also during this period that a new generation of Buddhist priests with Christian knowledge developed in Canton. I firmly believe that only a comprehensive investigation exploring the temple’s interrelated roles in religion, literature, recreation and diplomacy can properly highlight its pivotal significance in Chinese-Western relations and reveal the full picture of how those relations developed. It is in this sense that the proposed project constitutes unique research on the temple. This project will also represent the first China-, human activity- and literature-centred research on Haichuang Temple: a China-centred viewpoint to reveal the actual situation of China-Western contacts, with the Haichuang priests serving as the backdrop and first-hand Chinese-Western sources collected to rewrite its largely unknown history. My research exploring Protestant missionary Robert Morrison’s (1782-1834) connections with the temple confirms that only in-depth original research pursuing such an innovative approach can shed new light on four major and largely unexplored academic issues directly related to the Canton Trade and Christianity in China: the spiritual life of Westerners in Canton, the semi-official role of a provincial non-institutional organisation in handling Western affairs, Buddhist-Protestant (including Anglican) first encounters and exchanges, and the social networks of Canton Buddhist establishments. To successfully tackle these issues, the project will comprise three parts: (1) analysis, from the perspective of religious tourism, of descriptions of the temple written by local and Western visitors and elaboration of Haichuang’s accommodation strategies; (2) examination of the temple’s local and overseas connections in alignment with the Canton Trade and features of its semi-official roles; and (3) investigation of Protestants’ exchanges with the Buddhist priests and the latter’s differing attitudes towards Christianity. A large database comprising detailed information on the Haichuang inhabitants and literature will be created to serve as a multi-functional platform to implement all of the research activities. The project’s long-term impacts lie in: (1) constituting the first comprehensive research on Haichuang Temple, (2) providing valuable reference materials for teaching and research in multiple disciplines related to Chinese historical studies, (3) creating a new platform for regional and international collaborative research, and (4) resulting in an extensive range of research and educational activities of benefit to young researchers and the public at large. 在十九世紀，西方人對海幢寺的認識較廣州其他佛寺為深，主要原因是該寺經常用作中西交往活動的場所。也是在這個時期，廣州培育出新一代對基督宗教有所認識的佛教僧侶。筆者深信，只有對該寺在宗教、文獻、娛樂、外交這些相互關連的角色進行全面探索，才能正面突顯它在中西關係中的關鍵作用，並展示這種種關係的發展全貌。在這個意義上，本計劃將會對該寺進行獨特的研究。 本計劃也會是首個以中國—僧侶—文獻為中心對海幢寺進行的研究：以中國為本位反映中西接觸的實況，以海幢僧侶為依據、以搜集所得中西原手史料重寫該寺已瀕於湮沒的歷史。本人探究基督教傳教士馬禮遜(1782-1834)與該寺的聯繫表明，只有進行窄而深的原手研究並採用上述的創新路徑，始能為與廣州貿易、在華基督宗教直接有關的四大尚待開發的課題提供新的啟發。這四個課題包括：廣州西方人的精神生活、涉西方事務中一個非建制組織負起的半官方角色、佛教與基督教（包括聖公會）的初次接觸和交流、廣州佛教組織的社會網絡。 本計劃分為三個部份以處理這些問題：(1)從宗教旅遊的視角，分析海幢寺的本地和西方訪客的記載，並闡述該寺的管理策略；(2)考察該寺的本地、海外聯繫網如何配合廣州貿易和發揮它的半官方功能；(3)探究基督教徒和佛教僧侶的來往和後者對基督宗教的不同態度。為此，本計劃會建構一個包括海幢群體和文獻的大型數據庫，作為支援各項學術活動的多功能平台。 本計劃的長遠影響在於：(1)成為首個全面研究海幢寺的項目；(2)為與中國歷史研究相關的不同學科提供教學和研究的重要參考資料；(3)建立地區和國際共同研究的新平台；(4)以廣泛的研究和教育活動，為年青研究者及公眾帶來得益。

27606817.label: Realisation of objectives
27606817.value: 1. In meeting the first objective, this project achieved highly satisfactory results. The PI has shown that the modern concept of Religious Tourism is helpful for the study of this historical case. It provides a theoretical foundation and points of reference to illustrate the strategy that Haichuang, as the religious host, pursued by undertaking various tasks, including receiving guests, arranging itineraries, protecting the temple from potential menace, promoting Buddhist teaching, and welcoming visitors from overseas, including Christians. In discussing the utility of the concept of Religious Tourism, the PI used studies that applied this concept to Chinese Buddhist temples (e.g., Mount Putuo) as his major reference. (1) As anticipated by the PI, the first task necessary to achieve this sub-objective was to reconstruct the pedigree of the Haichuang priests, and this required the collection of historical materials from the Haichuang texts. The most prominent priests in this pedigree belonged to different generations of monastic publishers. It was precisely this group of priests (or at least some of them) who were responsible for receiving Western visitors and embassy officials, confronting Protestant missionaries’ propagating activities, and building up a social network in and beyond the region. To understand the multiple roles played by Haichuang, it is necessary to begin with a detailed investigation of its priests. (2) Although the narratives recorded Western visitors to Haichuang focused on different aspects of the temple, they also shared some common themes, and thus they can be regarded as a sort of “collective memory.” When their works were published, their impressions of this temple exerted some influence on contemporary readers and later generations. On the other hand, to deal with Western visitors, who were distinctly different from local visitors, the temple gradually developed a tourist management strategy. The temple made every effort to satisfy visitors’ demands, but it also censured the behaviour of visitors who breached the temple’s regulations. The PI thinks that only after this management strategy and visitor regulations had been established could the temple balance the interests of all parties and fully play the role of a multi-functional venue in China-West exchanges. 2. Regarding the second objective: This project achieved highly satisfactory results in the key issues under study, and the PI gained deeper insights into the objective. The PI believes that the temple had both semi-official and non-governmental features that were similar, although not identical to those of the Hong merchants who were responsible for looking after or monitoring the Western community in Canton. (1) The PI believes that the temple’s semi-official status was mainly manifested in two activities: assisting the government to entertain Western visitors when Canton was the sole port open to Western merchants, and receiving several Western diplomatic missions to China. However, we should not put too much emphasis on this semi-official status of the temple. The Western diplomatic missions stayed at Haichuang only for a short time, and they did not have any important cultural or religious exchanges with the temple’s priests. Furthermore, by the early 19th century at the latest, many Westerners who visited the temple failed to comply with government regulations, which required them to come only on prescribed days, yet they were still hospitably received at the temple, and individual priests of the temple aided visitors in transporting Buddhist texts and artefacts to the West. The facts show that the temple’s official status was eclipsed by its non-governmental orientation. Explorations of the conflicts between and changes in the temple’s semi-official and non-governmental features have been one of the most noteworthy issues in the present project. (2) The fact that the officials, gentry, and merchants had little to do with the publication and circulation of Buddhist texts also demonstrates the temple’s non-governmental status. To sustain the enterprise of publishing Buddhist texts, the priests had to develop a fundraising network in the community. The network mainly comprised the temple’s connections with fellow priests, Buddhist laymen, and general Buddhist believers. This kind of connection became increasingly important in the later period. As for the introduction of the temple, its Buddhist texts, and its artifacts to the Western world, the major figures who undertook this task included Robert Morrison, Nathan Dunn, and Karl Friedrich Neumann. 3. With respect to the third objective, this project achieved highly satisfactory results. The PI came to the conclusion that Morrison’s visits to Haichuang provide a convenient starting point for tracing the whole process of Buddhist-Protestant negotiations in the entire 19th century, from initial encounters to the missionaries’ advocacy of communion and co-existence, which was founded on the assumption that aspects of Buddhism could be Christianized. Exchanges of religious thought in the temple provided an important context for understanding how the attitude of Protestant missionaries towards Chinese Buddhism gradually changed, and their impact should be understood in this chronological and ideological framework. (1) The PI chose Morrison, George Smith, and John Henry Gray as the major objects of study for this sub-objective and conducted two investigations: (a) Exploring how Morrison, as a sinologist and an educator, learned about Chinese Buddhism; and tracking down how he integrated the notes he wrote in his copies of the Haichuang texts into his A Dictionary of the Chinese Language. (b) Investigating how Smith and Gray established personal relations with the Haichuang priests, and how step by step they achieved their targets of studying and living in the temple, handing out preaching pamphlets, and carrying out religious activities. (2) This project contributes to the popular academic domain of “Buddhist-Protestant encounters” by highlighting the response of the Buddhist priests. The PI made the following findings: (a) The publication of the Haichuang texts was a deliberate strategy on the part of the priests to strengthen the existing religious and cultural tradition of Buddhism against the challenge posed by a foreign religion. (b) The quantity of Christian tracts distributed to the Haichaung priests was far larger than the number of converts to Christianity. It is more reasonable to conclude that Buddhists read the tracts out of curiosity but were not moved to convert. 4. The fourth objective of this project also achieved highly satisfactory results. Academics agree that Haichuang was a bridge for China-West exchanges in the 19th century, but in-depth investigations into the activities of its priests and the circulation of Buddhist texts show just how varied the role of this bridge could be, as the following three cases indicate. (1) The vast quantity of descriptions of Haichuang written by Westerners throughout the nineteenth century witnessed that their zeal to visit the temple remained undiminished after other treaty ports besides Canton were opened for trade. Thus, Haichuang remained a highly reputable Buddhist temple in the eyes of the Western world. (2) The ex-abbot of the temple, “Chaou Chung,” assisted Dunn in collecting Chinese Buddhist artifacts to be shipped back to America, which Dunn featured in exhibitions in Britain and the USA. Such exhibitions had a direct impact, in the mid- and late 19th century, on Western people’s understanding of Chinese Buddhism. (3) Morrison and Neumann acquired from the temple a large quantity of Buddhist texts that they shipped to the West. These three cases were not isolated incidents but rather manifestations of a long-standing tradition of private communication and cooperation between China and the West.

27606817.label: Major findings and research outcome
27606817.value: 1 Regarding the Haichaung Buddhist texts: Through field trips and various channels, the PI assembled the latest and most comprehensive data on this collection of literature (122 items in total) to date. After a systematic collation, they have been introduced to international academics and the public. These data enable a clear understanding of the history and process of the publication and collection of the Haichaung texts. 2 Regarding the history of the Buddhist temple Haichuang: By choosing the monastic publishers, plus the publication and circulation of Buddhist texts, as the focus of the study, this project was able to reconstruct the temple’s missing history in the 19th century. The PI thinks that this group of Buddhist priests forms another representative sample in addition to the “poetry monks” who previously attracted great attention, and that this new theme has not yet been adequately explored by researchers. 3 Regarding Haichuang temple’s multiple roles in China-West relations: Whereas the early Western visitors treated the temple as “the Other” in their discussions, this project stressed its role as a “religious host” in cross-cultural and cross-religious exchanges. Thus, the project analysed the temple’s tourist management strategy and investigated the Buddhist priests’ responses to the preaching of Protestant missionaries. The PI thinks that by making a concerted effort to continue the enterprise of publishing Buddhist texts, the priests made a strategic decision to strengthen the temple’s religious tradition when they faced the challenge of Christianity. 4 Regarding the temple’s semi-official status: Unlike earlier researchers who stressed the temple’s “official” status, this project laid more emphasis on the temple’s “non-governmental” nature. The PI believes that the temple manifested both features, but in different circumstances; according to the situation, one feature became manifest while the other remained concealed. Only by investigating the multiple roles played by the temple can we recover the changes and development of these two features. 5 Regarding the academic significance and value of the study of Haichuang temple: The study not only helps to reconstruct the history of the temple, but it also interconnects three major research domains—namely, the Canton trade and the Western community in Canton, the cultural enterprise of Buddhism in the Lingnan region, and the propagation of Christianity in China—so as to re-portray the history of China-West relations in the 19th century.

27606817.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27606817.value: (1) The PI believes that there are still a certain number of Haichuang Buddhist texts preserved in other libraries and academic institutions all over the world (especially in North America), and that only by continuing to track down and collate these texts can we enhance our knowledge of this topic. (2) Through this research project, the history and process of the Haichuang priests’ contacts with Protestant missionaries is well understood. But the history of their contacts with Catholic missionaries is still little known, and this question will be explored in subsequent research. (3) The study of the history of Haichuang should be considered against the general background of the history of Buddhism in the Lingnan region as a whole. A further understanding of the temple’s connections with other temples (i.e., the Dafo and Hualin temples), together with a collection of additional historical materials from other temples, will advance our knowledge of development of the enterprise of publishing and circulating Buddhist texts in or beyond the region.

27606817.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27606817.value: Taking the Canton (Guangzhou) Buddhist temple Haichuang as its subject, the present project attempts to reconstruct its history by examining four aspects: religion, literature, recreation, and diplomacy. The temple was an important venue for Chinese-Western exchanges in the 19th century. Therefore, to reconstruct its history, we have to collect and make use of records found in historical materials written in Chinese and in European languages; it is of particular importance to assemble the Haichuang Buddhist texts that are scattered in various libraries all over the world. In the belief that greater emphasis should be put on the contributions of Haichuang priests who, as monastic publishers, promoted the publication and circulation of Buddhist texts, this project investigates their various activities, which did not receive sufficient attention from previous academics. Last but not least, a study of the history of Haichuang and its multiple functions enables us to offer new historical materials and perspectives that can be utilized in important research domains such as the Canton trade and the Western community in Canton, Buddhist-Protestant encounters, and the regional and cross-regional development of Lingnan Buddhism.

27608717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27608717.value: It is widely known that effective teaching requires more than familiarity with subject matter. Shulman (1986, 1987) identified a distinct province of knowledge required for effective teaching called pedagogical content knowledge (PCK). Since publication of his seminal articles, science educators have been investigating and discovering ways to enhance pre-service science teachers’ PCK. However, most prior research initiatives have focused on investigating and improving teachers' PCK in the lesson planning stage. Few have investigated the PCK that directly informs teachers’ action during the interactive phase of teaching. An emergent line of research (represented by Alonzo and Kim [2016] and Chan and Yung [2015]) is beginning to investigate in-service teachers’ in-the-moment pedagogical reasoning to better understand the “useable” form of PCK that directly informs teachers’ in-the-moment decision-making (i.e., dynamic PCK). Building on the premise that the classroom environment is often unpredictable, requiring teachers to make on-the-spot teaching decisions, these researchers argue that dynamic PCK (as opposed to planned PCK) is the most practice-relevant form of PCK, and directly influences teachers’ moment-to-moment teaching practices. An important finding from this line of research is that strong dynamic PCK enables teachers to capitalize on classroom experiences to develop new PCK during the interactive phase of teaching. Given the important role of dynamic PCK in informing teachers’ spontaneous teaching decisions and developing their new PCK during the interactive phase, an important question remains: How can the dynamic PCK of pre-service teachers be enhanced? The proposed project will be a multiple-case study that is qualitative and interpretive in nature. Its purpose is twofold. First, it will investigate the development of dynamic PCK in one entire cohort of pre-service teachers enrolled in a postgraduate diploma science methods course designed to enhance such PCK. The course engages participants in multiple cycles of lesson planning, video-mediated discussion and reflection activities. Second, the project will examine how and in what ways video-based learning experiences can enhance the development of teachers’ dynamic PCK. The project findings will advance the field by extending the scope of PCK investigation to dynamic PCK of pre-service teachers and offering a refined understanding of how dynamic PCK develops in pre-service science teachers. They will also have implications for pre-service teacher education, particularly with regard to how authentic classroom videos can be deployed to enhance dynamic PCK in pre-service teachers.

27610117.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27610117.value: Psychotic disorders affect about 3% of the population and are among the most disabling conditions. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is increasingly recognized as an important treatment target in people with early psychosis. It is one of the most common comorbid conditions in psychotic disorders, found in up to 23% of outpatients, and has significant negative impact on the quality of life and functioning of people living with psychosis in the community. Effective psychotherapies for social anxiety are available for the general population, with strong evidence for cognitive behavioural approaches. Initial evidence suggests cognitive behavioural intervention can be effectively applied to reduce social anxiety in people with psychosis. Theoretically based adaptation of cognitive behavioural intervention for this population with robust evidence support is lacking. Social anxiety is putatively linked to psychosis via several pathways. The main hypotheses are that social anxiety develops (1) as a consequence of residual delusional ideation (RDI); and (2) as a response to social stigma due to insight of a psychosis diagnosis. Empirical evidence to-date from populations with paranoia and psychotic symptoms provided support for the RDI hypotheses, including the principal investigator’s pilot data in a local consecutive sample of 137 outpatients with early psychosis, with RDI of social nature (e.g. reference delusions) specifically implicated. From a cognitive-behavioural conceptual model, RDI can directly cause anxiety in related social situations, leading to avoidance of those situations, and the avoidance behaviour contributes to the maintenance of the RDI, forming a vicious circle that maintains both RDI and social anxiety. This study is designed to test the RDI model of social anxiety in early psychosis. Outpatients with early psychosis (n=90) receiving community care will be randomly allocated to one of two intervention arms on top of their usual care: (1) a 18-session RDI-targeted cognitive behavioural intervention; and (2) 18 sessions of unstructured recreational activities. The primary outcome is severity level of social anxiety. We hypothesized that participants in the RDI-targeted cognitive behavioural intervention arm will achieve significantly higher rate of treatment response and remission of social anxiety. Secondary outcomes are severity level of RDI, quality of life, and functioning. The knowledge implication of this study is evidence for the RDI model of comorbid social anxiety in early psychosis. The service implication of this study is evidence to inform psychotherapy design for comorbid social anxiety in early psychosis, with potential benefits in quality of life, functioning and symptom reduction in this disadvantaged population. 思覺失調影響大約3%的人口，而且是最致殘的疾病之一。在早期思覺失調患者中，共發的社交焦慮症越來越被視為重要的治療目標。社交焦慮是思覺失調最常見的共發病之一，佔門診患者的23%，對社區內思覺失調患者的生活質素和功能表現造成顯著的負面影響。現已有適用於一般人口的心理療法，可有效治療社交焦慮。初步證據顯示，認知行為介入可有效地應用於思覺失調患者，以減低社交焦慮。然而，目前尚未有基於理論為這類患者而設計、而且具有力證據支持的認知行為介入法。 社交焦慮可能透過幾種途徑與思覺失調相關。一些主要的假設指社交焦慮的出現是 (1) 殘餘妄想的結果；以及 (2) 對思覺失調診斷的病識感所引致的社會污名的反應。現有的實證來自偏執與思覺失調症狀患者研究——包括本研究主要研究員所收集、來自連續137名早期思覺失調門診患者的先導數據——為殘餘妄想假設提供了支持，尤其是具有社交性質的殘餘妄想 (例如關係妄想)。基於認知行為概念模型，殘餘妄想可以在相關的社交場合直接引起焦慮，導致患者迴避這些場合；迴避行為又有助於維持殘餘妄想，從而形成一個殘餘妄想和社交焦慮的惡性循環。 本研究旨在測試早期思覺失調中社交焦慮的殘餘妄想模型。正在接受社區照顧的早期思覺失調患者 (n=90) 除了接受常規照顧外，將被隨機分配進入兩個介入組別之一：(1) 共18節針對殘餘妄想的認知行為介入；以及 (2) 共18節非結構性的康樂活動。主要結果是社交焦慮的嚴重程度。我們假設接受針對殘餘妄想認知行為介入的參加者，將會達到顯著較高的社交焦慮治療反應及緩解率。次要結果是殘餘妄想的嚴重程度、生活質素、以及功能表現。 在知識層面上，這項研究會為早期思覺失調共發社交焦慮的殘餘妄想模型提供證據。在服務層面上，本研究將為早期思覺失調共發社交焦慮的心理治療設計提供證據，從而對這類處於逆境的人士的生活質素、功能表現、以及症狀改善帶來潛在益處。

27610117.label: Realisation of objectives
27610117.value: The two objectives of this research were partially realised. In relation to the development of the theory for the cognitive-behavioural therapy being tested in this study, a journal paper has been published in the journal Anxiety, Stress, & Coping in 2020. The paper is entitled “Social Anxiety within a Network of Mild Delusional Ideations, Negative Symptoms and Insight in Outpatients with Early Psychosis: A Psychopathological Path Analysis”, with due acknowledgement to the ECS funding. To achieve the two objectives, as part of the research project, the PI has set out the following intervention development and training plan in the proposal: “The intervention will be delivered in the regular community facilities of the NGOs where the participants are recruited. To ensure treatment fidelity, a 2-day training workshop will be provided to the therapists in this study, who possess a social worker qualification. Ongoing clinical supervision will also be provided. A practitioner’s manual and intervention materials will be provided to the therapists after the training workshop.” Given that hourly compensation for therapists in the original budget was not supported, the PI has re-strategized to encourage voluntary-based participation of therapists from community mental health settings by providing free ongoing training opportunities throughout the project. This step in achieving the project objectives has therefore been fulfilled: a detailed intervention manual has been developed and trained 23 therapists by organising two 2-day training workshops for partnering NGOs and 21 regular skills training sessions with supervision from a psychiatrist, a social worker, and a clinical psychologist experienced in cognitive behavioural therapy. In terms of participant recruitment for the randomised controlled trial, we have under-achieved in terms of the planned number of participants. In the interim report (period ending 31-10-2018), the reviewer noted “problems encountered in engaging NGO partners and staff recruitment due to the non-funding of the therapist positions,” and that the PI has been “able to overcome the problems and… should be able to collect sufficient data in the remaining period”. This improved recruitment situation unfortunately lasted only slightly more than half a year, when social unrest and the outbreak of COVID-19 set in and caused disruption in community services, at a time when we have recruited only 20% of the target number of participants, with disruption to ongoing interventions and significantly increased difficulty in participant recruitment in the past years. Attempts to overcome the problems include: 1. applying for project extension for 6 months (reaching the maximum time limit); 2. expansion of sources of participant recruitment: including project briefs with multiple NGOs and operators of various settings such as Integrated Community Centre for Mental Wellness (ICCMWs), schools, sheltered workshops, vocational rehabilitation units, and half-way houses; 3. interim analysis of available data; 4. adoption of in-depth case analysis method to inform the effect of the theory-driven intervention; and 5. development of a bilingual remote intervention guidelines with clinical psychologist input to in preparation of prolonged disruption of face-to-face intervention. To evaluation the therapeutic effects of the theory-driven cognitive behavioural intervention for social anxiety in people with psychosis (objective 1), and the effect of this intervention on secondary outcome measures of residual delusional ideation, functioning, and quality of life in this group (objective 2), action items 3 & 4 above were carried out, with caution: as at the date this report is prepared, only 30 people have been randomised. Given the underpowered sample, as well as the unknown impacts of the social unrest and pandemic since late 2019 that have both disrupted the intervention (duration ranged from 4 months to 23 months) and affected the mental health of participants, interpretation of findings from this study would be complicated. With a preliminary paired t-test analysis on within-subject difference between the two timepoints for exploratory purpose, no significant change can be observed in either group for the four outcomes in this small sample. To be able to provide some insight on the research questions within all constrains of the current situation, and make the best use of available information, we have been working on in-depth case analysis to understand whether and how the intervention components exert their effect on social anxiety, residual delusional ideation, functioning, and quality of life. Here we describe four cases illustrative of the changes with cognitive-behavioural intervention and control (exercising with the company of a volunteer). We noted from the baseline and post-intervention assessment, session content, and case note of the therapist/volunteers some themes to inform the research objectives. From the detailed case notes of these in-depth case studies, we identified potential mechanisms in the cognitive-behavioural intervention given the unique context. For example, in case A, despite worsened symptoms and functioning, there was a reduction in social anxiety with a timing coinciding with social events; case B where increased social anxiety seen at a time when social isolation becoming the norm during COVID; case C with overall improvement despite relapse and intervention disruption, and case D with apparent worsening of social anxiety but improved quality of life and functioning. Other case studies have showed more minute psychological / psychopathological changes, such as reduced emotional valence despite unchanged attentional anomalies with residual ideas of reference. Findings from these in-depth case studies are being prepared as further research output in journal publication format and knowledge exchange materials. Findings from in-depth case analysis of remotely conducted cognitive behavioural intervention in this group suggested feasibility and possibly higher user acceptability. Such insight may be particularly relevant during COVID-19 outbreak but also applicable beyond the pandemic situation. In an illustrative case (case E, male, age 50 years) with a long duration of illness (24 years) had the following changes from baseline to post-intervention assessment: reduced social anxiety (LSAS, 55 at baseline to 45 post-intervention), ideas of reference (IRIS, 3 to 1.5), improved functioning (SOFAS, 46 to 62) and quality of life (WHOQoL-BREF-HK, 77 to 83). The intervention was conducted with an in-person first session followed by the remaining sessions delivered using secured information and communication technology in accordance with available, generic remote psychotherapy guidelines and one specifically developed for this research project (action item 5 above). Apart from the initial suggestions of feasibility in achieving clinical benefits with remote cognitive behavioural intervention in this population, we have two potentially useful observations: (1) certain therapeutic components of cognitive behavioural intervention could be more effectively delivered remotely, namely guided exposure in-situ with the presence of a therapist, which could be infeasible otherwise in some situation where social anxiety and other psychopathology may be triggered; and (2) less intrusive investigation by the therapist or researcher on the mechanisms of action with complex psychotherapies and symptom formation/extinction. In this case, the therapist was able to observe a lack of change in automatic attention towards self-referential stimuli (a residual delusional ideation), which was the source of social anxiety and avoidance, while a reduction in social anxiety level can be attributed to cognitive reappraisal. These discoveries, albeit preliminary, could be the beginning of a breakthrough in non-pharmacological intervention for people with psychosis.

27610117.label: Major findings and research outcome
27610117.value: We have tested a theoretical model of relationship between social anxiety, insight, persecutory delusions, ideas of reference, negative symptoms, and depression was tested using path analysis. The final model suggested a direct link between ideas of reference (standardized path coefficient, β = 0.26, p < 0.002) and negative symptoms (β = 0.29, p < 0.001) to social anxiety. Insight was related to both persecutory delusions and negative symptoms but had no direct relationship with social anxiety. The model has excellent goodness-of-fit (Chi-square 6.62, comparative fit index 1.00, root mean square error of approximation 0.00). This model provided a new framework for understanding the complex interplay between psychosis symptoms and social anxiety, which may be unique to outpatients with early psychosis and require further confirmatory research and targeted intervention strategies (Wong, 2020). With this new model for understanding the complex interplay between psychosis symptoms and social anxiety, a cognitive behavioural intervention protocol informed by the theoretical model developed. We also noted that intervention delivered by trained social workers feasible with regular supervision and support (Wong, 2019). References: Wong, G. H. Y. (2019). 27610117.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27610117.value: Because of the disruption of research intervention with COVID-19, we have piloted within the context of this research the use of remote psychotherapy in this population of stablised psychosis outpatients. Apart from the initial suggestions of feasibility in achieving clinical benefits with remote cognitive behavioural intervention in this population, we have two potentially useful observations: (1) certain therapeutic components of cognitive behavioural intervention could be more effectively delivered remotely, namely guided exposure in-situ with the presence of a therapist, which could be infeasible otherwise in some situation where social anxiety and other psychopathology may be triggered; and (2) less intrusive investigation by the therapist or researcher on the mechanisms of action with complex psychotherapies and symptom formation/extinction. These discoveries, albeit preliminary, could be the beginning of a breakthrough in non-pharmacological intervention for people with psychosis. The PI proposes to continue develop and test this platform in the post-COVID era, with rigorous study design to examine the effectiveness of remote cognitive behavioural therapy as compared with traditional in-person therapy, and to conduct qualitative study to investigate the user acceptability and feasibility of the new platform for delivering intervention and conducting interventional research on psychosis and social anxiety.

27610117.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27610117.value: People with psychosis are often faced with social anxiety even when they are stablised in terms of other symptoms. This can impact on their functioning, in terms of social interactions and occupation, as well as poorer quality of life. Using an advanced statistical method (called ‘path analysis’), we have identified certain contributors to social anxiety in these people, including ideas of reference (e.g., the feeling that others are talking about yourself) and ‘negative symptoms’ (e.g., facial expression flattening). They can be potentially targeted in psychotherapy to improve social anxiety in psychosis. In this study, we randomly assigned people with psychosis to receive a type of psychotherapy (called ‘cognitive behavioural intervention’) designed to address these contributors and social anxiety, or to receive support from a trained volunteer to engage in exercise(s) of their choice. Initial observations suggest that external factors such as COVID outbreak could have an impact on social anxiety and other outcomes, although the relative effect of the intervention in the context of these strong external factors requires further studies. We noted the potentials of using remote psychotherapies in advancing both research and practices, such as non-invasive presence of the therapist during sessions requiring exposure to anxious-provoking situations.

27610617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27610617.value: Not all of our past experiences are equally welcome: there are painful memories that we would prefer not to think about. Although constructive reflections on painful and unpleasant memories can lead to useful insights, when left uncontrolled, these memories are also unwanted in the sense that they can be intrusive, distracting and distressful. Specifically, unwanted memories can automatically intrude into awareness, distract people from concentrating on on-going tasks while eliciting stressful emotional responses. Therefore, the ability to effectively control unwanted memories and their automatic expressions is critical for maintaining cognitive functioning and for promoting psychological well-being. Previous research has shown that people can voluntarily control unwanted emotional memories and reduce their conscious recall. However, it remains unclear whether controlling emotional memory can similarly influence their involuntary, automatic expressions. Here, three experiments are proposed to answer this question. Experiment 1 will employ an implicit, affective priming task to test whether controlling unwanted emotional memories can reduce their elicited automatic affective responses. Experiment 2 will investigate whether controlling emotional memories from watching traumatic films can causally reduce real-life, involuntary memory intrusions. Electrophysiological measures will be employed to investigate the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms. Experiment 3 will build on Experiment 2 to test whether sleep can aid in emotional memory control to reduce real-life involuntary intrusions. The proposed research will have significant theoretical and translational implications. Theoretically, its focus on the automatic memory expressions will provide new knowledge on memory control’s downstream effects on explicit and implicit memory processes. Moreover, it will provide novel information regarding whether sleep can help people control emotional memories, thereby deepening our understanding of the implications of sleep for emotion and memory processes. This research will also have translational implications because impaired memory/thought control characterizes a range of psychopathological disorders including post-traumatic stress disorders (PTSD), depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorders (OCD), etc. The proposed research will thus inform the development of novel cognitive interventions to help people better control unwanted memories and distracting thoughts. Ultimately, this research will benefit cognitive functioning and promote psychological well-being. 並不是我們過去的所有經驗都是讓人愉快的：有一些痛苦的記憶是我們寧可不要再次憶起。雖然對這些痛苦且不快的記憶作建設性的反思有可能帶來有用的見解，但是當人無法控制這些記憶時，這些記憶也會是不想要的，因為它們有可能讓你分心以及令你不堪其憂。更具體地說，這些不想要的記憶可能自動地侵擾到你的腦海，使你從正在進行的作業中分心，同時誘發緊張的情緒反應。因此，能夠有效控制這些不想要的記憶以及其自動化表現，對於維持認知能力和保持心理健康都是很重要的。 過去的研究顯示人們能自願地控制不想要的情緒記憶，以及減少有意識的回想。可是，人們是否能控制情緒記憶的無意識的自動化的表現，則仍然是未知的。該專案將提出三個實驗以回答此問題。實驗 1 計畫使用情緒啟動任務來測試控制不想要的情緒記憶能否減少記憶自動誘發的情緒反應。實驗 2 將使用創傷性電影範式來考察是否控制情緒記憶可以減少現實生活中的記憶自動化入侵。同時我們將考察腦電生理活動來考察其背後的認知神經機制。實驗 3 將建立於實驗 2 之上，來考察睡眠对記憶控制及自動化入侵的影響。 此研究提案將會有重要的理論上和轉化性的影響。理論上，研究集中在自動的記憶表現上，這將提供記憶控制對外顯記憶和內隱記憶的影響的嶄新知識。此外，此研究將提供有關睡眠能否幫助人們控制情緒記憶的嶄新資訊，因此將會使我們更瞭解睡眠對情緒和記憶過程的意義。該研究也會有轉化性的影響，因為低效的記憶/想法控制會導致一些心理障礙，包括創傷後應激障礙、抑鬱症、焦慮症、強迫症等。因此，此研究提案將能帶來更多知識以促進新的認知干預的發展，讓人們更佳地控制不想要的記憶和讓人分心的想法。最終，此研究將有益於人們的認知功能以及促進心理健康。

27610617.label: Realisation of objectives
27610617.value: Unwanted emotional memories can be voluntarily forgotten by suppressing their recall. This project addressed three questions: We first examined the neurocognitive processes underlying retrieval suppression, when participants intentionally suppress the retrieval of aversive scenes in response to their reminders. We next examined whether and how such retrieval suppression impacts the spontaneous/implicit and deliberative/explicit emotional reactivity towards suppressed emotional memories upon their re-exposure. Third, we examined how sleep vs. sleep deprivation influenced real-life involuntary intrusions of lab-analogue trauma experience. First, We tracked, in real time, individual memories as they are suppressed remains elusive. Here we used multivariate decoding on EEG data to track how suppression unfolds in time and to reveal its impact on cortical patterns related to individual memories. We presented reminders to aversive scenes and asked people to either suppress or to retrieve the scene. During suppression, mid-frontal theta power within the first 500 ms distinguished suppression from passive viewing of the reminder, indicating that suppression rapidly recruited control. During retrieval, we could discern EEG cortical patterns relating to individual memories-initially, based on theta-driven, visual perception of the reminders (0-500 ms) and later, based on alpha-driven, reinstatement of the aversive scene (500-3000 ms). Critically, suppressing retrieval weakened (during 420-600 ms) and eventually abolished item-specific cortical patterns, a robust effect that persisted until the reminder disappeared (1200-3000 ms). Actively suppressing item-specific cortical patterns, both during an early (300-680 ms) window and during sustained control, predicted later episodic forgetting. Thus, both rapid and sustained control contribute to abolishing cortical patterns of individual memories, limiting awareness, and precipitating later forgetting. These findings reveal how suppression of individual memories from awareness unfolds in time, presenting a precise chronometry of this process. Second, to gauge neural and behavioural indices of participants’ spontaneous/implicit emotional reactivity, we combined EEG recording with an adapted affect misattribution procedure (AMP). For deliberative/explicit emotional reactivity, we measured participants’ self-reported affect ratings towards cues of emotional memories and towards emotional memories per se. We found behavioural evidence that suppressing the retrieval of emotional memories induced forgetting in the post-eTNT cued recall task. In terms of emotional rating, we found that retrieval suppression enhanced deliberative/explicit negative emotional reactivity towards previously suppressed negative memories when they were directly re-encountered. Memory suppression did not alter the implicit and explicit emotional ratings toward memory cues. EEG analyses showed that during the eTNT task, suppression enhanced neural signals associated with inhibitory control (frontocentral N450) while reducing electrophysiological activity associated with episodic recall (parietal P300), working memory maintenance (prefrontal NSW), and emotional reactivity (parietal LPP) relative to voluntary retrieval. Multivariate EEG-based decoding during the eTNT revealed that neural activity pattern was distinct upon viewing cues associated with emotionally negative vs. neutral memories during suppressed trials, only during 210-340 ms post cue onset. During later time window (400-3000 ms post cue), the neural activity pattern for cues associated with negative vs. neutral memories was indistinguishable during suppressed trials. In voluntarily retrieved trials, there was distinct neural activity pattern for cues paired with negative vs. neutral memories at multiple clusters, specifically during 190-260 ms and 1960-2050 ms post cue onset. The decoding evidence suggests that suppressing emotional memories deteriorated their valence-dependent neural representation. Neural marker sensitive to emotional reactivity (parietal LPP) recorded during the AMP was also attenuated for No-Think cues than for Think-cues, suggesting that the emotional after-effects of memory suppression persisted after eTNT. Further corroborating the emotional after-effects of memory suppression, multivariate decoding analyses revealed that neural activity pattern was indistinguishable only between suppressed negative and neutral memory. Taken together, our results suggest that suppressing unwanted memories can induce their forgetting as well as disrupt emotion-dependent neural representation in response to cues. However, suppression also amplified negative emotional reactivity towards previously suppressed negative memories when they are re-confronted. Our findings offer fine-grained insight into the dynamic influence of memory suppression on the implicit and explicit affect reactivity and bear theoretical implications for future research on the link between active forgetting and affect regulation. Third, despite the critical role of sleep in memory and emotion processing, large remains unknown regarding how sleep influences trauma-related symptoms arising from maladaptive memory/emotional processes, such as those among patients with posttraumatic stress disorder. Employing a trauma film paradigm, we showed how post-trauma sleep versus sleep deprivation influenced involuntary intrusions and voluntary recognition of traumatic memories. Participants were randomly assigned to sleep or total sleep deprivation group following experimental trauma induction. Participants were assessed with: (a) lab-based and 7-day diary-based involuntary intrusions; (b) voluntary recognitions of traumatic memories 12-hr and 7-day post-trauma induction; and (c) post-traumatic stress disorder-like symptoms measured by the Impact of Event Scale-Revised. We found that compared with sleep deprivation, slept participants experienced fewer traumatic intrusions across 7 days, reported lower emotional hyperarousal, and showed more accurate recognition of trauma-related stimuli. Moreover, higher subjective sleep quality was associated with fewer intrusions only in the sleep group, while a reversed pattern emerged in the sleep deprivation group. These results provide novel evidence supporting the therapeutic benefits of sleep in protecting mental well-being from trauma exposure. To the extent that sleep modulates trauma-related symptoms, sleep can be conceived as the potential target for early interventions among trauma victims.

We found that during retrieval suppression, mid-frontal theta power within the first 500 ms distinguished suppression from passive viewing of the reminder, indicating that suppression rapidly recruited control. During retrieval, we could discern EEG cortical patterns relating to individual memories-initially, based on theta-driven, visual perception of the reminders (0-500 ms) and later, based on alpha-driven, reinstatement of the aversive scene (500-3000 ms). Thus, both rapid and sustained control contribute to abolishing cortical patterns of individual memories, limiting awareness, and precipitating later forgetting. This work is now under review. Second, to gauge neural and behavioural indices of participants’ spontaneous/implicit emotional reactivity, we combined EEG recording with an adapted affect misattribution procedure (AMP). Multivariate EEG-based decoding during the eTNT revealed that neural activity pattern was distinct for emotionally negative vs. neutral cues during suppressed trials, only during 210-340 ms post cue onset. During later time window (400-3000 ms post cue), the neural activity pattern for cues associated with negative vs. neutral memories was indistinguishable during suppressed trials. This work is now under preparation, and we plan to submit in the second half of 2022. Third, we examined how sleep vs. sleep deprivation influences trauma-related symptoms arising from maladaptive memory/emotional processes. Supported by the grant, I and my team also published the first comprehensive meta-analysis of targeted memory reactivation in sleep and memory consolidation. This work is published in Psychological Bulletin (2020). Other work supported by the grants were published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience (2021), Memory (2020) and Cognition (2019).

27610617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27610617.value: First, we are working on the submission of the main results to high impact journals. We expect 2-3 papers published based on these results. Second, we are examining how emotion regulation, combined with memory control, can facilitate memory control. This is a new research direction, as previous research largely examined these two topics separately. Based on preliminary results (funded by this ECS project), we submitted one GRF grant on this topic. If the application is successful, we will systematically investigate this research question in the following years. Third, continuing the work along sleep, we aim to extend prior work that focused on sleep vs. sleep deprivation to memory manipulation directly during sleep. We are currently funded by the NSFC to investigate this research question.

27610617.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27610617.value: After experiencing trauma, unwanted memories can be intrusive and distressful. How to effectively control unwanted memories and their influence is important for maintaining well-being during difficult times, such as during the global pandemic. In this research, we studied how people voluntarily control unwanted aversive memories, while confronting with their reminders. This particular memory control strategy is known as retrieval suppression. We identified brainwave activity associated with retrieval suppression, such as attenuated brain activity implicated in memory retrieval. We also found that retrieval suppression weakened brain activity implicated in emotional processing. In a third study, we found that compared to sleep deprivation, sleep benefited processing of lab-analogue traumatic experiences, as evidenced by reduced flashbacks and hyperarousal. Together, these results suggest that retrieval suppression weakened both memory and emotional activity, and sleep can be adaptive in protecting mental well-being in the aftermath of trauma.

27611017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27611017.value: The thinking around guardianship, with its rationale of protecting the fundamental rights of mentally incapacitated individuals, has undergone significant change in the past few decades. Originating from a largely paternalistic philosophy, there has been a gradual shift towards respect for autonomy and human agency, together with an increasingly nuanced view towards capacity and decision-making capability. With the ratification of the UN Convention for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the principle of equality of social participation of all individuals, including those with mental disability, has been placed at the forefront of the discussion on guardianship. As a result, guardianship systems (mostly in Western jurisdictions such as Australia, Canada and the United States) have been moving towards a supported decision-making model whereby a mentally incapacitated individual is supported in making his own decisions, instead of a substituted decision-making model whereby decisions are made on his behalf once he is assessed as lacking requisite mental capacity. Alternative legal mechanisms to guardianship have also been developed in order to promote respect for the mentally incapacitated individual’s autonomy and self-determination. While encouraging developments have been made and written about in Western jurisdictions, the developments in guardianship systems in Asia have been much slower. Together with a dearth in scholarship on Asian guardianship systems from a theoretical and human rights perspective, there is an urgent need for this gap to be filled. This project aims to begin to fill this gap by constructing a theoretical framework with which to assess the guardianship system in Hong Kong and those of its East Asian neighbors, namely China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. Specifically, the resulting theoretical framework will assess (i) the extent to which these guardianship systems are underpinned by a set of consistent ethical and legal principles (such that the rules can be applied in a consistent and principled manner) and (ii) the extent to which these systems are compliant with local and international human rights standards. Where the systems fail to meet such standards, suggestions for reform will be made (with a particular focus on Hong Kong). It is envisaged that this project will lead to further research on guardianship systems in the larger Asia region in the future. 我們對監護權這個為保障無精神行為能力人仕的基本人權而設的機制的理解，在過去數十年起了很大變化。監護權相關的法律雖然起初為家長式思維的產物，但已慢慢地變得傾向於尊重人的自主權和能動性，並對精神行為能力及決擇能力有愈來愈深入細緻的詮釋。《聯合國殘疾人權利公約》被承認後，所有人—— 包括精神上有殘障人仕—— 在社會應享有平等參與的原則成為監護權討論的焦點。結果，監護權制度（主要為西方的司法管轄區， 如澳洲、加拿大和美國）正由以往由第三方為一旦被評為無精神行為能力的人仕代為作決定的「替代決定模式」，過渡到盡量支持無精神行為能力人仕為自己作決定的「支緩決定模式」。此外，其他以尊重無精神行為能力人仕自主自決權為本的監護權法律機制亦相繼被發展出來。 當西方司法管轄區在監護權法律上取得令人鼓舞的發展成果時，亞洲地區在這範疇的發展卻甚為緩慢。加上我們十分缺乏從理論和人權角度探討亞洲的監護權制度的研究，我認為有急切需要去填補這發展的差距。本研究項目的目標是初步建構一個適合用作評估香港及其比鄰的東亞地區—— 中國，日本，南韓及台灣—— 監護權制度的理論框架。此理論框架將會評估(i)這些監護權制度多大程度上以共同的倫理及法律原則為基礎，及(ii) 這些制度有多大程度符合當地及國際的人權標準。如果有制度不符合標準，我會提出改革建議（會特別集中於香港的情況）。我預期本項目會在將來引起關於大亞洲區監護權制度進一步的研究。

27611017.label: Realisation of objectives
27611017.value: Objective 1: To examine guardianship systems in Hong Kong and other East Asian jurisdictions including China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan within their legal context, as well as any alternative mechanisms in the law such as advance directives, living wills or durable/enduring powers of attorney (100%) This project began with an examination of adult guardianship systems in East Asia, following which the two jurisdictions of Hong Kong and mainland China were chosen as the focus of in-depth exploration and analysis due to the intriguing similarities and differences between them in terms of socio-cultural context and legal culture. The project examined the key features of the adult guardianship regimes in each of these jurisdictions, highlighting relatively recent changes in the mainland Chinese regime and the implications of these changes. The adult guardianship regime in Hong Kong was further examined in relation to the broader framework of values and participation in the context of an invited contribution to an international project on values and participation in mental capacity law (please see Collaboration with Other Institutions for further information). This research, in particular the research on the Hong Kong context, highlighted in particular a significant area of further research that has previously been underdeveloped, specifically the alternative legal mechanism/decision-making tool of the advance directive (as described in Objective 1) and the law and practice in relation to advance directives across Asia. Thus, this project undertook a broad examination of advance directives in 16 jurisdictions across Asia as an alternative to adult guardianship, in the context of a collaboration with Dr Michael Dunn (please see Collaboration with Other Institutions for further information). Under this project, we were able not only to present the first comprehensive and systematic analysis of the law and practice of advance directives across Asia, we were also able to identify key trends across these jurisdictions, and draw important conclusions about the manner in which advance directives have been taken up in these jurisdictions. Objective 2: To develop a theoretical framework for the assessment of such guardianship systems, relying on established bioethical principles such as autonomy and justice (100%) In the analysis of the Hong Kong and mainland Chinese adult guardianship regimes, the PI developed a framework on the basis of Hong Kong and mainland China’s international commitments under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), building upon previous work done by the PI and some collaborators regarding strong and weak interpretations of CRPD obligations and what they entail. Factors to be considered under this framework include (i) the extent to which supported decision-making, which has as its goal the promotion of respect for autonomy for all persons (no matter their level of mental capacity), has been implemented; (ii) the manner in which the concept of mental capacity is applied in these regimes and (iii) the sufficiency of safeguards under the regime in terms of (a) whether the individual’s wishes and preferences have been prioritized; (b) how conflicts of interest and the potential for undue influence are dealt with under the regime; and (c) how proportional, tailored, and subject to regular review the measures are. This framework was used to assess the two adult guardianship regimes and is envisaged to be applicable in assessments of adult guardianship regimes more generally as well. The assessment of the regimes itself is discussed further in Objective 3 below. Objective 3: To critically assess such guardianship systems for (i) consistent and principled application of ethical and legal principles, (ii) compliance with local and international human rights standards (including sufficiency of safeguards against abuse) (100%) As discussed above, a framework was developed on the basis of international commitments under the CRPD to assess the adult guardianship regimes in Hong Kong and China for their compliance with international human rights standards. This framework includes as its third step an assessment of the sufficiency of safeguards against abuse, addressing points (ii) and (iii) of Objective 3. In relation to point (i), this was addressed throughout the discussion of how the framework should be applied in the assessment of these adult guardianship regimes, but in particular, this was addressed in the second step of the framework. This second step considered how the concept of mental capacity has been applied in these jurisdictions. Apart from considering specifically whether the concept of mental capacity has been applied in a disability-neutral manner, the assessment considers more broadly whether there are any major concerns with how mental capacity is defined and conceptualized in these two jurisdictions. For example, problems were identified in terms of (i) inconsistent application of capacity tests in Hong Kong (between the adult guardianship regime and other parts of the Mental Health Ordinance which contain capacity tests), (ii) inconsistent and varying definitions of capacity across different guidance documents in mainland China, raising concerns about whether the assessment of capacity can be carried out in a consistent and principled manner. Additionally, the Hong Kong adult guardianship regime was also assessed in relation to the weight and emphasis that is given to the views and wishes of the individual under guardianship as part of the international project on values and participation in mental capacity law mentioned under Objective 1. The lack of weight and emphasis given to these views and wishes was critically evaluated in light of Hong Kong’s sociocultural context as part of this invited contribution. Objective 4: To suggest possibilities for reform where appropriate, particularly in the Hong Kong context (100%) This objective was addressed in both parts of the project. In the edited collection on advance directives, of which the PI co-wrote the chapter on Hong Kong, the PI and co-author raised clear concerns with the proposed legislation on advance directives and suggested that, for example, an overhaul of Hong Kong’s mental capacity law was necessary for the provisions to be coherent and consistent. Possibilities for reform were also suggested in relation to the other 15 jurisdictions in the book; while the PI was not a co-author of those chapters, the PI was heavily involved in shaping the content of many of the chapters in the processes of editing and revision. In terms of adult guardianship regimes, the PI proposed several key questions to consider when planning for the reform of the adult guardianship regimes in Hong Kong and mainland China. In addition, specifically in relation to the role of views and wishes of the individual under guardianship, a number of specific reform directions were suggested. For example, it was proposed that the coherence and effectiveness of having entirely separate regimes to deal with different aspects of substitute decision-making on behalf of persons lacking mental capacity be examined, and that the problematic paternalistic values underlying the relevant legislative provisions be addressed. At the minimum, it was suggested that legislative provisions about best interests and how decisions should be made on behalf of persons without capacity (if at all) should mandate the consideration of both the past and current views and wishes of the person lacking capacity, and Practice Directions issued by the Courts and other such policy documents and/or guidance should emphasise the need for and encourage persons lacking mental capacity to attend and participate in court and tribunal hearings about them where they are able to do so.
