27611017.label: Major findings and research outcome
27611017.value: Adult Guardianship As argued in my article entitled, “Bringing the Adult Guardianship Regime in Line with the UNCRPD: The Chinese Experience” (see Part C), both the adult guardianship regimes in Hong Kong and mainland China cannot be said to be compliant with even a weaker interpretation of its obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Additionally, as argued in my book chapter entitled, “Values and participation of individuals without mental capacity in Hong Kong” (see Part C), the views and wishes of an individual under guardianship (and individuals without capacity more generally) are generally given very little weight or emphasis in Hong Kong, which in turn leads to an absence of meaningful participation in court proceedings. In this way, Hong Kong’s archaic and paternalistic construction of the individual without capacity as a passive object of protection has resulted in a worrying absence of concern for the subjective values of the individual. Much thought needs to be given to how Hong Kong’s adult guardianship regime (and mental capacity law more generally) can be brought in line with modern standards. Advance Directives (ADs) As demonstrated in the Conclusion of our edited collection Advance Directives Across Asia: A Comparative Socio-legal Analysis (see Part C), there were a number of interesting similarities and differences across the Asian jurisdictions in terms of the law and practice of ADs. For example, a clear trend was the conservative approach adopted in most of the jurisdictions, whereas variations among jurisdictions included the specificity of regulation and the complexity of formalities. We also found that while the influence of the family was immensely significant in most jurisdictions, the nature of, and justification for, this influence was much more nuanced and complex than is typically recognised in the literature. Finally, we argue that our novel concept of ‘generative accommodation’ can be used to make sense of how ADs have been taken up in Asian jurisdictions. While a number of factors suggest that ADs, as well as the underlying principle of autonomy, have been incorporated as a form of accommodation, we also suggest that this process of incorporation is ‘generative’ in that distinctive, locally specific approaches have arisen, been set in motion, or been proactively produced in ways that are unique to these jurisdictions as they marshal their own commitments and expectations alongside this emerging international consensus.

27611017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27611017.value: On the basis of this project’s work, and to develop further my research on decision-making on behalf of persons without mental capacity in Asian jurisdictions, I have applied for and been very fortunate to be granted a GRF from the RGC on best interests decision-making in Chinese jurisdictions, for which I am very grateful. I will use this funding to expand on my research, and I look forward to contributing further in this field. Separately, I am working on three other lines of research that are further developments of the research conducted under this project, and intend to seek further support for this work where necessary: 1) Development of our findings on the family’s influence in end-of-life care, arguing that the current understanding is not sufficiently nuanced to capture the different roles that the family plays in medical decision-making at the end of life. 2) Development of concept of generative accommodation beyond the end-of-life context, as a way to understand medical law and ethics in Asia more generally. 3) Looking at how CRPD will and preferences model can be implemented in Confucian societies using an interpretation of Confucian theory consistent with the prioritisation of wishes of the individual under guardianship.

27611017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27611017.value: Population ageing has been described as one of the four global demographic ‘megatrends’. The growth in the proportion of the elderly has many implications, including the inevitable increase in individuals who may be subjected to adult guardianship regimes, and may need to consider advance care planning mechanisms such as advance directives (AD) to retain autonomy over their end-of-life care. It is thus crucial that these alternative mechanisms and regimes be scrutinised for their effectiveness and compliance with human rights obligations. This project examines both adult guardianship regimes and ADs, looking at important questions such as (i) whether substitute decision-making regimes such as adult guardianship in Hong Kong and mainland China are compliant with international human rights obligations, and (ii) what ADs in Asia look like, a vastly understudied area despite the relative abundance of literature in Western jurisdictions. In relation to (ii), the project takes the first comprehensive and systematic look at the law and practice of ADs in 16 jurisdictions across Asia, bringing out key similarities and differences among the jurisdictions. It also draws important preliminary conclusions about how ADs have been taken up in Asia, via what we call a process of ‘generative accommodation’.

27611517.label: Realisation of objectives
27611517.value: The research team published a paper entitled “How Effective are Social Safety Net Programs in Reducing Poverty Risks? A Comparative Study of Taiwan and Southeast China” in a Q1 journal, Journal of Asian Public Policy. This paper achieves the objectives #1, 2, 3, and 4. Using the harmonized Panel Study on Family Dynamics 2006, 2011, and 2013/14 data, this is the first study to examine poverty dynamic patterns and investigate the role of public safety nets in alleviating poverty over time in East Asia through a comparative lens, focusing on Taiwan and southeast (SE) China. We compared the extent to which public transfers alleviate poverty utilizing multilevel regression models. Our findings indicate that, firstly, the extent of poverty increased at a faster rate in rural areas and among migrants in SE China compared to residents in Taiwan and urban SE China, suggesting widening regional inequality. Secondly, public safety nets reduced poverty in all locations, and the reductions increased over time to a greater extent in rural areas and among migrants in SE China. However, such reductions remained insufficient to narrow the disparity in regional poverty trends. Thirdly, public safety nets in SE China lagged behind Taiwan’s on participation rates in elder, disability and education assistance and led in low-income assistance. Finally, although welfare policy design is more generous in Taiwan than SE China, our findings based on welfare outcomes indicate that Taiwan’s safety net did not alleviate poverty to a greater extent compared to SE China’s. Overall, this paper makes several contributions to existing literature. First, we provide an in-depth investigation of poverty dynamics as enabled by the panel data in the East Asian context. Tracking income changes over time, we were able to classify families into four groups: persistently non-poor, entering poverty, exiting poverty, and persistently poor, which affords new insights into patterns of poverty dynamics. Second, emphasis on the roles of public safety nets yields valuable lessons on poverty-reduction policies and programs, especially considering ongoing developments and changes in social safety nets in East Asia and elsewhere. Third, our focus on Taiwan and SE China can particularly illuminate how social welfare buffers poverty risks in the context of declining family support and limited social welfare investment. Taken together, this study offers new insights into poverty transition patterns and government responses within and between SE China and Taiwan. This contrast in welfare outcomes can enrich the literature on East Asian welfare systems, where discussions are often based on welfare policy design rather than welfare outcomes. Based on the qualitative phase of this study, the research team interviewed 35 individuals in Taipei and Shanghai. We are currently working on a manuscript entitled “Public and private safety nets for low-income families in Taipei and Shanghai: A qualitative examination.” Chinese societies have traditionally been characterized by relying on strong informal networks in meeting welfare needs, and government provided welfare have played a subsidiary role in assisting families in need. With the rapid transformation in demographic, economic, and social development in the past decades, does the welfare mix in Chinese societies still adhere to these traditional arrangements? Can the informal networks sustain families at times of crisis? This study examines strategies of low-income Chinese families in using public and private welfare support in meeting their needs in the face of financial hardships. We use a quota sampling approach to recruit families in Taipei and Shanghai who have been persistently in poverty or who exited poverty in the past decade through local organizations and residents’ committees. We conduct qualitative in-depth interviews with these families, utilizing life history interview methods. Findings reveal that, different from western literature, community-level government institutions served as important resources for low-income families in both Shanghai and Taipei. Other acquaintances (e.g., landlords, neighbors) are also identified as unexpected crucial sources of support. In Taipei, the prominent roles of family members in providing support at times of financial crisis showed signs of weakening, and there is a growing sense of entitlement to utilize public safety nets as a strategy to achieve self-sufficiency. In Shanghai, family members remain a fundamental source of financial buffers for many, and the roles of friends and neighbors remain strong. Findings from this study can contribute to the on-going discussion on the evolving welfare mix in East Asian Welfare Regimes. Further, in order to adequately address the second objective to investigate the relationships between public and private safety nets, the research team published another paper entitled “The effects of an old-age allowance programme on intergenerational interactions in Taiwan” in Journal of Social Policy, a Q1 and a top journal in the fields of social policy. In this paper, we examined the effects of a public safety net program, the Senior Citizens Welfare Living Allowance (SCWLA), on private safety nets. Here, we captured private safety nets as intergenerational financial transfers, living arrangements and contact. We further examined the heterogeneity of its effects by adult children’s five types of motives for giving: altruism, exchange, reciprocity, affection, and sense of responsibility. Similar to the first publication, we used 2002, 2004, 2005 and 2006 data from the Panel Study of Family Dynamics. We employed a difference-in-difference individual fixed effect model to compare the outcomes across the treatment (aged 65 and older) and comparison groups (aged 55 to 64) before and after the introduction of SCWLA. Our results indicate that SCWLA crowds in intergenerational contact but does not significantly change financial transfer and co-residence patterns. The increase in intergenerational contact is primarily driven by adult children having lower motives for giving. This suggests that old-age allowances may reduce financial entanglement between adult children and older parents and change the social norm by raising “low motivators’” awareness, respect and concern for elderly. Providing public transfer to the elderly should not be hampered by the fear of distorting family support functions. This paper contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, theoretically, the coverage of outcomes on non-financial transfer (e.g., co-residence and contact) and financial transfer provides new evidence enriching understanding of the effects of public transfer on the financial, structural and associational forms of intergenerational interactions. Second, we investigate the heterogeneous policy effects by adult children’s motives for giving. This enriches theoretical knowledge on pathways through which public financial transfer impacts intergenerational interactions. Third, practically, the examination of non-financial outcomes and heterogeneous effect can improve policymakers’ understanding of the costs and benefits of a public financial transfer programme. Fourth, the adoption of rigorous causal identification strategies contributes to understanding the causal relationship between old-age public transfer and intergenerational interactions.

27611517.label: Major findings and research outcome
27611517.value: This study published two papers in Journal of Social Policy, a leading social policy journal, and Journal of Asian Public Policy, a leading policy journal on Asian policy issues. Both journals are top-ranking (Q1 journals). This study has two additional manuscripts that will be submitted for journal publications in due course. In addition, based on findings from this project, the research team engaged in 14 presentations at international conferences or as invited talks at leading institutions such as the London School of Economics and Political Science, National University of Singapore, Seoul National University, and Academic Sinica in Taiwan. This demonstrated the academic community’s strong interests on this topic and the spread of finding dissemination. Regarding the poverty dynamic patterns and the role of public safety nets in alleviating poverty over time in Taiwan and SE China, our findings indicate that, firstly, the extent of poverty increased at a faster rate in rural areas and among migrants in SE China compared to residents in Taiwan and urban SE China, suggesting widening regional inequality. Secondly, public safety nets reduced poverty in all locations, and the reductions increased over time to a greater extent in rural areas and among migrants in SE China. However, such reductions remained insufficient to narrow the disparity in regional poverty trends. Thirdly, public safety nets in SE China lagged behind Taiwan’s on participation rates in elder, disability and education assistance and led in low-income assistance. Finally, although welfare policy design is more generous in Taiwan than SE China, our findings based on welfare outcomes indicate that Taiwan’s safety net did not alleviate poverty to a greater extent compared to SE China’s. Regarding the roles of public and private safety nets in buffering poverty risks, we found that, different from western literature, community-level government institutions served as important resources for low-income families in both Shanghai and Taipei. Other acquaintances (e.g., landlords, neighbors) are also identified as unexpected crucial sources of support. In Taipei, the prominent roles of family members in providing support at times of financial crisis showed signs of weakening, and there is a growing sense of entitlement to utilize public safety nets as a strategy to achieve self-sufficiency. In Shanghai, family members remain a fundamental source of financial buffers for many, and the roles of friends and neighbors remain strong. Findings from this study can contribute to the on-going discussion on the evolving welfare mix in East Asian Welfare Regimes.

27611517.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27611517.value: This project prepared the PI to engage in comparative research and to study welfare regimes in East Asia. This led the PI to further expand the inquiry to more East Asian societies. Currently, the PI is finalizing a manuscript to investigate generosity, coverage, redistribution, and work incentives in East Asian welfare systems. The PI engages in the comparative analyses using a model family approach. The geographic coverage is expanded from mainland China and Taiwan in the ECS project to six societies in total, including mainland China, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan. This work is further supported by a GRF grant “Shock-Responsive Social Protection Systems for Low-Income Families under COVID-19 in East Asia” to investigate East Asian social safety nets during the COVID-19 pandemic.

27611517.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27611517.value: This study first investigated the poverty dynamic patterns and the role of public safety nets in alleviating poverty over time in Southeast (SE) China and Taiwan. Our findings suggest that although public safety nets reduced poverty to a larger extent in rural SE China and among migrants in SE China than in urban SE China or Taiwan, such reductions remained insufficient to narrow the disparity in regional poverty trends where poverty rates grow faster among these two groups. We also found that although welfare policy design is more generous in Taiwan than SE China, our findings based on welfare outcomes indicate that Taiwan’s safety net did not alleviate poverty to a greater extent compared to SE China’s. This provides implications for governments to take policy actions. Next, this study examined the roles of public and private safety nets in buffering poverty risks using a qualitative interview approach in Shanghai and Taipei. We found that, different from western literature, community-level government institutions served as important resources for low-income families in both Shanghai and Taipei. In Taipei, the prominent roles of family members in providing support at times of financial crisis showed signs of weakening, and there is a growing sense of entitlement to utilize public safety nets as a strategy to achieve self-sufficiency. In Shanghai, family members remain a fundamental source of financial buffers for many, and the roles of friends and neighbors remain strong. However, the support from NGOs were lacking in Shanghai. Findings from this study can contribute to the on-going discussion on the evolving welfare mix in East Asian Welfare Regimes.

27612617.value:  To investigate how central government agencies, local governments, courts, and individual parties deal with the legal risks and uncertainties of local land reforms.  To explore whether the top-down legalist approach to Chinese land reform is the right direction in which to go.  To explore reform of the numerus clausus principle in the PRC Property Law to accommodate decentralized innovations to land institutions.  To articulate a functional model with clear boundaries and effective interaction between the Chinese central and local governments in land governance and to make legal and policy reform proposals accordingly.  To address the tension between respecting the law and promoting social and economic change in Chinese land reform.  To shed light on the internal structure and politics of government and add it to the theoretical model on the evolution of property rights.

27612617.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27612617.value: I will carry out the first-ever systematic analysis of decentralized land reforms in contemporary China, focusing on the conflicts between local practices and national laws and how central government agencies, local governments, local courts and individual parties deal with legal risks and uncertainties in the reform process. Article Five of the 2007 PRC Property Law states that “the types and contents of property rights shall be stipulated by law.” This means that the establishment of new types of property rights and the content of those rights can be stipulated only by law made by the National People’s Congress (NPC) or its standing committee (Committee of Legal Affairs of NPC Standing Committee 2007), a principle called numerus clausus, i.e., the number (of property types) is closed (物权法定 in Chinese). The principle is also the legal basis of the central government’s recent requirement that all local land reforms seek authorization from the NPC Standing Committee if they conflict with national laws. However, as I have argued elsewhere, the logic of Chinese land reform has not followed this principle, as evidenced by the rise of the Household Responsibility System in rural areas and Land Use Rights Reform in urban areas in the first two decades of China’s market reform (Qiao 2016b; Qiao & Upham 2017). The decentralized, bottom-up logic also applies to the contemporary Chinese land regime. There are several national laws related to property, mainly the Constitution, the Land Administration Law, the Rural Land Contract Law, and the Property Law, but hundreds of local land reforms. Local reforms can serve as laboratories of national legal reform, but, without proper authorization reforms that get ahead of national laws can be defined as illegal. I plan to investigate four categories of local reforms along the spectrum of legality: direct defiance, doctrinal migration (drawing legality from other effective legal reforms, such as trust law and corporation law), tying (tying local land reforms to higher and more general reform plans), and seeking authorization from the national legislature. The proposed research will examine different degrees of legality and their impact on local land reforms in China, and explore how national laws can be reconstructed to accommodate decentralized land reforms. 本研究旨在系统研究中国地方土地制度创新的原因、形式和内容，以及其与国家相关制度的关系。中国是一个单一制国家，体现在土地制度方面，则是地方的制度创新必须在中央法律的范围之内。特别是物权法中的物权法定原则和立法法中的立法保留原则都是地方土地制度创新的重要限制和约束。但地方政府的实践是否以上述原则或国家法律为基准则是另外一回事。很可能恰恰相反，地方政府的很多制度实践都突破了已有的国家法律。因此产生的问题是：如何评价“非法”的地方土地制度？中央政府在地方土地实践突破国家法律时如何引导和约束？是否需要改革现有的的以顶层设计为中心的土地制度？哪一级政府才是土地制度设计的最佳层级？

27612617.label: Realisation of objectives
27612617.value: Under this project, I have published three papers in top U.S. law journals. My article, Rights-Weakening Federalism, focuses on the first two objectives: (1) To investigate how central government agencies, local governments, courts, and individual parties deal with the legal risks and uncertainties of local land reforms; (2) To explore whether the top-down legalist approach to Chinese land reform is the right direction in which to go. It examines whether federalism protects land rights in China from two dimensions. I first compare national law with local institutions of eminent domain, revealing that local governments take much more land than the national government approves, frequently violating, tweaking, and challenging national law. I next examine the impact of interjurisdictional competition on the development of local land institutions, demonstrating that local governments are weakening individual land rights for the benefits of mobile capital. Overall, Chinese federalism weakens rather than strengthens individual land rights and should be called rights-weakening federalism. This article has generated general theoretical implications. Leading property law scholars in the U.S. have debated whether federalism protects land rights for decades but have achieved no consensus. The existing debate centers around the immobility of land, however, this article argues that land immobility is not an essential factor. The structure and power of local governance, the balance between land and capital in particular, matters much more. Hence, the better question to ask with respect to interjurisdictional competition is who benefits from the competition. This article also poses a more fundamental challenge to the literature on interjurisdictional competition by adopting agglomeration economics, which poses the question of whether such competition constitutes sorting or agglomeration. All the existing literature on property rights and federalism presumes a market of sorting, i.e., that investors are indifferent to location, and are thus attracted by local governments offering the best price or strongest protection. However, urbanization and industrialization in China are actually a process of agglomeration, which determines that a few cities with a natural, or at least initial, advantage are taking over, and the local governments of the remainder will therefore eventually lose in the competition. The implication is that interjurisdictional competition is actually a race to the bottom for most local governments rather than a win-win game as the sorting literature suggests. My article "Expropriation in the Name of Rights" focuses on the third and fourth objectives: to explore reform of the numerus clausus principle in the PRC Property Law to accommodate decentralized innovations to land institutions; to articulate a functional model with clear boundaries and effective interaction between the Chinese central and local governments in land governance and to make legal and policy reform proposals accordingly. It discloses for the first time how and why land reform programs in the name of empowering and enriching farmers have been serving the purpose of Chinese local governments to compromise the rights revolution in the Chinese national expropriation regime through an in-depth empirical investigation, . The concept of “transferable development rights” (TDRs) is simple: development rights from one parcel of land are lifted up and transferred to another. Upon a detailed examination of land tickets in Chongqing and Chengdu, the southwestern Chinese application of TDRs, this article reveals that local governments in both cities have created schemes of land tickets to circumvent the increasingly stringent national regulation of local governments’ expropriation power. But by reframing such practices as for rural rights and welfare, they have successfully gained acquiescence and even approval from the central government, eventually leading to the creation of a national market of land tickets. This case study demonstrates the “maximally protean and easily reformable” nature of the “bundle of sticks” and cautions against expanding the role of TDRs in China’s land reform. My article "Exclusionary Megacities" focuses on the sixth objective: To shed light on the internal structure and politics of government and add it to the theoretical model on the evolution of property rights. It investigates why, despite their many differences, the same type of exclusion is happening in both Chinese and U.S. megacities. This article is co-authored with University of Pennsylvania Professor and Provost Wendell Pritchett. Urban law and policy scholars argue that Not-In-My-Backyard (NIMBY) homeowners are taking over megacities in the U.S. and hindering housing development therein. They pin their hopes on an efficient growth machine that makes sure “above all, nothing gets in the way of building.” Yet the growth-dominated megacities of China demonstrate that relying on business and political elites to provide affordable housing is a false hope. Our comparative study of the homeowner-dominated megacities of the U.S. and growth-dominated megacities of China demonstrates that the origin of exclusionary megacities is not a choice between growth elites and homeowners, but the exclusionary nature of property rights. Our study reveals that megacities in the two countries share a property-centered approach, which prioritizes the maximization of existing property interests and neglects ultimate housing consumers’ interests, resulting in unaffordable housing. Giving housing consumers a voice in land use control and urban governance becomes the last resort to counteract this result. This comparative study shows that the conventional triangular framework of land use comprising government, developers, and homeowners is incomplete, and argues for a citizenship-based approach to urban governance. The essential component of this approach is clearly defining the boundary between the political and property markets, facilitating citizens’ equal access and participation in the political market that set general parameters for development while leaving individual development decisions to the property market. Combining together these three articles address local land reforms and property institutions in different parts of China and their complicated relationship with the central government and national law. The project objectives have been well achieved. These articles have been noted and cited by leading scholars and policy makers.

27612617.label: Major findings and research outcome
27612617.value: Local governments in China are both resisting and distorting the rights revolution in national law, at the core of which lies the imposition of constraints on those governments’ eminent domain power. At the same time, in the face of national legislative gridlock, local governments are experimenting with such initiatives as granting farmers land development rights. Why are Chinese local governments simultaneously endangering the tenure security of farmers and proactively expanding their land rights beyond what is permitted under national law? This article develops a bi-dimensional framework of federalism in China and demonstrates that the framework explains local governments’ seemingly contradictory attitudes to land rights much better than the conventional view of unidimensional federalism with interjurisdictional competition at its heart. The article’s core argument is that only the combination of horizontal federalism and vertical federalism can incentivize local governments to expand and protect individual land rights. Competition in one dimension alone, whether vertical or horizontal, cannot credibly commit local governments to protecting individual rights.

27612617.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27612617.value: I'm now reviewing findings of this project and draft a paper to summarize and theorize its contributions. The paper is titled "Federalism and the Rights Revolution: Why Do Chinese Local Governments both Endanger and Expand Individual Land Rights." I have presented drafts of this paper at Yale and Tsinghua Universities. I hope to publish a book eventually on this topic.

27612617.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27612617.value: This project furthers our understanding of the autonomy of local governments in designing their property institutions and implementing the national property laws. It also contributes to the discussion on comparative federalism and law and development. It has been the first study about the central-local relationship behind China's real estate regime.

27613017.label: Realisation of objectives
27613017.value: This project aimed to conduct a randomised controlled trial to examine the efficacy of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) and cognitive behavioural therapy for depression (CBT-D), as compared to waitlist control, in reducing depression and insomnia severity in adolescents with comorbid insomnia and depression. Eligible participants were invited to complete assessments at pre-treatment (week 0), during the treatment (week 2, 4, 6) and post-treatment (week 8/at the conclusion of the last group session). The two active treatment groups were additionally followed up at post-treatment one-month and post-treatment six months in order to determine the long-term changes following the treatment with CBT-I and CBT-D, respectively. The project was completed as planned and the objectives were fully achieved. We have successfully recruited the participants as planned and tested our study hypotheses. We screened 325 participants, and a total of 133 eligible youth participants were recruited and randomised into one of the following groups: CBT-I (n= 45), CBT-D (n=44), or waitlist control (n=44). In the CBT-I group, youth participants received an intervention programme designed to address the behavioural, cognitive and physiological perpetuating factor of insomnia and included: psycho-education about sleep and sleep hygiene, stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation training, structured worry time, cognitive restructuring (targeting sleep-related dysfunctional cognitions), and relapse prevention. In the CBT-D group, youth participants received an intervention programme designed to address common difficulties and problems encountered by depressed adolescents and included psycho-education about depression, self-monitoring, behavioural activation, cognitive restructuring (addressing negative and irrational thoughts often associated with depression in adolescents), relaxation techniques, and relapse prevention. Both treatments consisted of eight weekly 90-min group-based sessions, with 5-6 adolescents in each group, delivered over a 10-week window. Four out of 45 participants (8.9%) in the CBT-D group, five out of 44 participants (11.3%) in the CBT-I, and 4 out of 44 participants (9.1%) in the waitlist (WL) group dropped out during the intervention/waiting period. Thirty-nine (86.7%) from CBT-D, 38 (86.3%) from CBT-I, and 40 (90.1%) from WL completed assessment at post-treatment. In the CBT-D group, 38 completed follow-up and seven were lost to follow up at 1-month; and 34 completed a further assessment, with four lost to follow up at 6-month. In the CBT-I group, 38 completed follow-up and six were lost to follow up at 1-month; and 31 completed follow-up and seven were lost to follow up at 6-month. There were no differences in demographics and clinical characteristics for treatment completers and non-completers. The rates of missing data were similar between the groups across different time points. The majority of the recruited participants were late adolescents (aged 19.5 ± 2.4 years, female: 67.7%) and in tertiary education (n=106, 79.7%). All three groups were comparable in terms of demographics and clinical characteristics at baseline.

27613017.label: Major findings and research outcome
27613017.value: Three-group comparison showed a significant time x group interaction effect on the severity of insomnia symptoms (F(2, 118.14) = 7.97, p = .001) and depressive symptoms (F(2, 120.47) = 22.35, p <.001). Both CBT-I and CBT-D resulted in significant improvements of insomnia as assessed by ISI (CBT-I: d = -1.82, CBT-D: d = -1.52, WL: d = -0.29) and depressive symptoms as assessed by CDRS-R (CBT-I: d=-1.83, CBT-D: d = -1.57, WL: d = -0.71) at post-intervention, as compared to waitlist control (WL). CBT-D group also had a significant reduction of self-reported mood symptoms (HADS-D scores), as compared to WL group (P=0.011). At post-treatment, there were significantly more participants who achieved a clinically meaningful improvement in insomnia (as defined by a reduction of ISI score by 6 or above) in the CBT-I group as compared to the other two groups (CBT-I vs. CBT-D vs. WL: 64.9% vs. 38.9% vs. 27.5%, p = 0.026). Treatment effects on all primary outcomes (ISI, CDRS-R, HADS) were not significantly different between CBT-I and CBT-D groups at all time points except for HADS-D scores at one-month follow up, where CBT-D group showed a greater reduction in self-reported depressive symptoms from baseline compared to the CBT-I group. Regarding sleep diary parameters, significant improvements in sleep onset latency (CBT-I: d = -0.42, CBT-D: d = -0.26) and sleep efficiency (CBT-I: d = 0.85, CBT-D: d = 0.45) were observed in both CBT-I and CBT-D groups from baseline to post-treatment. However, only CBT-I group had a significant improvement in sleep efficiency at post-treatment relative to WL (p=0.05). In addition, CBT-I group had significantly higher sleep efficiency at one-month follow up (p=0.010), and 6-month follow up (p=0.009) relative to CBT-D group. Regarding objective sleep parameters (actigraphy), CBT-I showed a significant reduction in sleep onset latency (p=.013) and improvement in sleep efficiency (p=.032) at one-month follow up relative to CBT-D group. CBT-I group also showed significant improvements in sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, sleep-related cognitions and behaviours, and fatigue at post-treatment relative to WL group (all p<0.05). Treatment effect of CBT-I on sleep-related beliefs and behaviours (as assessed by Dysfunctional belief and attitudes scale) was significantly better relative to CBT-D at post-treatment (p=0.001) and at one-month follow up (p=0.001). There were no differences in the treatment effects between CBT-I and CBT-D on sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, pre-sleep arousal, fatigue, quality of life, and suicidality measures at post-treatment and two follow ups.

27613017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27613017.value: To our knowledge, this project was the first study in the literature to make a head-to-head comparison of the effects of cognitive behavioural therapy with two different treatment focuses (sleep vs. mood) in young people with comorbid sleep and insomnia. We showed comparable treatment effects of CBT-I and CBT-D in addressing both sleep and mood disturbances whilst CBT-I showed additional benefits of addressing sleep-related aspects which were evident by the improvements of both subjective and objective sleep as well as sleep-related dysfunctional cognitions. Nonetheless, CBT-D seemingly improved self-reported depressive symptoms better than CBT-I at one-month follow up but not at other time points. Our findings supported the efficacy of CBT-I in treating insomnia and depression in youths with both conditions, suggesting that targeting sleep disturbance could potentially change the trajectory of depression in youths. Further research is needed to examine the long-term treatment outcomes and to understand the mechanistic processes underlying treatment effects. Future studies should also explore sequential treatments and the groups of youths who are likely to benefit from sleep- vs. mood-focused treatment, as well as optimising treatment modality to increase accessibility and scalability of the interventions in this vulnerable group.

27613017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27613017.value: Adolescence is a challenging developmental period associated with increased vulnerability to developing sleep and mood disturbances. Whilst Insomnia is often comorbid with depression in youths and both may reciprocally exacerbate clinical outcomes and lead to a constellation of detrimental consequences, optimal treatment approach to manage this comorbid condition in young people remained unclear. The present study was a randomised controlled trial to test the efficacy of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for insomnia (CBT-I) and CBT for depression (CBT-D), when compared with waitlist control, in youths with comorbid insomnia and depression. The findings of this study extended our understanding of the interplay between insomnia and depression, and had important clinical implications, especially for informing clinical practice as to whether sleep complaints are necessarily a priority target for clinical intervention and the development of well-founded guidelines for managing insomnia and depression in adolescents. The results showed that the delivery of either CBT-I or CBT-D could effectively improve the clinical conditions of youths with comorbid insomnia and depression, with CBT-I showing additional benefits of addressing sleep-related aspects. In addition, the present study suggested that targeting sleep disturbance could potentially change the trajectory of depression in youths.

27615017.label: Project Title(Chinese)
27615017.value: 解讀運動式打黑模式何以在中國大陸持續存在

27615017.label: Project Objectives
27615017.value: To examine the underlying reasons for the persistence of campaign-style policing against organised crime in China. To investigate the extent to which political and institutional conditions have led to the continuity of this practice. To develop a new theory of policy persistence to interpret why the government continuously favours a policy that most academics and practitioners would prefer to change. To identify new directions for conducting research and making policy in response to the ineffective policing of organised crime.
rows: To examine the underlying reasons for the persistence of campaign-style policing against organised crime in China.
To investigate the extent to which political and institutional conditions have led to the continuity of this practice.
To develop a new theory of policy persistence to interpret why the government continuously favours a policy that most academics and practitioners would prefer to change.
To identify new directions for conducting research and making policy in response to the ineffective policing of organised crime.

27615017.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27615017.value: Why does the Chinese government persistently favour campaign-style policing to combat organised crime? Research to date has focused primarily on the legal issues and human rights concerns relevant to this crime control policy, offering insufficient knowledge to identify the underlying reasons for the persistence of such costly and controversial campaign-style policing. The proposed project will constitute a pioneering study of campaign-style policing in mainland China, examining why the Chinese government continues to favour the practice. Its aim is to develop a legitimacy-based theory of policy persistence by testing three hypotheses: (1) the deep-rooted political culture of ‘heavy penaltyism’ causes decision-makers to believe that campaign-style policing of organised crime is legally correct and morally justified; (2) the failure of routine enforcement encourages the Chinese government to continuously employ campaign-style enforcement to deal with stability-related problems, including organised crime; and (3) privileged groups (especially local political leaders) favour the constant use of campaign-style policing against organised crime in order to further their career prospects. To test these three hypotheses, the project will, after a systematic content analysis of published sources, conduct fieldwork in two Chinese cities (Chongqing and Qingdao). Based on contacts established from my previous work, I will conduct 60 individual interviews and at least five focus group discussions with (a) public security officials working at the grassroots level and (b) criminologists in public security colleges and other research institutions. This research will put forward a new perspective for interpreting policy persistence in mainland China and identify new directions for research and organised crime control policy. 為什麽中國政府始終堅持運動式打黑呢？迄今為止的研究主要集中在與這壹類犯罪控制政策相關的法律問題和人權問題上，然而目前的研究並未揭露這壹耗費巨大的運動式警務模式持續存在的根本原因。本項目是針對中國大陸運動式打黑模式的開拓性研究，深入探究中國政府為什麽持續使用運動式打黑模式。本項目旨在建立壹個“政策持續的合法性理論”，並且通過田野數據來驗證三個假設：（1）“重刑主義”作為根深蒂固的政治文化，使決策者相信運動式打黑是符合法理的，並且在道德上站得住腳；（2）常規執法的失效鼓勵中國政府不斷采取運動式執法來維護社會穩定和打擊有組織犯罪；（3）特權團體（特別是地方政治領導人）希望通過使用運動式打黑來建立其政治形象，從而提高其晉升的可能。 為了驗證這三個假設，該項目除了會對公開的資料進行內容分析之外，還會在兩個內地城市進行田野調查。研究人員將對處在執法壹線的公安人員和從事警務和犯罪控制研究的學者進行大約60次的個人訪談和至少5次小組討論。 這項研究將為理解運動式打黑模式的持續性提供新的視角，為研究有組織犯罪和完善犯罪控制確立新的方向。

27615017.label: Realisation of objectives
27615017.value: How an overview of published materials helps achieve project objectives The project objectives were partially achieved by a systematic review of both Chinese and English language materials. As mentioned in the ECS mid-term progress report, the PI and his RAs had conducted a systematic literature search to conduct an overview of the Chinese-language journal articles relevant to anti-crime policy in China. We paid special attention to CNKI, the most comprehensive academic database in China. We conducted a search in CNKI. By using “saohei” as a keyword, we collected 187 journal articles and 482 news reports. We also conducted a search in Xinhua Net (760 articles), legaldaily.com.cn (2136 articles) and southcn.com (500 articles). An overview of these articles helped us identify several dozens of articles and news reports that offered in-depth analysis of China’s anti-crime policy. The PI and his RAs also read all English-language books and articles relevant to China’s anti-crime policy. To gain insights from English-language literature, we also paid special attention to a number of books and journal articles discussing politics and American anti-crime and anti-drug policies. An overview of published materials, however, was not sufficient to address all research questions. This was because the existing literature failed to offer an up-to-date insights on this topic and most of them were written based on open sources rather than solid fieldwork. How empirical data helps achieve project objectives To effectively redress my research questions and achieve the project objectives, the PI and his RAs conducted 56 interviews with police officers, government officials, prosecutors, judges, lawyers, researchers and business people. These interviews and field notes generated 373,854 words of transcript materials. The empirical data collected from researchers are very helpful and enable the PI to pinpoint how academics view the origin, development and effectiveness of campaign-style policing and identify the essential causes of its continuity (Project Objective 1). The data also help the PI to develop a theory of policy persistence to interpret why the Chinese government favours campaign-style policing (Project Objective 3). Discussions with law and criminal justice researchers enable the PI to identify new directions for conducting research and making policy proposals in response to the ineffective policing of organised crime (Project Objective 4). Information obtained from criminal justice practitioners is particularly useful for helping the investigator to more deeply understand what political and institutional conditions are, how campaign-style policing works, how they perceive the persistence of campaign-style policing, and how they understand the major costs or concerns relating to a change or abandonment of this policy (Project Objective 2 &4). China has witnessed a significant change of political atmosphere in recent years; public officials (especially those from the criminal justice system) are now much more likely to decline interview requests from both local and overseas scholars in order to lower the risk of being criticized by their superiors or punished by the Party. This have brought significant challenges for this research project. The PI and his RAs planned to conduct a total number of 60 interviews and at least 5 focus group discussions with practitioners and academics focusing on these divergent viewpoints and understandings. The number of interviews conducted was slightly smaller than planned, and the planned focus group discussions were cancelled in order to protect interviewees. Several interviewees from law enforcement agencies asked investigators to delete all voice recordings, interview notes and transcripts after interviews. The deletion of these empirical data, obtained through weeks of hard work, was frustrating and significantly slowed the progress of the project. Despite these challenges, the PI and his RAs still managed to conduct a total number of 56 in-depth interviews, which were sufficient for achieving project objectives.

27615017.label: Major findings and research outcome
27615017.value: The key findings of this research include (1) the campaign-style law enforcement is an essential strategy for the party-state to sustain its authoritarian rule, which explains the government’s persistent employment of campaign-style policing to suppress organised crime; (2) the persistence of campaign-style law enforcement leads to the evolution of locally based criminal organizations. In the new century, criminal organizations have evolved from offline to online and they have developed new strategies of enforcement (e.g. soft violence and relational repression) to substitute traditional methods (e.g. physical violence). Two articles have already been published in The British Journal of Criminology, one of the world’s top criminology journals. The first article titled “Politics of crime control: How campaign-style law enforcement sustains authoritarian rule in China” aims to redress a research question of “How does campaign-style law enforcement sustain authoritarian rule?”. Drawing on fieldwork data and published materials, this article enhances the understanding of law and politics in authoritarian regimes by investigating the role of the ‘sweep away black' campaign—designed to combat organized and gang crime—in strengthening China's authoritarian regime. It argues that the campaign helps the party-state enhance its authoritarian rule by resolving the legitimacy crisis caused by economic slowdown, gangs' infiltration in grassroots political structures and problems of police corruption and shirking. But the campaign distorts the criminal justice system by demanding that criminal justice organs deliver severe and swift justice. It also harms China's private sector because local governments may expand the targets of repression to include private enterprises. The second article titled “Organized crime in cyberspace: How traditional organized criminal groups exploit the online peer-to-peer lending market in China” examines how traditional organized criminal groups run their offline businesses on the internet. It shows how Illegal lenders employ techniques of deception, the sharing of compromising information (e.g. social contacts and nude photos) and professional legal services to develop internet-based loan scams to trap student borrowers. To avoid police crackdowns and enforce loan repayment, lenders have developed a new strategy: relational repression, which is the use of cyberviolence and the threat of revealing damaging information to clients’ social contacts. In addition, this research project provides valuable materials for the PI and his collaborators to finish the third article article on “The Evolution of Protest Policing in a Hybrid Regime” which also comes out in The British Journal of Criminology.

27615017.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27615017.value: I plan to write a new article, tentatively titled “Policing organized crime in China: A critical review”. This article will critically examine the campaign-style policing employed by the Chinese government to combat organized and gang crime. The term ‘campaign-style policing’ refers to ‘short-term, zero-tolerance [policing] strategies’ focusing on all or certain types of crime in a country or particular geographical area (Dai 2008: 216). The proposed new article will first examine why the government persistently favours campaign-style policing from four perspectives, namely a political culture of ‘heavy penaltyism’, path dependency, interests of the advantage group (e.g. political elites), and a legitimacy-based theory of policy persistence. It will then critically evaluate the weaknesses and problems associated with the continuous employment of campaign-style policing in China. The article will also identify new directions for conducting research and making policy proposals in response to the ineffective policing of organized crime. The PI plans to submit a GRF proposal on “Authoritarian policing in China” in future. It will enable the PI to enrich his empirical data and write up a book on this topic.

27615017.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27615017.value: This research examines the campaign-style law enforcement in China, which remains an understudied area due to the secrecy of China’s public security organs. Based on rich empirical data, the research enriches our understanding of government’s persistent use of campaign-style policing in curbing organised crime, preserving social stability and retaining legitimacy. This research not only offers valuable data for understanding the rationale, strengths and limitations of the campaign-style law enforcement, but also enriches the knowledge on the evolution of organized crime. This research shows how traditional criminal organizations run their offline businesses on the internet and how they stay safe during anti-crime campaigns. Primary research outputs of this research project include three articles published in a world-leading criminology journal. These journal articles are core readings for researchers and others who are interested in the police and policing in China.

27617417.label: Project Title(Chinese)
27617417.value: 从法律区分看边疆内省化：以甘肃（1750-1850）和内蒙（1850-1920）为例

27617417.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27617417.value: Using the examples of Qing-era frontier regions Gansu and Inner Mongolia, this project examines the administrative creation of new criminal categories during transition from military to civilian order. In the inchoate phase of the Qing Empire, Gansu and Inner Mongolia were supervised by military governors controlling the garrisoned armies. The military order focused on prohibition of unpermitted population movement and treason, and quashing rebellious riots. The civilian rule focused on registration of households, taxation, enlistment of corvée labor, and settlement of legal disputes, all requiring close and meticulous control beyond the capacity of the military. The transformation from military to civilian rule was profound, not just because it functionally redefined the frontier, but also because it entailed drastic change in administrative vision. Different groups and behaviors were targeted as suspicious as new criminal categories emerged. Our study investigates the relationship between crime and state building and repositions it in the broader context of imperial transformation. We aim to reveal the various mechanisms of exclusion (legal, ethnic) in empire making which, to date, have remained poorly understood in historical sociology. Our project focuses on Gansu from the mid-18th to mid-19th century, and Inner Mongolia from the mid-19th to early 20th century. During these respective periods, civilian administration characterized by counties and sub-prefectures was established in these two regions. In Gansu, areas remotely controlled by garrison units were split into county administrative zones in order to facilitate close control. As the administration became more active, more local disputes, especially those related to Hui Muslims, were brought to its attention. In Inner Mongolia, land cultivation initiated by Han Chinese migrants escalated with the Qing court’s New Policy Reform (1900-1911), which formally abolished bans on opening up Mongolian land. These policies encouraged the fast growth of a civilian administration. Redressing injustice in land disputes became an urgent task. Using administrative archives and records of legal cases as our primary sources, we are interested in addressing the following questions: In the shift from military to civilian order, what were the most conspicuous changes to criminal categories used by the administrators to identify social deviants? To what extent did these newly defined criminalities adhere to and advance stigmatization of certain groups? How do these Gansu and Inner Mongolia case studies help us understand the discrimination entwined with the imperial administration in general? 疆域广延的大帝国在历史上开启了治理多元人口和社会构成的政治传统。而帝制国家如何改造其疆域的边陲，使其成为稳定的政治秩序的一部分，比起其疆域的扩展和统治人口的扩大来说更少得到社会科学的检讨。本研究项目从一个较为独特的角度，即新的刑名范畴（criminal categories）的形成来检讨清帝国对其边陲行政的塑造。本项目的研究对象是18世纪中期至19世纪中期的甘肃以及19世纪中期至二十世纪前期的内蒙古地区。两个边疆地区在上述时期经历了国家治理形式的深刻变化，在甘肃地区是明代以来的军事特别行政区向内省的变化，在内蒙古则是盟期制度将清代国家的力量以复杂的形式嵌入到了蒙古各部的政治生活当中。这一深刻的历史转折，相当丰富地留在了新的刑名范畴的变化轨迹里面。清代国家对国家基础性力量（infrastructural power）的重整，并将之安置在新的行政制度当中，和这些新的刑名范畴的关系是什么？国家是如何通过操作这些刑名范畴来继续国家建构的过程？这些问题是本项目关注的社会学机制问题。在18至19世纪中期的甘肃，卫所军户向州县的转变，使得回民的集体犯罪越来越多地进入到立法和司法的关注之中。19世纪中期开始，来自内地的汉族移民在内蒙地区的放垦最终成为清末新政改革（1900-1911）的一部分，其结果是放弃了清代数百年来控制蒙地边疆的政策。在这个过程中，不仅边疆的司法部门开始增设，蒙汉族群之间的法律纠纷也日益繁复。本项目通过大量使用行政和法律方面的史料，将系统梳理和对比上述两个过程。本研究的核心的研究问题如下，在两地的行政变革中，什么样的刑名范畴被制定出来描述当地的边缘性人群？这些新的法律-行政范畴给这些人群赋予了什么样的犯罪性（criminality）？如果说边疆和内地在行政与司法上的一体化是数百年来的历史趋势，那么如何理解这两个历史个案中体现的复杂的行政与法律区分？

28300317.label: Realisation of objectives
28300317.value: Objective 1: Determine the occurrence and distribution of CECs (e.g. PBDEs and PFASs), particularly their replacements in Hong Kong and/or the PRD by developing analytical methods for multi- class collection and quantification of these chemicals in various environmental compartments including air and/or aquatic samples In this study, all the collected specimens were processed for the analyses of the occurrence and distribution of CECs (e.g. PBDEs and PFASs), particularly their replacements such as hexabromocyclododecane (HBCD) and 1,2-dibromo-4-(1,2-dibromoethyl) cyclohexane (TBECH) in Hong Kong marine samples. These two types of alternatives have been regarded as possible replacements for PBDEs and have similar applications in expanded and extruded polystyrene. For PFASs, samples of marine food web were also collected for analysis of short- and long-chain PFASs including PFOS and its replacements. Levels of PFCAs and PFSAs and their composition profiles in biota samples have been identified and quantified by the LC-MS/MS. Among all biota samples, concentrations of total PFCAs and PFSAs in marine mammals were significantly higher (mean = 454642 ng/g wet weight (ww), range = 71.6-977 1180 ng/g ww) than shrimps (mean = 24 ng/g ww., range = 2.46-220 ng/g ww), and fishes (mean = 5.08 34 ng/g ww, range = 0.433-28.4 ng/g ww). Results have been published in Publication (1) and (2). Objective 2: Develop source apportionment and characterization methods for these CECs including studying their chirality and/or specific isotopic profiles Method development for analysis of chirality profiles of the target analytes HBCD and TBECH can exhibit optical activities as chiral compounds. HBCD can generate up to 6 pairs of enantiomers and 4 meso-forms, while TBECH can yield up to 4 pairs of enantiomers. The developed methods have been applied to analyze the marine biota samples and sewage samples and the results have been published in respective journals [Publications (1) and (2)]. Objective 3: Investigate and unravel the transport, source and fate of these CECs in the eastern and western coastal environment of Hong Kong by means of a variety of source identification and characterization approaches (1) BFRs in marine food web and wastewater treatment process Target analytes including HBCD and TBECH are used as physical additives in polystyrene foams and other polystyrene-based consumer products, they can easily leach from products and enter the environment during use or disposal, as such wastewater can act as an indicator reflecting the release of BFRs from local production and product usage, as a potential emission source. In this reporting period, these two chiral BFRs with sixteen different stereoisomers, in four Hong Kong wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) featuring diverse treatment processes have been investigated. Our results revealed that HBCD and TBECH were detected in all the influent samples with concentrations in the order of nanograms per liter, indicating that the release of these BFRs in domestic wastewaters was ubiquitous. Based on the developed analytical methods, HBCD and TBECH have been determined in sediments and different marine species in a marine food web to investigate their trophic transfer. Elevated biomagnification of each diastereomer from prey species to marine mammals was observed. A shift from γ- to α-HBCD when compared with sediments and technical mixtures were found in biota samples. Trophic magnification factors (TMFs) of 11.8 and 8.7 for (‒)-α- and (+)-α-HBCD, respectively were observed, suggesting apparent trophic magnification potential of in the marine food web. For TBECH, TMFs ranged from 1.9 to 3.5 for γ- and δ-TBECH and the relative abundance of these TBECH exhibited an increasing trend from abiotic matrices to biota samples. In general, trophic magnification was observed for these diastereomers. It is important to note that notable biotransformation of HBCD isomers were observed in the food web that biota samples showed a shift from γ- to α-HBCD when compared with sediments and technical mixtures. In contrast, less apparent biotransformation of TBECH isomers were found in the environmental samples with the exception of profile determined in cetacean. Based on these results, chirality of target analytes will be further tested and analyzed and then see whether it is a desirable tool for source apportionment [Publications (1) and (2)]. (2) PFASs in marine food web Among the PFCAs and PFSAs detected, PFOS (~ 45%) was found to be the most predominant compound, followed by PFUdA (~ 21%), PFODA (~ 6%), PFDoA, PFTrDA, PFHxDA, PFTeDA, PFOA, PFNA, PFDA, PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFBS and PFHxS. It is important to note that short-chain PFASs including PFBA and PFBS were detected in most of the samples collected. These results agreed well with that of the previous studies, which indicated that the potential replacements namely short-chain PFASs might widely distributed in the marine environment of South China, consequently they would accumulate in the marine organisms. Based on the newly developed method for non-targeted PFAS analysis, more than 50 individual new forms of PFASs were identified by using the LC-HRMS. Briefly, they were categorized into 8 classes including PFCAs, PFSAs, chlorinated polyfluorinated ether sulfonates (Cl-PFESAs), fluorotelomer sulfonic acids (FTSAs), N-Methyl perfluoroalkane sulfonamidoacetic acids (MeFASAAs), perfluoroalkane sulfonamidoacetic acids (FASAs), semi-fluorinated n-alkanes (SFAs) and unclassified. These results will be included in the publication which is still under preparation. Objective 4: Undertake an assessment of their risks to locally important marine organisms such as cetaceans In this reporting period, stereoisomeric compositions of HBCD and TBECH have been investigated in the blubber of two species of marine mammals, finless porpoises (Neophocaena phocaenoides) and Indo-Pacific humpback dolphins (Sousa chinensis), from the South China Sea. It’s noteworthy that a significant elevating trend of ΣHBCD was found in dolphin blubber over the past 10 years. The diastereomeric compositions showed a predominance of α-HBCD (mostly >90%), whereas the proportions of four TBECH diastereomers in the samples appeared similar. In most blubber samples, apparent enrichment of the (−)-enantiomers of α-, β-, and γ-HBCD was found. For TBECH, significant racemic deviations were also observed for α-, γ-, and δ-TBECH enantiomeric pairs. The results of risk assessment using hazard quotient approach indicates that concentrations of ΣHBCD would pose potential risks to dolphin, while the risk of TBECH exposure to marine mammals was low [Publication (2) and (3)]. Risk assessment for PFASs will be conducted based on the levels of PFASs detected in the marine biota samples and this will be elucidated in the next publication which is still under preparation. 28300317.label: Major findings and research outcome
28300317.value: (1) For the objective 1, the team has developed and validated the analytical methods to analyze other target analytes such as other potential replacements for PFOS in different marine samples by using LC-MS/MS and LC-HRMS. Method validation for PFASs were also done for the air samples collected by the CMS which was used to investigate a wide range of physicochemical properties of target analytes. (2) For objective 2, specific chirality profiles of target chemicals were successfully obtained from the environmental samples analyzed in the environmental samples by the LCMSMS and GCMS adopting chiral separation. There results have been published in the internationally referred journals. (3) For objective 3, we have summarized the results of the source identification and characterization method using chirality profiles of BFRs from the environmental samples analyzed. (4) For objective 4, based on the levels of alternatives for PBDEs determined in the environmental samples, we have carried out the ecological risk assessment to evaluate the potential risk posed on the assessment targets namely marine mammals. Chemical analysis of PFASs have been completed and the risk assessment for the PBDEs, PFOS and their potential replacements have been conducted, indicating the current levels were posing risk to the targets of the study.

28300317.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28300317.value: Concerns over the widespread occurrence and health effects on PFASs and PBDEs have resulted in the phasing out of these chemicals, and led to the production and use of other chemicals. These replacements originally are considered to be safe for use, are however, recently found to be equally or even more harmful than the phase-out chemicals. Our studies have indicated there is a high occurrence of these phase-out chemicals in a variety of environmental samples such as sewage and aquatic wildlife. We have elucidated that significant increasing trends of several shorter-chain PFASs and non-PBDE flame retardants have been found in the cetacean and fish samples from the Pearl River Delta (PRD) region. Explicitly, the levels of the substitutes for PBDEs and PFOS are elevating and associated with point source including sewage discharge, suggesting that the use of these unregulated substances is increasing in the region. These findings lend support to the idea that increasing usage of a wide range of these alternatives follow the restriction/voluntary withdrawal of the production and use of phase-out chemicals. Most importantly, the results indicated that these replacements posed risk to the targets of this study.

28300717.value: 近現代中國經濟對氣候變化脆弱性分析

28300717.label: Project Objectives
28300717.value: Statistically investigate the economic vulnerabilities under climate change in early modern China from a long-term temporal scale. • The long-term dynamics of the agrarian economy and climate change in early modern China will be quantitatively examined; • The economic impacts of climatic factors, including temperature, precipitation, ENSO, NAO, Asian monsoon and so on, will be scrutinized; • The Yangtze River Delta and Guangdong Province will be chosen as the regional cases to supplement the findings of the whole China. Formulate new theories or improve existing theories on the agrarian economy and its vulnerabilities to climate change. The proposed project could help to restructure the philosophical basis of research and policy making to address future threats of climate change. • Promote the development of Environmental Humanities with empirical evidence; • Incorporate the philosophical paradigm of Environmental Humanities into current research of history as well as other social sciences; • Review current economic theories under the background of climate change.

28300717.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28300717.value: Economic vulnerabilities to climate change are implied by how climatic impacts could affect the economic performance of a society. Thus, evaluating economic vulnerabilities is a key step in addressing climate change which could trigger socioeconomic disasters. This premise is particularly true for the past agrarian economy with low technological levels. However, the long-term dynamics (> 100 years) between climate change and economic vulnerabilities in early modern China have been insufficiently examined, particularly in a quantitative perspective. Furthermore, there is a large amount of historical documentary records on the past agrarian economy available in China. However, only a small proportion of these documents have been utilized. To fill the above research gaps, the PI will investigate the association between climate change and the agrarian economy in early modern China, especially with a statistical manner. The PI has taken a pioneering role in the relationship between climate change and economic fluctuation in the pre-industrial epoch. Therefore, with a special focus on early modern China, the following issues will be studied. First, the economic vulnerabilities of early modern China under climate change will be estimated. In particular, El Nino Southern Oscillation, North Atlantic Oscillation, and Asian monsoon will be studied together with temperature and precipitation to present a holistic picture on the economic impacts of climate change. Second, the Yangtze River Delta and Guangdong Province, as two agricultural centers, will be selected. The findings from these regions will supplement the findings of the project at the national scale. Furthermore, these two regions are located in different climatic zones. A comparison of these two regions will reflect the spatial differences of climatic impacts. Third, the project will take quantitative analysis as an essential method and qualitative analysis as a supplement. Chinese historical records will be evaluated and adopted. According to its quantitative nature and large amount of data basis, the project will be a “big data” research in historical studies. It is an attempt to search for a scientific way to use statistical methods to survey a historical society under climate change. This study is the first to quantitatively prove and evaluate the closeness of linkage between climate change and agrarian economy at both macroscale and microscale in early modern China. The associated findings are vital as the reference to adapt to and mitigate the climatic impacts. In this regard, this project is not only of academic interest but also of practical value. 評估經濟對氣候變化脆弱性是目前重點關注的議題，特別是氣候變化可能會導致社會經濟危機，而這種情況在技術低下的前工業化社會尤為明顯和突出。但是現有的研究中，近現代中國經濟對氣候變化脆弱性分析仍未從一個長期動態的層面得到充分的定量研究，雖然在中國有著大量的關於經濟情況的歷史文獻，但是只有一小部記錄得到了分析和應用。 為了應對以上的研究不足，本項目將定量地審視氣候變化和近現代中國經濟運行之間的關係，主要包括以下幾個方面。第一，除了傳統的溫度和降水因素之外，厄爾尼諾，北大西洋濤動和亞洲季風等都會納入到本研究中，共同描述氣候變化的綜合影響。第二，本項目將會特別關注長江三角洲和廣東作為傳統的農業中心，該尺度的研究發現將補充全國尺度的研究發現，可以識別不同尺度下的氣候變化的經濟影響。第三，本項目將採用大數據的理念，引入定量的研究方法，為定量使用歷史紀錄開拓新的方法學。 本文將首次定量地證明和評估氣候變化和農業經濟之間在宏觀和圍觀尺度上的關係，這對於適應和減緩氣候變化將提供歷史的實證依據。

Both national and regional scale findings were made by the PI through the pioneered effort in the quantitative analysis. To further understand the impact of climate system on social system, Asian summer monsoon, El Nino–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) have been additionally included besides temperature and precipitation in the study on economy of early modern China. The PI further scrutinized the similarities and differences between the notion of Mandate of Heaven and paradigm of Environmental Humanities. The quantitative evidences from the context of early modern China not only promoted the development of Environmental Humanities with empirical evidence, but also widened the application of Environmental Humanities from the western settings into eastern world. A global scope has been assigned to Environmental Humanities in this regard. Therefore, the global history and climate history, as two most related subjects of social sciences with the project, have been developed under the paradigm of Environmental Humanities. In the meantime, under the unprecedented warming trend of climate change, Environmental Humanities has great potential to re-interpret the human-nature linkage based on historical phenomena, just as the economic vulnerabilities under climate change in early modern China. The empirical studies in Environmental Humanities has also equipped this project with significant practical value. Notably, the biggest challenge in the project is how to analyse the records of social archives in China. The information on phenomena of weather/climate change or economic performance were only recorded in a generalized way without accurate quantitative details. 28300717.label: Major findings and research outcome
28300717.value: Under the support of the project from Jan 2018 to Dec 2019, the PI has published 12 research papers in peer-reviewed journals in academia and made 8 presentations in the international conferences. The project thus helped the PI establish a wide connection with fellow scholars in the world. All the outcomes through the project has helped the PI to exert impact in both academia and lay public. From the project, the PI utilized the social archives in China to study the economic impact of climate change. The study period is 1500-1900AD, early modern China. During this study period, Chinese economy has been examined by considering the external natural factors, for example, temperature, precipitation, ENSO, and etc., and internal social mechanisms, such as migration, war, and so on. The linkages between climate change and economy in early modern China were empirically examined in a quantitative manner. Based on the statistical results, the project findings confirm the significant role of climate change to affect economy in the past at both national and regional scales (Publications 3, 4, and 10). Even transitions from agrarian economy to industrialized economy in early modern China of 19-20th century, climate change did influence the process, although Chinese did not succeed in this transition. Furthermore, the economic deterioration due to climate change usually lead to mass migration in historical China, no matter in agricultural or nomadic societies (Publications 2, 7, 9, and 11). The project built up the linkage between climatic sciences and humanities by taking the example of economy under climate change in historical China. Furthermore, the social archives in China have been widely used by the PI in a quantitative way. Therefore, the social archives of China are useful to promote the development of climate sciences and quantitative history in the future (Publications 1, 5, 6, 8, and 12). With the basis of above findings and achievements, the PI was awarded several prestigious prizes based on the research performance, such as Higher Education Outstanding Scientific Research Output Awards, Second-class award in Natural Sciences. Ministry of Education, China in the year of 2019-2020; President’s Award for Outstanding Performance in Research (Early-Career Research Excellence Award), The Education University of Hong Kong, in 2019; and Carson Fellowship, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, Germany in 2018. Therefore, the project has proved its impacts both locally and globally according to the PI’s achievements.

28300717.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28300717.value: The project initiated and developed a new direction to empirically examine economic deterioration under climate change and related social responses based on a large number of social archives in China. Therefore, the potential for future development could be identified in terms of knowledge, theory and methods. First, climate change dampened economy in the past. Among different types of social responses, migration could be a major adaptive choice for past society, which was an instant and effective manner. Therefore, the study on climate-related migration deserves further research and the PI already has made the effort on this direction. Second, no matter economy or migration, the societies’ linkages with climate change could reflect the connection between nature and civilization in historical societies. Therefore, more existing theories could be reviewed by Environmental Humanities. Some new theories could even possibly be developed in the perspective of environmental change. Third, the quantitative practice on the social archives in China could be promoted further. There still lack of advanced methods to scientifically utilize the existing social archives in China. Along with more and more identified social archives, it will also require the progress in methods of analyzing these historical documents in the future.

28300717.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28300717.value: Evaluating economic vulnerabilities is a key step in addressing climate change, which could fundamentally trigger socioeconomic disasters. In this project, the PI investigated the association between climate change and the economy in early modern China, especially with a statistical manner. The quantitative analysis was based on a large amount of historical documentary records in China. The major findings and achievements are briefly listed as below. First, economic vulnerabilities of early modern China under climate change has been quantitatively evaluated. Furthermore, El Nino Southern Oscillation, Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Asian monsoon also held significant impact. Besides the national scale of whole China, the regional economic center, like Yangtze River Region and South China all were significantly influenced by climate change. Second, according to its quantitative nature and large amount of data basis, the project followed a “big data” research in historical studies. This is a pioneered attempt to search for a scientific way to use statistical methods to survey a historical society under climate change. The associated findings are vital as the historical reference to adapt to and mitigate the future climatic impact. In this regard, this project is not only of academic interest but also of practical value.
